en: Auspiciousness.

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The First Book, named "The Foundation of Stories. Long ago, it is said, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean that was the mouth of Hara, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Those who, having attained the two-fold wealth free from obstacles, forcibly bring about [the welfare of others], bear the burden of the gods upon this earth through the grace of Bhava.
First Wave.

May the dark throat of Śambhu bestow prosperity upon you— his throat which seems as if it were entwined by the nooses of the glances of Pārvatī, who rests upon his lap, and who is the very embodiment of the mind-born god of love.
May the Conqueror of Obstacles protect you, who, at the festival of the supreme twilight, raises the stars with his trunk,
as if fashioning others from the spray of his hissing breath.
Having bowed down to the speech that serves as a lamp illuminating all things without exception,
I compose this compendium of the essence of the *Bṛhatkathā*.

Herein, the first is the *kathāpīṭha* (the foundation of the tale), and after that, the *kathāmukha* (the introduction to the tale); following that, there shall be the third *lambaka*, named Lāvānaka.
After that comes the birth of Naravāhanadatta;
then the one called Caturdārika, and after that, Madanamañcukā.
Then there shall be the seventh book, named Ratnaprabhā;
and then the eighth book shall be that entitled Sūryaprabha.
Then Alaṃkaravatī shall become Śaktiyaśas,
and thereafter the eleventh shall be known as Velālambaka.
Then there would be the Śaśāṅkavatī, and likewise Madirāvatī;
following that, there would be the Pañcalambaka, accompanied by the Mahābhiṣeka.
Then Suratamañjarī shall become Padmavatī;
thereafter, the eighteenth chapter, named Viṣamaśīla, shall follow.
Just as it is in the root [text], so it is here; there is not even the slightest deviation.
There is only a difference in the expansion or brevity of the composition and a difference in the language.

Preservation of the connection with propriety is maintained according to one's ability, and the composition of the poetic portion is joined together without interrupting the flavor of the narrative. SoKss_1,1.11 //
This effort of mine is not at all for the sake of displaying cleverness or out of a desire for fame;
rather, it is for the purpose of facilitating the easy recollection of the various networks of stories.
There is a king of mountains, renowned as Himavat, frequented by kinnaras, gandharvas, and vidyādharas.
The majesty of that mountain has reached such a height that Bhavānī,
the mother of the three worlds, has become his daughter.
Its northern peak is the great mountain named Kailāsa,
which stands having ascended many thousands of yojanas.
Even when the ocean was churned, Mount Mandara did not attain the whiteness of nectar;
yet I, as it were, laugh at this with my own splendors, having achieved it without effort.
There dwells Maheśvara, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, accompanied by Ambikā and served by hosts of Gaṇas, Vidyādharas, and Siddhas.
The fresh moon, resting upon her mass of tawny, high matted locks,
enjoys the pleasure of clinging to the peak of the eastern mountain, ruddy with the twilight.
By him, as he thrust his trident into the heart of the Asura Andhaka alone, it was wondrously extracted from the hearts of even the three worlds.
Upon their crest-jewels, the gods and asuras shine as if they were half-moons obtained through his grace, marked by the reflection of the tips of his toenails.
Once, when confidence had arisen between them, his beloved wife, in private,
gratified the Lord Īśvara, the husband of Bhavānī, with hymns of praise.
Delighted by her words of praise, the Moon-crested Lord placed her upon his lap and said, "What pleasing thing shall I do for you?"
Then Girijā said: "If you are pleased, O Lord, tell me today some beautiful and new story, O God."
"O beloved, what could there be in this world—past, present, or future—that you would not know? Thus even Śarva spoke to her.
Then his beloved made a persistent request to her lord,
for the mind of a woman who cherishes love is devoted to the affection of her beloved.
Then, with the very intent of pleasing her, Śiva described to her a brief account concerning his own power as follows:
Formerly, Brahmā and likewise Nārāyaṇa came to behold me;
wandering over the earth, they arrived at the foot of the Himavat mountain.
Then they saw there before them a great flaming liṅga;
one set out to see its upper limit, while the other went downward.
Having failed to reach their goal through austerities, the two of them propitiated me;
and having appeared before them, I said, "Choose whatever boon you desire."
Upon hearing that, Brahmā said, "May you become my son.
Because he was thus born as one not worthy of worship, he was censured for his excessive arrogance.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa requested a boon from me:
"O Blessed One, may I be intent upon serving you."
Therefore, he has been born as my very body through your own self;
for that which is Nārāyaṇa is you, the power of me, the possessor of power.
When Śaṅkara said, "Why are you my wife from a former birth? Pārvatī replied, "How am I your wife from a former birth? (SoKss_1,1.33)
Then Bharga replied: "O Goddess, in former times, many daughters were born to the Prajāpati Dakṣa, both you and others."
He gave you to me, and those other daughters of his—Dharma and the rest—to various suitors; once, when they were invited to a sacrifice, all of them became my sons-in-law.
But I alone was excluded from that; therefore, you were questioned by him:
"Father, tell me, why was my husband not invited by you? (SoKss 1.1.36)
Then he spoke these words, which were like poison needles to your ears: "How can your husband, who wears a garland of skulls, be summoned to the sacrifice? (SoKss 1.1.37)
"Since this body was born from such a wicked man, what use have I for it?"—
thus, out of anger, was that body abandoned by you, my beloved.
And that sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed by me through that wrath;
from that you were born, O Himavat’s daughter, like a digit of the moon from the ocean.
Then, O Smara, I came to the Snowy Mountain for the sake of asceticism;
both my father and you appointed me to attend upon my guest.
Sent by the gods to obtain a son who would be the destroyer of Tāraka, the God of Love gained his opportunity there and pierced me; thus was he consumed.
Therefore, O wise one, I have been won over by you through your intense austerity;
and that [austerity], my beloved, was endured by me solely for the sake of its accumulation.
"In this way you were my wife in a former birth; what more need be said to you?
When Śambhu had spoken thus and ceased, the Goddess, agitated with anger, replied:
"You are a rogue; even when entreated, you do not tell a heart-pleasing story.
Have you not been defeated by me, who carries the Gaṅgā while observing the morning twilight?"
Having heard that, Hara, having offered his apologies, agreed to tell her the divine story; thereupon, she released her anger.
When she herself had said, "No one is to enter here," and Nandin had closed the door, Hara proceeded to speak.
Gods are exclusively happy, while humans are perpetually suffering;
yet the conduct of gods and humans alike is not captivating in its ultimate aspect.
"Therefore, I shall describe to you the life of the Vidyādharas"—
while Hara was saying this to the Goddess, [the sage] arrived.
Puṣpadanta, the foremost of Śambhu’s attendants, whose wealth was his devotion,
was stopped at the gate by Nandin, who stood there.
Thinking, "Today there is a prohibition against me as well, though for no reason," he entered that very moment, unobserved through the power of yoga, out of curiosity.
Having entered, he heard everything being described by the wielder of the Pināka bow—
the unprecedented and wondrous life-story of the seven Vidyādharas.
Having heard this, he went and described it to his wife Jayā;
for who indeed is able to conceal wealth or a secret from women?
Overcome with wonder at that, the female doorkeeper Jayā went before the Daughter of the Mountain and sang: "Among women, where is there any restraint of speech?"
Then Girijā became angry, saying, "You have not described anything unprecedented;
for even Jayā knows this," and thus she addressed Īśvara.
Then, having understood this from his vow, the Lord of Umā spoke thus;
Puṣpadanta, having become a yogin and entered therein, heard it.
"O beloved, who else indeed knows what was described by him regarding Jayā?
Having heard this, the Goddess summoned Puṣpadanta with great wrath.
She cursed him, who was distraught at being called a mortal and undisciplined,
as well as the attendant Mālyavat, who was pleading on his behalf.
Having prostrated at their feet,
Śarvāṇī, being exhorted by Jayā, slowly spoke these words regarding the end of the curse.
In the Vindhya forest, a yakṣa named Supratīka, having attained the state of a piśāca due to the curse of Kubera,
remained under the name Kāṇabhūti.
"O Puṣpadanta, when you see him and, remembering your former birth, recount this story to him, then you shall be released from the curse."
When Mālyavat hears that story from Kāṇabhūti,
he will eat at Kāṇabhūti’s house after having related the story, and then he will depart.
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the mountain ceased; and at that very moment, those two hosts vanished from sight like flashes of lightning.
Then, as time passed, the compassionate Gaurī asked Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, where on earth have those two excellent Pramathas, whom I cursed, been born?"
And the moon-crested Lord spoke: "There is a great city called Kauśāmbī;
in it, O beloved, that Puṣpadanta was born under the name Vararuci."
Moreover, O Queen, that one named Guṇāḍhya was also born in the excellent city called Supratiṣṭhita; such is the account of those two.

Having thus informed her, the Lord dwelt, delighting his beloved in pleasure-houses fashioned from wish-fulfilling creepers upon the slopes of Mount Kailāsa— she who was filled with remorse at the thought of the insults suffered by her ever-devoted servant.
Thus ends the first wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave:
Then Puṣpadanta, wandering about in a mortal body, [proceeded].
By name he was Vararuci, and he was also known as Kātyāyana.
Having attained mastery of the sciences and fulfilled his duties as a minister,
he once, feeling weary, went to visit the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.
Propitiated by his asceticism, the Goddess, through a command in a dream,
sent him to the Vindhya forest to visit Kāṇabhūti.
Wandering there in that place crowded with tigers and monkeys, where the trees were waterless and harsh, he beheld a tall banyan tree.
And he saw nearby that Piśāca Kāṇabhūti, surrounded by hundreds of Piśācas, his body resembling a sal tree in stature.
Having seen him, Kāṇabhūti performed the ritual salutation at his feet;
and after a moment, Kātyāyana sat down and spoke to him.
"How is it that you, who were always of such virtuous conduct, have come to this state?
Having heard that, Kāṇabhūti, showing his friendship, said to him:
"I possess no knowledge of my own; rather, I have heard it from Śarva.
Listen as I tell you what I heard in the cremation ground at Ujjayinī."
"Why, O Lord, do you take delight in skulls and cremation grounds?
When the Goddess asked this, the Blessed One then spoke as follows:
Long ago, when the dissolution of the eon had occurred and the world had become composed of water,
I then pierced my thigh and caused a drop of blood to fall.
Within the water, that egg came into being; from it, when divided into two parts, a Person emerged.
Then, for the sake of creation, Prakṛti was emitted by me.
And those two created other Prajāpatis and their progeny;
therefore, O beloved, that Puruṣa is called the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) in the world.
Having thus created the universe of moving and non-moving beings, he became arrogant;
therefore, I severed his head.
Then, out of remorse, I undertook the great vow;
henceforth, I carry a skull-bowl in my hand and have a fondness for the cremation ground.
Moreover, O Goddess, this world, which consists of skulls, rests in my hand;
for the two previously mentioned halves of the cosmic egg are celebrated as heaven and earth.
When Śambhu had spoken thus, and I stood there full of curiosity, saying "I shall listen," Pārvatī then spoke again to her husband.
"In how much time will that Puṣpadanta come to us?
Having heard this, Maheśvara spoke to the Goddess concerning me: SoKss_1,2.17
"This piśāca who is seen here is indeed a follower of Vaiśravaṇa;
he was a yakṣa named Sthūlaśiras who became his friend."
Having observed that he was joined with that evil, the Lord of Wealth,
the master of riches, ordained that he become a *piśāca* in the Vindhya forest.
Then his brother Dīrghajaṅgha fell at his feet and entreated him regarding the end of the curse; thereupon, the Lord of Wealth spoke.
Having heard the Great Story from Puṣpadanta, who had descended due to a curse,
he told it to Mālyavat, who had likewise attained the state of mortals through a curse.
"Accompanied by those two hosts, he shall cross over this curse"—
thus was the end of his curse ordained here at that time by Dhanada.
"And remember, O beloved, that he is indeed Puṣpadanta;
having heard these words of Śambhu, I have come here filled with joy."
"Thus this curse of mine shall last until the arrival of Puṣpadanta.
When Kaṇabhuji had spoken thus and ceased at that moment—
Having recollected his former birth, Vararuci spoke as if waking from sleep:
"I am that very Puṣpadanta; hear that story from me."
Having said this, Kātyāyana recounted seven hundred thousand verses and seven great narratives; thereupon, Kāṇabhūti spoke.
"O Lord, you are an incarnation of Rudra; who else knows this story?
By your grace, that curse has for the most part departed from my body."
Therefore, O Lord, tell me your own history from your birth onwards;
purify me once again, if there is nothing that should be hidden from one such as me.
Then, out of consideration for him who had bowed down,
Vararuci related this entire account of his life from birth in full detail.
In Kauśāmbī there was a twice-born man named Somadatta, also known by the name Agniśikha; his wife was called Vasudattā.
And that daughter of a sage, due to a curse, descended into her womb;
thus was I born from that best of the twice-born through the power of that curse.
Then, while I was still very young, my father passed away;
my mother remained, however, rearing me through arduous labors.
Then, on one occasion, two brahmins, dusty from a long journey, approached our house for the purpose of staying for a single night.
And as the two of them stood there, the sound of a drum arose;
remembering her husband, my mother spoke to me in a faltering voice because of it.
"O son, this Nanda, the dancer and friend of your father, is dancing.
I also said, "Mother, I too shall go to see this."
"I shall show all of that to you as well, along with its recitation.
Having heard these words of mine, those two brahmins were filled with wonder.
And my mother said to those two, "O sons, there is no doubt in this matter:
having heard it but once, this boy will indeed retain everything in his heart. (SoK 1.2.37)
Then, for the sake of inquiry, the Prātiśākhya was recited to me by these two;
likewise, it was all recited by me while they were looking on.
Then, having gone with those two and witnessed that very same dance,
I returned home and showed it all in its entirety before my mother.
Having ascertained me to be one who retains everything heard only once,
one of those two, named Vyāḍi, bowed to my mother and said this story.
In the city named Vetasā, O Mother, there were two brothers, Devasvāmin and Karambhaka,
who were both brahmins and exceedingly fond of one another.
Of those two, this Indradatta was born as the son of one, and I, Vyāḍi, was born as the son of the other; my father then departed for that [other] place.
Out of grief for him, Indradatta’s father departed upon the great path; and then, from sorrow, the hearts of our two mothers burst asunder.
Therefore, though we possess wealth, we are destitute; desiring knowledge, we have come from there to seek the Prince through ascetic practice.
And while we were established there in ascetic practice, that Lord commanded us in a dream:
"There is a city named Pāṭalika belonging to King Nanda."
"There is a certain brahmin there named Varṣa;
from him you two shall obtain the entirety of knowledge. Therefore, you two must go there."
Then we went to that city, and when we asked there,
the people said to us, "There is a foolish Brahmin here named Varṣa."
Then, having traveled that moment by means of a mind mounted upon a swing,
we two beheld the house of Varṣa in its state of desolation.
With an anthill built by mice, its walls crumbling and detached,
lusterless and bereft of a roof, it was like the very field of one's birth for calamities.
Then, having observed that he was established in meditation for a year within [the cave],
his two wives approached him and were offered the honors of hospitality.
With a body emaciated and greyish, and wearing tattered, soiled garments,
she was like his own misfortune personified, having come to him out of attachment to his virtues.
Then, preceded by a salutation,
he related to her our own story and the account of our husband's folly that we had heard.
"You two are my sons; what shame is there? Listen, I shall tell you both.
Having said this, that virtuous woman related this story to them.
In this city there was an excellent brahmin named Śaṃkarasvāmin;
my husband was Upavarṣa, and these two are both his sons.
"This man was foolish and poor, while his younger brother was the opposite;
therefore, his own wife was appointed by him to support the household."
Then, at one time, the rainy season arrived; and during that season, a woman [offered him] a loathsome object in the form of a secret [gift], made of flour mixed with molasses.
Having performed them, they indeed bestow these [merits] upon a foolish Brahmin;
for when performed, they remove the distress and fatigue of bathing during both the cold season and the summer heat.
"It is a contemptible custom that they do not accept what has been given;
therefore, this gift, along with its fee, was given by me to him through my husband’s wife."
Having taken that, he arrived here and was severely rebuked by me;
he then burned with inner resentment caused by his own foolishness.
Then he went to the feet of Svāmikumāra;
pleased by his asceticism, the latter revealed all the sciences to him.
"Having found a Brahmin who can retain what he hears but once, you shall reveal these [teachings] to him. Thus commanded by Him, he has come here with joy.
Having arrived, he reported the entire account to me;
from that time forth, he has remained constantly engaged in recitation and meditation.
Therefore, you two should search for and bring someone who possesses the learning of the scriptures;
through him, the accomplishment of all goals will surely come to pass, without a doubt.
Having heard this from the wife of the householder, they quickly gave her a hundred pieces of gold to eliminate her poverty, and then departed happily from that city.
Then we wandered over the earth, yet nowhere did we find one who had mastered the scriptures;
consequently, weary from our travels, we have arrived today at your home.
"Your son Bāla has now become a master of a single hearing;
therefore, give him to us so that we may go for the sake of attaining knowledge, wealth, and supernatural powers."
Having heard these words of Vyāḍi, my mother spoke with respect: "All this is indeed most agreeable; I have full confidence in this matter."

For when this only son was previously born to me, such a disembodied voice clearly arose from the sky: ||| SoKss_1,2.68 ||| When this only son was previously born to me, such a disembodied voice clearly arose from the sky. ||| SoKss_1,2.68 |||
This one has been born as Śrutadhara; he will acquire knowledge within a year, and furthermore, he will cause the grammar to attain firm establishment in the world.
"By name he is Vararuci, for whatever may be excellent indeed pleases him";
having said this, the voice ceased.
Therefore, now that this boy has grown, I ponder day and night as to where that preceptor might be.
"Today, having learned this from your own mouths, my satisfaction is supreme.
Therefore, take him away as your brother; what loss is there for you two?"
Having heard these words of my mother, Vyāḍi and Indradatta, filled with joy,
passed that night as if it were a mere moment.
Then, desiring that I become worthy of the Vedas, Vyāḍi quickly gave his own wealth for my mother’s festival and brought me back.
Then, having somehow been permitted by my mother, whose tears were restrained,
she took me with her, having allayed every distress of mine through her own resolve.
And considering that youthful favor to be like a flower in bloom,
Vyāḍi and Indradatta then departed swiftly from the city.
Then, in due course, we reached the house of our teacher; he regarded me, as I approached the temple of Skanda, as the deity himself in bodily form.
On another day, having seated us in front upon a pure ground,
the teacher Varṣa uttered the syllable *oṃ* with a divine voice.
Immediately thereafter, the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences appeared before him;
from that moment on, he began to teach us.
There, what was heard by me once was likewise heard twice by Vyāḍi, and thrice by Indradatta; thus was the word spoken by the teacher grasped.
Then, having suddenly heard that unprecedented, divine sound, the assembly of brahmins was instantly filled with a shimmering inner wonder.
Thinking, "What is this?", they approached from all sides to see the rain; their faces radiant with the beauty of voices raised in praise, they honored him with prostrations.
Upon beholding that marvel there, Upavarṣa was not merely overcome by joy;
indeed, the entire populace of Pāṭaliputra became immersed in a grand and widespread festival.
King Nanda, too, beholding that power of the boon granted by the Son of Giriśa, attained great satisfaction;
and he, of exalted glory, immediately filled the householder’s dwelling with riches out of his deep regard for him.
Thus ends the second wave in the Kathāpīṭha book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The third wave begins:
Having spoken thus, while Vararuci listened with a one-pointed mind,
In that forest, Kāṇabhūti spoke this once again.

Once, when some time had passed and the rite of Vedic recitation was completed, we questioned the teacher after he had performed his daily duties: "O Teacher, [how is it that] the year... SoKss_1,3.2 //
"O teacher, tell me why this city of such a kind has become a sacred field (kṣetra) for both Sarasvatī and Lakṣmī."
Having heard that, he said to us: "Listen to this story.
There is a purifying sacred site named Kanakhala at Gaṅgādvāra."
There, by means of the fall of his golden tusk, Devadatta split open the plateau of Mount Uśīnara and caused the Jāhnavī to descend.
A certain twice-born man from the Deccan was practicing austerities there together with his wife,
and three sons were born to him right there.
When he had passed away to heaven with his wife at the proper time, those sons of his went to the place named Rājagṛha, desiring to acquire knowledge.
And there, having completed their studies, those three, suffering from the misery of being without a protector,
went to the southern region to see the prince.
Having gone there to the city named Ciñcinī on the shore of the ocean, they dwelt in the house of a brahmin named Bhojika.
And that Bhojika, having given his three daughters and wealth to them,
went to the Ganges for asceticism, being without any other offspring.
Then, while they were living there in their father-in-law’s house,
a severe famine caused by drought broke out.
Having abandoned their virtuous wives, those three departed;
for kinship-affection does not touch the hearts of the cruel.
Then, among them, the middle one became pregnant;
thereafter, they took refuge in the house of Yajñadatta, the friend of their father.
There they remained, their conduct distressed as they meditated upon their own husbands;
for do noble women ever abandon the conduct of virtuous wives even in times of calamity?
In due time, she gave birth to a son among them;
and because of their mutual excellence, their affection for him increased.
Once, seeing Maheśvara traveling through the path of the sky with the mother of Skanda seated upon his lap, she spoke to him with compassion:
"Your Majesty, behold! Even these three women, bound by affection for this child, maintain hope that he might bring us back to life."
"Act in such a way that even this child may live," said his beloved;
thus addressed, the boon-granting Lord spoke to her.
"I favor this man first because he, together with his wife, has propitiated me;
therefore, he has been created on earth for the sake of enjoyment."
And she was born as the daughter of King Mahendravarman, named Pāṭalī, and she shall become his wife.
Having spoken thus, the Lord addressed those three virtuous women in a dream:
"This young son of yours is indeed named Putraka."
Day by day, at the end of his head as he awakens from sleep, there shall be a hundred thousand pieces of gold; and he shall become a king.
Then, when that boy had risen from sleep, those virtuous daughters of Yajñadatta obtained the gold and rejoiced, their vows having borne fruit.
Then, by means of that gold, King Putraka’s treasury soon became full; for the riches of those devoted to austerity are indeed immeasurable.
Then once, Yajñadatta spoke privately to his son:
"O King, due to the calamity of famine, your ancestors have gone elsewhere."
Therefore, always give to the Brahmins so that they may come to you;
and listen here as I relate to you this story of Brahmadatta.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta;
one night he saw a pair of swans traveling through the sky.
It possessed a shimmering golden luster and was surrounded by hundreds of royal swans,
like a mass of lightning encircled by sudden white clouds.
Then his longing to see him grew so great that he no longer found delight anywhere in the pleasures of royalty.
Having consulted with his ministers, that king then had a lake constructed according to his own design, and he granted safety from fear to all living beings.
Then, after some time, the king saw those two swans who had arrived;
he questioned them, for they were full of confidence, regarding the cause of their golden bodies.
Then those two swans, speaking clearly, said to the king:
"O lord of the earth, in a previous birth we were both born as crows."
And while fighting for the sake of alms in a sacred, secluded temple of Śiva,
they both fell down and perished within that very pit of the temple grounds.
"Then we were born as two golden swans possessing the memory of our former births.
Having heard that, the king rejoiced as he gazed upon them according to his desire.
"Therefore, you shall obtain [the fruits] from a gift to the ancestors that is not otherwise.
Having been told this by Yajñadatta, the son did exactly so.
Having heard that news of the gift, those twice-born ones arrived;
once they were recognized, they obtained supreme prosperity along with their wives.
It is a marvel that the innate nature of evil-minded people, whose intellects are blinded by a lack of discernment, cannot be abandoned even when their visible fortunes have perished. (SoK 1.3.37)
In due course, those twice-born men, desiring the kingdom and wishing to kill that son, took him away under the pretext of showing him the site, to the Vindhya-dwelling goddess.
And having stationed the executioners within the inner chamber of the queen's quarters, they said to him: "First, you alone must look upon the queen from within the courtyard."
Then, having entered out of trust and seeing the men prepared to kill him, Putraka asked, "Why do you slay me? SoKss_1,3.40 //
"We have been sent by our fathers to give gold," they said;
then the wise Putraka spoke to them, who were deluded by the goddess: SoKss_1,3.41 //
"I give you this priceless jewel-ornament of my own;
release me, for I shall not cause a disturbance here, but will depart to a distance."
Saying "So be it," the executioners took him from there and went away; they falsely told his parents, "The son has been killed."
Then those twice-born men, who had been killed while seeking the kingdom, returned;
for having been recognized by the ministers as traitors, how can there be welfare for the ungrateful?
In the meantime, that king, his little son,
true to his promise and detached from his own kinsmen, entered the Vindhya forest.
While wandering there, he saw two men intent solely on wrestling;
he then asked them, "Who are you two?"
"We two are the daughters of the asura Maya, and this wealth belongs to him:
this vessel, this staff, and these sandals."

Prostitutes are prone to deception, as are brahmins like my fathers;

Reflecting thus, the king reached a deserted house;
within it, he beheld an old woman in a dilapidated dwelling.
Having first gratified that old woman with gifts and being honored by her, he lived there in a dilapidated house, unobserved by others, like a son.
Once, being well-pleased, that old woman said to her little son:
"My son, I have a concern: that nowhere is there a wife suitable for you."
In this place, the king has a daughter, a maiden named Pāṭalī;
she is cherished as a jewel within the inner apartments.
As he listened with attentive ear to these words of the elderly woman,
the god of love entered his heart through that very same path, having found its opening.
Having resolved, "I must see that beloved this very day," he traveled through the sky at night there by means of his two sandals.
Having entered through a lofty window at the peak of a mountain ridge,
he beheld Pāṭalī asleep in private within the inner apartments.
Constantly attended by the moonlight clinging to her limbs,
she was like the embodied power of the Mind-born God, exhausted after conquering this entire world.
While he was thinking, "How shall I awaken her?",
a watchman outside suddenly cried out:
That which young men awaken their sleeping beloveds to in private— by embracing her as she utters sweet moans and opens her languid eyes— that alone is the fruit of their birth.
Upon hearing this introduction, he embraced his beloved with limbs trembling with agitation; and then she woke up.
As she watched the king, a mutual conflict arose in her eyes between shame and curiosity as they moved back and forth.
Then, when conversation had taken place and the Gandharva marriage rite was completed,
the affection of that couple increased, but not the night.
Then, having addressed his longing bride with a mind fixed solely on her,
the young man returned to the house of those two elders in the western quarter.
While he was thus making his comings and goings there every night,
the guards once beheld a sign of sexual enjoyment upon a trumpet-flower tree.
This was reported by them to her father, and he, in turn,
appointed a woman to observe [her] secretly within the inner apartments there at night.
And by her, for the sake of proving his supernatural powers there once he had arrived,
lac-dye was placed upon the garment of her sleeping son.
Informed by her in the morning, the king dispatched his spies;
and by means of those tokens, they found Putraka in the house of the old woman.
Having been brought into the presence of the king and seeing that monarch enraged,
he flew up into the air by means of his sandals and entered the Pāṭalī palace.
"Knowing this, arise; let us go by means of the sandals.
Having thus placed Pāṭalī on his lap, he then departed through the sky.
Then, descending from the sky near the bank of the Ganges,
he delighted his weary beloved with foods produced by the power of his alms-bowl.
Then, having been entreated by Pāṭalī’s son, who possessed the power of his glance,
he drew there with his staff a city equipped with a fourfold army.
There, having become that king when great power and truthfulness had been attained,
he caused his father-in-law, Śaśākha, to bow down before him as far as the ocean-bound earth.
This very divine city, fashioned by Māyā together with its citizens,
is therefore known by the name Pāṭaliputra, a field of Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī.
Thus, having heard this unprecedented and exceedingly wonderful tale from Varṣa and the others,
we remained for a long time with our hearts overflowing with wonder and joy, O Kāṇabhūti.

"I am Sarasvatī, always dwelling within your body;

Death is indeed better than infamy; for if your heart were to be discovered by your elders, it might perhaps lead to some misfortune.
"Therefore, do this, O blessed lady: restore life to that friend of mine and to me.

Then, in the course of time, his circle of disciples became great;

Wearied by his service and sent away by the wife of Varṣa,

There, having propitiated the Moon-crested Lord with intense austerity,

Then, having arrived, he challenged me alone to debate;

Then, having conceived a sense of world-weariness, he placed his own wealth in the hands of the merchant Hiraṇyagupta for the purpose of maintaining his household.

For Upakośā, desiring my welfare, remained day after day in her own home, bathing in the Gaṅgā with firm vows.
Once, when spring had arrived, she— emaciated, pale, yet beautiful,

and on another day, having attained the throne, he went to the house of Kālanemi.
Filled with indignation, he asked him, "Where is that son of yours, Śrīdatta? And he replied to him, "I do not know."
Thinking, "My son has been hidden by this man," King Kālanemi was impaled upon a stake in a fit of rage, as he had been accused of being a thief.
Seeing that, the heart of his wife burst asunder of its own accord;
for the evil deed of the cruel is indeed cruel, as it casts forth further evil upon itself.
And he, Vikramaśakti, is searching for Śrīdatta and his companions in order to kill them; therefore, you must depart from here.
Thus addressed by that man, Bāhuśālin and the other four, afflicted with grief, consulted together and went to their own land, Ujjayinī.
"O friend, I have been stationed here by them in concealment for your sake;
therefore, come, let us go right there to the presence of our friend."
Having heard these harsh words and mourned for his parents,
he repeatedly cast his gaze upon his sword, as if fixing his hope for retaliation upon it.
Then the hero, accompanied by Niṣṭhuraka and awaiting the proper time,
set out for that city of Ujjayinī in order to reach his friends.
Describing the entire account of his friend up to the point of their immersion,
Śrīdatta saw on the road a certain woman crying out.
To her who said, "I am a weak woman who have lost my way and am setting out for Mālava," he then,
out of compassion, made her his traveling companion.
And out of consideration for that woman's compassion, he stayed that day in a certain deserted city together with Niṣṭhuraka.
There, having suddenly woken from sleep during the night, he saw that woman, who,
having killed Niṣṭhuraka, was joyfully devouring his flesh.
Then, drawing forth his sword Mṛgāṅkaka, he rose up;
and that woman likewise resumed her own terrible form as a rākṣasī.
And he seized that night-stalker by the hair in order to kill her;
at that moment, she attained a divine form and said to him:
"Do not kill me, O illustrious one; release me! I am certainly not a rākṣasī.
This curse of such a nature befell me from the sage Kauśika."
For when he was previously performing austerities with the desire to attain that station, I was sent by this Lord of Wealth to create obstacles for him.
Then, unable to disturb him with my lovely form and feeling ashamed, I assumed a terrifying body to frighten her.
Seeing that, the sage then pronounced upon me a fitting curse:
"O sinful woman, become a rākṣasī who slays human beings!"
"When the seizing of my hair occurred at your hands, he brought about the end of my curse;
thus have I fallen into this miserable state of a rākṣasī."
"This city was swallowed by me alone today after a long time, and you have brought an end to that curse; therefore, accept now a boon."
Having heard these words of hers, Śrīdatta replied with respect:
"O noble lady, what need is there for any other boon? Let this friend of mine live."
"So be it," she said, and having granted him the boon, she vanished; and Niṣṭhuraka rose up again, alive with his limbs uninjured.
Then, together with him, Śrīdatta set out in the morning, joyful and amazed,
and reached Ujjayinī in due course.
There he greeted those friends who were looking out for his path,
with a sight as if he had arrived like a dark-blue cloud meeting peacocks.
Having performed the rites of hospitality, he was led to his own home by the mighty-armed one, while the curiosity of his entire life story was being recounted.
There, being cared for by his parents, Śrīdatta lived together with his friends like one who possesses great strength, as if in his own home.
Once, when the great festival of the month of Madhu had arrived,
he went with his friends to see the procession in the grove.
There he saw a maiden, the daughter of King Śrībimbaki,
who had arrived with perfect form, appearing like the very goddess of spring in person.
At that moment, she named Mṛgāṅkavatī entered his heart,
as if given passage by his blossoming gaze.
Her gaze, too, repeatedly moist with affection and proclaiming her first love, went back and forth toward him like a messenger sent to him.
Then, not seeing her for a moment after she had entered the thicket of trees,
Śrīdatta, his heart empty, could not even perceive the directions.
"Friend, I have understood your heart; do not deny it.
Come, let us go to that place where the princess has gone."
Thus addressed by his strong-armed friend, who was skilled in discerning gestures,
he agreed, saying "So be it," and went into her presence accompanied by his friend.
"Alas, what a tragedy! The princess has been bitten by a snake!"—at that moment, a cry arose there, causing a fever in the heart of Śrīdatta.
"The powerful-armed one went and said to him: 'I have a poison-neutralizing ring and a lore that belongs to my friend.'"
And at that very moment, the chamberlain approached, bowed at her feet,
and quickly led Śrīdatta into the presence of the princess.
He too placed the ring upon her finger;
then he recited a spell, and by that means she was restored to life.
Then, while all the people were delighted and intent on praising Śrīdatta,
King Bimbaki arrived at that very place, having learned of what had transpired.
Thus, having not taken the ring, Śrīdatta returned with his friends to the palace of Bāhuśālin.
There, whatever gold and other gifts the king, being pleased, sent to him,
he delivered in its entirety to his father, who was possessed of mighty arms.
Then, as he brooded over that beloved woman,
he was so consumed by anguish that his friends became bewildered as to what ought to be done.
Then a dear female friend of the princess named Bhāvanikā approached her under the pretext of delivering a ring.
And he said to him: "O fortunate one, regarding that friend of mine, you are now either the giver of her life as her husband, or death—this is certain."
When this had been said by Bhāvanikā, Śrīdatta, she herself,
Bāhuśālin, and the others gathered together and performed a consultation.
"Let us carry away this princess secretly and by means of a stratagem;
for the sake of a dwelling, let us go from here to Mathurā in concealment."
When they had thus deliberated and established a mutual understanding for the perfect accomplishment of their purpose, Bhāvanikā departed from there.
On another day, Bāhuśālī, accompanied by his three friends,
set out toward Mathurā under the pretext of trade.
As he went along, he stationed his mounts at every step—
clever and well-concealed— for the princess’s secret rendezvous.
Then Śrīdatta, having had the woman together with her daughter drink wine at the residence of the princess in the evening, placed them there.
Then, under the pretext of providing lamps, she secretly brought the princess outside to the chamber of Vāsava after setting fire to it with a bundle of cotton.
Having reached her at that very moment, Śrīdatta, who was standing outside,
sent word to Bāhuśālin, who had set out earlier.
He gave her two female companions as well as Bhāvanikā;
and in that house, that drunken woman was burned along with her daughter.
The world, however, believed that the princess had been burned along with her companions;
and in the morning, Śrīdatta was seen by the people there just as before.
Then, on the second night, Śrīdatta, holding the deer-marked moon [the sword],
set out toward his beloved who had departed earlier.
When that night had passed and he had traveled a long distance, eager as he was,
he reached the Vindhya forest at dawn, once a watch of the day had elapsed.
There, first he saw those omens on the road,
and afterwards all his companions from the same monastery, struck down by blows.
And seeing him approach in agitation, they said to him:
"We have been plundered today by an attacking army consisting of many horsemen."
And by a single horseman, that princess, overwhelmed with fear,
was mounted upon his horse and carried away while we were in such a state.
Before she has been led far away, go in this direction;
do not remain near us, for she is in every way superior.
Thus urged by those friends, Śrīdatta turned back and, looking repeatedly,
pursued that princess with speed.
Having traveled a great distance, he found that cavalry force;
and among them, he beheld a certain young kṣatriya.
There he saw that princess held up above the arena, and he gradually approached the presence of that young Kṣatriya.
When he would not release the princess from his feet despite gentle persuasion,
Śrīdatta pulled him from the horse and crushed him against a stone.
Having slain him, he mounted that very horse and struck down those many other enraged cavalrymen who were charging forward.
Then those who remained after the slaughter, having witnessed such superhuman valor of that hero, fled in fear.
And Śrīdatta, mounted upon his horse together with that princess Mṛgāṅkavatī, set out toward those friends.
Having gone but a short distance, his horse, severely wounded in battle,
fell as he and his wife dismounted, and it met its death.
And at that very moment, right there, his beloved Mṛgāṅkavatī became exhausted by fear and fatigue, and afflicted by thirst.
Having left her there, he went far away in this direction and that, searching for water; and as he was doing so, the sun reached its setting.
Then, although he had obtained water, wandering due to the loss of his way and crying out like a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), he passed that night in the forest.
In the morning, he reached that place, which was marked by fallen horses;
yet, he did not see his beloved princess there at all.
Then, out of delusion, having set down his sword Mṛgāṅka upon the ground,
he climbed to the top of a tree to look for her here and there.
At that very moment, a certain lord of the Śabaras came along that path;
having arrived, he seized Mṛgāṅkaka from the foot of the tree.
Even upon seeing him, Śrīdatta, overcome with intense grief, descended from the top of the tree and questioned the lord of the Śabaras regarding news of his beloved.
"Go from here to my village; I know she has gone there.
I shall come to that very place myself, and I will give this sword to you."
Having spoken thus, Śrīdatta, eager and sent by that Śabara,
went to that village together with the man's men.
"First, give up this exertion," he was told there by those men;
having reached the house of the village chief, exhausted, he fell asleep in an instant.
And having awakened, he saw his own feet bound by fetters,
as if they were two efforts toward the means of attaining his beloved, rendered powerless to reach their goal.
Then, grieving for his beloved there, he stood reflecting on her— she who granted happiness for a moment only to destroy it in the next, like the course of destiny itself.
Once, a maidservant named Mocanikā approached him and said:
"O illustrious one, where have you come here, alas, unto death?"
For that certain lord of the Śabaras has departed to accomplish his purpose;
having returned, he will offer you as a sacrifice to Caṇḍikā.
For this very purpose, having reached you here from the slopes of the Vindhya forest by means of a stratagem and having released you, he has now brought you into captivity.
Since you were conceived as an offering for the Blessed One,
for that very reason you are always served with garments and food.
"If you think that there exists a single means for your liberation, there is such a one:
the daughter of this Śabara chief, named Sundarī."
And upon seeing you, she will become exceedingly afflicted by love;
therefore, enjoy her as my companion, and from that you shall attain well-being.
Having been told "So be it" by her, Śrīdatta, seeking liberation,
replied "So be it" and secretly made that beautiful woman his wife according to the Gāndharva rite.
And night after night, she untied his bonds;
and before long, that Sundarī became pregnant.
Then his mother, having learned all that from Mocanikā,
went of her own accord out of affection for her son-in-law and spoke to Śrīdatta.
"My son, this man named Śrīcaṇḍa, the father of Sundarī, is prone to anger; he will not tolerate you. Therefore, depart; Sundarī must be forgotten."
Having spoken thus, Śrīdatta was released by his mother-in-law; having entrusted the sword in Śrīcaṇḍa’s hand to Sundarī, he departed from there.
Overcome with anxiety, he entered that very same forest once more,
desiring to seek out the path of Mṛgāṅkavatī again.
Having seen an auspicious omen,
he went to that very place where his horse had died and where that bride had been lost.
And there he saw a hunter approaching from the opposite direction;
having seen him, he asked for news of that fawn-eyed woman.
When he was asked by the hunter there, "Are you Śrīdatta?",
he sighed and replied, "I am that very same unfortunate man."
Then that hunter said: "In that case, friend, listen;
I have seen your wife weeping here and there for you."
Then, having inquired about his story and comforted him, I, overcome with compassion,
led that wretched man from this forest to my own village.
And there, having observed some young Pulinda hunters, she was led by me in fear to the village of Nāgasthala, near Mathurā.
And there, having respectfully entrusted it as a deposit, she placed it in the house of an elderly brahmin named Viśvadatta.
"Therefore, having learned your name from his mouth, I have come here;
go quickly from here toward Nāgasthala to search for her."
Having been addressed thus by the hunter, Śrīdatta departed immediately from there and reached that place,
Nāgasthala, on the following day at the close of the day.
Then, having entered the residence of Viśvadatta and beheld him,
he entreated him, saying, "Give me back my wife, who was placed with the hunter."
Having heard that, Viśvadatta said to Śrīdatta:
"In Mathurā, I have a friend who is a Brāhmaṇa beloved by the virtuous."
The preceptor and the minister of King Śūrasena—
into their hands I have placed that wife of yours.
For a village devoid of people is indeed fearful and cannot provide protection;
therefore, go there tomorrow morning, and rest here today.
Having been addressed thus by Viśvadatta, he spent that night right there;
at dawn he set out and reached Mathurā on the following day.
Exhausted from his long journey and stained with dust, he bathed right there outside the city in the clear water of a large pond.
Then, from the midst of the water itself, he unexpectedly recovered the garment placed there by the thief,
along with a necklace tied in a knot at its hem.
Then, taking that garment and not noticing the necklace,
Śrīdatta, desiring to see his beloved, entered the city of Mathurā.
There, having recognized him and recovered both the garment and the necklace,
the city guards seized him as a thief and led him away.
And they showed him in that state to the lord of the city;
he too reported it to the king, and the king ordered his execution.
Then Mṛgāṅkavatī saw him from afar being led away to the place of execution, with the drum beating behind him.
"This husband of mine is being led away to his execution! she cried out in agitation;
having gone there, she spoke to the chief minister exactly what had occurred in her house.
Then the minister, having restrained the executioners and petitioned the king,
had Śrīdatta released from execution and brought him home.
"How is it that this uncle of mine, who long ago went to another land,
has now by fate returned here, free from fear, and attained the position of minister?"
Then Śrīdatta, having arrived at that house,
recognized the minister after questioning him, and fell at his feet.
He too, having recognized his brother’s son, embraced him around the neck with wonder and inquired about the entire account of events.
Then Śrīdatta related his entire life story to his paternal uncle, beginning from the murder of his father.
Wiping away his tears in that secluded place, he said to his brother’s son:
"Do not despair, my son; for my yakṣiṇī has indeed attained her goal."
She gave me five thousand horses and seven crores of gold; since I am childless, all that wealth belongs to you alone.
Having said this, the paternal uncle presented his beloved to Śrīdatta;
and Śrīdatta, having acquired his wealth, married her there.
And then he remained right there, united with his beloved Mṛgāṅgavatī, full of joy like a bed of night-lotuses with the night.
But for him, whose prosperity was complete, the thought of possessing great learning and such qualities became a source of stain in his heart, like a streak of the moon’s dark spot.
Once, that paternal uncle spoke to Śrīdatta in private:
"Son, the king has a daughter; she is the maiden of Śūrasena."
"And by his command, she was to be led by me to the land of Avanti to be given [in marriage];
under that very pretext, I shall take her away and give her to you."
"Then, when his followers have arrived and my own forces are present,
you shall before long regain that kingdom which was ordained for you by Śrī."
Having decided this, Śrīdatta and his paternal uncle set out from there, taking that maiden with them, accompanied by their armies and retinues.
Then, as soon as these two had unexpectedly reached the Vindhya forest,
a vast army of bandits, raining down arrows, blocked their path.
Having bound Śrīdatta, who was unconscious from the blows and whose army had been broken,
those thieves took all his wealth and led him to their own village.
And they brought him to the terrifying abode of Caṇḍikā, which,
with the sounds of its bells, seemed to summon him toward death as an offering.
There, his wife—the daughter of the village headman—saw him;
Sundarī had come to visit the goddess, accompanied by her young son.
Then Śrīdatta entered her palace together with Niṣiddhavatī, who was full of joy and remained neutral toward the bandits.
At that very moment, he obtained that principality of the forest-dwellers which had been entrusted to him by his father—
who, having no other son, had already departed for heaven long before— after being bestowed upon Sundarī.
He recovered that thief along with his paternal uncle and retinue,
together with his wife, and he also obtained that sword, Mṛgāṅkaka.
And having married that very daughter of Śūrasena,
the great king Śrīdatta also established himself in the city.
Then he dispatched messengers to those two parents-in-law— namely,
Bimbaki and that King Śūrasena.
And those two, accompanied by their assembled armies, approached him;
having recognized that kinship, they were filled with joy, for they were both deeply affectionate toward their daughter.
When those companions, Bāhuśālin and the others, had healed their wounds and recovered their health,
they learned of this and approached him.
Then, accompanied by his father-in-law, that hero went to that patricide and made Vikramaśakti an offering to the fire of his wrath.
And then, having regained the earth encircled by the oceans, Śrīdatta rejoiced,
like the moon emerged from an eclipse, together with Mṛgāṅkavatī.
In this way, O Lord of Men, those of steadfast mind cross over the ocean of the calamity of long separation and attain what is auspicious.
Having heard this story from Saṅgataka, King Sahasrānīka, longing for his beloved, passed that night on the road.
Then, mounted upon his desire, with his mind directed forward,
Sahasrānīka set out at dawn toward his beloved.
And after a few days, he reached that hermitage of Jamadagni,
where even the deer had abandoned their restlessness.
There he beheld Jamadagni, who had prepared hospitality for him,
bowing before that man of purifying gaze, who was like the very embodiment of ascetic powers.
And that sage delivered Queen Mṛgāvatī, together with her son, to the king,
like long-awaited joy personified.
At the end of the curse, that mutual beholding of the couple rained down,
as it were, nectar upon their eyes, which were filled with tears of joy.
Embracing his son Udayana for the first time since that [long] ago,
the king released him from his distress, as if he were pinned down by the bristling of his own hair.
Then, taking Queen Mṛgāvatī along with Udāyana,
he followed her as far as the penance grove, even the deer following him with tears in their eyes.
Having taken leave of Jamadagni,
King Sahasrānīka departed from that peaceful hermitage toward his own city.
Listening to accounts of his beloved’s separation and describing them himself,
he gradually reached Kauśāmbī, where triumphal arches and banners were raised.
And together with his wife and son, he entered that city,
as if being drunk in by the eyes of the citizens, whose rows of eyelashes were upturned.
And there, impelled by his virtues, the great king immediately consecrated his son Udayana in the position of crown prince.
For the sake of that counsel, he entrusted to him his own ministers' sons:
Vasantaka and Rumaṇvat, as well as Yaugandharāyaṇa.
"With these excellent ministers, he shall obtain the entire earth"—
thus a divine voice arose at that time, together with a rain of flowers.
Then, having entrusted the burden of sovereignty to his son, that king enjoyed with Mṛgāvatī the pleasures of the world of the living, which he had long desired.
Then, suddenly beholding old age— the messenger of peace— approaching the monarch’s ear, his longing for sense-objects, alas, vanished far away in an instant.
Then, having installed that virtuous son Udayana— who was beloved by his subjects— as the ruler of his own kingdom for the sake of the world’s welfare,
King Sahasrānīka, accompanied by his ministers, his beloved wife, and his horse, departed for the Himalayas on the Great Journey.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Kathāmukha* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the third wave:
Then, having obtained the kingdom of Vatsa which had been entrusted to him by his father...
Established in Kauśāmbī, Udayana ruled his subjects with perfect justice.
Having entrusted the burden of governance to his ministers, beginning with Yaugandharāyaṇa,
the king gradually became solely devoted to pleasures.
He constantly pursued the hunt and that lute Ghoṣavatī;
he played it day and night, for it had been given to him previously by Vāsuki.

And he brought under control, having restrained them, the wild elephants that were always intoxicated and captivated by the delusive spells of the sound produced by the tuning of their respective lutes.
The King of Vatsa drank his wine, which was adorned by the moon-like faces of the women of Vārāṇasī,
and he drank at the same time as the reflection of the ministers' faces.
"A wife suitable to my family and appearance is not to be found anywhere;
however, it is heard that there is a maiden named Vāsavadattā."
And he, Caṇḍamahāsena, pondered this single thought: "How might she be obtained?"—thus he reflected while in Ujjayinī.
"There is no husband for my daughter equal to him in this world;
however, there is one named Udayana who is always my rival."
How then can he truly become a submissive son-in-law?
There is only one means: that he must wander in the forest.
"Alone and addicted to hunting, the king binds elephants;
through that vulnerability, I shall skillfully seize him and bring him here."
"I shall make this daughter of his a pupil of that master of music;
then, without doubt, his eye will surely become fixed upon her."
"In this way, my son-in-law will certainly become submissive;
there is no other means whatsoever by which he might be brought under control."
Having reflected thus, he went to the temple of Caṇḍikā for the sake of its accomplishment;
having worshipped Caṇḍī, he praised her and made a vow to her.
"O King, this which you desire shall be accomplished before long," he heard that incorporeal voice there.
Then, having arrived satisfied, Caṇḍamahāsena, together with the minister Buddhadatta, reflected upon that very matter.
Proud, free from greed, devoted to his servants, and possessed of great strength—
though he may be incurable by means such as conciliation, let him first be approached with gentle words.
Having deliberated thus, the king commanded a messenger:
"Go, and in my name speak these words to the King of Vatsa."
"My daughter wishes to become your pupil in the art of song;
if you have affection for us, then come here yourself and teach her."
Having spoken thus, the messenger was dispatched by him;
having gone, he delivered that very message to the King of Vatsa in Kauśāmbī.
Having heard those improper words from the messenger, Vatsarāja spoke thus in private to his minister Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"What was this sent by that arrogant king to me?
What is the intention of that evil-minded one in sending such a message?"
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, the great minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, who was devoted to his master's welfare, spoke to him harshly at that time.
O Great King, that reputation for addiction which has grown like a creeper upon you— this is its fruit, bitter with its astringent flavor.
For Caṇḍamahāsena, thinking you to be full of passion and tempting you with this jewel of a maiden, has taken you away and desires to keep you as his prisoner.
Therefore, abandon those vices; for kings who sink into them are easily seized by their enemies, like wild elephants in pits.
Having been addressed thus by his minister, the steadfast Vatsarāja dispatched a counter-embassy back to King Caṇḍamahāsena.
And he gave this command: "If there is a desire for your daughter to become my disciple, then let her be sent here by you."
Having done this, Vatsarāja said to his ministers:
"I shall go and bring here that Caṇḍamahāsena, having bound him."
Having heard that, the preeminent minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said to him:
"O King, this cannot be done, nor indeed is it appropriate."
For that king is powerful and worthy of being won over by you, O Lord;
listen as I tell you everything concerning him.
There is here a city named Ujjayinī, an ornament of the earth,
which seems to mock Amarāvatī with its palaces washed in white plaster.
In which city dwells Viśveśa himself in the form of Mahākāla— Hara, who has set aside his passion for residing on Kailāsa.
In that city there was a king named Mahendravarman, the best among rulers;
he had a worthy son named Jayasena.
Then, to that Jayasena was born a son of incomparable strength,
a preeminent elephant among kings named Mahāsena.
Then that king, while protecting his own kingdom, reflected:
"I have no sword worthy of me, nor a wife of noble birth."
Having reflected thus, the king went to the temple of Caṇḍikā;
staying there without food, he worshipped the Goddess for a long time.
Then, having cut off his own flesh, he performed the rite of oblation;
thereupon, the goddess Caṇḍī, being pleased, appeared before him in person and spoke to him.
"I am pleased with you; my son, take this supreme sword of mine.
By its power, you shall become invincible to your enemies."
Moreover, you shall soon obtain as your wife a maiden named Aṅgāravatī, the daughter of the asura Aṅgāraka, who is the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
"Because this exceedingly fierce deed has been performed here by you,
therefore your name shall be Caṇḍamahāsena."
Having spoken thus and given him the sword, the goddess vanished;
then, the king’s joy at the fulfillment of his resolve appeared once more.
O Lord, that sword Khaḍga and the lordly elephant Naḍāgiri were his two jewels,
just as the thunderbolt and Airāvaṇa are the two jewels of Śakra.
Then, at times made happy by the power of those two,
King Caṇḍamahāsena once went out to hunt in the great forest.
There he beheld a single, immense, and terrifying boar,
like nocturnal darkness that had suddenly assumed a solid form even in broad daylight.
That boar, though pierced by his sharp arrows, remained unwounded;
having struck the king’s chariot, it fled and entered a cave.
The king also, abandoning his chariot and pursuing him in fury with his bow as his only companion,
entered that very same cave.
Having entered deeply, he beheld a great and lovely city;
filled with wonder, he sat down on the bank of a long pond within it.
Standing there, he beheld a maiden accompanied by a hundred women,
moving about like an arrow of the God of Love that pierces through fortitude.
She too, as if bathing the king repeatedly with her eyes that rained down a shower of the essence of love, slowly approached him.
"Who are you, O fortunate one, and for what reason have you entered here now?"—
being thus addressed by her, the king described the matter exactly as it was.
Hearing that, the maiden simultaneously shed a stream of tears from her eyes, which were filled with passion, and she also cast away her fortitude from her heart.
"Who are you, and why do you weep?"— when asked thus by the king, she, who was obedient to her husband's great command, replied to him in this way:
"The boar who entered here is the Daitya named Aṅgāraka;
and I, O King, am his daughter, Aṅgāravatī by name."
And he, whose nature is as firm as adamant, having snatched these hundred princesses from the houses of kings, made them my retinue.
Moreover, this great asura, having become a rākṣasa due to the fault of a curse,
has abandoned you today even after reaching you, being afflicted by thirst and fatigue.
And now the eight-armed Varāha himself is resting;
having awakened from sleep, he will surely commit some evil against you.
Thus, as I behold no good fortune for you, these drops of tear-water fall from me like my very life-breaths, which are boiling with the heat of anguish.
Having heard these words of Aṅgāravatī, the king said to her:
"If you have affection for me, then do this which I say."
Once he has awakened, go and weep before your father;
then he will certainly ask you the cause of your distress.
"If someone were to strike you down, what would my fate be then?
'This suffering is mine alone'—this is how he should be addressed by you."
"When this is done, there will be welfare for both you and me.

And she, having seen her own mother from the top of the pillar,
immediately brought her down along with the people standing there, filled with bashfulness.
Then that procuress was questioned there by all of them with curiosity regarding what had occurred, and she related it to them.
Then, having reflected upon that wondrous account of the Siddhas and others, those people— the king, the brahmins, the merchants, and the common folk— spoke these words:
"Let him who has thus deceived her—she who was cheated by many lovers—be made manifest here; let the binding of the royal fillet be performed for him."
Having heard that, Lohajaṅgha revealed himself there;
and being questioned, he described the entire account from the very beginning.
And there he presented to the God offerings such as the conch and the discus,
sent by Vibhīṣaṇa, which caused wonder among the people.
Then, having immediately bound the turban upon him, all the people of Mathurā, being well-pleased,
made Rūpaṇikā subject to his will by royal decree.
And so, having avenged the humiliation and resentment inflicted by the procuress, Lohajaṅgha— his treasury now overflowing with vast accumulations of jewels— dwelt there happily with his beloved.
Having thus heard this story from the mouth of Vasantaka, who had assumed another form,
Queen Vāsavadattā felt supreme satisfaction within herself regarding her husband, the Lord of Vatsa, who was nearby in captivity.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the Kathāpīṭha-lambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fifth Wave.
Then Vāsavadattā, slowly [addressed] the Lord of Vatsa.
Turning her back on her father’s side, she bound her true affection firmly [to him].

"O King, you have been bound by Caṇḍamahāsena through his magical power."
"Having given his daughter and honored you, he now wishes to release her;

For in this way, a remedy for such an arrogant one would have been provided;
neither would there be any lack of human effort in the world, nor any loss of dignity for you.
And there is an elephant named Bhadravatī, O King, which was given by this king to the hand of his daughter Vāsavadattā.

And there is a mahout named Āṣāḍhaka here;
having given him abundant wealth, he was accepted and established by me.
Having mounted that female elephant together with Vāsavadattā,

And let a high official here, who understands the gestures of elephants,
bring him to a state of intoxication with liquor so that he does not perceive this [danger].
"I shall go to Pulindaka's side and ahead of you for the purpose of guarding the path," having said this, Yaugandharāyaṇa departed.
Vatsarāja also took all of that to heart as his duty;
then Vāsavadattā approached him.
Then, while engaged in various confidential conversations with her,
the king related to her what had been told by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Having understood and resolved upon that very course for her departure,
she summoned Āṣāḍhaka and prepared him as an elephant-keeper.
Under the pretext of worshipping the gods, she gave him wine that was intoxicating and mixed with all kinds of aphrodisiacs, thereby bringing about his great ruin.
Then, at twilight, amidst the tumultuous sound of shimmering clouds,
Āṣāḍhaka prepared that female elephant and brought her there.
As she was being readied, that female elephant let out a cry;
and then the mahout, who was skilled in understanding the sounds of elephants, heard it.
"I shall go sixty-three yojanas today," the female elephant said;
and he replied with words faltering from unrestrained intoxication.
Furthermore, the mind of that intoxicated elephant was not inclined toward reflection;
and the drunken mahouts did not hear his words at all.
Then the King of Vatsa, having taken up his own lute there,
had his bonds loosened by means of the stratagems obtained from Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Having been provided with weapons by Vāsavadattā, he mounted the female elephant at his own will,
accompanied by Vasantaka.
Then Vāsavadattā also, together with her friend Kāñcanamālā,
who shared her secrets, ascended that very same [palanquin].
Then, at night, the Lord of Vatsa departed from Ujjayinī with the elephant driver as his fifth companion, by way of a path through which a rutting elephant had broken down the city wall.
The king easily slew those two heroes who guarded that place,

Then the king, joyful and accompanied by his beloved, set out with speed,

And having seen those two guards of the wall slain in Ujjayinī,

Having searched in due course, Caṇḍamahāsena also discovered that the King of Vatsa had fled, having carried off Vāsavadattā.
Then his son, named Pālaka, when a clamor had arisen in the city,

The Lord of Vatsa also fought him as he approached with arrows;
and Naḍāgiri, seeing that female elephant, did not strike her.
Then that Pālaka was turned back by his brother,
the cowherd Gopālaka, who was skilled in speech and intent on fulfilling his father’s purpose.
Then Vatsarāja also set out to go with confidence;
as he proceeded slowly, the night gradually came to an end.
Then, having reached the Vindhya forest at midday,
the female elephant, who had come from sixty-three yojanas away, became thirsty for that king.
When that king had descended into the water with his wife,
that female elephant drank from it and, due to its defect, met her death instantly.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, despondent along with Vāsavadattā,

"O King, I am a Vidyadhara woman named Māyāvatī;

"O Lord of Vatsa, today I shall indeed repay your kindness,

"And this Vāsavadattā, your wife, is not at all human;

Then, delighted, the king sent Vasantaka down the slope of the Vindhya mountains to inform his friend Pulindaka of his arrival.
And he himself, traveling on foot slowly accompanied by his beloved,
