With his bow as his only companion, the King of Vatsa slew those one hundred and five bandits before Vāsavadattā.
At that very moment, Pulindaka, a friend of this king and a companion of Yaugandharāyaṇa, arrived there preceded by Vasantaka.
Having warded off those other bandits, the king of the Bhillas prostrated before the Lord of Vatsa and led him, along with his beloved, to his own forest settlement.
There, that night, the Lord of Vatsa rested together with Vāsavadattā, while his feet were lacerated by the darbha grass of the forest.
In the morning, his commander-in-chief Rumaṇvat arrived in his presence,
having been previously informed by Yaugandharāyaṇa who had dispatched a messenger.
And the entire camp, with its vastness pervading the quarters of the horizon,
reached a state of stifling congestion, just as the Vindhya forest does when it is filled.
Then, having entered that camp in that very forest region,
the Lord of Vatsa remained there to learn news of Ujjayinī.
And while he was staying there, a merchant from Ujjayinī, a friend of Yaugandharāyaṇa, arrived; having come, he spoke as follows:
"O King, Caṇḍamahāsena is pleased with you, his son-in-law;
he has sent this doorkeeper here to your presence."
As he was approaching and standing behind, I remained right in front,
having come quickly in concealment to inform the Lord.
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa rejoiced and recounted everything to Vāsavadattā; she, too, attained the highest joy.
Having abandoned her kinsmen and being eager for the marriage rites,
Vāsavadattā was then both bashful and full of longing.
Then, for her own diversion, she said to Vasantaka who was standing nearby, "Let some story be narrated by you to me."
Then the wise Vasantaka told this story to that lovely-eyed woman, which increased her devotion to her husband.
In this world there is a city renowned as Tāmraliptī;
and in it there was a merchant named Dhanadatta, who possessed great wealth.
Being childless, he assembled many brahmins and, bowing down, said:
"Act in such a way that I may have a son without delay."
Then those brahmins said to him: "This is not at all difficult;
for here, O twice-born ones, everything is accomplished through Vedic ritual."
And likewise, O King, in former times there was a certain king who was childless;
he had one hundred and five women in his inner apartments.
And by means of the *putrīyeṣṭi* sacrifice, a son named Janturna was born to him;
he was like the rising of the new moon to the eyes of all his wives.
Once, as the boy was crawling about on his knees, an ant bit him on the thigh,
causing him to let out a terrified cry of "cūt-kāra."
At that moment, a tumultuous cry of lamentation arose within the inner apartments;
even the king wailed, "O son! O son! like an ordinary man.
When the boy had recovered in an instant and the ants had been removed,
the king lamented his state of having only one son, which was the sole cause of his suffering.
"Is there some means by which I might have many sons?"—
with such distress, he questioned the brahmins.
They replied to him, "O King, you have this means here:
offer this son of yours into the fire; thus his entire flesh shall be consumed."
"By smelling that fragrance, all the queens shall obtain sons from you.
Having heard this, the king had everything performed accordingly.
That king obtained as many sons as there were wives;
therefore, we shall likewise procure a son for you through the performance of a fire-oblation.
Having spoken thus to Dhanadatta and provided him with the prescribed sacrificial fee, those brahmins performed the fire-oblation for that merchant; consequently, a son was born to him.
And that boy named Guhasena grew up gradually;
meanwhile, his father Dhanadatta began searching for a wife for him.
Then his father went together with that son to another island on the pretext of trade, for the sake of his daughter-in-law.
There, for the sake of his own son Guhasena, he requested the maiden named Devasmitā from Dharmagupta, the preeminent merchant.
But Dharmagupta,
out of affection for his daughter, did not accept that alliance, considering Tāmraliptī to be difficult to reach.
But at that very moment, having seen Guhasena, Devasmitā—
her heart drawn by his virtues and her mind firmly resolved upon the renunciation of her kin— [fell in love with him].
Having made an appointment with her beloved— who was accompanied by his father— through the mouth of a female friend, she departed from that island at night.
Then, having reached Tāmraliptī after the two had performed their marriage ceremony,
the minds of the husband and wife became bound to one another by the cord of mutual love.
Then, when his father had passed away, Guhasena was urged by his kinsmen to travel to the island of Kaṭāha, having set out there by chance.
But his wife Devasmitā, then full of jealousy and fearing the company of another woman out of passion, did not consent to that departure of his.
Then, while his wife was unwilling and his kinsmen were urging him on,
Guhasena became a fool, paralyzed as to what ought to be done.
Having gone there, he observed a fast and undertook a vow at the temple of the god, thinking:
"May the god here point out a means for me."
Devasmitā likewise undertook that vow together with him;
then Śiva granted a vision of himself to this couple in a dream.
Having presented two red lotuses, that god spoke to those two:
"Both of you, take one lotus each in your hand."
And even when they are far apart, if one should practice the abandonment of ethical discipline, the lotus in the hand of the other will wither; it cannot be otherwise.
Having heard this and awakened, the couple saw what appeared to be each other’s heart— a red lotus held in the hand.
Then Guhasena, holding a lotus, set forth;
but she remained there, gazing at Devasmitā with eyes fixed upon her lotus-like face.
Guhasena also quickly reached that island of Kaṭāha,
and there he proceeded to engage in the buying and selling of jewels.
And seeing that lotus in his hand, which was never at any time withered,
four sons of merchants there were filled with wonder.
Having led him to that house by means of a stratagem and made him drink copious amounts of wine, they questioned him about the story of Padma; and he, being intoxicated, related it to them.
Then those four merchant sons, having reflected upon Guhasena’s long-standing business of buying and selling jewels and other goods, [acted].
Having consulted together out of curiosity, those wicked men, desiring to bring about the ruin of her wife's virtue,
went quickly and unobserved to Tāmraliptī.
Seeking a means there, they approached a female renunciant named Yogakaraṇḍikā, who resided at the Sugata’s shrine.
And with affection they said to her, "O Blessed One,
if that which we desire can be accomplished by you, then we shall give you many riches."
She also said: "Surely some woman desired by you young men is here;
therefore, go and accomplish that very thing, for I have no desire for wealth."
I have a disciple named Siddhikarī who is endowed with great intelligence;
indeed, by her grace, I have acquired immeasurable wealth.
"How was such great wealth obtained by you through the lack of faith in your disciples?"—
thus questioned by those merchant sons, the female ascetic replied:
If you have curiosity, O sons, listen as I describe it to you: once upon a time, a certain merchant came here from the Northern Region.
While he was staying here, my female disciple went to his house and, having altered her appearance, took up the role of a maidservant through a clever stratagem.
Having gained the merchant's trust and secretly stolen the entire hoard of gold from his house, she then departed at dawn.
Seeing her having departed from the city with a hurried gait as if out of apprehension, a certain *ḍomba* musician, mridaṅga drum in hand, quickly followed after her for the sake of plunder.
Having reached the foot of a banyan tree and seeing that the Domba had approached,
the deceitful Siddhikarī spoke these words with feigned distress:
"Having quarreled with my husband today, I have left my home;
O good sir, please bind this noose for me here so that I may die."
Thinking, "Let her die by the noose; why should I kill this woman? that Domba fastened the noose to that tree.
Then Siddhikarī, as if bewildered, said to that Domba:
"How can this hanging be performed by you? Let it be shown to me."
Then that Domba, having placed the mṛdaṅga drum beneath his feet and saying,
"Let it be done thus," fastened the noose around his own neck.
That [spell] also, which brings about success, instantly crushed that mṛdaṅga drum with a kick from his foot; then that Ḍomba also perished in the noose.
Arriving at that time to search for her, he saw from a distance at the foot of the tree that merchant woman Siddhikarī, whose entire treasury had been plundered.
She too, seeing him approaching, climbed that tree unobserved and remained upon a branch, her form concealed by a mass of leaves.
And when that merchant, along with his servants, arrived, he saw only that *ḍomba* bound in fetters; he did not see Siddhikarī anywhere at all.
Thinking, "Perhaps she has climbed that tree," at that very moment,
one of the merchant's servants climbed up that tree.
"Always my love has been fixed on you alone, and you have likewise ascended upon me.
Therefore, O handsome one, this wealth is yours; come, enjoy me."
Having spoken thus, she embraced and kissed his face; while doing so, that Siddhikarī bit off the tongue of the foolish-minded merchant’s servant with her teeth.
Overcome by agony and vomiting blood from his mouth,
he fell from that tree, uttering some indistinct sound like "lalala."
Seeing that, the merchant was terrified; realizing he had been seized by a spirit, he fled from there with his servants and went to his own home.
Then, having descended from the treetop, the female ascetic, likewise terrified,
went home taking with her that wealth which brings success.
For such is my disciple, endowed with abundant wisdom;
and thus, by her grace, O sons, this wealth has been obtained by me.
Having spoken thus to those sons of merchants, the female ascetic then showed them her own disciple who had arrived at that time.
And he said to them, "O sons, tell me now your true intention: which woman do you desire? I shall quickly procure her for you."
Having heard that, they said to her: "This woman named Devasmitā is the wife of the merchant Guhasena; unite us with her."
Having heard this, that female ascetic then promised to perform that task and gave her own house for these sons of merchants to stay in.
Then, having delighted the people there by giving them food and other gifts,
she entered the house of Guhasena together with her female disciple.
Then, as she approached the door of Devasmitā’s residence,
the dog, which had never before obstructed her, barred her way while bound by a chain.
Then Devasmitā, having seen her, sent a maidservant and, thinking to herself, "What could she have come for?", personally ushered her inside.
Having entered and offered her blessings, that wicked female ascetic, having feigned great respect, spoke to the virtuous Devasmītā: SoKss_2,5.120 //
"I have always had a desire to see you; today, moreover, I saw you in a dream, and for that reason I have come here eager to behold you."
And seeing you deprived of your husband, my mind is pained; for beauty and youth are indeed fruitless and barren when devoid of the enjoyment of a lover.
Having comforted that virtuous woman for a long time with these and other words,
the female ascetic took her leave and returned to her own home.
On the second day, having taken a piece of meat thoroughly saturated with powdered black pepper,
she went once more to the house of Devasmitā.
There he gave that piece of meat to the dog at the door;
the bitch immediately devoured it along with the pepper.
Then, due to the defect caused by the pepper,
unobstructed tears flowed from her eyes, and her nose began to run.
At that moment, that deceitful female ascetic entered the presence of Devasmitā; having been offered hospitality by her, she began to weep.
And when questioned by Devasmitā, she spoke thus with great difficulty:
"Daughter, look now at this bitch weeping outside."
For today, having recognized me as one with whom she was associated in a previous birth, she has begun to weep; therefore, tears have arisen in me out of compassion.
Having heard that and looking outside at the bitch who seemed as if she were weeping, Devasmitā reflected for a moment: "What is this wonder?"
Then that female ascetic said: "Daughter, in a previous birth, this woman and I were both the two wives of a certain brahmin."
And that husband of ours, by the king’s command, traveled repeatedly to various distant lands on embassies.
And while he was away on his travels, by engaging in sexual union with men at my own will,
I did not deceive the collection of elements and senses with worldly enjoyments.
"Non-injury toward living beings and the senses is indeed considered the supreme dharma;
therefore, O daughter, I have become one who remembers my past births in this life."
But at that time, she protected her virtue alone, not out of wisdom;
therefore, though she fell into the womb of a dog, she remembered her former birth.
"What dharma is this? Surely this is a clever ruse devised by her.
Having reflected thus, Suprajñā said to Devasmītā:
"O Blessed One, for so long this Dharma has not been known by me;
therefore, bring about my union with some beloved man who possesses the truth."
Then she said to the female wanderer: "Some sons of merchants who have come from another island are staying here; I will bring them to you."
Having spoken thus, the female ascetic departed for her home in high spirits; and Devaśmitā, at her leisure, addressed her own maidservants as follows: SoKss_2,5.139 //
"Surely, having seen that unfading lotus in my husband's hand, and having questioned him out of curiosity as to how it came to be while he was drinking wine," SoKss_2,5.140.
"These certain deceitful sons of merchants have come here from that island to destroy me; it was by them that this wicked ascetic woman was employed."
"Bring quickly wine mixed with that dhattūra;
then go and have an iron foot made for the dog. (SoKss 2.5.142)
Thus addressed by Devasmitā, those maidservants did exactly as they were told;
and one maidservant then assumed her form according to her word.
That female ascetic also, having taken one from those four merchant sons who had been designated in order of seniority, then departed.
Having brought him— who was disguised as his own disciple— into Devaśmitā’s house that evening, he departed and went away unobserved.
Then, there, that maidservant disguised as Devasmitā respectfully made the merchant’s son drink that honey infused with dhattūra.
His consciousness stolen by that intoxication which is like wine,
he robbed the maidservants of their garments and other belongings, and there he was made naked by them.
Having marked his forehead with the foot of a dog,
they led him away and threw him at night into a pit filled with impurities.
Then, having regained consciousness during the final watch of the night, he saw himself as if plunged into a pit of Avīci hell brought about by his own evil deeds.
Then, having risen and bathed, that merchant’s son, still naked, went to the house of the female ascetic while touching the mark upon his forehead.
"Lest I alone be an object of ridicule," he said to his other friends there, "I have been robbed as I was coming here. (SoKss 2.5.151)
Having attributed his headache to staying awake and excessive drinking,
he stood in the morning with his head wrapped in a cloth, marked by the signs [of intoxication].
And in the same way, that second merchant's son also came to Devasmitā’s house in the evening and met with the same humiliation.
He too, having arrived there naked, said: "Even though I had placed my ornaments right there, I went out and was robbed by thieves."
In the morning, he too, under the pretext of a headache,
wrapped a turban and covered his forehead, which was marked with the sign.
Thus, all those sons of merchants, full of denial, were successively humiliated,
disgraced, and suffered the loss of their wealth, filled with shame.
Thinking, "Let it be so for her as well," they departed from there after having humiliated that female ascetic, without revealing the matter to her.
Then one day, the female ascetic Devaśmitā, joyful at the thought that she had accomplished her purpose, went to the house [of the king] together with her disciple.
There, Devasmitā, having shown her respect,
made her drink wine mixed with dhattūra, as if it had been brought forth out of sheer delight.
Then that virtuous woman had Mattā, along with her disciples, have their ears and noses cut off and cast into the midst of a foul mire.
"Lest these merchant's sons go and kill my husband at any time," she said,
and being thus distressed, she related that entire account to her mother-in-law.
Then her mother-in-law said to her, "Daughter, you have done well;
however, some harm might perhaps come to that son of mine."
Then Devasmitā said to him, "Just as Śaktimatī formerly protected her husband through her wisdom, so shall I protect this man."
"How did you, O capable daughter, protect your husband? Let it be told.
Thus questioned by her mother-in-law, Devasmitā then spoke.
In our country, within the city,
there is a powerful great yakṣa known as Maṇibhadra, whose installation was performed by our ancestors.
The people living there come before him and perform various offerings for the sake of accomplishing their respective desires.
Whatever man is caught there at night with another's wife is placed by her together with her in this yakṣa’s inner chamber.
In the same manner at dawn, having brought him along with his wife to the royal assembly and made that conduct public, he is to be punished; such is the established rule.
Once, at night, a merchant named Samudradatta, who had met with his wife there, was caught by the city guard.
And having led him there, the merchant was thrown by him, along with the other man's wife,
into that temple of the Yakṣa which had its bolts firmly fastened.
At that very moment, the merchant’s wife, named Śaktimatī, who was possessed of great wisdom and devoted to her husband, learned of this event.
Then, at night, assuming the form of a steadfast yakṣī and taking offerings for worship, she went confidently to that abode of the yakṣa accompanied by her circle of friends.
Having gone there out of greed for the sacrificial fee, he became the worshiper of this very [image];
opening the door and announcing the city governor, he granted him entrance.
Having entered and seeing her husband together with his wife, he looked embarrassed;
he had the woman assume his own dress and said to her, "Go out."
And having departed at night, that woman went from there in that very disguise;
Śaktimatī remained there together with her husband.
And when the king’s officials arrived in the morning and began their investigation,
they saw that merchant accompanied by his own wife.
Having learned of this, the king— like one escaping from the mouth of Death—
punished the city governor and released that merchant from the yakṣa’s abode.
Thus, in the past, Śaktimatī protected her husband through her wisdom;
in the same way, I shall go and protect my husband by means of skillful means.
Having spoken thus in private to her mother-in-law, the ascetic Devasmitā,
accompanied by her own maidservants, assumed the guise of a merchant.
And having embarked upon a ship under the pretext of trade,
she then went to the island of Kaṭāha, where her husband resided.
Having gone there, she saw her husband Guhasena among the merchants, like consolation itself embodied in visible form outside.
He too, seeing that figure in human form from afar as if drinking it in, thought:
"Who might this be who resembles my beloved? Could he be a merchant? (SoKss_2,5.182)
And that Devasmītā, having gone there to the king, petitioned him: "I have a request; therefore, let all the subjects be assembled."
Then, having summoned all the citizens with curiosity, the king spoke to her who was dressed as a merchant, asking, "What request do you have?"
Then Devasmitā said: "Four slaves of mine are standing here in the midst [of this crowd]; let the King give them back to me."
Then the king said to her: "All these citizens are standing here;
having recognized them all as your own servants, take them."
Then she took those four merchant's sons into her own house; they had been previously humiliated and their heads were bound with cloths.
"How can these sons of a caravan leader become your slaves?
the merchants standing there then said to her in anger.
Then she replied to them: "If you have no conviction, let the foreheads of these dogs be examined; they are marked by my footprints."
Saying "So be it," he untied the head-cloths of those four;
then everyone there beheld the footprint of Śuna upon their foreheads.
Then, as the guild of merchants was filled with shame, the king, overcome with wonder,
asked Devasmitā himself, "What is this?"
She related the events exactly as they had occurred, and all the people laughed;
the king then said to her, "Those men are indeed your slaves."
Then other merchants gave abundant wealth and a fine to the king for that virtuous woman, so that those four might be released from slavery.

Having taken that wealth and recovered her own husband, Devasmitā—honored by all virtuous people—returned to her own city of Tāmraliptī; and thereafter, she never again experienced separation from her beloved.

Thus, O Goddess, women born of noble families worship their husbands with pure and steadfast conduct, their minds never turning elsewhere; for the husband is indeed the supreme deity of virtuous wives.

Having heard this noble tale from the mouth of Vasantaka while on the road— she who had recently left her father’s house with Vāsavadattā— the mind of that woman, which had been bound by mature affection for her husband, the Lord of Vatsa, became solely intent upon devotion to him, even as she established that shame within herself.
Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Kathāmukha* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the sixth wave: Then, while the King of Vatsa was staying there in the midst of the Vindhya mountains...
And Caṇḍamahāsena’s doorkeeper approached his side.
Having arrived and paid homage to the king, he said this to him:
"King Caṇḍamahāsena has sent this message to you."
It was right that Vāsavadattā was carried off by you yourself;
for it was for that very purpose that I brought you here.
And this gift was not given by me personally to you while you were self-restrained,
because I was apprehensive that such might not be your affection toward us.
Therefore, O King, you should wait a little while so that the marriage of this daughter of mine may not take place now in an improper manner.
For my son Gopālaka will indeed come here before long;
he shall perform his sister's marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites.
Having thus delivered this message to the King of Vatsa,
the doorkeeper announced each point to Vāsavadattā.
Then, together with that Vāsavadattā who was filled with joy,
the delighted Lord of Vatsa set his mind upon going to Kauśāmbī.
"You two should wait here for the arrival of Gopālaka;
afterwards, you shall come to Kauśāmbī together with him."
Having spoken thus, the lord of the earth stationed his father-in-law,
the warder, and his own friend Pulindaka right there.
He was followed by the lords of the nāgas, who were shedding streams of rut-fluid like mobile slopes of the Vindhya mountains that had come out of affection.
The earth, as if offering praise with the sound of the hoofbeats from the massed cavalry—
surpassing the compositions of professional bards— resounded.
With the uplifted masses of dust from his army that leaped into the sky,
he aroused in Indra the suspicion that the winged mountains were rising up once more.
Then, on the very next morning, that king of kings set out for his own city together with Queen Vāsavadattā.
Then, having reached that region after two or three days,
the king rested for one night in the palace of Rumaṇvat.
And on the following day, accompanied by his beloved, he entered Kauśāmbī, where after a long time a great festival had begun and the people stood looking up with eager anticipation on the road.
And then, with auspicious bathing and adornment begun by the women,
that city shone like a woman when her husband has returned after a long absence.
And there the citizens beheld the King of Vatsa with his bride,
their grief now stilled, like peacocks beholding a rain-cloud accompanied by lightning.
And the women of the city, standing upon the tops of the palaces, covered the sky with their faces,
which possessed the splendor of golden lotuses blooming on the banks of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Then the King of Vatsa entered his own royal palace together with Vāsavadattā, who was like a second royal splendor.
Crowded with kings who had come for service and filled with the auspicious songs of the Magadhas,
that city of Rājagṛha then shone as if it had just awakened from sleep.
Then Vāsavadattā’s brother Gopālaka arrived shortly thereafter,
bringing with him the warder and Pulindaka.
Vāsavadattā, her eyes wide with joy, approached him as he had risen to welcome her like another Ānanda.
"Lest there be shame for me as I behold this brother of hers"—
with this very thought, she restrained the tears in her eyes at that moment.
Then, encouraged by those words of her father’s message,
she considered herself to have achieved her purpose, as if reunited with her own kin.
Then, on the following day, Gopālaka busily attended to the great wedding festival of her and the Lord of Vatsa, which proceeded according to tradition.
Then the Lord of Vatsa took the hand of Vāsavadattā, which was as radiant as a fresh, newly blossomed sprout upon the creeper of love.
She too, with her eyes closed from the intense bliss of the touch of her beloved’s hand,
her limbs drenched in trembling sweat and covered in a dense horripilation, [was transformed].
At that moment, he appeared as if pierced by the flower-bowed god of love with a continuous stream of the Susaṃmohana, Vāyavya, and Vāruṇa weapons.
As she circumambulated the fire, her gaze was copper-red with smoke;
it was as if Madirā were making the first tentative stroke of the thread of intoxication’s sweetness.
With his treasury filled by the jewels offered by cowherds and the tribute-gifts of kings at that time,
the Lord of Vatsa truly embodied the sovereignty of a king of kings.
Having completed their marriage, the bride and groom first appeared before the eyes of the world, and afterwards entered their own dwelling.
Then, on his own festival, King Vatsarāja himself honored Gopālaka and Pulindaka with the investiture of the turban and other marks of distinction.
For the purpose of honoring the kings and the citizens as was appropriate,
Yaugandharāyaṇa and Rumaṇvat were appointed by him.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke thus to Rumaṇvat:
"We have been appointed to a difficult task by the King; for the minds of people are indeed hard to grasp."
Even a fool, when provoked, will certainly give rise to anger;
therefore, my friend, listen to this story of a fool’s ruin.
In former times, there was a certain Brahmin named Rudraśarman;
that householder had two wives.
One [wife] passed away immediately after giving birth to a son;
then, that son was placed into the hands of his stepmother by him.
And when he had grown somewhat, she gave him coarse food;
by that, the boy became one with dusty limbs and a protruding belly.
"How was this infant of mine, deprived of his mother, neglected by you?
Rudraśarman then said this to that other wife.
"Even when served with affections, he remains just like this;
what can I do for him? she said thus to her husband.
And that twice-born man thought, "Surely this is her very nature";
for who would believe the false and artless words of women to be anything but a lie?
Thinking, "This boy has perished while still a child," he became known by the name Bālavinaṣṭaka (Perished-in-Infancy) in his father's house.
"This mother of mine oppresses me constantly;
it would be better if I were to perform some counter-action against her. (SoKss 2.6.44)
Thus he reflected, that Bālavinaṣṭaka, who,
though only five years of age, was indeed possessed of great intelligence.
Then, having arrived from the royal palace, he spoke to his father in private with an indistinct voice: "Father, I have two fathers. (SoKss 2.6.46)
Thus that boy spoke every day, and his father,
suspecting that his wife was with a paramour, avoided even touching her.
She too reflected: "Why is my husband angry with me when there is no fault?
Could something have been done by some misdeed of a child?"
Having bathed him with respect and given him wholesome food,
she placed the ruined boy on her lap and questioned him.
"Son, has my father Rudraśarman been provoked to anger by you because of me? Upon hearing this, the boy spoke to his stepmother.
If you do not desist even now, I shall do even more than this to you:
why do you, who are nourishing your own son, constantly torment me?
Having heard that, she bowed to him and spoke these words following her oath:
"I shall never do so again; therefore, grant my husband his life through your favor."
Then that boy said to her: "In that case, let one maidservant show a mirror to my father when he has arrived; I shall know for certain."
Having said "So be it," she appointed a maidservant to show the mirror to Rudraśarman when he arrived a moment later.
There, showing him his own reflection at that very moment, the boy said, "This is my second father, Father! SoKss_2,6.55.
Having heard that, Rudraśarman was immediately freed from his suspicion; he became gracious toward his wife, who had been unjustly defamed.
Thus even a fool, having fallen into a state of corruption, would produce such a fault;
therefore, this entire retinue of ours is worthy of being properly delighted.
Having spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Rumaṇvat,
then honored all the people at the festival of the King of Vatsa.
And they so delighted the circle of kings that everyone thought, "These two are devoted to me alone."
And the king honored those two ministers,
along with Vasantaka, by bestowing upon them garments, unguents, ornaments, and villages from his own hand.
Then, having celebrated the marriage festival, the Lord of Vatsa, united with her,
Vāsavadattā, considered himself to have attained the very fruits of his heart's desire.

After a long time, there arose between them a certain sequence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), ever unfolding through affection, as delightful as the movement of a pair of *cakravāka* birds distressed by the end of night.
And just as the intimacy of the couple reached maturity, so too did their love attain, as it were, a state of ever-newness.
Then Gopālaka, requested by the King of Vatsa to return quickly, set out at once upon his father’s command to arrange the marriage.
Once, that King of Vatsa, being fickle, secretly consorted with a female attendant of the harem named Viracitā, who had been his companion in a previous life.
Having stumbled over her name and clinging to her feet to appease the queen,
he obtained the empire of good fortune, consecrated by her tears.
Moreover, there was a princess named Bandhumatī, won by his own arm;
sent by Gopālaka as a gift for the Queen, she was a maiden.
By her, she was concealed under the very name Mañjulikā,
like another goddess of fortune risen from the ocean of loveliness.
Accompanied by Vasantaka, that king beheld her in a bower of creepers in the garden and married her in secret according to the Gāndharva rite.
Standing there in concealment, Vāsavadattā saw this;
she became enraged, bound Vasantaka, and led him away.
Then the king took refuge with her female ascetic friend, named Sāṃkṛtyāyanī, who had come from his father’s family.
Having propitiated that queen, she herself, acting upon her command, gave Bandhumatī to the king; for the mind of a virtuous woman is indeed gentle.
Then the queen released Vasantaka from his bonds;
and he, having come before the queen, spoke to her thus with a smile:
"And what offense have I committed against you, O Queen Bandhumatī?
You, being angry with the snakes, strike at the *duṇḍubhas*."
"Explain this analogy to me," the queen asked out of curiosity;
thereupon Vasantaka replied to her once more.
Long ago, a certain son of a sage named Ruru,
while wandering at will, beheld a maiden of wondrous appearance.
Born from a Vidyadhara upon the celestial maiden Menakā,
she was raised by the sage Sthūlakeśa in his own hermitage.
And having seen her, named Pramadvarā, she captivated the mind of that Ruru;
he then went and requested her from Sthūlakeśa.
Sthūlakeśa also promised that maiden to him;
and when the wedding was near at hand, a serpent bit her unexpectedly.
Then, with a despondent heart, he heard this voice in the sky:
"O Brahmin, restore this one whose life has reached its end by giving her half of your own lifespan."
Having heard that, he gave her half of his own life at that very moment;
by means of it she was restored to life, and he too married her.
Then Ruru, being constantly enraged, would kill whichever snake he saw, thinking,
"My wife might have been bitten by one of these."
Then a certain *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, wishing to kill him, spoke to him in human speech:
"O Brahmin, you are angry with snakes; why do you kill *ḍuṇḍubhas*?"
"Your beloved has been bitten by a snake; both the snake and the *duṇḍubha* have been torn apart. All snakes are venomous, but *duṇḍubhas* are without venom. (SoKss 2.6.84)
Having heard that, he replied to him, "Friend, who indeed are you?
The Dundubha also said, "O Brahmin, I am a sage fallen [from his state] due to a curse."
"This curse of mine has reached its limit with your conversation";
having said this, he vanished, and the Guru did not strike them again.
This has been spoken by me to you for the sake of comparison, O Goddess: "May you strike at the buffalo-demons with fury, as if they were mere water-snakes."
When Vasantaka had finished speaking these words with a playful laugh,
Vāsavadattā, standing at her husband’s side, was pleased with him.
Thus the amorous Udayana, the King of Vatsa, at the feet of the Queen, constantly performed various springtime arts— sweet as honey— to entreat her who was angry.

The tongue was ever devoted to the flavor of wine, the ear was enamored with the sound of the sweet lute, and the gaze was fixed steadily upon the face of his beloved; such was the state of that happy king.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the Kathāmukha book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And this second book, the Kathāmukha, is completed. Śrī!
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The third book, named Lāvāṇaka.
This nectar of stories, it is said, was long ago churned forth from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the churning of the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain King.
Those who, having attained the two-fold wealth free from obstacles, forcibly savor [the nectar] and bear the burden of the gods upon this earth, do so by the grace of Bhava.
The First Wave.
Salutations to that Conqueror of Obstacles, whose grace even the Creator sought for the sake of achieving the unimpeded manifestation of the universe.
Even Śaṅkara trembles when embraced by his beloved at his command;
victorious is he of the peerless arrow who conquers the world.
In this way, that King of Vatsa gradually became even more so,
having obtained Vāsavadattā, with his mind solely intent upon the joy of her company.
And his great minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, along with the commander-in-chief Rumaṇvat, bore the burden of the kingdom day and night.
Once, having brought Rumaṇvat to his house at night, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa, filled with anxiety, spoke to him.
"This Lord of Vatsa was born into the lineage of the Pāṇḍavas;
and the entire earth, as well as the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), has come to him through the succession of his family."
All that was renounced by this king without any desire for conquest;
yet here, in this very land, his kingdom has arisen within a single province.
For he remains free from care, devoted to women, wine, and hunting;
all responsibility for the kingdom has been entrusted by him to us. (SoKss 3.1.8)
Therefore, we ourselves must act with our own intelligence in such a way that he shall indeed obtain this hereditary sovereignty over the entire earth.
For when this is done, both devotion and the practice of mantra will have been accomplished;
everything is achieved through intelligence—listen therefore to this discourse.
In former times, there was a king named Mahāsena;
he was attacked by another king who was exceedingly powerful.
Then, having assembled with his ministers who were intent on preventing the failure of their own interests,
Mahāsena was made to pay a fine to that enemy.
Having inflicted punishment, that proud king was deeply tormented, thinking: "Why have I performed a prostration before the enemy? (SoKss 3.1.13)
And by that very [sorrow], a tumor arose within him;
overcome by both the tumor and his grief, the king became one on the verge of death.
Then, considering that the queen was incurable by medicine, a certain wise physician falsely said to the king: "O King, your queen is dead."
Upon hearing that, as the king suddenly fell to the ground,
his abdominal tumor burst open of its own accord due to the powerful force of his grief.
Recovered from his illness, the king enjoyed his desired pleasures for a long time together with that very queen, and he once again conquered his enemies.
Just as that physician, through his wisdom, acted for the king's benefit, so do we act for the king's benefit; we shall accomplish the governance of his earth.
And there is one adversary there, Pradyota, the lord of Magadha;
for he is a rear-enemy who always raises a rebellion against us from behind.
"He possesses a jewel of a daughter named Padmāvatī;
we shall request her for the sake of this King of Vatsa."
Having concealed Vāsavadattā by means of our own ingenuity and having set fire to the bedchamber,
let us proclaim everywhere that the queen has been burnt.
The Lord of Magadha will not give that daughter to any other king;
for this reason, when he was previously entreated by me, he spoke thus.
"I will not give this daughter, who is dearer to me than my own self, to the King of Vatsa;
for his affection for Vāsavadattā is indeed very great."
And while Queen Satyavatī is alive, the Lord of Vatsa will never marry another;
however, once the report that the queen has been burned has arisen, everything will be accomplished.
And once Padmāvatī has been obtained, the King of Magadha, as her kinsman,
will no longer harbor resentment and will instead become an ally.
"Then we shall go to conquer the eastern direction, and the others in their proper order;
in this way, we shall bring the entire earth under the sovereignty of the Lord of Vatsa."
And while we have exerted ourselves, this king shall surely obtain the earth; for previously, a divine voice spoke thus.
Having heard these words from Yaugandharāyaṇa, the bull among ministers,
Rumaṇvat spoke to him, suspecting this to be a rash act.
If a pretext were ever made for the sake of Padmāvatī, it would lead only to our own ruin; therefore, hear the story regarding this matter.
There is a city named Mākandikā on the bank of the Jāhnavī;
in it there once lived a certain wandering mendicant who observed a vow of silence.
Subsisting on alms and surrounded by many wandering mendicants,
he took up residence in a small cell within a temple.
Once, having entered the house of a certain merchant for the sake of alms,
he saw a beautiful maiden coming out, carrying alms.
And having seen her of wondrous form, that rogue, fallen under the power of desire, cried out, "Alas! Alas! What misery! while that merchant was listening.
Having accepted alms, he then went to his own home;
thereafter, that merchant approached him in private and questioned him out of wonder.
"Why have you suddenly abandoned your silence and spoken thus this very day?
Hearing that, the wandering mendicant spoke to the merchant as follows:
"This daughter of yours possesses ill-omened marks; when her marriage takes place, the destruction of you, along with your sons and wife, will certainly occur."
"Seeing this, sorrow has arisen within me, for you are my devotee;
it was for your sake that I broke my silence and spoke thus. (SoKss 3.1.37)
"Therefore, let this girl, placed within a chest at night with a lamp set upon it, be cast by you into the Ganges."
Having agreed, saying "So be it," that merchant then went there and did everything accordingly at night out of fear; for the fearful are indeed devoid of reflection.
At that time, the renunciant also said to his own followers:
"Go to the Ganges; go there and find whatever river flows within it."
"Bring here that casket which has a lamp placed upon its back;
it must be kept secret, and it is not to be opened even when the internal sound is heard. (SoK 3.1.41)
Saying "So be it," they set out, but before they had reached the Ganges,
one of the princes descended into that very river.
There, seeing that casket which had been cast in by the merchant, he had it brought by his servants and, out of curiosity, suddenly opened it by the light of a lamp.
And within, he beheld that maiden who maddened his heart,
and at that very moment, he united with her by the Gāndharva rite.
Having placed that casket and likewise the lamp held upright within it, he cast them into the Ganges,
having thrown a fierce monkey inside.
Then, when that prince had departed with the jewel of a maiden,
those disciples of the wandering mendicant arrived, searching for him.
They saw that basket and, taking it, brought it to the presence of the wandering mendicant; then he, being delighted, said to them:
"I alone shall accomplish the mantra here above;
you must lie silently below for this night."
Having said this, that wandering mendicant, desiring the merchant’s daughter, placed her upon that chest atop his hut and opened it.
Then, emerging from her, a monkey of terrifying form rushed at him like his own misconduct incarnate.
In that instant, with his teeth and claws, the monkey tore away the nose and ears of that wicked one,
like one skilled in subduing enemies acting out of wrath.
Then, having become thus, that wandering mendicant descended;
and his disciples, their strength restrained by effort, beheld him at that time.
Having awakened in the morning and learned all of that, every person laughed;
the merchant rejoiced, as did his daughter, who had now attained her goal.
Just as that wandering mendicant fell into ridicule,
so too might we at some time fall into ridicule if our employment of a stratagem were to fail.
"Separation from Queen Vāsavadattā is indeed fraught with many evils";
when Rumaṇvat had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
Success in effort cannot be achieved otherwise, and it is certain that in the absence of effort, even what is already established would perish if the king were to fall into calamity.
Even if we have attained renown as ministers, it might turn out otherwise for us;
furthermore, we would become betrayers of our master’s confidence.
For since wisdom is considered the instrument for a king whose success depends on his own efforts,
what need is there for ministers, whether they are employed or not?
But for one whose success depends upon ministers, their wisdom alone is the means to achieve his ends; yet if they themselves lack zeal, a final farewell has been offered to prosperity.
Now, if you have no doubt regarding Caṇḍamahāsena, the father of the Goddess,
then he, along with his son and the Goddess, will surely do my bidding.
To Yaugandharāyaṇa, the foremost among the wise, who had spoken thus,
Rumaṇvat, his heart apprehensive of negligence, spoke again:
"Even one possessed of discernment is tormented by the pain of separation from a beloved woman;
how much more so this King Vatsa? In this regard, hear this story."
In former times there was a king named Devasena, the best among the wise;
Śrāvastī was his capital city.
And in that city there was a certain merchant of great wealth;
it is said that to him was born a daughter who had no equal.
That maiden also became renowned by the name Unmādinī;
for upon seeing her beauty, every person who encountered her would go mad.
"The daughter must never be given away by me without first informing the king;
for he might become angry," thought her father, that merchant.
Then, having gone there, he addressed King Devasena:
"O King, I have a jewel of a daughter; if she is of use to you, let her be accepted."
Having heard that, the king then dispatched trustworthy brahmins with the instruction:
"Go and determine whether she possesses the auspicious marks or not."
"So be it," said those twice-born men; having gone and seen that merchant's daughter, Unmādinī, they were instantly agitated, for passion had arisen within them.
Once she is married, the king will abandon everything with his mind fixed solely on her; royal affairs will perish, and thus, what is the use of her?
Having thus returned to their natural state and consulted together, those twice-born ones went away and falsely told the king, "That girl possesses the marks of a low family."
Then that merchant gave Unmādinī, who had been abandoned by the king, to his general, even though she felt inward resentment.
Then, once while staying in the palace in her husband’s residence,
she perceived that the king had arrived by that path and showed herself to him.
And as soon as the king beheld her, that medicine for the bewilderment of the world,
he became like one possessed by madness, as if love had cast its spell upon him.
Having returned to his own abode and realized that she had previously been disregarded by him,
he became despondent and fell into a state of intense suffering from the fever of torment.
"Let it be understood that she is a maidservant and not another's wife; or else, I shall abandon her at a temple, and then let my lord take her as his own."
Thus, being earnestly entreated by his own general, who was also his husband, the king spoke as follows.
"I shall not take another's wife, nor will you abandon her; otherwise, your dharma will perish and you shall be punished by me. (SoKss 3.1.78)
Having heard that, the other ministers remained silent, and in due course,
the king passed away from that very fever of love.
Thus that king perished, even though he was steadfast, because of being without Unmādinī;
but how could the King of Vatsa fare without Vāsavadattā?
Having heard this from Rumaṇvat, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke again: "Suffering is endured by kings who keep their objectives in view."
Did Rāma not endure the agony of separation from Queen Sītā, even though he was separated from her by the gods who devised a stratagem for the destruction of Rāvaṇa?
Having heard this, Rumaṇvat spoke once more:
"For those such as Rāma were gods; their minds were capable of enduring everything."
But I cannot endure [the presence of] humans; therefore, let this story be heard:
here there is a great city called Mathurā, rich in many jewels.
In that city there was a certain merchant’s son named Yaïllaka;
he had a beloved wife whose mind was entirely fixed upon him alone.
Then, while living with her, the merchant's son once resolved to go to another island due to the weight of his business affairs.
His wife also desired to go with him;
for the hearts of women, when devoted out of affection, cannot endure separation.
Then that merchant’s son set out after performing the auspicious rites;
yet he did not take his wife, who was already adorned with her finery, along with him.
Then, watching him depart from behind with tearful eyes,
she stood leaning against the edge of the door-panel at the entrance of the courtyard.
When he had passed from her sight, she, unable to endure the separation, was so bewildered that she could not go out; her life-breaths departed.
Having understood that, the merchant’s son returned at that very moment and beheld his beloved, overwhelmed and with her life departed.
With its beautiful, pale luster and marked by dangling locks of hair,
it was like the lunar splendor upon the earth, as if fallen from heaven while asleep.
And as he held her on his lap and wept,
his life-breaths immediately departed from his body, which was ablaze with the fire of grief, as if terrified.
Thus, through their mutual separation, the couple perished;
therefore, the king and the queen must protect each other from being parted.
When Rumaṇvat had finished speaking and ceased, having become apprehensive,
the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, an ocean of fortitude, said:
"All these matters have been determined by me; the affairs of kings are indeed of such a nature, so hear a story regarding this."
Formerly, there was a king in Ujjayinī named Puṇyasena; once, he was attacked by another powerful king who came against him.
Then his wise ministers, seeing that enemy to be invincible,
spread a false report everywhere that the king was dead.
They placed King Puṇyasena in concealment,
and they cremated another corpse according to the rites befitting a king.
"Now, become our king, for we are without a ruler; you alone must do so for us.
Thus they spoke to that enemy through the mouth of a messenger.
When the enemy, being satisfied, had said "So be it," they then gathered together with their armies and gradually broke through his camp.
When the army was broken, those powerful ministers revealed King Puṇyasena to him and struck down that enemy.
"Royal affairs are of such a nature;
therefore, we shall carry out this task with fortitude under the pretext of the Queen's cremation."
Having heard this from Yaugandharāyaṇa, whose mind was thus resolved, Rumaṇvat spoke as follows: "In that case, if this is the firm decision..."
"Having brought that cowherd, the respected brother of the queen,
and having consulted with him, let everything be properly arranged."
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa said, "So be it," and because of his confidence,
Rumaṇvat also made the firm resolve to act.
On another day, those two chief ministers dispatched their own messenger,
Gopālaka, under the pretext of longing to see him.
Having previously departed on account of his business, that cowherd returned there upon hearing the words of the messenger, appearing like the festival itself incarnate.
On that day, when he had arrived, Yaugandharāyaṇa took Gopālaka along with Rumaṇvat to his own house at night at his leisure.
And there he recounted to him that enthusiasm for what he intended to do—
everything that had previously been deliberated upon by him together with Rumaṇvat.
And Gopālaka, desiring the welfare of the king, consented even to that which brought suffering to his sister; for the word of the virtuous must indeed be carried out.
"All this has been well-arranged; however, considering that the Queen has been burned, let it be considered how the Lord of Vatsa is to be protected while he gives up his life."
Indeed, even when the assembly of favorable conditions such as skillful means is present,
the primary limb of mantra is the counteraction of misfortune.
When Rumaṇvat had thus spoken once more at that time, Yaugandharāyaṇa, who had deliberated upon every course of action, replied: SoKss_3,1.114 //
There is no doubt in this matter that the princess Gopālaka’s younger sister,
the queen, is dearer to him than even his own life.
And seeing his grief to be slight, the Lord of Vatsa will then regain his composure, thinking, "Perhaps the Queen still lives."
Moreover, this supreme being will soon be led away in marriage;
therefore, Queen Padmāvatī shall be revealed before long.
Having thus reached this decision, Yaugandharāyaṇa,
Gopālaka, and Rumaṇvat then held this consultation.
"By means of this stratagem, let us go to Lāvāṇaka together with the Queen and the King;
for that is a border district situated near Magadha."
Because it is a land of easy prey and because the king is absent,
if they set fire to the inner apartments there, whatever was intended will be accomplished.
And the queen shall be taken by a stratagem and established in the house of Padmāvatī, so that she, remaining there in concealment, may serve as her witness to her virtue.
Having thus conferred with one another during the night, all of them—
Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others— entered the royal palace on the following day.
Then, having been thus addressed by Rumaṇvat, Vatsarāja said:
"Your Majesty, all is well with us who have gone to Lāvāṇaka."
And that region is exceedingly delightful; there, O King, the hunting grounds are beautiful, with abundant grass and easy to traverse.
"And that lord of Magadha oppresses everyone because of his proximity;
therefore, you should go there for the sake of protection and for diversion."
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa, together with Vāsavadattā—
who was solely intent on their amorous play— set his mind on going to Lāvāṇaka.
When the departure had been decided upon and the auspicious moment for the next day had been determined,
the sage Nārada suddenly appeared, illuminating the quarters of the sky with his radiance.
Descending from the midst of the sky, providing a festival for the eyes,
he approached that Lord of Vatsa out of affection for his own family, like the moon approaching the lord of the night-lotuses.
Having accepted the hospitality and honors, that sage, being pleased, gave a garland made of *pārijāta* flowers to the king who stood before him in humble reverence.
"You shall obtain a son who is a lord of the Vidyādharas and an emanation of Kāmadeva";
thus he greeted Vāsavadattā with great respect.
Then, while Yaugandharāyaṇa stood by, he said to the Lord of Vatsa:
"O King, having seen Vāsavadattā, alas, I have been reminded [of her]."
In former times, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others were your great-grandfathers;
Draupadī was the single wife of those five.
And she was peerless in beauty, like Vāsavadattā herself;
then, apprehensive of that very fault, I spoke to them thus:
One must guard against enmity with women, for that is indeed the seed of calamities in this world;
listen therefore, as I relate this story to you.
There were two brothers named Sunda and Upasunda,
two asuras who were difficult to conquer and who had overwhelmed the three worlds with their prowess.
And Brahmā, desiring their destruction, gave his command to Viśvakarman and had him fashion the divine woman Tilottamā.
It is said that even Śarva, though possessing four faces, had to circumambulate her while looking at her form in all four directions.
At the command of the Lotus-born One, she went to the side of Sunda and Upasunda,
who were dwelling in the gardens of Kailāsa, in order to seduce them.
As soon as they saw Sundarī approaching nearby, both of those two Asuras,
infatuated with desire, seized her by both arms.
Seizing her at that very moment, they both fell into mutual conflict;
and because they engaged in combat, both met their destruction.
Thus, for whom is the object known as "woman" not a cause of calamities?
And yet, Draupadī alone is the beloved of many of you here.
"Indeed, you must guard against any conflict arising from various causes;
by my word, let this agreement always hold for you."
The mother who stays near the eldest son should be regarded as such by the younger;
and the one staying near the youngest should be known as a daughter-in-law by the eldest. (SoKss 3.1.143)
"O King, your great-grandfathers,
their minds set on what is auspicious, accepted these words of mine, saying, 'So be it.'"
They were my friends, and out of affection for them I have come here to see you, O Lord of Vatsa; therefore, listen as I tell you this.
Just as you have carried out these words of mine, so should you act toward the ministers;
in a short time, you shall attain great prosperity.
For a short time you will experience suffering, but you must not fall into excessive delusion regarding it; for that shall end in happiness.

Having spoken thus correctly, at that very moment the sage Nārada, who was skilled in the art of indicating future events through indirect hints, vanished from the sight of the King of Vatsa regarding his impending prosperity.
And then, at the word of that bull among sages, all those ministers, headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa,
perceiving the imminent success of their own intended purpose, exerted themselves with even greater effort to bring it to fruition.
Thus ends the first wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The second wave begins:
Then, according to the previously mentioned stratagem, [he approached] the King of Vatsa together with his beloved.
Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others led them toward Lāvāṇaka.
With the swelling roar of his army, that king reached that region,
as if it were proclaiming to his ministers the successful fulfillment of their desires.
Thereupon, having learned that the Lord of Vatsa had arrived with his retinue,
the King of Magadha trembled, fearing an attack by surprise.
Sad-buddhi dispatched a messenger to the presence of Yaugandharāyaṇa;
that wise minister, who understood the nature of affairs, welcomed him with joy.
The Lord of Vatsa, while residing in that country,
wandered day after day through the distant forest for the sake of hunting.
One day, when that king had gone out for a hunt, [the sage],
having made an agreement regarding his duties, set out accompanied by a cowherd boy.
The wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Rumaṇvat and Vasantaka,
went into the presence of Queen Vāsavadattā in private.
There, with various words, he entreated her— who had already been persuaded by her brother— to provide assistance in this royal matter, as she bowed before him.
And she consented to that which caused her heart such pain of separation;
for what indeed do noble women devoted to their husbands not endure?
Then the skillful Yaugandharāyaṇa, having bestowed upon her a transformative yoga, turned that goddess into the form of a brahmin woman.
And he made Vasantaka one-eyed and disguised him in the form of a young brahmin student;
he himself likewise assumed the appearance of an elderly brahmin.
Then, having taken that queen who was of such a form, the high-minded one set out at his own will toward Magadha, accompanied by Vasantaka.
Thus Vāsavadattā, having departed from her own home,
went toward her husband with her mind, while going along the path with her body.
Then, having set that palace ablaze with fire, Rumaṇvat proclaimed aloud:
"Alas, alas! The Queen, together with Vasantaka, has been consumed by the flames!"
And so, both the fire and the wailing arose there simultaneously;
the fire gradually subsided, but the sound of the wailing did not.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa, together with Vāsavadattā and Vasantaka,
reached the city of the Lord of Magadha.
Having seen the princess Padmāvatī there in the garden, he approached her together with those two, even though he was being restrained by the guards.
And as soon as Padmāvatī saw Queen Vāsavadattā, who was wearing the form of a Brahmin woman, love arose in her eyes.
Having dismissed the guards, the princess then had Yaugandharāyaṇa,
who was in the guise of a Brahmin, summoned to her presence.
And he asked, "O Great Brahmā, who is this young girl of yours?
For what purpose have you come? He, too, replied to her.
"Thus, this daughter of mine is the princess named Āmāvantikā;
and her husband, being addicted to vice, has abandoned her and gone off somewhere."
"Therefore, O illustrious lady, I entrust her to your care today,
so that I may go and bring back her husband after searching for him without delay."
"And let this brother Kāṇabaṭu remain right here near her, so that she does not experience the sorrow of being alone. (SoKss_3,2.23)
Having spoken thus, and having had his words accepted by her, that excellent minister took leave of the princess and went quickly to Lāvāṇaka.
Then [he saw] Vāsavadattā standing there under the name of Āvantikā,

Taking her with him and having shown her noble hospitality,

There, Vāsavadattā entered and, beholding Sītā within the painted walls during the account of Rāma’s life, she endured her own anguish.
By her physical form, her delicacy, the elegance of her posture while reclining or sitting,
and even by the fragrance of her body, which was as sweet as the blue lotus;
Having determined her to be the most excellent, Padmāvatī attended upon her as she desired with costly honors equal to her own.
And he thought: "Surely this is some woman staying here in disguise;
was Draupadī not hidden while we dwelt in Virāṭa's kingdom?"
Then Vāsavadattā, on the occasion of visiting this queen,
prepared for her a fresh garland and a forehead mark (tilaka), which she had previously learned from the Lord of Vatsa.
Seeing Padmāvatī adorned with those ornaments in private, her mother asked,

Padmāvatī said to her: "A certain woman named Āvantikā, staying here in my palace, did this for me."
Having heard that, her mother said to her: "Daughter, she is not some mere human; she is surely a goddess who possesses such supernatural knowledge."
Deities and sages likewise remain in the homes of the virtuous for the sake of testing them;
therefore, my daughter, listen to this story.
There was a king named Kuntibhoja,
and into his palace came and stayed the sage Durvāsas, whose sole delight was in deception.
For the sake of serving him, King Kuntibhoja commanded his own daughter Kuntī; she too attended upon the sage with great diligence.
Once, that sage, desiring to test Kuntī, said to her:
"Cook some excellent rice-milk porridge quickly, so that I may return as soon as I have bathed."
Having spoken thus, that seer quickly bathed and came to eat;
Kuntī then presented him with a vessel filled with that food.
And with food that was too hot, the sage cast his gaze upon Kuntī’s back— she who was like a blazing fire and unfit for him to take by the hand.
Having discerned the sage’s intention, she also placed that bowl upon her back;
then he ate as he pleased, while Kuntī’s back burned with pain.
Because she remained unshaken even while being severely burned, the sage was pleased; having eaten, he then granted her a boon.
Thus was that sage there; and this Avantikā of yours is likewise some such being. You should propitiate her for the sake of truth.
Having heard this from her mother’s mouth, Padmāvatī esteemed that Vāsavadattā— who was there in another form— all the more highly.
Vāsavadattā too, deprived here of her own lord,
remained distressed and lusterless, like a lotus at midnight.
And those various compositions of the poet Vasantaka, suited for children, repeatedly provided occasions for a smile upon the face of that woman separated from her lover.
In the meantime, after wandering through hunting grounds at a great distance,
the King of Vatsa finally returned to Lāvāṇaka again in the evening.
And he saw that the inner apartments had been reduced to ashes by the fire there;
moreover, he heard from his ministers that the queen, along with Vasantaka, had been burnt.
As soon as he heard this, his consciousness was stolen away by delusion and he fell to the ground,
as if wishing to cast off the affliction of experiencing that sorrow.
In an instant, having regained consciousness, he blazed with grief in his heart,
as if possessed by the fire of the sight of the goddess burning there.
Then, lamenting and afflicted by grief, with his mind solely intent on abandoning his body,
the king, after a moment, recollected this and reflected:
"The son of that goddess shall become the lord of the Vidyādharas;
the sage Nārada told this to me, and it is not false."
For some time, suffering was proclaimed to me by that very sage;
yet the grief of this cowherd appears to be quite slight.
"Nor do Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others appear to be in extreme distress;
therefore, I know that the queen must somehow still be alive."
"This must be some kind of stratagem devised by the ministers;
therefore, O Queen, there might eventually be a reunion with me through it."
Thinking, "I shall see the end of this matter here," that king,
though being exhorted by his ministers, fixed his heart in steadfastness.
And Gopālaka, having instructed him regarding the matter exactly as it was,
immediately dispatched a scout there unobserved for the sake of reassurance.
When his own account had thus been related by those who were in Lāvāṇaka,

Having learned of this, the king, who knew the proper time, desired to give his daughter Padmāvatī— who had previously been sought by the minister— to the King of Vatsa.
Then, through the mouth of a messenger, he sent word to the King of Vatsa and also to Yaugandharāyaṇa regarding this matter, exactly as he desired.
And at the word of Yaugandharāyaṇa, the Lord of Vatsa consented to that, thinking:
