Then, having determined an auspicious moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa quickly dispatched a counter-messenger to that King of Magadha.
"Your wish has been accepted by us; therefore, on the seventh day from now, the King of Vatsa will come here for the marriage of Padmāvatī."
"And quickly arrange for Vāsavadattā in such a way that he will forget her"—
this the great minister instructed the king.
Having gone as a return messenger, he delivered the message exactly as instructed;
then the King of Magadha received him with great joy.
Then the Lord of Magadha prepared the wedding festivities and their requisite materials, according to his affection for his daughter, his own desire, and his wealth.
Upon hearing of her desired boon, Padmāvatī attained joy,
while Vāsavadattā fell into grief upon hearing that news.
That news, reaching Karna and causing her to lose her complexion,
seemed to provide assistance to the concealment of his own deformity caused by his secret dwelling [in her womb].
"In this way, even an enemy can be made a friend, and not otherwise;
such was the speech of Vasantaka to her, which, like a friend, restored her composure."
Then, for Padmāvatī, whose wedding was imminent,
that wise woman once again fashioned two divine garlands and forehead marks that would never fade.
Then, on the arrival of the seventh day, the Lord of Vatsa,
accompanied by his army and ministers, reportedly came there to marry her.
How could that man separated from her even mentally touch the effort toward her?
If he did not have the hope: "May I obtain that very goddess in this way."
And the Lord of Magadha immediately went out to meet him with joy,
as the ocean approaches the moon when it has risen, a festival for the eyes of the subjects.
Then that Lord of Vatsa entered the city of the King of Magadha;
meanwhile, a great festival entered the minds of the citizens on all sides.
There the women beheld him, his body emaciated by separation and causing delusion to the mind, like the god of love deprived of Rati.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, having entered the palace of the Lord of Magadha, went to the bridal chamber,
which was filled with women whose husbands were living.
There the king beheld Padmāvatī within, who had performed the marriage ceremony; her full moon-like face surpassed the orb of the full moon itself.
And beholding those two divine garland and forehead-mark of his own, the king reflected: "From where do these belong to her?"
Then, having ascended the altar, he took her hand;
that very act constituted the commencement of his taking the hand of the Earth.
As if thinking, "This man, whose beloved is Vāsavadattā, cannot bear to see this," the smoke from the sacrificial altar veiled his eyes with tears.
As she circumambulated the fire, Padmāvatī’s face,
having understood her husband’s intention, then appeared as if agitated with anger.
Having completed the marriage, the Lord of Vatsa released his bride from his hand;
yet he did not abandon that Vāsavadattā from his heart for even a moment.
Then the Lord of Magadha bestowed such jewels upon him that the earth seemed to realize it had been milked dry and was now empty of its treasures.
And having made fire his witness at that moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa caused the King of Magadha to give a pledge of non-hostility toward the king.
With garments and ornaments bestowed, with excellent bards singing,
and with noble women dancing, the great festival spread forth.
At that time, Vāsavadattā remained unobserved, as if asleep, awaiting the rising of her husband; she was like the lunar splendor during the day.
Then, when the King, the Lord of Vatsa, had entered the inner apartments,
the skillful Yaugandharāyaṇa became apprehensive regarding a meeting with the Queen.
Out of fear that his secret counsel might be leaked, he thus addressed the Lord of Magadha:
"The King of Vatsa will not depart from your palace this very day."
Having agreed with "So be it," he immediately informed the King of Vatsa of that very matter; and the king, for his part, believed it to be so.
Then the Lord of Vatsa set out, having finished eating and drinking,
taking with him his retinue and his bride Padmāvatī along with his ministers.
Having mounted the vehicle sent by Padmāvatī,
he set out together with those high officials who had been commanded by her.
Vāsavadattā also arrived secretly behind the army,
placing Vasantaka— who had assumed a disguised form— in front of her.
In due course, having reached Lāvāṇaka, the Lord of Vatsa entered his own residence together with his bride; yet he was entirely preoccupied with the Queen’s mind alone.
Then Vāsavadattā also, having stationed her attendants there, entered the palace of Gopālaka at midnight.
There, seeing her brother Gopālaka showing such respect,
she embraced him around the neck while weeping, her eyes clouded with tears.
At that very moment, Yaugandharāyaṇa,
accompanied by Rumaṇvat, arrived there while remaining steadfast in his resolve, having been received with honor by the queen.
While he was still dispelling her sorrow caused by the separation from his encouragement,
those high officials arrived at the side of Padmāvatī.
"O Queen from Avantī, having arrived, you have somehow left us and entered the house of the prince Gopālaka."
Thus addressed by her own chief ministers, Padmāvatī,
filled with apprehension, spoke thus to the King of Vatsa in their presence.
"Go to Avantī and say: 'Indeed, you have remained as my deposit;
therefore, what is it to you here? Come to that very place where I am.'"
When they had departed after hearing that, the king asked Padmāvatī in private, "By whom were these two— the garland and the tilaka— made for you?"
She then said: "This woman named Āvantikā was deposited in my house by a certain Brahmin;
this is her great craft."
Upon hearing that, the Lord of Avanti went to the cowherd’s house,
thinking, "Surely she must be Vāsavadattā here."
And having gone there, he entered that place where the high minister stood at the gate, together with the queen within,
the two chamberlains, and Vasantaka.
There he beheld Vāsavadattā, who had returned from her exile,
like the lunar orb released from an eclipse.
Then, overwhelmed by the poison of grief, he fell upon the surface of the earth;
a tremor arose within the heart of Vāsavadattā.
Then she too fell to the ground, her limbs pale from the pangs of separation,
and lamented, reproaching her own conduct.
Then that couple, wretched with grief,
wept in such a manner that even Yaugandharāyaṇa had his face washed with tears.
Having heard such a clamor at that time,
Padmāvatī also approached him right there in a state of agitation.
And as she gradually came to understand the situation of both the King and Vāsavadattā, she too found herself in exactly the same state; for virtuous women are indeed tender and guileless.
"What use have I for life that brings such suffering to my husband?
Vāsavadattā said, weeping again and again.
"O Lord, desiring imperial sovereignty for you through the acquisition of the daughter of the King of Magadha, this was done by me; there is no fault whatsoever on the part of the Queen."
"But this [other woman] is like a co-wife to her, acting as a witness to her virtue during her absence," said the steadfast Yaugandharāyaṇa to the Lord of Vatsa.
"I shall enter this fire for the sake of manifesting her purity," Padmāvatī said there, with a heart free from malice.
"I alone am at fault,
for whose sake this great suffering was endured even by the Queen," the king also declared.
"I must enter the fire for the sake of proving the king's heart pure," Vāsavadattā declared with firm resolve.
Then that wise Yaugandharāyaṇa, the foremost among the successful,
having sipped water and facing the east, uttered the words, "I am pure."
"If I am a benefactor to the king, and if Queen Śuddhimatī is pure, then speak, O World-Protectors! If it is not so, I shall cast off this body."
When he had finished speaking and ceased, this divine voice arose:
"O King, you are blessed, for you have Yaugandharāyaṇa as your minister."
"The one whose wife Vāsavadattā was his deity in a previous birth—
there is no fault whatsoever in her," having said this, the voice ceased.
Having heard that sound, which filled all the quarters of the sky with the splendor of the deep thundering of fresh rain-clouds,
they all— having long since abandoned their distress and clearly emulating the blue-throated god (Śiva)— stood with their necks outstretched.
And even while accompanied by Gopālaka, the King of Vatsa praised the conduct of Yaugandharāyaṇa and considered the earth already within his grasp.
Then the king, beholding both his beloved wives standing near him like the personified forms of Rati and Nirvṛti,
experienced a supreme festival of joy through the affection born of their daily companionship.
Thus ends the second wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the third wave.
Then, on another day, the Lord of Vatsa, together with Vāsavadattā—
And he engaged in the sport of drinking with Padmāvatī, having retired to a secluded place.
Having brought Yaugandharāyaṇa along with Gopālaka, Rumaṇvat, and Vasantaka, he engaged them in confidential conversations.
There, on the occasion of his own departure and the resulting upheaval, the lord of the earth related this story while all of them were listening.
There was a king named Purūravas, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu,
whose movement was unimpeded both upon the earth and even in heaven.
Once, as he was wandering in the Nandana grove, an Apsaras named Urvaśī— like another bewitching weapon of Kāma— beheld him.
As soon as she was seen by him,
her heart was so captivated that it caused the hearts of her friends, including Bhaya and Rambhā, to tremble with fear.
Seeing her, who was like a cascading torrent of the essence of beauty, the king,
overcome by thirst, fainted because he did not obtain her embrace.
Then Hari, the omniscient one dwelling in the ocean of milk,
gave instructions to the excellent sage named Nārada, who had approached him for a vision.
O divine sage, King Purūravas, while staying in the Nandana grove,
had his heart stolen by Urvaśī and remained unable to endure the pangs of separation.
"O Sage, having gone there and informed Śatakratu with my words, cause that Urvaśī to be given quickly to that king."
Having been thus commanded by Hari, Nārada replied, "So be it," and returning,
he awakened Purūravas in that state and spoke to him.
"Arise, O King! I have been sent here by Viṣṇu on your account;
for He indeed never neglects the calamities of those who are devoted to Him with sincere devotion."
Having spoken thus, the sage Nārada, together with Purūravas who had been comforted by him, went into the presence of the king of the gods.
Having reported Hari’s command to Indra, who was bowed down in devotion,
he then caused Urvaśī to be given to Purūravas.
To him, the gift of Urvaśī was like a life-restoring elixir for heaven;
to Urvaśī, however, it was the very medicine that restores the dead to life.
Then Purūravas returned to the world of mortals, taking her with him,
offering to the eyes of humans the wonder of beholding a celestial bride.
Then those two, Urvaśī and that king, remained inseparable,
as if bound to one another by the noose of their mutual glances.
Once, when the wielder of the thunderbolt had entered into battle with the Dānavas,
Purūravas went to heaven, summoned for the sake of providing assistance.
When that lord of the asuras named Māyādhara had been slain,
there was a festival for Śakra, with throngs of celestial nymphs breaking into dance.
Then, seeing Rambhā dancing with her gestures faltering while the teacher Tumburu stood by, that Purūravas laughed.
"Do you know this divine dance, or do you know it as a human being? Thus Rambhā spoke to him at that time with resentment.
Then Purūravas said to her: "I know that which even Tumburu does not know, and even your guru does not know, arising from my union with Urvaśī."
Having heard that, Tumburu, out of anger, then pronounced a curse upon him:
"Your separation from Urvaśī shall occur until you have performed worship of Kṛṣṇa."
Having heard the curse, Purūravas went to Urvaśī and reported his own story, which was as terrible as an untimely stroke of lightning.
Then, it is said, Urvaśī was suddenly snatched away and carried off somewhere by invisible Gandharvas, while the king did not see her.
Then, having understood that fault of the curse, Purūravas went and performed the propitiation of Hari at the hermitage of Badarī.
But Urvaśī, pained by the separation and dwelling in the realm of the Gandharvas,
remained as if dead, as if asleep, as if painted, devoid of consciousness.
It is a marvel that she did not lose her life while clinging to the hope for an end to the curse,
released as she was from nights made long by separation, like a female cakravāka bird.
And Purūravas, through that asceticism, gratified Acyuta;
by his grace, the Gandharvas released Urvaśī to him.
Reunited with that very apsarā upon the termination of her curse,
the king enjoyed divine pleasures even while remaining on the surface of the earth.
When the king had finished speaking, Vāsavadattā, who had heard of Urvaśī’s passion for him, felt ashamed because she herself had endured separation from him.
Seeing the queen thus rebuked by the king with skillful artifice and looking abashed,
Yaugandharāyaṇa then spoke in order to reassure the monarch.
If you have not heard it, O King, then let this story be heard by you:
there is here a city named Timirā, the abode of Śrī.
In that city there was a famous king named Vihitasena;
he had a wife named Tejovatī, who was like an apsaras upon the surface of the earth.
With his sole focus on grasping her neck, that king, greedy for touch,
could not endure even his body being quickly brushed by a mere bodice.
Once, that king was afflicted with the disease of chronic fever;
the physicians prevented him from having union with that queen.
In the heart of that king, who was deprived of the company of his queen,
there arose a disease that could not be cured by the application of medicines.
"Due to fear, grief, or some affliction, the king's illness may suddenly burst forth," the physicians thus said to the minister in private.
He who formerly did not tremble when a great serpent fell upon his back,
nor was he agitated even when a hostile army entered the inner apartments.
"How could fear arise for this courageous king? We have no idea of a means [to counter him]; what can we ministers do against him? (SoKss 3.3.40)
Having reflected thus and consulted together with the queen, those ministers concealed her and told the king, "The queen is dead."
As that king was being tormented by the excessive weight of his grief,

Then, once that king had been delivered from the calamity of disease, the ministers presented to him that great queen, who was like another perfection of happiness.
And that king, though wise, highly valued her as the savior of his life; he did not, however, become angry with her, for she had concealed her true nature.
For that which is the desire for the husband's welfare is the cause of being a queen;

And that which consists solely in reflecting upon the burden of state affairs is "counsel"; that which consists in following the whims of others is the characteristic of a "parasite. (SoK 3.46)
Therefore, this effort has been made by us for you, so that you may conquer the earth, having reconciled with the King of Magadha who stands as your adversary.
Therefore, O King, the Queen has committed no offense against you; rather, she has rendered you a full service by enduring an unbearable separation out of devotion to you.
Upon hearing these words of the prime minister, which were both truthful and principal,
the King of Vatsa considered himself at fault and was pleased.
And he said this: "I know that the earth has already been given to me by the Goddess through Nīti, who was dispatched by you and possesses a beautiful form."
However, out of excessive affection, I have spoken this which is improper;
for how can those whose minds are blinded by passion possess the capacity for discernment?
With such words and many others, the King of Vatsa removed on that very day both his own sense of shame and the queen's flush of embarrassment at once.
On another day, a messenger sent by the Lord of Magadha, bearing a gift of knowledge,
approached the King of Vatsa and announced his message.
"We have already been deceived by these ministers;
therefore, act now in such a way that this world of living beings shall no longer be filled with grief for us."
Having heard this and then having honored him, the Lord of Vatsa dispatched that messenger to the side of Padmāvatī in order to receive a reply.
She too, bowing solely before Vāsavadattā, presented herself to the messenger in her presence; for modesty is indeed the vow of a virtuous wife.
"Under the pretext of [your father's] devotion to another, my daughter, you were led away; and your husband is attached to others.

When the messenger had thus delivered his father’s message, Padmāvatī then said to him: "O good man, let my father and mother be informed of this by my word."
What is the use of grieving? For my noble husband is supremely compassionate toward me, and Queen Vāsavadattā is affectionate toward me like a sister.
Therefore, my dear father, you must not be one who wavers, if my life is as dear to you as your own innate truth which is never to be abandoned.
When Padmāvatī had thus delivered her appropriate reply,
Vāsavadattā then honored that messenger and sent him on his way.
When that messenger had departed, Padmāvatī, remembering her father’s house, remained there for a while as if her mind were distracted by longing.

There is a city named Pāṭaliputra, an ornament of the earth;
and in that city there was a certain great merchant named Dharmagupta.
He had a wife named Candraprabhā, and she once became pregnant;
she then gave birth to a daughter who was beautiful in all her limbs.
As soon as she was born, that girl, illuminating her chamber with her radiance,
spoke clearly and sat up.
Then, seeing the women in the birth-chamber struck with wonder and terror,
Dharmagupta himself came there filled with fear.
Bowing down at that moment in private, he asked that maiden:
"O Blessed One, who are you that have descended into my house?"
She too replied: "I must not be given by you to anyone at all;
I am your auspicious wife staying in your home. Why ask me this, father?"
Thus addressed by her, Dharmagupta, being afraid, kept her hidden in his own house,
while announcing abroad that she was dead.
Then that maiden named Somaprabhā gradually grew up with a human body, yet possessed divine beauty and luster.
Once, however, a merchant’s son named Guhacandra beheld her from atop his palace as she stood there joyfully watching the spring festival.
As if struck instantly by the arrow of love lodged in his heart,
he then fainted as it were, and only with great difficulty did he return home.
There, when persistently questioned by his parents regarding the cause of his ill health, he— distressed by the pangs of love— spoke through the mouth of his companion.
Then his father, named Guhasena, went out of affection to the house of the merchant Dharmagupta to ask for his daughter.
There, Dharmagupta rejected Guhasena, who had made his request seeking a daughter-in-law, saying, "O fool, where would I have a daughter? *Sūtrakṛtāṅga Sūtra* 3.3.76.
Thinking that his daughter had been hidden by him, Guhasena went home; seeing his son overcome by the fever of love, he reflected:
"I shall urge the king in this matter, for he was previously served by me;
he will even cause that daughter to be given to my son, though he is on the verge of death."
Having thus resolved and gone there, that merchant gave him an excellent jewel and made his own request known to the king.
The king, being well-pleased, granted him the assistance of the city governor; together with him, he went to the house of Dharmagupta.
And with his forces, he besieged the house of that Dharmagupta, while [Dharmagupta],
fearing total destruction, besieged his own throat with his vital breaths.
Then Somaprabhā spoke to that Dharmagupta:
"Give me up, father; let there be no calamity for you on my account."
"I must never be placed upon the bed by my husband;
you must ensure that such a verbal agreement is observed by our relatives."
Thus addressed by his daughter,
Dharmagupta agreed to give her away, provided she was told to avoid being placed upon a bed.
And Guhasena, with a suppressed smile, consented to it exactly as requested, thinking:
"Let my son's marriage take place for now."
Then, having taken that bride Somaprabhā after her marriage was performed,
Guhacandra, the son of Guhasena, set out for his own home.
And in the evening, his father said to him: "Son, place this bride upon this bed;
for whose bed indeed shall one's own wife ever be?"
Hearing that, the bride Somaprabhā looked at her father-in-law in anger and brandished her forefinger like the command of Yama.
Upon seeing that finger of his daughter-in-law at that very moment,
the merchant’s life-breaths departed, and fear came upon the others.
When his father had met his death, Guhacandra also thought:
"My wife Mārī has entered my house."
Thereupon, not enjoying the company of his wife who remained in the house,
Guhacandra observed a vow as perilous as the edge of a sword.
Burning within with the pain of that [realization], he became dispassionate toward the abundance of enjoyments;
having undertaken his vow, he fed the Brahmins every day.
And his wife as well, assuming a divine form, always gave sacrificial fees to those twice-born ones after they had eaten, while remaining observant of silence.
Once, an elderly brahmin came alone for a meal and beheld her,
who produced wonder in the world by the perfection of her beauty.
Then, filled with curiosity, the twice-born one asked Guhacandra in private: "Whose daughter is this child of yours? Tell it to me."
Being questioned persistently, Guhacandra, with a heavy heart, related to that brahmin the entire account concerning her.
Having understood that, the best of the twice-born, feeling compassion for him,
then gave him the mantra for the propitiation of Agni for the sake of attaining his desired goal.
Then, as Guhacandra was performing the recitation of that mantra in secret, a man emerged from the midst of a fire.
And that fire, assuming the form of a twice-born, said to him as he bowed at his feet:
"Today I shall eat in your house, and I will stay there for the night."
"Having shown you the truth, I shall accomplish your desire," said that brahmin to Guhacandra, and he went to his house.
There, having eaten like the other brahmins, he attended to his bed for about one watch of the night in the presence of Guhacandra, remaining unwearied.
And at that moment,
Somaprabhā, the wife of Guhacandra, departed from his palace during the night while the people were fast asleep.
At that time, the Brahmin there awakened Guhacandra and said to him,
"Come, go see the account of what has happened to your wife."
Having assumed the form of a bee through his yogic power, he likewise transformed himself and,
emerging from it, showed him his wife as she had departed from the house.
The beautiful woman went a great distance outside the city together with Guhacandra, and the brahmin followed after her as well.
Then, there he beheld a single nyagrodha tree, providing great enjoyment with its beautiful, shady trunk. (SoKss_3,3.106)
And beneath that, he heard the sound of divine music, accompanied by the resonance of lutes and flutes, sweet with the melody of shimmering song.
And at the place where the trunk was, he saw a divine maiden seated upon a great throne, possessing a form exactly like that of his own wife.
She surpassed the moonlight with her own radiance and was fanned by white yak-tail whisks;
she was like the presiding deity of the moon, the treasury of all its loveliness.
Then, having climbed that very tree, Guhacandra saw his own wife seated upon half of her seat.
At that moment, as he gazed upon those two divine maidens who had come together with equal splendor,
the night shone for him as if it possessed three moons.
Then, overcome with curiosity, he reflected for a moment thus:
"Is this a dream, or a delusion? Or fie upon both! (SoKss 3.3.112)
This association with the learned is the cluster of blossoms on the tree of the true path;
this emergence of flowers is for me the precursor to its appropriate fruit.
While he was thus reflecting at his ease, those two divine maidens,
having eaten food suitable for themselves, drank divine liquor.
"Today a certain brahmin of great splendor arrived at our home;
therefore, sister, my mind is apprehensive, and I shall depart."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of that second divine maiden, she,
the wife of Guhacandra, descended from the tree.
Having seen that, Guha, Candra, and the brahmin, who were in the form of bees,
returned to the front of the house and stood there as before during the night.
Then that divine maiden, the wife of Guhacandra,
having arrived here unobserved, entered her own residence.
Then that brahmin spoke freely to Guhacandra:
"You have seen that this wife of yours is divine, not human."
Moreover, you have seen her second sister today;
how can a divine woman desire union with a human?
To achieve this, I give you the mantra to be inscribed on the door;
I also teach you the external reasoning that serves as its reinforcement.
Even a pure fire blazes; what need is there to mention it when joined with a wind?
In the same way, a mantra alone bestows its purpose; how much more so when combined with the proper method!
Having spoken thus and given the mantra to Guhacandra, that best of the twice-born instructed him in that method and vanished at dawn.
Guhacandra also, having written that mantra on the door of his wife's house,
again employed this persuasive stratagem in the evening.
Having gone there, adorned with magnificent ornaments, he engaged in conversation with a certain excellent woman while she was looking on.
As soon as she saw him, that divine maiden, with words unsealed by mantra, called out to him and asked with jealousy, "Who is this?"
"That beautiful woman is devoted to me,
and today I am going to her house"— thus he falsely replied to her.
Then, with her face turned sideways, her eyes averted, and her brows arched,
she looked at him, stopped him with her left hand, and spoke to him.
"Hūṃ! I have understood this; this attire has such a meaning, so do not go there.
What use have you for her? Leave her alone, for I am indeed your wife."
Thus addressed by her, who was agitated by the trembling of horripilation and possessed as if by the malevolent seizure of his mantra-servant, he—
Having entered the bedchamber immediately with her,
even though he was a mortal, he experienced a divine enjoyment that had never been touched by the desires of the mind.
Having thus obtained her, who was full of love and perfected through the power of mantras,
Guhacandra abandoned his celestial state and dwelt with her at his ease.
Thus, by means of meritorious deeds such as the performance of sacrifices and other good works,
women who have fallen from their divine state due to a curse remain in the position of housewives for those of virtuous karma.
For the service of the gods and the twice-born is considered by the wise to be the wish-fulfilling cow;
what indeed cannot be obtained from her? The descriptions of the Sāman and other [Vedic chants] are merely its remnants.
But for you, who were born into a most exalted station among the gods, this misdeed is the sole cause of your downfall, like a high wind that causes flowers to fall to the ground.
Having spoken thus, Vasantaka said again to the princess:
"Moreover, hear this account of what happened to Ahalyā."
In former times there was a great sage named Gautama, who knew the three periods of time;
and his wife was Ahalyā, who surpassed the Apsarases in beauty.
Once, Indra, lusting after her beauty, solicited her in secret;
for the minds of lords, blinded by power, run toward what is improper.
And that foolish woman, longing for a bull, consented to the lord of Śacī;
but the sage Gautama, having perceived this through his supernormal power, arrived there.
And at that very moment, even Indra assumed the form of a cat out of fear;
then Gautama asked Ahalyā, "Who is standing there?"
"Indeed, this cat is standing right here," she replied to her husband with words that were Apabhraṃśa yet crooked, and which adhered to the truth.
Saying, "It is true, this is indeed your cat," the sage laughed and then cast a curse upon her,
which was destined to reach its end through adherence to the truth.
"O you of evil character, may you attain the state of being stone for a long time,
until the sight of Rāghava wandering within the forest."
For you, who are covetous of the finest limb, that thousandfold [of women] shall exist upon your body—
those celestial women whom Viśvakarman shall fashion as Tilottamā.
"Upon seeing her, at that very moment your eyes shall become a thousand," Gautama thus cursed Indra even at that time.
Having uttered the curse as he desired, that sage departed for his ascetic penance;
Ahalyā, too, underwent the dreadful state of being turned into stone.
Then even Indra became possessed of excellent limbs covering all his body;
otherwise, his name would have been "Ill-favored," which would surely have been a cause for humiliation.
Thus, the evil deed of everyone always bears fruit within oneself;
for whatever seed one sows, that is the fruit one receives.
Therefore, those of great magnanimity do not take pleasure in opposing others;
for this is the established rule of the virtuous vow of those who possess the highest nature.
"You two are both goddesses who were elder sisters, fallen due to a curse;
likewise, your hearts are devoted to each other's welfare and free from all dualities."
Having heard this from Vasantaka, both Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī completely abandoned even the slightest trace of jealousy toward one another.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, having made her husband common to both,
was intent on Padmāvatī’s welfare and treated her as dear as herself.
Having learned from the messengers sent by Padmāvatī that her majesty was indeed such as described, the Lord of Magadha was greatly pleased.
Then on another day, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa approached the Lord of Vatsa in the presence of the Queen while the others stood by, and spoke to him.
O Lord, exert yourself now; why is Kauśāmbī not being gone to?
There is no longer any fear even from the King of Magadha, for he has been deceived.
For how could he, having been properly restrained by the *sāman* chant named "The Betrothal of the Daughter," and having entered into a formal agreement,
abandon his daughter, who is dearer to him than life itself?
Truth must be upheld by him and by you, and he was not deceived;
for this was done by me myself, and it brings no suffering to him.
And from our spies I learned that he does not employ his supernatural powers;
for that very reason, we have remained here for these days.
While Yaugandharāyaṇa was speaking thus, having accomplished his task,
an envoy related to the Lord of Magadha arrived there.
At that moment, announced by the doorkeeper, he entered;
having sat down after making his salutation, he addressed the King of Vatsa.
"Delighted by the message sent by Queen Padmāvatī,
the Lord of Magadha has now addressed this to Your Majesty."
What is the use of my knowing everything? I am pleased with you;
therefore, do that for which this undertaking was begun—we are prostrate before you.
The Lord of Vatsa joyfully welcomed these words of the messenger at his own pleasure,
like the blossom of the tree of policy produced by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Then, having summoned Queen Padmāvatī and together with her,
he honored that envoy who had brought the gifts and dismissed him.
Then the messenger of Caṇḍamahāsena also arrived there;
having entered, he bowed to the king and spoke as was appropriate.
"O King, King Caṇḍamahāsena, who understands the true nature of affairs,
having learned of your situation, has joyfully sent this message:"
Your excellence has already been sufficiently described by this much alone:
that Yaugandharāyaṇa is your minister; what is the use of further words?
Blessed indeed is Vāsavadattā, for through her devotion to you she has performed that deed by which our heads have been held high for a long time among the virtuous.
"Padmāvatī is not different from Vāsavadattā for me;
indeed, the two share one heart. Therefore, exert yourselves quickly."
Upon hearing these words of his own father-in-law’s messenger, joy instantly arose in the heart of the Lord of Vatsa;
moreover, an indescribable excellence of affection grew for the queen, and a profound bond of friendship was formed with the preeminent minister.
Then, having dispatched that messenger— who had been received with due hospitality by the two queens— with an impetuous mind,
the king, desiring to set forth his exertion quickly, consulted with his ministers and resolved to go toward Kauśāmbī.
Thus ends the third wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the fourth wave.
Then, on the following day, from that city of Lāvāṇaka, together with his ministers...
Accompanied by his beloved, that King Vatsa set out for Kauśāmbī.
And his forces, filling the surface of the earth with their resounding shouts,
surged forward like the waters of the ocean overflowing its bounds out of season.
An analogy for that king as he proceeded, seated upon his lordly elephant,
would be the sun traveling through the sky together with the mountain of sunrise.
Provided shade by a white parasol,
the king shone as if being attended by the moon, which was pleased that the splendor of the sun had been surpassed.
The neighboring vassal kings hovered all around him— who was radiant with his own splendor and stood above them all— just as the hosts of planets revolve around the Pole Star.
Behind him, two goddesses riding female elephants shone as if they had followed him in person out of love for Śrī and Bhuvā.
The ground along his path was scarred by the tips of the hooves and the nails of the throngs of galloping horses, as if it had been enjoyed by the king himself.
Thus the Lord of Vatsa, being praised by bards as he went along,
reached Kauśāmbī, where festivities were widespread, after a few days.
Covered by crimson banners like silken garments, with windows as her wide-open eyes,
she displayed a pair of full, lofty jars at the gateway like breasts.
With the joyful chatter of the people's clamor and the palaces appearing like smiles,
that city shone at that moment when her husband had returned from his journey.
Accompanied by his two queens, the king entered that city;
and for the women of the citizens, there was an indescribable festival of joy at the sight of him.
The sky was filled by the hundreds of faces of the women situated in the golden palaces,
as if by the armies of the moon— who had been surpassed by the beauty of the queens' faces— come to pay their respects.
And others, standing at the windows with unblinking eyes, gazed upon him and created the illusion that he was a celestial being (sara) descended from his vimāna out of curiosity.
Some, with their eyelashes clinging to the edges of the lattice windows,
seemed to create cages of arrows for the god of love.
The gaze of one woman, eager and blossoming at the sight of the king,
seemed to come toward the side of her ear as if to tell it what she saw, for she could not see it herself.
The breasts of a certain woman who had arrived in haste heaved repeatedly,
as if they wished to emerge from her bodice out of a desire to see him.
The pearls from the necklace of another, broken by her agitation,
shone like droplets of tears of joy falling from her heart.
If one were to commit a sin against this [teaching], then Agni would cast a blinding darkness upon the world, even though he is its illuminator. (SoK 3.4.18)
Thus, having seen Vāsavadattā and remembering those events,
some women, as if filled with longing, spoke regarding the report of her cremation.
"By good fortune, the queen was not put to shame by her co-wife,
who is like a friend," said one female companion to Padmāvatī upon seeing her.
Surely this beauty of these two has never been seen by Hara and Murāri;
otherwise, why would Umā and Śrī bestow such great honor upon them?
Thus spoke others, having seen those two goddesses together,
casting garlands of blue lotuses from their eyes that were blossoming with joy.
Thus the Lord of Vatsa, creating a festival for the eyes of the people,
entered his own palace together with the Queen, having performed the auspicious rites.
At that moment, the splendor of the royal palace was like that of a lotus pond at dawn or of the ocean at the rising of the moon.
In an instant, it was filled with the auspicious offerings from neighboring vassals,
as if signaling the arrival of tributes from all the kings of the earth.
Having honored the assembly of kings and celebrated the festival, the King of Vatsa then entered the inner apartments, just as he had entered the hearts of all the people.
Standing there between the two queens like Smara between Rati and Prīti,
the king spent the remainder of the day in the playful enjoyment of drinking and other diversions.
And on the following day, while that king was seated in his assembly hall in the presence of his ministers, a certain brahmin cried out at the gate.
"O Lord, in this wilderness, an act of sacrilege has been committed against me by sinful cowherds;
my son’s feet have been severed without cause."
Having heard that, the king immediately had two or three cowherds seized and brought before him, and questioned them; they then spoke as follows:
"O King, let us become cowherds and play together in a secluded place. Among us, O King, there shall be one named Devasena who stands as the leader of the cowherds."
And sitting upon a stone seat in a certain part of the forest,
he says to us, "I am your king," and instructs us.
"And among us, no one transgresses his command;
thus, O Lord, does Gopālaka rule the kingdom in the forest."
And today, as the son of this brahmin was traveling along that same path,
he did not offer a salutation to that king of cowherds.
"Go away! Do not speak to us with the command of the king, 'Do not bow'!"—shaking off us who spoke thus, that young brahmin departed even though he had been instructed, smiling as he went.
"Therefore, O boy, we have been commanded by the cowherd king to carry out the punishment of that undisciplined fellow by cutting off his feet."
And having run from there, O Lord, we cut off his foot;
for who like us is capable of transgressing the command of the Lord?
When the cowherds had thus addressed the king,
the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa reflected upon it and spoke to the king in private.
"Surely that place must contain a treasure or the like, for by its power even a cowherd has become so influential; therefore, let us go there."
Thus addressed by the minister, the king placed the cowherds in front and proceeded to that forest region with his army and his retinue.
As the ground was being excavated by the workmen after it had been inspected,
a yakṣa with a form like a mountain rose up from beneath it.
And he said: "O King, take possession of this treasure which has been guarded by me for a long time—a treasure buried by your grandfather."
Having spoken thus to the Lord of Vatsa and having accepted his worship,
the Yakṣa vanished, and a great treasure appeared in the excavation.
Then a highly precious lion-throne made of jewels was obtained;
for at the time of one's rise, a succession of auspicious events indeed comes to pass.
Then, having taken possession of the entire treasure and celebrated a festival,
the Lord of Vatsa, after instructing those cowherds, departed for his own city.
There, with the spreading rays of its rubies and emeralds,
the Lord’s future conquest of the quarters through his majesty seemed to be displayed as if already present.
Jagged with rows of pearls threaded through the openings of silver sprouts,
it seemed to gaze repeatedly at his minister’s astonishment as if laughing.
The people beheld that golden lion-throne brought by the king,
and they rejoiced in the beauty of the sound of the drums that had destroyed all sorrow.
The ministers also celebrated a festival, having determined the victory of the king;
for a good omen appearing at the very outset portends the successful accomplishment of one's purpose.
Then, amidst the expanse of the sky filled with banners like flashes of lightning,
that royal cloud rained down gold upon his followers.
When this day had been spent in celebration, on the following day Yaugandharāyaṇa,
wishing to test the king's mind, spoke to the Lord of Vatsa.
"Having ascended this great lion-throne, which has come down through the lineage of your family and which you have now obtained, may Your Majesty be consecrated."
"Where my great-grandfathers ascended after conquering the earth,
what fame shall be mine if I ascend there without having conquered all the quarters?"
"Having conquered this earth, bounded by the oceans and adorned with vast treasures,
I shall grace the great jeweled lion-throne of my ancestors."
Having spoken thus, the king did not mount at that time;
for among those of noble birth, a natural sense of self-respect indeed persists.
Then Yaugandharāyaṇa, being pleased, said to the king:
"Excellent, O King! Then first make an effort for victory in the eastern direction."
Upon hearing that, the king, in the course of conversation, asked his minister:
"Even though the northern and other directions exist, why do kings travel toward the east first?"
Having heard this, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke to him again:
"O King, although the northern region belongs to Kubera, it is censured due to its contact with barbarians."

The western direction is not worshipped because it is the cause for the setting of the sun and other luminaries; the southern direction is avoided as it is inhabited by wicked rākṣasas; and the northern direction is not relied upon.
The sun rises in the east, Indra presides over the east, and the Ganges flows toward the east; for that reason, the east is praised.
And even among countries situated between the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains,
that which is purified by the waters of the Ganges is considered the most praiseworthy.
Therefore, kings seeking auspiciousness first set out toward the east,
and they also dwell in the land situated along the celestial river.
For even by his ancestors, following the ancient tradition, the quarters were conquered,
and a residence was established at Hastināpura on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
But Śatānīka took refuge in Kauśāmbī out of a sense of its beauty,
seeing that sovereignty depends upon personal prowess and that the land itself is not the cause [of success].
When Yaugandharāyaṇa had spoken thus and ceased,
the king, out of his singular high regard for human effort, addressed him:
Truly, no restriction of place is the cause of sovereignty here;
for in times of prosperity, one's own manly effort is the sole cause for those of noble character.
Even one who is alone and even one who lacks a support attains prosperity if he possesses courage;
have you not heard here the story of that courageous man?
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Vatsa, at the request of his ministers,
related this auspicious and wonderful tale in the presence of the two queens.
There is this city of Ujjayinī, renowned throughout the world;
in it there formerly lived a king named Ādityasena.
Like that of the sun, his chariot— being the abode of majesty through his status as a sole universal monarch— never indeed stumbled anywhere in this world.
When that high umbrella, white as the moon, shone forth in the sky,
the parasols of other kings— whose heat had already subsided— were set aside.
He became the receptacle for all the jewels produced throughout the entire expanse of the earth, just as the ocean is for the waters.
Once, for some reason, that king set out on a journey and,
having reached the bank of the Jāhnavī with his army, took up residence there.
There, a certain wealthy man born in that region named Guṇavarman approached the king, bringing a jewel of a maiden as a gift.
"This maiden, a jewel born even in the three worlds, has been produced in my own house;
she cannot be given to anyone else, for such a lord as you, O God, is her master."
Having thus informed him through the mouth of the doorkeeper,
Guṇavarman then entered and presented his own daughter to the king.
He beheld her, named Tejasvatī, who illuminated the quarters of the sky with her brilliance,
like the flame of a jewel-lamp that serves as the auspicious abode for the God of Love.
Beholding him, the king, composed of affection, embraced by the splendor of his beauty, was as if scorched by the fire of desire; perspiring, he began to dissolve.
And having at that moment accepted her as worthy of the rank of Great Queen,
Guṇavarman, being highly pleased, made her equal to himself.
Then, having married that beloved Tejasvatī, the king,
considering his purpose fulfilled by her, went with her to Ujjayinī.
There, with his gaze fixed solely upon her face, the king became so absorbed that he did not perceive even the most important affairs of state.
As if pinned down by the sweet conversation of Tejasvatī,
his hearing could not be drawn away by the cries of the distressed subjects.
The king, who had long been inside, did not emerge from the inner apartments;
rather, the fever of pain emerged from the hearts of his enemies.
In due time, there was born to that king by Queen Tejasvatī a daughter who was beloved by all, and in his intellect there arose a desire for conquest.
Exceedingly wonderful in form, that maiden made the three worlds seem like blades of grass,
and she inspired joy in him through her splendor and her desire for conquest.
Then, on one occasion, King Ādityasena set out from Ujjayinī to attack a certain neighboring vassal who was arrogant and intent on aggression.
And he made Queen Tejasvatī, mounted upon her female elephant,
a traveling companion who was like the presiding deity of the army.
And he mounted his excellent horse,
which was like a moving mountain— tall, with its girth-band, its auspicious tree-mark, and its flowing stream of sweat rising from pride.
[In the case of the mountain, *śrīvṛkṣa* refers to the *bilva* tree;
however, in the case of the horse, Mallinātha states in his commentary on the *Śiśupālavadha* (5.56) that "the *śrīvṛkṣa* is a particular kind of curl of hair."]
With his feet raised as high as his mouth, he was practicing in the sky the flight of Garuḍa,
which he had previously seen, as if he were a fellow-student of its speed.
Lifting his neck, he gazed with a steady look at the earth as if measuring it, wondering, "Would this speed be sufficient for me?"
Having traveled some distance and reached level ground,
that king urged on his horse, showing it to Tejasvatī.
Struck by that heel-strike of his, like an arrow released from a mechanical device,
he went off somewhere with extreme speed, invisible to the eyes of the world.
Seeing that, while the army was in a state of agitation, horsemen by the thousands pursued him,
yet they did not catch the king who had been carried away by his horse.
Then, fearing an undesirable outcome, the ministers, along with their army,
took the weeping queen and returned to Ujjayinī out of fear.
There, having closed the gates and secured the city walls,
they remained, consoling the subjects while seeking news of the king.
In the meantime, that king was also carried by that horse in an instant to the difficult Vindhya forest, where fierce lions roam.
There, by fate, that horse having come to a halt, the king suddenly became bewildered and distressed, his sense of direction lost within the vast wilderness.

Seeing no other course and descending from his chariot, the king—who understood the nature of horses—bowed down and spoke to that excellent steed: *The king, who knew the breeds of horses, having descended and paid homage, spoke to that noble steed.* (Sūtra-khaṇḍa 3.4.98)
"O Lord, one such as you ought not to commit treachery against his master;
therefore, you alone are my refuge—lead me by an auspicious path."
Having heard that, the horse, who remembered his former births, felt remorse;
and that best of steeds, being like a deity, accepted those words in his mind, thinking, "So be it."
Then, once the queen had mounted, that horse set forth along a path with clear,
cool-watered lakes that dispelled the fatigue of the journey.
And at evening, that best of horses brought the king, who was a hundred yojanas away, into the vicinity of Ujjayinī.
Seeing that even his own seven horses had been surpassed by their speed, the sun,
as it dissolved into the cave of the western mountain, seemed to hide in shame.
Seeing that the gates of Ujjayinī were closed as darkness spread abroad, and that the cremation ground outside was terrifying at that hour, he [proceeded].
The intelligent horse led the king to his dwelling,
a secret Brahmin monastery situated in a secluded spot outside the city, during the night.
And seeing that monastery suitable for passing the night,
King Ādityasena, whose mounts were exhausted, began to enter it.
The Brahmins living there blocked his entrance, saying, "Who is this? Is he a cemetery-keeper or perhaps a thief?"
And they departed, engaged in quarrels, fickle and harsh;
for Vedic scholars are indeed the abode of fear, cruelty, and anger.
While they were thus shouting, a certain virtuous brahmin named Vidūṣaka, the foremost among those possessed of courage, emerged from that monastery.
A youth, possessed of mighty arms, having propitiated the Fire-god through asceticism,
obtained from him a supreme sword that appeared as soon as it was thought of.
Seeing that king of noble appearance who had arrived at night,
the steadfast Vidūṣaka thought, "This must be some god in disguise."
Having dismissed all those other brahmins, he, whose disposition was now contrary [to his former state],
bowed with humility and led the king into the interior of the monastery.
And when the king had rested and was brushed free of the dust of the road by female servants, they prepared for him in an instant food suitable for his own status.
And he removed the saddle from that noble steed of his and,
by providing fodder and other necessities, relieved him of all fatigue.
"I shall protect your body; therefore, sleep in peace, O Lord," he said to the king, who was exhausted and lying upon his prepared bed.
While he was asleep, that twice-born man remained awake at the gate for the entire night,
with a sword of fiery power appearing in his hand as soon as it was thought of.
And in the morning, as soon as that king had awakened,
Vidūṣaka himself, even without being told, made the horse ready.
The king also, having taken leave of him and mounted his horse,
entered Ujjayinī, seen from afar by the people who were overwhelmed with joy.
As soon as he had entered, all the subjects approached him in an instant,
their confused clamor dulled by the joy born of his arrival.
Accompanied by his ministers, the king returned to the royal palace;
and from the heart of Queen Tejasvatī, the great fever departed.
At that moment, the sorrows of the city seemed to be driven away by the rows of silken banners on the festive poles, which were tossed about by the wind.
And the queen held that great festival until the end of day,
until the people of the city, along with the sun, became tawny with vermilion.
On another day, King Ādityasena had Vidūṣaka summoned from that monastery along with all the brahmins.
Having made public the events of the night, he immediately gave a thousand villages to that benefactor, Vidūṣaka.
And the grateful king appointed that brahmin to the office of domestic priest, providing him with an umbrella and a vehicle, while he was watched with curiosity by the people.
Thus, at that very moment, Vidūṣaka became equal to his peers;
for how could a great service rendered to the mighty ever be in vain?
And all those villages which he received from the king, that magnanimous man made them common property,
shared together with the brahmins residing in his monastery.
And he remained there, serving that king and depending upon him,
while enjoying the abundance of the village together with those other brahmins.
As time passed, all those others who desired preeminence—
those brahmins, arrogant with the intoxication of wealth— did not take him into account at all.
Divided into seven factions yet residing in a single place,
they oppressed the villages through mutual conflict, like wicked planets.
Vidūṣaka remained indifferent toward those who were unrestrained;
for among the wise, disdain alone is appropriate toward those of little character.
Once, seeing them engaged in a quarrel,
a certain brahmin named Cakradhara, who was naturally harsh, approached them.
In the assemblies of those who propounded heterodox doctrines, the Brahmin spoke to them constantly—though he was one-eyed, his vision remained undimmed;
though he was hunchbacked, his speech was perfectly clear.
"O deceitful ones, this prosperity was obtained by you all after becoming mendicants;
why then do you destroy villages, being intolerant of one another?"
This is the fault of the jester by whom you were neglected;
therefore, without doubt, you shall soon again wander for alms.
For it is better to have a single leader whose prosperity depends on fate than to have many divided leaders through whom all affairs fall into ruin.
Therefore, by my word, appoint one steadfast leader,
if you have a purpose for a stable prosperity protected by a capable guardian.
Having heard that, when they all desired the leadership for themselves, the Wielder of the Discus reflected upon those fools and spoke to them again: SoKss_3,4.138 //
"In that case, I grant you a period of time.
In this cemetery, three thieves have been impaled upon a stake."
"Whosoever among you, being a man of great courage, should cut off their noses at night and bring them here, he shall be your leader; for a hero indeed deserves to be your master."
Standing nearby, Vidūṣaka said to those brahmins whom Cakradhara had thus addressed, "Do this;
what is the harm?"
Then those brahmins said to him, "We are not capable of doing this;
let whoever is able do it, for we remain bound by our agreement."
Then Vidūṣaka said, "O sir, I shall do this:
I will go to the cemetery at night, cut off their noses, and bring them back."
Then, considering that to be difficult to perform, those fools also said to him:
"If you do this, you shall be our master; this is our agreement."
Having thus explained the agreement, and when night had arrived,
Vidūṣaka took leave of those brahmins and set out for the cremation ground.
And that hero entered his own [palace], which was as terrifying as his own past karma,
taking up as his sole possession a fiery sword that appeared the very moment he thought of it.

In that place where the cries of ḍākinīs have increased and vultures and crows shriek, where the fire of the funeral pyre is fanned by the flames from the mouths of those with faces like meteors; SoKss_3,4.147.
And there in the midst, he saw those men impaled upon stakes, their faces turned upward as if out of fear of having their noses cut off.
And as soon as he reached their vicinity, all three of them,
possessed by the vetālas, struck him with their fists.
Unshaken, he too struck them back with his sword;
for effort that has not been trained does not find a place in the hearts of the steadfast due to fear.
Once they were freed from the transformations of the vetālas, that skillful man cut off their noses,
bound them, and seized them by their garments.
And as he was coming, Vidūṣaka saw a wandering mendicant standing upon a corpse in that cemetery, muttering prayers.
Approaching him out of curiosity to observe his movements and play,
he remained hidden behind that wandering mendicant.
In an instant, the corpse beneath the wandering mendicant let out a shriek;
flames issued from its mouth, and mustard seeds emerged from its navel.
Then, taking those mustard seeds, the wandering mendicant rose up and struck the corpse with the palm of his hand.
Then that corpse, possessed by a frantic vetāla, rose up;
and thereupon the mendicant climbed onto its very shoulder.
Having mounted it, he then suddenly set out from there;
Vidūṣaka also followed him silently and unobserved.
Having traveled not very far, Vidūṣaka beheld a deserted temple, presided over by an image of Kātyāyanī.
[This story imitates the narrative of Aghoraghaṇṭa, Kapālakuṇḍalā, Mādhava, Mālatī, and others found in the fifth act of the *Mālatīmādhava*:
Having descended from the shoulder of the vetāla, the wandering mendicant then entered the inner sanctum,
while the vetāla fell to the ground.
And Vidūṣaka remained there, observing by means of his skillful artifice yet remaining unobserved;
the mendicant, having paid homage to the goddess there, made this request:
"If you are pleased, O Goddess, then grant me my desired boon;
otherwise, I shall gratify you with the sacrifice of my own self."
To that wandering mendicant, who had spoken thus and was proud of his intense practice of mantras,
a voice emerged from within the inner sanctum and spoke these words:
"Bring here the maiden daughter of King Ādityasena and offer her as a sacrifice; then you shall obtain what you desire."
Having heard this, the mendicant went out and, striking him again with his hand,
raised up that vetāla, who let out a hissing roar.
And mounting his shoulder, whose mouth emitted flames of fire,
he flew up into the sky to bring back that princess.
The vidūṣaka, having seen all of that, reflected there:
"How can the princess be killed by him while I am alive?"
"I shall remain right here until that rogue arrives," having reflected thus,
Vidūṣaka remained concealed in that very place.
And that wandering mendicant, having gone by way of the window and entered the inner apartments, found the king’s daughter sleeping there at night.
And Rāhu, consisting of darkness, came through the sky seizing her, just as he seizes the digit of the moon that illuminates the quarters with its luster.
Crying out "O father! O mother!
as the maiden wailed, he descended from the sky right there into the temple of the goddess.
And at that moment, having released the vetāla and taking that jewel of a maiden, he entered the inner sanctum of the goddess.
Just as he was seeking to kill that princess,
Vidūṣaka entered there with his sword drawn.
"O wretch! You seek to strike down a *mālatī* flower with a stone;
you who desire to employ a weapon against this form."
Having spoken thus, Vidūṣaka drew back the hair of that wandering mendicant as he writhed, and severed his head with his sword.
And he comforted that princess, who was overwhelmed by fear and who,
as if shrinking into her own limbs, was only faintly recognizing him.
"How might I lead this princess from here into the king's inner apartments?"— this was what that steadfast man thought at that time.
"O Vidūṣaka, listen to this: as for this ascetic who was killed by you, he had mastered a great Vetāla as well as mustard seeds."
Then, a desire for sovereignty over the earth and for the king’s daughters arose within him;
because of that, he has now been deceived as a fool.
"O hero, take these mustard seeds belonging to him,
by means of which you shall have the power to travel through the sky for this one night tonight."
Thus a voice from the sky spoke to him, who was filled with joy;
for even the gods generally bestow their grace upon such a person.
Then, from the hem of that wandering mendicant’s garment,
he took those mustard seeds in his hand and placed the princess on his lap.
And as he was departing from that place, the palace of the queen,
another voice once more resounded in the sky:
O great hero, you must come here again at the end of the month to the abode of the Goddess; you must not forget this.
Having heard that, Vidūṣaka said, "So be it," and by the immediate grace of the goddess,
he flew up into the sky while carrying the princess.
Having traveled swiftly through the air, he brought the princess into the interior of the inner apartments while she was still comforted, and spoke to her.
"In the morning I shall have no way to travel through the sky, and consequently everyone will see me departing; therefore, I shall go right now."
Thus addressed by him, the young woman, trembling with fear, said to him:
"If you depart, these life-breaths of mine, overcome by terror, will flee."
Therefore, O illustrious one, do not depart; restore my life to me once more.
For the fulfillment of a promise undertaken is indeed the innate vow of the virtuous.
Having heard that, the noble-minded Vidūṣaka reflected:
"Whatever may happen to me, I will not go; lest she give up her life out of fear."
Then, reflecting, "What devotion can I possibly offer to the king? he remained right there in the inner apartments during the night.
Exhausted from physical exertion and staying awake, he gradually fell asleep;
the princess, however, remained sleepless and passed the night in fear.
"Let him rest for a moment," she thought, her mind moist with love;
thus, even at dawn, she did not awaken him as he slept.
Then, having entered, the attendants of the inner apartments beheld him;
and in great agitation, they went at once and informed the king.
The king also dispatched a doorkeeper to investigate the truth;
and the doorkeeper, having gone inside, saw Vidūṣaka there.
And he heard from the mouth of that princess exactly what had occurred;
having gone there, he reported it all in its entirety to the king.
Having heard that from Vidūṣaka, the king, who knew his character,
quickly became as if bewildered, wondering, "What could this be?"
And he had Vidūṣaka summoned from his daughter’s palace,
accompanied by a retinue provided at her request, as her heart was overcome with affection for him.
And the king questioned him as he had approached regarding everything that had occurred;
and that brahmin also related the entire account to him from the very beginning.
And he showed her those mustard seeds, tied within the hem of his garment,
which belonged to the wandering ascetic and were capable of piercing the earth.
Then, having confirmed that to be true, he summoned those brahmins of the monastery,
including all those led by Cakradhara, and questioned them regarding the root cause of the matter.
Having gone to the cremation ground himself and seen those men with their noses cut off,
as well as that lowest of mendicants with his throat slit, [he reflected].
The high-minded king, having gained confidence, was filled with joy toward the skillful Vidūṣaka, who had given back his daughter’s life.
And at that very moment, he gave his own daughter to him;
for what is there that the noble cannot give to those who have rendered them assistance and in whom they find satisfaction?
Surely it was through her love for the lotus that Śrī took hold of the hand of the princess’s son,
by which Vidūṣaka obtained the fortune of this [princess].
Then, with that beloved wife,
he of praiseworthy fame dwelt in the palace of King Ādityasena, treated with royal honors.
Then, after some days had passed, one night, impelled by fate,
that princess said to Vidūṣaka:
"O Lord, do you remember what was said there in the goddess's house at night by a divine voice: 'At the end of the month, you shall come here'?"
"An entire month has passed since you went there, yet you have forgotten that.
When his beloved said this, Vidūṣaka remembered and rejoiced.
"O slender one, you have remembered well, while I, on the other hand, have forgotten," saying this,
he gave her an embrace as a reward.
Then, while she was asleep, he went out from the inner apartments at night;
taking up his sword and composed, he proceeded to the temple of that goddess.
Saying aloud, "O sir, here I am, Vidūṣaka," he heard a voice from within, uttered by someone, saying, "Enter."
Having entered there, he beheld within a divine dwelling,
and inside it, a maiden of celestial form with divine attire.
With the darkness dispelled by her own radiance, she was like a night ablaze with light;
she was the life-restoring herb for Smara, who had been consumed by the fire of Hara’s wrath.
Filled with wonder, asking "What is this?", he was greeted by her, who was herself joyful,
with a welcome full of affection and great respect.
When he was seated and had become confident through the manifestation of her affection,
she spoke to him as he was eager to fully understand her true nature.
"I am a maiden of the Vidyādharas named Bhadrā, born of a noble lineage;
because I roam here at will, I saw you at that time."
And at that moment, my heart drawn by your virtues,
I myself produced that invisible voice for you to return once more.
Today, the applications of my spells, having been sent forth by me to cause delusion,
have restored your memory regarding this task, O princess.
"I remain here for your sake;
therefore, O handsome one, I offer this body of mine to you—take my hand in marriage."
Thus addressed by Bhadrā, the Vidyādharī, the fortunate Vidūṣaka agreed,
saying "So be it," and then married her according to the Gāndharva rite.
Then, having obtained divine enjoyments right there, he remained together with that beloved woman, as if through the supernatural power that is the fruit of his own manly effort.
In the meantime, at the end of the night, that princess woke up;
not seeing her husband, she was suddenly overcome with despair.
Rising up, she went toward her mother with faltering steps,
overwhelmed, her eyes rippling with flowing tears.
And she, both fearful of her own transgression and filled with remorse, said to her mother: "My husband has gone somewhere during the night."
Then, as his mother became agitated out of affection for him, the king gradually learned of this; he too went there and fell into a state of extreme distress.
"When the princess said, 'I know he has gone outside to the cemetery; he has gone to that temple,' the king went there himself."
There, by the power of the Vidyadhara woman’s spell, the king could not find Vidushaka even after searching for him with great care; he had become invisible.
Then, when the queen had departed, a certain wise man approached that princess, who was now hopeless and intent on abandoning her body, and said this:
No fear of misfortune should be entertained, for that husband of yours is indeed alive;
endowed with divine enjoyments, he will come to you before long.
Having heard that, the princess sustained her life,
for it was held back by the desire for his return, which had entered her heart.
Then, while the Vidūṣaka was still staying there,
a certain female friend named Bhadrāyogeśvarī approached his beloved.
Approaching Bhadrā in secret, she then said this to her:
"Friend, the Vidyādharas are angry with you because of your association with humans."
They wish to do you harm; therefore, you must depart from here.
On the far shore of the eastern ocean, there is a city named Kārkoṭaka.
Having passed beyond that, there is the purifying river named Śītodā;
having crossed it, one reaches the great mountain called Udaya, a field of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra).
Go there now, for you cannot be overcome by the Vidyādharas;
and do not harbor anxiety on account of this dear mortal.
Having told him all this, you shall depart,
so that this courageous one will later return to that very place.
Thus addressed by her friend, Bhadrā,
though she was devoted to Vidūṣaka, consented to it, saying "So be it," as she was overcome by fear.
Having spoken thus to him with that stratagem and having given her own ring to Vidūṣaka,
she vanished at the end of the night.
In an instant, Vidūṣaka found himself standing in that same empty temple as before, yet he saw neither Bhadrā nor the palace.
Remembering that expansion of magic and beholding the ring,
Vidūṣaka fell under the sway of despondency and astonishment.
And he reflected on her words, remembering them as if they were a dream:
"She has already departed for Mount Udaya, having announced me to her."
Therefore, I too must go there quickly to attain that;
for if the King were to find me here as seen by the world, he would surely abandon me.
"Therefore, I shall employ a stratagem here so that my purpose may be accomplished.
Having reflected thus, the wise one assumed another form.
Then, wearing tattered clothes and covered in dust, he emerged from the temple of the goddess, crying out, "Alas, O noble lady! Alas, O noble lady!"
And at that moment, seeing him, the people living in that region raised a great clamor,
crying out, "This is Vidūṣaka who has arrived!"
Having learned of this, the king went out in person, saw him in such a state,
and having restrained that man of mad behavior, he was led back to his own palace.
There, whatever was said to him by his servants and kinsmen who were overwhelmed with affection, he gave this reply in every instance: "Alas, my dear lady!"
Although he was massaged with ointments prescribed by physicians, at that very moment he smeared his limbs with abundant dust and ashes.
The food, which had been served with his own hands out of affection by the princess,
was suddenly struck with his foot and cast aside by him.
Thus Vidūṣaka remained there for several days, free from desire,
tearing his own clothes and feigning madness.
This [suffering] is impossible to remedy; why then is it being made so wretched?
One might even lose one's life, and from that would come the sin of killing a Brahmin.
"However, by moving about according to his own will, he may eventually attain well-being.
Having reflected thus, King Ādityasena released him.
Then, moving about at his own will,
the hero Vidūṣaka set out freely the following day toward Bhadrā, carrying the ring with him.
Traveling day by day toward the eastern direction,
he gradually reached the city of Pauṇḍravardhana, which lay on his path.
Having said, "Mother, I shall stay here for one night," he entered the house of a certain elderly Brahmin woman there.
Having accepted his hospitality and rested for a moment,
that Brahmin woman approached him and, with inner sorrow, spoke to him thus:
"O son, this entire house has been given by me to you alone;
therefore, take it, for my life now no longer remains."
"Why do you speak thus? she was asked by him in astonishment;
saying, "Listen, I shall tell you this," she spoke again.
"O son, there is a king named Devasena here in this city;
to him was born a daughter who is an ornament to the earth."

"This daughter was obtained by me with great hardship"— thinking thus, the king, who was exceedingly affectionate toward her, gave that daughter, who had been won through suffering, the name Duḥkhalabdhikā.
When she had reached her youth in due time, this king brought her to his own palace and gave her to the king who was the lord of Kacchapa.
That lord of tortoises entered the bedchamber of his bride at night,
but at that very moment, upon entering, he met his death.
Then, with a dejected mind, the king gave that daughter once more to another monarch; he too met his end in the same manner.
And when other kings, out of fear of that, no longer even desired her,
the king then commanded his own general in this manner:
"From this region, you must bring back one person at a time, from each individual household,
every day— a Brahmin or perhaps a Kshatriya— for the sake of my sons."
"Having brought them here, they should be introduced at night into my daughter's house;
let us see how many perish here and for how long."
And whoever shall cross over here will become her husband;
for the course of destiny, which ordains such wonders, cannot be fathomed.
Thus commanded by the king, the general day after day leads men away from their homes here in turn according to the sequence of their watches.
And thus, although hundreds of men have perished there,
for me, who have performed no merit, this one son remains here.
"Today his turn has arrived to go there for his own ruin;
in his absence, I must enter the fire this morning."
While still alive, with my own hand, I give my entire house to you, who are virtuous,
so that I may never again be a partaker of suffering.
When she had spoken thus, the steadfast Vidūṣaka said to her:
"If this is so, mother, then you must not yield to despondency."
"I shall go there myself today so that your only son may live;
do not harbor such thoughts as 'Why should I have him killed? and let there be no lack of compassion toward me."
"Indeed, through the power of this perfected yoga, there is no fear at all for me who have gone there.
When Vidūṣaka had spoken thus, that Brāhmaṇī said to him:
"In that case, you must be some god who has come here by virtue of my merits.
Therefore, O son, grant us our lives and likewise safety for yourself."
Thus followed by her, he went in the evening to the princess's palace together with a servant appointed by the commander-in-chief.
There he beheld that princess, exultant with the pride of youth,
like a creeper bent down by the weight of its abundant, ungathered blossoms.
Then, when the princess had retired to her bed at night,
he held in his hand the fiery sword that appeared as soon as it was meditated upon.
In that residence of Vāsava, Vidūṣaka remained awake,
thinking, "I shall see who it is that kills men here."
And while the people were fast asleep, he beheld a terrible rākṣasa approaching from the gateway, having quickly flung open the door-panels.
And that Rākṣasa, standing there at the door within his dwelling,
thrust forth an arm like the staff of Yama, which instantly struck down hundreds of men.
And Vidūṣaka, having rushed forward in a rage,
instantly severed that arm of the rākṣasa with a single stroke of his sword.
With his arm severed, that night-stalker fled quickly,
never to return again out of fear of that man’s excellence of character.
Having awakened and seen the fallen arm of the Rākṣasa,
the princess became afraid, filled with joy, and struck with wonder.
And in the morning, King Devasena saw him there at the gate of his daughter’s inner apartments, standing with his arm severed and fallen off.
"From this point forward, no other men shall enter here"—
thus was a very long iron bolt placed by Vidūṣaka.
Then, pleased with that man of divine power,
the king gave his daughter to Vidūṣaka along with magnificent wealth.
Then Vidūṣaka remained there for some days with that beloved woman, as if with the very personification of beauty itself.
And one day, leaving the princess while she was asleep,
he departed from there in haste toward Bhadrā during the night.
And that princess, distressed at not seeing him in the morning,
was comforted by her father with the hope of his return.
Traveling day by day, Vidūṣaka eventually reached the city of Tāmraliptikā, situated not far from the eastern ocean.
There at Cakrā, he formed an alliance with a merchant named Skandadāsa, who was desirous of crossing to the other side of the ocean.
Together with him, he embarked upon a ship laden with no small amount of that man's wealth and set out by way of the ocean.
Then, as that ship reached the middle of the ocean,
it was suddenly obstructed, as if held fast by something.
When that [ship] did not move even though the ocean was filled with jewels,
then the distressed merchant Skandhadāsa spoke this:
"To whoever releases this carriage of mine that is stuck,
I shall give half of my own wealth and my daughter."
Upon hearing that, the resolute-minded Vidūṣaka spoke thus:
"I shall descend here and search within the waters of the ocean."
"In an instant, I shall release this ship of yours that is bound;
you too must hold on, binding me with ropes of cord."
And when the ship has been set free, at that very moment,
I must be lifted up from the midst of the waters by you using supporting ropes.
When the merchant had assented to those words with "So be it," the helmsmen bound him to the two side-posts with ropes.
Bound by that, Vidūṣaka descended into the ocean;
for a person of courage never desponds when the right moment has arrived.
Having meditated upon and taken into his hand a sword produced by the power of fire,
that hero entered beneath the ship into the midst of the waters.
And there he beheld a man of massive body sleeping;
he saw that the ship was caught fast upon his shank.
At that very moment, he cut off his shank with a sword,
and the ship, released from its obstruction, moved forward immediately.
Upon seeing that, the wicked merchant,
out of greed for the promised wealth, cut those ropes of Vidūṣaka.
And by means of that well-constructed, swift-moving vessel,
he reached the far shore of the ocean as if it were the shore of his own great greed.
The wit, too, his support of rope severed, found himself in the midst of the water;
having emerged and seen that state of affairs, the resolute man reflected for a moment:
What is this that has been done by that merchant, or rather, what can be said?
Ingrates, blinded by greed for wealth, are incapable of even looking upon a favor received.
Therefore, this is precisely the time for absolute composure;
for even a minor calamity is not overcome by a collapse of spirit.
Having reflected thus at that time, he climbed onto that thigh which had been pressed down upon the man who was sleeping beneath the water.
With her, he crossed the ocean as if by a boat, with water scattered by his hands;
for destiny itself provides assistance to those endowed with courage.
To that powerful one, who had come for the sake of Rāma like Mārutī to the far shore of the ocean,
a voice from the sky spoke thus:
"Excellent, excellent! O Vidūṣaka, what other being is there as virtuous as you?
I am pleased by this fortitude of yours; therefore, listen to this."
"You have now reached this realm of the Nagnas;
furthermore, from here you will reach the city named Kārkoṭaka in seven days."
Then, having regained your fortitude, you shall go and quickly attain what you desire;
for I was formerly the lord of the gods, the consumer of your sacrificial offerings to the gods and ancestors.
"And by my boon, hunger and thirst shall no longer afflict you from this time forth; therefore, go with confidence toward your accomplishment. Having said this, the voice fell silent.
And Vidūṣaka, having heard that, was delighted by the fire of his affection;
he set out and on the seventh day reached the city of Kārkoṭaka.
And there he entered a certain monastery presided over by noble ones—
by various twice-born men from many lands who were fond of receiving guests.
It was built by the illustrious local king, Āryavarman;
it was prosperous and endowed with delightful temples made entirely of gold.
There, after all had extended hospitality to that single guest, a certain brahmin led him home and attended to him with baths, meals, and garments.
"Whether he be a Brahmin or even a Kṣatriya, whoever desires to marry the king’s daughter shall stay in her house tonight."
Having heard that with its underlying cause and suspecting it at that moment, he,
who was fond of daring deeds, desired to go at once to the residence of the king’s daughter.
