Those brahmins of the hermitage said to him, "O Brahmin, do not act rashly!
That is not the prince's palace; it is the wide-open mouth of Death."
For whoever enters there at night does not live;
many such reckless men have thus met their destruction here.
Although addressed thus by those brahmins, Vidūṣaka did not accept their words and went to the royal palace along with their servants.
There, having been personally seen and welcomed by King Āryavarman,
he entered his son’s dwelling at night like the sun entering the fire.
And he beheld that princess, who was enamored with him because of his appearance,
looking at him with tearful eyes, distressed by the sorrow of her despair.
And there he remained awake throughout the night, watching over them,
holding in his hand a sword of fire that appeared as soon as it was thought of.
And suddenly he saw at the door a most terrible Rākṣasa, who,
because his right arm had been severed, was stretching out his other arm.
Seeing him, he thought: "Alas, this is that very night-stalker whose arm was severed by me in the city of Pauṇḍravardhana."
Therefore, today I shall not strike him again on the arm, for he might flee as before; thus, I shall properly slay him.
Having reflected thus, Vidūṣaka rushed forward, seized the rākṣasa by the hair, and began to sever his head.
At that moment, the Rākṣasa, trembling with fear, said to him:
"Do not kill me! You are a man of great virtue; therefore, show me mercy."
"What is your name, who is she, and what is this activity of yours?"—
thus questioned by that hero, the rākṣasa released him and spoke again.
"These two daughters are mine, named Yamadaṃṣṭrā;
one is here, and the other resides in Pauṇḍravardhana."
Since the king’s son must be protected from association with unheroic men,
such was the grace of Śaṅkara’s command bestowed upon me.
"In that regard, first my arm was severed by one at Pauṇḍravardhana;
and today I have been conquered here by you. Thus, this [hostility] of mine has come to an end."
Having heard that, Vidūṣaka laughed and replied to him:
"That very arm was cut off by me there in Pauṇḍravardhana."
The Rākṣasa also said: "In that case, you are a portion of a god, not a mere human;
I believe it was for your sake alone that Śiva’s command and favor were bestowed upon me."
Therefore, you are now my friend; whenever you remember me, I shall be present for your success, even in times of distress.
Thus that rākṣasa, having won over Vidūṣaka with friendliness,
vanished while Yamadaṃṣṭra’s words were still being welcomed by him.
The Vidūṣaka also, his valor joyfully acclaimed by the princess, spent that night there in great delight.
In the morning, having learned the news, the king was pleased and gave that daughter to him along with great riches— as if giving him the very banner of heroism.
Vidūṣaka remained there with her for several nights,
as she did not leave even a single step behind him, bound to him by his virtues like Lakṣmī herself.
And once, at night, he departed from there of his own accord, longing for his beloved;
for who, having tasted divine nectar, would take pleasure in any other flavor?
Having departed from the city, he called that rākṣasa to mind; as soon as he was remembered, the rākṣasa arrived, and [the prince], having performed a prostration, spoke to him.
"Friend, I must go to the mountain of sunrise, a field of accomplishment, for the sake of the Vidyādharī Bhadrā; therefore, lead me there."
When he had spoken thus, he mounted upon the shoulder of the *rākṣasa* and traveled sixty *yojanas* of difficult terrain during that night.
And at dawn, having crossed the Śītodā river, which is impassable for humans,
he then effortlessly reached the vicinity of the Mountain of Sunrise (Udayādri).
"This is that glorious mountain called Udaya situated before you;
and above this, in the abode of the Siddhas, there is no path for me to go."
Having spoken thus, when that Rākṣasa had received permission and vanished,
Vidūṣaka beheld there a single beautiful oblong pond.
And he sat down on its bank, which seemed to offer a welcome with the humming of wandering bees, while it possessed the beauty of a blooming lotus for its face.
There he saw a very extensive trail of footprints, as if belonging to women,
which seemed to say, "This is the path for the arrival of your beloved."
"This mountain is impassable for mortals; therefore, it is better that I remain right here for a moment and see whose footprints this trail is."
While he was thinking thus, many beautiful women arrived there for the sake of water, carrying golden jars.
And he asked those women, who were carrying jars filled with water, with words tender with affection: "To whom is this water being carried? (SoKss 3,4.357)
"O auspicious one, a Cid-yādharī named Bhadrā dwells here on this mountain;
this is her bathing water," they said to him.
It is truly marvelous how the Creator, as if delighted, brings together the necessary conditions for those wise ones who have undertaken such magnificent deeds.
Then, one woman among them suddenly spoke to him:
"O fortunate one, let the jar be lifted onto my shoulder. (SoKss 3.4.360)
Saying "So be it," when the jar had been lifted by her onto his shoulder, that wise man placed the jeweled ring previously given by Bhadrā inside it.
And he sat down right there once more upon the bank of the pond;
those women, taking that water with them, went to the house of Bhadrā.
There, as they were pouring bathing water over Bhadrā,
the ring fell into her lap.
Having seen that and recognized it, Bhadrā asked those friends:
"Has any unprecedented man been seen by you here?"
"We saw a certain young man on the bank of the pond;
by him this jar was lifted up," they replied.
Then Bhadrā said: "Go quickly and bring him here who has prepared his bath and ornaments; for he, my husband, has arrived."
When Bhadrā had spoken thus, she went and reported the matter as it truly was;
and Vidūṣaka, having bathed, was brought there by her companions.
And having arrived there, he beheld Bhadrā after a long time,
standing at the entrance of the path like the manifest glory of the ripened fruit of the tree of his own goodness.
She too, seeing him, rose up and, as if offering him the guest-offering (*argha*) with the spray of her tears of joy,
bound the garland of her vine-like arms around his neck.
As the two of them embraced one another, their long-accumulated affection seemed to flow forth like sweat due to the intensity of their pressing embrace.
Then, as they sat down, insatiable in gazing at one another,
both bore an intensity of longing that seemed to have increased a hundredfold.
When Bhadrā asked him, "How have you come to this land?", Vidūṣaka then spoke these words.
Having taken hold of [you] as my object, I have felt affection and have risked many dangers to my life; I have come here for this, O beautiful one—what more need I say?
Having heard that and seeing his disregard for his own life, Bhadrā, her affection having reached its peak, spoke to him with joy: SoKss_3,4.374 //
"Noble son, I have no need for friends nor for supernatural powers;
you are my life, purchased by your virtues, and I am your slave, O Lord."
Then the Vidūṣaka said: "In that case, come with me, my dear;
leaving behind this divine enjoyment, let us dwell in Ujjayinī."
"So be it," Bhadrā immediately accepted those words;
and her magical sciences, fallen away due to that resolve, she cast off like blades of grass.
Then Vidūṣaka rested there for that night with her,
having been provided with every hospitality by her friend Yogeśvarī.
And in the morning, having descended from the Mountain of Sunrise together with Bhadrā,
that virtuous man again called to mind the Rākṣasa Yamadaṃṣṭra.
Having spoken of his own route to be traveled once she had arrived as soon as he was thought of,
he placed Bhadrā before him and mounted upon her back.
She too endured that mounting upon the shoulder of an exceedingly fierce rākṣasa;
for what will women not do when they are subject to passion?
Then, mounted upon the Rākṣasa and accompanied by his beloved,
Vidūṣaka set out and once again reached that city of Kārkoṭaka.
There, while being watched by the people with terror at the sight of the Rākṣasa,
he saw King Āryavarmā and sought out his own wife.
Having accepted that daughter given by him, whom he had won by the strength of his arms,
he set out from that city mounted upon the Rākṣasa just as before.
Having gone to the shore of the ocean, he found that wicked merchant by whom his ropes had previously been cut when he was cast into the sea.
And he carried off that merchant’s daughter along with his wealth—
wealth which had previously been acquired as a stake for releasing a ship upon the ocean.
He considered the mere seizure of that wicked man's wealth to be his execution;
for among the miserly in this city, their lives generally consist of nothing but the accumulation of riches.
Then, having mounted the chariot of the rākṣasa and brought that merchant’s daughter,
he flew up into the sky together with the two princesses, Bhadrā and Rājaputrī.
Displaying his own splendor to his beloveds, he crossed the ocean by way of the sky, as if crossing over his own prowess characterized by the exuberance of a radiant being.
And he reached that city of Pauṇḍravardhana once again;
beheld by everyone with astonishment, he had made the rākṣasa his mount.
There he took as his wife the daughter of King Devasena, who had long yearned for him, won by his conquest of the Rākṣasa.
Although his father tried to restrain him, he, longing for his own country,
took her as well and set out from there toward Ujjayinī.
And before long, through the power of the rākṣasa, he reached that city, which was like his own native land come out to meet him, bringing the bliss of seeing his homeland.
Then he stood upon the shoulder of that giant-bodied rākṣasa,
whose own presence was made manifest by the radiance of the circle of wives resting upon his shoulder.
There, upon the mountain peak where the medicinal herbs were glowing, Vidūṣaka was seen by the people like the moon rising over the eastern mountain.
Then, perceiving that the people were struck with wonder and terror,
his father-in-law King Ādityasena emerged from the city at that time.
But Vidūṣaka, seeing him, quickly descended from the Rākṣasa, bowed to the king, and approached him; the king also greeted him with joy.
Having lowered all those wives of his from his shoulders,
Vidūṣaka then released the Rākṣasa so that he might go wherever he pleased.
When that *rākṣasa* had departed,
he, together with his wife and his father-in-law the king, entered the royal palace.
There, having approached his first wife, the daughter of that king—
who had been overcome by long-standing longing— he gladdened her.
"How were these wives obtained by you, and who is this Rākṣasa?"—
thus questioned by the king, he related all of that to him there.
Then, pleased by his power and knowing what ought to be done, that king gave half of his own kingdom to his son-in-law.
And at that very moment, having become a brahmin, Vidūṣaka became a king,
with a white parasol raised high and fanned on both sides by chowries.
And then, resounding with the blare of auspicious musical instruments and filled with the cries of those released from joy, the city of Ujjayinī shone forth.
Thus, having attained the splendor of sovereignty and having gradually conquered the entire earth, his feet honored by all kings, he—
accompanied by Bhadra and together with those wives who were free from envy and full of contentment— enjoyed himself for a long time with his own beloveds.
Thus, when destiny is favorable, for the steadfast,
their very own nature becomes like a mantra that has achieved great joy through its power to irresistibly attract prosperity.
Having thus heard this wonderful tale of marvelous meaning from the mouth of the King of Vatsa,
all his ministers seated at his side, as well as his two queens, attained the highest joy.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Lāvāṇaka* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fifth Wave.
Then, there, Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke to the Lord of Vatsa:
O King, both the favor of destiny and human effort are present in you.
We too have exerted some effort here on the path of policy;
therefore, swiftly achieve the victory of the quarters as you have intended.
When this had been said by the chief minister, the King, the Lord of Vatsa, replied:
"Let it be so; however, the accomplishment of auspicious goals is always beset with many obstacles."
Therefore, for that purpose, I propitiate Śambhu through austerity;
for without his grace, how can there be the attainment of desired goals?
Having heard that, the ministers also approved of his asceticism,
just as the lords of the monkeys did when Rāma was intent on building a bridge across the ocean.
Then Śiva appeared to the king in a dream as he remained engaged in asceticism with his two queens and his ministers, having fasted for three nights.
"I am pleased with you; therefore, arise, for you shall attain victory without obstacle and, before long, a son who is the sovereign lord of all the Vidyādharas."
Then the king, his fatigue removed by her grace, became aware [of her],
like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight when its nourishment has been restored by the rays of the sun.
And in the morning, he gladdened his ministers with that dream,
as well as the two queens, who were tender as flowers and exhausted by their vows and fasts.
For those two, who were already satiated by the description of that dream— which was like nectar for the ears—
a course of sweet medicines arose solely for the sake of their physical restoration.
Through his ascetic power, that king attained an influence equal to that of his ancestors;
and his two wives acquired the holy fame of devoted wives.
When the citizens were occupied with the festival and the breaking of the vow had been performed,
on the following day Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke thus to the king:
Blessed are you, for the Lord Hara is thus pleased with you;
therefore, having now conquered your enemies, enjoy the prosperity won by your own arms.
For she was born of her own dharma and remained steadfast in the lineage of kings;
indeed, there is no destruction of wealth acquired through one's own dharma.
And likewise, a treasure long buried in the earth, accumulated by your ancestors, has been lost and then found by you; moreover, hear this story regarding it.
In the city of Pāṭaliputra,
there was once a certain merchant’s son named Devadāsa, born into a family of great wealth.
And his wife was the daughter of a certain wealthy merchant from the city of Pauṇḍravardhana, whom he had married.
When his father had passed away, Devadāsa, gradually overcome by misfortune,
lost all his wealth at gambling.
Then his wife, afflicted by the suffering of grief and poverty,
was taken by her own father to his home in Pauṇḍravardhana.
Gradually, Devadāsa too, distressed by his misfortune yet desiring to remain in his own work and seeking payment, went to ask his father-in-law for it.
Having reached that city of Pauṇḍravardhana at the time of twilight,
he beheld it covered in dust and its people stripped of clothing, and reflected within himself:
"How can I enter my father-in-law's house in such a state?
For a man of honor, death is better than wretchedness before one's own kin."
Having reflected thus, he went to the marketplace and stood somewhere outside the shop at night, shrinking like a lotus during that time.
And in an instant, he beheld a certain young merchant entering that shop, having thrown open its door.
And in another moment, he saw a certain woman approaching that very spot with silent steps and quickly entering within.
And as long as he cast his gaze within that space where the lamp was burning,
he recognized her at once as his very own wife.
Then, seeing his wife— who had gone to another man— standing before him with the door bolted shut, Devadāsa, struck by the thunderbolt of grief, reflected:
By one devoid of wealth, even the body is lost; what then need be said of women?
Their fickleness is as natural as that of lightning flashes.
This, then, is the calamity for men who fall into the ocean of misfortune;
this is the fate of an independent woman remaining in her father’s house.
Reflecting thus, he remained outside and heard, as it were, the conversation of his wife, who was enjoying the confidence of the end of their dalliance.
Having approached, she placed Karṇa at the door; at that very moment, that wicked woman spoke thus to her paramour, the merchant, in private:
Listen, for today I shall tell you this secret, O devoted one:
in former times, my husband’s great-grandfather was named Vīravarman.
In the courtyard of his own house, he placed four jars filled with gold,
hidden underground at the four corners.
Then he made that known to his own wife;
and at the time of her death, that wife spoke it to her daughter-in-law.
"She [told it] to her daughter-in-law, and my mother-in-law told it to me;
such is the tradition concerning the succession of mothers-in-law in my husband's family."
And I did not describe that to my husband, even though he was poor;
for he was addicted to gambling and detestable, whereas you are most dear to me.
Therefore, go there and purchase that house from my husband with wealth; having obtained it and acquired the gold, return here and enjoy me happily.
Thus addressed by that crafty woman, the merchant, her paramour,
was delighted with her, imagining he had found a treasure without effort.
Devadāsa too, having gone outside, felt at that moment as if his hope for wealth were pinned within his heart by those word-thorns of his wicked wife.
Then he departed immediately for the city of Pāṭaliputra;
having reached his own home and obtained the treasure, he took possession of it.
Then that merchant, whose secret lover was his wife,
arrived at that very place under the pretext of trade, greedy for treasure.
And he purchased that house from Devadāsa;
Devadāsa, moreover, gave it to him for a higher price.
Then, having established a household by means of a stratagem at his father-in-law’s house,
that Devadāsa quickly brought back his wife.
When this had been done, that deceitful merchant, who was lusting after his wife,
not having obtained the treasure, approached Devadāsa and said to him:
"This house of yours is dilapidated; it truly does not please me.
Therefore, give me its proper price and take back your own house."
Thus the merchant spoke, and Devadāsa likewise replied;
both, intent on their dispute, went before the king.
There, Devadāsa recounted before the king the entire account of his wife, which was as unbearable as the poison lodged in his chest.
Then, having summoned the merchant's wife and investigated the truth of the matter, the king punished that adulterer by confiscating all his property.
Devadāsa, having made that woman with the severed nose his wife,
married another and remained there happily, having obtained a treasure.
Thus, wealth acquired through righteousness remains steadfast and does not perish;
but other wealth is as fleeting as a drop of frost or a spray of water.
Therefore, a man should strive to acquire wealth through righteous means;
a king, however, must do so all the more, since wealth is the very root of the tree of sovereignty.
Therefore, having duly honored the circle of ministers for the sake of success,
O Lord, undertake the conquest of the quarters to obtain prosperity preeminent in Dharma.
Through the successive involvement with their fathers-in-law and kinsmen,
many kings do not act perversely, and they meet together.
But this lord of the earth in Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta is your constant enemy; therefore, conquer him first.
When that [eastern quarter] is conquered, you shall achieve victory over all directions by proceeding from east to west;
indeed, raise high the fame of Pāṇḍu, radiant as a white water-lily.
Thus addressed by the chief minister, "So be it," the King of Vatsa, intent on victory, ordered the commencement of the expedition among his subjects.
And that king, for the sake of honoring his brother-in-law who was following him, gave the kingdom of the Vaideha country to Gopālaka.
Furthermore, having honored him, he bestowed the region of Cedi upon Siṃhavarman, the brother of Padmāvatī,
who had arrived together with his armies.
And that Lord summoned Pulindaka, the king of the Bhillas and his friend, who filled the quarters with his forces like the rainy season with clouds.
And there was a great stir for the expedition in the kingdom of that mighty lord,
while a strange agitation arose in the hearts of his enemies.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa dispatched spies ahead toward Vārāṇasī to ascertain the activities of King Brahmadatta.
Then, on an auspicious day, accompanied by omens foretelling victory,
the Lord of Vatsa joyfully set out toward the east toward Brahmadatta, just as before.
Mounted upon his lofty elephant of victory, over which a high umbrella was raised,
he was like a rutting lion ascending a mountain with a single tree in full bloom.
Receiving great joy from the autumn season, which was like a messenger of accomplishment that had arrived,
he saw a path that was exceedingly easy to traverse, with its shallow streams of water.
Filling the surface of the earth with armies accompanied by many sounds,
he created the confusion of an unseasonable rain falling from a cloudless sky.
And then, the quarters of the sky, filled with the echoes of the army's roar,
seemed to announce to one another the fear of its arrival.
And his horses, equipped with golden trappings and possessing the brilliance of the sun,
moved along as if followed by the fire that had been gratified by the lustration ceremony.
And his elephants shone on the road, their white ear-fans flickering,
with streams of ichor flowing red from the vermilion upon their temples.
Marked by autumn clouds as white as ash and possessing waterfalls of liquid minerals,
they were sent forth on their journey like sons dispatched by the mountains out of fear.
"This king cannot endure the spreading splendor of others"—
as if for this reason, the dust of his army concealed the brilliance of the sun.
And two goddesses followed the king on the path, step by step— Fame and the Glory of Victory— as if drawn by his quality of statesmanship.
"Bow down or flee!"—
thus it seemed as if he were speaking to his enemies by means of the silken banners of his army, tossed and scattered by the wind.
Thus he traveled through the various regions, beholding the blossoming white lotuses that appeared like the hoods of Śeṣa,
tossed upward in terror at the crushing of the earth.
In the meantime, those spies, who had undertaken the vow of the Kāpālikas and were dispatched by Yaugandharāyaṇa, reached the city of Vārāṇasī.
Among them, one who was skilled in deception displayed his own knowledge and assumed the role of a teacher;
the others became his disciples.
Those disciples proclaimed that teacher— a mendicant wandering here and there— to be a "false guru" who claimed to know the three times.
Whatever that wise man spoke regarding future events, such as fires and other calamities, to those who questioned him, his disciples kept it secret; by that means, he became renowned.
And he won over a certain lay follower, a prince who was beloved by the king there and delighted in inferior supernatural attainments.
Through that very person, he became a knower of the secrets of King Brahmadatta when the latter inquired about them upon the arrival of the war with the Lord of Vatsa.
Then, as Vatsarāja was approaching on the road, Brahmadatta’s minister, Yogakaraṇḍaka, devised various stratagems against him.
He defiled the path at every turn with mixtures of poisonous substances,
and he poisoned the trees, flowering creepers, waters, and grasses.
He placed poison-maidens among his army disguised as courtesans,
and he dispatched men to strike during the nights by means of treachery.
Having understood that, the spy, bearing the marks of a sage,
then quickly reported it to Yaugandharāyaṇa through the mouths of his own companions.
Yaugandharāyaṇa, having understood this, purified along the entire path the grass, water, and other provisions at every step by means of counter-measures.
He prohibited the union with an unprecedented woman within the camp,
and together with Rumaṇvat, he put those assassins to death once they were captured.
Having understood that, Brahmadatta’s illusions being destroyed, he considered the Lord of Vatsa— whose quarters were filled with his army— to be truly invincible.
Having consulted together and dispatched a messenger, he then approached the Lord of Vatsa in person, with his hands joined in reverence upon his head.
Vatsarāja, for his part, honored with affection the king who had arrived bringing gifts; for the brave are fond of those who bow before them.
Thus, having conquered him, he pacified those to the east and humbled the mild ones, while uprooting the hard ones—like the wind among trees. (SoKss 3.5.89)
And the powerful one reached the eastern ocean, which was agitated by rolling waves and seemed to tremble with fear at his conquest of Vaṅga.
And on the edge of that shore, he erected a pillar of victory,
which rose up like the King of the Nāgas emerging to beg for protection from the underworld.
Then, as the Kalingas advanced and offered their hands for him to grasp, he ascended Mount Mahendra; it was the glory of that illustrious king.

Having conquered the forest of rival kings with elephants that seemed as if they had come from the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, fearing an assault by Mahendra, he proceeded toward the southern direction.
There, on that wheel, he [saw] his enemies— pale and devoid of substance, like clouds resting upon mountains in the autumn season when they have ceased thundering.
As the Kāverī was being overstepped by that cause of great commotion,
both she and the fame of the Lord of the Colas simultaneously fell into turbidity.
He could not tolerate the lack of elevation on the heads of the Muralas,
even when their hands were striking his beloved’s breasts.

The elephants drank the waters of the Godāvarī, which had been divided into seven streams by him; under the pretext of intoxication, they seemed to release those very waters back again in seven separate flows.
Then, having crossed the Revā, that Lord of Vatsa went to Ujjayinī;
and he entered it, preceded by Caṇḍamahāsena.

And there he became the very target of the side-long glances of the Mālava women, which were characterized by a lack of restraint due to the beauty of their loosened flower-garlands and disheveled braids.
And there he remained, at ease and honored by his father-in-law,
forgetting even those desired pleasures born of his own country.
And Vāsavadattā remained by her father’s side,
remembering her childhood, appearing as if despondent even in the midst of happiness.
And King Caṇḍamahāsena rejoiced upon her arrival just as much with Padmāvatī as he had with his own daughter.
And after resting for some nights, the King of Vatsa, being pleased,
then set out toward the western direction accompanied by his fathers-in-law's armies.
Surely his sword-blade was the smoke from the fire of his majesty,
for it caused the eyes of the Lāṭa women to become clouded with tears.
"May he not uproot me while churning the ocean!"—
as if thinking thus, Mount Mandara trembled when its forests were shaken by those elephants.
Truly, he was some extraordinary being of splendor, unlike the sun and other luminaries;
though he had already reached his zenith, he attained a further rising in the west.
Then he set out toward the quarter adorned by Kubera’s tilaka-mark, which betokens union with Alakā and is made beautiful by the laughter of Kailāsa.
Having brought the King of Sindhu under his control, Rāghava, pursued by the monkey armies,
destroyed the Mlecchas as if they were Rākṣasas.
The throngs of Turuṣka horses, like the waves of an agitated ocean,
were shattered into fragments upon the forests on the shore by the herds of his lordly elephants.
The illustrious Supreme Person,
having seized his sword, severed the head of the King of the Persians, just as Rāhu seizes the head of the moon.
[In this context, Puruṣottama is Viṣṇu;
in his case, there is the discus, meaning he has taken the discus in his hand.]
His fame, which caused the destruction of the Hūṇas and made the faces of all directions resound, spread across the Himalayas like a second Gaṅgā.
While his armies were roaring, the enemies stood paralyzed with fear;
their own cries were heard only in the mountain caves, turned back toward them.
That even the Lord of Kāmarūpa, bowing with his head uncovered by a parasol,
attained a state of lusterlessness— that was no wonder at all.
Then the emperor set forth, accompanied by the elephants given by him,
as if by moving mountains offered up like the trunks of elephants.
Having thus conquered the earth, the Lord of Vatsa, together with his retinue,
reached the city of the King of Magadha, the father of Padmāvatī.
And when he had arrived there together with his two queens, the Lord of Magadha became filled with joy, like the god of love in the moonlight of a night bright with moonbeams.
And he regarded Vāsavadattā— who had previously remained unrecognized and had now become manifest again— as a vessel for even greater courtesy.
Then, honored by that King of Magadha together with his city, and followed by the hearts of all the people who had come out of affection,
the victorious Vatsarāja— having swallowed the surface of the earth with the weight of his army— departed for his own domain of Lāvāṇaka.
Thus ends the fifth wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Sixth Wave:
Then he remained there in Lāvāṇaka for the rest of his army.
Rahasa said to King Vatsa and Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"By means of your wisdom, all the rulers on earth have been conquered by me;
having been won over through strategic means, they do not at all deviate from my service."
"This lord of Vārāṇasī, Brahmadatta, is evil-minded;
I know he is unfaithful alone. What trust can there be in the crooked?"
When the Lord of Vatsa had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa said:
"O King, Brahmadatta will not transgress against you again."
But he, though previously oppressive, has now been thoroughly subdued and highly honored by you;
for what conscious person would do evil to one of virtuous conduct?
Or, if one were to perform it, that very same evil would accrue to oneself;
listen, therefore, to a story in this regard which I shall relate to you.
In ancient times, in the land of Padma, there was a certain eminent brahmin named Agnidatta, who was renowned and enjoyed a royal grant of land bestowed by the king.
To him was born an eldest son named Somadatta,
and a second son was born known by the name Vaiśvānaradatta.
Of those two, the first was a fool, handsome in appearance but ill-mannered;
the other was learned, well-behaved, and fond of study.
Once both of them were married and their father had passed away,
they divided his land-grants and other property, each taking half.
Among them, the youngest was honored by the king,
while the eldest, Somadatta, was fickle and performed the duties of a warrior.

Once, seeing Somadatta engaged in conversation with Śūdras, a certain twice-born friend of his father spoke to him thus: SoKss_3,6.12: "Once, seeing Somadatta engaged in conversation with Śūdras, a certain twice-born friend of his father spoke to him thus:"
Having become the son of Agnidatta, you act like a fool, O Śūdra;
seeing your own younger brother honored by kings, you feel no shame.
Hearing that, Somadatta then became enraged; casting aside all decorum, he rushed at the brahmin and struck him with a kick.
Thereupon, that brahmin, having immediately summoned other twice-born men as witnesses, went in a rage caused by the blow to the king's feet and addressed him thus: SoKss_3,6.15.
The king also dispatched soldiers to seize Somadatta;
but having gone out, they were struck down by his friends, who held weapons in their hands.
Then, having dispatched even more troops, the king,
blinded by rage, ordered the impalement on a stake of Somadatta, who was thus held in check.
Then, as he was being placed upon the stake, that brahmin suddenly fell to the earth as if thrown down by someone.
Fortune itself protects future welfare,
since it was through fortune that the executioners became blind as they prepared to impale him.
At that moment, having heard the account, the king was pleased;
at the request of his younger brother, he released him from execution.
Then, having escaped from death, Somadatta, along with his household,
desired to go to another land because of the king’s insult.
And when his assembled kinsmen did not wish for him to depart,
he then adopted a state of life in which he had renounced half of the royal lands and revenues.
Then, because there was no other means of livelihood, he desired to practice agriculture;
on an auspicious day, he went into the forest to look for land suitable for that purpose.
There he found a beautiful site, anticipating the perfection of its fruit;
and in the midst of it, he beheld a great, prosperous *aśvattha* tree.
Seeing him, who was cool as the rainy season because the rays of the sun were shielded by the dense shade of his auspicious body, that seeker of the fruits of cultivation attained great satisfaction.
Having declared, "I am a devotee of him who is the presiding deity here," he circumambulated that Aśvattha tree and bowed down before it.
Then, having yoked a pair of oxen and performed auspicious rites,
he made an offering at that tree and began his cultivation there.
He remained day and night beneath that very tree,
and his wife always brought him food right there.
And when his crops had ripened there in due season,
that land was unexpectedly plundered by a foreign kingdom, which arrived there by the turn of fate.
Then, when the enemy force had departed and the grain was destroyed,
that courageous man comforted his weeping wife and took what little remained.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation as before, he then remained right there beneath the tree;
for it is the natural disposition of the steadfast that they become even more firm in times of adversity.
Then, as he stood alone at night, sleepless with anxiety,
a voice issued forth from that aśvattha tree.
"O Somadatta, I am pleased with you; therefore, go to the kingdom of the king named Ādityaprabha, located in the region of Śrīkaṇṭha."
There, at the gate of that monarch,
you should recite this speech after having chanted the mantras for the twilight fire-sacrifice without interruption.
"I am a brahmin named Phalabhūti; listen to what I say:
one who performs good deeds shall obtain good fortune, and one who performs evil deeds shall obtain misfortune."
By speaking thus, you shall attain great supernatural power there;
now, recite from me alone the mantras for the twilight fire-sacrifice.
Having said, "I am a yakṣa," and having instantly taught those mantras to him by means of his own power at the banyan tree, the voice vanished.
In the morning, that virtuous Somadatta set out together with his wife,
having received the name Phalabhūti bestowed by the Yakṣa.
Having traversed various rugged and winding forests,
he reached the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha, which was like a state of misfortune.
There, having performed the twilight rites, the fire-oblation, and so forth, he duly announced his own name as Phalabhūti at the gate of the king.
"He who does good shall obtain good, and he who does evil shall obtain evil"—such is the saying that arouses curiosity among the people. (SoKss 3.6.41)
And as he was speaking thus, King Ādityaprabha,
having learned of Phalabhūti’s presence there, being filled with curiosity, had him ushered in.
He too, having entered, repeated those very same words before him again and again;
at that, the king laughed along with those standing by his side.
And having given him garments and ornaments, the king, together with his vassals, granted him villages; for the satisfaction of the great is never in vain.
And thus, at that very moment, Phalabhūti— having become emaciated— attained through the favor of the Guhyaka the splendor bestowed by the king.
Constantly repeating that very same thing he had said before, he attained the favor of the king;
for the minds of lords indeed delight in diversion.
Gradually, in this city of Rājagṛha, throughout the kingdoms and the inner apartments,
he won the affection and great respect of the king under the name "Rājapriya" (the King’s Favorite).
Then once, having returned from hunting in the forest,
King Ādityaprabha suddenly went into the inner apartments.
Entering with apprehension due to the agitation of the doorkeeper,
he beheld the queen named Kuvalayāvalī, who was intent upon the worship of the gods.
[He saw her] naked, with hair standing on end, eyes closed,
bearing a large tilaka mark of vermilion, and her lower lip quivering as she muttered prayers.
She stood in the center of a great maṇḍala laid out with powders of various colors,
performing a fierce bali-offering prepared with blood, wine, and human flesh.
When the king had entered, she too, her garments disarrayed by her agitation,
was questioned by him and, having been granted safety, spoke thus after a moment:
At that very moment, I performed worship for the sake of attaining my rise [to power].
O Lord, hear from me now the account of this scripture and its accomplishment.
Long ago, while I was still a maiden living in my father’s house,
I was addressed in this way by my female companions as we gathered together in a garden during the great festival of spring.
Here, in the pleasure garden, situated in the midst of a circle of trees,
dwells the god of gods, Vināyaka, whose power has been witnessed and who bestows boons.
Approaching him with devotion, worship him who grants all that is requested,
so that you may swiftly obtain a husband worthy of you without any obstacle.
Having heard that, out of my naivety, I asked those friends:
"Do maidens obtain a husband through the worship of Vināyaka?"
Then they replied to me: "Why do you say this?
If he is not honored, no success whatsoever exists here for anyone."
"And so, listen as we describe its power to you.
Having said this, my friends told me this story.
Long ago, when Śakra was oppressed by Tāraka and the flower-armed god [Kāma] had been consumed by fire, he desired to obtain a commander-in-chief who would be the son of Purāri.

Having performed austerities, Gaurī sought out and obtained as her husband Tryambaka, who is one whose vital energy is drawn upward, exceedingly fierce, and established in very long-term ascetic practice.
She longed for the birth of a son and for the life of Madana,
yet she did not remember to worship Vighneśvara for the sake of attaining success.
And Śiva spoke thus to his beloved, who was entreating him for her desired object:
"O dear one, in former times, Smara was born from the mind of Prajāpati."
And as soon as he was born, he spoke out of pride, saying, "Whom shall I delight?
For that reason, the Four-Faced One gave him the name Kāndarpa.
"If you are so excessively arrogant, my son, then do not transgress against the Three-Eyed One;
otherwise, you will surely meet death at his hands."
And thus, although he was commanded by Brahmā, that rogue came to cause a disturbance;
having been consumed by me, there shall be no further rebirth for him while his body still exists.
"I shall produce a son for you by my own power alone;
for my offspring is not caused by the impulse of passion, as is the case with worldly people."
Even as the bull-bannered god was speaking thus to Pārvatī,
Brahmā appeared before him, accompanied by Indra, the lord of a hundred sacrifices.
Having been praised by him, Śiva was entreated for the pacification of the demon Tāraka;
he consented to procreate a legitimate son from his own body through the Goddess.
And he consented to the birth of desire within the minds of embodied beings, for the sake of the creation,
interruption, and preservation [of the world], even though that [desire] is formless, by means of his word.
And he gave even his own heart room for the god of love;
pleased by this, the Creator departed, and Pārvatī attained joy.
Then, after some days had passed, Śaṅkara, remaining in seclusion, enjoyed the sport of amorous union with Umā.
When no end to his passion occurred even after hundreds of years had passed,
then, by the crushing of that [desire], the three worlds trembled.
Then, out of fear for the destruction of the world and for the sake of obstructing the trident-bearer’s pleasure,
the gods, at the command of the Grandfather, called upon Agni.
That fire, too, as soon as it was remembered, realizing that the Destroyer of Madana was unassailable,
fled from the gods and entered the depths of the water.
And there, the frogs, being scorched by that heat,
informed the gods who were searching for him about that fire situated within the water.
Then, having instantly turned them into frogs whose voices were indistinct by means of a curse,
Agni vanished and went back to Mount Mandara.
There the gods found him within the hollow of the tree, in the form of a snail, as had been described by the elephant and the parrot; and he granted them his vision.
Having caused the reversal of the tongues of Śuka and Dantila by means of a curse,
he accomplished the purpose of the gods after being praised by them.
Having gone there, that fire, having warded off Śiva from sexual union by means of its own heat,
bowed to him out of fear of a curse and informed him of the task of the gods.
Śarva, his impetus having mounted, deposited his seed into that fire;
for neither Vahni nor Ambikā was able to sustain it.
Then Hara spoke thus to the queen, who was distressed by grief and anger as she said, "I have not obtained a son from you."
"This obstacle has arisen for you here because of the failure to worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa).
Therefore, worship him so that a son may quickly be born to us from the fire."
Thus addressed by Śambhu, the Goddess performed the worship of Vighneśvara;
by that seed of Dhūrjaṭi, Anala also became pregnant.
Bearing that Śambhu-derived splendor, he then shone even during the days like the seven-rayed fire with the sun having entered within it.
Then, by the command of Hara, Gaṅgā discharged that unbearable energy into her waters; Gaṅgā, in turn, cast it onto Mount Meru into a sacrificial fire-pit.
While being thus protected there by the hosts of Śambhu,
that embryo emerged after a thousand years and became the six-faced Kumāra.
Then, having drunk from the breasts of the six Kṛttikās who were appointed by Gaurī with his six mouths, he grew in very few days.
In the meantime, the king of the gods, defeated by the demon Tāraka,
abandoned the battle and took refuge on the inaccessible peaks of Mount Meru.
The gods, together with the ṛṣis, sought refuge with the Six-faced One;
and the Six-faced One, surrounded by them, remained protecting the deities.
Having understood that and considering his kingdom lost, Indra then became agitated;
filled with envy, he went and fought against Kumāra.
Likewise, from the limb of Ṣaṇmukha struck by that vajra,
there arose two sons named Śākha and Viśākha, both of incomparable splendor.
Approaching his son, who had surpassed the prowess of Indra,
Śarva himself restrained him from the battle.
"You have been born to slay Tāraka and to protect the kingdom of Indra;
therefore, perform your own duty," he thus instructed him.
Then, having bowed with a joyful heart at that very moment, the enemy of Vṛtra began the consecration of Kumāra as the commander-in-chief.
When his arm became paralyzed because he had himself lifted the water-jar, Śakra fell into grief; then Śiva spoke to him.
Because you did not worship Gajamukha while desiring a commander-in-chief, this obstacle has arisen for you; therefore, perform his worship.
Having heard that and having done accordingly, the Lord of Śacī, with his arms released,
duly performed the consecration festival for the commander-in-chief.
Then, before long, the commander-in-chief slew the demon Tāraka;
the gods rejoiced at having accomplished their task, and Gaurī became a mother of a son.
Thus, O Goddess, even for the gods there are no accomplishments when Heramba is not honored; therefore, as one who desires boons, worship him.
Having been told this by my companions, I went previously to the one dwelling in a secluded part of the garden, O noble son, and worshipped Vighnarāja.
And at the conclusion of the worship, I suddenly beheld those companions of mine soaring up and moving through the courtyard of the sky by means of their own supernatural power.
Having seen that, out of curiosity, I summoned them from the sky and brought them down; when I asked them about the nature of their supernatural power (*siddhi*), they immediately replied as follows:
These are the mantra-attainments of the ḍākinīs born from the consumption of human flesh;
she is known as Kālarātri, a brahmin woman who is our guru in this matter.
Thus addressed by my friends,
I was for a moment filled with doubt— eager for the power of flight yet terrified of eating human flesh.
Then, out of greed for that success, I said to those friends:
"This instruction must be given to me by you as well."
Then, at my request, they went at that very moment and brought back Kālarātrī, who was there with her hideous form.
With meeting eyebrows, timid eyes, a sunken and flat nose,
thick cheeks, protruding lips, bumpy teeth, and a long neck.
With sagging breasts, a protruding belly, and feet cracked and swollen,
she appeared as if the Creator had displayed his skill in fashioning deformity.
Having bathed and performed worship to Vighneśvara, she prostrated at my feet; then, while I was naked within the mandala, that formidable woman caused me to perform the worship of Bhairava.
And having consecrated me, she gave me those various mantras of her own,
as well as human flesh that had been prepared as an offering for the worship of the gods, for me to eat.
At that very moment, having consumed the great flesh and recited the assembly of mantras,
I flew up into the sky with my companions, entirely naked.
Then, O Lord, having finished my play and descended from the sky with my guru’s permission,
I went to my own inner apartments among the maidens.
Thus, even when born in childhood, I was a sovereign of the circle of ḍākinīs;
there, having gathered together, we devoured many men.
In this interval of the story, O Great King, hear this tale:
there was a brahmin named Viṣṇusvāmin who was the husband of that Kālarātri.
And in that region, that preceptor, who was an expert in the knowledge of the Vedas, taught his disciples who had come from various directions.
And among his disciples was one youth named Sundaraka, whose body was radiant with virtue and whose qualities were distinguished by his moral conduct.
Once, when her husband had gone out somewhere, that wife of the preceptor— Kālarātri— being afflicted by desire, chose him in secret.
Surely Smara sports excessively with hideous laughter, since,
disregarding his own form, he has conceived a longing for Sundaraka.
But he, though entreated with every means, did not desire disorder;
for however women may behave, the mind of the virtuous remains unshakable.
Then, when he had withdrawn, Kālarātri, filled with rage,
tore her own body with the wounds of her own teeth and nails.
With her garments and hair disheveled,
she remained weeping until the preceptor Viṣṇusvāmī entered the house.
And when he had entered, she said to him: "Behold, my lord, the state to which I have been reduced by Sundaraka, who lusts after me by force."
Upon hearing that, the teacher flared up with anger at that very moment;
for confidence in women robs even the wise of their discernment.
And in the evening, when Sundaraka had arrived home, he rushed toward him and,
together with his disciples, struck him with fists, feet, and clubs.
Moreover, having instructed his disciples to leave him outside while he lay motionless from the blows,
he had him cast out onto the street at night with total indifference.
Then, fanned by the night breeze, Sundaraka slowly reflected thus upon himself as he perceived his own state of being so utterly overwhelmed: *SoKss_3,6.127*
Ah! The instigation of women is like a whirlwind that stirs the depths of men whose minds are overcome by passion, agitating their hearts as it does the waters of lakes.
Because of which, despite being elderly and learned, my preceptor acted improperly toward me out of excessive anger, without due reflection.
Or rather, even for the wise, as long as creation exists,
desire and anger— though perfected by destiny— are both the bolts on the door to liberation for brahmins.
For instance, why did the sages not formerly become enraged with Śarva in the Devadāru forest, fearing the loss of their own wives?
And they did not recognize this god, who had assumed the form of a mendicant,
as he intended to show Umā the lack of tranquility even among the sages.
Having immediately realized that they had incurred a curse which would cause the agitation of the three worlds,
they sought refuge in that very Lord, the Sovereign God.
Thus, even sages who have been deceived by the sixfold group of enemies—desire, anger, and the rest—become utterly deluded; what then need be said of those who are merely learned in the Vedas?
Thus, meditating there at night out of fear of bandits,
Sundaraka climbed onto a nearby empty cow-pen building and stayed there.
While he remained unobserved in that one spot for a moment,
Kālarātri arrived right there at the palace.
Drawing her heroic dagger, terrifying with the hissing breath she emits,
vomiting flames from her eyes and mouth, she is joined by a circle of ḍākinīs.
Seeing that such a night of doom had arrived there,
Sundaraka, filled with fear, then called to mind the mantras that destroy demons.
Then, deluded by his mantra, she did not see him as he stood silently in a secluded spot, his limbs drawn together in fear.
Then, having recited the mantra for flight,
Kālarātrī, together with her companions, her cow-pen, and her palace, soared up into the sky.
Having heard that mantra at that time, Sundaraka took it up;
and she too, along with her palace, quickly traveled through the sky to Ujjayinī.
Having brought her there into the palace, she was led by means of mantras to a vegetable garden;
having gone to the cremation ground, she sported in the midst of a circle of ḍākinīs.
And at that moment, overcome by hunger, Sundaraka descended into a vegetable garden and there made his sustenance from uprooted radishes.
When he had thus satisfied his hunger and taken refuge in the cow-pen as before,
Kālarātri returned from her dwelling in the middle of the night.
Then, having mounted the cow-pen by means of the accomplishment of the mantra as before,
she, together with her disciples, returned to her own home through the sky during the night.
Having placed that cow-pen carriage in its proper place and dismissed those female attendants, she entered the bedchamber.
Sundaraka, too, having passed that night amazed by the obstacles,
abandoned the cow-pen at dawn and went into the presence of his friends.
There, having related his own story and being intent on departing for a foreign land,
he was comforted by those friends and took up residence among them.
Leaving the preceptor’s house and eating at a public almshouse,
he dwelt there, wandering at his own will together with his friends.
Once, having gone out to purchase household goods,
Kālarātri beheld that Sundaraka at the marketplace.
Having approached him, she, once again afflicted by love, said to him:
"O Sundaraka, even now favor me, whose life is dependent upon you."
Thus addressed by her, the virtuous Sundaraka then said:
"Do not speak thus; this is not dharma, for you are my mother, the wife of my guru."
Then Kālarātri said: "If you know what is dharma, then give that;
for what dharma could be greater than the gift of life by giving me my life?"
Then Sundaraka said: "Mother, do not harbor such a thought in your heart;
where could there be righteousness in approaching the bed of one's guru?"
Thus repulsed by him, she, threatening him in her rage,
tore her own upper garment with her own hand and went home.
"See, Sundaraka has run here and torn this [garment] of mine," she said to her husband there, showing him her upper garment.
And her husband, having gone there in a fit of rage and having proclaimed her as one deserving of death,
immediately forbade Sundaraka’s food at the sacrificial feast.
Then Sundaraka, knowing the mantra for flying through the sky that had been taught by Govāṭa, prepared to abandon that place out of distress.
Then, even as he was descending, he heard another lesson that he had forgotten;
at night, he went once again to that very same empty cow-pen palace.
While he was staying there, Kālarātri approached as before;
leaping up from her palace in that very same manner, she departed for Ujjayinī through the sky.
Having caused the cow-pen to be moved there by means of a mantra into the vegetable garden,
she went once more to the cemetery for her nocturnal wanderings.
And although Sundaraka heard that mantra once more, he did not grasp it;
for how can there be complete accomplishments without the instruction of a guru?
Then, having eaten some radishes and other roots there,
he threw them into the cow-pen to take away and remained as before.
Then, having mounted her carriage of oxen and traveled through the sky at night,
Kālarātri entered her own abode after setting down her vehicle.
Then Sundaraka, having emerged from the cow-pen in the morning,
went to the marketplace with roots in hand, seeking money for his meal.
While he was selling it there, the Mālava royal servants, seeing that it was produced in their own country, seized the radishes without paying any price. (SoKss 3.6.166)
Then, while making a commotion and being pursued by his friends,
he was led before the king by them on the charge that he was throwing stones at them.
"Why have you brought radishes here from Mālava to sell in Kānyakubja?"— when asked this by us, he did not speak at all.

"Instead, he strikes them with stones"—thus was the king addressed by those rogues; he then asked about that marvel, and his friends replied: SoKss_3,6.169: "Instead, he strikes them with stones"—thus was the king addressed by those rogues; he then asked about that marvel, and his friends replied: [as follows].
"O King, if he is raised up to the palace together with us, then this curiosity will be fully explained; it cannot be otherwise."
"So be it," said the king; and while he looked on, Sundaraka, together with the palace, immediately flew up into the sky by means of the mantra.
Having traveled with his friend and reached Prayāga in due course, he,
being exhausted, saw a certain king there who had just bathed.
Having stabilized the palace there and descended into the waters of the Gaṅgā,
he was gazed upon with wonder by all as he approached that king.
"Who are you, and for what purpose have you descended from the sky? Tell us.
Thus questioned by the king who was bowing before him, Sundaraka spoke as follows:
"I am a Gaṇa named Murajaka, belonging to the god Dhūrjaṭi;
by his command, I have come into your presence seeking human enjoyment."
Hearing that and suspecting it to be true, the king gave him a city rich in crops, filled with jewels, together with its women and all its equipment.
Then, having entered that city and flown up into the sky with his followers,
Sundaraka wandered for a long time at his own will, free from all want.
Reclining on a golden couch and being fanned with yak-tail whisks,
while being attended by excellent women, he attained the bliss of Indra.
Then once, a certain perfected being (siddha) who traveled through the sky gave him a mantra for descending from the heavens, having become acquainted with him.
Having thus obtained the mantra for descent, Sundaraka then went and descended from the path of the sky into his own country, Kānyakubja.
Having learned that the city, endowed with full splendor, had descended from the sky,
the king himself approached it out of curiosity.
Then, having been fully questioned by the king who knew the proper time, he, being aware of the right moment,
reported his entire account of what had been done during the Night of Doom.
Then the lord of the earth summoned Kālarātri and questioned her;
she, being fearless, confessed all her own misconduct.
When the king was enraged and prepared to cut off her ears,
she vanished even while everyone looked on, despite having been seized.
Then her residence within his own kingdom was forbidden by the king;
honored by him, Sundaraka once again took to the sky.
Having spoken thus to her husband, King Ādityaprabha,
Queen Kuvalayāvalī addressed him once more.
"O King, such are the accomplishments of the mantras of the ḍākinīs;
and this event, which occurred in my father's country, is renowned everywhere."
"I am a disciple of Kālarātri," and so forth was described by me;
yet because of my devotion to my husband, my spiritual attainment (*siddhi*) is even greater than that.
And today you saw me, having performed worship for the sake of your welfare;
I was intent on summoning a man by means of a mantra for my sacrificial offering.
Therefore, enter now into this system of ours as well;
place your foot upon the heads of those kings who have been conquered through the yoga of supernatural powers.
Having heard that, the king said, "Where is the eating of human flesh according to the way of the ḍākinīs, and where is kingship? and thus he forbade it.
But when the queen was intent on giving up her life, he consented to that;
for how can those who are dragged away by sense-objects remain upon the path of the righteous?
Then, having led him into the previously consecrated mandala, she spoke these words to the king, who had taken the vow: SoKss_3,6.193 //
"This Brahmin named Phalabhūti who stands here in your presence has been prepared by me to be drawn away for the purpose of a sacrificial offering."
And attracting [others] is laborious; therefore, it would be better to appoint some cook in this matter—one who both kills and cooks that [animal] himself.

And one should not feel aversion, because by consuming the meat and the sacrificial offering (bali) once the worship has been completed, there shall be perfect accomplishment; for he is indeed the most excellent.
Thus addressed by his beloved, the king, though fearful of sin, accepted that once more;
alas, fie upon the wretched subservience to women!
Then, having summoned the cook named Sāhasika,
they gained his trust, initiated him, and the husband and wife spoke together.
"Today the king, accompanied by the queen, shall eat; therefore, make haste.
Anyone who approaches you to speak regarding this meal, you must strike them down."
"And you should prepare a delicious meal for the two of us in private this morning using his flesh.
Thus instructed, the cook said, "So be it," and went home.
In the morning, when Phalabhūti had arrived, the king said to him:
"Go and speak to the daring cook in the kitchen."
"Today the king, accompanied by the queen, shall eat delicious food;
therefore, prepare the finest meal with all haste. (SoKss_3,6.202)
When Phalabhūti had thus departed and gone outside,
the prince named Candraprabha approached him and spoke these words.
"With this gold, have earrings made for me this very day,
just like those you previously had made for my noble father."
Thus addressed by the prince, Phalabhūti then,
having complied with his request, was dispatched and went forth for the sake of the two earrings.
The prince also went at his own will to the kitchen alone, having received that royal command as described by Phalabhūti.
There, that cook, firm in his resolve and acting with reckless courage, immediately slew the prince with a knife, carrying out the royal command as it had been spoken.
Having performed their worship, the queen and the king ate the meal prepared with his flesh, unaware of the true reality of the matter.
Having passed that night with remorse, the king saw Phalabhūti approaching him in the morning with the earrings in his hand.
Wandering about from place to place, he questioned him at that very moment;
having had his own story related by him, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Crying out, "Alas, my son! he lamented, blaming both his wife and himself;
and when questioned by his ministers, he described everything exactly as it had happened.
And Phalabhūti replied:
"It has been said that one who performs good deeds shall obtain what is good, and one who performs evil deeds shall obtain what is evil."
Like a ball struck against a wall, repeatedly rebounding,
a fault intended for another generally falls back upon oneself.
"Because we, following evil conduct and desiring to commit the murder of a Brahmin,
killed our own sons and ate their flesh, that [sin] has been obtained."
Having spoken thus and having enlightened his own ministers who were hanging their heads,
he consecrated that very Phalabhūti in his own kingdom.
Having bestowed his gifts, the king, being childless,
entered the fire along with his wife for the purification of his sins, even though he was already consumed by the fire of remorse.
And Phalabhūti, having obtained that kingdom, ruled the earth;
thus, whether good or evil, what one has done is imputed to oneself.
Having thus related this story in the presence of the Lord of Vatsa,
Yaugandharāyaṇa spoke again to that king:
Therefore, O Indra among kings, even if you have conquered him and are practicing virtue, Brahmadatta might still act perversely; if he does, you alone must slay him.
Thus addressed by his chief minister, the Lord of Vatsa welcomed those words,
rose up, and performed his daily duties.
And on another day, having successfully completed his conquest of all directions,
that accomplished king set out from Lāvāṇaka toward his own city, Kauśāmbī.
In due course, the lord of the earth, together with his retinue, reached the city,
which seemed to be dancing out of joy, its creeper-like arms of banners uplifted.
And he entered into her— the forest of blue-lotus eyes of the city women—
spreading at every step the agitation of a rising gale.
Being celebrated by wandering minstrels, praised by bards,
and saluted by kings, the king returned to his palace.
Then, having established his command over all the kings of every land who had bowed before him,
that King Vatsa forcibly ascended that lion-throne which had been obtained from a former treasure-trove and was worthy of his lineage.
At that time, the sky was filled with the echoes of the loud and steady sounds of musical instruments struck for the auspicious occasion, as if by shouts of "Well done!
from the world-protectors, who were gratified by the chief minister and had granted their approval in every direction.
Then, free from greed, having distributed in various ways the wealth acquired through his conquest of the earth to the twice-born, he—
having celebrated a great festival— rendered the circle of kings and his own ministers successful in their aims.
When that king caused rain to fall upon the fields in accordance with their needs, resounding with the noise of thundering clouds and drums,
the people of that city also celebrated in every house, anticipating the future fruit of abundant grain.
Having thus conquered the world, that virtuous King of Vatsa, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to Rumaṇvat and Augandharāyaṇa,
remained there at his pleasure together with Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī.
Standing between those two goddesses as if between Fame and Fortune, he was praised by excellent bards;
he enjoyed the rising of the moon, white with his own glory, and constantly drank the wine that was like the majesty of his enemies.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the Lāvāṇaka book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
And this third book, the Lāvāṇaka, is completed. Śrī!
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Lambaka, named "The Birth of Naravāhanadatta.
This nectar of stories indeed emerged long ago from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the King of Mountains.
Those who, having attained supernatural power through the removal of obstacles, forcibly cause [others] to remember [the Dharma], bear the burden of the gods upon this earth by the grace of Bhava.
The first wave:
Victorious is the Conqueror of Obstacles, who parts the great mountain ranges as if with the forceful stroke of his ear-flap, pointing the way, as it were, to the spiritual attainments.
Then King Udayana, the lord of Vatsa, residing in Kauśāmbī,
enjoyed the conquered earth under his single umbrella.
Having entrusted the burden of governance along with Rumaṇvat to Yaugandharāyaṇa,
he lived happily as a friend of Vasantaka, finding his sole delight in pleasure.
Playing the lute himself, accompanied by Queen Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī, he enjoyed the performance of music.
While there was no distinction between the soft song of the goddess and the sound of her lute, the trembling of her thumb during playing served as an indicator of their difference.
And on the roof of his palace, white with moonlight as if with his own fame,
he drank wine dripping from a stream, like the intoxication of his enemies.
In private, beautiful women brought him honey, glowing with passion, from golden jars as if it were the water for his consecration to the kingdom of Love.
Between the two of them, he offered wine that was slightly reddish, delicious, and clear, with his own face shimmering within it, as if it were his own heart.
Even though envy and anger were absent, their gaze did not reach satiety upon the face of that passionate woman with arched brows.
His drinking hall, with its many goblets of honey and crystal,
shone like a lotus pond where white lotuses are reddened by the morning sun.
And in between, a hunter met him, clad in a tunic of dark *palāśa* leaves; with his bow and arrows, he entered the deer-forest that resembled himself.
He struck down swarms of boars muddied by the mire with his arrows,
just as the sun dispels masses of darkness with its dense rays.
As he rushed forth, the terrified black antelopes fled;
they appeared like the glances of the quarters of the sky, which had previously been overcome by him.
And the earth, reddened with blood, appeared like a forest lotus-pond that had fled from the falling of his horns to seek refuge at his service after the slayer of the buffalo had struck it.
He rejoiced even at the lions as they fell, impaled by spears dropped from their gaping mouths, with their lives departing amidst internal roars.
In that forest, dogs were placed in pits and snares were set along his paths;
such was the preparation for the pleasure of the hunt, even though he had already achieved perfection through his own weapons alone.
While the king was thus engaged in the enjoyment of pleasures, one day the sage Nārada approached him as he sat in the assembly hall.
Forming a halo with the radiance of his own body, he was an ornament of heaven,
like the sun descended out of affection for the noble race of luminaries.
Having been offered hospitality by that king who bowed repeatedly before him,
he stayed for a moment and spoke to the monarch with pleasure.
Listen, O Lord of Vatsa, as I tell you this in brief:
there was once a king named Pāṇḍu, who was your great-grandfather.
He, of great majesty, had exactly two wives worthy of him:
one was Kuntī and the second was named Mādrī.
Having conquered this earth girt by the oceans, that Pāṇḍu,
being happy, once went to the forest out of a passion for hunting.
There, having released his arrow, he struck the sage named Kindama together with his wife as they were engaged in sexual union in the form of deer.
Abandoning that deer-form,
the sage cursed the dejected Pāṇḍu, who had dropped his bow, with words that issued from his very life-breath as it turned back toward his throat.
"Since I was slain by you while standing at ease and without reflection,
therefore your death shall come like mine at the time of sexual union with your wife."

Thus, having received this curse from the seer, Pāṇḍu— out of fear of its fulfillment and having abandoned all desire for sensual enjoyment— dwelt in a peaceful penance grove accompanied by his two wives.
Although staying there, once impelled by that curse,
he suddenly desired his beloved Mādrī and met his death.
Thus, O King, that which is called hunting is a source of negligence for rulers;
for by this very practice, even those various other kings have been destroyed like deer.
With a terrifying roar, intent on flesh, harsh, with smoke-colored hair standing erect,
and teeth like spears— how indeed could she, like a rākṣasī, bring about auspiciousness?
Therefore, abandon this fruitless exertion and the passion for hunting;
for those who kill wild animals and those who are their prey, the danger to life is equal.
And you, out of affection for your predecessor, are dear to me and a vessel of auspiciousness;
now hear how your son shall become a portion of Kāma.
Praised with hymns by Rati for the sake of restoring the limbs of the Ancient One who had lost his body,
Śiva, being pleased, spoke these words to her in private in brief.
"Having descended to earth with a portion of himself and having worshipped me personally,
this Gaurī, desiring a son, shall give birth to Kāma."
Therefore, O lord of men, this queen Vāsavadattā was born as the daughter of Caṇḍamahāsena and has become your consort.
Therefore, having propitiated Śambhu, she will give birth to a son who is a portion of Kāma,
who shall become the universal monarch (cakravartin) of all the Vidyādharas.
When the king had spoken thus with words that were not respected, the seer Nārada returned to him the earth that had been offered to him and vanished from sight.
When he had departed, the King of Vatsa, together with Vāsavadattā—
who was now desirous of a son— spent that day in anxious reflection upon him.
On another day, the eminent doorkeeper named Nityodita, approaching the Lord of Vatsa as he sat in the assembly hall, addressed him thus:
O Great King, a certain destitute Brahmin woman, accompanied by two young children, stood at the gate, longing for a vision of the Lord.
As soon as she heard that and the king had granted her entrance,
that Brahmin woman entered there, emaciated, pale, and greyish-white.
Distressed as if by a tattered garment,
she bore both her young sons upon her lap, appearing like two children of sorrow and wretchedness.
Having performed the appropriate salutation, she addressed the king:
"I am a brahmin woman of noble birth, yet I have fallen into such a miserable state."
"By fate, these two sons were born to me simultaneously;
therefore, O Lord, I have no breast milk for them without food."
Therefore, O Protector who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, I, being miserable, have now reached the Lord as my refuge; he is my authority and my master.
Having heard that, the compassionate king commanded his doorkeeper:
"Let this be taken and presented to Queen Vāsavadattā."
And then, led by that very doorkeeper as if by her own auspicious karma acting as a precursor, she was brought into the presence of the Queen.
Having learned from the doorkeeper that she had been sent by the king,
Queen Vāsavadattā placed even greater trust in the brahmin woman.
Seeing her, who had twin children, yet so wretched, she reflected:
"Aha! This is some truly perverse way of acting on the part of the Creator."
"Alas, what stinginess regarding a real thing! Alas, what devotion to a non-existent thing!
Even now not a single son has been born to me; yet in this birth, these twins have appeared."
Reflecting thus, the queen, desiring to bathe,
gave instructions to the Brahmin woman’s maidservants regarding her bath and other preparations.
Washed, given garments, and fed delicious food by them,
that Brahmin woman, like parched earth sprinkled with water, breathed a deep sigh of relief.
Once she had been comforted through skillful conversation, Queen Vāsavadattā addressed her after a short interval in order to test her.
"O Brahmin lady, let some story be told by you to us.
Having heard that, she said, "So be it," and proceeded to tell a story.
In former times, there was a certain ordinary king named Jayadatta,
and a son named Devadatta was born to him.
Then, when his son had reached youth, the wise king, desiring to arrange his marriage, thought as follows:
Royal fortune is exceedingly fickle, like a courtesan to be enjoyed by the powerful;
but the prosperity of merchants is stable and devoted to no other, like a woman of good family.
Therefore, I shall arrange my son’s marriage with the daughter of a merchant,
so that no misfortune shall befall him in this kingdom which has many claimants to the throne.
Having thus resolved, for the sake of his son,
that king requested the hand of the daughter of the merchant Vasudatta from Pāṭaliputra.
Vasudatta, desiring a praiseworthy alliance,
gave his daughter to that prince even though he was in a distant foreign land.
And he likewise filled his son-in-law with jewels,
so that his great respect for him surpassed even his own father’s wealth.
Then King Jayadatta dwelt happily together with his son, who was accompanied by the daughter of a wealthy merchant whom he had obtained.
Once, having arrived there at his relative's house full of longing,
that merchant Vasudatta led his daughter to his own home.
Then, suddenly, that King Jayadatta went to heaven;
his kinsmen rose up and took possession of that kingdom.
Out of fear of him, his son Devadatta was led away at night by his own mother to another country, unobserved.
Thereupon, her mind distressed with grief, the mother said to that prince:
"We have a lord, a Cakravartin king, the sovereign of the eastern quarter."
"Go to his side, my child; he will secure the kingdom for you.
Having been addressed thus by his mother, the prince then spoke to her:
"Who will think much of me when I have gone there without any retinue?
Having heard that, his mother spoke to him once more in this way:
Having gone to your father-in-law's house and obtained wealth from there,
go to the presence of the universal monarch after having prepared your equipment.
Thus urged by his mother, the prince, though filled with shame,
set out in due course and reached his father-in-law’s house that evening.
Deprived of his father and with his fortune ruined, he was unable to enter there at an improper time during the night, fearing the shedding of tears and overcome by shame.
Then, standing nearby outside the sacrificial hall, he suddenly beheld a woman descending by means of a rope from her father-in-law’s house at night.
And in an instant, recognizing his own wife— resplendent with the luster of jewels— to be like a meteor fallen from the clouds, he was consumed by anguish.
Seeing him, though he was pale and emaciated, she did not recognize him and asked, "Who are you? Upon hearing that, he replied, "I am a traveler."
Then that merchant’s daughter entered the interior of the sacrificial hall;
the prince also followed her secretly to observe her.
And she approached a certain man there, and that man,
thinking "you have come after a long time," struck her with kicks of his feet.
Then that wicked woman, her passion redoubled, propitiated the man and remained there with him at her pleasure.
Having seen that, the wise prince reflected:
"This is not the time for my anger; indeed, another task remains to be accomplished."
And how could this treatise spread among these two wretched ones—this woman of mine, who is fit for a foe, or this beast of a king? (SoKss 4.1.78)
What business has this wicked woman with this? For it is the work of that evil fate, which rains down suffering and is skilled in the sport of observing my fortitude.
She belongs to an incomparable family; what offense has she committed?
How could a female crow, abandoning the crow, take pleasure in a cuckoo?
Having reflected thus, he neglected his wife who was full of desire;
for in the minds of the virtuous, when intent on conquering their masters, how insignificant is a woman, like a blade of grass?
And at that moment, it is said, due to the force of her passion,
a beautiful ornament rich with pearls fell from the ear of that merchant’s daughter.
And she did not see that at all; then, at the conclusion of the amorous encounter, she quickly took leave of her lover and went home by the way she had come.
When that secret lover had also quickly departed for some place,
the prince, seeing those jeweled ornaments, took them.
With its mass of crest-jewels sparkling, it was like a hand-lamp bestowed by the Creator to dispel the darkness of delusion for one who had lost his fortune and sought it again.
And beholding that [treasure] of great value, the prince,
having accomplished his purpose, departed at that very moment and went from there to Kānyakubja.
Having given that ornament there for the sake of his release, he purchased elephants and horses with a hundred thousand pieces of gold and went into the presence of the universal monarch.
Having arrived together with the forces provided by him and having slain his enemies in battle,
the virtuous prince regained his paternal kingdom and was greeted with joy by his mother.
And having released that ornament from its binding, she sent it unhesitatingly to her father-in-law to reveal that secret.
Her father-in-law, too, seeing that very earring which was his daughter’s ear-ornament,
arrived there in that manner and, filled with confusion, showed it to her.
She too, seeing that [ring] as if it were her own conduct fallen away in former times,
and realizing it had been sent by her husband, remembered everything with great agitation.
"This fell upon me that night inside the sacrificial hall,
on which night some traveler was seen by me standing there."
Surely he came here as my husband, desiring to test my character;
but I did not recognize him, and for that reason this ornament was obtained by me.
As she was thinking thus, the merchant’s daughter’s heart, distressed by the manifestation of her own misconduct and filled with terror, broke apart.
Then, having skillfully questioned a maidservant who knew her secret,
that merchant father understood the truth and abandoned his grief for her.
Then the prince, having attained the kingdom and having won as his wife the daughter of a universal monarch— acquired through his virtues— enjoyed another form of glory.
Thus, in such daring acts, the hearts of women are as hard as adamant; yet that very same heart becomes as delicate as a flower at the onset of the agitation of fear.
But some of those women, born of noble lineage like pearls,
who are well-conducted and pure-hearted, become ornaments upon the earth.
And royal fortune, like a doe, is always thus prone to flight;
yet some wise men know how to bind it with the tether of fortitude.
Therefore, even in times of adversity, those who desire prosperity must not abandon their integrity;
this is the very principle here, and my own experience serves as the illustration in this matter.
