"O Queen, that my conduct was maintained even in this adversity has indeed borne fruit for me through the attainment of the auspicious sight of you."
Having heard this story from the mouth of that brahmin woman at that very moment,
Queen Vāsavadattā reflected with respect.
This Brahmin woman is surely of noble birth;
for her graceful bearing and the maturity of her speech testify to her refined character.
Thinking, "She possesses such proficiency in entering royal assemblies," the queen spoke again to that brahmin woman:
"To whom do you belong as a wife, or what is your story? Let it be told by you.
Having heard that, the Brahmin woman then proceeded to speak further.
In Mālava, O Queen, there was a certain brahmin named Agnidatta,
who was the abode of Śrī and Sarasvatī, having personally bestowed his wealth upon those who sought it.
And to him were born in due course two sons suited to himself:
the elder named Śaṅkaradatta, and the other known by the name Śāntikara.
O illustrious lady, Śāntikara, seeking knowledge, suddenly departed from his father’s house while still a child and went away somewhere.
And his second brother, the elder one, married me—
the daughter of Yajñadatta, whose wealth was maintained for the sake of sacrifice.
In time, that father of my husband, named Agnidatta,
being old, passed away to the other world, followed by his own wife.
And because my husband had set out for a sacred ford, he abandoned me while I was pregnant;
having gone to the bank of the Sarasvatī, blinded by grief, he cast off his body.
When this account had been told, my companions arrived;
I was able to inform my own people, but I could not follow them, being pregnant.
Then, while I was still reeling with fresh grief, bandits suddenly arrived and plundered our entire agrahāra settlement, including our very home.
At that moment, out of fear of losing my virtue, I fled from there with three Brahmin women, clutching a small garment to our bodies.
Having gone to a distant land because of the ruin of my country, I remained there for about a month with her, subsisting on difficult labor.
Having heard from the world that the Lord of Vatsa was a refuge for the helpless,
I have therefore come here with my Brahmin wife, carrying virtue alone as our provisions for the journey.
I gave birth to both sons simultaneously as soon as I arrived,
even while these three Brahmin women, my friends, were standing by.
Sorrow, exile, poverty, and even this double birth—alas!
the Creator has flung wide open for me the door to calamities.
"Therefore, there is no way for these two children to grow up; they must be abandoned by me,"—having reflected thus, she cast aside shame, which is the ornament of women.
Having entered the assembly, I entreated the King of Vatsa:
"Who is able to endure the sight of the suffering of a woman whose child has met with calamity?"
And by his command, I have come into the presence of your feet;
my misfortunes have ceased, as if repelled at the very threshold.
Such is my story; I am also named Piṅgalikā, for my two eyes have been turned tawny by the smoke from the fire-rituals since childhood.
But that husband of mine, O Goddess, who brings peace, has gone abroad;
even now it is not known in which country he dwells.
When she had thus related her own story, the queen, perceiving that she was of noble birth, reflected upon this Brahmin woman with affection and spoke as follows:
"Here stands our family priest named Śāntikara;
I know him to be a foreigner, and he shall become your brother-in-law."
Having spoken thus to the eager Brāhmaṇī and having passed that very night,
the queen summoned Śāntikara in the morning and inquired about his lineage.
And to him who had thus explained the lineage, she, having reached a firm conviction,
showed that Brahmin woman, saying, "This is your brother's daughter."
And once full comprehension had arisen, he, having learned of the destruction of his kinsmen,
then led that Brahmin woman, his brother’s wife, to his home.
There, having lamented for his parents and brother as was appropriate,
he comforted her as she sat with her two young children.
Queen Vāsavadattā also appointed those two boys, her sons,
as the future priests for her own son.
Of those two, the elder was named Śāntisoma and the other Vaiśvānara;
they were so named by that very goddess, who bestowed upon them abundant prosperity.
For this world, which is like a blind man being led by his own past actions acting as guides toward the ground of its fruit, one's own human effort serves merely as the instrumental cause.
When they had arrived and attained their respective fortunes, they all gathered there:
those two boys, their mother, and Śāntikara.
Then, as the days passed, on one occasion he took along five sons and approached a female potter who had arrived carrying earthenware bowls.
Having seen a certain woman in her own palace, that Brāhmaṇī Piṅgalikā was addressed by Queen Vāsavadattā as she stood by her side: SoKss_4,1.135 //
"O friend, let even one of her five sons be seen by me today;
such a worthy recipient of merits is rare, and even one such as I am not so."
Then Piṅgalikā said: "O Queen, this progeny, being full of evil, arises for the sake of suffering;
it is most abundant among the poor."
Whoever might be born among those like you would surely be someone most excellent;
therefore, enough with this haste—you shall soon obtain a son worthy of yourself.
Thus addressed by Piṅgalikā, Vāsavadattā remained eager for the birth of her son, her mind overcome with anxiety regarding that matter.
"Nārada told you that a son is to be obtained through the worship of Girīśa;
therefore, O Goddess, that Śiva, the granter of boons, must certainly be propitiated by us in this matter."
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, who had arrived at that very moment,
the queen, having grasped his intention, quickly made her resolve for the vow.
When she had undertaken her vow, that king, together with his ministers and his entire kingdom,
also performed the vow for the propitiation of Śaṅkara.
Then, having fasted for three nights, that Lord, having manifested his grace, personally commanded the couple in a dream.
"Arise! That portion of your desire shall be born as a son, who by my grace will become the lord of the Vidyādharas."
Having uttered these words, as the moon-crested Lord suddenly vanished, the couple awoke; having swiftly obtained the boon, they, their purpose fulfilled, experienced genuine joy.
Then, having risen at dawn and informed the ministers, who were gratified by the nectar-like essence of the narration of that dream,
both the queen and the king, together with their kinsmen and servants, celebrated with great festivity and performed the breaking of their fasts.
After the lapse of a few days, a certain man with matted hair appeared in a dream to Queen Vāsavadattā and, approaching her, gave her a fruit.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, having been delighted by her who had clearly related such a dream, and being congratulated by his ministers,
reflected and considered that the wish-granting son, bestowed by the moon-crested Lord Śiva as if it were already a fruit, was no longer far off.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Naravāhanadattajanana* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave:
Now follows the festival for the heart of the Lord of Vatsa, occasioned by Vāsavadattā.
Before long, the embryo was formed, radiant as an incarnation of a portion of Kāma.
With her face of pale luster and its flickering eyes,
she shone like the moon containing within it the god of love and his passion.
As she sat there out of love for her husband, two reflections appeared on the sides of her jeweled couch as if Rati and Prīti had arrived.
Desiring to serve the womb of the future lord of the Vidyādharas, her friends, who grant all desires,
attended upon her like personified sciences (vidyās) come to life.
Then she bore two breasts, dark-faced like fresh blue sprouts,
which were like two jars for the consecration of her son from the womb.
In the center of the palace, she shone as she lay upon a comfortable couch, graced by a jeweled floor that was clear, radiant, and possessed a true luster.
As if being attended from all sides by heaps of jewels that had approached, their waters trembling with the fear of being trodden upon by the Son of the Embodied One.
In the center of her celestial palace, an image fashioned from jewels shone like the splendor of the Vidyādharas, having come through the sky for the purpose of prostration.
And she became pregnant while listening to stories concerning the foremost practitioners who were intent upon the accomplishment of mantras,
which arose as incidental topics.
Excellent Vidyādhara women, engaged in melodious singing,
attended upon her in a dream as she had ascended into the lap of the sky.
Having awakened, she longed to experience that very thing directly:
the playful sport of roaming through the sky and the wonder of beholding the surface of the earth.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa fulfilled that pregnancy longing of the queen through the employment of mechanical devices, spells, illusions, and other such means.
And she remained there in the sky, performing various feats that inspired wonder in the women of the city with their long-lashed eyes.
Once, while she was staying in her dwelling,
there arose in her heart a curiosity to hear the noble tales of the Vidyādharas.
Then, entreated by the queen, Yaugandharāyaṇa related this story there while she and everyone else listened.
"There is Himavat, the lord of mountains, the father of Ambika;
he who is not only the preceptor of all mountains, but also of the Lord of Gauri."
And on that great mountain, the abode of the Vidyādharas, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas,
a king named Jīmūtaketu, dwelt.
In his house there was a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) descended through his paternal lineage,
renowned by its appropriate name as the "Bestower of Desires."
And once, King Jīmūtaketu approached that celestial tree,
a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), in the garden and made a request of it.
"Everything we desire is always obtained by us from you;
therefore, O God, grant me, who am childless, a son endowed with virtuous qualities."
Then the wish-fulfilling tree said: "O King, a son shall be born to you who remembers his past lives, a hero among givers, and a benefactor to all beings."
Having heard that, the king was filled with joy; he bowed to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, went [to his queen], and informed her, thereby bringing delight to his own queen.
Then, not long after that, a son was born to the king,
and his father gave him the name Jīmūtavāhana.
Then, together with his innate compassion for all living beings,
that Great Being Jīmūtavāhana attained growth.
And in due course, having been installed as crown prince, he, compassionate toward the world, addressed his father in private after the latter had been propitiated by his service: SoKss_4,2.25.
I know, dear father, that all things in this world are momentary and subject to destruction;
yet the one thing that remains steadfast for great beings until the end of the aeon is their stainless fame.
If that very thing which arises from benefiting others is indeed so, alas!
What else could be the wealth of the noble, dearer to them than their own lives?
And prosperity, like lightning, causes distress to the eyes of the world;
flickering, it vanishes somewhere or other—that which brings no benefit to others.
If this wish-fulfilling tree that we possess were to be employed for the sake of others, then its fruit would truly be attained.
Therefore, I shall act here in such a way that by means of his riches,
this entire assembly of seekers may no longer be poor.
Having thus informed his father and obtained his permission,
Jīmūtavāhana went to that wish-fulfilling tree and spoke to it:
"O Lord, you are the constant bestower of our desired fruits;
therefore, fulfill this one wish of mine today."
"Make this entire earth free from poverty, my friend;
may it be well with you. You have been bestowed upon the world that seeks wealth."
Thus addressed by that steadfast one, the wish-fulfilling tree rained down abundant gold upon the earth, and all the subjects rejoiced.
Who else besides Jīmūtavāhana— a compassionate portion of a Bodhisattva— could,
being so skillful, have made even the wish-fulfilling tree the property of those who seek it?
Thus, as affection arose among them, Jīmūtavāhana’s pure fame spread far and wide through the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, seeing that the kingdom of Jīmūtaketu was firmly rooted in the fame of his son, those born of his lineage became envious and fell into a state of agitation.
And they considered that abode, which possessed a magnificent wish-fulfilling tree suited for giving,
as easily conquerable because it was devoid of splendor.

Then, when they had gathered together and resolved upon battle, the steadfast Jīmūtavāhana spoke thus to his father: [-yuktāspadaṃ em. for -muktāspadaṃ] Then, when they had gathered together and resolved upon battle, the steadfast Jīmūtavāhana spoke thus to his father.
Just as this very body is like a bubble on the water,
and fortunes are as flickering as a lamp in a gale— for whose sake are they [to be desired]?
Who that is wise would desire even those [pleasures] by means of crushing others?
Therefore, I must certainly not fight with my kinsmen.
"Having abandoned the kingdom, I must go from here to some forest;
let these wretched ones remain, so that there be no destruction of my own lineage."
When Jīmūtavāhana had spoken thus, his father Jīmūtaketu,
having likewise made up his mind, replied as follows:
I too must go, my son; for what desire can there be in me, who am old, now that the kingdom has been cast aside like a blade of grass by you, though you are young, out of compassion?
When his father had spoken thus, Jīmūtavāhana, together with his wife, agreed, saying "So be it," and departed for Mount Malaya.
There, at the hermitage site where the perfected ones dwell by a waterfall shaded by sandalwood trees, he remained devoted to the service of his father.
Then, there the self-controlled son of Viśvāvasu, the lord of the Siddhas, named Mittrāvasu, became his friend.
And once in a secluded place, the wise Jīmūtavāhana beheld his sister, a maiden who had been his beloved in another birth.
And at that moment, the mutual gaze of those two youths was like a gentle snare for the deer of the mind.
Then, on one occasion, Mitrāvasu, having approached Jīmūtavāhana— who is honored by the three worlds— suddenly and joyfully addressed him:
"I have a younger sister named Malayavatī;
I shall give her to you. Do not disregard my wish."
Upon hearing this, Jīmūtavāhana also said to him:
"O Prince, she was my wife even in a previous birth."
And you were born right there as my second heart and dear friend;
I am one who remembers former births, and I recall all of that previous life.
When he had spoken thus, Mitrāvasu said to him at that time:
"Tell me first this story of another birth, for I have great curiosity."
Having heard this from Mittrāvasu, the virtuous Jīmūtavāhana related this story of his previous birth to him.
Formerly, I was a Vidyādhara who traveled through the sky; once, I went along the path of the Himalayan peaks.
Then Hara, standing below there and playing with Gaurī, cursed me, saying:
"Fall into a mortal womb," being enraged by my leaping over him.
Having obtained a Vidyadhari as your wife and having installed your son in your own position,
you will remember your former birth and again enter a Vidyadhara womb.
Having thus heard the end of the curse and Śarva having vanished,
before long I was born on earth into a family of merchants.
In the city named Valabhī, I was the son of a very wealthy merchant;
being named Vasudatta, I grew up there.
In due time, having reached youth and being provided with a retinue by my father,
I went to another island for the sake of trade by his command.
Then, as I was coming through the forest, bandits fell upon me;
having bound me and stripped me of my possessions, they led me to their own village, to the temple of Caṇḍikā.
With its long, flickering, and terrible banner of red silk,
it was like the tongue of Death as he seeks to devour the life-breaths of living beings.
There, I was brought by them as an offering into the presence of their own lord,
named Pulindakā, who was worshipping the Goddess.
Upon seeing me, even that Śabara became soft-hearted;
his mind felt affection without cause, as if remembering a love from a previous birth.
Then, having released me from execution, that lord of the Śabaras desired to complete his act of worship by offering himself as a sacrifice.
"Do not do so; I am pleased with you, ask me for a boon.
Being thus addressed by a divine voice, he spoke, filled with joy:
Since you are pleased, what other boon could there be? Nevertheless, I request this much:
may I have friendship with this merchant even in another birth.
When Śāntā had spoken thus, "So be it," that Śabara then sent me to his own home, having provided me with special provisions.
When I had returned from my exile and from the jaws of death,
my father, having learned the news, held a great festival for me.
In due course, I saw there that very same lord of the Śabaras, who had been seized and brought before the king for plundering a merchant caravan.
At that moment, having informed my father and petitioned the king,
I released him from the penalty of execution by paying a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
Having thus performed this act of reciprocal service for the favor of saving his life,
he was brought home with affection and honored fully for a long time.
Then, having been sent off with due honor and having entrusted his heart— tender with love—
to me, that lord of the Śabaras departed for his own village.
There, reflecting on how to offer a gift to me in return for my favor,
he considered even his own pearls, musk, and other possessions to be too meager.
Then, with me as his companion and his bow, he set out for the Himalayas to slay elephants in order to obtain for my sake pearls of the highest excellence.
Wandering there, he reached a great lake with a temple situated on its shore, where he found delight among the lotuses that were like friends, sharing his passion for them.
Suspecting that wild elephants might come there to drink water,
he stood hidden in a secluded spot with his bow, desiring to slay them.
Meanwhile, there she beheld a maiden of wondrous form, mounted upon a lion, who had come to worship Hara at the edge of the lake.
He beheld her, like another daughter of the king of snowy mountains,
remaining in the state of maidenhood and devoted to the service of Śambhu.
And having seen her, the Śabara was overcome with wonder and thought:
"Who might this be? If she is a mortal woman, then how can she have a lion for a mount?"
"Now, how could that divine being be seen by those such as me?
Therefore, this is surely the personified fruition of my former merits for my two eyes."
If, by means of this, I were to unite him with that friend,
then I would have performed for him a truly extraordinary act of requital.
"Let me first approach her to inquire about the boon," having thus reflected,
that Śabara friend of mine drew near to her.
And at that moment, having descended from the lion as he sat in the shade,
a maiden approached and began to gather lotuses from the lake.
And seeing that Śabara who had approached her, she,
having bowed down, delighted him with a welcome out of unprecedented affection for a guest.
"Who are you, and why have you come to this land that is so extremely difficult to traverse?
To her who had thus questioned him, the Śabara replied:
"I am the lord of the Śabaras, whose sole refuge is the feet of Bhavānī;
I have come to this forest for the sake of the pearl released by the Mātaṅga."
And now, O Goddess, having seen you, I have remembered my own life-giving friend,
the illustrious Vasudatta, the son of a merchant leader.
For in beauty and in youth, O beautiful one, you alone are like him,
an unrivaled cascade of nectar for the eyes of this entire world.
Blessed is that maiden in this world whose hand is taken by him here—
the treasury of loving-kindness, generosity, compassion, and fortitude— as her marriage bracelet.
If this form of yours is not united with one such as that, then my pain is this: that Kāma carries his bow in vain.
Thus, by the words of the lord of hunters, the maiden’s mind was instantly captivated,
as if by the syllables of a spell for enchanting with the god of love.
And, impelled by the god of love, she said to that Śabara:
"Where is that friend of yours? Bring him here and show him to me."
Having heard that and saying "So be it," the Śabara took leave of her at that very moment; considering his purpose accomplished, he departed from there in high spirits.
Having reached his own village and taking with him pearls, musk, and other such things—
a vast amount that could only be carried by hundreds of loads— he then returned to our house.
Honored by all, he entered there and presented that gift,
worth many hundreds of thousands of gold pieces, to my father.
When this day had passed in festivities, at night he described to me in private that entire account of seeing the maiden, from its very beginning.
Saying, "Come, let us go right there," the lord of the Śabaras took me, who was eager, and set out freely in the night.
And in the morning, having learned that I had gone somewhere with the Śabara chief,
my father remained there, maintaining his composure out of confidence in his affection for me.
And I was gradually led by that swift Śabara,
who had prepared the way, to the Snowy Mountain.
Having reached that lake in the evening and bathed, both he and I, eating sweet fruits,
spent that single night there in the forest.
It was strewn with flowers from the creepers, made beautiful by the songs of female bees,
carrying auspicious fragrances, enchanting, and illuminated by the lamps of glowing medicinal herbs.
That mountain forest became for us, as we drank the water of that lake at night, like the residence of Indra for the sake of rest.
Then, on the following day, my mind— bearing a longing for each successive step and racing along that path— seemed as if it were coming out to meet me.
With her right eye, which had already signaled her arrival and was now twitching as if out of a desire to see him, that maiden came here.
And I beheld her, with beautiful eyebrows, seated upon the back of a maned lion,
like a digit of the moon resting upon the lap of an autumnal cloud.
And as I gazed upon her, filled with shimmering wonder, longing, and trepidation,
I do not know how my heart then came to be.
Then, descending from the lion, that girl gathered flowers,
bathed in the lake, and worshipped Hara who was situated upon its shore.
And at the conclusion of the worship, that Śabara friend of mine approached,
prostrated himself, announced his identity, and spoke to her with respectful devotion.
"O Goddess, that worthy suitor, a friend to me, has been brought by me;
if you so desire, I shall show him to you this very moment."
Having heard that and being told, "Show him," the Śabara then approached,
led me near, and presented me to her.
She too, casting a sidelong glance at me with eyes overflowing with affection,
fell under the sway of the onset of passion and addressed that lord of the Śabaras:
"This human being is not your friend; some god has come here by his own will. Today he has assumed this mortal form for the sake of deceiving me; whence could such a shape belong to a mortal?"
Having heard that, I spoke to her myself in order to convince her:
"It is true, O beautiful one, that I am a mortal; why use a pretext toward a person so honest?"
For I am the son of a caravan leader named Mahādhana, a resident of Valabhī,
who acquired his wealth through the grace of Maheśvara.
For while he was performing austerities with the moon-crested Lord as his goal for the sake of a son,
the God, being pleased, commanded him thus in a dream.
"Arise! A certain Great Soul shall be born as your son;
this is a supreme secret, so enough with further elaboration here."
Having heard this, as he was awakening, in the course of time a son was born to him,
known by the name Vasudatta.
And this lord of the Śabaras, a friend from my own choosing, was previously encountered by me while I was traveling to another land; he is now my sole kinsman in this time of distress.
When I had finished speaking, saying, "This is the summary of reality for me," the maiden then addressed me, her face bowed down with modesty.
"This is true; and today in a dream, Hara, being pleased, commanded me after I had worshipped him: 'In the morning, you shall obtain a husband.'"
"Therefore, you alone are my husband, and this friend of yours is my brother.
Having gladdened me with these words, which were like nectar, she became silent.
Then, having consulted with her regarding the marriage according to the prescribed rites,
I made the decision to go to my own home accompanied by my friends.
Then that beautiful woman, having summoned her mount, the lion, with a sign of her own, said to me, "O noble son, mount here."
Then, followed by that friend, the Śabara,
I mounted the lion and took my beloved onto my lap.
Then, having accomplished my purpose, I set out for my own home with my beloved seated upon the lion, while that friend proceeded before us.
Subsisting on the flesh of deer pierced by his arrows,
we all eventually reached the city of Valabhī.
Seeing me arrive there, mounted upon a lion together with my beloved, the people were filled with wonder; they went quickly and told my father.
He too, having come forward with joy from his lion-throne as I descended,
saw me bowing at his feet and greeted me with wonder.
Beholding her, who was peerless and had performed the salutation at his feet,
my wife who was worthy of me, he could not contain himself for joy anywhere.
Having led us into the temple and inquired about our circumstances,
he celebrated a festival while praising the friendship of the Śabara lord.
Then, according to the instructions of the astrologers, on the following day, that excellent maiden was married by me,
having assembled all my kinsmen.
And upon seeing that,
my son-in-law’s mount, the lion, suddenly assumed human form while everyone was looking on.
While all the people standing there were bewildered, wondering "What is this?", he—adorned with divine garments and ornaments—bowed and spoke to me thus: ||| SoKss_4,2.135 |||
"I am a Vidyādhara named Citrāṅgada, and this is my daughter, a maiden named Manovatī, who is dearer to me than my own life."
Constantly wandering through the forest with her held in my arms,
I once reached the Ganges, whose banks were filled with ascetic groves.
As I was passing through her midst out of fear of disturbing an ascetic,
my flower garland fell by chance into that water.
Then, rising suddenly while standing within the water, the sage Nārada,
enraged by her falling upon his back, cursed me.
"O evil one, by this arrogance you shall become a lion;
having gone to the Himalayas, you shall carry this daughter on your back."
And when this daughter of yours is married by a human being, then,
simply by the sight of him, you shall be released from this curse.
Thus cursed by the Sage, I became a lioness and remained on the Himalayas,
carrying this daughter of mine who was devoted to the worship of Hara.
Immediately thereafter, how this all-auspicious result was achieved through the efforts of the Śabara chief is already well known to you.
"I shall accomplish that; may it be well with you; this curse has been crossed by me.
Having said this, he immediately flew up into the sky as a Vidyādhara.
Then, overcome with wonder at that, my father— rejoicing with his kinsmen and relatives, delighted by such a praiseworthy alliance— celebrated a great festival.
For who indeed would contemplate the conduct of friends with such sincerity?
For those who, even by sacrificing their own lives, never tire of benefiting their friends.
And thus, no one there uttered anything with wonder,
as they repeatedly contemplated that noble deed of the Śabara chief.
The king also, having learned that to be so,
was exceedingly pleased with the noble-minded Śabara chieftain for his affection toward us.
And being pleased, my father immediately caused the entire kingdom of the forest to be granted to him, who presented me with gifts of jewels.
Then, having achieved my purpose through that wife Manovatī and that friend, the lord of the Śabaras, I remained there in happiness.
And that lord of the Śabaras, his passion for dwelling in his own country having been slackened,
resided for the most part in our very houses.
In their mutual acts of assistance, never satiated at any time,
that period of time passed for both of us, my friend and his.
And not long after, a son was born to me by Manovatī;
he was like a festival for the hearts of an entire lineage that had been cast out.
And he, named Hiraṇyadatta, gradually grew up;
having completed his studies, he was then duly married.
Having seen that and considering his life’s purpose fulfilled, my father,
though old, went with his wife to the Bhāgīrathī to cast off his body.
Then, afflicted by grief for my father, I was somehow made to take heart by my kinsmen,
and I resolved to bear the burden of my own household.
Then, on one hand, the sight of Manovatī’s charming face, and on the other,
my meeting with the lord of the Śabaras, brought me joy.
Then those days of mine passed away, filled with the joy of a virtuous son, the delight of a good wife, and the happiness of meeting with friends.
Then, in the course of time, when I had grown up, old age seized me by the chin, as if out of affection saying for my own benefit: "Son, why are you still in the house even now? (SoKss 4.2.159)
Therefore, with sudden detachment having arisen within me, I appointed my own son to bear the burden of the household, while I myself desired to go to the forest.
Then, together with my wife, I went to Mount Kālañjara along with the Śabara king, who had renounced his kingdom out of affection for me.
Having arrived there, I suddenly remembered my own birth as a Vidyādharī and that curse of Śiva which had reached its end.
And at that very moment, desiring to cast off my human body, I informed my wife Manovatī and my friend, the king of the Śabaras.
"May these two alone be my wife and friend even in another birth as I remember them"— having spoken thus and placed Śaṅkara in his heart, he [departed].
Then, having thrown myself down violently from that mountain slope,
I cast off my body along with those two, my wife and friend.
Thus, having been born from that [state], I am now known by the name Jīmūtavāhana,
born into this family of Vidyādharas and possessing the memory of my former births.
And you, that very lord of the Śabaras, were born again as Mitrāvasu,
the son of King Viśvāvasu of the Siddhas, through the grace of the Three-eyed One.
That Vidyādharī, my friend, was my wife Manovatī;
she has been reborn as your sister, known by the name Valayavatī.
"Thus, this former wife of mine is your sister, and you were my friend in the past; therefore, it is fitting that she should marry me."
"But first, go from here and inform my parents;
once they have given their approval, this desire of yours will be accomplished."
Having heard this from Jīmūtavāhana, Mitrāvasu, with a joyful heart,
went and related everything to his parents.
His words welcomed by them, he was then filled with joy;
approaching his parents, he informed them of that very matter.
When those two were satisfied by the fulfillment of their desire, the crown prince quickly made preparations for his sister’s marriage.
Then, preceded by the King of the Siddhas, Jīmūtavāhana duly took the hand of Malayavatī in marriage.
And there a festival took place, with celestial *cāraṇas* dancing about,
throngs of *siddhas* gathering together, and *vidyādharas* leaping up exultantly.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony, Jīmūtavāhana remained on that Malaya mountain together with his bride, amidst magnificent splendor.
And once, together with his brother-in-law Mitrāvasu,
he went to behold the forested shores of the ocean.
There he saw a young man, distressed and having arrived, turning back his mother who was crying out, "Alas, my son! (SoKss 4.2.178).
Having been abandoned by another man, who was like a soldier following behind him,
he reached a certain broad and lofty rocky surface.
"Who are you? What do you seek? And why does your mother grieve for you?
he asked him; then he too told him his story.
Long ago, it is said, two wives of Kaśyapa, Kadrū and Vinatā,
engaged in a dispute with one another during the course of a conversation.
One woman drove the dark horses of the Sun, while the other drove the white ones;
they entered into a wager there, staking their mutual status as slaves upon it.
Then Kadrū, desiring victory, at her own will caused the horses of the Sun to be fouled by the poisonous hissing of her own sons, the Nāgas.
Having displayed such beings and having deceitfully defeated Vinatā, he made her his slave; for the intolerance of women toward others is indeed a painful thing.
Having learned of this, Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, then approached and,
with gentle words, requested Kadrū to release his mother from her state of servitude.
Then the Nāgas, the sons of Kadrū, having reflected thus, said to him:
"O Vainateya, the ocean of milk has been begun to be churned by the gods."
"Therefore, having gathered the nectar, bestow it upon us for each object;
then accept our mother as yours, for you are the foremost among the powerful."
Having heard these words of the Nāgas and having gone to the Ocean of Milk,
Garuḍa displayed his great prowess for the sake of the nectar.
Then the god Hari himself, pleased by his prowess, commanded him: "I am satisfied with you; choose some boon."
"May the nāgas become my food," he said; thereupon, Vainateya, provoked by his mother's servitude, chose this boon from Hari.
Having been thus commanded by Hari, he who had obtained the nectar through his own prowess was then addressed in this manner by Śakra, who understood the true state of affairs.
"O Lord of Birds, you must act in such a way that this nectar is not consumed by the deluded snakes, so that I may recover it from them."
Having heard this and saying "So be it," Tārkṣya, empowered by the boon of Viṣṇu, took the jar of nectar and approached the nāgas.
To those fools who were terrified by the power of his excellence, he said from afar:
"This nectar has been brought; let it be taken, setting aside my mother."
"If you have fear, I shall set this down for you upon a bed of darbha grass;
having released my mother, I shall depart. Accept the nectar from here."
When those nāgas replied, "So be it," he placed the jar of nectar upon a pure bed of kuśa grass, and they brought his mother there.
And having thus made his mother free from slavery, when Garuḍa had departed,
the nāgas, being now without fear, began to take that nectar.
Then, having suddenly prostrated himself and bewildered them by his own power,
Śakra seized that jar of nectar from the bed of Kuśa grass.
Then those dejected nāgas licked that mat of darbha grass, thinking,
"Perhaps there might be some smear of nectar upon this."
Because of that, their tongues were split and they obtained the state of being double-tongued in vain;
for what else could be the fruit of those who are excessively greedy, other than ridicule?
Then, by the boon of Hari, Tārkṣya, the enemy of the snakes, began to devour those nāgas who had not yet tasted the essence of nectar, swooping down upon them again and again.
And at its impact, the underworld became devoid of life among its serpents due to terror,
its pregnant women miscarried their fetuses, and its snakes were destroyed.
Seeing that, Vāsuki, the lord of the serpents, thought daily that the entire world of the nāgas had perished in a single moment.
Then, having reflected upon that one of irresistible prowess,
he immediately made this agreement with Garuḍa, preceded by a formal request.
"O Lord of Birds, I shall send you one nāga each day for the sake of food, upon the mountain on the shore of the ocean."
"You must not enter the underworld as one who causes destruction;
for by the ruin of the world of the Nāgas, your own self-interest will surely perish."
Having been addressed thus by Vāsuki, Garuḍa said, "So be it," and began to eat one snake sent by him here every day.
In that manner, countless hooded serpents have perished here;
I am the nāga named Śaṅkhacūḍa, and today is my turn.
Therefore, for the sake of being food for the Garuḍa, I have come to this execution stone,
having become an object of grief for my mother due to the command of the Naga king.
Having heard these words of Śaṅkhacūḍa,
Jīmūtavāhana, distressed and filled with inner grief, spoke to him.
"Alas! What a truly cowardly kingship this is for Vāsuki, that his own subjects are led by his own hand to become the prey of his enemy!"
Why did he not first give himself to Garuḍa?
What kind of cowardly witness to the destruction of his own lineage was this that he offered when entreated?
Even Tārkṣya commits some evil after being born from Kaśyapa;
what kind of delusion is this, even for the great, that they act for the sake of the body alone?
Therefore, for now, I shall protect you alone today from Garuḍa by offering my own body; do not despair, my friend.
Having heard that, Śaṅkhacūḍa also spoke this to him with composure:
"Be quiet, O Great Being; do not speak thus again."
It is never fitting for a pearl to suffer damage for the sake of glass;
nor shall I enter into a conversation that brings disgrace upon my family.
Having spoken thus and restrained Jīmūtavāhana, that virtuous one,
perceiving that the hour of Garuḍa was approaching within that very moment, [acted accordingly].
At the time of his end, Śaṅkhacūḍa went there to pay homage to the Lord of Umā, known as Gokarṇa, who dwells upon the shore of the ocean.
When he had departed, Jīmūtavāhana, that treasury of compassion,
perceived that the opportunity had been gained for his own sacrifice in order to save him.
Then, having quickly made it as if forgotten through his own ingenuity,
he sent his own friend Mitrāvasu home under the pretext of some business.
And at that moment, struck by the wind from the wings of the nearby Tārkṣya,
that earth seemed to reel as if from the wonder of beholding that being.
Thinking that the enemy of snakes was approaching, Jīmūtavāhana,
out of compassion for others, ascended that execution stone.
In an instant,
Garuḍa, covering the sky with his shadow, swooped down right there and seized that Great Being, striking him with his beak.
Having led him to the mountain peak, he began to devour him as he flowed with streams of blood and had his crest-jewel torn away and fallen.
At that moment, a rain of flowers fell from the sky;
seeing this, Tārkṣya was struck with wonder, thinking, "What indeed could this be?"
Meanwhile, having bowed there, Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived at Gokarṇa and beheld the surface of the execution stone drenched by a torrent of blood.
"Alas! Fie upon me! Surely that Great-souled One has given his very self for my sake;
where has he been taken by Tārkṣya? What will become of him in this very moment?"
"I shall search quickly; perhaps I might find him.
Thinking thus, that virtuous man went on, following the trail of blood.
In the meantime, seeing Jīmūtavāhana so joyful,
Garuḍa abandoned his meal and reflected with astonishment:
Is this someone else entirely, who, even while being devoured by me,
does not perish but, on the contrary, remains steadfast and even rejoices?
While Tārkṣya was thus reflecting within himself, Jīmūtavāhana, despite being in such a state, spoke to him for the sake of accomplishing his own desired goal.
"O King of Birds, there is indeed flesh and blood in my body;
why have you suddenly desisted from eating, even though you are not yet sated?"
Hearing that, overcome by wonder, the king of birds asked him:
"O virtuous one, you are certainly not a nāga; tell me, who are you?"
"I am indeed a nāga; eat, and complete what you have begun.
For why would an undertaking that has been started be abandoned by the wise before it is finished? (SoKss 4.2.234)
Even as Jīmūtavāhana was thus replying to him,
Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived there from afar and spoke.
"O Garuḍa, do not [seize] me! This is no serpent; indeed, I am a serpent to you.
Therefore, release him! What is this sudden delusion that has arisen in you?"
Upon hearing that, the lord of birds became utterly bewildered,
and Jīmūtavāhana fell into a state of despondency at the failure of his desire.
Then, having learned from the lords of the vidyādharas who were crying out to one another that he had been devoured through delusion, Garuḍa was filled with remorse.
"Alas! A sinful deed has befallen me, a cruel man;
for indeed, those who follow the wrong path find sin easily."
But praiseworthy is this one Great-Souled One, who, by giving his life for the sake of others,
has cast the entire world beneath him, having brought it under the sole power of the delusion that "this is mine."
Then Jīmūtavāhana spoke to Garuḍa, who was thus reflecting on how to purify his sin and was about to enter the fire:
"O Lord of Birds, why are you despondent? If it is true that you fear sin, then from now on these serpents shall no longer be your food."
Furthermore, you must exercise vigilance toward those enjoyers who have already consumed [the offerings];
for this is the remedy in this matter—any other concern you have is in vain.
Thus addressed by him who was compassionate toward all beings, Tārkṣya was pleased and accepted those words as "so be it," just as one would the command of a guru.
And he went swiftly from the celestial realm to fetch the nectar in order to restore to life him whose limbs were wounded there, as well as the other serpents who remained nothing but bones.
Then, having appeared in person, Gaurī, pleased by the devotion of her husband’s wife, sprinkled Jīmūtavāhana with nectar.
By that, his limbs became even more radiant,
together with the joyful sounds of the celestial drums of the gods.
Then, once he had risen up healthy, Garuḍa also brought that nectar from the sky and rained it down here upon the entire shore of the sea.
By that [power], all those serpents there rose up alive;
and then that place shone, crowded with a vast multitude of snakes.
Then Velāvana was freed from the fear of Vainateya,
like Pātāla when Jīmūtavāhana arrived to behold it.
Then, perceiving him resplendent with a body free from decay and with glory,
his kinsmen rejoiced in Jīmūtavāhana.
His wife, his kinsmen, and likewise his parents rejoiced;
for who would not be gladdened by suffering that turns into happiness? (SoKss 4.2.252)
Dismissed by him, Śaṅkhacūḍa departed for the netherworld (rasātala),
while his fame, not being dismissed, wandered at will even through the three worlds.

In the meantime, that young Brahmin Śaktideva was despondent.

Alas, even though the earth is devoid of cohesion through water, and even though it is being constantly trampled, it remains distant from misfortune! SoKss_5,2.10 //

"O Blessed One, I have come from Vardhamānapura;

"In that place there is my noble elder brother named Dīrghatapas; go to him, for that old man might perhaps know that city."

And they gradually led me to the presence of their own lord of the Rākṣasas;
upon seeing me, he too was pleased and appointed me to the office of commander-in-chief.
Then once, having gone there in his pride to attack the Gandharvas,
that lord of the Rākṣasas was slain in battle by his enemies.
At that very moment, my command was accepted by his servants;
thus, remaining in that city, I ruled the kingdom of the Rākṣasas.
There, by chance, he beheld him who had arrived for the sake of the golden lotus.
That state of mine has been stilled by the noble Aśokadatta.
Immediately thereafter, the noble one will relate to you in its entirety how we ourselves recovered our own vidyās through the power of the release from the curse.
When Vijayadatta had thus reported there,
Aśokadatta then described it from the very beginning.
Formerly, while we were two Vidyādharas, we beheld from the sky the daughters of sages bathing in the Gaṅgā at the hermitage of Gālava. (SoKss 5.2.282)
Having suddenly perceived that they both desired her in secret with equal longing, her kinsmen, who possessed divine vision, rebuked them out of anger.
"Both of you, having practiced evil conduct, shall be born in a mortal womb;
even there, a manifold separation shall befall you both."
When one of you has arrived even in a remote region beyond the range of human perception,
and the second shall attain wisdom upon seeing him.
Then, having obtained the lore from the preceptor of the Vidyādharas,
you two shall once again become Vidyādharas, joined with your kinsmen and liberated from the curse.
Thus cursed by those sages, we two were both born here;
how our separation occurred is all known to you.
Now, for the sake of the lotus and by the power of my mother-in-law’s accomplishment,
I have gone to the city of the lord of the rākṣasas and this younger brother of mine has been found by me.
And having received the vidyās from our teacher Prajñaptikauśika right there,
we immediately became holders of vidyās and have swiftly come here.

Having spoken thus to his parents and to that most beloved daughter of the king, Aśokadatta— whose conduct was wondrous and who rejoiced at their immediate liberation from the darkness of the curse— then distributed among them various special sciences by which they instantly became Vidyādharas with awakened minds.
Then, having taken leave of that king together with his parents and his two beloved wives,
the fortunate one, swift as thought, flew up and departed through the path of the sky toward the abode of his own universal monarch.
Having seen him there and received his command, he took the name Aśokavega;
and his brother likewise took the name Vijayavega.
The two brothers, the most excellent youths among the Vidyādharas, accompanied by their own kinsmen, went to their own abode,
the best of mountains known as Govindakūṭa.

Pratāpamukuṭa, the king of Vārāṇasī, was likewise overcome with wonder; having placed a single golden lotus upon the second water-jar in his own temple and having worshipped Tryambaka with other golden lotuses given by him, he rejoiced at the greatness of that connection and considered his lineage to have achieved its purpose.
Thus, by means of a divine cause, beings descend and are born into this world of living creatures;
maintaining the courage and energy appropriate to them, they attain the fulfillment of their goals, even those that are difficult to reach.
Therefore, O ocean of being, I know that you too must be some portion of a divinity, for your success is as you desire;
generally, enthusiasm for even difficult undertakings speaks of the excellence of one's nature.
Moreover, that divine princess Kanakarekhā, who is desired by you, is surely a maiden;
for otherwise, how could she wish for a husband who has seen the Golden City?
Having thus heard this collection of charming tales from Viṣṇudatta in private, Śaktideva,
longing in his heart to behold the City of Gold, maintained his fortitude and passed the night.
Thus ends the second wave in the Caturdārikā-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Third Wave:
Then, on that island of Utsthala, at dawn, while he was staying in that monastery—
That lord of fishermen, Satyavrata, approached Śaktideva.
Having previously committed himself, he approached him and said:
"O Brahmin, for the sake of accomplishing your desired goal, a means has been devised by me."
In the midst of the ocean there is an excellent island called Ratnakūṭa;
there the Blessed Lord Hari dwells, established by the ocean.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, during that festival procession,
people always come from all the continents with great effort to offer worship.
"In that case, it may be that the city of Kanakapurī can somehow be found;
therefore come, let us go there, for that auspicious day is drawing near."
Having been addressed thus by Satyavrata, Śaktideva said,
"So be it," and joyfully accepted the provisions for the journey prepared by Viṣṇudatta.
Then, having boarded the vessel presented by Satyavrata,
he set out swiftly along the path of the ocean together with him alone.
And as he proceeded there to that wondrous abode where crocodiles resembled islands,
he questioned Satyavrata, who stood as the helmsman.
"What is this that appears in the ocean far from here, possessing great splendor,
resembling a lofty winged mountain suddenly risen by chance?"
Then Satyavrata said: "That deity is the banyan tree;
they say that beneath it lies the great whirlpool, the Mare's Mouth."
And having avoided this very place, one goes to that region;
for those who have entered this whirlpool, there is no returning again.
While Satyavrata was speaking thus,
that vessel began to move in that very direction, driven by the force of the waters.
Seeing that, Satyavrata said again to Śaktideva:
"O Brahmin, this time of our destruction has surely arrived."
That this carriage has suddenly sped away right here, and cannot now by any means be stopped by me—how strange! (SoKss_5,3.14)
Thus we have been cast into this deep whirlpool, as if into the very mouth of Death,
having been drawn in by the water as if by a powerful karma.
And this is not at all a source of suffering for me, for whose body is indeed stable?
But it is a source of suffering that your heart's desire has not been accomplished even through great hardship.
"Therefore, while I hold back this carriage for just a moment,
you must quickly grasp a branch of the banyan tree."
Perhaps some means of survival might exist for you, who possess such auspicious form;
for who indeed can fathom the playful whims of Fate or the waves of the ocean?
While this Satyavrata, of resolute character, was thus speaking,
his ship then arrived near that tree.
At that moment, Śaktideva, having leaped up and freed from his trepidation,
seized a broad branch of that banyan tree by the sea.
But Satyavrata, with his body and his vehicle still moving,
entered the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha) here, having dedicated himself to the welfare of others.
And Śaktideva,
though he had clung to a branch of that tree whose branches filled the quarters, became hopeless and reflected:
I have not yet seen that city of Kanakapurī;
while perishing on this pathless way, even this lord of fishermen has been lost to me.
Or rather, whose wish can prevail against the power of destiny, which has its feet ever-planted upon the head of all? (SoKss 5.3.24)
As that young man, reflecting thus on what was appropriate for his situation,
sat upon the trunk of a tree, the day passed away.
And in the evening, he saw many great birds from all sides entering that banyan tree, filling the quarters of the horizon with their cries.
He saw vultures being greeted, as it were, out of affection for their long acquaintance by the waves of the ocean tossed by the wind from their broad wings.
Then, concealed by a mass of leaves, he heard the conversation of those birds perched on the branches as they spoke to one another in human speech.
One described another continent, another a mountain, and another a distant region;
each one recounted that place where [the Buddha] had set foot during that day.
And one aged bird from among them spoke:
"Today I went to the City of Gold to roam about."
And tomorrow morning I shall go there again to wander at my ease;
for what purpose is a long journey that brings only fatigue?
Thus, his distress being stilled by the bird’s words, which were like a sudden shower of nectar, Śaktideva reflected:
"By good fortune, that city truly exists, and this very means for reaching it is mine:
this bird of immense body who has been made my vehicle."
Having reflected thus, Śaktideva then approached slowly and hid himself within the back and wings of that sleeping bird.
In the morning, after those other birds had departed,
that bird displayed its wondrous partiality, just like the way of fate.
Carrying Śaktideva unobserved upon his back,
Dattāskanda went in an instant to that City of Gold once more to roam about.
While that bird was seated there in the midst of that garden,
Śaktideva quietly alighted from its back.
Having moved away from his side, as he was wandering there,
he beheld two women intent on gathering flowers.
Having approached slowly, while they were struck with wonder at the sight of him, he asked: "What region is this, and who are you two, ladies?"
This city named Kanakapurī is the abode of the Vidyādharas;
and in it, O friend, dwells a Vidyādharī named Candraprabhā.
"And know us to be her garden-keepers here in this grove;
this collection of flowers is for her sake," they both said to him.
Then that brahmin also said: "Do for me likewise, so that I too may see your mistress here."
Having heard this and said "So be it," those two women led the young man from within the city to the royal palace.
Having arrived there, he beheld that mansion of Saṃketa, radiant with pillars of rubies and walls of gold, as if it were the very abode of all prosperity.
And seeing him arrived there, all the attendants went and reported that marvel of a human's arrival to Candraprabhā.
Having thus instructed the doorkeeper, she then had that brahmin ushered without delay into her presence within the inner apartments.
Having entered, he too beheld her there, a feast for the eyes,
as if she were the personified perfection of the Creator’s wondrous craftsmanship.
And she, rising from her couch of fine jewels even from afar,
honored him herself with a welcome, being captivated by the sight of him.
And when he was seated, he asked: "O auspicious one, who are you, being such as this?
And how have you reached this earth, which is inaccessible to mortals?"
Having been addressed thus by Candraprabhā, Śaktideva, with curiosity, announced his own country, his birth, and his name.
He described how he had come to obtain that princess named Kanakarekhā by wagering his vision of her city.

Having understood that and reflected for a moment, Candraprabhā then sighed deeply and spoke to Śaktideva in private: tad buddhvā kim api dhyātvā dīrghaṃ niḥśvasya sā tataḥ / candraprabhā taṃ vijane śaktidevam abhāṣata // SoKss_5,3.52 //
Listen, O fortunate one; I shall now tell you something:
there is on this earth a lord of the Vidyādharas named Śaśikhaṇḍa.
We four were born to him as his daughters in succession;
I am the eldest, Candraprabhā, and another is Candrarekhā.
Śaśirekhā was the third, and Śaśiprabhā the fourth;
we have all grown up here in our father’s house in that order.
And once, while I was observing the vow of maidenhood, all three of my sisters went together to the bank of the Mandākinī to bathe.
There, having begun their water sports, they drenched with water a sage named Agryatapas who was standing in the water, out of pride in their youth.
Being excessively persistent, the sage became enraged and cursed them all, saying:
"May you all be born as wicked daughters in the world of mortals!"
Having learned of that, our father went and propitiated him;
he then declared the end of the curse for each of them individually, according to their respective circumstances.
The great sage bestowed upon all of them the recollection of their past births, augmented by divine knowledge, even while they remained in their mortal state.
Then, after those queens had abandoned their bodies and departed for the mortal world,
my father, having given this city to me, went to the forest out of weariness.
Furthermore, while I was dwelling here, the goddess Ambikā appeared to me in a dream and commanded:
"Daughter, you shall have a human husband."
Because I held back my father as he was pointing out various excellent Vidyādharas to me, I remain even now a mere maiden.
And now, having captivated you by this wondrous arrival and by my very form, I have been surrendered to you alone.
"Therefore, on the coming fourteenth day, I shall go for your sake to the great mountain named Ṛṣabha to present my petition to my father."
On that lunar day every year,
all the foremost of the Vidyādharas gather from every direction to worship the god Hara.
"My father will come to that very place; having obtained his permission, I shall return here quickly. Thereafter, you may marry me."
Having said, "Therefore, stay here for now," Candraprabhā attended to Śaktideva with various enjoyments suitable for Vidyādharas.
And as he stood there, saying "So be it," there arose for him at that moment a bliss such as one feels when plunging into a pool of nectar after being scorched by a forest fire.
And when the fourteenth day had arrived, Candraprabhā said to him:
"Today I shall go to make a request to my father on your behalf."
"All these attendants shall go with me;
you must not experience suffering alone for two days."
Furthermore, even while residing in this temple,
you must by no means ascend to the middle level.
Having spoken thus to that youth, Candraprabhā, having surrendered her heart to him and following his mind, departed from there.
He too, remaining there alone,
wandered from place to place of great splendor, diverting his mind.
Then, his curiosity aroused, he thought, "What indeed has she forbidden me here? Is it the mounting upon her back because I am the daughter of a Vidyādhara?"
He ascended that middle floor of the palace;
for the inclinations of the human mind generally turn away from what is forbidden.
Having ascended there, he saw three jeweled pavilions guarded [by spirits];
one had its door open, and he entered into its midst.
And having entered within, he beheld someone lying on a couch made of excellent jewels, provided with a mattress, his body covered by a cloth.
As soon as he lifted the cloth and looked, he saw that the excellent maiden, the daughter of King Paropakārin, was likewise dead.
Having seen this, he then reflected: "What is this great marvel?
Is she asleep in a state of unconsciousness, or is this some uncontradicted illusion?"
She for whose sake I am on this journey stays right here;
she has lost her life in that land, while I remain alive.
And her splendor remains unfading; therefore, it is certain that for some reason the Creator is spreading this illusion before me.
Having reflected thus and gone out, he entered those two other pavilions in succession; inside, he beheld likewise other maidens.
Having emerged from that temple as well, he, filled with wonder,
sat down and beheld an exceedingly excellent pond below.
On its bank he saw a horse with a jeweled saddle;
having dismounted there, he then approached its side out of curiosity.
Seeing it empty, he desired to mount it;
but by that horse, having been struck with its hoof, he was cast into that pond.
Plunged therein, he quickly emerged in great agitation from the middle of a garden pond in his own city of Vardhamāna.
And in his birthplace, he suddenly beheld himself standing in the water of a pond,
resembling a white water-lily, yet miserable without the radiance of the moon.
Where is this city of Vardhamāna, and where is that city of the Vidyādharas?
Oh, what is this manifestation of the grand display of illusion?
"What a misery! I, unfortunate as I am, have been deceived by someone for some reason; or rather, who here knows what the course of destiny will be?"
Reflecting thus, Śaktideva then emerged from the middle of the pool and, filled with wonder, went to his own father’s house.
There, having feigned the wandering about with the drum that had been assigned to him,
he remained together with his joyful kinsmen, who were delighted by his father.
On the second day, having gone outside the house, he again heard these words being proclaimed with the beating of drums throughout that city: SoKss_5,3.93 //
The king bestows his daughter, along with the rank of crown prince, upon whoever has seen Kanakapurī in its true nature from among the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
Upon hearing that, the capable Śaktideva went to those criers of the proclamation and spoke again: "I have seen that city."
He was quickly led before the king; and the king, recognizing him, considered him once again to be a liar, just as he had been before.
"If I speak falsely, if that city was not seen by me,
then let my wager now be the punishment of this body."
When it was said, "Let that princess question me today," the king then went with his attendants and had his daughter brought to that very spot.
Having seen that brahmin whom she had seen before, she said to the king:
"Father, he will surely speak something false once again."
Then Śaktideva said, "O Princess, I shall tell you whether this is true or false;
but first, speak thus to me, for I am curious."
In Kanakapurī, I saw you lying on a couch, lifeless;
how is it that I see you here alive?
Having been addressed thus by Śaktideva with the token of recognition,
that princess Kanakarekhā immediately spoke in this manner before her father:
"Father, that city has indeed been seen by this great-souled one;
and before long, he will become my husband while I remain there."
There he will marry my three sisters and others as well,
and he will exercise sovereignty over the Vidyādharas in that city.
But today I must enter both my own body and that city;
for by the sage’s curse, I was born here in your house.
When a human being, still bearing the state of a mortal, beholds your body in Kanakapurī,
he will achieve the penetration of reality.
"Then there shall be your release from the curse, and he shall become your human husband"—
thus did that sage further prescribe the end of my curse.
Even in this human state, I am thus possessed of knowledge and the power of recollecting my past lives;
therefore, I shall now go to my own Vidyādhara realm for the sake of attaining perfection.
Having spoken thus, the princess cast off her body and vanished;
and a tumultuous cry of lamentation arose in that royal palace.
Śaktideva, too, fallen from both sides and brooding upon those two beloved ones he had failed to reach despite undergoing various insurmountable hardships, remained lost in thought.
Though he reproached himself and was distressed by his unfulfilled desires,
he departed from the royal palace and reflected thus for a moment:
"What was desired by me shall indeed come to pass," so it was said by Kanakarekhā;
why then do I despair? For spiritual accomplishments depend upon one's own inner strength.
"I shall go once again to that City of Gold by that very same path;
surely fate will provide me with a means to reach it."
Having reflected thus, Śaktideva departed from that city;
for the wise, having undertaken an effort, do not turn back until their purpose is accomplished.
And after traveling for a long time, he once again reached that city named Viṭaṅkapura, situated upon the shore of the ocean.
There he saw that merchant approaching before him—
the one with whom he had previously gone to sea when the ship was wrecked.
Could this be Samudradatta? And how did he fall into the ocean and then emerge from it?
It is no wonder; I myself am the proof of this.
Having reflected thus, as soon as the brahmin approached that merchant,
the merchant recognized him and, filled with joy, embraced him around the neck.
And having led him to his own home and offered him hospitality, he asked:
"When the ship was wrecked, how did you emerge from the ocean?"
Śaktideva also related that entire account exactly as it had happened,
including how he had previously reached the island of Utsthala after being swallowed by a fish.
And immediately thereafter, he questioned that excellent merchant as well: "Tell me, how did you yourself cross the ocean at that time?"
Then that merchant also said: "At that time, having fallen into the ocean, I wandered for three days, clinging to a single plank."
Then, by that path, a ship suddenly arrived;
seeing me crying out from there, those on board took me up onto it.
And having ascended it, I then saw my father there,
who had previously gone to another continent and had returned at that time after a long interval.
Seeing me and recognizing me, my father embraced my neck and, weeping, asked for news of me; and I spoke to him thus: SoKss_5,3.125 //
"O father, although you had been away for a long time and had not yet returned,
I myself engaged in trade, thinking it to be my own duty."
Then, while traveling to another island, I was submerged in the ocean today due to the wrecking of my ship, and having been found, I have been rescued by you.
When I had spoken thus, my father addressed me reproachfully:
"For what purpose do you expose yourself to such dangers to your life?"
"For I have wealth, my son, and I am established in its acquisition;
see this ship brought by me for you, filled with gold."
Having spoken thus and comforted me, he brought me by that very same vehicle to his own home in Viṭaṅkapura; from there, I was brought here by him.
Having heard this from the merchant, Śaktideva rested that night and spoke to him on the following day.
"O caravan leader, I must go once again to the island of Utsthala;
therefore, tell me now, how shall I go there? (SoKss 5.3.132)
"My merchants have set out there today;
you should board their ship and travel along with them."
Having been addressed thus by that merchant,
Śaktideva then departed for the island of Utsthala together with those traders.
"That noble kinsman of mine, Viṣṇudatta, who stays here—
just as before, I wish to dwell near him in that very monastery."
Having thus reached the island and reflected upon that moment,
the brahmin set out to proceed along the central path of the marketplace.
And at that moment, by chance, the sons of the fisherman’s lord saw him there;
having recognized Satyavrata from close by, they spoke as follows: SoKss_5,3.137 //
"O Brahmin, you went from here at that time to Kanakapurī together with my father; how is it that you have come back alone today?"
Then Śaktideva said, "Your father fell into the ocean;
his ship was dragged away by the waters and he was cast into the mouth of the submarine fire."
Having heard that, the sons of the fisherman became enraged and said to their servants:
"Bind this evil-minded man! By him our father has been killed."
Otherwise, how could it be that while there is but one ship, one person falls into the submarine fire and the second emerges from it? (SoKss 5.3.141)
Therefore, this slayer of his father must be offered as a sacrificial victim by us before the goddess Caṇḍikā tomorrow at dawn.
Having said this, those sons of the fisherman then bound their servant Śaktideva and led him from there to the terrifying temple of Caṇḍikā.
With its vast belly perpetually swallowing many living beings,
and with rows of tinkling bells for its row of teeth, it was like the gaping mouth of Death.
There, bound and staying through the night, doubting his own life, that Śaktideva made this petition to the goddess Caṇḍī: SoKss_5,3.145 //
O Blessed One, by you, with a form resembling the orb of the rising sun,
the world was saved as if it were the blood from the throats of the Dānavas, which had been drunk up and then poured forth again.

Therefore, O Giver of Boons, protect me— who am constantly prostrate before you, who have fallen into the hands of a group of causeless enemies, and who have come from afar— with the thirst to attain my beloved.
Having thus addressed the goddess and somehow obtained sleep,
he saw in a dream a woman emerging from that inner chamber.
Approaching him with a divine form, she spoke to him as if out of compassion:
"O Śaktideva, do not fear; no misfortune shall befall you."
Among these ten sons of the fisherman, there is a sister named Bindumatī;
seeing you as a maiden in the morning, she will request you for the sake of marriage.
And you should practice that; she alone will liberate you.
She is not a fisherwoman, for she is a divine woman fallen from her state due to a curse.
Having heard this, as he awoke, that fisherman’s daughter came to the temple of the goddess at dawn like a shower of nectar for his eyes.
Approaching him and announcing herself, she spoke to him with eager longing:
"I shall release you from here; therefore, do what I desire."
"These suitors were indeed approved by my brothers, yet they were rejected by me;
however, upon seeing you, affection has arisen within me, so please accept me."
Thus addressed by Bindumatī, the daughter of the lord of fishermen,
Śaktideva recalled his dream and, filled with joy, accepted her proposal.
He was liberated by her very self and married that beautiful-faced woman,
whose union was desired and arranged by his brothers through the instructions of Ambikā obtained in a dream.
And he remained there together with that divine woman, who had assumed another form and was obtained solely through his merit, as if she were the very accomplishment of his happiness.
Once, while standing on the roof of his palace, he saw a Caṇḍāla coming along the road carrying a load of beef; seeing him, he spoke to his beloved wife.
O slender-waisted one, behold how this evildoer eats the flesh of those cows who are worthy of worship even by the three worlds! SoKss_5,3.159
Having heard that, Bindumatī then said to her husband:
"Noble son, this is inconceivable; what can be said regarding this evil?"
"By the power of my [past] cows, though for even a very slight offense, I was born into this family of fishermen; what atonement can there be for this?"
Even as she was speaking thus, Śaktideva said to her:
"It is strange; speak, my dear, who are you, and how did you come to be born as a fisherman's daughter?"
To him who was thus questioning her with such persistence, she said:
"I shall tell you this, even though it is a secret, if you will do my bidding."
When he replied with an oath, "Certainly, my dear, I shall do so," she then spoke to him thus regarding her initial desire: SOkss_5,3.164.
"In this island, your second wife shall now also be yours;
and, noble son, she will soon become pregnant."
And in the eighth month of pregnancy, you must tear open her belly and pull out that fetus; you must not feel any compassion in this matter.
When she had spoken thus, while he was wondering "What is this?
and filled with increasing compassion, that daughter of the lord of fishermen spoke again.
"O compassionate one, you must follow my word for some reason;
now hear this: who I am and how my birth as a fisherman came about."
"In a previous birth, I was once a certain Vidyādharī;
now, by a curse, I have fallen from that state into the world of mortals."
And when, in my state as a Vidyādhara, I cut the strings of lutes with my teeth and rejoined them, because of that I was born here in the household of a fisherman.
Thus, when the mouths of cows are touched by even a single dry tendon, such is their downward destiny;
what then can be said of those who eat their flesh?
While she was speaking thus,
her brother approached in great haste and addressed Śaktideva.
"Arise! This great boar has emerged from somewhere;
having killed many people out of pride, he is now advancing here toward us."
Having heard that, Śaktideva immediately descended from his own palace,
mounted his horse with his spear in hand, and galloped toward the boar.
And as soon as he saw that hero rushing toward him,
the boar fled wounded and entered a cave.
Śaktideva also, searching for him, entered that very place and in an instant beheld a great, secluded garden grove containing a dwelling.
And standing there, he beheld a maiden of most wonderful form,
approaching with agitation as if she were a forest deity moved by affection.
And he asked her, "O auspicious lady, who are you, and what is this agitation of yours?
Hearing that, the fair-faced woman replied to him in this way:
"There is a king named Caṇḍavikrama, the lord of the southern quarter;
O fortunate one, I am his daughter, a maiden named Bindurekhā."
And here today, that wicked Daitya, with blazing eyes, having seized me by a ruse, has brought me from my father’s house all of a sudden.
Seeking meat, he had gone outside having assumed the form of a boar;
today, while afflicted by hunger, he was pierced by a certain hero with a spear.
As soon as he was pierced, he entered [the fire] and met his death;
and I, my maidenhood remaining untainted, fled and emerged.
Having heard that, Śaktideva said to her: "Then why this agitation?
For it was by me alone, O princess, that the boar was slain with my spear."
Then she also said, "In that case, tell me, who are you?
And he replied, "I am a Brahmin named Śaktideva."
Then, having been addressed by her, "In that case, you alone shall be my husband," the hero agreed, saying "So be it," and taking her with him, he emerged through the opening of the cave.
Having gone home and informed his wife Bindumatī of that,
she trusted him and he married that maiden Bindurekhā.
Then, while that Śaktideva, who had two wives, was living there,
one of those wives, Bindurekhā, became pregnant.
And in the eighth month of her pregnancy,
her first wife, Bindumatī, approached him in private and said to Śaktideva:
O Hero, remember that which was promised by you to me;
this is now the eighth month of pregnancy for your second wife.
Therefore, go and, having ripped open her womb, take out the fetus;
for your own word of truth must not be transgressed.
Thus addressed by her, Śaktideva— agitated by affection and compassion,
yet constrained by his vow— was for a moment at a loss for what to do.
Filled with agitation, he went out and approached Bindurekhā;
she too, seeing him approaching dejected, spoke to him thus:

Listen, O Lord, to this story of Devadatta:
formerly there was a brahmin named Haridatta in the city called Kambuka.

And there he saw, all alone, a solitary practitioner of great vows named Jālapāda, who had accomplished many magical feats and was engaged in silent recitation.

Having heard these words of Queen Tārādattā,

Truly, even a small dharma properly performed becomes of great fruit;

"And thus, even this cow has perished in this forest devoid of water, trees, and humans; what small matter for my teacher could possibly remain after that?"

Therefore, until death, a wise person should act for the benefit of sentient beings in all desired circumstances, in order to attain perfect awakening, by turning back from all worldly hopes.
And so, in former times, seven exceedingly beautiful daughters were born in succession to a certain king named Kṛtanāman.

even with this very body, we shall perform what is beneficial for sentient beings.
"Let us cast this living body, O Jīvadeva, into the cemetery for the use of the hosts of flesh-eaters; for what is the use of even such a beloved one?"
And so, in former times, there was a certain prince here who became disenchanted;
though he was young and very handsome, he took up the life of a wandering mendicant.

"Blessed is that woman who is gazed upon by this eye of yours.

"Tell me, what is so charming about these two that they are just like this?

Long ago, O beloved, there was a certain ascetic in a certain grove by the Ganges,
desiring to test the very limit of dispassion.
And while he was practicing austerities, a certain king happened by fate to arrive at that very place to sport together with the women of his harem.

And having seen that sage established in meditative absorption in one part of that place,

When they had remained there for a long time, the king then woke up;
not seeing his beloveds by his side, he wandered everywhere.
And there he saw those queens standing surrounding the sage;
enraged by jealousy toward him, he struck the sage with his sword.
What could sovereignty, envy, cruelty, intoxication, and lack of discernment not accomplish individually? What need is there to speak of their power when they are all five present together?

Listen now as I relate here the story of Sulocanā.

Thus, having descended from the midst of the sky with a display born of her longing,

And seeing her suddenly approached, the king was filled with wonder and thought: "Aha! Who might this be, possessing such an inconceivable form?"
She cannot be human, since her feet do not touch the dust and her eyes do not blink; therefore, she is surely some divine being.
However, she must not be questioned by me, for she might flee at any time;

Meditating thus, that king, having conversed with her,

"Such is our agreement; therefore, you must protect this maiden. Through her marriage, our reunion shall take place again in heaven."

Having been addressed in this way by his ministers, the king, who understood the matter,

"Oh, how truly extraordinary is the beauty of this maiden!
If she does not become my wife, what other fruit is there for my asceticism?"
While the young sage was thus meditating, he was beheld by that Sulocanā,

Beholding him, who held a rosary and a water-pot, she too, filled with affection, thought:

"If this desire of yours is not free from guile, then,

"O illustrious one, let it be investigated how this could have happened. SoKss_6,2.86 //
Having heard that, the son of the sage reflected thus for a moment:
"Was not Pramadvarā, born of Menakā, formerly bitten by a serpent?"

why then was the hunter Triśaṅku not led to heaven by Viśvāmitra?
"By expending a portion of my own ascetic merit, why should I not do this?
Having reflected thus, the sage said, "This is no burden," and spoke.

When that sage had spoken thus while the royal assembly was listening, a divine voice, clearly articulated, arose from there, saying: "So be it."

"Thus, O Lord, Suṣeṇa attained his purpose through the maiden;

Having heard this story from the twice-born man who had grown old in his service,
King Kaliṅgadatta abandoned his anxiety and was filled with joy.
And he gave that young daughter of his, who brought joy to the eyes and resembled a digit of the moon, the name Kaliṅgasenā.
Then, in her father’s house, that princess Kaliṅgasenā gradually grew up, surrounded by her playmates.
