Beholding her, who was enchanting the minds of sages with her beauty,
Somaprabhā, while still stationed in the sky, felt a surge of affection and thought:
"Who is she? Is this the form of the daughter of the Moon? Whence comes such radiance for her by day?
Or if she is Rati, where is Kāma? As for this maiden, I understand her to be something else."
"Someone here in Rājagṛha must be a divine being fallen due to a curse;
I know that surely there was friendship between her and me in a previous birth."
"For this very reason my mind, agitated by excessive affection for her, speaks thus to me;
therefore, it is right that I myself should once again make her my own chosen companion."
Having reflected thus, out of fear that the young woman might be terrified,
Somaprabhā descended unobserved from the sky.
Resorting to the guise of a human maiden as a means of consolation,
she gradually drew near to this Kaliṅgasenā.
"By good fortune, some princess of most wonderful form has come of her own accord to my side; she is a fitting companion for me."
Thus, reflecting upon that very sight, Kaliṅgasenā rose up with reverence and then affectionately embraced Somaprabhā.
Having seated her, he asked after a moment for her lineage and name;
and Somaprabhā said to him, "I will tell you everything, but please wait."
Then, through the very course of their conversation, friendship was established by those two with words,
preceded by the grasping of each other's hands.
Then Somaprabhā said: "Friend, you are a princess;
friendship with princes is maintained with great difficulty, even under the most trying circumstances."
For they become excessively angry even at a slight offense;
in this regard, I shall relate to you the story of the prince and the merchant's son.
In the city of Puṣkarāvatī, there was a king named Gūḍhasena;
it is said that he had only one son born to him.
That prince, being arrogant because he was an only son, endured whatever his father did, whether it were auspicious or inauspicious.
Once, while wandering in the grove, he saw the only son of the merchant Brahmadatta, whose wealth and appearance were equal to his own.
And upon seeing him, he immediately made him his own friend for the svayaṃvara;
at that very moment, the prince and the merchant's son became identical in appearance.
They were unable to remain for long out of each other's sight;
for affection quickly binds those who have been acquainted in a previous life.
The prince never consumed that enjoyment which had been prepared for him at the very outset for the merchant’s son.
Once, having first resolved upon his marriage with his friends,
that prince set out for Ahicchatra for the sake of the wedding.
Mounted upon an elephant together with that friend and his army,
he proceeded and, having reached the bank of the Ikṣumatī, took up residence there in the evening.
There, having indulged in drink at the rising of the moon and retired to his bed,
he began to tell a story when requested by his own nurse.
Having begun their conversation, the nurse was overcome by exhaustion and intoxication and fell asleep;
she likewise, and the merchant’s son as well, remained awake out of affection.
Then, while the others were asleep, that merchant’s son, remaining awake, heard in the sky a conversation like that of women among themselves.
"This man has fallen asleep without finishing his story; therefore, I shall curse him.
In the morning, he will see this necklace, and if he should seize it—" ||| SoKss_6,2.124 ||
"By this [snake] clinging to his throat, he will meet death at that very moment.
Having said this, one [demoness] fell silent, and then the second spoke:
Therefore, if he has crossed over, he will see the mango tree;
he will partake of its fruits, and from that he will be released from his life.
Having said this, she too ceased speaking; then the third one spoke:
"If he has even crossed over this, then let him go home for the sake of marriage."
"If he has entered, that very thing will fall upon his back to kill him.
Having said this, she too turned back; then the fourth spoke:
Therefore, even if he has crossed over [the danger], should he enter the residence of Vāsava at night,
he will immediately sneeze a hundred times.
If no one here were to say "Live! to him even a hundred times, then he would fall under the power of death.
"If he who heard this should speak of it for the sake of protecting him,
his death too will come"— having said this, she turned back.
And the merchant’s son, having heard all that [news] as terrible as a thunderbolt,
was agitated by affection for the prince and reflected:
"Fie on this story that has begun but remains untold, if the deities have come to listen unobserved and, out of curiosity, are now cursing! (SoK 6.2.133)
"Therefore, if this prince were to die, what purpose would my life serve?
Thus, he must be protected by me," said that friend who was as dear to him as his own life.
"I must not even speak of this matter, lest I too incur blame because of it.
Having reflected thus, the merchant’s son passed the night with great difficulty.
The prince also set out in the morning with his companion,
and on the road he saw that necklace ahead and desired to take it.
Then the merchant’s son said: "Friend, do not take the necklace;
this is an illusion, for otherwise how could these soldiers not see it?"
Having heard that, the prince left him and, proceeding further, saw a mango tree; he desired to eat its fruits.
And as before, he was dissuaded from that course by the merchant’s son;
with inner distress, traveling slowly, he reached his father-in-law’s house.
There, as he was entering the house for the sake of marriage, he was turned back at the door by that very friend; and just then, that house collapsed.
Then, having somehow emerged from that with some degree of confidence, the prince, accompanied by his bride, entered another dwelling at night.
Then, while that merchant's son had entered and remained there unobserved,
he lay down upon his bed and sneezed a hundred times.
Having uttered "Live long! to him here even a hundred times, the merchant's son, his purpose accomplished, went out joyfully at his own will.
And seeing him departing accompanied by his bride, the prince—having forgotten his affection for him due to jealousy—spoke angrily to the gatekeepers: SoKss_6,2.144 //
"This evil-souled man has entered my inner apartments while I was in private;
therefore, let him be bound and kept until he is apprehended at dawn."
Having learned of this, the merchant’s son was bound by the guards and taken through the night;
as he was being led to the place of execution by them in the morning, he said to them:
"First, lead me for a moment to the presence of the prince, so that I may state a certain reason; thereafter, you may carry out my execution."
When he had spoken thus, those ministers went and informed the prince; and after being exhorted by other counselors, the prince ordered her to be brought.
Once he had been brought, he related the account to the prince; and through that proof, the prince also believed it to be true, concluding that the house had indeed collapsed and then risen again.
Then, being gratified by that friend who had been released from execution,
the prince returned to his own city with his wife.
There, that friend of his, the merchant’s son who had taken a wife,
remained at ease while his virtues were being praised by all the people.
Thus having become unrestrained and crushing their own controllers,
the princes do not heed what is beneficial, like elephants in rut.
What friendship can there be with those vetālas who snatch away one's life while laughing?
Therefore, O Princess, never let our friendship ever waver.
Having heard this story from the mouth of Somaprabhā in the palace, Kaliṅgasenā affectionately replied to her friend: SoKss_6,2.154 //
"These are piśācas, my friend; they are not considered to be princes.
Listen as I relate to you the story of the evil possession by a piśāca."
Long ago, in an agrahāra named Yajñasthala, there lived a certain twice-born man;
once, having fallen into poverty, he went to the forest to fetch firewood.
There, a piece of wood being split by an axe fell by the power of fate; having struck his shank, it pierced through and entered inside.
Then, seeing him unconscious with blood flowing from his wounds,
a man who recognized him picked him up and carried him home.
There, his agitated wife washed away his blood,
comforted him, and bound a bandage upon his calf.
Then, as he was being treated, his wound not only failed to heal day by day, but moreover, it developed into a sinus tract.

Then, distressed by that sinus ulcer, the poor man, intent on death, approached a certain Brahmin friend who spoke to him in private: SoKss_6.2.161: "Then, distressed by that sinus ulcer, the poor man, intent on death, approached a certain Brahmin friend who spoke to him in private."
My friend, named Yajñadatta, having long been extremely destitute,
performed the rite for propitiating a piśāca, obtained wealth, and remained happy.
And since I have told you that very means of accomplishment, therefore, my friend, accomplish the piśāca; he will heal your wound.
Having spoken thus, he who had received the mantra said to him:
"Rising in the final watch of the night, with hair disheveled and naked as the sky, perform this rite."
And without having sipped water, taking two handfuls of rice as much as he can with both hands while reciting the mantra, he should go to a crossroads.
"Having set aside two handfuls of rice there, O friend, you should then proceed in silence; do not look back."
"Act thus always until the piśāca becomes manifest;
he will himself say to you, 'I shall indeed destroy your disease.'"
"Then he will rejoice in that, and he will take away your disease.
Having been told this by his friend, that brahmin did exactly as instructed.
Then that perfected piśāca, having brought great medicinal herbs from the lord of mountains, the Himalayas, healed the wound of that suffering man.
Then, with the auspicious moment having arrived, he joyfully said to that brahmin:
"Give me a second wound, so that I may heal it."
"If I do not create misfortune for you, I shall destroy your body.
Hearing that, the brahmin became terrified and immediately spoke to him for the sake of liberation.
"I shall inflict a second wound upon you in seven days," he said;
thereupon, abandoned by him, that brahmin became hopeless of life.
Having spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā ceased from the midst of her speech out of shame for having uttered such indecent words; then she spoke this again to Somaprabhā:
Then, seeing and questioning that distressed brahmin, the clever widow spoke to him, finding an opening in his wounds: SoKss_6,2.174 //
"I shall deceive that piśāca; go and tell him again:
'Let a sinus ulcer be inflicted by you upon my daughter.'"
Having heard that, the brahmin went away delighted; and having spoken exactly as instructed, he then brought that piśāca into the presence of his daughter.
And she showed her own private parts to that piśāca,
saying in secret, "O noble one, heal this wound of mine."
And that foolish piśāca constantly applied medicinal pastes and ointments to her noble limb, yet he was not able to heal it.
And after several days, becoming weary, he placed her two calves upon his own shoulders and gazed at that beautiful limb, wondering, "Why does it not grow?"
When he saw a second one beneath that, which was a festering wound,
the piśāca was immediately seized with alarm and thought to himself:
"One wound has not yet healed when this other one arises; the popular saying is true: that misfortunes multiply through one's vulnerabilities. (SoKss 6.2.181)
From whom the worlds arise and by whom they go to their dissolution—
who is capable of closing that which has opened wide as the path of saṃsāra?
Having reflected thus, and fearing imprisonment due to the realization of a contrary outcome,
that foolish piśāca then fled and vanished from sight.
And having thus deceived that piśāca, she released him;
that twice-born man remained at ease, like one who has emerged from a disease.
In this way, those fools who are like Piśācas and even princes—though they may have attained success, O friend, they lead to misfortune; therefore, they must be guarded by means of wisdom.
"Princesses of noble lineage have never been heard of anywhere as being like this;
therefore, my friend, you must not think otherwise regarding our union."
Having thus heard from the mouth of Kaliṅgasenā this account, which was full of laughter, wonder, and sweetness, Somaprabhā attained satisfaction in due order.
"My home is sixty yojanas from here, and the day is drawing to a close;
I have stayed for a long time, O slender one, so I must go," she said to her.
Then, as the lord of the day was slowly approaching the peak of the western mountain, Somaprabhā took leave of her affectionate friend and,
having caused a momentary wonder by leaping into the path of the sky, departed with great speed for her own dwelling.
And having beheld that most wonderful and marvelous sight, Kalingasenā entered and reflected with many conjectures:
"Alas, I do not know what this is; could my friend perhaps be a Siddha woman, or an Apsaras, or even a Vidyādharī?"
This celestial [power] is indeed real and unfailing, moving at the very summit of the sky; and divine beings go into union with human women, drawn by incomparable affection.
Did Arundhatī not share friendship with the daughter of King Pṛthu? And out of love for her, did Pṛthu not bring Surabhi from heaven down to the surface of the earth?
"By drinking her milk, did he not go to heaven even though he had fallen? And have not perfect cows appeared on the earth ever since then?
Therefore, I am blessed by this auspicious turn of fortune; this divine friend has come to me, and tomorrow morning I shall skillfully ask her about her lineage and her name when she arrives."
Reflecting thus in her heart, Kaliṅgasenā, the daughter of the king, passed that night there;
and Somaprabhā, her mind once more longing for the sight of him, spent the night in her own dwelling.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the third wave. Then, in the morning, Somaprabhā [prepared] that which would provide him with diversion.
He saw many wooden figures and iron mechanical dolls placed there.
Taking up the karaṇḍas, she, moving through the expanse of the sky,
returned once more to the presence of that Kaliṅgasenā.
Kaliṅgasenā, too, seeing her, was filled with tears of joy;
rising up, she embraced her by the neck as she sat at her side and said:
"O friend, without the sight of the full moon of your face,
this night of three watches has passed for me as if it were a hundred watches, filled with darkness."
What kind of connection from a previous birth could there have been between you and me, such that you have now become my wife? O Goddess, if you know, tell me.
Having heard that, Somaprabhā spoke thus to the princess:
"I possess no such supernatural knowledge; indeed, I do not remember my former birth."
And there are no sages here who possess supernormal knowledge; yet if some do know, it is because they previously performed such [practices], and they are knowers of the supreme reality.
When she had spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā, full of curiosity, questioned her again in that secluded place with words tender with love and confidence.
"Tell me, friend, of what divine lineage is your father,
by whose birth this family has been adorned by you, like a well-fashioned pearl?"
Furthermore, O lady of auspicious marks, what is your name, which is nectar to the ears of the world?
For what purpose is this basket, and what object is contained within it?
Having thus heard these affectionate words from Kaliṅgasenā,
Somaprabhā proceeded to relate everything in due order.
There is a great asura renowned throughout the three worlds named Maya;
having cast off his asuric nature, he has taken refuge in Śauri.
He granted him protection, and he [Vajrabhṛt] entered the assembly;
but the Daityas, thinking "this one belongs to the side of the gods," became enraged at him.
Out of fear of that, he constructed on the Vindhya mountain a palace within a cave of illusions,
filled with many wonders and inaccessible to the lords of the asuras.
"We have two daughters of that Maya who are practicing celibacy;
the elder is a maiden named Svayaṃprabhā, who remains in his house."
"I am the youngest, named Somaprabhā; that is who I am, my friend.
I have been given in marriage to the one named Nalakūbara, the son of Dhanada."
"I have been instructed here by my father in many kinds of magical mechanisms;
out of affection for you, this full casket has been brought by me."
Having said this, Somaprabhā, full of many wonders, opened up for her wooden mechanical dolls created by her own magic power.
By the mere stroke of a pin, one woman went through the air and,
by his command, quickly returned bringing a garland of flowers.
One brought water in that same manner by chance;
another danced, and yet another engaged in conversation.
Having entertained her for some time with such great wonders as these,
he placed that mechanical casket in a well-guarded location.
Then Somaprabhā, having taken leave of the longing Kaliṅgasenā,
went through the air to her own palace, devoted to her husband.
Kaliṅgasenā too, her hunger dispelled by the sight of that marvel,
remained on that day exceedingly joyful, turning away from all food.
Having seen that, her mother, fearing it was a disease,
had it examined by a physician named Ānanda, who declared it to be free from ailment.
"For some reason, her hunger has vanished through joy and not from disease";
thus speaks her face, as if smiling, with its eyes wide open. (SoKss 6.3.25)
Having been addressed thus by the physician, the mother asked her about the cause of her joy; she, in turn, related to her exactly what had occurred.
Then, perceiving her to be delighted by the company of her praiseworthy friends,
her mother congratulated her and had her take food as was appropriate.
Then, having come on another day and gradually learned the facts of the matter, Somaprabhā spoke in private to that very Kaliṅgasenā: SoKss_6,3.28 //
Having informed you of my friendship, I have obtained the daily permission from my husband, who is wise and understands the matter, for coming to your side.
Therefore, you too should now obtain the permission of your parents,
so that you may sport with me freely and without hesitation.
When she had spoken thus, Kaliṅgasenā took her by the hand at that very moment and went into the presence of her father and mother.
There, having first introduced her by name and lineage,
she presented her friend Somaprabhā to her father, King Kaliṅgadatta.
And he showed her likewise to his mother, Tārādattā;
and having seen her according to the description, they both rejoiced in her.
Then that couple, delighted by her form,
spoke after honoring that beautiful great asura woman out of affection for their daughter.
"O child, this Kaliṅgasenā is now entrusted into your hands;
therefore, let both of you now enjoy yourselves as you desire."
Having welcomed these words of theirs, both Kaliṅgasenā and Somaprabhā then departed together from that place.
And they went to the monastery built by the king for their residence,
and there they brought that basket containing the illusory mechanical contrivances.
Then, by her own magical power, Somaprabhā took a mechanical yakṣa and dispatched it to bring back an image of the Buddha.
That yakṣa, having traveled through the sky over a long distance,
returned bringing with him a collection of pearls, excellent jewels, gold, and blue lotuses.
Having thus honored the Sugatas,
Somaprabhā, together with her attendants, caused them to blaze there with that which bestows all wonders.
Having learned of this, King Kaliṅgadatta arrived and, seeing it, was struck with wonder; accompanied by his queen, he asked her about the operation of the mechanical device.
Then, O King, by the power of Soma, he said: "These various arts, such as illusory machines and the like, were created for me by my father in the past."
Just as this machine of the world consists of the five elements, so too do all these machines; hear now about them individually.
The machine that primarily consists of earth is that which closes the doors and so forth;
once closed by it, another is unable to open it.
The form arising from a water-engine appears as if it were alive;
however, whatever engine consists of light, that emits flames.
It creates a wind-mechanism that performs activities such as coming and going,
and it makes manifest speech arising from space.
"I have obtained these from my father; but as for that protective wheel-mechanism of the Truth (*ṛta*), my father alone knows it, and no one else."
While she was speaking these words, as if they were being accepted with faith,
the sound of conch shells being filled at midday arose.
Then, having requested the king to provide food appropriate for her,
and having obtained his permission, she placed her and her attendants in a mechanical celestial chariot.
Taking Kaliṅgasenā with her, Somaprabhā set out through the sky toward her father’s house, to the presence of her elder sister.
And in an instant, having reached her father’s palace situated on the Vindhya mountains,
he led her to the side of his sister Svayaṃprabhā.
There Kaliṅgasenā saw that self-luminous female ascetic, adorned with a mass of matted hair and a long rosary of beads.
Clad in white garments, she was like the smiling Pārvatī,
having undertaken the practice of fierce asceticism despite being possessed of the great enjoyments of desire.
And Svayaṃprabhā, having herself offered hospitality to that princess named Somaprabhā who stood before her bowed in salutation, shared with her a meal of fruits.
"O friend, by eating these fruits, old age shall not come upon you;
it will be like the frost striking a lotus, destroying this perishable form."
"It was for this reason that I brought you here out of affection," Somaprabhā said to the princess.
Then Kaliṅgasenā ate those fruits there,
and her limbs immediately became as if sprinkled with a shower of the essence of nectar.
And as she wandered there out of curiosity, she beheld a city garden containing ponds with golden lotuses and trees bearing fruits as sweet as nectar.
It is filled with various birds made of gold, possesses the splendor of jeweled pillars,
produces the perception of walls where there is only emptiness, and conveys the cognition of emptiness within the wall itself.
Creating the perception of land upon water and the perception of water upon land,
it is like a previously unseen other world fashioned by the magic of Maya.
This place had previously been entered by the monkeys while they were searching for Sītā;
through the grace of Svayaṃprabhā, they had finally achieved their exit after a long time.
Then, having taken leave of that Svayaṃprabhā— who had become a fit vessel for agelessness and was astonished by the extensive sight of that wondrous city— [he departed].
Having placed Kaliṅgasenā upon the mechanical device, Somaprabhā once again brought her through the air to her own residence in Takṣaśilā.
There, Kaliṅgasenā related everything to her parents exactly as it had happened; they, too, attained the highest satisfaction.

Thus, as those two friends were passing their days, Somaprabhā one day spoke to Kaliṅgasenā in this manner: SoKss_6,3.65: "Thus, as those two friends were passing their days, Somaprabhā one day spoke to Kaliṅgasenā in this manner."
"As long as you are not married, so long shall there be friendship between me and you;
but after you have gone to your husband's house, how could I have access there?"
For the husband of one's friend is not to be seen, nor is he to be accepted in any way;
like a she-wolf to a sheep, the mother-in-law devours the flesh of her daughter-in-law.
And so listen as I relate this story of Kīrtisenā to you:
long ago, in the city named Pāṭaliputra, there was a merchant who was the foremost among the wealthy; he was known by his true name, Dhanapālita.
And a daughter named Kīrtisenā was born to him,
peerless in beauty and dearer to him than his own life.
And she, being of equal status with him, was given by him as a daughter to a merchant named Devasena, who possessed great prosperity in Magadha.
And that virtuous Devasena had a wicked wife who was the mistress of the household, while his father had passed away.
Seeing that daughter-in-law Kīrtisenā, who was so highly esteemed by her husband,
she burned with rage and, out of her son's absence, tormented her.
And Kīrtisenā was not at all able to say that to her husband;
for the condition of a wife dependent on a harsh and crooked mother-in-law is indeed painful.
Once, urged by her kinsmen, that husband of hers, Devasena, set out for the city of Valabhī on a trading expedition.
Then Kīrtisenā spoke thus to her husband:
"O noble son, I have not told you this for so long."
"This mother of yours treats me with contempt even while you are present;
I do not know what she might do to me when you have departed on your journey."
Having heard that, Devasena became greatly agitated; out of affection for her and filled with fear, he went slowly and spoke to his mother with prostration.
"O Mother, now that I am departing, you must not harbor any lack of affection for Kīrtisenā in your heart; for she is the daughter of a noble family."
Having heard that, her eyes wide with alarm, the mother summoned Kīrtisenā and at that moment spoke to Devasena.
"What have I done? Ask her; it is she who thus impels you, O son. She is the one who causes the ruin of the household, yet for me, both of you are equal."
Having heard this, that excellent merchant became peaceful in mind on her account—
he who could not be deceived by his mother’s words of feigned affection.
But Kīrtisenā remained silent, her smile tinged with agitation;
meanwhile, on another day, the merchant Devasena set out for Valabhī.
Then, as she gradually succumbed to the suffering of separation from him,
her mother Kīrtisenā removed the maidservants from her side.
Having made an agreement with her own maidservant who moved about the house,
she had her brought into a secret inner room and stripped her of her clothes.
Having said, "You are taking my son away through your wickedness," she seized her by the hair and,
together with the maidservant, tore her apart with her feet, teeth, and claws.
And he cast her into an underground chamber that was sealed with a lid and secured by firm bolts,
wherein every accumulation of wealth inherited from his ancestors had been extracted.
And every day at the close of the day,
that wicked woman placed half a bowl of food there for her while she was in such a state.
And while her husband was still far away, she thought: "I shall say, 'In a few days, she died of her own accord; lift her up and go. (SoKss 6.3.89)
Thus cast into an underground cellar by her evil-doing mother-in-law,
Kīrtisenā, who deserved happiness, wept there and reflected:
Wealth, a husband, birth in a noble family, good fortune, and virtuous conduct—
even these, alas, have become such a calamity for me through the favor of my mother-in-law.
And for this reason, relatives disparage the birth of daughters, [seeing it] as defiled by the terror of mothers-in-law and sisters-in-law, and by ill fortune and the like. (SoK 6.3.92)
While she was thus lamenting, Kīrtisenā suddenly found a small spade in that underground chamber,
as if the Creator had extracted a thorn from her mind.
With that iron [rod], she dug a tunnel there until,
by fate, she emerged from her own residence.
Then, by means of that former lamp which had not been exhausted, she beheld that house illuminated by her very own dharma.
Having taken his garments and his own complexion at the end of the night,
he departed secretly from there and went outside the city.
"It is not fitting for me to go to my father's house in such a state;
what shall I say there, and how will the people believe me?"
Therefore, by my own resolve, I must go to my husband's very side,
since for virtuous women the husband alone is the sole refuge both in this world and the next.
Having reflected thus, Kīrtisenā, having bathed in the waters of the lake there, assumed the full attire of a prince.
Then, having gone to the marketplace and purchased some gold for a certain price,
she stayed that day in the house of a merchant.
On another day, a merchant named Samudrasena, who desired to go to Valabhī, formed a friendship there with her.
Together with him and his attendants, she set out toward Valabhī to reach her husband, who had already departed; she proceeded while wearing the fine attire of a prince.
And he said to that merchant, "I am being oppressed by my kinsmen;
therefore, I shall go with you to Valabhī, to the presence of my own people."
Having heard that, the merchant’s son followed her along the road out of respect, thinking,
"This must surely be some noble prince."
And that merchant caravan set out,
taking the forest path which had been abandoned by other people due to the fear of heavy tolls.
Having reached the entrance of the forest after several days and having halted with the caravan at evening,
a jackal let out a terrifying cry like a messenger of Death.
In that merchant community, which was conversant with those [perils] and apprehensive of the sudden onset of thieves and the like,
enemies were present on all sides in their eyes, which held weapons in their hands.
When the darkness, resembling the vanguard force of fleeing bandits,
was rushing forward, Kīrtisenā, seeing it and dressed in male attire, reflected:
"Alas! The karma of evildoers increases through its very continuity.
Behold, the calamity brought about by my mother-in-law has borne fruit even here for me."
First, as if by Death itself, I was devoured by my mother-in-law's anger;
thereafter, I entered an underground cellar, like another dwelling in a womb.
By fate, having emerged even from that, I was as if born again;
having returned here today, I have once more fallen into a state where my life is in doubt.
If I am killed here by thieves, then my mother-in-law, who is my enemy, will say to your husband: "She has gone off somewhere, infatuated with another."
"If I am recognized by anyone as a woman while my garments are being stripped away,
then death is better for me than the violation of my virtue."
Therefore, I must protect myself alone; this merchant friend need not be looked after.
For the duty of virtuous women is what must be considered, not friends and the like.
Having thus resolved, she reached a pit shaped like a house situated among the trees, which seemed as if the earth had opened a passage out of compassion for her as she searched.
Having entered there and covered her body with grass, leaves, and other such things,
she remained, sustaining herself through the longing for union with her husband.
Then, at midnight, a vast army of thieves suddenly descended with raised weapons and surrounded that caravan.
Then there occurred a stormy day of battle, where the clouds were the shouting barbarians, the lightning-flashes were the flames of weapons, and the showers were streams of blood.
Having slain that merchant leader Samudrasena along with his followers,
the powerful bandits then departed, taking away their accumulated wealth.
And at that time, Kīrtisenā, having heard the clamor, did not forcibly give up her life;
the sole cause for that was destiny alone.
Then, when the night had passed and the one of fierce splendor had risen,
she emerged from that pit from the midst of the branches.
Granted that for virtuous women who are devoted solely to their husbands and whose splendor is unswerving,
it is the deities themselves who provide protection in times of distress.
That even when a lion saw her there in that desolate wilderness, he left her alone;
moreover, no ascetic came from anywhere to approach her.
Having comforted her after she had asked for news, and having given her water to drink from his water-pot and pointed out the way, he vanished somewhere.
Then, as if satiated by nectar and freed from hunger and thirst,
that devoted wife set out upon the path described by the ascetic.
Then, seeing the sun mounted upon the peak of the setting mountain with its rays extended,
as if saying, "Endure this one night," she—
He entered a hollow at the root of a great forest tree that resembled a house, and he closed its entrance with another piece of wood.
And at twilight, through a crack in the door, she saw there a terrible rākṣasī who had arrived, accompanied by her sons, the children.
"Today I have crossed over misfortune because I have been devoured by her"— thinking thus,
the terrified rākṣasī climbed up the tree at that very moment.
And his sons, having climbed up after her, spoke to that rākṣasī there at that very moment: "O Mother, give us some food."
Then that rākṣasī said to those children: "O little sons, even though I went to the great cremation ground today, no food was obtained by me."
Although the host of ḍākinīs was requested, they did not grant me a share therein;
then, out of weariness with that, I petitioned Bhairava after making my request known.
And having asked his name and lineage, the god commanded me thus:
"O Bhayaṅkarī, you are of noble birth, born of the lineage of Khara and Dūṣaṇa."
Therefore, go from here to the city of Vasudatta, which is not far away;
there dwells a great king named Vasudatta who is devoted to righteousness.
He who, stationed at the boundary, protects this entire forest,
collects the toll himself, and suppresses the thieves.
And while that king was sleeping in the forest from the fatigue of hunting,
a centipede quickly and unnoticed entered his ear.
And she gave birth to many children within his head over time;
because of that disease, this king now exists as nothing but sinews.
If his physicians do not recognize that disease, and if no one else should know it either,
then he will perish in a few days.
When he has perished through his own magic power, you should eat his flesh;
by eating it, you will then remain fully satisfied for six months.
"In this way, even with Bhairava, my distribution [of the sacrifice] was accompanied by doubt;
and today, a time-bound [sacrifice] has been prescribed. O sons, what shall I do?"
When she had spoken thus, those sons said to her:
"Mother, now that this disease has been recognized and removed, does that king still live?"
"And tell me, how can such a disease as that be removed?
To those sons who had spoken thus, the rākṣasī replied:
Once this disease has been diagnosed and removed, that king will indeed live;
hear now how this great illness of his is to be cured.
Having first smeared his head with ghee and applied warm clarified butter to it,
he should place it for a long time in the harsh heat of the midday sun.
Having inserted a hollow bamboo tube into the cavity of the ear,
[one should direct it] so that it connects with the hole of a shallow bowl placed upon the back of a jar filled with cold water.
Exhausted by the heat of the sweat and the sun, he emerged from within his head and,
entering that very bamboo tube through the same ear-cavity, reached her.
Just as centipedes, longing for coolness, fall into a jar,
so too that king is liberated from that great disease.
Having spoken thus to her sons who were perched in the tree, the rākṣasī fell silent;
and Kīrtisenā, remaining within a hollow, heard all of that.
And having heard this, he reflected: "If I am to escape from here, then I shall go and restore that king to life by means of this very stratagem."
He protects this very forest with little tax while stationed at its edge;
and because of that convenience, all the merchants travel by this path.
The merchant Samudrasena, who had gone to heaven, said this:
"Therefore, my husband shall come by this very same path."
Therefore, having gone to the edge of the forest to the city of Vasudatta,
I shall deliver the king from his illness and, remaining there, await my husband’s arrival.
Reflecting thus, she passed that night with great difficulty;
when the rākṣasas had vanished in the morning, she emerged from the hollow.
Then, proceeding in due course through the middle of the forest while wearing male attire,
she saw a virtuous cowherd in the afternoon.
Approaching him, who was softened by the sight of that long journey despite his delicate frame, she asked: "Tell me, what region is this?"
The cowherd also said:
"This city standing before us is named Vasudattapura, belonging to King Vasudatta."
The king, that great-souled one, remained there afflicted by disease and on the verge of death;
having heard this, Kīrtisenā spoke to Gopālaka.
If someone were to lead me into the presence of that king, then I know how to cure him of his malady. (SoKss 6.3.158)
Upon hearing this, the cowherd said: "I am going to this very city;
therefore, come with me while I make an effort on your behalf."
When Kīrtisenā had said, "So be it," the cowherd Vasudatta led her away at that very moment, disguised as a man, to the city of Vasudattapura.
Having thus presented that object there at that very moment,
he entrusted her, who possessed auspicious marks, to the doorkeeper.
The doorkeeper, having informed the king, ushered that blameless woman into his presence by the king's command.
And King Vasudatta, afflicted there by disease, was comforted the moment he beheld her of such wondrous form; for one knows for oneself what is beneficial and what is harmful.
And he said to her while she was in male attire: "O woman of auspicious marks, if you will remove this pain from me, I shall give half of my kingdom to you."
"I know that in a dream a woman took away from my back a black woolen blanket;
therefore, it is certain that you will remove this disease of mine."
Having heard that, Kīrtisenā said to him: "O King, today's day has passed;
tomorrow I shall remove your illness; do not speak thus in distress."
Having said this, he had cow's ghee applied to the head of the king;
by that, sleep came upon him and that intense pain departed.
"This is some deity who has come to us through our merits in the form of a physician"—
thus did they all then praise Kīrtisenā there.
And the Great Queen attended upon her with various services;
she also provided her with a separate residence at night, complete with female attendants.
Then, on the following day at midday, while the ministers and the women of the inner apartments were looking on,
Kīrtisenā dragged him away from that king.
Through the path of the ear in her head, she [the Rākṣasī] entered along with a hundred centipedes,
by means of that previously mentioned, most wonderful artifice.
Having placed those centipedes in a small jar,
she then satisfied the king by sprinkling him with clarified butter, milk, and other substances.
When the king had gradually recovered and was freed from disease,
who there did not marvel upon seeing those living beings inside the jar?
And the king, beholding those worms emerging from his head,
was terrified, reflected, rejoiced, and felt as though he had been born anew.
Having celebrated the festival and performed his ritual ablutions, he honored Kīrtisenā—
who had shown no regard for half the kingdom— with villages, elephants, horses, and gold.
The queen and the ministers filled him with gold and garments, saying,
"This physician, who has restored the life of our lord, is worthy of honor."
And she placed those objects in the hands of that very king, saying,
"I am observing a vow for some time," while looking toward her husband.
Then, while being thus honored by everyone, she remained there for some days in the guise of a man, as Kīrtisenā.
Then, from her chamber, she heard from the world outside that her own husband,
the caravan leader Devasena, had arrived on that very path.
Then, having learned that the caravan had arrived at the city, she went out to meet him;
and she beheld her husband as a peahen beholds a fresh rain-cloud.
With his very mind, which dissolved the long-standing fever of longing and offered the water of honor through tears of joy, he fell at his feet.
And he too recognized her upon observing her in her disguised form,
just as one might recognize the lunar orb by day when its splendor is obscured by the fierce rays of the sun.
As Devasena gazed upon that moon-like face of Candrakānta, it was a marvel that his heart did not melt away.
Then, while Kīrtisenā stood thus with her true nature revealed,
and while her husband stood there in wonder, wondering "What is this?", [the following occurred].
When the merchant community was astonished upon learning of that,
King Vasudatta himself, filled with wonder, reportedly went there in person.
Questioned by him, Kīrtisenā described her entire history before her husband, arising from the wicked conduct of her mother-in-law.
And having heard that, Devasena, her husband, turned his face away from his own mother, filled with anger, forbearance, astonishment, and joy.

Victorious are the virtuous women, whose devotion to their husbands is firmly established, who are protected by the armor of moral conduct, who have dharma as their charioteer, and whose intellects are their weapons.
Having heard this wondrous account of Kīrtisenā’s conduct, all the people standing there spoke thus with joy.
The king also said:
"By this Queen Sītā, who has endured suffering for the sake of her husband, even Rāma—who brought her such hardship—has been conquered."
"This sister of mine, who gave me my life," said the king; then Kīrtisenā replied to him:
"O King, let that gift of your favor which has remained in your hand—
consisting of villages, elephants, horses, jewels, and so forth— be bestowed upon my husband."
Having been addressed thus by her, the king, being pleased, gave those villages and other gifts to him,
and he bound the turban of honor upon his husband, Devasena.
Then, with those floods of wealth bestowed by the king and acquired through trade, Devasena— his treasury filled to overflowing—
remained in that very city, having left his mother behind and dwelling there while praising Kīrtisenā.

Having reached that place, Kīrtisenā—whose fame was won by her incomparable conduct and who had become free from the wicked mother-in-law—dwelt there, partaking in all enjoyments and sovereignty; she was like the abundance of the fruits of merit personified, remaining close to her husband even while he was bound in a body.
Thus, having endured the decree of adverse fate, virtuous women who have preserved the wealth of their conduct in times of calamity—
protected by the greatness of their own innate strength— bring about the welfare of both their husbands and themselves.
"O princess, such are the many faults inflicted upon brides by mothers-in-law and sisters-in-law.
Therefore, I pray that your husband’s home may be one where there is neither a mother-in-law nor a treacherous sister-in-law."
Having heard this wonderful tale of Ānandikā from the mouth of Somaprabhā, the daughter of the Asura king,
Kaliṅgasenā, the princess, was filled with great joy.
Then, seeing that the discourse on various matters had come to an end and that they were preparing to depart,
Somaprabhā embraced the longing Kaliṅgasenā and returned to her own abode.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the fourth wave:
Then, as she had gone to her own home, [he] followed behind to observe her path.
Out of affection for Somaprabhā, she stood upon the roof-terrace of the palace on the road.
From the sky, a young lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega happened by chance to see Kalingasenā nearby.
As soon as he saw her, who could enchant the three worlds with her beauty, he fell into agitation like a magician at the sight of his own wand.
Enough with the women of the Vidyādharas; what need is there even to mention the Apsarases? For such is this wondrous beauty of this human woman.
Therefore, if she were not my wife, what would life be worth to me?
And how could I, even though being a Vidyādhara, engage in union with a human woman?
Having reflected thus, he meditated upon the vidyā known as Prajñapti;
and she, appearing before him in bodily form, then spoke to him in this way.
"In reality, she is not a human being; she is an Apsaras fallen by a curse, born in the house of King Kaliṅgadatta, O fortunate one."
When this was said by Vidyā, he then went to his own abode joyful; there, the Vidyādhara, turning away from others and afflicted by desire, reflected thus: SoKss_6,4.8 //
"If I carry her off by force, that would not be right for me;
for there is a death-dealing curse upon me for the forcible enjoyment of women."
To attain this, Śambhu must be propitiated by me through austerity;
for spiritual perfections depend upon austerity, and no other means is known to exist.
Having thus resolved, he went to Mount Ṛṣabha on another day and,
standing on one foot without food, performed austerities.
Then, soon after, the Lord of Ambikā, having granted him a vision of himself, being pleased by his intense austerities, commanded Madanavega in this way:
This girl named Kaliṅgasenā is renowned on earth for her beauty; yet there is no husband even for her who is equal to her in the perfection of her form.
There is, however, one Vatsarāja who desires her;
yet, out of fear of Vāsavadattā, he does not openly seek her hand.
This princess too, being greedy for beauty, heard this from the mouth of Somaprabhā and now desires the King of Vatsa for herself in a svayaṃvara.
In the meantime, before her marriage could take place,
she assumed the form of the Lord of Vatsa, who was as if unable to endure the delay.
"Having gone there, you should take this woman as your wife according to the Gāndharva rite;
in this way, the beautiful Kaliṅgasenā will become yours."
Having been thus commanded by Śarva, Madanavega prostrated before him and departed for his own home on the slope of Mount Kālakūṭa.
In the meantime, she traveled to her own palace every night and returned at every dawn by means of a sky-going machine.
Once, while Kaliṅgasenā was sporting with Somaprabhā in the city of Takṣaśilā, she spoke to her in private:
"O friend, you must not tell this to anyone;
listen, for I shall tell you why: I know that my marriage has now arrived."
"Here, messengers have been sent by many kings to request me;
they were turned back by my father and dispatched from here in that very same manner."
But as for the king named Prasenajit who resides in Śrāvastī,
he was merely his [the Buddha's] messenger and was honored by him with great respect.
And since Ambā has also consecrated him with these words, I believe that king is my chosen husband;
he is thus esteemed by my father and mother as one of noble birth.
For he was born into that family where Ambā, Ambālikā, and the others—
the grandmothers of both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas— were born.
"O friend, it is now certain that my father has given me to that King Prasenajit in the city of Śrāvastī."
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, Somaprabhā wept immediately with a stream of tears, as if creating another necklace out of her grief.
Having seen the entire world of mortals, that daughter of the Asura Maya spoke to her companion who was asking the cause of her tears.
"O friend, regarding the qualities of a bridegroom that are sought—namely age, appearance, lineage, character, and wealth—the first is age; after that come lineage and the rest."
And that King Prasenajit was seen by me to be advanced in years;
what is the use of the lineage of one who is as decayed as a jasmine flower?
O Queen, by that man who is as bright as snow, you will become as pitiable as a lotus pond whose faces of blossoms have withered, even though you were joined with him.
Therefore, despondency has arisen in me; yet, O auspicious lady, joy would come to me if that Udayana, the King of Vatsa, were your husband.
Indeed, there is no other king on earth equal to him in physical form, in beauty, in lineage, in valor, or in majesty.
If you are united with such a husband, O slender-waisted one,
then the Creator’s craftsmanship of beauty has truly borne fruit in you.
Thus, impelled by the words fashioned by Somaprabhā as if by mechanical devices,
Kaliṅgasenā’s heart went toward the Lord of Vatsa.
Then the princess questioned her daughter:
"Friend, who is this man called the King of Vatsa, and from what lineage is he descended?"
"And how was it that you were named Udayana? Tell me this.
Then Somaprabhā said, "Listen, friend, I shall tell you."
There is a renowned land called Vatsa, an ornament of the earth;
there lies the city of Kauśāmbī, like a second Amarāvatī.
He exercises his sovereignty over that land;
therefore, O blessed one, hear from me as I recount the lineage of that Lord of Vatsa.
It is said that Abhimanyu was the son of Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava;
by him, through his breaking of the wheel-array, the Kuru army was brought to destruction.
From him was born Parīkṣit, the sustainer of the Bharata lineage and king;
from him also came Janamejaya, who was the initiator of the snake sacrifice.
From him was born Śatānīka, who dwelt in Kauśāmbī;
he was the one who perished after slaying the Daityas in the host of gods and asuras.
Therefore, that king became celebrated throughout the world as Sahasrānīka,
he who, with a chariot sent by Śakra, made his journey back and forth across the heavens.
To him, by his queen Mṛgāvatī, was born this King Udayana—
the ornament of the lunar dynasty and a festival for the eyes of the world.
Hear also the reason for his name: she was indeed Mṛgāvatī, the pregnant mother of this noble-born king.
Having developed a pregnancy-longing for a bath in blood,
she was made to bathe in a pool of lac and other red juices prepared by her husband, who feared the consequences of sin.
A bird of the lineage of Tārkṣya, swooping down with the suspicion that it was meat, carried her away;
by the power of fate, she was released alive upon the Udaya mountain.
There she was seen by the seer Jamadagni standing in that hermitage, having been further comforted by him with words concerning her reunion with her husband.
For a certain period of time, indeed, such was the curse from Tilottamā, born of her contemptuous jealousy, which brought about the separation of her husband from her.
And after some days, right there in the hermitage of Jamadagni, she gave birth to a son,
just as the sky gives birth to the new moon upon the mountain of sunrise.
This Udayana has been born as a sovereign lord of the earth,
and a son shall be born to him who will become the ruler of all the Vidyādharas.
Then, having uttered these words from the sky as an incorporeal voice,
the gods bestowed upon him the name Nāgodayana because of his birth from Udaya.
Bound by hope for the end of his curse and informed by Mātali,
Sahasrānīka passed the time with great difficulty without that Mṛgāvatī.
When the end of the curse arrived through the power of destiny from the Śabara,
he came from the Mountain of Sunrise and obtained proof of his own identity.
At that moment, his purpose having been announced by a voice arising from the sky,
he set out for the Mountain of Sunrise, placing that Śabara at the head of his procession.
There, having obtained Mṛgāvatī as his wife— like the fulfillment of a long-cherished desire— and Udayana as his son— like the realization of a kingdom of the mind— [he rejoiced].
Then, having taken them both and arrived at Kauśāmbī, he—
satisfied by the excellence of that son's virtues— consecrated him in the position of crown prince.
And he gave him the sons of his ministers, beginning with Yaugandharāyaṇa;
with that burden taken up by them, he enjoyed pleasures for a long time in the company of his wives.
In due time, having installed his son Udayana upon the throne,
the aged king, together with his wife and ministers, departed for the Great Path.
Thus, having obtained that ancestral kingdom and conquered the entire earth,
Udayana, with Yaugandharāyaṇa as his companion, ruled the world.
Having thus quickly told that story in private, Somaprabhā spoke again in this manner to her friend Kaliṅgasenā.
Thus, O fair-limbed one, he was called Vatsarāja because he ruled over the Vatsas;
and in age, prosperity, and likewise in his birth from the Lunar dynasty, he surpassed the Pāṇḍavas.
He was called Udayana by the gods because of his birth from the rising sun;
and in this world, even Kandarpa himself is not his equal in beauty.
O beauty of the three worlds, he alone is your equal as a husband;
and he, greedy for your loveliness, surely desires you when you are sought after.
"But, my friend, there is a chief queen of his named Vāsavadattā, who is the daughter of King Caṇḍamahāsena."
Likewise, having abandoned his kinsmen out of excessive passion,
he was chosen by Uṣā, Śakuntalā, and other maidens who had cast aside their modesty.
In her was born his son named Naravāhanadatta,
who was indeed ordained by the gods as the future sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
Therefore, that Lord of Vatsa, fearing her, does not ask for you here;
moreover, she was seen by me and does not rival you in the perfection of her beauty.
When her friend Somaprabhā had spoken thus,
Kaliṅgasenā, filled with longing for the Lord of Vatsa, then replied to her.
"I know this to be the will of my parents; but what can be done by me?
Since she is omniscient and possessed of power, the truth alone is my refuge in this matter."
"This matter depends on destiny; therefore, listen to a story regarding this.
Having said this to Somaprabhā, he related this tale to her.
In former times, there was a king named Vikramasena in Ujjayinī;
he had a daughter named Tejasvatī, who was peerless in beauty.
And for her, there was generally no king who was a desirable suitor;
then one day, while staying in her own palace, she saw a certain man.
Because of his handsome appearance, she longed for union with him by fate;
and having communicated her intention to him, she sent her own female friend to him.
Having gone there, that friend of his, after earnestly entreating him— even though he was unwilling and apprehensive of the man’s rashness— arranged a secret meeting.
"O noble one, behold this secluded temple here;
you should wait for the arrival of the princess there during the night."
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, she went and told this to Tejasvatī; thereafter, she too remained gazing at the sun.
And that man, having been reasoned with, fled elsewhere out of fear;
for the frog was not one who knew how to savor the filaments of the red lotus.
In the meantime, a certain prince of noble birth,
having lost his father, came there to see the king, who was his friend.
And there, at evening, arrived a youth named Somadatta— handsome in appearance, solitary, and one whose kingdom and inheritance had been seized by his kinsmen.
By fate, she entered that very temple to spend the night,
where the princess’s companion had designated a rendezvous with a man.
Approaching him as he stood there at night, the princess, blinded by passion and unable to discern who he was, chose him as her husband of her own accord.
The wise man also silently welcomed that [garland] offered by the ritual,
which indicated his future union with royal fortune.
Then, in an instant, upon seeing him in this very way, the princess considered herself to have been truly blessed by the Creator with one most desirable of all things.
After they had conversed with one another according to their mutual understanding,
one went to her own residence, while the other spent that night there.
Having gone there in the morning and announced his name through the mouth of the doorkeeper,
the prince was recognized and entered into the presence of the king.
There, showing great respect for the suffering caused by the aforementioned seizure of his kingdom and other misfortunes,
the king accepted the role of an ally in crushing that enemy.
And he resolved to give her to him— the daughter whom he had previously intended to give—
and at that very moment, he disclosed this intention to his ministers.
And the queen, who had previously been informed by that very friend through the mouths of trusted attendants, related the account of her son to the king.
Then, while the king was astonished by the unexpected success of his unproven desire,
a certain minister spoke to him there at that time:
For destiny alone remains awake in bringing about the fulfillment of the goals of those destined for success,
even as they remain unconscious of it, just like a loyal servant attending to his masters.
And so I shall tell this; O King, listen here to this story:
there was once a certain twice-born man named Hariśarman in a particular village.
Poor and foolish, ill-situated due to a lack of livelihood,
he was born with many children as a result of experiencing his past misdeeds.
Wandering for alms with his family, he eventually reached a certain city and took refuge with a very wealthy householder named Sthūladatta.
Having placed his sons, who were protectors of cattle and other livestock, as well as his wife and his own servant near his house, he lived there performing menial service for him.
Once, there occurred for Sthūladatta a wedding festival for his daughter,
crowded with people who had come from various regions on their journey.
And at that time, Hariśarman, together with his family, established a habit of eating to his heart's content of ghee, meat, and other delicacies in that house.
Then, observing that time and being remembered by no one there,
he became despondent due to lack of food and spoke thus to his wife at night:
"Because of my poverty and my folly in this world, I have met with such disrespect;
therefore, I shall here employ a fabricated knowledge through skillful means."
By this means, I shall become an object of respect for this Sthūladatta;
and when the opportunity arises, you should inform him that I am a man of knowledge.
Having spoken thus and reflected upon this with his intellect while the people were asleep,
he carried off the horse that was the vehicle of his son-in-law from the house of Sthūladatta.
Although the bridegroom’s party searched here and there in the morning, they did not find the horse that had been placed by him in a hidden spot far away.
Then, approaching Sthūladatta— who was terrified by ill omens and searching for the thief of his horse— Hariśarman’s wife said to him:
"My husband is wise and an expert in the science of astrology and other fields;
why is he not asked for what reason he is causing you to lose this horse?"
Having heard that, Sthūladatta summoned Hariśarman, who was saying, "Yesterday I forgot it, but today, now that my horses have been stolen, I remember it."
Having requested the brahmin, "Forgive us for our forgetfulness," he asked him,
"Tell me, by whom has our horse been carried away?"
Then Hariśarman, drawing false lines, said:
"At the southern boundary from here, a horse has been stationed by thieves."
"While he remains hidden until the end of the day, let that horse be fetched quickly; go and bring it back before he is led far away."
Having heard that, many men ran and reached him in an instant;
praising Hariśarman’s discernment, they brought back the horse.
Then, honored by all people as a man of wisdom and revered by Sthūladatta, Hariśarman lived there in happiness.
Then, as the days passed, a great deal of gold, jewels, and other wealth was carried away from within Rājagṛha by some thief.
When it was not known who the thief was, the king then quickly had that Hariśarman brought before him by virtue of his renown as a man of wisdom.

And having been brought there, wasting away his time while saying, "I shall speak tomorrow morning," he was placed in a dwelling by the king and guarded with great care, for he was agitated by his knowledge [of the truth].
In that royal household there was a maidservant named Jihvā,
by whom that wealth had been taken from the interior along with her brother.
Having gone there at night to Hariśarman’s dwelling,
she pressed her ear against the door out of curiosity, suspecting that he possessed such knowledge.
And at that time, Hariśarman, standing alone within,
thus censured his own tongue, which speaks with false knowledge.
"O tongue, greedy for enjoyments, what is this that you have done?
O you of wicked conduct, now endure here your punishment."
Having heard that, the maidservant named Jihvā, out of fear that she had been discovered by this wise man, skillfully entered his presence.
Falling at his feet, she spoke in the guise of a wise woman:
"O Brahmin, I am that very tongue of yours, who carries away the meaning you have understood."
And having taken that wealth, I buried it here in the ground beneath a pomegranate tree in the garden behind this very temple.
"Therefore, protect me; take this gold that is in my hand.
Having heard this, Hariśarman spoke to her with pride:
"Go; I know all that has been, that is to be, and that is currently happening.
But I will not reveal you, for you are a miserable woman who has come to me for refuge."
"And whatever you have in your possession, you shall give that back to me.
Having been addressed thus by him, the maidservant said, "So be it," and quickly departed from there.
And then Hariśarman, out of astonishment, thought thus:
"When fate is favorable, it accomplishes even an impossible goal with ease."
When this misfortune has occurred, my purpose here is accomplished beyond doubt;
for as I censure my own tongue, my tongue—my thief—has fallen right before me.
"Alas! These are secret sinners who reveal themselves only through their very suspicion!"—reflecting thus and other such thoughts, he spent that night there in great joy.

which are devoid of desire and firmly resolved upon the renunciation of life.
Therefore, you must protect your own interest, for even animals know how to protect themselves;
O King, how much more so should wise men such as yourself?
Having heard this from the excellent minister Yaugandharāyaṇa at his own leisure,
and having properly attained the path of discernment, the Lord of Vatsa said:
"It is so; there is no doubt that all this of mine will perish.
Therefore, what purpose would I have in marrying Kaliṅgasenā?"
"The astrologers have done what was appropriate when they declared that the auspicious moment was far off;
or how much unrighteousness could there be from abandoning those who have come to the svayaṃvara?"
Thus addressed by the King of Vatsa, the delighted Yaugandharāyaṇa reflected: "Our task is as good as accomplished, exactly as we desired."
Sprinkled with the essence of skillful means and nourished by the proper place and time,
what fruit indeed would this great creeper of policy not bear?
Having reflected thus and meditating upon the proper time and place,
the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa paid homage to the king and departed for his home.
The king also, having approached her while she was performing secret acts of hospitality, spoke thus to Queen Vāsavadattā as he comforted her: SoKss_6,7.87 //
"Why do I speak? You yourself know, O fawn-eyed one, that your love is my very life, just as water is to the lotus."
For how could I venture even to utter the name of another?
Yet Kaliṅgasenā has come to my house by force.
And it is well known in this regard that Rambhā, having approached Pārtha while he was established in asceticism,
was rejected by him and consequently cast upon her a curse of impotence.
While remaining there, he spent that year in the house of Virāṭa in female attire, which was of most wonderful appearance, thereby fulfilling his curse.
Therefore, I did not prevent this Kaliṅgasenā at that time;
indeed, without your consent, I do not venture to say anything at all.
Having thus consoled him and then perceived his cruel intention with her heart— as if with wine reddened by passion applied to her face— she [spoke].
Together with Queen Vāsavadattā, the Lord of Vatsa spent that night in the company of his chief minister, gratified by the latter’s profound sagacity.
In the meantime, Yaugandharāyaṇa employed that [spell] which he had previously used day and night in order to ascertain the news concerning Kaliṅgasenā.
That Brahmarākṣasa, named Yogeśvara, having approached him as a friend,
spoke freely to that excellent minister on that very same night.
I have always remained both inside and outside Kaliṅgasenā’s residence,
yet I do not see the arrival of any beings, whether divine or human.
Even now, an indistinct sound was heard by me suddenly in the sky at the onset of night, while I was hidden here near the top of the palace.
Even though I applied my spells to discern his power, they proved ineffective; therefore, reflecting on this, I thought to myself: ||| SoKss_6,7.99 |||
"This is certainly the sound of someone possessing divine power,
wandering through the sky, lusting after the beauty of Kaliṅgasenā."
I observe some slight interval by which knowledge does not proceed;
for a clever person remaining awake, another's flaw is not difficult to find.
"This is the desire of the divine ones," so it was said by the excellent minister;
and I have heard this being spoken by her friend Somaprabhā.
Having thus resolved, I have come here to tell this to you;
in this connection, I ask this question, so let it first be explained by you to me.
"Indeed, even animals protect themselves;
this which you said to King Rajā, O Sage, I heard through my yogic power while remaining unobserved."
"If there is an illustration for this, tell it to me, O wise one," said Yogeśvara; thus addressed, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
There is a friend; likewise, I shall relate a story to you here—listen.
Long ago, there was a great banyan tree outside the city of Vidiśā.
Four living beings lived there in that great tree:
a mongoose, an owl, a cat, and a mouse, each with its own separate dwelling.
The mongoose and the mouse remained each in their own separate holes,
while the cat stayed in a great hollow in the middle of the tree.
The owl, however, is in the upper part of the head in a bower of creepers inaccessible to others;
here the mouse is to be killed by three [enemies], while the other three are to be killed by the cat.
Out of fear of the cat for its food, the mouse, as well as the mongoose,
and the owl by its very nature— these three roamed about at night.
And that cat wandered about fearlessly day and night nearby a field of barley, always with the desire to catch mice.
Others also, at that time, followed that path through reasoning because of their lack of desire for food;
then once, a certain Caṇḍāla hunter arrived there.
Seeing the trail of cat's footprints leading toward that field,
he set snares all around the field for the sake of killing it and then departed.
There, during the night, that cat, having approached with the desire to kill the mouse,
entered that field and was caught in its snares.
Then the mouse, seeking food, approached that place in secret;
seeing the cat bound, he rejoiced and danced.
As soon as he entered that field from afar by a single path,
both the owl and the mongoose also arrived there.
Seeing the cat and the mongoose, both desired to catch the mouse;
and the mouse, seeing them from afar, was distressed and reflected:
If I take refuge with a cat that brings fear to both the mongoose and the owl,
this enemy, though already bound, might kill me with a single blow.
"The cat will kill me from afar, and the owl and the mongoose as well;
fallen into such a crisis with enemies on all sides, where shall I go, and what shall I do?"
"Alas! I shall take refuge with this very cat here, for he has fallen into distress;
he might protect me for his own preservation when I am useful for cutting his snares."
Reflecting thus, the mouse went slowly toward the cat and said:
"I am in great distress because you are bound; therefore, I shall cut your snare."
Affection arises even toward enemies through living together;
however, I have no confidence in you, as I do not know your mind.
Having heard that, the cat said: "My good sir, you may trust me;
from this day forward, you are my friend and the giver of my life."
Having heard this from the cat, he immediately took refuge on its lap;
seeing that, the mongoose and the owl departed from there, their hopes dashed.
Then the cat, tormented by the snare, said to the mouse:
"Friend, the night is nearly spent; therefore, cut these snares of mine quickly."
The mouse also, while slowly gnawing and looking out for the arrival of the hunter,
made a prolonged sound of "kaṭakaṭa" with his teeth as if they were grinding in falsehood.
In an instant, when night had turned to dawn and the hunter was drawing near,
the mouse quickly cut the snares as the cat was demanding its prey.
Then, when the cat’s bonds were severed and it had fled in terror from the hunter,
the mouse, having escaped death, ran away and entered its hole.
Not trusting when called back by the cat, he said:
"For by the exigency of time, an enemy becomes a friend, and not always."
Thus, when one's self is protected by wisdom from many enemies—
even by a mouse, which is a mere animal— how much more so should it be guarded against those among human beings?

O Queen, that which was said by me to the king at that time—which you have heard—is this: "One should protect one's own duty with intelligence, for it is through protection [of the self] that [all is preserved]."
And in all matters, intellect is the primary friend, not physical prowess;
O Lord of Yoga, listen now to this story regarding that very point as well.
There is a city called Śrāvastī; formerly, King Prasenajit reigned there, and once a certain unprecedented brahmin arrived in that city.
While he was eating the food of a Śūdra, a certain merchant, thinking him to be virtuous,
established that twice-born man in the house of a particular Brāhmaṇa.
Right there, it was replenished daily by him with gifts of dry food and other offerings,
and then gradually by other excellent merchants who had learned of it.
Having gradually accumulated a thousand gold dīnāras,
that miser went to the forest, buried them there, and cast them into the ground.
Going there alone every day, he inspected that place;
one day, he saw that pit, which had been empty of gold, gaping open.
As he gazed at that empty pit with his mind destroyed,
not only did emptiness enter his heart, but wondrously, emptiness pervaded even the directions.
Then, lamenting, he approached the brahmin in whose house he had stayed;
and when questioned, he reported his entire history to him.
Having gone to the sacred bathing place, he desired to give up his life while fasting;
and the merchant who was his provider of food, having learned of this, arrived there along with others.
He said to him: "O Brahmin, why do you wish to die for the sake of wealth?
Wealth comes and goes unexpectedly, like an unseasonable cloud."
Although addressed with these and other words by him, he did not relinquish his grip on death;
for to a miser, even a mere object of value is dearer than life itself.
Then, as that twice-born man was going to the sacred ford to die,
King Prasenajit himself, having learned of this, came into his presence.
And he asked him: "Is there any identifying mark there, O Brahmin, by which those dinars buried by you in that ground may be recognized?"
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "O King, there is a small tree here in the forest;
at its base, that wealth was buried by me."
Having heard this, the king said: "I shall find that wealth for you from my own treasury and give it to you; O twice-born one, do not abandon your life."
Having spoken thus, the king dissuaded him from his efforts toward death, placed that brahmin in the hands of a merchant, and entered his inner apartments.
There, having instructed the doorkeeper under the pretext of a headache,
he summoned all the physicians by the proclamation of a drum.
"How many patients are there here? Whose are you? What medicine have you given?
Thus he asked each one individually, having brought them together while remaining in seclusion.
Then each one of them told the king everything at that time;
then, one physician among them, being questioned in turn, spoke as follows.
"O King, today is the second day that I have administered *nāgabalā* medicine to the merchant Mātṛdatta while he was unwell."
Having heard that, the king summoned the merchant and said to him: "Tell me, by whom was this *nāgabalā* brought for you?"
When the merchant had replied, "By a laborer,
Your Majesty," the king then had that laborer quickly brought before him and spoke to him.
"Since you, while digging at the base of a tree for the sake of *nāgabalā*, obtained a quantity of silver coins— that which was the property of a Brahmin, restore it."
Thus addressed by the king, the frightened laborer immediately agreed; having brought those dinars, he abandoned them there at that very moment.
The king also, having summoned that brahmin who had observed the fast,
gave him those dinars won at gambling, as if they were his own life-breaths moving outside his body.
Thus, by means of his intelligence, the king, knowing that the medicinal herb had grown from that tree, obtained it— having brought it down from the root of the tree— for the sake of the twice-born.
Thus, in this way, the supremacy of the intellect always triumphs over human effort;
and in such matters as these, what could mere physical prowess accomplish?
Therefore, O Lord of Yoga, you too should act with such wisdom that some fault may be discovered in Kaliṅgasenā.
This is indeed so: just as the gods and asuras here are infatuated with her, so too was the sound of someone in heaven heard by you one night.
If a fault were found in her after she had been obtained, it would not be unwholesome for us;
the king would not have taken her as a wife, and no unrighteousness would have been committed.
Having heard all this from Yaugandharāyaṇa,
the noble-minded Brahmarākṣasa Yogeśvara was satisfied and said to him:
Who else besides the god Bṛhaspati is your equal in statesmanship? You are the sprinkling of nectar for this tree of his kingdom; your counsel is its root.
"Thus, I shall always investigate the course of Kaliṅgasenā through both my intellect and my power," having said this, Yogeśvara then departed.
At that time, Kaliṅgasenā, staying in her own palace, grew faint as she gazed again and again at the Lord of Vatsa as he was wandering about on the palace rooftops and other places.
With her mind fixed on him, tormented by love, wearing bracelets of lotus stalks and anointed with sandalwood paste,
she found no peace anywhere.
In the meantime, that lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega, having seen her before, stood there afflicted by the intense arrows of the god of love.
Although she performed austerities to attain him and obtained a boon from Śaṅkara, she remained attached to another man living in a different land; thus, she was not easily accessible to him.
Because that lord of the Vidyādharas had found an opportunity,
he was wandering through the sky at night above his palace.
But remembering that command of Dhūrjaṭi, who was pleased by his asceticism,
he assumed the form of the Lord of Vatsa during one night by means of his own magic power.
And assuming that form, he entered his palace, saluted by the doorkeepers,
like the God of Death himself who had arrived in secret with his ministers, impatient for the delay.
Seeing him, Kaliṅgasenā also rose up, trembling with agitation;
she seemed to be restrained by the cries of her ornaments, as if saying, "This is not he!"
Then, having gradually gained her confidence by assuming the form of the Lord of Vatsa, he,
Madanavega, made her his wife according to the Gāndharva rite.
And at that moment, having entered there unobserved through his yogic power,
the Lord of Yoga became despondent due to the delusion of seeing the King of Vatsa.
Having gone and told this to Yaugandharāyaṇa, and by his direction,
he skillfully observed that Vāsavadattā was standing beside the King of Vatsa.
Delighted by the words of his chief minister, he went once more to ascertain the appearance of Kaliṅgasenā’s secret lover while she was asleep.
Having gone to the bed of the sleeping Kaliṅgasenā,
he beheld Madanavega lying there, restored to his own natural form.

His lotus-feet are marked by the parasol and banner and are free from dust; he possesses both divine and human [qualities], and he has transcended the transformation of form through the mastery of those very sciences that were previously hidden within his sleep.
Having gone there, the Lord of Yoga, filled with joy and satisfaction at what he had seen, spoke thus to the delighted Yaugandharāyaṇa: SoKss_6,7.179.
One such as I knows nothing at all, whereas you know everything through the eye of political wisdom;
by your counsel, this task of our lord, which was difficult to accomplish, has been achieved.
What is the sky without the sun? What is a lake without water? What is a kingdom without counsel? What is speech without truth?
Having addressed the Lord of Yoga who had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa, being pleased,
then went in the morning to see the King of Vatsa.
Approaching him in the proper manner, he spoke to the king during the course of conversation regarding Kaliṅgasenā, having been asked for his decision on the matter at hand.
"O King, she is independent; she does not deserve the touch of your hand here.
For she has come of her own free will to see Prasenajit."
Having seen that you were old, she became detached [from him] and came to you out of greed for your beauty;
moreover, she now indulges at her own will in union with other men.
Having heard that, [he thought: "How could this daughter of noble family act in such a way?
Who has the power to enter the interior of my inner apartments?"
When the king had spoken thus, the wise Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
"O King, this very night I shall show this to you directly."
The divine beings, such as the Siddhas and others, long for her; what mortal man is there in this world?
And who here, O King, is able to obstruct the course of the divine?
"Come, see it for yourself," said that minister;
at these words, the king resolved to go there with him during the night.
"O Queen, as for what was said— that no other woman is to be married except Padmāvatī— that vow has been fulfilled by me today."
Then, having approached that queen and spoken to her, Yaugandharāyaṇa told her the entire account concerning Kaliṅgasenā.
"This is the fruit of practicing your instructions for me," said Queen Vāsavadattā, and she too, bowing down, congratulated him.
Then, at midnight while the people were fast asleep, the Lord of Vatsa departed for the house of Kaliṅgasenā, accompanied by Yaugandharāyaṇa.
And having entered there unobserved into the presence of her who was enjoying sleep,
he saw Madanavega lying asleep in his own natural form.
And while that king was still wishing to kill that reckless man,
he was awakened by his magic power and became a Vidyādhara.
And having awakened, he emerged and suddenly flew up into the sky;
in an instant, Kaliṅgasenā also woke up from that state.
Seeing the bed empty, she said: "How is it that the Lord of Vatsa, having previously awakened, goes away after leaving me while I am still asleep?"
Having heard that, Yaugandharāyaṇa said to the Lord of Vatsa:
"Listen, she has been ruined by this man who assumed your form."
