Having known him through the power of yoga, he has been shown directly to you by me;
however, because of his divine majesty, he cannot be slain.
Having said this, he and the king went together toward her;
and Kaliṅgasenā, seeing them, stood there showing them respect.
To her who was saying, "O King, where have you just now gone, having arrived with your ministers? that Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
"Kaliṅgasenā, you have been deluded and married by someone using the illusory form of the Lord of Vatsa; you were not married by this husband of mine."
Hearing that, Kaliṅgasenā was greatly agitated, as if pierced in her heart by an arrow; with eyes full of tears, she spoke to the Lord of Vatsa.
"Even though I was married to you by the Gāndharva rite, I have been forgotten;
is this not just as it happened before with Śakuntalā and King Duṣyanta?"
Having been addressed thus by her, the king, with his face bowed down, said to her:
"It is true that you have not been married by me; for I have only just now arrived."
When the Lord of Vatsa had spoken thus, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said,
"Come," and then led him at his ease to the royal palace.
Then, when the queen had departed with her ministers,
she remained there like a deer strayed from the herd, having been abandoned by her own kinsmen.
With the lotus-face of her petals blossoming through sexual enjoyment,
she was like a lotus pond pressed by an elephant, with the rows of bees being the mass of her braided hair.
Her maidenhood destroyed and left without any means of recourse, Kaliṅgasenā, gazing at the sky, spoke these words: SoKss_6,7.209 //
"By someone in the form of the Lord of Vatsa, I have been married;
let that childhood husband be made manifest, for he alone is my husband."
When she had spoken thus, that lord of the Vidyādharas,
possessing a divine form and adorned with necklaces and armlets, descended there from the sky.
And when asked by her, "Who are you?", he said this to her:
"O slender one, I am a lord of the Vidyādharas named Madanavega."
And previously, having seen you while you were staying in your father’s house,
I performed austerities and obtained from Maheśvara a boon that would grant me union with you.
And because you were so enamored of the Lord of Vatsa, I quickly married you through a stratagem, even though his marriage had not yet taken place, by means of your own form.
Thus, by his nectar-like words entering the path of her hearing,
Kaliṅgasenā’s lotus-heart was somewhat revived.
Then Madanavega, having comforted his beloved and restored her composure, bestowed upon her a heap of gold;
and she, inwardly bound by devotion to her noble husband as being worthy of him, immediately flew back up to heaven to return once more.
Considering that her husband’s home was a divine abode inaccessible to mortals, and that she had left her father’s house out of love,
Kaliṅgasenā then resolved to dwell right there, having been granted permission by Madanavega.
Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the eighth wave.
Then, remembering the incomparable body of Kaliṅgasenā...
Once, at night, the Lord of Vatsa became possessed by the god of love.
Rising up with sword in hand, he went and entered her palace alone,
where he was received with the honors of hospitality by her.
Thereupon, as that lord of the earth was seeking her for the sake of a wife,
he was rejected by her with the words, "I am the wife of another," and he replied:
Since you have reached a third man, you are an unchaste woman;
therefore, the fault of approaching another's wife does not apply to me in approaching you.
Thus addressed by the king, Kaliṅgasenā replied to him:
"O King, I have indeed come here for your sake, sent by a Vidyādhara."
I was approached at will by the force of passion, who assumed your form;
he alone is my husband, so why am I a harlot?
What indeed can be said of these calamities that befall women who have transgressed their kin and whose souls are ruined by self-willed conduct; what even need be said of unmarried maidens?
Although I was forbidden by my friend, who perceived an ill omen, I nevertheless dispatched a messenger to your side; this is the fruit of that action for me.
If you touch me by force, I shall then give up my life;
for what woman of noble birth would indeed commit treachery against her husband?
And so I shall tell you a story here; listen, O King.
Long ago there was a lord of the Cedi country named Indradatta.
Desiring a body of fame and seeing that his own body was fragile, he built a great temple at the sacred ford of Pāpaśodhana for the sake of renown.
And that king went there constantly to behold that [liṅga] with the sentiment of devotion (bhaktirasa),
and all the people always came there for the sake of bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
And once, that king saw there a merchant’s wife who had come for the purpose of bathing at a sacred ford, her husband being away on a journey.
Sprinkled with the nectar of her own pure luster, adorned with ornaments of wondrous form,
she was as delightful as the moving capital city of the God of Love.
By you, O Vijayā, I have been embraced at my feet as if out of affection, saying "I am the universe," by the two quivers of the Five-Arrowed One that grace both sides.
As soon as he saw her, she so captivated the mind of the king that,
searching for her house, he went there at night, utterly helpless.
And as he was pursuing her, the king was addressed by her:
"You are a protector; it is not fitting for you to violate another's wife."
If you touch me by force, great unrighteousness will be yours;
I shall die instantly, and I will not endure such defilement.
Even though she spoke thus, as the king desired to use force against her,
her heart suddenly burst from the fear of losing her virtue.
Seeing that, he was immediately overcome with shame; having returned just as he had come, the king met his death within those days due to that remorse.
Having told this tale, Kaliṅgasenā, bowing with a mixture of fear and humility,
spoke again to the Lord of Vatsa.
Therefore, do not set your mind on unrighteousness by taking my life;
grant me a place to dwell here as one who has sought refuge, or otherwise I shall go elsewhere.
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, the King of Vatsa,
who was knowledgeable in dharma, reflected upon it, desisted, and then spoke to her.
"O princess, dwell here now with your husband as you please;
I shall not say anything further to you now, so do not be afraid."
When the king had spoken thus and departed at his own will for his palace,
Madanavega heard of this and descended from the sky.
"My dear, you have done well; had you not acted thus, O auspicious one, no good would have come of it, for I could not have endured it."
Having spoken thus and comforted her, that Vidyādhara spent the night with her; thereafter, he remained coming and going to that very place.
And Kaliṅgasenā, while her husband was the lord of the Vidyādharas,
remained there, even though she was in human form, endowed with the happiness of divine enjoyments.
Vatsarāja, too, casting aside that anxiety and remembering the words of his minister,
rejoiced, considering himself to have regained the queen, the kingdom, and likewise his son.
And Queen Vāsavadattā and the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa became filled with joy when the fruit of the *Nītikalpalatā* had been accomplished.
Then, as the days passed, Kaliṅgasenā, her lotus-like face turning pale, conceived a child and experienced the longings of pregnancy.
Her two high breasts, with their nipples dark as fresh clouds,
shone like two treasure-jars of Love, marked with the seal of intoxication.
Then Madanavega, her husband, approached her and said:
"O Kaliṅgasenā, this is the custom for us who are divine beings."
Why did Menakā not abandon Śakuntalā at Kaṇva’s hermitage, when we could have gone far away, leaving behind this human offspring?
O Goddess, although you were formerly an apsaras, you have now attained human birth due to your own lack of discipline and the curse of Śakra.
"By that very act, the title of 'unchaste woman' has been applied to you here, even though you were virtuous.
Therefore, you must protect your offspring; I shall go to my own place."
"When you remember me, I shall then appear before you.
Having spoken thus to Kaliṅgasenā, whose eyes were filled with tears, [he departed].
Then, having comforted her and given her that collection of jewels,
the lord of the Vidyādharas, his mind fixed on her and drawn by their mutual agreement, departed.
Kaliṅgasenā, too, remained there, leaning upon the king of Vatsa’s arm-shade as if it were a friend, while clutching her hope for offspring.
In the meantime, the Lord of Ambikā commanded Rati, the wife of Anaṅga, who had performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a husband endowed with all his limbs.
Born in the house of the King of Vatsa, that husband of yours named Naravāhanadatta was previously consumed by fire; he is not born of a womb because of my transgression.
But through your propitiation of me, you shall be born in the world of mortals not from a womb; then, by that husband, you shall be united with him in his entirety.
Having spoken thus to Rati, Śambhu then commanded Prajāpati:
"Kaliṅgasenā shall give birth to a son of divine origin."
Having abducted her by means of illusion, you should create this Rati as a human maiden at her place, and cast off her divine body.
Having thus received the command of the Lord upon his head, the Creator then departed;
and Kaliṅgasenā, when her time for delivery had arrived, gave birth.
As soon as her son was born, the Creator, having taken him away by his own power of illusion and transformed that girl into Rati, placed her there unobserved.
And everyone there perceived that very girl as if she were the crescent of the new moon risen unexpectedly even during the day.
She illuminated her dwelling with her radiance,
making the rows of jewel-lamp flames appear lusterless as if they were ashamed, having been surpassed by her.
Seeing that she had given birth to such an extraordinary daughter, Kaliṅgasenā,
out of joy exceeding even the birth of a son, held a great festival.
Then the King, the Lord of Vatsa, together with his queen and his ministers,
heard that such a daughter had been born to Kaliṅgasenā.
And having heard this, the king, suddenly impelled by the Lord,
spoke to Queen Vāsavadattā while Yaugandharāyaṇa stood nearby.
"I know that this Kaliṅgasenā is a divine woman fallen due to a curse;
and this daughter born of her is likewise divine, possessing a wondrous form."
Therefore, this maiden is equal in beauty to my son Naravāhanadatta; she is worthy to become his chief queen.
Having heard that, King Vāsavadattā said to him:
"O Great King, why do you speak thus so suddenly today?"
This son of yours is pure on both sides of his lineage; where indeed is that Kaliṅgasenā, from whose womb as an unchaste woman he was conceived?
Having heard this and reflecting upon it, the king said: "Indeed, I do not say this of my own accord;
it is as if someone, having entered within me, is making me speak."
And I seem to hear a voice from the sky saying: "This maiden was ordained of old to be the wife of Naravāhanadatta."
Furthermore, this Kaliṅgasenā was a devoted wife of noble birth;
however, due to the power of her past karma, she has incurred the reputation of being an unchaste woman.
When the king had spoken thus, the minister Yaugandharāyaṇa said:
"O Lord, it is heard that when Smara was consumed by fire, Rati performed austerities."
Having descended to the world of mortals in bodily form,
you shall be reunited with your own husband once he has entered the state of a mortal.
Thus Śarva granted a boon for the sake of pleasure to her who desired him as her husband;
and previously, your son was declared by divine speech to be an incarnation of Kāma.
And by the command of Hara, she was to descend into the state of a mortal through Rati;
thus was it described to me in secret today by Garbhagrāhikā.
Previously, I saw Kaliṅgasenā’s embryo joined with the bed of the womb;
at that very moment, I saw it again, devoid of that.
"Having seen that wonder, I have come here to tell you," said that woman to me; "this intuition has arisen in you as well."
Knowing this, the gods created through their illusory power this daughter of Kaliṅgasenā, born not from a womb, as a source of delight produced by the theft of an embryo.
O King, she was the wife of your son, who is an incarnation of Kāma;
likewise, listen here to this story concerning a yakṣa.
There was a servant of Vaiśravaṇa known as Virūpākṣa,
a yakṣa who had attained the position of chief superintendent over hundreds of thousands of treasures.
And he appointed a yakṣa to guard a treasure situated outside Mathurā,
who was as immovable as a stone pillar.
Then, at one time, a certain twice-born Pāśupata living in that city, who was a seeker of hidden treasures and an expert in the science of mining, arrived there in search of a treasure.
As he searched with a human corpse for a lamp in his hand,
at that very spot, the lamp fell from his hand.
Having recognized that a treasure was situated there by that sign,
he began to dig it up together with his other brahmin friends.
Then that yakṣa who had been appointed to the task of guarding,
having seen this, went and informed Virūpākṣa of the situation exactly as it was.
"Go and quickly slay those base practitioners of subterranean lore," thus the wrathful Virūpākṣa commanded that yakṣa.
Then that yakṣa, having gone there, by his own stratagem slaughtered those brahmins who had been proclaiming the treasure, before they could attain their desire.
Having learned of that, the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) became enraged and said to Virūpākṣa:
"O sinful one, how was the murder of a Brahmin suddenly committed by you?"
What indeed would a person in a low station not do out of greed?
He is restrained by being terrified with various obstacles; he is not killed.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Wealth cursed Virūpākṣa, saying:
"Be born in a mortal womb because of your practice of evil deeds."
Then, having received a curse from a certain brahmin on earth,
that Virūpākṣa was born as the son of a brahmin who had seized a land grant.
Then his wife, the yakṣiṇī, addressed the Lord of Wealth:
"O Lord, cast me into that very place where my husband has been thrown."
"Be gracious, for I am not able to live separated from him.
When she, the virtuous woman, had thus entreated him, Vaiśravaṇa replied:
O blameless one, he who was born in the house of that brahmin shall be your husband;
you, however, shall be born not from a womb, but fall into the house of his very slave-woman.
There, you will be reunited with that husband;
and by your grace, having crossed over his curse, he shall come to my side.
Thus, by the command of Vaiśravaṇa, that virtuous woman fell from there and became a human girl at the door of that maidservant's house.
And suddenly that maidservant saw a girl of wondrous appearance;
having seized her, she showed her to her master, the twice-born man.
"This is some divine maiden, undoubtedly not born from a womb"—so my own soul tells me here; bring her without hesitation.
"Indeed, I think this woman deserves to be the wife of my son.
Thus that brahmin spoke to the maidservant and rejoiced.
Gradually growing up there, that girl and the son of the Brahmin became bound by intense mutual affection upon seeing one another.
Then, having performed their marriage with that brahmin, the couple remained as if they had emerged from a period of separation, even though they did not possess the recollection of their past lives.
Then, in due time, at the end of her body, that husband followed her;
his sins destroyed by that asceticism, he became a yakṣa and attained his own station.
Thus, being free from sin and not born from a womb, these divine beings created by fate descend here upon the earth due to the power of causes.
"O King, what is her lineage? Therefore, this daughter of Kaliṅgasenā is ordained by fate to be the wife of your son, just as it was declared."
When Yaugandharāyaṇa had spoken thus,
both the Lord of Vatsa and Queen Vāsavadattā resolved in their hearts, "So be it."
Then, after that chief minister had gone home,
the king spent that day happily with his wife, engaged in drinking and other diversions.
Then, as the days passed, that daughter of Kaliṅgasenā— though her own memory had been lost through delusion— remained possessed of the fullness of her beauty.
In due course, she grew up and was given the name Madanamañcukā by her mother and by the people, because she was the daughter of Madanavega.
Surely she must have assumed the beauty of all other excellent women;
otherwise, how could they have appeared so deformed in her presence?
And having heard of that Rūpavatī, Queen Vāsavadattā once brought her into her own presence out of curiosity.
There, King Vatsa beheld her clinging to the nurse’s face,
while Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others saw her like the flame of a lamp within its wick.
And having seen that body of hers, never before seen, which was nectar to the eyes,
who there did not think, "This must be Rati herself descended here"?
Then Queen Vāsavadattā had her son Naravāhanadatta, a festival for the eyes of the world, brought there.
There, he did not see that radiant Madanamañcukā upon her full-blown lotus-face,
just as a bed of lotuses does not see the splendor of the new sun.
Beholding him, the delight of her eyes, with her face blossoming,
that young woman found no satiety, just as a female cakora bird never tires of the moonlight.
From that time forth, even though they were but children, those two were unable to remain apart for even a moment,
as if bound by the snares of their glances.
Having determined over several days that their relationship was indeed ordained by the gods,
the Lord of Vatsa set his mind upon the performance of their marriage ceremony.
Having learned that, Kaliṅgasenā rejoiced and,
out of affection for her son-in-law Naravāhanadatta, she fixed her heart’s resolve upon him.
After consulting with his ministers,
the King of Vatsa then had a separate palace built for his son, as if it were his own.
Then, having gathered the necessary materials, that king, who knew the proper time, consecrated his son—
who had already demonstrated his grasp of praiseworthy virtues— in the position of crown prince.
First, there fell upon his head the water born from the tears of joy of his parents;
thereafter, the water from sacred bathing places, purified by Vedic mantras.
When his lotus-face was washed with the waters of consecration,
it is a marvel that even the faces of the quarters attained stainless purity.
When auspicious garlands and flowers were thrown at him by his mothers,
even the heavens at that moment released a rain of celestial flower garlands.
In the vault of the sky, the echoes of the sounds of the drums of bliss swelled as if in rivalry with the resonance of the celestial drums.
Who there did not bow down to that consecrated crown prince? For at that time, he alone rose up by his own power.
Then the Lord of Vatsa summoned the seventy sons of his own ministers, who had been the childhood friends of his son, and appointed them to the office of minister.
Then he appointed Marubhūti, the son of Yaugandharāyaṇa,
to the office of minister, and Hariśikha, the son of Rumaṇvat, to the command of the army.
He appointed Tapantaka, the son of Vasantaka, as his playmate,
and Gomukha, the son of Ityaka, to the office of chamberlain.
And for the office of domestic chaplain, both sons of Piṅgalikā mentioned previously—
Vaiśvānara and Śāntisoma, the two sons of his brother the chaplain— were appointed.
When the king had thus commanded them to assist his son,
a voice arose from the sky, preceded by a rain of flowers.
These shall accomplish all the goals of this practitioner;
Gomukha, moreover, shall be inseparable from his very body.
Having been thus addressed by the divine voice, the delighted Lord of Vatsa honored them all with garments and ornaments.
And while that king was raining down wealth upon his dependents,
the word "poor" had no application there for even a single person.
The city was filled with dancers and wandering minstrels who seemed as if summoned by the rows of banner-cloths fluttering and tossed by the wind.
The future wife of Kaliṅgasenā, who was none other than the goddess Lakṣmī herself,
arrived there for the upcoming festival of her mother-in-law.
Then Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī likewise danced with joy, like three powers united as one.
With their creepers swaying in the wind, the trees here seem to be dancing on all sides;
what need is there even to mention the sentient beings?
Then, having performed his ablutions and mounted the elephant Jayakuñjara,
the crown prince Naravāhanadatta set forth.
And he was showered by the women of the city with upturned eyes— blue, white, and reddish— that shone like handfuls of blue lotuses, parched grain, and red lotuses.
And having seen that, being praised by bards and panegyrists, he entered his own palace together with his ministers, while the deities worthy of worship in that city [were honored].
There, Kaliṅgasenā first presented him with divine foods and drinks that surpassed her own royal splendor.
Overcome with affection for her son-in-law, she gave him fine garments and divine ornaments, along with his ministers, friends, and servants.
Thus, with such great festivities, that day passed for the King of Vatsa and all the others, as beautiful as the taste of nectar.
Then, when night had arrived, Kaliṅgasenā, reflecting upon her son’s marriage, remembered her friend Somaprabhā.
As soon as she was remembered by her, the great wise Nalakūbara spoke then to that worthy daughter of the Asura Maya.
"O beloved, Kaliṅgasenā remembers you today with eager longing;
therefore, go to the divine garden and perform this for the sake of your daughter."
Having spoken thus and related both what was to come and what had already occurred concerning that matter,
the husband then and there sent his wife Somaprabhā away.
Having arrived and embraced her friend Kaliṅgasenā— who had long yearned for such a greeting— Somaprabhā inquired after her welfare and said:
First, you were married by a Vidyadhara of great supernatural power;
and by the grace of Śiva, Rati and your daughter were brought down [to earth].
And she was fashioned as the former wife of Naravāhanadatta, who was born to the King of Vatsa through his descent into the realm of desire.
He shall exercise divine sovereignty over the Vidyādharas for an eon (kalpa),
and she will be honored above all his other queens.
And you, an Apsaras fallen to the world of mortals due to Śakra’s curse,
having completed the remainder of your task, shall obtain release from the curse.
"O friend, all this has been told to me by my wise husband;
therefore, you should have no anxiety on his account, for everything will turn out well for you."
"And here I am creating this divine garden for the sake of your daughter;
there is nothing that does not exist in Pātāla, on earth, or in heaven."
Having spoken thus, Somaprabhā took leave of the longing Kaliṅgasenā and departed for her own divine garden by means of her magic power.
Then, when night had turned to dawn,
the world suddenly beheld that garden there, as if it had fallen from heaven to the earth.
Having learned of this, King Vatsarāja arrived there with his wife and ministers,
as did Naravāhanadatta with his followers.
They beheld that garden, which was always filled with trees bearing flowers and fruit,
and possessed pillars, walls, grounds, and ponds made of various kinds of jewels.
With its golden-colored birds and winds of divine fragrance,
that place— descended to earth by the command of the gods— was like another heaven upon the ground.
Having seen that marvel, the King of Vatsa then asked Kaliṅgasenā, who was busy with her hospitality, "What is this? (SoKss_6,8.147)
She replied to that king while everyone was listening:
"There is a great asura named Maya, who is an incarnation of Viśvakarman."
She who built the beautiful city for Yudhiṣṭhira and for the wielder of the thunderbolt—
her daughter, named Somaprabhā, is my friend.
Having come to my presence by her own supernatural power during that night,
she out of affection created this divine garden for the sake of my daughter.
Having said this,
she then related everything, saying, "Whatever was spoken by my friend regarding the past and the future, all that was spoken by her exactly as it was."
Then, observing that Kaliṅgasenā’s statement was consistent with the facts,
they all cast aside their doubts and attained incomparable satisfaction.
And the King of Vatsa, together with his wife, sons, and others, spent that day in this very garden through the hospitality of Kaliṅgasenā.
On another day, having gone out to see the deity at the temple,
the king saw many women there, beautifully dressed and adorned with ornaments.
When asked by him, "Who are you?", they replied to him:
"We are these sciences and arts; we have come here for the sake of your son."
"Let us go and enter the sky," they said, and having spoken thus, they vanished;
the King of Vatsa, the sovereign, also entered his inner apartments, filled with wonder.
There he announced this to Queen Vāsavadattā and to the group of ministers;
they rejoiced in it and recognized it as a favor from the gods.
Then, by the king's command, as Naravāhanadatta entered there, Vāsavadattā instantly took up her lute.
Then, with humility, the prince said to his mother as she was playing it, "This lute has slipped from its place. (Suttanipāta 6.8.159)
When his father said, "Take this and play it," he then played the lute,
causing even the Gandharvas to be filled with wonder.
Thus, having been examined by his father in all branches of knowledge and the arts, he himself came to know everything that they had selected for him.
Seeing that his son was endowed with such qualities, the King of Vatsa instructed Madanamañcukā,
the daughter of Kaliṅgasenā, in the art of dance.
Just as Pūrṇakalā became like the body of the moon,
so too did that ocean of Naravāhanadatta become agitated.
And he took delight in beholding her as she sang and danced,
appearing as if she were reciting the commands of Love through the expressive gestures of her limbs.
Not seeing her nectar-like beloved for even a moment, she too sat at dawn with tears in her eyes,
like a night-lily wet with dew.
Unable to remain constantly without gazing upon her face,
Naravāhanadatta went to various gardens.
There, having brought his daughter Madanamañcukā to his side,
he remained, being filled with joy by Kaliṅgasenā’s affection.
And Gomukha, who knew his master’s mind and wishing for him to remain there for some time, told various stories to Kaliṅgasenā.
The prince was pleased with her by means of that grasp upon his heart;
for entry into the heart is indeed the supreme means of enchantment for a lord.
There, in that garden-located music hall, he himself made Madanamañcukā fit for dancing and other arts.
While his beloved was dancing, Naravāhanadatta played all the musical instruments, putting even the finest wandering minstrels to shame.
And he likewise defeated various learned men who had come from all directions—
experts in elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, missiles, painting, literature, and other arts.
Thus did the days of Naravāhanadatta’s childhood pass away as he lived in this manner, chosen by the sciences themselves in their own selection.
And once, during a festival, that prince went with his beloved and his ministers to a garden called Nāgavana.
There, a certain merchant’s wife, who had been rejected by him despite her longing for him,
desired to kill Gomukha by bringing him a drink mixed with poison.
And Gomukha learned of this from the mouth of his friend;
he did not take that drink and thus censured women.
"Aha! First the Creator fashioned recklessness, and after that, women. For these women, nothing is difficult to accomplish here by their very nature."
Surely this thing called "woman" was created from both nectar and poison;
for when she is attached, she is indeed nectar, but when she is detached, she is just poison.
By whom can a woman of beautiful face be known to have hidden sins?
A wicked woman is like a lotus pond in full bloom, yet conceals crocodiles within.
But another woman falls from heaven, impelled by the wheel of her virtues— a noble wife unable to endure the praise of her husband— like the stainless radiance of the sun.
Once she has been seized, that wicked woman— infatuated with another, devoid of desire for her husband, and bearing the poison of dispassion— swiftly destroys him, just like a female serpent.
For instance, in a certain village there was a man named Śatrughna,
and his wife was unchaste.
One evening, he saw his wife united with her lover;
standing within the inner chamber, he struck down that lover with his sword.
Waiting for the night, he remained at the door, having barred his wife;
and at that moment, a traveler seeking lodging arrived there.
Having provided him with shelter by means of a stratagem, he took that adulterer— who had been killed by him—
and went to the forest there at night.
While he was throwing that corpse into the blind well,
his wife arrived from behind and threw him in there as well.
"What kind of reckless deed does a wicked woman not commit? Thus did Gomukha, though but a youth, there censure the conduct of women.
Then, having personally worshipped the Nāgas there in the Nāga grove,
Naravāhanadatta went to his own residence together with his retinue.
Thereupon, on another day, although he already knew them, he questioned his ministers, Gomukha and the others, regarding the compendium of royal policy.
"Although you are omniscient, we speak thus because we have been questioned by you";
having said this and determined the essential point among themselves, they spoke as follows.
Having first mounted the horses of the senses which have been brought under control, and having conquered those internal enemies such as desire, anger, and the rest, the king [proceeds].
One should first conquer one's own self for the sake of conquering other enemies;
for how can one who has not conquered his own self, being powerless, bring another under control?
Then he should appoint as ministers those endowed with qualities such as being native-born to the realm,
and as domestic priest one who is skilled, possessed of ascetic merit, and learned in the Atharva Veda.
Having examined them for fear, greed, righteousness, and passion through various tests,
the king, who knows the inner thoughts of others best, should appoint those ministers as suitable for their respective duties.

One should examine their speech as they converse with one another regarding mutual affairs— whether it be truthful, motivated by hatred, spoken out of affection, or consistent with their own self-interest.
One should be satisfied with the truth, but regarding untruth, one should inflict punishment as deserved;
and one should always investigate their conduct separately by means of spies.
Thus, seeing with unobstructed vision,
having uprooted the thorns and acquired treasury, army, and so forth, he should achieve firm rootedness.
Then, endowed with the three powers of energy, sovereignty,
and counsel, he should desire to conquer foreign lands after having deliberated upon the difference between himself and his enemy.
One should deliberate on counsel with those who are trustworthy, learned in the scriptures, and wise, without haste;
once it has been determined by them, one should refine every aspect of it with one's own intelligence.
One who knows the means such as conciliation and bribery should secure the acquisition and preservation of what has been gained;
thereafter, one should employ the six measures of policy, beginning with peace and war.
Thus, free from sloth and applying his mind to both his own country and that of his enemies, a king surely conquers and is never again defeated.
But the ignorant man, blinded by desire and greed, is led astray by those who show him false paths;
having been cast into pits, he is plundered by the servants of rogues.
No other person finds any opportunity in the presence of that king,
just as farmers find no access to rice whose field has been fenced off by rogues.
For by entering into the secrets, he is indeed brought under their control;
consequently, the Goddess Śrī, distressed by that knower of the specific [truth], flees from him.

Therefore, a king should be one who has conquered himself, who applies punishment appropriately, and who discerns distinctions; for by acting thus out of regard for his subjects, he shall become a vessel of prosperity.
And formerly, a king named Śūrasena, who placed sole reliance on his servants, was brought under control by his ministers, who formed a clique and consumed his wealth.
When the king wished to give even a blade of grass to that servant of his, those ministers there did not wish to grant it to him.
But whoever was a servant among them, they themselves gave to him;
and having petitioned the king, they caused even those unworthy to be given [alms].
Having seen that and understood it, the king gradually caused those ministers— who were a band of rogues— to be divided from one another through wisdom and skillful means.
When they had been divided and destroyed, and were engaged in mutual slander,
that king ruled his kingdom properly, uncheated by others.
And Harisiṃha became king, together with his ministers who knew the principles of policy; he maintained devoted and wise counselors, possessed strong fortresses, and accumulated great wealth.
Having made his subjects devoted, he acted in whatever manner was appropriate;
even when attacked by a universal monarch, he did not suffer defeat.
"Thus, deliberation and reflection are the essence; what indeed could be more important for a kingdom?
Having said this and other such things, Gomukha and the others ceased speaking, each according to his own nature.
And Naravāhanadatta, placing faith in their words,
declared that although human effort is to be considered, destiny is inconceivable.
Then, rising up, he went with them to see his beloved Madanamañcukā, whose longing had been intensified by his delay.
When he had reached that palace and was seated upon his throne,
Kaliṅgasenā, having paid him her respects, spoke for a moment to Gomukha with wonder:
While Naravāhanadatta, the prince, had not yet returned there,
Madanamañcukā was anxious to see his path.
While I had ascended to the top floor of the palace accompanied by Gomukha, at that very moment,
a certain man descended there from the sky.
Wearing a crown and bearing a sword, he of divine appearance said to me:
"I am the king named Mānasavega, the lord of the Vidyādharas."
"The celestial woman named Surabhidattā and you yourself have fallen to earth due to a curse;
and this daughter of yours is divine—it is indeed known to me."
"Give this daughter of yours to me, for this alliance is indeed fitting.
When he had spoken thus, I suddenly laughed and said to him:
"Naravāhanadatta has been ordained by the gods as her husband;
he shall become the sovereign emperor (cakravartin) over all of you here."
Having been addressed thus by me, that Vidyādhara flew up into the sky and departed,
like a sudden flash of lightning that causes distress to the eyes of my daughter.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O Mistress, when this prince was born here, we learned from a voice in the sky that he would be our future lord."
For those Vidyādharas immediately desired even to inflict evil upon him;
for who would wish for a powerful master to be unrestrained?
Then this Rakṣita was personally instructed by Śambhu regarding the Gaṇas;
this speech of Nārada, as it was being spoken by my father, was heard by me.
"Therefore, these Vidyādharas are now our enemies.
Having heard this, Kaliṅgasenā spoke out of fear for her own life: SoKss_6,8.227 //
In that case, why is Madanamañcukā not married to the prince by means of an illusion, so that she is not deceived by him as I have been?
Having heard this from Kaliṅgasenā, Gomukha and the others said to her: "Let the Lord of Vatsa himself be urged to undertake this task."
Then, his mind fixed upon her, Naravāhanadatta spent the day in that garden,
gazing at Madanamañcukā.
Her face was like a full-blown lotus, her eyes like opening blue water-lilies,
her lips lovely as the bandhūka flower, and her breasts like clusters of mandāra blossoms.
Her limbs as delicate as the *śirīṣa* flower, like one made of five blossoms,
she was fashioned by Smara as the sole arrow capable of conquering the world.
On another day, Kaliṅgasenā herself went to the Lord of Vatsa and,
for the sake of her daughter’s marriage, made her request according to her desire.
The Lord of Vatsa, having dismissed her and summoned his own ministers,
spoke to them while Queen Vāsavadattā remained present.
"Kaliṅgasenā is hastening toward her daughter's wedding; how then shall we act, since the world calls this most excellent woman an unchaste woman? (SoKss_6,8.235)
The world must always be protected; why was it not so in the past? By his mere reputation, Rāmabhadra abandoned Queen Jānakī, even though she was pure.
Even though Ambā was abducted by Bhīṣma with great effort for the sake of his brother,
why did he not abandon her when she acted contrary to his will and had previously chosen another husband?
Thus, although this Kaliṅgasenā chose me in a svayaṃvara, she was married by Madanavega; for that reason, people reproach her.
"Therefore, let this Naravāhanadatta himself marry this daughter of his, who is a worthy match for him, according to the Gāndharva rite."
When the King of Vatsa had spoken thus, Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
"O Lord, how could Kaliṅgasenā desire such impropriety?"
"For she is divine and not ordinary, along with her son"—this has been understood by me repeatedly;
and this was told to me by my friend, the wise Brahmarākṣasa.

While they were thus deliberating with one another, there suddenly emerged from the sky a voice belonging to Maheśvara: SoKss_6,8.242: "Thus, while they were reflecting upon it among themselves, a voice of Maheśvara appeared from heaven."
This [woman] was created by me alone for Naravāhanadatta, who was born from the mind and consumed by the fire of Manmatha’s eye.
His wife, Madanamañcukā, was the delight [of his senses] through her satisfaction with his asceticism;
and he was accompanied by her, the foremost of all the women in the harem.
"By my grace, having conquered his enemies, he shall exercise divine sovereignty over the Vidyādharas for an eon," she said, and then her voice ceased.
Having heard these words of the Blessed One, the King of Vatsa, together with his retinue,
bowed to him and, filled with joy, made the firm resolve for the auspicious marriage.

Then the king, having honored and summoned his chief minister—who already knew the truth of the matter—as well as the astrologers, asked them for an auspicious moment that would yield favorable results; and they, having received honors, told him that it would occur within a few days.
"Your son will experience some slight separation from this wife here for a short time;
we know this, O Lord of Vatsa, through the insight of our own science," so those astrologers declared to you once again.
Then the king prepared for his son the marriage rites befitting his own majesty,
in such a manner that not only his own city, but the entire earth itself was thrown into agitation by those preparations.
Then, on the day the wedding arrived, Kaliṅgasenā’s father provided her with his own divine ornaments,
while Somaprabhā— having come under the influence of her husband’s command— performed the rite of adorning his daughter.
Then, having had the divine marriage-thread fastened, Madanamañcukā shone forth exceedingly;
indeed, it was just like the lovely moonlight when it follows the full moon of Kārtika.
And by the command of Hara, divine women, their songs being heard, performed auspicious rites for her; though overcome by her beauty, they remained concealed as if out of shame.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, compassionate toward your devotees, you have today come in person and made the penance of Rati successful!"—
with such words, accompanied by the music of divine and excellent celestial bards, they celebrate Gaurī’s attainment of her goal here.
Then Naravāhanadatta entered the wedding chamber,
which was occupied by Madanamañcukā and adorned with the splendor of the auspicious marriage-thread, while he himself bore various great musical instruments.
Having there completed the auspicious marriage rites for the bride and groom with great zeal and care,
they both ascended the altar where the blazing fire stood, which was like the crown of kings adorned with the lamps of pure jewels.
If, at some point, the moon and the sun were to revolve simultaneously around the Golden Mountain here,
then only would there be a resemblance to the circumambulation of the bride and bridegroom around the fire in this world.
Just as the drums in the sky drowned out the sounds of the wedding festival trumpets,
so too did the showers of flowers released by the gods here overwhelm the parched grain scattered for the bride during the sacrifice.

Then the noble-minded Kaliṅgasenā indeed honored her son-in-law with heaps of gold and jewels made of gems, such that even the Lord of Alakā himself was perceived by the people there as utterly destitute in her presence; what then need be said of other wretched kings?

And when the ceremony for the marriage rite— which had been long desired and was now accomplished in such a manner— was completed, the bride and groom entered the inner apartments, which were filled with joy, like the mind of the world entering a pure painting of variegated patterns.

O one honored by the whole world, that city was swiftly filled by kings who, though accompanied by excellent armies and possessed of splendor through their valor, were themselves conquered and bowed down; they arrived with noble gifts and jewels in their hands, like the lords of the waters (oceans) filling it.
In this great festival, that king also showered gold upon his subjects;
indeed, there was no one in his kingdom who was not born of gold within their mother’s womb.
Then, with throngs of excellent wandering actors and dancers gathered there from various quarters,
the world of living beings was awakened as if consisting entirely of that [festivity], surrounded by hymns, dances, songs, and instrumental music.
And at this festival, Kauśāmbī, with its creeper-like arms of banners fluttering in the wind,
seemed to dance itself, the city adorned with the ornaments fashioned by the women of the citizens.
And so, as that great festival continued to grow day by day, it was brought to a conclusion after a very long time;
meanwhile, all his friends, kinsmen, and the people were constantly joyful, and thus their desires were fulfilled beyond measure.
And that Crown Prince Naravāhanadatta, together with Madanamañcukā,
pursued the long-desired pleasures of the world of the living, seeking their fulfillment.

Thus ends the eighth wave in the *Madanamañcukā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. And here concludes this sixth book, the *Madanamañcukā*. May there be prosperity!
*Śrīḥ!*
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The seventh book, named Ratnaprabhā.
Long ago, it is said, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, stirred by the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Those who, having attained supernatural power through the removal of obstacles, forcibly cause others to remember [the truth], bear the divine burden upon this earth by the grace of Bhava.
May the head of Śarva protect you— its forehead covered by the fingernails of Gaurī as she busily grasps his hair in play, appearing as if adorned with many moons. (SoKss_7,1.1)
May that elephant-faced one protect you, who, extending his trunk with its tip curled and moistened by the water of his gift, appears as if bestowing spiritual accomplishment.
Thus, in Kauśāmbī, that youth, the son of the Lord of Vatsa,
having married Madanamañcukā, who was as dear to him as his own life, [remained there].
Naravāhanadatta remained together with his own ministers, Gomukha and the others, as he pleased, his desires completely fulfilled.
And once, when the air resounded with the cries of intoxicated cuckoos in full flight and was filled with the Malaya breeze, which stirred the dance of swaying creepers; // SoKss_7,1.5 //
When the spring festival had arrived, made beautiful by the singing of bees,
the prince went with his ministers to the park to enjoy himself.
Having wandered there, his own companion Tapantaka suddenly approached him and, with eyes wide open in great joy, spoke to him: SoKss_7,1.7 //
"O Prince, I saw a certain maiden not far from here;
having descended from the sky, she stood beneath an aśoka tree."
And I was sent by that very maiden, who, accompanied by her friends and illuminating the quarters with her own splendor, approached me to summon you.
Having heard that, Naravāhanadatta, eager for a sight of him, went quickly to the foot of that tree together with his own ministers.
There he beheld that beloved woman, whose tremulous eyes were like bees,
whose sprout-like lips were crimson, and who was adorned with the clusters of her full breasts.
Her limbs were as fair as a mass of pollen, she dispelled heat with her shadow,
and she possessed a form so fitting that she seemed like the presiding deity of the grove manifest in person.
And the prince approached her as she bowed down,
and he greeted that celestial maiden, his eyes captivated by her beauty.
Then, when everyone had sat down, Gomukha, his minister, asked her: "O auspicious lady, who are you, and for what purpose have you come here?"
Having heard that, she— casting aside her shame due to the command of Love (Manmatha), which is difficult to transgress—
gazed repeatedly at the lotus-face of Naravāhanadatta.
Looking askance with her eyes, which were streaming with tears of equal measure,
she described the account of her own life story in detail as follows:
In the three worlds there is a renowned lord of mountains called Himavat;
of that mountain with many peaks, one peak is the mountain of the Lord of Gaurī.
Garlanded by the radiance of shimmering jewels and gleaming with the brilliance of snow,
he cannot be circumscribed, just like the vast expanse of the sky.
Whose mountain slopes are a treasury of medicinal herbs and of spiritual accomplishments— attainable through the grace of the Lord— which sever the fear of old age and death.
By its peaks, which are tawny with the radiance from the bodies of hosts of Vidyādharas,
the splendor of the summit of the king of the gods’ mountain is surpassed.
Therein lies a golden city named Kāñcanaśṛṅga,
which shines brilliantly with its splendors like the abode of the sun.
In that place, extending for many yojanas, there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Hemaprabha, who possesses firm devotion to Umāpati.
And among his many wives, he had a beloved queen named Alaṃkāraprabhā, who was like Rohiṇī to the moon.
In the morning, that righteous king, having risen together with her,
bathed and worshipped Maheśvara, accompanied by Gaurī, according to the prescribed rites.
And having come to the world of men, he bestows a hundred thousand pieces of gold, mixed with jewels, day after day upon brahmins who are poor.
Then, having returned and attended to his royal duties in accordance with dharma,
he partakes of food, drink, and so forth like a sage, firm in his vows.
Thus, as the days passed,
it is said that due to his lack of offspring, a concern regarding the king's sonlessness eventually arose.
Seeing him so deeply distressed, his beloved queen Alaṃkāraprabhā asked him the cause of his despondency.
Then the king said to her: "O Queen, I possess every kind of prosperity;
however, the single sorrow that I have no son afflicts me."
This thought has arisen in me because of the recollection of that discourse on the being endowed with spiritual power which I heard previously from a man who was childless. SoKss_7,1.30 //
When asked by the goddess, "O Lord, what kind of story is that?",
the king described that very story to her in brief.
In the city named Citrakūṭa, there was an eminent brahmin king, devoted to the worship of brahmins, whose name was truly significant.
He had a victorious servant named Sattvaśīla, who was devoted solely to battle;
and month after month, he received a hundred pieces of gold from that king.
And that gold was not sufficient for his needs,
because he was childless and his mind was solely intent on the joy of giving.
The Creator has granted me a son as a source of diversion,
yet he has also bestowed upon me a passion for giving, which is now rendered meaningless by the lack of wealth.
Better is the birth of a withered, decayed tree or even of a stone than that of one who is poor in this world and whose sole passion is renunciation.
Thus constantly reflecting, that man of virtuous character,
while once wandering in a park, by chance discovered a treasure-trove.
And taking it along with his servants, he brought by force that [treasure]— resplendent with abundant gold and beautiful with highly precious jewels— to his home.
Then, while remaining there in a state of sattva, he enjoyed pleasures, giving wealth to brahmins,
servants, and friends.
Having seen that, his kinsmen inferred it was the discovery of a treasure;
he went to the royal court and reported it freely to the king.
Then, summoned by the king at the command of the doorkeeper,
Sattvaśīla stood for a moment in a secluded corner of the royal courtyard.
There, digging the earth with a playful fist-closed vajra held in his hand,
he discovered another great treasure contained within a copper jar.
Having given this heart of his own to the King as something pleasing, it was revealed by the Creator, who is pleased with his virtuous nature, as if it were made manifest.
In that very same way, he covered it with clay and entered it;
then, announced by the doorkeeper, he approached the presence of the king.
"I have learned that you have found a treasure;
surrender it to us!"—thus was he addressed by the king himself there, after having been prostrated before him.
"What shall I offer to the God today? What is said to be appropriate for this day?
To him, Sattvaśīla spoke there to the king: "Let that [be offered] as well."
Thus addressed by the king with the words, "Offer that which you have newly obtained," he went and delivered the treasure to him in a secluded corner of the royal courtyard.
Then, having been sent off by the king— who was pleased with his treasure— with the words, "Enjoy this first treasure as you wish," Sattvaśīla went home.
There he lived, making his name true to its meaning through the practice of giving and enjoyment,
and somehow dispelling the mental distress and sorrow caused by childlessness.
Thus have I previously heard this account of Sattvaśīla;
remembering it, I dwell in sorrow, reflecting upon the non-existence of my son.
When the lord of the Vidyādharas, Hemaprabha, had spoken thus to his queen Alaṃkāraprabhā, she replied to him:
It is true that fate favors the virtuous;
for what other treasure is found in times of distress than the character of a noble being?
By the power of your own being, you too shall obtain what you desire;
hear now the story of Vikramatuṅga as an illustration of this.
There is a city named Pāṭaliputra, an ornament of the earth,
inlaid with various excellent jewels that possess a perfect array of colors.
In that place, there was formerly a king named Vikramatuṅga who possessed great courage;
he was never averse to giving to those in need, nor did he turn his back on his enemies in battle.
Once, having entered the forest for the sake of hunting,
the king beheld there a brahmin performing a fire sacrifice with *bilva* fruits.
Seeing him, although he wished to question him,
he departed from his presence and went far away with his army, out of a passion for hunting.
Having played for a long time with lions and deer as if they were balls— some leaping up, some falling down, and others being struck by his own hand.
Having returned and seeing that twice-born man there, likewise intent on the fire-oblation,
he approached him, bowed, and asked his name and the fruit of the oblation.
Then that brahmin, having offered his blessing, addressed the king:
"I am a brahmin named Nāgaśarman; hear from me the result of my sacrificial rite."
When the fire is propitiated by this oblation of bilva fruits,
then golden bilva fruits emerge from the sacrificial pit.
Then Agni, having become manifest, personally grants a boon:
"A great deal of time has passed for me while I have been offering *bilva* fruits."
"Yet that fire is not satisfied even now with one of such meager merit.
When he had spoken thus, the king, firm in his resolve, addressed him:
"In that case, O Brahmin, give me one *bilva* fruit so that I may offer it; I shall propitiate your fire this very moment."
How can you seek to propitiate that fire while being undisciplined and impure— a fire which is not satisfied even with me, who am thus established in my vows and purified?
Having been addressed thus by that brahmin, the king spoke to him again:
"Do not give me the wood-apple in this manner; wait a moment and behold a marvel!"
Then that brahmin, filled with curiosity, gave a bilva fruit to the king;
and the king, at that time, accepted it there with a mind of firm resolve.
"If he is not satisfied by this offering of a bilva fruit,
then I shall offer my own head to you, O Agni," he thought, and meditating thus, he offered it into him.
And the seven-flamed fire emerged from the sacrificial pit, itself taking up a golden bilva fruit,
like the fruit of the tree of being.
And Jātavedas himself spoke to that lord of the earth:
"I am pleased with this quality of yours; therefore, O King, choose a boon."
Having heard that, the Great Being, bowing before the king, said:
"What other boon do I have? Grant this twice-born man whatever he desires."
Having heard these words of the king, Agni, well-pleased, said to him:
"O King, this Brāhmaṇa shall become a lord of wealth through the Maghā constellation."
"By my grace, you too shall possess the glory of an inexhaustible treasury.
To Agni, who had thus granted the boon, that brahmin made this request:
"You have suddenly appeared before the king who wanders according to his own will;
but what is this to me, who am under vows? O Blessed One, why is this so? (SoKss 7.1.74)
Then Agni, the giver of boons, said: "If I had not granted him my vision, this king, possessed by such intense devotion, would have offered his own head into me."
For one of sharp faculties, the accomplishments indeed come without delay;
but for one of dull faculties such as yourself, O Brahmin, they come only after a long time.
Having spoken thus, when the fire had vanished, that brahmin Nāgaśarman took leave of the king and departed; thereafter, he gradually became a man of great wealth.
King Vikramatuṅga, having witnessed that virtuous being and being praised by his followers,
departed for his own city, Pāṭaliputra.
Once, while the Lord was staying there, a doorkeeper named Śatruñjaya entered unexpectedly and addressed him in private:
"O King, a young Brahmin named Dattaśarman stands at the gate, desiring to make a representation in this secluded place. SoKss_7,1.80 //
When the king commanded, "Let him enter," he was ushered in;
having first offered a blessing, the young student bowed to the king and sat down.
And he informed [the king]:
"O Lord, I know how to produce excellent gold from copper instantly by means of a certain formulation of powder."
For that method was indeed taught to me by my guru, and by means of that method,
I myself directly perceived his gold as it was fully accomplished.
When that student had spoken thus, the king had copper brought;
once it had been melted, the student threw the powder into it.
And as that powder was being scattered, some invisible being carried it away;
a certain yakṣa saw him, while the king’s fire was satisfied.
The copper, not having reached the powder, did not turn into gold;
thus, as the young brahmin performed this three times, his labor became fruitless.
Then, taking the powder from that despondent boy himself, the king—
the best among the radiant— cast it into the molten copper.
The Yakṣa smiled and departed, taking that powder with him;
through the application of that powder, the copper turned into gold.
Then, to that astonished young Brahmin who questioned him,
the king related the account of the Yakṣa exactly as it had been witnessed.
Having learned the formulation of medicinal powders from that young brahmin at that very time,
the king made him successful in his purpose once he had taken a wife.
And Pūrṇakoṣaśrī, having made the twice-born free from poverty, sent them away with unequalled enjoyments along with gold produced from that [alchemical] process, together with his harem.
Thus, as if out of fear or perhaps out of satisfaction,
it is indeed the Lord alone who grants what is desired to those of intense resolve.
"O Lord, who else besides you possesses such steadfast courage and is so generous?
Śambhu, when propitiated, will grant you a son; do not grieve."
Having heard these words from the mouth of Queen Udāramalaṃkāraprabhā, King Hemaprabha believed them and was filled with joy.
And he considered the attainment of a son to be certain through the propitiation of Gaurī’s Lord,
as indicated by his own heart, which was filled with enthusiasm.
Then, on another day, having bathed together with his queen and worshipped Śaṅkara,
he bestowed ninety million pieces of new gold upon the brahmins.
For the sake of a son, he performed austerities without food before Hara,
resolved that either his body would be cast away or Śarva would be gratified.
And standing there in ascetic penance, he praised the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the giver of boons,
who had effortlessly bestowed the Ocean of Milk upon Upamanyu when he sought refuge in him.
Salutations be unto you, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world;
O Lord of Gaurī, whose eightfold forms are distinguished by the various elements such as space and the rest.
Salutations to you, Śambhu, who reclines upon the ever-blooming lotus of the heart,
the swan dwelling within the pure lake of the mind.
Homage to you, O Moon, who possesses divine radiance, who is stainless, whose nature is water,
who is visible to those whose defects have been extinguished, and who is most wonderful!
Salutations to you, who are composed of the universe, who bear your beloved upon half your body, who remain a perpetual celibate student, and who have fashioned the entire world by your mere will.
To the king who had thus offered praise and who had fasted for three nights, the Lord of Girijā appeared in person in a dream and spoke as follows:
"Arise, O King! A heroic son shall be born to you who will uphold your lineage;
and by the grace of Gaurī, an excellent daughter shall also be yours."
She shall become the queen of Naravāhanadatta, your future universal monarch, that treasury of splendors.
When Śarva had vanished after saying this, Hemaprabha, the lord of the Vidyādharas, awoke delighted at the end of the night.
Having reported his dream, he greatly delighted Alaṅkāraprabhā,
who confirmed the correspondence by relating that Gaurī had told her exactly the same thing in a dream.
Then, having risen from there, bathed, worshipped Dhūrjaṭi (Śiva),
given gifts, and broken his fast, the king held a festival.
Then, after some days had passed,
Queen Alaṃkāraprabhā conceived a child by that king.
And she gladdened her beloved with her mouth, fragrant as honey,
with its rolling eyes like bees, as a pale lotus might gladden one with its face.
Then, in due time, she gave birth to a son whose noble birth was proclaimed by her magnificent pregnancy longings, just as the sky gives birth to the sun.
By him, as soon as he was born, his innate splendors illuminated even the dwelling where he was born,
turning it the color of vermilion-red.
And his father, the king, gave that infant— who brought fear to the clans of his enemies—
the name Vajraprabha, as instructed by a divine voice.
Then that boy grew gradually like the moon on the day of the full moon,
being filled with its digits for the sake of the increase of the ocean of his lineage.
Then, not long after, Queen Alaṃkāraprabhā became pregnant once again by that King Hemaprabha.
And she, pregnant and possessing a special radiance arising from her physical form,
truly became the jewel of the inner apartments, seated upon a golden throne.
And she, whose pregnancy-longings were thus manifesting, wandered through the sky in a celestial palace made of lotuses fashioned by her magic power.
And when the time had arrived, a daughter was born to that queen;
it would be superfluous to describe her birth, which resulted from the grace of Gaurī.
Then, a voice from the sky was heard, which accorded with the words of Śiva’s command: "She shall be the future wife of Naravāhanadatta."
Then King Hemaprabha, having celebrated a festival no different from that for the birth of a son,
gave his daughter the name Ratnaprabhā.
And that Ratnaprabhā, refined by her own learning, grew up in her father’s house, while her radiance spread throughout the quarters of the world.
Then that king, having performed the marriage rites for his son Vajraprabha, the wearer of armor,
consecrated him as the crown prince.
Having transferred the burden of the kingdom to him, he was not at ease;
at that time, the single concern of his heart was the thought of his son's marriage.
Once, seeing that daughter worthy of being given away as she sat nearby,
the king spoke to Queen Alaṅkāraprabhā, who was close at hand.
"Behold, O Goddess, how even in the three worlds a maiden, though she has become an ornament to her family, is a source of great suffering; fie, alas, even upon the great! (SoKss 7.1.125)
Although she is disciplined, though she has acquired knowledge, and though she possesses beauty and youth—
since Ratnaprabhā causes me such pain despite having obtained this boon.
"This woman has been declared as the wife of Naravāhanadatta by the gods;
why then is she not given to him, who is destined to be our emperor?"
When he had been addressed thus by the goddess, the king spoke again:
"Indeed, that maiden is blessed who shall obtain him as her husband."
For he has indeed entered into the realm of desire here, yet he has not as yet attained divine status;
therefore, I await his acquisition of the sciences (vidyā).
As his father was speaking thus, those words—
which were like the syllables of a mantra for the delusion of Kandarpa— immediately entered his ears.
Her heart was stolen by that excellent man, and Ratnaprabhā became as if possessed by delusion, as if her mind were entranced, as if asleep, and as if licked away.
Then, having somehow paid homage to his parents and gone to his own inner apartments,
he was overcome with anxiety and only after a long time did he finally fall asleep.
"Daughter, this morning is an auspicious day;
therefore, you must go to the city of Kauśāmbī and see that chosen husband of yours, the son of the Lord of Vatsa."
And then, O auspicious one, your father himself will bring you back to this city of his and arrange the marriage between you and him.
Thus, while he was dreaming, Gaurī, filled with compassion, instructed him;
and having awakened from that dream, she reported it to her mother in the morning.
Then, permitted by him and having learned [his location] through the power of her knowledge,
she set out from her own city to see the bridegroom who was staying in the garden.
"Noble son, you know me as this Ratnaprabhā;
you know that I have arrived today, eager [for you] in an instant, and nothing beyond this."
Having heard these words of hers, which surpassed nectar in sweetness,
and having beheld that body of the Vidyādharī, which was nectar for the eyes;
Naravāhanadatta inwardly reproached the Creator, thinking:
"Why did he not make me entirely composed of ears and eyes?"
And he said to her: "I am blessed; today my birth has become fruitful, O slender one, since I have been thus approached by you yourself out of affection."
Thus, while the two of them were engaged in conversation born of mutual affection,
suddenly the army of the Vidyādharas was seen there in the sky.
When Ratnaprabhā immediately exclaimed, "Father has come here," King Hemaprabha descended from the sky along with his son.
And he approached Naravāhanadatta together with his son Vajraprabha, having offered him a respectful welcome.
While they remained for a moment, engaged in mutual conversation,
the King of Vatsa arrived there, having learned of the situation, accompanied by his ministers.
Then Hemaprabha informed the king— who had already offered him hospitality—
of that entire account exactly as Ratnaprabha had told it.
And he said: "By the power of my knowledge, I have known that this daughter has come here; I know the entire account of what has occurred here.
For such a celestial chariot of a universal monarch (cakravartin) will indeed belong to him in the future."
Give your consent; before long you shall behold this son of yours, the crown prince, returned here accompanied by his bride, who possesses the radiance of jewels.
Having thus entreated the Lord of Vatsa and having had his desire granted by him, he,
together with his son, fashioned that celestial chariot by means of his own magic science.
There, he placed Naravāhanadatta— who was accompanied by Ratnaprabhā and his companions, Gomukha and the others— with his face bowed down in modesty.
And Hemaprabha, sent by his father, was led by Yaugandharāyaṇa to his own city, Kāñcanaśṛṅgaka.
And Naravāhanadatta, having reached that city of his father-in-law,
beheld it made of gold, resplendent with its golden ramparts.
With rays of light streaming forth,
it was as if adorned on all sides by many outstretched arms, due to the agitation of joy for his son-in-law.
There, the king Hemaprabha, with great magnificence, gave Ratnaprabhā to him according to the prescribed rites, just as the ocean gave Śrī to Hari.
Then he presented him with heaps of radiant jewels,
which possessed the splendor of many blazing wedding fires.
And in this king’s city, which was full of festivity as he showered wealth,
even the houses, adorned with banners, appeared as if they had obtained new garments.
And Naravāhanadatta, having completed the auspicious marriage rites,
remained there together with Ratnaprabhā, enjoying celestial pleasures.
And he took delight in divine gardens, ponds, and temples,
having ascended into the sky by the power of that vidyā while gazing upon them with her.
And so, having stayed there for some days in the city of the lord of the Vidyādharas along with his bride,
the son of the Lord of Vatsa resolved, according to the counsel of Yaugandharāyaṇa, to return to his own city.

Then, having had the auspicious rites performed for him by his mother-in-law, and being honored once more by his father-in-law along with his ministers, he set out together with that very man and his son; accompanied by his beloved wife, he ascended the celestial chariot once again.
Having quickly reached that city, which was filled with joy and where the King of Vatsa had organized a great festival, he— who was a flood of nectar to his mother’s eyes—
entered his own capital together with Ratnaprabhā, his son Hemaprabha, and his attendants.

The Lord of Vatsa, possessing formidable splendor, together with Vāsavadattā, greeted the son and daughter-in-law who had prostrated at his feet; he then honored his new relative Hemaprabha along with his son in a manner befitting his wealth.
Then, after taking leave of the King of Vatsa and the others, that king of the Vidyādharas,
Hemaprabha, flew up into the sky with his daughter and departed for his own city.
Accompanied by his own friends, Naravāhanadatta spent that day happily with Ratnaprabhā and Madanamañcukā.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave:
In this manner, he obtained as his wife the beautiful and new Vidyādharī, Ratnaprabhā.
On another day, when he had arrived at her house together with her, [he saw...]
In the morning, while Naravāhanadatta was staying there, his ministers, Gomukha and the others, came to the gate to see him.
When they had been stopped for a moment by the female gatekeeper and then announced, and had entered with due respect, Ratnaprabhā said this to the gatekeeper: SoKss_7,2.3 //
The door must not be barred against these friends of my noble son as they enter here again; for they are indeed our own bodies.
"Such protection as this within the inner apartments is not at all my view," she said to the gatekeepers, and then she spoke to her husband.
"Noble son, I speak to you by way of an incidental remark; listen to that.
I consider the guarding and restraining of women to be merely a matter of worldly policy."
Or perhaps it was delusion caused by envy;
yet that can achieve nothing, for women of noble family are protected by their own virtue alone.
Even the Creator is generally not the master in the protection of the fickle;
by whom can a river in flood and a woman in passion be restrained?
And so, listen; I shall tell you a story on this matter:
there is here, in the midst of the great ocean, an island named Ratnakūṭa.
In that place, in former times, there was a king named Mahotsāha, a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu,
who was known by the meaningful title Ratnādhipati.
That king performed great asceticism as a means of propitiating Viṣṇu in order to obtain victory over the earth, as well as all the daughters of kings to be his wives.
Pleased by his asceticism, the Blessed One appeared in person and commanded him:
"Arise, O King! I am pleased; therefore, listen as I speak these words to you."
In the region of Kaliṅga, a certain Gandharva, having been born as an elephant due to a sage’s curse, was known as Śveta or Śvetaraśmi.
Through the power of asceticism accomplished in a previous birth, as well as through devotion to me,
that elephant became a man of knowledge, capable of traveling through the sky, and one who remembered his former births.
"I have given my command in a dream: that great elephant of yours shall come of its own accord through the path of the sky and become your mount."
Mounting that white elephant like the wielder of the thunderbolt upon the celestial elephant,
whichever king you shall approach by way of the sky, [he will be yours].
Terrified by your divine majesty,
he will offer you tribute under the guise of giving his daughter in marriage, having been commanded by me in a dream.
"In this way, you shall conquer the entire earth and the inner apartments;
you shall obtain eighty thousand princesses."
When Viṣṇu had vanished after saying this, the king, having broken his fast,
beheld on another day that auspicious elephant arrived through the sky.
Having mounted that [chariot] which had been brought to him as directed by Viṣṇu,
he likewise conquered the earth and brought back the daughters of kings.
Then, together with those eighty thousand women,
the king dwelt there on Rātnakūṭa, sporting as he pleased.
For the sake of pacifying that divine elephant of cool rays,
he fed five hundred brahmins every day.
And once, having ascended it and wandered through other islands, that king Ratnādhipati returned to his own island.
As he was descending from the sky toward that excellent elephant,
a bird born of Tārkṣya by chance struck him on the head with its beak.
Struck by the king with a sharp goad, that bird fled;
but the elephant, fainting from the blow of the beak, fell to the ground.
When the king had descended, that elephant, though still conscious, was unable to rise;
even as it was being raised up, it refused to stand, having abandoned its grasping for morsels of food.
In that same manner, as he lay fallen upon this elephant, the king remained there for five days, distressed and without food, and spoke thus: SoKss_7,2.27.
"O World-Protectors, tell me a means in this crisis;
otherwise, I shall offer my own head to you today after cutting it off."
As soon as he had said this and was prepared to cut off his own head with his drawn sword,
an incorporeal voice spoke thus from the sky at that very moment:
"O King, do not act rashly! If some virtuous woman makes physical contact with this elephant's trunk, he will rise; otherwise, he will not."
Upon hearing that, the king was delighted and had his own principal queen, Surakṣitā, named Amṛtalatā, summoned.
When the elephant did not rise even though touched by her hand,
the king then summoned all his other queens.
Having clearly felt the touch of their hands by all of them together,
the king, seeing this in the presence of the people, was truly overcome with shame.
Seeing those eighty thousand women of the harem clearly abashed in the presence of the people, that king, feeling embarrassed,
summoned all the women from his city.
In due course, he caused him to touch the trunk of that elephant.

Therefore, O fair-hipped one, if you desire that Somasvāmin be dear to you,
