"Therefore, taking him under the pretext of play, go to Mathurā;
and I shall teach you these two methods involving counsel and stratagem."
"You shall provide such means that you will bring this man, who has the form of a monkey yet stands by your side,
into a secluded place and make him your beloved husband."
Having been addressed thus by her friend, Bandhudattā likewise brought me into that secret place and affectionately informed me of her purpose.
And having granted me permission, that friend of hers, at that very moment, placed a mantra-thread tied around my neck and laid me down comfortably like a young monkey.
In that form, Bandhudattā brought me to her own husband and showed him,
saying, "This one has been given to my friend for his amusement."
And he was delighted upon seeing me, that plaything resting on his lap;
and I was indeed a monkey, though wise and possessed of articulate speech.
"Ah, how strange is the conduct of women!"—thus laughing inwardly, I remained there; for who indeed is not mocked by desire?
On another day, having been taught that mantra by her friend Bandhudattā,
she set out from her father’s house toward Mathurā together with her husband.
And then that husband of Bandhudattā, desiring to do what was pleasing to her, placed me upon the shoulder of a single servant on the road.
Then we all, traveling along, reached after two or three days a forest standing in the middle of the path, terrifying with its many monkeys.
Then, seeing me, the monkeys rushed toward me from all sides in great numbers,
shouting "kila-kila" cries and calling out to one another.
And those monkeys,
difficult to restrain, arrived and began to devour that merchant's servant upon whose shoulder I had been sitting.
Agitated by that, he abandoned me from his shoulder and fled on the ground out of fear;
then those monkeys seized me there.
Out of affection for him, Bandhudattā, her husband, and his followers,
though striking with stones and clubs, were unable to defeat those monkeys.
Then those monkeys, as if enraged by his evil deed, tore out hair by hair from every limb of the fool with their claws and teeth.
Then, through the power of the neck-thread and by the recollection of Śambhu,
I regained my strength, broke free from their bonds, and fled.
Having entered their dense thicket and passed beyond the range of their vision,
traveling gradually from forest to forest, I have reached this grove.
How is it that for you, fallen from [virtue], this very birth with Bandhudattā has resulted in the fruit of monkeyhood due to your union with another's wife?
Thus, while I was wandering here in the rainy season, blinded by the darkness of suffering,
the dissatisfied Creator has bestowed upon me yet another sorrow.
Suddenly approaching me, a female elephant seized me with her trunk and thrust me into the mud inside an anthill saturated with rainwater from the clouds.
"I know that she must be some divinity appointed by destiny,
since even with effort I am not able to move from this mire."
While he was being thus consoled, not only did I not die,
but knowledge arose within me as I meditated incessantly upon Hara.
And for that long, O friend, neither hunger nor thirst ever afflicted me,
until today when I was pulled out by you from the mound of dry mud.
Even though knowledge has been attained, I do not possess such power by which I might liberate myself from this state of being a monkey.
When someone releases this neck-thread with that very mantra,
I shall once again become a human yoginī here on earth.
Such is my story; but you, my friend, tell me now: why have you come to this inaccessible forest, and how?
Thus addressed by the brahmin Somasvāmin in the form of a monkey,
Niścayadatta told him his own story.
Just as he had come from Ujjayinī for the sake of the Vidyādharī,
so too was he brought back at night by that Yakṣiṇī, who had conquered him with her steadfastness.
Then, having heard that wondrous account, the wise Somasvāmin, who had assumed the form of a monkey, spoke to Niścayadatta.
Great suffering was experienced by you on my account because of a woman;
yet in this world, neither prosperity nor women are ever stable for anyone.
Women are as fleeting as the twilight, as crooked in disposition as rivers,
as untrustworthy as female serpents, and as fickle as lightning.
Therefore, even though that Vidyādharī is passionate, she may in an instant become devoted to another of her own kind and turn away from you, a mere mortal.
Therefore, enough now with this exertion on account of a woman,
which is like the fruit of the *kiṃpāka* tree— sweet at first but bitter in its final consequence.
"Friend, do not go to that city of the Vidyādharas, Puṣkarāvatī;
instead, mount the shoulder of the Yakṣiṇī and go to this very Ujjayinī."
"O friend, follow my words! Because I, being full of passion, did not previously heed the words of a friend, I now suffer remorse."

For at that time, my very affectionate friend, the Brahmin named Bhavaśarman, who was devoted to Bandhudattā, restrained me and spoke thus: SoKss_7,3.148: "For at that time, my very affectionate friend, the Brahmin named Bhavaśarman, who was devoted to Bandhudattā, restrained me and spoke thus."
"O friend, do not fall under the power of a woman, for the mind of a woman is exceedingly difficult to fathom.
Listen, and I shall tell you this account of what happened to me."
Right here in Vārāṇasī, there lived a young woman of great beauty named Somadā, a Brahmin woman who was fickle and a secret practitioner of yoga.
And by chance, I had a secret union with her;
through the course of that union, my love for her increased.
Once, out of jealousy and anger, I struck her at my own will;
that cruel woman endured it, concealing her wrath at that very moment.
On another day, under the pretext of a playful act of affection, he tied a string around my neck; at that very moment, I became tamed.
Then, having become strong, I was sold by her for a desired price to a certain man who lived by training camels.
There, a yoginī named Badhamocanikā, filled with compassion, beheld me suffering, having been made to bear that burden.

Having learned through her supernatural knowledge that I had been turned into a sacrificial animal by Soma and others, she released the cord from my neck while my mistress, Madgosvāminī, was not looking.
Then, having become human, my master, looking about quickly and thinking that I had fled, wandered through all directions.
And as I was departing from there with her, who releases one from bondage,
I was seen from afar by Somadā, who had arrived there by chance.
Blazing with anger, she said to that wise woman who liberates from bondage: "Why has this sinner been released by you from his state as an animal?"
"Shame on you, O woman of evil conduct! You shall reap the fruit of this wicked deed;
tomorrow morning I will slay you along with that sinner."
When she had departed after saying this, that Siddha-yoginī,
Bandhamocinī, spoke to me for the purpose of counteracting her [spell].
"She will approach to slay me in the form of a black mare,
and I shall assume the form of a red mare here."
Then, when the battle has commenced, you must strike Somadā from behind with a sword in hand, remaining vigilant against her.
"In this way we shall kill her; therefore, you must come to my house tomorrow morning. Having said this, she showed me her own home.
When she had entered there, I went to my own home,
having experienced many wonders even in this very life.
In the morning, sword in hand, I went to that house;
then Somadā arrived there, assuming the form of a dark mare.
She too, the liberator from bondage, assumed the form of a chestnut horse;
then a battle ensued between the two with blows from hooves and teeth.
Then that wretched Śākinī, who had dealt me a blow with a sword, was slain by Bandhamocinī; by her, Somadā was subsequently released.
Then, having become fearless and having crossed over the miserable destinies of animal existence,
I did not again even mentally contemplate union with a wicked woman.
Fickleness, recklessness, and [the influence of] *śākinīs*, *śambaras*, and the like—
these three faults in women generally bring fear to the three worlds.
"Why do you run after Bandhudattā, the friend of that Śākinī?
How can she, who has no affection for her own husband, have any affection for you?"
Although I was thus addressed by that friend Bhavaśarman, I did not follow his advice; consequently, I have reached this state.
Therefore I tell you: do not cause distress for the sake of a woman who is devoted to passion;
for when a man of her own kind arrives, she will surely abandon you.
Just as a bee desires flower after flower, so does a woman desire man after man;
therefore, O friend, remorse will come to me alone, and likewise to you.
Thus, these words of Somasvāmin, who was in the form of a monkey,
did not enter the heart of Niścayadatta, which was overflowing with passion.
He said to that monkey: "She will certainly not be unfaithful to me, for she was born into the pure lineage of the lords of the Vidyādharas."
While the two of them were thus conversing, the sun, red with the twilight,
went to the mountain of setting as if desiring to please Niścayadatta.
Then, when night had come, that yakṣiṇī Śṛṅgotpādinī approached his presence there, like a vanguard messenger.
Mounted upon the shoulder of that monkey, Niścayadatta set out toward his beloved,
having taken leave of the ape as it said, "I should be remembered."
And at midnight on the Himālaya, he reached his father’s city, Puṣkarāvatī, belonging to the lord of the Vidyādharas, where she was devoted to him with love.
Having understood this by its power,
she, devoted to her affection, then went out from the city to meet him.
"Your beloved approaches at night, bestowing a festival for the eyes; she is like a second form of the moon. Therefore, I shall now depart."
Having spoken thus and shown him that [jewel] which she had taken down from the tip of her shoulder,
the Yakṣiṇī bowed to Niścayadatta and then departed.
Then she too, devoted to him with passion, approached her beloved and greeted him with embraces and other gestures, her agitation born of long-standing longing.
He too, having embraced her and experiencing the festival of union obtained after much suffering,
ceased to abide in his own body and entered her very form.
Having become his wife according to that Gandharva rite, she,
devoted to him with passion, immediately fashioned a city by means of her magic power.
There, Niścayadatta stood outside with her,
unobserved by his parents, whose vision was obscured by her magic spells.
When questioned, he described to her those hardships of the journey;
because of that, she held him in high esteem and attended to him with desired enjoyments.
Then Niścayadatta related this wonderful tale of Sīmasvāmin, who had become a female monkey, to that Vidyādharī.
And he said to this friend of mine: "If, through some effort of yours, he were to be released from his animal state, that would be a great merit for my beloved."
Having been addressed thus by him, she, though overcome with passion, said to him:
"Furthermore, this path of mantra belongs to the Yoginīs; it is not within our domain."
Nevertheless, I shall accomplish this dear wish of yours by entreating my companion named Bhadrarūpā, a perfected yoginī.
Having heard that, the merchant’s son was delighted and said to his beloved:
"In that case, come, let us go to the presence of my friend so that you may see him."
When she said, "So be it," Niścayadatta, seated upon her lap,
went through the air on the following day to the forest that was the abode of his friend.
There, seeing his friend who had assumed the form of a monkey,
he approached him together with his beloved, bowed, and then inquired after his welfare.
"Today is my good fortune that you, filled with affection,
have been seen by me"— so indeed spoke the monkey Somasvāmin.
He greeted him and bestowed a blessing upon his beloved;
then they all sat down there upon that delightful stone surface.
And they engaged in conversation concerning various matters for the sake of that monkey;
meanwhile, Niścayadatta first deliberated with his beloved.
Then, having taken leave of that monkey and of her beloved’s dwelling,
Niścayadatta flew up into the sky and departed, held in her embrace.
And on another day, he spoke again to her who was devoted to him:
"Come for a moment to the presence of that monkey friend."
Then she said to him: "Go yourself this very day;
receive from me the science of ascending as well as that of descending."
Having been addressed thus, Niścayadatta then took those two sciences and went through the air to the presence of that friend, the monkey.
There, while he engaged in long conversations with her,
she, intent on passion, eventually departed from the house for the garden.
Then, while she was seated there, a certain young Vidyādhara arrived through the air, wandering about at his own pleasure.
As soon as he saw her, overcome by the onset of passion,
he approached that Vidyādharī, having perceived through his supernatural knowledge that she was the wife of a mortal.
Beholding him approaching, she too, with her face bent down, asked him slowly out of curiosity: "Who are you, and for what purpose have you come?"
Then he replied to her:
"O charming girl, know me to be a Vidyādhara, endowed with the knowledge of my own sciences, named Rājabhañjana."
O fawn-eyed one, at the mere sight of you, I was suddenly brought under the sway of the mind-born god [Kāma] and surrendered to you alone.
Therefore, O Goddess, enough of serving a mortal who dwells upon the earth;
as long as your father does not know of you, so long do you enjoy me, your equal.
While he was speaking thus, she, casting sidelong glances,
thought with a fickle mind, "This man is suitable for me."
Then, having perceived her intention, he made her his wife right there;
for when two minds are one, what need is there for Love in secret?
Then, once that Vidyādhara had departed from there,
Niścayadatta arrived in the presence of Somasvāmin.
Though he had arrived, she did not offer him a greeting, an embrace, or the like;
being devoted to him with passion, she made an excuse by citing a headache.
But he, being straightforward and deluded by affection, unaware of that pretext,
considered her illness itself to be her sorrow and passed that day [with her].
And in the morning, being again dejected toward that monkey friend,
he departed through the sky by the power of his two sciences to visit Somasvāmin.
When he had departed, that lustful Vidyādhara returned again to her who was devoted to him; for, deprived of her, he could not sleep throughout the night.
And embracing her by the neck, she who was longing for him during their separation at night,
he, exhausted from the end of their lovemaking, became overcome by sleep.
Having concealed her beloved who was sleeping in her lap by means of the power of her magic knowledge, she,
devoted to passion, fell asleep because of staying awake all night.
Meanwhile, Niścayadatta also reached the presence of that monkey;
and his friend the monkey, having offered him a welcome, questioned him.
"Why do I see you appearing so dejected today? Tell me.
Then Niścayadatta spoke to that monkey:
"O friend, she remains extremely ill due to her excessive passion;
because of that, I am in distress, for she is dearer to me than my own life."
Thus addressed by him, that wise monkey spoke to him:
"Go now, having made her who stands there with her limbs entwined fall asleep."
"Bring her to my presence through the sky by means of the spell granted by him,
so that I may now show you this great wonder."
Having heard that, Niścayadatta went through the air and, seeing Anurāgaparā there asleep, quickly took her into his arms.
But he did not see that Vidyādhara clinging to her body,
for he had been rendered invisible at the outset by her through the power of his magic spell.
And leaping into the air, he brought that woman, who was devoted to him with passion, in an instant into the presence of that monkey, Somasvāmin.
Then that monkey, possessing divine vision, instructed him in a yoga by means of which he beheld the Vidyādhara clinging to her throat.
And having seen him speaking thus, "Alas! Fie upon this! What is this?", the monkey—who was himself a seer of reality—informed him of exactly what had occurred.
Then, while Niścayadatta was thus enraged, that Vidyādhara,
desiring his beloved, woke up there, flew into the sky, and vanished from sight.
She too, having awakened at that time and seeing that disclosure of the secret by him whose soul was overcome with passion, stood with her face cast down in shame.
Then Niścayadatta, with eyes full of tears, said to her:
"Alas, how have I, who trusted you, been thus deceived by you, O wicked woman!"
While a method for binding quicksilver, which is fickle in this world,
is indeed known, no such method exists at all for the mind of a woman.
While he was speaking thus, she, weeping softly and overcome with passion,
ascended and went to her own abode in heaven.
Then his friend the monkey said to Niścayadatta:
"Since you have pursued this beloved of yours even though you were forbidden by me."
This is the fruit of that fire of intense passion that you now regret:
for what reliance can there be on fleeting prosperity or upon women?
Therefore, enough with this lamentation; now find peace.
For even by the Creator himself, that which is destined to be cannot be avoided.
Having heard this from the monkey, Niścayadatta abandoned that grief and delusion;
detached from the world, he went there for refuge to Śiva.
Then, while he was staying in that forest with his friend the monkey,
a female ascetic named Mokṣadā approached him from nearby by chance.
Having seen him bowing down in due order, she asked him, as he was still a human being:
"It is strange; how is it that this monkey has become your friend here?"
Then he related his own story to her, and subsequently recounted the piteous history of his friend; and then he spoke to her thus:
"If the Blessed Lady knows any ritual application or mantra, then let her now release this good friend of mine from his monkey-state."
Having heard that, she agreed to the monkey's request and, through the application of mantras, released that thread from his neck.
Then, casting off that monkey form, Somasvāmin became a human being as before.
Then, when she— who possessed divine power— had vanished like a flash of lightning after he had performed abundant austerities,
Niścayadatta and the brahmin Somasvāmin, it is said, attained the supreme goal there in the course of time.
Thus, women are by nature fickle, their many evil deeds forming a continuous stream that bestows only a lack of discernment and detachment;
yet among them, there may be some virtuous woman who adorns her vast family like the fresh crescent of the moon adorning the sky.
Having heard this wonderful tale from the mouth of his minister Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta, together with Ratnaprabhā, was filled with joy.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Wave:
Seeing that [the king] was pleased with the story of Gomukha, [Vetāla], out of a desire to rival him, said: "Indeed..."
Then Marubhūti spoke to that Naravāhanadatta:
Generally, women are indeed fickle, yet not invariably so;
for even courtesans are seen to be rich in virtuous character, let alone others.
And so, O King, hear this famous story here:
there was once a king named Vikramāditya in Pāṭaliputra.
He had two intended friends:
King Hayapati and King Gajapati, both of whom possessed vast forces of horses and elephants.
His enemy was the powerful king named Narasiṃha, the lord of Pratiṣṭhāna, who possessed a vast army of infantry and was himself full of pride.
Filled with indignation toward that enemy and proud of his allies' strength,
Vikramāditya rashly made this vow:
I shall conquer that king,
the lord of men, in such a way that he will be announced at my gate by bards and heralds as my servant.
Having thus made his vow, he summoned his two friends, the lords of horses and elephants;
together with them, he shook the earth with his elephants and horses.
To attack that lion among men, the lord of men, by force,
King Vikramāditya set out accompanied by his entire army.
When he arrived, King Narasiṃha, having learned that he was near Pratiṣṭhāna, armed himself and went out to meet him.
Then a battle took place between those two kings, causing great wonder,
wherein even the foot soldiers fought together with elephants and horses.
And gradually, by the forces of King Narasiṃha, consisting of ten million foot soldiers,
that army of King Vikramāditya was broken.
Defeated, Vikramāditya fled to the city of Pāṭaliputra,
and his two friends each departed for their own respective countries.
The lion among men, the lord of men who had conquered his enemies, entered his own city of Pratiṣṭhāna, his valor being extolled by bards.
Then Vikramāditya, his purpose unaccomplished, reflected:
"It is better that I conquer that enemy, who is invincible by weapons, through wisdom alone."
"Let some people censure me as they wish; let my vow not be otherwise than true.
Having reflected thus, he entrusted the kingdom to capable ministers.
Having departed secretly from the city together with one chief minister named Buddhivara, as well as with the excellent princes, [he went forth].
Accompanied by five brave men born of noble families, he, assuming the guise of a pilgrim, went to that city of his enemy, Pratiṣṭhāna.
There, he went to the excellent palace of the courtesan known as Madanamālā, which was like the residence of a king.
It was as if calling out with its banners— whose silken cloths were tossed and drawn back by the gentle breeze, rising high upon the peaks of the lofty ramparts— with their fluttering fronds.
At the main eastern gate, it was guarded day and night by twenty thousand foot soldiers, resplendent with various weapons.
In the other three directions, at every gate,
it was guarded by ten thousand brave warriors, arrogant with pride, stationed in groups of ten thousand.
Having been announced by the doorkeepers, he entered in that state and beheld a place adorned in one spot by rows of many excellent horses spread out in array.
In some places, the passage was crowded by the jostling of herds of tethered elephants;
in other places, it was filled with the profound appearance of an array of weapons.
In some places it was radiant with many treasury-houses shining with the luster of jewels;
in other places it was filled with circles formed by throngs of attendants.
In some places it was filled with the tumultuous clamor of crowds of bards reciting aloud;
in others, it resounded with the sound of drums accompanied by fixed musical performances.
Beholding that [palace] divided into seven courtyards, he, together with his retinue,
reached the lofty residential palace of Madanamālā.
Having heard from her attendants that he had been looking meaningfully at the horses and other things in the stables, she concluded that he was some distinguished person in disguise.
Then, having gone out to meet him and bowed down with longing and curiosity,
she led him inside the palace worthy of a king and seated him upon a throne.
His mind captivated by her beauty, grace, and modesty,
the king greeted her while remaining unrecognizable to her.
Then Madanamālā honored that king with baths, flowers, ointments, garments, and highly precious ornaments.
Having provided daily sustenance for them and their followers,
he attended upon him along with his ministers with various kinds of food.
And she spent that day with him in the pleasure of drinking and other diversions;
captivated by the sight of him, she surrendered herself to him.
In this very manner, even while remaining concealed, Vikramāditya stayed day after day being propitiated by her with the conduct appropriate for a universal monarch.
He constantly gave whatever wealth he had to beggars;
when Madanamālā saw this, she brought her own wealth to him.
As she was being enjoyed by him, she considered that body and that wealth to have fulfilled their purpose, while turning her back on any other man or any other object.
Out of that very affection, he indeed restrained that lion among men— the devoted local king who was approaching— with reasoned arguments.
While he was being served by her in this manner, the king once spoke in private to his minister, his companion there, Buddhi-vara:
A courtesan seeking wealth does not even take pleasure in sexual union without it;
for greed was bestowed upon them by Fate, which created them as if they were beggars.
But while this Madanamālā was enjoying my wealth, she did not become detached; rather, due to her excessive affection, she was instead pleased with me.
How then shall I now perform a return service for her,
by which my own vow may also be fulfilled in due course?
Having heard that, the minister Buddhivara said to the king:
"If it is so, then as for those priceless jewels which he brought forth—"
"O monk, you have a mind for conceptual proliferation; give some of these to them.
Thus addressed by that minister, the king replied to him:
Even if all those things were given, nothing at all would have been done for him;
rather, what other expiation could there be for him than that which is connected with this very account?
Having heard that, the minister said: "Your Majesty, what was done by that monk?
Let this account of how he performed service to you be told by you."
Thus addressed by that minister Buddhivara, the king said:
"Listen; I shall relate that story to you."
Formerly, having entered the assembly hall in Pāṭaliputra every day, a monk named Prapañcabuddhi would present a casket to me. (SoKss 7.4.47)
In that very same manner, I continuously offered [the offerings] for one year,
leaving them unopened in the hands of the treasurer.
Once, that casket was offered by the monk; by chance, as it fell from my hand, it broke into two pieces upon the ground.
And from that [lotus] emerged a great jewel, blazing with fire;
it revealed his heart, which previously I had not understood.
Having seen that, I took it and brought back others; then, having opened all the caskets and distributed them, I obtained the jewels from everyone.
Then, out of wonder, I asked that man of worldly intellect:
"Aha! Why do you serve me with such jewels as these?"
Then, having cleared the place of people, that monk said to me:
"On the coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the arrival of night..."
"There is a certain vidyā that must be accomplished by me in a cremation ground outside of this place; O hero, I request your arrival there to assist me."
"For accomplishments easily attained are indeed free from obstacles when aided by heroes";
having been told this by that monk, I then undertook it.
Then, after he had departed joyful, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight arrived; on that day, I remembered the words of that ascetic.
Then, having performed my daily rites and waiting for the onset of night,
I completed the twilight ritual and, by fate, quickly fell asleep.
At that moment, the Lord Hari, who is compassionate toward his devotees, mounted upon Garuḍa with his lap marked by a lotus, thus commanded me in a dream:
"O son, this man named Prapañcabuddhi, who is true to his name, will take you to the cremation ground during the worship of the mandala and offer you as a sacrifice."
Therefore he will say: "Do not do that which he desires to kill you for;
first train yourself and then tell him, 'I shall do it. (SoKss 7.4.60)
Then, while he is acting in that manner, you should strike him at that very moment through that very vulnerability;
thus, the success desired by him will become yours.
When Viṣṇu had vanished after saying this, I awoke and thought:
"By the grace of Hari, that master of illusion has been identified by me today as one who must be slain."
Having reflected thus, when the first watch of the night had passed,
I went alone to that cemetery with a sword in my hand.
Having seen him there, I approached that monk who was honored by the circle [of disciples];
he too, looking at me, greeted me and then spoke, being deceitful:
"Close your eyes, stretch out your limbs, and fall face-down upon the ground;
O King, in this way, success shall come to both of us."
Then I replied to him: "Do this first:
show it to me; having learned it, I shall perform it exactly in that way."
Hearing that, the deluded ascetic fell upon the ground in such a way that I severed his head with a stroke of my sword.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "Excellent, O King!
For today you have indeed offered this wicked monk as a sacrifice."
"That which was to be accomplished by you has today been achieved; you possess the power of movement through the sky.
I am pleased with your fortitude; I am the Lord of Wealth, who moves at will."
"Therefore, choose from me another boon, whatever you desire.
Having been addressed thus, I bowed to him as he appeared before me and spoke.
"But when I shall request a boon from you that is suitable, then,
O Blessed One, having been remembered, you will appear and grant it to me."
Having said to me, "So be it," that Lord of Wealth vanished;
and having attained the siddhi, I went quickly to my own home.
"Thus was my own history told to me by Kubera’s boon;
therefore, I must perform a service in return for this Madanamālā."
"Therefore, O excellent buddhi, go for now to Pāṭaliputra,
taking with you the retinue of the prince, disguised in their attire."
And having performed this fresh service for my beloved,
I shall now return there once more in order to come back here again.
Having spoken thus to his minister, King Vikramāditya, after performing his daily duties, dismissed him along with his retinue.
When he had departed saying "So be it," the king spent that night with Madanamālā, longing for the impending separation.
She too, as if her inner self were foretelling his departure, embraced him repeatedly with longing; she did not find sleep that night.
Then, at dawn, having performed his necessary duties, that king entered the temple for the daily worship of the deity alone, under the pretext of reciting prayers.
There, having called to mind the god Vaiśravaṇa, who appeared before him, he bowed to that deity who had previously offered his boon and made this request:
"O Lord, grant me today, by virtue of that boon you have accepted for me,
those five great golden men who are inexhaustible."
Those very same limbs, which are incessantly cut off for the sake of their desired enjoyments,
grow back again and again.
"Let those men be of such a form as you desire," having said this, the Lord of Wealth vanished in an instant.
At that very moment, the king also saw there in the temple five great golden men standing there suddenly.
Then, having entered, he emerged without forgetting his vow;
having ascended to the sky, he went to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
There, welcomed by his ministers, the citizens, and the women of the inner apartments,
he remained performing his duties with a mind fixed on Pratiṣṭhāna.
And at that moment, his beloved entered that city of Pratiṣṭhāna to see her husband, who had been gone from that temple for so long.
Having entered there, she did not see her beloved king anywhere;
however, she saw five very tall men made of gold.
Seeing them but not finding him, she became distressed and reflected:
"Surely my beloved is some Vidyādhara or a Gandharva."
"He who, having shared me with these men, has flown up into the sky—
what can I do now that I am separated from him, who was equal to Bhārata?"
Having reflected thus, she repeatedly questioned her own attendants;
then, having gone out, she wandered everywhere in search of news of him.
She found no pleasure anywhere— in palaces, gardens, houses, or elsewhere—
lamenting, afflicted by separation, and intent on abandoning her body.
"Do not despair, O Queen; for he is a wanderer at will. That god will, by his own volition, approach you again, O blessed lady."
Consoled with some difficulty by her attendants through such words as these, which were offered with renewed hope, she made this vow:
"If he does not grant me an audience within six months,
then I must enter the fire after having surrendered all my possessions."
Having thus steadied herself with this resolve,
she thereafter remained giving gifts day after day while meditating upon her beloved.
On one occasion, she, being solely intent on the practice of giving, cut off the two arms of one of those golden men and gave them to the twice-born.
And on the second day, filled with wonder, she beheld those two arms of his, exactly as they were, having appeared in the middle of the night.
Then, in due order, she cut off the arms of the others for the sake of giving;
and for all of them, those [arms] grew back again exactly as they were.
Then, seeing that those arms were inexhaustible, she cut them off day after day and gave them to the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, according to the number of Vedic recensions they knew.
Having heard from various directions that she had departed with only a few attendants,
a brahmin named Saṅgrāmadatta came there from Pāṭaliputra.
That poor man, though learned in the four Vedas and endowed with virtues, approached his presence seeking a gift; he was then announced by the gatekeeper.
To him, who had been honored by her with limbs emaciated by vows and pale from separation, she gave golden arms equal in number to the Vedas.
Then that brahmin, surrounded by his followers, heard from the one afflicted by grief the entire account of that most terrible vow in its entirety.
Both joyful and dejected, having mounted these two golden camels upon his arms,
he went to his own residence in Pāṭaliputra.
"Security would not exist for me in this city of Kāñcanā if it were not protected by a king";
having reflected thus, he entered and approached the one seated upon the throne.
That Brahmin addressed King Vikramāditya:
"O Great King, I am a twice-born man residing right here in this city."
Thus, poor and seeking wealth, I set out for the southern region and reached Pratiṣṭhāna, the capital of King Narasiṃha.
There, seeking a gift, I went to the house of the courtesan Madanamālā, whose fame was renowned.
Indeed, some divine man had lived for a long time in her presence;
having given five inexhaustible golden men, he departed for some other place.
Then, pained by separation from him, she regarded life as the agony of poison,
the body as fruitless exertion, and food as the torment of a thief.
Thinking thus, her fortitude gone, that high-minded woman was somehow consoled by her attendants and made a solemn vow.
"If he does not honor me within six months, then I,
my soul stricken by misfortune, must enter the fire."
Thus, having made her vow and resolved upon death,
she, desiring the fruits of great merit, gave gifts every day that were exceedingly vast.
And she was seen by me, O Lord, standing with her feet free from fetters, exceedingly beautiful even with a body emaciated by lack of food.
With hands moistened by the water of charity and swarming with a multitude of bees,
she was like the embodied state of rut in the elephant of desire, yet remained ill-at-ease.
I consider that lover both blameworthy and worthy of praise who abandons her—that beloved without whom that beautiful woman gives up her very life. (SoKss 7.4.117)
By her, four golden human arms were here duly presented to me, who am learned in the four Vedas, according to the number of those Vedas.
"Having made that a house for a long-term sacrifice, I wish to practice my own dharma here; may Your Majesty grant me assistance in that matter."
Having heard this pleasant news from the mouth of that twice-born man,
King Vikramāditya’s mind was immediately captivated by it.
And having instructed the doorkeeper for the sake of accomplishing the brahmin’s desire,
he reflected upon her, who was possessed of firm passion and had held her very life as cheap as grass.
Eagerly anticipating the assistance that would ensure the success of his vow,
he took account of his beloved woman and calculated that the limit for her sacrifice of her body was now but a short time away.
Having quickly departed through the air, that king, who had entrusted the kingdom to his ministers,
entered the palace of his beloved at Pratiṣṭhāna.
There he beheld that beloved woman, emaciated yet radiant as moonlight, her splendor bestowed by the gods, like a digit of the moon on a full-moon night.
And Madanamālā, seeing him unexpectedly arrived— the very essence of nectar for her eyes— became, for a moment, as if bewildered.
Then, as if out of fear of fleeing, she embraced him even more closely and cast the noose of her vine-like arms around his neck.
"O pitiless one, why have you departed, abandoning me who am innocent?
Thus she spoke to him in a voice whose syllables were choked with tears.
Saying, "Come, I shall speak in private," the king, welcomed by his retinue, went with her into the interior seclusion.
There, having revealed himself, he described his own history,
explaining how he had come there to conquer King Narasiṃha through strategic means.
Just as he attained the state of moving through the sky after destroying the mind of conceptual proliferation,
and just as, having received a boon from the Lord of Wealth, he shared it with her.
And just as he had come there after hearing news from a brahmin,
he spoke all of that again, up until the point of his vow's fulfillment, and then spoke further to her.
"Beloved, this Narasiṃha is invincible and exceedingly powerful with his forces;
he shall now engage in a duel with me."
Though I was a sky-dweller and he a dweller of the earth, I did not slay him;
for what kṣatriya, being himself, would desire victory through unrighteous combat?
Therefore, assist me in that which is to be accomplished by my vow: the announcement to this king as he stands at the gate, made by bards.
Upon hearing this, the courtesan said, "I am blessed," and after consulting with the king, she summoned her own bards and spoke to them.
"When King Narasiṃha comes to my house, you must remain stationed at the door, keeping your eyes fixed upon him."
"O King, King Narasiṃha is devoted to and affectionate toward you"—
this is what you must say repeatedly as he enters.
And if he should ask, "Who stands here?", having reflected for a moment,
one must simply say to him, "Vikramāditya stands here."
Having spoken thus and dismissed them, she then said to the female doorkeeper:
"King Narasiṃha must not be prevented from entering here."
Having done this, Madanamālā, having regained her lord of life, remained at her ease, bestowing incalculable wealth.
Then, having heard of that extraordinary gift arising from the golden man,
King Narasiṃha abandoned [his duties] and came to see that house.
And as he entered there, unforbidden by the doorkeepers,
all the bards cried out loudly from as far as the outer gate:
"O Lord, King Narasiṃha has bowed down with devotion"—
hearing this, the king became filled with indignation and apprehension.
Having asked, "Who stands here? and having learned that it was King Vikramāditya who stood there, he reflected for a moment as follows:
This very thing which I previously promised— the announcement of my arrival at the gate— has been fulfilled by this king, who has forcibly entered within for me.
"Aha! This king is full of vigor, by whom I have been defeated this very day;
yet he is not to be slain by force, for he is alone and has come to my home."
Thinking, "I shall enter for that purpose," King Narasiṃha entered the inner apartments, announced by a multitude of bards.
As soon as he saw that the king had entered, Vikramāditya, with a smiling face,
rose up and embraced the monarch around the neck.
Then, once those two kings were seated, they inquired after each other’s welfare while Madanamālā stood by their side.
And in the course of their conversation, Narasiṃha asked Vikramāditya, "From where did these golden men here come?"
Then, there Vikramāditya, having slain that lowest of śramaṇas,
was granted the power of traveling through the sky by the excellent Lord of Wealth.
Having attained the five marks of a Great Man of inexhaustible gold,
he related to him his entire wondrous life story.
Then Narasiṃha, perceiving that the king was a great power who moved through the sky and possessed a mind free from malice, chose him as his ally.
Having then conducted him through the rites of hospitality and established his friendship,
he led him to his own capital and attended upon him with personal services.
Honored and dispatched by that king,
King Vikramāditya returned once more to the home of Madanamālā.
Then Vikramāditya, having fulfilled the difficult vow through the power of his own majesty,
set his heart on returning to his own city.

Desiring to go with him, Madanamālā too, unable to endure separation and intending to abandon that region where she had made her dwelling for the sake of the Brahmin, was likewise desirous of departing.
Then, followed by her elephants, horses,
and footmen, that moon among kings, Vikramāditya, went together with her— whose mind was fixed on no other— to his own city, Pāṭaliputra.
There, having formed a friendship with that lion-like king,
he dwelt happily, accompanied by Madanamālā, who had abandoned her own country out of love for him.
"Thus, O King, even the women who delight in pleasure become noble-minded and firmly devoted;
this is true for the wives of kings, let alone for other women of good family."
Having thus heard this noble tale from the mouth of Marubhūti, King Naravāhanadatta and his new bride Ratnaprabhā, born of a lineage of the highest Vidyādharas, experienced great joy.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The fifth wave begins:
When Marubhūti had spoken thus, the commander-in-chief [Vaiśampāyana] said:
In the presence of Naravāhanadatta, Hariśikha spoke:
For virtuous women, there is truly no other ultimate refuge than their husband;
and in this regard, let this even more wonderful story be heard.
There was a city on earth named Vardhamānapura;
there lived a king named Vīrabhuja, the best among those who uphold the Dharma.
Although hundreds of women were present in his inner apartments,
the lord had a single queen named Guṇavarā, who was dearer to him than his own life.
And even among his hundred wives,
due to the power of fate, not a single son was born to him from any one of them.
He questioned a physician named Śrutavardhana, asking:
"Is there perhaps such a medicine by which the birth of a son might occur?"
Having heard that, the physician said: "Your Majesty, I shall accomplish this;
however, let a wild goat be brought to me by Your Majesty."
Having heard these words of the physician, the king commanded his doorkeeper and had a goat brought for him from the forest.
Having handed over that goat to the royal cooks,
the physician then prepared an excellent broth from its meat for the sake of the king.
Having ordered the queens to assemble in one place to worship the deity,
when the king had departed, those queens gathered together there.
But one had not joined them: that Guṇavarā, who at that time was standing near the king as he was engaged in the worship of the gods. SoKss_7,5.11 //
And when they had come together, the physician gave them the medicinal extract mixed with powder for their drink, so that it was consumed entirely without even being noticed.
Having performed his worship there in an instant, the king returned accompanied by his beloved; seeing that all those materials had been consumed, he spoke to that physician: SoKss_7,5.13 //
"Alas! Nothing has been established by you for the sake of the one who possesses excellent qualities;
that which is the primary purpose of this undertaking has been forgotten by you."
Having said this, the king spoke to the embarrassed physician and the cooks:
"Is there any meat remaining from that goat here?"
When the cooks said, "There are two horns," the physician then replied:
"Excellent! For rasaka produced from within a horn would indeed be of the highest quality."
Having said this and having had that prepared from the horn and flesh,
the physician gave it to Guṇavarā mixed with powder.
Then, ninety-nine queens of that king became pregnant, and in due time, they all gave birth to sons.
And that great queen, having conceived the embryo not long ago, subsequently gave birth to a son of supreme marks and excellent qualities.
King Vīrabhuja, having celebrated a great festival, made him— born from the essence of the horn and flesh, and named Śṛṅgabhuja— his heir apparent.
Though Vardhamāna was the youngest among those other brothers by age,
he became their eldest by virtue of his qualities.
In due course, that prince became equal to Kāma in beauty,
equal to Arjuna in the science of archery, and equal to Bhīmasena in strength.
Then, seeing that beloved queen Guṇavarā, the wife of King Vīrabhuja, together with her son, the other queens became exceedingly envious.
Then, among them, a queen named Ayaśolekhā, who was evil-minded,
consulted with those other women and made a secret agreement with them.
When the king had returned home and questioned him, she— feigning a weariness of countenance before all her co-wives— spoke with great difficulty.
"Noble son, how can you endure the defilement of your home?
You who protect the faults of another, how is it that you do not protect yourself?"
This youth named Surakṣita is the master of the inner apartments;
for it is said that your Queen Guṇavarā is indeed attached to him.
No other man has access here in this inner apartment, which is guarded by eunuchs; therefore, she was united with him.
"This is well known throughout the entire inner court and is sung here," having been told this by her,
the king reflected and deliberated.
And having gone, he questioned each of the other queens one by one in turn;
and they all, having devised their deceptions, spoke to him in the same manner.
Then that wise king, having conquered his anger, reflected:
"This cannot be possible for those two, yet such is this report."
Therefore, without reaching a definitive conclusion, I must not disclose this to anyone;
rather, those two [objections] should be refuted through reasoning so that the ultimate truth may be examined.
Having thus resolved, on the following day at the assembly hall,
he summoned his well-guarded superintendent of the inner apartments and, feigning anger, addressed him.
"O sinner, it has been understood by me that you have committed the murder of a brahmin;
therefore, I cannot bear to look upon you unless you have completed a pilgrimage to sacred fords."
Having heard that, as he was bewildered and crying out, "O God, how could I have committed the murder of a Brahmin?",
the king spoke to him again.
Do not act with such audacity; go to Kaśmīra, which destroys all evil, where lies that field of victory and the purifying field of Nandi.
Where there is the sacred field of Vārāha, where those purified by the wielder of the discus dwell, and where the Jāhnavī flows under the name Vitastā; SOkss_7,5.37.
When you have been purified by a pilgrimage to that Maṇḍavakṣetra and to Uttaramānasa, you shall see me again; it cannot be otherwise.
Having spoken thus, King Vīrabhuja, by means of a stratagem regarding his pilgrimage to sacred sites, sent him away far off, well-guarded and rendered powerless.
Then the king, full of affection, anger, and reflection, went first to Queen Guṇavarā.
There, seeing him with a dejected mind, she asked him in agitation:
"Noble son, why are you so suddenly despondent today?"
Having heard that, the king spoke these feigned words:
"Today, some great sage came and addressed me, O Queen."
"O King, Queen Guṇavarā should be placed by you in an underground chamber for some time,
and you yourself must remain a celibate student."
"Otherwise, you will certainly suffer the loss of your kingdom, and she will surely die.
Having said this, that wise man departed; therefore, this is my despondency.
When the king had spoken thus, Queen Guṇavarā,
devoted to her husband and bewildered by fear and affection, said to him:
"In that case, noble son, why do you cast me into a subterranean cell this very day?
For I am blessed if even by my life I might bring about your welfare."
"Let death come to me, but let there be no lack of peace for you;
for in this world and the next, the husband is indeed the supreme refuge for women."
Having heard these words of hers, the Lord, with tears in his eyes, reflected:
"I suspect there is no sin in her, nor in him who was so well-guarded."
For he was seen by me with an unfaded complexion on his face and free from apprehension;
yet, alas, I still wish to ascertain the truth of this report.
Having reflected thus, the king, filled with sorrow, said to that queen:
"Therefore, grant me this very boon: let an underground chamber be constructed here."
Having said "So be it," and having easily constructed an underground chamber right there in the inner apartments, the king then placed the queen within it.
He consoled his son Śṛṅgabhuja, who was despondent because of the matter of the hunt,

She too, thinking it was for the king's benefit, regarded the earth-cave as heaven;
for virtuous women have no happiness of their own—their husband’s happiness is their happiness.
When this had been done, that other queen, Ayaśolekhā, spoke privately to her own son, named Nirvāsabhuja: SoKss_7,5.54 //
"If the king were to cast one like me into a pit and entrust Guṇavarā to him,

Therefore, my son, together with your other brothers, devise some stratagem so that Śṛṅgabhuja may be banished from this country without delay.
Thus addressed by his mother, he spoke to his other brothers with resentment and remained there, eating only leftovers while contemplating a means [to leave].
Once, while those princes were discharging great weapons,
they all beheld a giant crane upon the roof of the palace.
As they were looking on with astonishment at that deformed bird,
a certain wise mendicant (kṣapaṇaka) who had come along that path spoke to them:
"O princes, this is not a crane; by this form he is a *rākṣasa*.
Known as Agniśikha, he wanders about destroying cities."
"Then pierce him with this arrow so that, being slain, he may depart from here.
Having heard this from the Kṣapaṇaka, ninety-nine [arrows] were [discharged].
The eldest [brothers] threw arrows, yet not even one of them struck the crane;
then that naked mendicant spoke to them once again.
"This younger brother of yours, Śṛṅgabhuja, is capable of slaying this crane; therefore, let him take up this suitable bow."
Upon hearing those words of his mother, which he now had the opportunity to recall,
that wicked Nirvāsabhuja reflected at that very moment:
"This may be the means for the exile of this Śṛṅgabhuja;
therefore, let us present our father’s bow and arrow to him as a gift."
If Baka, having been pierced, takes that golden arrow and departs, he too will later follow this path; therefore, [aim] that arrow at him among us.
And when he does not find this *rakṣobaka* while searching,
he will wander here and there and remain [elsewhere], not returning here without his arrow.
Reflecting thus, that wicked man gave to Śṛṅgabhuja his father’s bow, along with an arrow, for the purpose of killing the crane.
Having seized and drawn it back, the powerful Śṛṅgabhuja pierced that crane with that gold-tufted arrow, which was feathered with jewels.
As soon as he was pierced, the crane, taking up that arrow which remained fixed in his body,
fled from there, streaming with a flow of blood.
Then that deceitful Nirvāsabhuja spoke to the hero Śṛṅgabhuja,
and his other brothers, incited by his signal, said to him:
"Give us back that gold-tipped arrow belonging to our father;
otherwise, today we shall cast off our bodies before you."
"Father, without him he will surely cause us to dwell here in misery;
nor is it possible to create or find a substitute for him."
Upon hearing this, the hero Śṛṅgabhuja said to those sycophants:
"Be steadfast; let there be no fear in you; cast away your wretchedness."
"I shall go and bring back an arrow after slaying that lowest of rākṣasas," having said this, Śṛṅgabhuja took up his own bow along with an arrow.
And he went toward that direction in which the crane had gone,
quickly following the stream of blood fallen upon the earth.
When they and the others had departed joyfully to their mother's side,
Śṛṅgabhuja, proceeding by stages, reached a vast wilderness.
Searching within that forest, he beheld a great city,
like the fruit of a most meritorious tree brought forth in due time for his enjoyment.
There, having rested at the foot of a garden tree for what seemed like a moment,
he beheld a maiden of wondrous form approaching.
In separation she robs one of life, yet in union she bestows life;
she is a wondrous stream fashioned as if composed of both poison and nectar.
And as she approached slowly, gazing at him with eyes raining forth love, the prince, his mind fixed upon her, asked her:
"O deer-eyed one, what is the name of this city and to whom does it belong?
And who are you, and for what reason have you come here? Please tell me."
Then, with her face turned aside and her gaze fixed upon the ground,
that woman of beautiful teeth addressed him in a sweet and affectionate voice.
This city, named Dhūmapura, is a home of all prosperity;
in it dwells a preeminent rākṣasa named Agniśikha.
Know me to be his daughter, named Rūpaśikhā, who am worthy of him; having come here, my mind has been captivated by your extraordinary beauty.
"Tell me now, who are you and why have you come here?
When she had spoken thus, he told her everything concerning Śṛṅgabhuja for a moment.
Who he was, what his name was, whose son he was of that lord of the earth,
and by whom— on account of an arrow— he came to that city of smoke.
Then, having learned the facts of the matter, Rūpaśikhā said to him:
"O one of noble vision, there is no other archer like you even in the three worlds."
By means of that great arrow, even my father was pierced while in the form of a crane;
and that golden arrow was taken by me as a plaything.
But his father was immediately made free of wounds by the minister Mahādaṃṣṭra,
who was an expert in the foremost great medicinal herbs, such as the Viśalyakaraṇī.
"Therefore, my noble son, having informed my father, I shall quickly lead you inside;
for now, this self of mine has been entrusted by me to you."
Having spoken thus and having stationed Śṛṅgabhuja there for a moment,
Rūpaśikhā went to the side of her father, Agniśikha.
"Father, a certain prince named Śṛṅgabhuja has arrived here;
he is peerless in beauty, lineage, character, youth, and virtues."
"I know that someone who has descended here is a portion of a god and not a mere mortal;
if he does not become my husband, I shall surely give up my life."
Having been addressed thus by her there, the Rākṣasa father said to her:
"O daughter, humans are our food; nevertheless, if you have a desire for them," so he spoke.
"Therefore, let him be brought right here and shown to you.
Having heard this, Rūpaśikhā went into the presence of Śṛṅgabhuja.
Having said this and related how it had been done, he led him into the presence of his father;
and his father, Agniśikha, having honored him as he stood bowed before him, spoke to him.
"O prince, I give this Rūpaśikhā to you,
provided that you never at any time transgress my word."
When he had spoken thus, Śṛṅgabhuja, bowing low, replied to him:
"Certainly; I shall by no means transgress the word of your command."
Thus addressed by Śṛṅgabhuja, Agniśikha was pleased and said:
"Rise then; having bathed, come from the bathing chamber."
Having spoken thus to him, he said to his daughter Rūpaśikhā:
"Go, and taking all your sisters with you, return quickly."
When they had been addressed thus by Agniśikha, both Śṛṅgabhuja and Rūpaśikhā said, "So be it," and departed from there.
Then that wise Rūpaśikhā said to Śṛṅgabhuja:
"Noble son, I have a hundred sisters who are maidens."
We are all alike, wearing identical ornaments and garments;
upon the necks of us all hang those same strings of pearls.
"O dear one, having gathered us together from that place in order to delude you, he will say: 'Choose for yourself the one among these who is your beloved.'"
"I know this deceptive intention of his;
for what other purpose would he bring us all together in such a manner?"
Then I shall place it upon my head, and from my neck I shall wear a garland;
once you have obtained that token of recognition, you should cast the forest garland upon me.
Moreover, this father of mine is mostly composed of the material elements; his intellect is not discerning.
Thus, where can he go, following the path established by his birth even toward me?
Therefore, whatever he may say to you for the sake of deception, you must accept it all; tell me that, for I alone shall know the ultimate truth.
Having spoken thus, Rūpaśikhā went to the side of her sisters;
and saying "So be it," Śṛṅgabhuja also departed to bathe.
Then Pārśvarūpaśikhā arrived together with her sisters;
Śṛṅgabhuja also returned there once more, having been bathed by his maidservants.
Then Agniśikha, saying, "From among these, give this one to your own beloved," gave the forest garland to Śṛṅgabhuja.
The prince also took it and placed it around the neck of Rūpaśikhā, upon whose head the necklace— the sign previously agreed upon— had been set.
Then Agniśikha said to Rūpaśikhā, who was accompanied by Śṛṅgabhuja: "I shall perform the auspicious marriage ceremony for you both tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus, she dismissed both him and those other women to their homes;
and in a moment, having summoned Śṛṅgabhuja, she spoke to him as follows.
"Take this pair of tamed horses and go outside the city;
sow there today one hundred khārīs of sesame seeds that are heaped upon the ground."
Having heard that, Śṛṅgabhuja said, "So be it," and went;
he spoke [to Rūpaśikhā], and she, being distressed, replied to him in this way.
"Noble son, you should not feel even the slightest bit of despair in this matter.
Go; I shall accomplish this quickly by means of my own magical power."
Having heard that, he went there and saw the sesame seeds lying in heaps; overwhelmed, the prince began to eat them as he pulled them up.
Then, by the power of his beloved’s illusion, he beheld that entire ground being ploughed and those sesame seeds being sown, one after another, and was utterly amazed.
Having gone, he reported this deed that had been accomplished to Agniśikha;
then that deceitful Rākṣasa spoke to him once more.
"I have no need for these sown sesame seeds; go, heap them up.
Having heard that, he approached Tadrūpaśikhā and spoke to her again.
Having released that earth and created countless ants upon it,
she joined those sesame seeds together by means of her own illusory power (*māyā*).
Having seen that, Śṛṅgabhuja went back again and informed Agniśikha that those sesame seeds had been turned into heaps.
Then that foolish and deceitful Agniśikha spoke to him once more:
"Go two yojanas from here toward the south."
"O noble one, there is an empty temple dedicated to Śambhu in the forest;
in it dwells my dear brother named Dhūmaśikha."
Therefore, go now from here to the front of the temple of Vedī;
O Dhūmaśikha, you are the messenger for the invitation of yourself and your followers.
"Sent by Agniśikha, I say: you must come quickly, for tomorrow morning the marriage festival of Rūpaśikhā will take place."
Having said this much, come here today with all haste;
marry my daughter Rūpaśikhā tomorrow morning.
Having been addressed thus by that wicked man, Śṛṅgabhuja said, "So be it," and having gone accordingly, he told all of that to Rūpaśikhā.
Having given him earth, water, thorns, and fire, as well as her own excellent horse, that virtuous woman spoke to him thus:
Having mounted that horse and bowed to that temple of the gods,
he quickly delivered the invitation as spoken by his father to Dhūmaśikha.

having reflected thus, he then cast a skeleton from the top of the tree.

Announced by the doorkeeper, the physician entered, bowed at his feet, and when asked about his welfare by the king, related the news to him.
Then, having cleared the place of people, the king himself said to him:
"Friend, you have seen that source from which the golden lotuses arise."
That field is indeed supreme, and there you saw him;
know that skeleton upon the banyan tree was my body from a former life.
In former times, hanging there with my feet upwards, I performed austerities by withering away my body.
Then, by the power of his asceticism,
through the waters of the clouds falling upon that skeleton, golden lotuses are born there.
"That skull which was thrown by you into that sacred bathing place—

This Bhaiṣajyacandra and likewise that Padmadarśana—

O friend, it is by the power of that former austerity that memory of my past lives, wisdom, and sovereignty have been bestowed upon me.
This very thing has been demonstrated to you by me through reasoning and direct perception;
the heap of bones cast away by you has been described along with its identifying marks.
"Therefore, you must not harbor the conceit that 'the kingdom was given to you by me,' nor should your mind be set in an unstable state."
Indeed, without prior karma, no one is a giver to anyone;
from the womb onward, a living being partakes of the fruit of the tree of its own past actions.
Having been addressed thus by the sick king, and seeing that very same thing,

Together with his harem and his friends, may he dwell in happiness, enjoying the earth won through policy, attained through merit, and free from thorns.
Thus it is in this world, O Lord, for everyone at all times:

Therefore, I consider you to be our master from a previous birth;

Having thus heard from the mouth of Tapantaka this story, so unprecedentedly delightful and wonderful, Naravāhanadatta rose up with his beloved to bathe there.

Having bathed, he then went into the presence of his father, the King of Vatsa; repeatedly shedding a rain of nectar from his eyes upon his mother, he took his meal with them, and accompanied by his beloved and his ministers, he spent that day and night in pleasures such as drinking parties.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.

Then, together with Ratnaprabhā, he [remained] in that dwelling.
On another day, he remained engaged in various conversations with his ministers.
There, in the courtyard outside the palace, Naravāhanadatta suddenly heard the sound of lamentation, as if from a man.
When someone asked, "What is this?", the maidservants who had arrived replied:
"O Lord, this Kañcukī Dharmagiri is weeping."
For now, having come here, a foolish friend has told me that his brother,

In the city named Cirāyu, there was formerly a king named Cirāyu, who was indeed long-lived and the abode of all prosperity.
He had a minister named Nāgārjuna, born from a portion of a Bodhisattva, who was compassionate, generous, virtuous, and possessed of great wisdom.
He who knew the application of all medicinal herbs and had perfected the elixir of immortality made both himself and that king free from old age and long-lived.
Once, the young son of that minister—
his most beloved child among all the sons of Nāgārjuna— passed away.
Having seen that suffering, he prepared the nectar for the pacification of death among mortals through the power of his austerities and gifts, using various substances.
While he was waiting for the proper time to combine the one remaining medicinal herb, Indra became aware of that.
Indra, having consulted with the gods, commanded the two Aśvins as follows:
"Go to Nāgārjuna on earth and speak these words to him in my name."
"What is this injustice that you, even as a minister, have begun to commit here?
Alas! Are you now prepared to conquer Prajāpati himself?"
Mortals are subject to death; therefore, those who were indeed created by you, you now wish to make immortal by accomplishing the nectar of immortality.

If this were done, what indeed would be the distinction between gods and humans? Furthermore, due to the absence of those to be sacrificed for and those who sacrifice, the very order of the world would collapse.
Therefore, at our word, withdraw this means of attaining immortality;
otherwise, the gods, being enraged, will certainly bestow a curse upon you.
"Since this effort of yours arises from grief, your son remains in heaven";
having thus instructed them, Śakra dispatched both the Aśvins.
Having arrived and accepted the guest-offering,
they then related that message of Śakra to Nāgārjuna, who was pleased by their arrival.
And they told him that his son was dwelling in heaven together with the gods;
then Nāgārjuna, being despondent there, reflected:
"If I do not carry out Indra's command, let the other gods be;
why would these two Aśvins themselves not cast a curse upon me?"
Let this remain as it is; my nectar has not been attained, and my heart's desire remains unfulfilled.
Yet, by virtue of his past merits, my son has gone to a state beyond sorrow.
Having reflected thus, Nāgārjuna said there to the two Aśvin deities:
"The command of Indra has been carried out by me; I shall now withdraw the process of the nectar."
"If you two had not come, this earth would have been made free from old age and death by me within five days, once the Immortal was accomplished."
Having said this in his presence,
Nāgārjuna then buried that nectar, which was almost perfected, in the earth according to those various instructions.
Then the Aśvins, having taken leave of him and gone to heaven, reported to Śakra that their task was accomplished; and the king of the gods rejoiced.
Meanwhile, that lord King Nāgārjuna, being long-lived,
consecrated his son named Jīvahara as the crown prince.

Queen Dhanaparā, seeing her son joyful, spoke to him:

For there is no such sequence for attaining the kingdom through asceticism."
For many princes, your father’s sons, have passed away;
no one has obtained the kingdom, but all have obtained only mockery.
For Nāgārjuna gave this elixir to this king,

O King, I remember ninety-nine births;
in birth after birth, my own head was given by me.
"O Lord, this is my hundredth birth for the sake of giving away my head;
therefore, do not say anything to me, for a petitioner does not leave me disappointed."
"Therefore, I now give my own head to this son of yours;

Then, by that stroke of his sword,
the prince severed Nāgārjuna’s head like a lotus from its stalk.

"Do not do what should not be done, O King, for this friend of yours is beyond grief;

When Marubhūtika had finished telling this story and ceased speaking, Naravāhanadatta rose together with his ministers and performed his daily duties.
Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Ratnaprabhā* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.

Then, on the following day, he reached his beloved Ratnaprabhā, who was longing for him.

surrounded by horses and elephants.
There, with the pearls fallen from the interiors of the claws of lions that had slain and then slept upon the split temples of elephants, it was as if seeds had been sown.

and as if possessed of young leaves by the flowing blood of deer.

then, laughing slightly, that female ascetic spoke to him.
In the same way, if you should ever obtain Karpūrikā as your wife, what will become of this pride of yours?

Having heard that, and saying, "My son, I have no anger," that female ascetic,

Then, perceiving that Satyataspinī was self-controlled and awakened,
Naravāhanadatta questioned her with humility.
"O Blessed One, who is this one named Karpūrikā whom you have mentioned?
If you are pleased with me, please instruct me on this, for I am indeed curious."
To him who had spoken thus and was bowing down, the female ascetic said:
"Beyond the ocean, there is a supreme place named Karpūrasambhava."
There dwells a king whose name is truly significant, known as Karpūraka;
he has a daughter, an excellent maiden named Karpūrikā.
Having observed that one Kamalā had been carried away by the gods after being churned,
the ocean deposited a second one as it were there and concealed it.
She is averse to men and does not desire marriage;
only if you approach her will she become desirous of that.
Therefore, go there, my son, and you shall find that beautiful woman;
however, as you travel through this forest, you will encounter great hardship.
"You should not feel any delusion in this matter, for all of that will surely have a happy end.
Having said this, the female ascetic flew up into the sky and vanished.
Then Naravāhanadatta, drawn by the command of Madana through her voice,
spoke to Gomukha, who was standing at his side.
"Come, let us go to Karpūrasambhava, the city at the side of Karpūrikā;
for without seeing her, I cannot bear to remain for even a moment."
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O King, enough of this rashness!
Where are you, and where is the ocean? Where is that city, where is that road, and where is that maiden?"
When merely his name is heard, why do you, alone and having abandoned celestial women, run toward a human woman with such aimless and uncertain intent?
Thus addressed by Gomukha, the son of the King of Vatsa then said:
"The word of that perfected female ascetic is not false."
"Therefore, I must certainly go to obtain that princess," he said,
and mounting his horse, he set out from there at that very moment.
And Gomukha followed him in silence, even though he was unwilling;
for a master, though he may not comply with the words of his servants, must still be followed by them.
Meanwhile, the Lord of Vatsa also returned to his own city after hunting,
thinking that his son was approaching in the midst of his own forces.
And his own army, along with Marubhūti and the others,
returned to that very city, believing their lord to be stationed in the midst of the troops.
Having arrived there and searched, the King of Vatsa and all the others, realizing that he had not yet returned, went to Ratnaprabhā.
And she, first distressed by hearing that news, then by her own meditative power,
and having been told the tidings of her beloved, spoke to her grieving father-in-law.
"The noble son has gone to the city of Karpūrasambhava to find Karpūrikā, the king’s daughter, who was described to him by the female ascetic in the forest."
"And having accomplished his task, he will return here quickly along with Gomukha;
therefore, enough of this anxiety, for I have obtained this through my knowledge."
Having spoken thus, she comforted the Lord of Vatsa along with his retinue;
and her husband employed another science, Ratnaprabhā, for him.
For noble women who desire their husband’s welfare indeed consider the means to alleviate Naravāhanadatta’s hardships on the road.
And for such a long distance did Naravāhanadatta travel on the back of his horse through this forest, accompanied by Gomukha.
Then, suddenly approaching him on the road, a young woman said to him:
"I am a spell named Māyāvatī, sent by Ratnaprabhā."
"I shall protect you invisibly on the way; go now without anxiety. Having said this, the personified Vidyā vanished from his sight as he looked on.
By her power, as he traveled along the road with his hunger and thirst stilled,
Naravāhanadatta praised his beloved Ratnaprabhā.
Having reached a clear lake in the forest in the evening, he and Gomukha bathed and performed their eating, drinking, and other needs with very sweet fruits and water.
And there, having restrained the two horses that had been given fodder for the night,
he climbed a great tree with his minister as a companion to find a place to stay.
Resting upon its branch, he was awakened by the neighing of terrified horses; looking down from within, he saw a lion that had arrived below.
Seeing him wishing to descend for the sake of the horse, Gomukha said:
"Aha! Being indifferent to your own body, you act without even consulting a counselor."
For kings have their foundation in the body, and sovereignty has its foundation in counsel;
how then do you wish to fight with those beasts whose weapons are claws and fangs?
"It was precisely for the sake of protecting him that we two have now mounted here.
Thus restrained by Gomukha’s words, the crown prince at that very moment—
Seeing that lion killing the horse, he quickly struck it from the back of a tree with a knife that he had hurled and which sank deep into its body.
Though pierced by him in that manner, the powerful one killed that horse and slaughtered the second steed as well, just as a lion kills its prey.
Then the son of the Lord of Vatsa took a sword from Gomukha;
with that [sword] thrown, he split the lion in two in its midst.
Having descended and taken a sword from the body of the lion,
he mounted his own sword [as a seat] and spent that night right there under the tree.
Then, having descended in the morning, Naravāhanadatta set out accompanied by Gomukha toward that Karpūrikā.

Then, seeing him traveling on foot after his mount had been killed by a lion, Gomukha spoke these words on the road to console him: SoKss_7,8.52: "Then, seeing him traveling on foot after his mount had been killed by a lion, Gomukha spoke these words on the road to console him:"
"O King, I shall relate to you this incidental story; listen.
There is here a city named Irāvatī, which surpasses Alakā."
In that city there was a lord of the earth named Parityāgasena,
and he had two queens who were as dear to him as his own life.
