the second, born of a royal lineage, was named Kāvyālaṃkārā.
Together with those two, that childless king, seeking a son,
performed austerities while fasting and sleeping on *darbha* grass, propitiating Ambikā.
Then Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, being pleased by his asceticism, appeared to him in person in a dream and, having given him two divine fruits, commanded him: SoKss_7,8.57.
"Arise and give these two fruits as food for your wife;
from them, O King, two heroic sons shall be born to you."
Having spoken thus, Gaurī vanished; and that king, having awakened, rose in the morning and rejoiced upon seeing both fruits in his hand.
Having delighted his wife with that description of the dream,
he bathed, worshipped Mṛḍānī, and performed the breaking of his vow.
Having approached that queen first at night, when she was most eager for union,
he gave her a single fruit, and she then ate it.
Then, out of respect for his own chief minister, who was her father, the king stayed that night in her palace.
And he placed it right there, near the head of his own bed, for the sake of the second queen; it was the second fruit that had been prepared.
Then, while the king was asleep there, the queen, having had excessive sexual union,
rose up and desired two sons of her own who were like unto herself.
She ate that second fruit as well, down to its core;
for envy toward co-wives is indeed innate to women.
And rising in the morning, she said to that lord of the earth as he was gathering those fruits: "I myself have already eaten those fruits; these are the second."
Then that king, dejected, departed and, having passed the day,
went at night to the bedchamber of that second queen.
There, as she was begging for that very fruit, he said to her:
"While I was asleep, your co-wife ate it by means of a trick."
Then, having failed to obtain that fruit which was the cause for the birth of a son,
Queen Kāvyālaṃkārā remained silent and deeply distressed.
As those days passed while she remained there, the queen, having had excessive sexual union, became pregnant; then, in due time, she gave birth to two sons simultaneously.
The king too, his own desire having borne fruit through that birth,
rejoiced as Parityāgasena celebrated a great festival.
And of those two sons, the king gave the name Indīvarasena to the elder, who had eyes like blue lotuses and a wondrous appearance.
And he gave his younger brother the name Anicchasena,
because his mother had enjoyed the fruit of that [merit] against her will.
Then, having observed that [ornament] of the king there, his second queen, skilled in poetic figures, became indignant and reflected thus:
"Alas! I have been deceived by this co-wife regarding the acquisition of a son;
therefore, I must certainly take revenge for her offense."
Thinking, "These two sons of his must be destroyed by my own ingenuity," she remained there, searching for a means to achieve that end.
And just as those two princes grew up there,
so too did the tree of enmity grow within her heart.
In due course, having reached the prime of youth, those two princes, mighty of arm and desirous of victory, made their request to their father.
Having been trained in the arts of weaponry and having reached the prime of youth,
how can we endure bearing these arms of ours now rendered so fruitless?
"Shame on the arms of a Kṣatriya who does not seek victory, and shame on his youth!
Therefore, father, grant us now permission for our world-conquest."
Having heard these words of his two sons, King Parityāgasena was delighted; with their approval, he made preparations for their departure.
If at any time you should encounter distress here, then the goddess Ambikā, the remover of suffering, should be remembered; for it was she who granted you both to me.
Having spoken thus, the king dispatched his two sons on their expedition,
accompanied by armies and vassal lords, and having had auspicious rites performed for them by their mother.
And afterwards, I dispatched their maternal grandfather, my own chief minister,
named Prathamasaṃgama, who was accompanied by Prajñā.
Then those two princes, brothers endowed with great prowess, having marched in due order toward the eastern direction together with their armies, first conquered it.
Then those two invincible heroes, whose majesty was perfected and who had assembled many kings, set out for the southern direction to conquer.
Upon hearing that news from the two of them, their parents rejoiced;
however, the stepmother burned with the fire of internal hatred.
"Having conquered the earth by the pride of their arms and having slain me,
these two sons of mine have intended to seize my kingdom for themselves."
Therefore, if you have devotion toward me, then these two sons of mine must be slain by you both here, without any hesitation whatsoever.
Thus, at that time during the night, that deceitful woman wrote out the king’s command in the very name of him who was staying in that camp among the vassal princes.
The secretaries of peace and war, having brought together stores of wealth,
dispatched couriers with poetic compositions adorned with ornaments in private.
And that letter-carrier, having gone secretly to the camp of those two princes,
delivered those letters to the vassal chiefs from them.
Having made them recite it, they all reflected upon that exceedingly harsh royal policy, and realizing that the command of their lord was not to be transgressed.
Having met and deliberated at night, they— though captivated by his virtues— helplessly resolved to kill those two princes.
Having understood that very thing from the mouth of one friend among them,
the minister, who was their maternal grandfather, remained together with those two princes.
Having awakened him to the truth as it is and having mounted the two excellent horses,
he then secretly removed him from that camp at that very moment.
Dismissed by him, those two princes traveled through the night illuminated by his splendor, and,
not knowing the way, entered the Vindhya forest.
There, as the night had passed and the two were proceeding by stages,
at midday, overcome by intense thirst, the two horses met their death.
And that aged maternal grandfather, his palate parched by hunger and thirst and exhausted by the heat, passed away while the two of them looked on in their weariness.
"How have we two, though innocent, been brought to this state by our father,
who fulfilled the desire of that wicked stepmother?"
Thus, while those two brothers were grieving and suffering there,
they then meditated upon the Goddess Ambikā, who had previously been pointed out to them by their father.
By the power of that refuge-providing meditation, at that very moment,
those two became free from hunger, fatigue, and thirst, and were restored to strength.
Then, comforted by that assurance and their fatigue from the road forgotten,
they went forth to see her who dwells in the Vindhya forest.
There, at the place of attainment and in its presence, both those brothers began a fast and undertook ascetic penance to propitiate her.
In the meantime, those neighboring chieftains stationed at the camp,
having gathered together, arrived there desiring to do harm to the two of them.
Searching everywhere, they did not see those two princes— the son and his maternal grandfather— anywhere, even though they had fled.
Then, fearing that their secret counsel might be betrayed, they all,
out of fear of King Parityāgasena, went into his presence.
Having shown him the letters, they told him exactly what had occurred;
then, having understood that, he became bewildered and, filled with anger, spoke to them thus: SoKss_7,8.108
"These letters were not sent by me; this is some kind of sorcery. Do you fools not know even this much? SoKss_7,8.109.
"How can I kill my two sons, who were obtained through no small amount of austerity?

There was a daughter of the king of Tāmraliptī named Madanasenā,
the son of one called Vīrabhaṭa, a maiden who was the most beautiful woman in the world.
The second was Candrikāvatī, the daughter of the king of Aparānta named Subhaṭa; she had been carried off by the Siddhas and abandoned elsewhere.
The third daughter of the king named Kumbhīra of the city of Kāñcī was the renowned Varuṇasenā, endowed with great beauty.
The daughter of the king named Paurava, the sovereign of Lāvāṇaka,
was Sulocanā by name, the fourth [princess] with beautiful eyes.
The fifth daughter of King Suroha, the ruler of the land of Cīna, was named Vidyunmālā; her limbs were as radiant as gold and the color of tigers.
The daughter of King Kāntisena, the lord of the Śrīkaṇṭha region, was named Kāntimatī; as the sixth [princess], she surpassed the celestial nymphs in beauty.
The seventh daughter of King Janamejaya, the lord of the city of Kauśāmbī, was named Parapuṣṭā, who spoke with sweet charm.
And when their kinsmen learned that those women had been carried off without their knowledge,
they behaved like reeds before him, who was arrogant with the power of his magic.
There, Sūryaprabha, having assumed multiple bodies created by his magic sciences, sported simultaneously with those women who had likewise mastered the sciences.
Thus, together with those women and his ministers such as Prahasta, he sported in celestial dwellings, musical gatherings, drinking parties, and other diversions.
Skilled in the divine art of painting, he drew figures of Vidyādhara women and,
by making playful and sarcastic remarks, provoked his beloveds to anger.
And he took delight in their faces with their arched brows and reddened eyes,
and in their words with syllables faltering from trembling lips.
Accompanied by his wife, that prince traveled to Tāmraliptī and, as a wanderer through the air, enjoyed himself in the gardens together with Madanasenā.
Having left his beloved ones there, he traveled in a celestial chariot drawn by living beings to the city named Vajrasāra, accompanied solely by Prahasta as his friend.
There, while King Rambha looked on, he took as his wife the king’s daughter named Tārāvalī, who was enamored with him and burning with the fire of love.
He went to Tāmraliptī, and there again he brought another princess, a maiden named Vilāsinī.
For that purpose, he paralyzed with his magic power the arrogant brother of hers named Sahasrāyudha, who had arrived in a state of rage.
Having subdued his maternal uncle, who had arrived as an ally along with his followers and was seeking to abduct her beloved, he caused him to have his head shaved.
Though enraged, he did not speak those words "wife and kinsmen" to them both;
instead, laughing at their embarrassment over the shattering of their pride, he replied:
Then Sūryaprabha, accompanied by his nine beloved wives and summoned by his father, departed for his own city, Śākala, by means of a celestial chariot.
Then King Vīrabhaṭa sent a messenger from Tāmraliptī to his father, King Candraprabha.
And he sent this message: "Since my daughter has been carried off by your son, let it be so;
for he is indeed praiseworthy as the husband of those two, having attained mastery over the sciences."
And if you have affection for us, then come here now,
so that we may perform the marriage rites, hospitality, and friendship.
Having heard this, King Candraprabha then honored the messenger and quickly resolved to depart for that place on the very next day.
Thinking that the coming and going of messengers would take a long time, he dispatched Prahasta to ascertain King Vīrabhaṭa’s certainty regarding the truth.
Having gone swiftly, Prahasta saw Vīrabhaṭa,
and upon seeing the king and that matter, he was trusted and highly honored by him.
Having told that man, who was filled with wonder, about the arrival of his masters in the morning,
he returned through the air in a moment to the side of Candraprabha.
He informed the king that Vīrabhaṭa was standing ready;
and the king, pleased with his minister for his son's sake, honored him.
Then the lord Candraprabha was with Queen Kīrtimatī,
and Sūryaprabha was with Vilāsinī as well as Madanasenā.
Having ascended that celestial chariot, the seat of the *bhūtas*, together with their retinue and ministers, the two of them departed from there on the following morning.
In just one watch of the day, they reached Tāmraliptī,
visible in the sky to the people who raised their eyes in wonder.
Having descended from the surface of the sky,
they entered the city together with King Vīrabhaṭa, who had come out to meet them.
With its beautiful streets sprinkled at every step with sandalwood water,
the city appeared as if strewn with blue lotuses by the side-long glances of the women of the townsfolk.
There, having performed the worship for the bridegroom and his relative according to tradition, Vīrabhaṭa carried out the proceedings of their daughter’s marriage.
For Viśuddha carried a thousand loads of gold,
and a hundred camels laden with burdens of jeweled ornaments.
Five hundred camels laden with loads of various garments,
seven thousand horses, and five thousand elephants.
King Vīrabhaṭa bestowed upon his two daughters a thousand courtesans adorned with ornaments of gold and jewels upon the sacrificial altar.
Furthermore, he honored both his son-in-law Sūryaprabha and his father with excellent jewels as well as with territories.
He summoned Prahasta and his other ministers according to their rank,
and held a festival that caused all the people of the city to rejoice.
And Sūryaprabha was there, accompanied by his father and his beloved wife,
enjoying at that time various pleasures such as food, drink, and song.
And at that moment, a messenger arrived there from Rambha’s presence by way of Vajrarātra; he spoke the words of his master in the assembly hall.
Our defeat, arising from the abduction of our daughter, was inflicted upon us by Prince Sūryaprabha, who is arrogant with the power of his magic sciences.
And today we have learned that you have entered into an alliance with King Vīrabhaṭa,
who shares our common calamity.
If you likewise agree to a treaty with us quickly, then come here;
otherwise, there will be no escape for us from death.
Having heard that and having honored the messenger, King Candraprabha, who was revered by Vīrabhaṭa, spoke again to Prahasta there.
"You yourself go to that Rambha and say these words on our behalf:
'Why do you grieve in vain? For you have been ordained to become a universal monarch.'"
"O Lord of the Mountain, it has now been declared by the Siddhas that this Sūryaprabha shall be the husband of the Vidyādharas, and that these daughters of yours and others shall be his wives."
Your son has attained that state, but you were not asked for it;
therefore, be pleased, for you are our friend, and we shall come here as well.
Having been thus given his message by the king, Prahasta traveled through the sky and reached Vajrarātra in just one watch.
Having delivered the message there to Rambha and being granted his approval by him,
he returned in that same manner and spoke it thus to King Candraprabha.
Then Candraprabha, having dispatched his minister Prabhāsa from Śākala,
had Tārāvalī, the daughter of Rambha, brought to his side.
Then he departed by means of the celestial chariot, accompanied by King Sūryaprabha, by Vīrabhaṭa as well, and attended by all the others.
He reached Vajra-rātra, which was crowded with people looking out for him on the road; welcomed by Rambha, he entered the royal capital.
There, Rambha also, having arranged the festival of the marriage ceremony,
gave his daughter countless gold, elephants, horses, jewels, and other riches.
And he attended to his son-in-law, Sūryaprabha,
in such a manner that all of his own personal enjoyments were cast into oblivion.
And while they remained there in happiness, delighted by the festival,
a messenger from the city of Kāñcī arrived at the presence of Rambhā.
Having received that message, Rambha said to King Candraprabha:
"The Lord of Kāñcī, a king named Kumbhīra, is my elder brother."
Therefore, a trusted messenger has been sent by him today to speak these words to me:
"First my daughter was taken by Sūryaprabha, and after that yours."
"I have heard that you have already established friendship with them today;
therefore, you should likewise establish such friendship for me as well."
"Let them come to my house until, at the light of the sun,
I here with my own hand bestow my daughter Varuṇasenikā upon him."
When Rambha spoke these words, "Let this request of his be granted," King Candraprabha then placed his trust in his speech.
And having quickly looked at Prahasta,
he had Varuṇasenā brought from the city of Śākala into the presence of his father, Kumbhīra.
And on the following day, Rambha, Sūryaprabha, Vīrabhaṭa, and all of them with their followers went to Kāñcī by means of a celestial chariot.
Emerging from the crocodiles, they entered that city of Kāñcī, which was inlaid with various jewels and bound together with virtues, like the girdle of the earth.
Having given his daughter to Sūryaprabha there according to the prescribed rites,
the Kumbhīra bestowed abundant wealth upon the bridegroom and the bride.
When the wedding was concluded and Candraprabha was seated in the pleasure following the meal, Prahasta spoke thus to him in the presence of everyone:
"O King, while wandering through the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha, I arrived there;
having seen me by chance, King Kāntisena spoke to me."
"Let Sūryaprabha come to my house taking with him my abducted daughter Kāntimatī; I shall perform for him the rites of hospitality according to tradition."
"If I am deluded by affection for my daughter, I shall not cast off this body"—
this was said by him, and in that context, I spoke as follows.
When Prahasta had spoken thus, King Candraprabha replied:
"Go then, and bring Kāntimatī into his presence."
Then, having been told by that king, "Therefore, we shall go there," Prahasta went through the sky at that very moment and did exactly as he was instructed.
And at dawn, all of them— Candraprabha and the others,
together with Kumbhīra— departed for the realm of Śrīkaṇṭha by means of a celestial chariot that travels through the sky.
Thereupon, King Kāntisena, having led his daughter into his own palace as the foremost of all, performed the auspicious marriage ceremony.
Then he gave to Kāntimatī and to Sūryaprabha an immeasurable collection of jewels that caused wonder even among kings.
Then, while they were all standing there enjoying various pleasures,
a messenger arrived from Kauśāmbī and spoke as follows:
King Janamejaya says this to you:
"My daughter Parapuṣṭā has been carried off by someone not long ago."
And it has been understood here that since she has come into the hands of Sūryaprabha,
let him come to our house with her without hesitation.
"I shall send him off with due honor and according to the prescribed rites, together with his wife;
otherwise, you are my enemies, and I am yours."
Having spoken these words of his master, the messenger became silent;
then King Candraprabha spoke to them all in private.
"How is it understood from such words spoken with pride that [the enemy] is in his palace?
Having heard this, the minister named Siddhārtha spoke thus:
"O King, you must not think otherwise; for he alone is worthy to speak thus.
For he is a king, a great donor, wise, and born of a noble lineage."
A hero, a performer of the horse sacrifice, and always undefeated by others—
what indeed could be contradictory that he has said, since he speaks according to reality?
Whether it was Śatrughna who spoke thus, or Vāsava himself, [the prince replied:
"In that case, we must go to his house; for that king is true to his promise."
"Let someone else be sent as well to perceive his mind"—
all there placed their trust in these words of Siddhārtha.
Then, wishing to investigate that Janamejaya,
Candraprabha dispatched Prahasta and had him bring back a messenger from that king as well.
And Prahasta, having gone there, made an agreement with that lord of Kauśāmbī and,
having brought back his letter, satisfied Candraprabha.
That king also, having quickly dispatched Prahasta from Śākala,
had that female cuckoo brought to the presence of Janamejaya.
Then those kings, Candraprabha and the others, led by Sūryaprabha and accompanied by Kāntisena, arrived at Kauśāmbī by means of a celestial chariot.
There, King Janamejaya honored his kinsmen and sons-in-law, who had approached him with humble prostrations, by rising to meet them and other marks of respect.
And having performed the auspicious rites for his daughter’s wedding,
he gave five thousand elephants and a hundred thousand choice horses.
He also gave five thousand camels laden with burdens filled with jewels, gold, fine cloth, camphor, and agallochum.
And he held a great festival for the world consisting solely of music and dance,
in which the most excellent brahmins were honored and all the kings were respected.
Meanwhile, the sky there unexpectedly turned a golden-brown,
as if announcing its own imminent state of blood-red hue.
And suddenly the quarters of the sky became filled with tumultuous and confused sounds,
as if terrified upon seeing the enemy army approaching through the air.
And at that very moment, a great wind began to blow,
as if lifting up the earth-dwellers to do battle with those who move through the sky.
And in an instant, a great army of Vidyādharas was seen in the sky,
illuminating the circle of the quarters with its brilliance, raising a mighty roar, and possessing immense speed.
In the midst of them, Sūryaprabha and the others, filled with great wonder, beheld a single, exceedingly beautiful young Vidyādhara.
Victorious is this Crown Prince Dāmodara, the son of Āṣāḍheśvara!
O mortal who dwells upon the earth, Sūryaprabha, fall at his feet!
"O Janamejaya, bow down! Why have you given away your daughter in such an improper place?
Propitiate this very god; he will not tolerate anything otherwise."
At that moment, from the sky, a Vidyadhara bard then spoke these lofty words in front of that Dāmodara.
Having heard that and seen his army, Sūryaprabha took up his sword and shield and flew into the sky in anger by means of his own magic power.
And all his ministers followed him, bearing their weapons:
Prahasta, Prabhāsa, Bhāsa, and Siddhārtha.
Prajñāḍhya, Sarvadamana, Vītabhīti, and Śubhaṃkara—
along with these [others], a great battle ensued against the vidyādharas.
And Sūryaprabha ran toward where Dāmodara was,
striking down his enemies with his sword and parrying their weapons with his shield.
As for those beings, how many in number? There were hundreds of thousands of sky-dwellers;
fighting with one another, they met their end in equal measure.
And here, sword-blades, red with blood and agitated,
appeared as they fell upon the bodies of the heroes like the glances of Kṛtānta.
And the Vidyādharas, as if seeking refuge out of fear on the earth,
fell before Candraprabha with their heads and their bodies.
Sūryaprabha shone with the splendor of a sky-dweller as seen by the world;
the sky became as red as blood, as if strewn with vermilion.
And Sūryaprabha, having reached him, fought face-to-face with that Dāmodara,
who was likewise equipped with sword and shield.
And while fighting, having entered by means of the application of his skillful technique,
he struck down his enemy to the ground, whose shield had been shattered by his sword.
And just as he desired to cut off his quivering head,
Viṣṇu arrived through the sky and uttered the syllable "Huṃ."
Having heard that and beheld Hari, Sūryaprabha bowed down out of reverence for him and then released Dāmodara from execution.
Taking that devotee who had been spared from execution, Hari went somewhere;
for the Blessed One protects his true devotee both in this world and the next.
And all those followers of Dāmodara went here and there;
Sūryaprabha also descended from the sky to his father’s side.
The father of Candraprabha welcomed him as he returned unharmed along with his ministers; other kings, having witnessed his prowess, praised him.
Then, while they all remained there delighted by that conversation,
another messenger belonging to Subhaṭa arrived from that place.
And he presented the letter right before Candraprabha;
having opened it, Siddhārtha read it aloud in the midst of the assembly: SoKss_8,1.158 //
The illustrious King Candraprabha, a pearl-jewel upon his exalted lineage, was respectfully informed by Śrī Subhaṭa from Śrī Koṅkaṇa:
"My daughter was carried away by some being during the night; she has been recovered by your son, and we are satisfied that this has come to light."
Therefore, along with that son Sūryaprabha who is endowed with such qualities, you should exert yourselves here without restraint to bring him to our home;
so that we may behold our daughter as if she had returned from the other world, and we may now perform her marriage rites.
When the letter had been read thus,
King Candraprabha honored the messenger with the words "So be it," and he rejoiced.
And having swiftly dispatched Prahasta to that western region, he had Candrikāvatī, the daughter of Subhaṭa, brought into the presence of Subhaṭa himself.
And in the morning, having placed Sūryaprabha at their head, they all departed by means of the celestial chariot toward the western region,
accompanied by Janamejaya.
Thereupon King Subhaṭa,
delighted by the birth of his daughter, honored them greatly and held a grand festival for her marriage.
And he gave to Candrikāvatī such jewels and other gifts that Vīrabhaṭa and the others were put to shame by what had been given to her.
Then, while Sūryaprabha remained there in his father-in-law’s house,
a messenger related to the Pauravas also arrived from Lāvāṇaka.
He too spoke these words of his own master to Candraprabha:
"My daughter Sulocanā has been carried off by the illustrious Sūryaprabha."
Therefore, I feel no distress at all; rather, let him be brought by you to my home, so that we may perform the customary rites for him.
Upon hearing this, King Candraprabha, having honored the messenger with joy,
had Sulocanā brought by Prahasta to his father’s presence.
Then all of them, together with their warriors and accompanied by Sūryaprabha,
went to Lāvāṇaka by means of the aerial chariot that arrives as soon as it is thought of.
There, having performed the marriage festival for Sūryaprabha and Sulocanā,
that Paurava king, who had honored the assembly of monarchs, filled them with jewels.
While they were being thus attended to and remained in comfort there,
Suroha, the lord of Cīna, dispatched a messenger.
That king also, like the others, made a request through the mouth of a messenger for their arrival at his palace together with the maiden who had been taken away.
Then King Candraprabha, delighted, had his daughter Vidyunmālā brought by Prahasta to that dwelling.
And on another day, Candraprabha and all the others, together with Sūryaprabha and the citizens, departed by means of a celestial chariot for the land of Cīna.
Thereupon the king went out first, led them into his own fortress,
and that King Surūha also performed the marriage ceremony for his daughter.
And from him he took for Vidyunmālā and for Sūryaprabha countless numbers of gold, elephants, horses, jewels, Chinese silks, and other such things.
And there Candraprabha and all the others remained for some days, honored by Suroha with various enjoyments.
And there was Sūryaprabha, radiant with the full bloom of youth,
who shone like the rainy season graced by a garland of lightning.
Thus Sūryaprabha, accompanied by his various beloveds and his kinsmen, enjoyed pleasures here and there in the house of his father-in-law.
Then, having deliberated with his ministers headed by Siddhārtha,
he [dispatched] those kings, Vīrabhaṭa and the others, along with their cavalry, in succession.
Having dismissed that excellent king Suroha to his own lands,
and having taken leave of him, he departed together with his parents, accompanied by his son and his followers.
Having ascended that celestial chariot, the seat of the spirits,
the virtuous Sūryaprabha traveled by way of the sky to his own city, Śālaka.

In that city, there was the joy born of his arrival: in one place attachment to dancing, in another a passion for music, in some places the sport of drinking, in others the adornment of beautiful women, and in yet others the sound of bards made vocal by the praise they had obtained. SoKss_8,1.184 //
There, having summoned other wives who were residing in their fathers' houses, he arrived together with them and the multitudes of elephants and horses given by their fathers;
and with countless camels bowed down under loads filled with various jewels, displaying the wealth arising from his playful conquest of the quarters, he aroused the wonder of the people.
Abounding in wealth and vast treasures, inhabited by that man of great fortune,
Śākala shone as if it were a city fashioned by the gods, Kubera, and the Nāgas.
Then Sūryaprabha dwelt there together with Madanasenā, enjoying all desired pleasures and happy in the fullness of every prosperity;
accompanied by his father, his ministers, and his other wives, he awaited day by day Maya, who had promised to visit him.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave.
Now, once while King Candraprabha was seated there in his assembly hall—
And while Sūryaprabha remained there, accompanied by his entire assembly of ministers.
While I was recollecting the story told by Siddhārtha,
the earth suddenly split open right here in the midst of the assembly.
Then, from the opening in the earth, first there arose a fragrant wind accompanied by sound;
after that, the Asura Maya emerged.
With his dark, lofty head like a mountain peak and his blazing hair like great medicinal herbs,
he appeared like a mountain at night with its red garments like gushing minerals.
Having been honored by King Candraprabha as was fitting,
the Lord of the Dānavas sat upon a jeweled throne and spoke.
These earthly enjoyments have now been experienced by you;
it is time for others, so apply your minds now to that endeavor.
"Dispatch messengers to bring our own kings, kinsmen, and relatives;
then we shall meet with Sumeru, the lord of the Vidyādharas."
"We shall conquer Śrutaśarman and obtain the sovereignty of the sky-dwellers;
and Sumeru stands here by our side as an ally, regarding us with the affection of a kinsman."
"Protect Sūryaprabha and give him your own daughter"—
thus was he indeed commanded at the very outset by the god who wields the Pināka bow.
When the asura Maya had spoken thus,
Candraprabha dispatched Prahasta and the other sky-dwellers as messengers to all the kings.
And by Mayā’s command, Sūryaprabha shared his magical sciences with all his wives and ministers, those who had not previously been so endowed.
While they were still standing there, the sage Nārada arrived, descending from the vault of the sky and illuminating the quarters of the horizon with his radiance.
Having accepted the guest-offering and sat down, he said to Candraprabha:
"I have been sent here by Indra, and this was said to you by him: SoKss_8,2.13 //
I have understood that you,
friends of the asura Maya, deluded by ignorance, acted against Sūryaprabha at the command of Maheśvara.
It is desired that this mortal body shall achieve the great status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the lords of the Vidyādharas.
That which was given by us to Śrutaśarman is improper;
for that [kingdom] belongs to him by hereditary succession, as he is the moon of the ocean of the Vidyādhara lineage.
Whatever you do in opposition to us and by obstructing the Dharma will certainly lead to your own destruction.
Previously, when you were performing a sacrifice to Rudra, I told you,
"Sacrifice first with the horse-sacrifice," yet you did not do so.
Therefore, that which you have practiced out of pride, disregarding the gods and relying solely on hope for Rudra, will not lead to your welfare.
When Śakra’s message had been thus spoken by Nārada, Maya laughed and said to him:
"O great sage, what has been said by the Lord of the Gods is not well-said."
That which says Sūryaprabha is mortal is meaningless;
for what was not known by him in the battle with Dāmodara? What did that matter to him?
For mortals alone, being rich in spiritual essence, are entitled to all accomplishments;
was not the position of Indra previously attained by Nahuṣa and others?
And as for what he said— that the empire we gave to Śrutaśarman belongs to him by right of succession— that too is inconsistent.
Where Maheśvara is the giver [of authority], who has any authority over what?
And how was the sovereignty of Indra, which had passed to Jyeṣṭha, taken away from Hiraṇyākṣa?
And whatever else he calls an adversary or unrighteousness, that is false;
for it is he himself who forcibly makes us his adversary for his own sake.
And what unrighteousness do we seek to overcome, for we merely wish to remove an obstacle;
we do not carry off the wife of a sage, nor do we commit the murder of a Brahmin.

As for his talk about the non-performance of the horse sacrifice and his contempt for the gods—that is false; for once the sacrifice to Rudra has been established by others, what is the use of other rituals?
When Śambhu, the God of gods, is worshipped, what god is not thereby worshipped?
And as for the claim that there is only one Rudra and no Śiva— that too is false.
What need is there for other hosts of gods where Hara is prepared? When the sun has risen, do other lights shine?
"O Sage, you must tell all of this to the King of the Gods;
we shall do what is required, and let him do whatever he knows to be right."
Thus addressed by the Asura Maya, the seer Nārada said "So be it," and taking that message back, he went toward the Lord of the Gods.
When that sage had departed, the asura Maya spoke thus to King Candraprabha there, who was filled with apprehension regarding Śakra’s message: SoKss_8,2.32 //
"You need not fear Śakra; he will be on the side of Śrutaśarman in battle against us, together with the hosts of gods, out of hatred for us."
Therefore, O Great King, we, who are presided over by Prahlāda, are innumerable;
we stand firmly on your side, united with the Daityas and Dānavas.
When the Destroyer of Tripura has shown us favor and is exerting himself on our behalf,
what other wretched being in the three worlds possesses such power?
When Maya had declared, "Therefore, O heroes, exert yourselves in this task," they were all delighted and agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then, following the message delivered by the messengers, all those kings led by Vīrabhaṭa, as well as other friends and kinsmen, arrived there in succession.
When these kings, together with their armies, had performed the appropriate honors,
the asura Maya spoke thus once more to King Candraprabha:
"O King, perform today during the night a great bali-offering for Rudra;
then you shall carry out everything exactly as I shall instruct."
Having heard these words of Māyā, King Candraprabha then immediately had the preparations for Bali made for Rudra.
Then, having gone to the forest at night with me as his ritual instructor,
Candraprabha himself performed an offering to Rudra with devotion.
And while that king was engaged in the rite of fire-offerings,
Nandin, the lord of the hosts of spirits, appeared there visibly and without hesitation.
Having been honored according to the prescribed rites by the delighted king, he spoke this:
"This was commanded by the Lord Śambhu himself through my mouth."
"By my grace, let there be no fear for you even from hundreds of Śakras;
Sūryaprabha shall surely become the universal monarch of the sky-dwellers."
Having received such an instruction from Śaṅkara and having taken his portion of the sacrificial offering,
Nandīśvara vanished there along with the hosts of spirits.
Then Candraprabha, having gained confidence regarding the birth of his son,
completed the sacrificial offering at the conclusion of the *homa* and, observing the proper time, entered the city.
And in the morning, Maya spoke to King Candraprabha, who was seated in private with the queen, his son, the kings, and his ministers.
Listen, O King, I shall tell you today a secret long preserved:
you are the mighty Dānava named Sunītha, my own son.
Sūryaprabha and he known as Sumuṇḍika, your younger brothers, were slain in the battle of the gods; now you two have been born here as father and son.
Having anointed that body of the Dānava with divine medicinal herbs and ghee through skillful means, I preserved it and established it here.
Therefore, having entered the opening and reached Pātāla,
enter your own body by means of that method taught by me.
And having entered that body, you shall become superior in brilliance, heroism, and strength,
such that you will conquer the sky-dwellers in battle.
But Sūryaprabha, with this very same beautiful body,
shall before long become this Sumuṇḍīka, the lord of the sky-goers.
Having heard this from the asura Maya, King Candraprabha joyfully accepted it, saying "So be it," while Siddhārtha, his purpose accomplished, spoke as follows:
"O best of Dānavas, when we were deluded by the thought, 'Has he entered another body, or has he met his death?', what stability could there have been for us then?"
Moreover, when he has entered another body and gone to the next world, he forgets us; just as [one does], who then is he and who are we?
Having heard this from Siddhārtha, the asura Maya said:
"By means of yogic power, enter this very body. (SoKss 8.2.57)
"Come of your own accord and see for yourselves right there;
he does not forget you in this way—listen to the reason."
One who is not independent dies and is born elsewhere in a womb;
he does not remember anything, being obscured by those afflictions such as death and so forth.
But by means of yoga, one who independently enters another body,
having entered the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the sense faculties, [attains mastery].
With his mind and intellect undisturbed, that wise one, a master of yoga, suddenly remembers everything, just as one might go from one house to another.
Therefore, let there be no doubt in you; on the contrary, this king shall attain a great, divine body, free from old age and disease.
And you all, O Dānavas, having entered Rasātala,
shall become possessed of healthy, divine bodies through the drinking of the nectar of immortality.
Having heard these words of the Asura Maya, they all said, "So be it," and,
their doubts abandoned through that conviction, they accepted them.
And on the following day, at his word, Candraprabha, having assembled the entire circle of kings, went to the confluence of the Candrabhāgā and Airāvatī rivers.
Having stationed the kings there and cast them outside,
Sūryaprabha approached those who were blocking his way, as directed by Maya.
Candraprabha entered the opening in the water together with Sūryaprabha, along with the queen and his ministers, Siddhārtha and the others.
Having entered and traveled a long distance along that path,
he beheld a divine temple and entered it together with all of them.
And at that moment, the kings who were stationed there outside the opening were attacked from the sky by the Vidyādharas together with their armies.
Having paralyzed them with their magical powers, they carried off those wives of Sūryaprabha; and at that very moment, a voice arose from the sky: SoKss_8,2.70.
"O wicked Śrutaśarman! If you touch these wives of the universal monarchs, then you shall immediately meet your death along with your army."

Therefore, looking upon them with reverence as if they were your own mother, you should protect them; for it was precisely because I did not kill you this very moment that these women have been set free by me.
"There is a certain reason for this; let that matter rest for now.
When this was spoken by a divine voice, those sky-dwellers vanished from sight.
Having seen those queens led away, Vīrabhaṭa and the others drew near and,
through mutual combat, made an effort to give up their lives.
There is no destruction for these; you shall obtain these daughters again.
Therefore, you must not commit such a rash act; may it be well with you!
Thus a celestial voice restrained their exertion;
thereafter, those kings remained right there, waiting.
In the meantime, Maya, standing in that temple in Pātāla and surrounded by all [the demons], spoke thus to Candraprabha:
O King, becoming single-minded, listen now to this unsurpassed [teaching];
I shall instruct you in the yoga that grants entry into another body.
Having spoken thus and having explained Sāṃkhya and Yoga along with their secret doctrines, he taught him the method for entering another body.
And that lord of yogis said: "This is that very perfection, and this is that knowledge, sovereignty, and mastery—the abode of the powers such as *aṇimā*."
Established in this sovereignty, the lords of the gods do not desire liberation;
for this very purpose, others as well undergo the hardships of recitation and austerity.
Noble-minded persons do not desire even the enjoyment of heaven when it has been attained;
in this regard, listen as I tell you a story.
In a former age, there was a certain great brahmin named Kāla;
having gone to the sacred site of Puṣkara, he performed recitation day and night.
As he was reciting, two hundred divine years passed there;
then, a great, unbroken flame appeared from his head.
By him, who rose into the sky like ten thousand suns,
the movement of the *siddhas* and others was obstructed, and the three worlds blazed forth.
"O Brahmin, choose whatever boon you desire; these worlds are ablaze with your radiance," said Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods as they approached him.
"May I have no delight in anything other than japa;
this alone is my boon, I choose nothing else"—thus he replied to them.
While they persisted in their pursuit,
that practitioner of recitation went even further away and remained on the northern side of the Himalayas, engaged in his silent chanting.
When even that [effort] became increasingly unbearable for him due to his extraordinary splendor,
Indra then dispatched celestial nymphs to create obstacles for him.
That steadfast one did not consider those seductive women even as much as a blade of grass;
therefore, the gods dispatched Death to him with full authority.
Approaching him, he said: "O Brahmin, mortals do not live for such a long time; therefore, abandon yourself and do not transgress the natural order."
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "If my limit for life is full, then why do you not lead me away? Why do you wait?"
And I myself would not abandon my own life, O wielder of the noose;
for by casting off this body out of desire, I would become a self-killer.
When death was unable to lead him away despite his power because he had spoken thus,
death turned its face away and departed just as it had come.
Then, at that very moment when he had been defeated, Indra seized the twice-born man, who was still possessed by resentment,
with his two arms and forcibly carried him to the abode of the gods.
There, turning away from those enjoyments and never ceasing his recitation,
he was brought down by the god and returned once more to that very Himālaya.
There, Indra and the other gods further urged him for the sake of a boon;
at that very moment, King Ikṣvāku arrived by that same path.
Having understood that as it truly was, he spoke to the reciter:
"O sir, if you do not accept a boon from the gods, then receive one from me."
Having heard that, the reciter laughed and addressed the king:
"You are capable of granting me a boon, even though you do not receive one from the gods."
To that brahmin who had spoken thus, Ikṣvāku replied:
"I am not capable of giving to you; you are capable of giving to me. Therefore, grant me this boon."
Then that reciter said, "Choose whatever you desire;
I shall surely grant it. Having heard this, the king reflected within himself.
"It is the proper rule that 'I give' and 'this brahmin takes';
yet this is the reverse, that I take while he gives."
While the king was thus delaying in doubt,
two Brahmins arrived there, engaged in a dispute.
Seeing the king, the two of them spoke before him for the sake of justice;
one said, "A cow was given to me by this man along with a sacrificial fee."
"Does he not take that [gift] from my hand as I am giving it?
Or rather," another replied, "I have not previously performed the act of receiving."
"And yet I have no desire for it; why then does he force it upon me by force?
Having heard this, the king said, "This accuser is not cleared."
To the king who had asked, "Having accepted [the cow], how can you give it back by force to the donor? Śakra, having found an opening, replied:
O King, if you know this to be just, why do you not accept from that twice-born reciter the excellent gift he has obtained after making a formal request?
Then King Niruttara said to that reciter:
"O Blessed One, grant me this boon: from half of your own recitation, bestow its fruit upon me."
"Very well; let half of the fruit of my recitation be yours.
Thus did that reciter then grant a boon to the king.
By that [practice], both the king and the reciter attained the state of all the worlds;
and he, known as Śiva, reached the world of the gods.
Having remained there for many eons, he returned once more to the surface of the earth;
having attained autonomy through yoga, he achieved eternal perfection.
Thus, by the wise who are indifferent to heaven and the like, only spiritual perfection (siddhi) is sought;
that has been attained by you, O King, as one who is independent—therefore, enter your own body.
Having been addressed thus by Maya through the application of his supernatural power,
King Candraprabha, together with his wife, son, and ministers, then rejoiced exceedingly.
Then, having led him to the second underworld, that Maya introduced the king,
together with his sons and others, into a celestial palace.
There, they all saw a single great man lying fallen upon an excellent bed, as if asleep.
Anointed with great medicinal ghee, terrifying with a deformed appearance,
and surrounded by the daughters of the Daitya king whose lotus-faces were downcast.
"Therefore, this very body of yours stands here occupied by your former wife;
enter it," Maya then said to Candraprabha.
Then, having applied himself to that yoga taught by him,
the king entered within that human body, abandoning his own physical form.
Then, having yawned and slowly opened his eyes,
that man rose from his bed as if waking from sleep.
"By good fortune, our lord Sunītha has today been restored to life!"—
such was the cry that arose there, uttered by the joyful wives of the asuras.
But Sūryaprabha and all the others suddenly became despondent upon seeing the body of Candraprabha fallen and lifeless.
And Candraprabha, the son of Sunītha, as if rising from a pleasant sleep,
saw Maya and paid homage to him, falling at his father’s feet.
The father also embraced him and asked in the presence of everyone:
"My son, do you now remember those two births?"
Having said, "I too remember," he recounted that which occurred during his birth as Candraprabha and during his birth as Sunītha.
Calling them by name, he comforted each one individually— Sūryaprabhā and the others who were with their queens, as well as his former wives who were daughters of the Dānavas.
Thinking that his body, born during the time of Candraprabha, might one day prove useful through the principle of dual sovereignty, he preserved it and established it in safety.
Then Sūryaprabha and the others, joyful, bowed down and offered their praise to Candraprabhasunītha, having gained confidence and attained peace of mind.
Then the asura Maya, having led all those delighted ones out from that city,
caused them to enter another city adorned with gold and jewels.
Having entered there, they beheld a pool of lapis lazuli filled with the essence of nectar, and they all sat down upon its bank.
And there they drank that nectar-like beverage, which surpassed even the ambrosia of the gods,
from various jeweled vessels brought by the wife of Sunītha.
Then, having awakened from their intoxicated sleep by that drink,
they all attained divine bodies endowed with great strength and prowess.
Then the asura Maya spoke to Candraprabha-sunītha:
"Come, my son, let us go; behold your own mother after a very long time."
Then, saying "So be it," Sunītha prepared himself and, with Maya leading the way,
proceeded to the fourth underworld together with Sūryaprabha and the others.
Beholding there various cities composed of diverse elements,
they all reached a single city that was entirely made of gold.
There, in that palace made of jewels, the abode of every perfection,
they beheld that wife of Maya, the mother of Sunītha.
Named Līlāvatī, she surpassed the celestial nymphs in beauty;
surrounded by asura maidens, she was adorned with every ornament.
As soon as she saw Sunītha, she rose up in agitation;
Sunītha, for his part, fell at her feet, having offered his salutation.
Then, having embraced her son—who had not been touched for so long—she wept;
and she praised her husband Maya as the cause of that reunion.
Then Mayā said, "O Goddess, that other son of yours was Sumuṇḍīka;
and this Sūryaprabha has been born as the son of that very son."
"O Goddess, this one has been ordained by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva) to become the universal emperor of the Vidyādhara lords,
even in this very body."
Upon hearing this, as she gazed at him with eyes full of longing,
Sūryaprabha, together with his ministers, approached and fell at her feet.
"My child, what is the use of this shaven-headed body? You look beautiful just as you are," Līlāvatī said to him after bestowing her blessing.
Then, on this occasion of his son’s exaltation, Maya called to mind his daughter Mandodarī and Vibhīṣaṇa; and as soon as they were remembered, the two of them arrived.
Having accepted the festive honors, Vibhīṣaṇa said to him:
"O Lord of Dānavas, if you will follow my word, then I shall speak it."
Among the Dānavas, you alone are a doer of good deeds and one who lives a virtuous life;
therefore, you should not harbor groundless enmity toward the gods.
For if you oppose them, there is no benefit for you other than ruin;
indeed, in battles, it is the asuras who were slain by the gods, not the gods by the asuras.
Having heard that, Maya said to him: "We do not act out of force;
but tell me, how can we endure it if Śakra acts with violence?"
Those asuras who were slain by the gods were negligent;
but why were Bali and the others, who were vigilant, not slain at all? (SoKss 8.2.149)
Having been addressed with these and other words by Māyā,
the lord of the Rākṣasas then took leave of him and, together with Mandodarī, went to his own dwelling.
Then Sunītha, accompanied by Sūryaprabha and the others,
was led by Maya to the third underworld to see King Bali.
There, they all beheld Bali, who was even greater than heaven itself,
wearing a necklace and a crown, and surrounded by the sons of Diti and the Dānavas.
Sunītha and the others fell at his feet one after another;
he too honored them with hospitality as was appropriate.
Then Bali, delighted by the account related by me, quickly summoned Prahlāda and the other Dānavas to that place.
There, Sunītha and the others also bowed at his feet; and he, filled with joy, greeted them as they stood humbly before him.
Then Bali said here: "Having become Candraprabha on earth, this Sunītha has been restored to life for us by regaining his own body."
Sumuṇḍīkāvatāra has been attained by this Sūryaprabha as well,
and he has been commanded by Śarva that he shall become the sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
And by the power of this sacrifice, I have been born with my bonds loosened;
therefore, since these two have been obtained, our prosperity is certain.
Having heard these words of Bali, his preceptor Śukra said:
"For those who conduct themselves according to dharma and abide in truth, there is never a lack of prosperity."
"Therefore, conduct yourselves according to the Dharma; even now, carry out my word.
Having heard that, the Dānavas there established a rule, saying, "So be it."
The lords of the seven netherworlds who had assembled there at that time,
as well as Bali, celebrated a festival out of joy at the recovery of Sunītha.
In the meantime, the sage Nārada arrived there once again;
having accepted the guest-offering and sat down, he spoke to those Dānavas.
"I have been sent here by Indra, and he says this to you:
'My supreme satisfaction comes from the recovery of Sunītha's life.'"
Therefore, we must no longer engage in this groundless enmity;
nor should Śrutaśarman, who is on our side, be opposed by us.
When Indra had spoken these words, Prahlāda said to the sage:
"Is there any other way to understand that Indra’s satisfaction comes from Sunītha’s life?"
We certainly do not engage in groundless opposition;
indeed, this very day a rule was established by all of us in the presence of our teacher.
If Śrutaśarman, relying on his allies,
should by force act in opposition to us, what blame can we incur for that?
Indeed, this had already been commanded by Śambhu, the God of gods, on the side of Sūryaprabha, because he had previously propitiated him.
"Therefore, what can we do regarding this task ordained by the Lord?
Śakra speaks this without cause and in a most improper manner."
Thus addressed by Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, the sage Nārada said,
"So be it," and while censuring Vāsava, he vanished from sight.
When he had departed, Uśanas addressed those lords of the Dānavas:
"In this matter, a persistent enmity toward Indra is clearly observed."

But while Maheśvara has girded his loins solely for the sake of showing grace toward us, what power does he have? What could his Vaiṣṇava energy possibly do? Or rather, what reliance can we place in it?
Having heard these words of Śukra and having given their assent, those Dānavas took leave of Bali along with Prahlāda and departed for their own abodes.
Then, after Prahlāda had returned to his own abode in the fourth underworld,
King Bali rose from the assembly hall and entered the inner apartments.
Maya, Sunītha, and all the others, including Sūryaprabha and his companions,
paid homage to Bali and returned to their own respective abodes.
Then, when they had finished their appropriate meals and drinks,
his mother Līlāvatī approached Sunītha and said to him:
"Son, you know that these wives of yours are the daughters of great beings:
Tejasvatī, the daughter of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), and Maṅgalāvatī, the daughter of Tumburu."
And she who was wedded by you with the body of Candraprabha, the lord of wealth—
know her to be Kīrtimatī, the daughter of Prabhāsa Vasu.
"O son, you should regard these three with an equal eye.
Having said this, she entrusted those three principal wives to him.
Then, on that night, Sunītha entered the bedchamber together with his elder wife, Tejasvatī.
There he enjoyed with her, who had long been filled with longing,
various pleasures of amorous play— pleasures that, though experienced before, seemed ever new.
But Sūryaprabha, together with his ministers, sat that night on a couch in another chamber, without his wife.
"Why does he abandon his own beloveds outside with such lack of affection?"— thinking thus, sleep did not come to him, who was solitary and constant.
And Prahasta, as if out of envy because he was solely intent on contemplating his duties,
[remained awake], while the others around Sūryaprabha fell into a pleasant sleep.
Then Sūryaprabha and Prahasta beheld there that peerless maiden, the daughter of a noble family, entering accompanied by her female companions.
"Let not the creation of celestial nymphs appear lusterless before her," thinking thus,
the Creator, as if having produced them, placed them in the netherworld.
And while Sūryaprabha was reflecting, "Who might this woman be?",
she approached his sleeping companions and gazed at each one of them individually.
Leaving aside those who lacked the marks of a universal monarch,
she saw Sūryaprabha endowed with those very characteristics as he lay in their midst, and she approached him.
And he said to his friend: "Friend, touch his feet;
awaken him with these two hands, cool with water."
Having heard this, her friend did exactly as instructed;
and Sūryaprabha, having abandoned his feigned sleep, opened his eyes.
Having observed them, he said, "O maidens, who are you two, and why have you come here?
Hearing this from him, her companion spoke to him.
Listen, O gods: in the second netherworld (pātāla) there is a victorious sovereign, the powerful lord of the Daityas named Amīla, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
"This daughter of his, Kalāvatī, is dearer to him than even his own life-breaths;
her father has come here today from the presence of Bali and said this."
"By good fortune, Sunītha has regained his life today and is seen again;
and the youth Sūryaprabha, the incarnation of Sumuṇḍīka, has been beheld."
"He who was created by Hara as the future sovereign of the circle of sky-goers—
therefore, I shall here perform this honoring of Sunītha with joy."
"I shall give this daughter Kalāvatī to Sūryaprabha;
however, because she belongs to the same lineage as Sunītha, it is not proper for me to give her to him."
And Sūryaprabha was his son when he was born as a king, not an asura;
by honoring his grandson, one would have honored him.
Having heard these words of her father, my friend, her mind drawn by your virtues,
has come here out of curiosity to see you.
When she had spoken thus, Sūryaprabha then feigned sleep so that his friend might truly fall asleep, in order to ascertain her intention and purpose.
Then that maiden, having gone slowly to the side of the sleepless Prahasta and spoken everything to him through the mouth of her friend, went outside.
And Prahasta, having approached, said to Sūryaprabha, "O Lord, are you awake or not? and he, opening his eyes, replied to him:
"Friend, I am awake; for how could there be sleep for me today while I am alone?
Yet I shall tell you this distinction; listen, for what is there to be hidden from you?"
Just now, as soon as I entered here, I saw a certain maiden accompanied by her friend; her like is not seen even in the three worlds.
In an instant she has gone somewhere, having truly stolen my mind;
therefore, search for her immediately, as she must be staying somewhere right here.
Thus addressed by Sūryaprabha, Prahasta then went outside;
seeing the maiden standing there with her friend, he spoke to her.
At your request, I have awakened this master of mine;
therefore, at my request, grant him your sight once again.
Behold his form once more, which brings fulfillment to the eyes;
let him too behold you, for he is captivated by the mere sight of you.
"For when he was awakened, he said to me, 'Having told your story, bring her to me from wherever she may be; otherwise, I shall not live.'"
"Therefore I have come to you; so come, look for yourself.
Thus addressed by Prahasta, she, with the modesty natural to a maiden, [replied].
When she was unable to go on by force and began to reflect,
he then took her by the hand and led her into the presence of Sūryaprabha.
And Sūryaprabha, seeing Kalāvatī approaching his side, said: "O fierce one, what is this that you have done here today against me?"
"While you were asleep, you entered by stealth and stole my heart;
therefore, O thief, since you have not been caught here, I shall not let you go."
Having heard this, that clever friend said to him:
"Her father already knew of this beforehand, and it was he himself who sent this thief to capture you."
Since you have resolved to hand her over, who then is your restrainer?
Why do you not simply inflict upon her the punishment appropriate for a thief?
Hearing that, as Sūryaprabha desired to embrace her, Kalāvatī, feeling ashamed, said, "O noble son, do not; I am a maiden."
Then Prahasta said to her: "O Queen, let there be no doubt in you;
for this Gāndharva rite is indeed the best among all forms of marriage here."
Having spoken thus, as soon as Prahasta had gone out together with all of them,
Sūryaprabha then took Kalāvatī as his wife.
And together with that maiden from Pātāla, he enjoyed the delights of sexual union, which are difficult for mortals to attain and involve an inconceivable, ever-new encounter.
And at the end of the night, when Kalāvatī had gone to her own dwelling,
Sūryaprabha went to the side of Sunītha and Maya.
Then they all gathered together and went into the presence of Prahlāda;
having honored them according to their rank while seated in his assembly hall, he spoke to Maya.
"At this festival of Sunītha, we must certainly do what is pleasing to him;
therefore, let us all eat together in one place today."
When Maya said, "We shall do so; what fault is there in this?", Prahlāda then invited the lords of the asuras there through messengers.
And they all arrived there from all the netherworlds in succession;
first came King Bali, accompanied by innumerable great asuras.
Anantaramāmila, Durāroha, the valiant Vīryavān, Sumāya, Tantukaccha, Vikaṭākṣa, and Prakampana.
Dhūmaketu, Mahāmāya, and whoever other lords of the asuras there were,
each arrived surrounded by a thousand of his own vassals.
The assembly was filled by them as they exchanged mutual salutations;
and once they were seated in order, Prahlāda honored them.
When the time for food arrived, they all, together with Maya and the others,
bathed in the Ganges and came to the great assembly hall to eat.
It was a hundred yojanas in extent, with floors inlaid with gold and jewels,
adorned with jeweled pillars, and set with various precious gem-vessels.
There, those asuras, together with Prahlāda, Sunītha, and Maya, were accompanied by Sūryaprabha and his ministers.
Together with the asuras,
they partook of various kinds of divine food— consisting of edibles, chewables, lickables, and so forth, possessing the six flavors— and they drank the most excellent drink.
And having gone elsewhere to another assembly hall made entirely of jewels,
they all beheld the supreme dance of the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas.
In that context, Sūryaprabha saw there the daughter of Prahlāda, named Mahallikā, who was dancing by her father's command.
Illuminating the quarters with her splendor and raining nectar upon the eyes,
she was like the very form of the moon descended to the underworld out of curiosity.
Adorned with a tilaka on her forehead and beautiful anklets upon her feet,
she appeared as if created by the Creator himself as a personification of dance, with a smiling gaze.
With her curling locks and pointed teeth, she bore breasts that formed a circle upon her chest,
as if performing a brand-new dance.
And as soon as Caṇḍī saw Sūryaprabha at that time,
she forcibly stole his heart away, even though it had already been claimed by others.
Then she too, from afar, beheld him in the midst of the lords of the asuras,
like another Smara created by the Creator after the original Smara had been consumed by Śiva.
As soon as she saw him, her mind became fixed upon him so that she remained motionless,
just as her physical gestures seemed to freeze in anger upon seeing his lack of decorum.
Those present in the assembly perceived that state of mind in both of them;
and they concluded their gazing, saying, "The prince is weary."
Then Mahallikā, casting a sidelong glance at Sūryaprabha, was dismissed by her father; having paid homage to the lords of the Dānavas, she went home.
And all those lords of the dānavas went to their respective homes;
Sūryaprabha also returned to his own residence at the close of day.
And at nightfall, having slept secretly within with Kalāvatī who had returned, he lay there while all his followers slept outside.
Meanwhile, that Mahallikā also, eager for a sight of him,
arrived there accompanied by two confident female companions.
At that moment, Sūryaprabha’s minister named Prajñāḍhya, who had been momentarily abandoned by sleep, saw her as she desired to enter within.
"O Queen, stay for a moment until I have gone inside and returned," he said; and she, recognizing him, rose and spoke.
When she asked him with apprehension, "We are besieged; why are you outside, and who are you? Prajñāḍhya spoke to her once more.
"Why have you entered so suddenly into the presence of one who is sleeping at his ease? Moreover, this master of ours is alone because of his vow."
Then, having been told by that daughter of the Daitya Prahlāda, who was filled with bashfulness, "Enter," Prajñāḍhya entered within.
Seeing Kalāvatī asleep, he woke Sūryaprabha and privately told him that Mahallikā had arrived.
And Sūryaprabha, having understood this, slowly rose and went out;
seeing Mahallikā, he spoke even though she was the third person with him.
This guest has already been brought to the fulfillment of his purpose;
let him also be led to his place, and let this seat be accepted.
Having heard that, Mahallikā then sat down together with the other two;
Sūryaprabha also sat down there, accompanied by Prajñāḍhya.
Having sat down, he said: "O slender one, even though you have shown me contempt while I was in the assembly, it must be forgiven by you as you look upon me now with increasing affection."
Nevertheless, O fickle-eyed one, by the mere sight of you,
my two eyes have been made fruitful by your dance, as it were, through your beauty.
Thus addressed by Sūryaprabha, that daughter of Prahlāda said:
"O noble son, this is not my fault; it is he who is at fault in this matter."
"By whom I was made to appear broken and ashamed in the assembly?
Having heard this, Sūryaprabha said with a laugh, "I am conquered."
Then that prince took her hand with his own,
as if it were perspiring and trembling from the fear of being seized by force.
To her, who was saying, "Release me, noble son; I am a maiden under the power of my father," that Prajñāḍhya then spoke to the daughter of the lord of the asuras.
Moreover, O Goddess, the Gāndharva form of marriage exists for maidens;
yet your father, having discerned your intention, will not give you to another.
And he will certainly show him honor here;
therefore, enough with this anxiety—let such a meeting not be in vain.
While Mahallikā and all the others, up to Prajñāḍhya, were speaking with her,
Kalāvatī woke up inside there.
Not seeing Sūryaprabha on his bed, she waited for a moment, then, becoming anxious and apprehensive, she went outside.
Seeing her own beloved there accompanied by an elderly woman,
she became filled with anger, shame, and fear.
Upon merely seeing her, the old woman was struck with fear and shame;
and Sūryaprabha stood motionless, as if he were a painted figure.
"If I am seen, how could I flee? If I feel shame or envy," she thought;
and so Kalāvatī then went right up to her side.
