Therefore, tell us where it is spread out so that it may be seen all at once.”
"Just one yojana from here there is a region known as the village of Kalāpa;
go there and, having reached that vast place, let this be observed."
When this was said by that sage, all those [gods], together with Sumeru and accompanied by their own forces, went to that village of Kalāpa.
There, standing on the elevated ground, they beheld separately the various arrays of the asuras' and the kings' armies.
Then Sumeru said: "Śrutaśarman is superior in strength;
for he has one hundred and one lords of the Vidyādharas."
And each one of those sovereigns shall have a separate lord over thirty-two kings;
having split some of them, I shall bring them together for you.
Therefore, we shall go tomorrow morning to that place known as Valmīka;
for the morning of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna is indeed a great lunar day.
And when that [constellation] arises there, the characteristics of a Cakravartin appear;
for his sake, the Vidyādharas quickly come here on that lunar day.
When Sumeru had thus spoken regarding the military arrangements for the day,
they spent the time until morning and then set out with their forces and chariots toward that anthill.
There, on the southern slope of the Himalayas, those forces with their shouting troops encamped and beheld many lords of the Vidyādharas who had arrived.
And those Vidyādharas there, having kindled fires in the sacrificial pits,
became engaged in fire-oblations, while some were intent on silent recitation.
Then Sūryaprabha also prepared a great fire-pit there;
by the power of his magic science, the fire blazed up spontaneously within it.
Upon seeing that, joy arose in Sumeru, but envy arose again;
among the Vidyādharas, one then spoke to him: SoKss_8,3.57
Having abandoned the sovereignty of the Lord of Vidyādharas, fie on you, O Sumeru,
that you follow this one named Sūryaprabha, who dwells within the realm of the earth!
Having heard that, Sumeru rebuked him angrily,
and to Sūryaprabha, who was asking for his name, he spoke as follows:
There was a Vidyadhara named Bhima, and Brahma lustfully desired his wife; from that [union], he (Vasistha) was born.
That which is the secret of Brahman, born from Brahman, is called *brahmagupta*;
therefore, this speech of his is consistent with his own birth.
Having said this, Sumeru also prepared a fire-pit;
then Sūryaprabha offered oblations into the sacrificial fire along with him.
And in an instant, from the fissure in the earth, there emerged an exceedingly terrifying great python. Why [did this happen]? 8.3.63.
Then that lord of the Vidyādharas,
named Brahmagupta, by whom Sumeru had been reviled, ran in pride to seize him.
There, by the wind from the breath of that serpent's mouth,
he was carried a hundred cubits and cast down like a withered leaf.
Then a lord of the Vidyādharas named Tejaḥprabha approached, desiring to seize him; but he too was likewise hurled away by that [snake].
Then the lord of the Vidyādharas named Duṣṭadamana approached him, and he too was cast away by that same breath as the others.
Then the lord of the Khecaras named Virūpaśakti approached him;
he too was struck by that very same breath as if it were a blade of grass.
Likewise, as the two kings Aṅgāraka and Vijṛmbhaka were charging toward him simultaneously from afar, he cast them away with a single breath.
Thus all those lords of the Vidyādharas were cast down by him one after another; somehow they rose up again with their limbs covered in pulverized stone.
Then, out of pride, Śrutaśarman approached that serpent, desiring to seize it;
but the serpent, in turn, cast him down there with its breath-winds.
Then, having fallen short, he rose up again and ran;
but having been led even further away by him, he was cast to the ground by his breath.
When Śrutaśarman had risen up, his limbs crushed and his face disfigured,
Sūryaprabha was dispatched by Sumeru to seize the serpent.
"Look! Even this one has risen to seize the python.
Oh, these humans are as thoughtless as monkeys! (SoKss 8.3.74)
"Whatever another is doing, they see and imitate that"—
thus did those Vidyādharas then laugh at Sūryaprabha.
While they were still laughing, Sūryaprabha went and seized that python by the mouth, holding it motionless as he dragged it out from its hole.
At that very moment, that serpent attained the state of a jewel for his quiver;
moreover, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the head of Sūryaprabha.
"O Sūryaprabha, this inexhaustible jewel-quiver has been perfected for you;
therefore, take it!"—thus a divine voice resounded loudly at that time.
Then the Vidyādharas fell into dejection; Sūryaprabha took up his quiver, while Maya, Sunītha, and Sumeru experienced great joy.
Then, after Śrutaśarman had departed accompanied by his Vidyādhara forces,
his messenger approached Sūryaprabha and spoke as follows:
"The illustrious Lord Śrutaśarman commands you:
deliver this quiver to me, if you have any regard for your own life."
Then Sūryaprabha replied: "Go, messenger, and say this to him:
'The quiver shall exist within your own body, filled with my arrows.'"
Having heard this reply and seeing the messenger turn away and depart,
all those followers of Śrutaśarman laughed at that impetuous speech.
Then Sūryaprabha, joyfully embraced by Sumeru, said:
"By good fortune, the word of Śambhu has today undoubtedly borne fruit."
"For when this jewel of a quiver is mastered, your status as a universal monarch is secured.
Therefore, come now and, free from distraction, master the jewel of the bow."
Having heard this concerning Sumeru,
Sūryaprabha and the others then departed for Mount Hemakūṭa, with that very leader at their head.
And on its northern side, they reached the lake named Mānasa,
which was like a palette for the Creator in the creation of the ocean.
The faces of divine women sporting within the water were concealed by full-blown golden lotuses shaken by the wind.
And while they were beholding the splendor of that lake,
Śrutaśarman and all the others also arrived there.
Then Sūryaprabha and they performed a fire sacrifice with ghee and lotuses;
in an instant, a terrible cloud rose up from that lake.
Having pervaded the sky, that cloud released a great rain;
and from within it, a single black serpent fell from the cloud.
And when he rose up from Sumeru's words, though he was being pierced, he was firmly grasped by Sūryaprabha; thus that nāga became a bow.
When he had become that bow, a second [bow] fell from the cloud,
a serpent that terrified all sky-dwellers with the fire of its venom and caused them to flee until none remained.
Sūryaprabha seized him there as well, and by that act, he attained the state of being a bowstring as before, and that cloud quickly vanished.
"This bow of yours has been perfected with the immeasurable power of the sun's radiance; this string is likewise indestructible. Therefore, take these jewels."
Thus a divine voice was heard, preceded by a rain of flowers,
and Sūryaprabha took up that excellent bow along with its qualities.
Śrutaśarman, too, went dejected to the ascetic grove along with his followers;
meanwhile, Sūryaprabha and all those led by Maya were filled with joy.
Then, questioned by them regarding the origin of the bow, Sumeru said:
"In this place there is a great, divine forest of hollow bamboos."
Then, those kīcaka reeds which, having been cut, are thrown here into this lake,
become these great and divine bows.
And those very [mantras] were accomplished by those various gods of old,
as well as by the asuras, the gandharvas, and the highest vidyādharas.
Their names are distinct, yet they are bows of universal monarchs; known as "Immeasurable Strength," they were deposited here in ancient times by the gods.
And these [medicines] are prepared by means of these afflictions for those of virtuous karma;
for some, they are prepared by the will of Īśvara for future universal monarchs (cakravartins).
And this great bow has now been mastered by Sūryaprabha;
therefore, let these friends of his prepare those [other weapons] appropriate for him.
For those heroes who have mastered the vidyās and possess the requisite capacity,
those [mantras] indeed still succeed even today for those who are worthy, in accordance with their fitness.
Having heard these words of Sumeru, those companions of Sūryaprabha,
Prabhāsa and the others, went to that Kīcaka forest.
Having conquered the king who protected it— Caṇḍadaṇḍa—
they brought the kīcakas there and placed them within the lake.
And for those of virtuous character who fasted on its banks, recited mantras, and offered oblations,
their bows became perfected within seven days.
Then, having been informed of the events by those who had arrived, Sūryaprabha set out together with Maya and the others and reached that penance grove on Mount Sumeru.
Thereupon Sumeru said to him: "It is a marvel that Caṇḍadaṇḍa, though invincible, has been conquered by your friends in the Veṇuvana forest."
He possesses a spell named Mohinī, by which he is difficult to conquer;
surely it was placed there by him for the sake of his chief enemy.
Therefore, these [mantras] have not been employed against your friends at this time;
for that [efficacy] of his yields fruit only once, and not again and again.
For she was indeed directed by him toward the teacher himself for the purpose of observing his power;
therefore, he bestowed such a curse upon him.
This is indeed a matter for reflection, for the power of the sciences (vidyās) is difficult to overcome;
therefore, let the cause of this be asked of the venerable Maya by you.
"What can I say before him? What lamp is there before the sun?
When Sumeru had spoken thus to Sūryaprabha, Maya replied:
What Sumeru has spoken to you is true; listen as I tell it to you in brief:
from the Unmanifest (avyakta) arise here those various powers and subordinate powers.
There, the resonance (nāda) arising from the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), resting upon the path of the point (bindu),
attains the state of mantra beginning with Vidyā, conjoined with the digit of the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
And by means of knowledge of those mantra-sciences, or even through austerity,
or by the command of the perfected ones (siddhas), their power is difficult to overcome.
Therefore, my son, all the sciences have been mastered by you, yet you lack two;
the *mohinī* and *parivartinī* sciences have not been accomplished by you.
"And Yājñavalkya knows it; go and entreat him.
Having been told this by me, Sūryaprabha went into the presence of that ṛṣi.
That sage, having caused him to dwell for seven days in the snake-pool,
made him perform ascetic practice for three days in the midst of fire.
Within seven days, he bestowed upon him the deluding spell (mohinī-vidyā) that withstands the bite of snakes;
and within three days, [he bestowed] the counteracting spell (viparivartinī) that overcomes fire.
The sage commanded him to enter the fire-pit once more even after he had attained the vidyā; and he did exactly as he was told.
And at that very moment, the great lotus-palace of Sūryaprabha, which travels at will through the sky, appeared before him.
It was adorned with one hundred and eight petals and a hundred ancient [ornaments],
fashioned from various forms of great jewels.
This celestial palace of a universal monarch has been accomplished for you;
you shall establish the harems of that king within all these cities.
"By means of which those [missiles] shall become invincible to your enemies"—
thus did Sarasvatī then speak to that wise one from the intermediate space.
Then, bowing low before his teacher Yājñavalkya, he requested:
"Please command me; what kind of sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall I bestow?"
"Remember me at the time of your own consecration; this indeed shall be your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Go now to your own army," the sage said to him.
Then, having bowed to that sage and ascended his celestial chariot,
Sūryaprabha went to his army stationed on Mount Sumeru.
There, Mayūra and the others— along with Sunītha and Sumeru— joyfully greeted him, who had narrated his own adventures and whose chariot was now a perfected vehicle of magic power.
Then Sunītha remembered that young Suvāsaka;
and he, having arrived, spoke thus to Maya and the others, together with the king:
"The celestial chariot is ready and all the sciences are at his disposal; O Sūryaprabha, why do you remain indifferent even now regarding the conquest of your enemy?"
Having heard that, Maya replied: "What the Blessed One has said is fitting;
however, let a messenger be sent first; let diplomacy be employed for now."
When the asura had spoken thus, that son of a sage said:
"Let it be so; what harm is there? Let this Prahasta then be dispatched."
He is quick-witted, eloquent, and knows the proper course of action for both the task and its timing;
he is firm yet patient, endowed with all the qualities of an envoy.
Having thus placed their trust in his words, they all then dispatched Prahasta,
having given him his instructions, as an envoy to Śrutaśarman.
When he had departed, Sūryaprabha said to all his own people:
"Listen to the unprecedented wonder of a dream that was seen by me."
"Today, as the night wanes, I see that we shall all be carried away by a great flood of water."
"Even as we were being carried away, we danced and did not sink in any way;
then that flood turned back due to a contrary wind."
Then, having been approached by a certain man of blazing splendor,
we were lifted up and thrown into fire, yet we are not consumed by the flames.
Then a cloud arrived and rained down a torrent of blood;
by that blood the quarters were overspread, and consequently my sleep vanished along with the night.
To him who had spoken thus, that youth Suvāsaka replied:
"Prosperity preceded by toil has been indicated by this dream."
That which was the flood of water was the battle; that which was the non-sinking was fortitude;
and for those being carried away by the waters while dancing, that was the turning over.
Whosoever among you is Marut, he too is some refuge and protector;
and that man of blazing splendor who is the deliverer is Śaṅkara himself in person.
And because they were cast into the fire, you have been stationed in this great battle;
and that which was the rising of clouds was the subsequent onset of fear.
That which rains down a torrent of blood is the destruction of fear;
that the quarters of the sky are filled with blood is a great prosperity for you.

And a dream has many types of meanings: one that accords with reality, one that is meaningless, and one that indicates an immediate result; that which indicates an immediate result is called "another-meaning" (anyārtha).
A dream that takes the form of an instruction from a serene deity is true to reality;
they say that [a dream] produced by intense experience, reflection, and so forth, is devoid of meaning.
Indeed, with a mind deluded by passion and turned away from external objects,
a living being under the sway of sleep perceives various dreams through those respective causes.
The slowness or swiftness of its fruition depends on the specific time [of the dream].
A dream seen at the end of the night, however, bestows swift results.
Having heard this from that young sage, Sūryaprabha and the others were thoroughly relieved; rising up, they performed their daily duties.
Just then, Prahasta returned from the presence of Śrutaśarman;
questioned by Maya and the others, he described everything exactly as it had happened.
From here I went swiftly to that city called Trikūṭapatākā, situated on Mount Trikūṭa and constructed of gold.
Having entered it, announced by the doorkeeper, I beheld that Śrutaśarman surrounded by those various lords of the Vidyādharas.
By his father Trikūṭasena, as well as by Vikramaśakti,
Dhuraṃdhara, and other heroes such as Dāmodara and the rest.
Then, having sat down upon Dhara, I said to that Śrutaśarman:
"I have been sent into your presence by the illustrious Sūryaprabha."
And this was commanded by him to you through my favor: "By the grace of Dhūrjaṭi, the sciences, jewels, wives, and even companions have been accomplished."
Therefore, come and join my army along with these lords of the sky-dwellers;
I shall be the slayer of those who oppose us and the protector of those who bow before me.
And that maiden whom you abducted while she was unapproachable and unaware—
the crest-jewel of desire— release her, for that act was indeed inauspicious.
When I had spoken thus, they all became enraged and said this right there:
"Who indeed is he who, out of arrogance, issues such a command to us?"
"Let him thus command among mortals; but who is he among the Vidyādharas?
Being a mere wretched human, he shall perish for being so arrogant."
Having heard that, I said: "What? What? Who indeed is he? Let him be heard!
He has been appointed by Hara here as your universal monarch."
Whether it was a mortal or even if divinity was attained by mortals,
the prowess of that mortal has been witnessed by the Vidyādharas as well.
"For if he were to come here, your destruction would surely be seen at some point.
When I had spoken thus, that assembly became enraged and fell into agitation.
And as Śrutaśarman and Dhuraṃdhara were rushing toward me to kill me, I said to them both: "In this way, I behold your valor."
Then Dāmodara rose up and restrained them both, saying, "Peace! Neither the messenger nor the brahmin is to be slain."
Then Vikramaśakti said to me: "Go, O messenger!
For we all, indeed, have been created by the Lord just like your master."
"Therefore, let him come; we shall see whether we are capable of receiving him as a guest.
When he had spoken thus with pride, I laughed and said:
The swans remain happily making their cries in the lotus grove only so long as they do not see a cloud approaching to cover the sky. (SoKss 8.3.169)
Having spoken thus, he rose and departed with contempt; I have come here after hearing this from Prahasta, and satisfaction was attained by me and the others.
Having resolved upon their exertion for battle, Sūryaprabha and all the others then appointed Prabhāsa, who was fierce in combat, as their general.
And on that day, having received instructions from Suvāsakumāra regarding the initiation for battle, they all entered [the fray] with their vows firmly restrained.
And there at night, Sūryaprabha, remaining awake, beheld an unprecedented and excellent maiden who had entered the interior of his vow-chamber.
Approaching him at her ease while he was feigning sleep and his ministers were fast asleep, she said to a female companion standing nearby:
If even while asleep, when his playful charms have come to rest, his beauty of form is such as this, O friend, what must it be like when he is awake?
Let it be so; he is not to be awakened, for the curiosity of my eyes has been satisfied. What further use have I here for this heart that is bound [with longing]?
"For he shall have a battle with Śrutaśarman;
who there truly knows what will happen to whom?"
For heroes, the festival of battle arises even at the cost of their lives;
let there be well-being for him in that regard for now, and thereafter we shall know again.
Furthermore, what woman like me could possibly delight the heart of this man, who is the crest-jewel of desire and who wanders through the sky?
When she had spoken thus, her friend said to her: "What are you saying this?
O fierce one, how can your heart's attachment to him be under your control?"
If he whose heart was stolen by the sight of her— the crest-jewel of all desire— could not steal the heart of any other woman, even if she were Arundhatī herself before his eyes.
And by the power of your knowledge, do you not know his welfare in battle?
For you have been declared by the Siddhas to be the wives of this true universal monarch.
"You are Kāmacūḍāmaṇi, and Suprabhā is born of the same lineage;
during these very days, Suprabhā was married by him."
So why should there be anything inauspicious for him in battle? For the words of the perfected ones are never false. And what can happen to one whose heart has been captivated by Suprabhā?
"O blameless lady, you should not take [him], for you are superior in beauty;
or if you have a hesitation out of regard for your kinsmen, that is not right."
"For indeed, apart from her husband, there is no other kinsman for virtuous women.
Having heard these words of her friend, that excellent maiden said:
"Truly, friend, you have spoken; I have no need for other kinsmen.
And by my own supernatural power, I know that this noble son will be victorious in battle."
His jewels and his spells have already been mastered; how much more so, then, his medicinal herbs? Since these herbs have not yet been mastered by him, my mind is distressed.
And all of them are located within the caves on Mount Candrapāda;
they are attained by those possessing merit, and only by universal monarchs (cakravartin).
If he were to go there and procure all those medicinal herbs, it would be well;
for his great battle is close at hand tomorrow morning.
Having heard all this, Sūryaprabha abandoned his feigned sleep, rose up, and spoke with humility to that maiden.
"O lady with most charming eyes, you have shown me great partiality;
therefore, I am going there—tell me, who are you?"
Having heard this, that maiden became bowed with shame, thinking, "He has heard everything," and she remained silent; but her friend spoke to him.
This maiden named Vilāsinī, the younger sister of Sumeru, the lord of the Vidyādharas, is filled with curiosity at the sight of you.
Even as her friend had spoken thus, that playful woman said,
"Come, let us go now," and departed from there.
Then, having awakened Prabhāsa and the others to that matter,
Sūryaprabha explained to his ministers the means for obtaining the medicinal herbs as they had described it.
And he dispatched Prahasta, who was capable of accomplishing that task,
to inform Sunītha, Sumeru, and Maya.
Accompanied by those who had arrived with faith and by his ministers,
Sūryaprabha set out at night toward the Moonbeam Mountain.
And as they proceeded by stages, there arose before them, obstructing their path,
yakṣas, guhyakas, and kūṣmāṇḍas, with various weapons raised for the purpose of creating obstacles.
Having bewildered some of them with weapons and paralyzed others with magic spells,
Sūryaprabha and his companions reached that Candrapādagiri mountain.
There, as they had reached the entrance of that cave, the hosts of Śaṅkara approached and blocked their entry, possessing faces of various distorted shapes.
One must not fight with these, for the Lord Hara might become enraged;
therefore, let us praise that very giver of boons with his eight-thousand-name hymn.
"By that very means those hosts become pleased," said the youth Suvāsaka to Sūryaprabha and the others.
Then, saying "So be it," they all praised Hara in that very manner;
and those attendants, pleased by their master's praise, spoke to them:
"O Muktā, this cave has been opened for you by us; take the great medicinal herbs within it.
But Sūryaprabha himself must not enter it."
"Let Prabhāsa enter this [city], for it is easy for him to traverse;
all those members of the assembly agreed, saying, 'So be it.'"
Then, as soon as Prabhāsa entered, that cave,
though filled with dense darkness, became somehow brilliantly illuminated.
And having risen, even those four *kiṃkara* rākṣasas of most terrible form, bowing down, said to him, "Enter."
Then, having entered and gathered those seven divine medicinal herbs,
Prabhāsa emerged and gave them all to Sūryaprabha.
"O Sūryaprabha and the others, these seven herbs of great power have been perfected,"— at that moment, such a voice arose from the sky.
Having heard that, Sūryaprabha and all the others were delighted;
they quickly returned to their own army, which was stationed at the abode of Mount Sumeru.
Then Sunītha asked that youth Suvāsaka:
"O Sage, why was Prabhāsa admitted while leaving Sūryaprabha behind?"
"Why is he honored by hosts in the cave, and even by the *kiṃkaras*?
Having heard this, while everyone was listening, the sage replied:
"Listen, O assembly; I shall tell this: Prabhāsa is the supreme benefactor.
He is the very self of Sūryaprabha; there is no difference between these two."
Moreover, there is no other equal to Prabhāsa in terms of valor and power;
this cave belongs to him as a result of his meritorious deeds in previous lives.
I shall tell you this: who he was and what he was like in the past.
Formerly, there was a preeminent Dānava named Namuci.
For that great hero who was devoted to generosity,
there was nothing whatsoever that he would not give to one who asked, even if it were something harmful.
Having performed the smoke-inhalation penance for ten thousand years,
he obtained from Viriñca the boon of being incapable of being slain by iron, stone, or wood.
Then, having defeated Indra once and for all, he made him flee in all directions;
thereupon, the seer Kaśyapa, being entreated by the gods, brought about a peace treaty with him.
Then, their hostilities having ceased, those gods and asuras consulted together,
approached the Ocean of Milk, and churned it with Mount Mandara.
Then, just as Acyuta and the others obtained their respective shares, such as Kamala and the rest,
so too did Namuci obtain the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
Other gods and asuras, each separately designated by Brahmā,
received various portions arising from the churning of the ocean.
And when the nectar had been obtained from the churning-vessel and taken away by the gods,
enmity arose once again between those Asuras and them.
Then, in the battle between the gods and the asuras, whichever asura was slain by the gods,
Uccaiḥśravas would smell him and restore him to life at that very moment.
By that [means], the Daityas and Dānavas became invincible even to the gods;
thereupon, Bṛhaspati spoke in private to the despondent Śakra.
"You have one means here; employ it without delay:
go yourself and beg that excellent horse from Namuci."
Even though you are his adversary, he will not fail to give you that horse;
nor will he destroy the reputation for generosity he has accumulated throughout his life.
Having been addressed thus by the preceptor of the gods, Mahendra, together with the thirty deities,
went and begged Namuci for that horse Uccaiḥśravas.
"Even Indra himself does not depart from me with his face turned away when he comes as a petitioner;
therefore, having become Namuci, how could I not give him the horse?"
If that fame for generosity which I have long cultivated throughout the worlds has now withered away, then what is the use to me of prosperity or even of life?
Having reflected thus, the noble-minded Namuci gave that horse Uccaiḥśravas to Śakra,
even though he was being restrained by Śukra.
Then Namuci, having gained the horse’s trust, was slain by him with a wave of the Gaṅgā;
for he was incapable of being killed by weapons or other means, just as Vṛtra was slain by the slayer of Vṛtra with foam upon which the thunderbolt had been placed.
Alas! The thirst for enjoyments in saṃsāra has such a miserable end that even the gods do not fear impropriety or infamy because they are carried away by it.
Having learned of that, Danu, his mother, tormented by grief, made a resolve through the power of her asceticism for the sake of allaying her sorrow.
"May that same powerful Namuci be born again in my womb,
so that he may be invincible by all the gods in battles."
Then, having been conceived in her womb, that asura was born again,
composed of all kinds of jewels, named Prabala because of his possession of great strength.
That powerful lord of the Dānavas, a man of merit who performed intense austerities and delighted even in giving his own life to those who sought it, conquered Indra a hundred times.
Then, having deliberated together, the gods approached him and made this request:
"By all means, give us your body for the sake of the human sacrifice."
Having heard that, he gave his own body even to those enemies;
for the noble, when solicited, do not turn their backs on those who seek their help.
Then that powerful Dānava was cut into pieces by the gods;
today he has been born again in the world of men with the body of Prabhāsa.
Thus, at first he was Namuci, and then he became Prabala;
this very Prabhāsa, through the power of that merit, has become invincible to his enemies.
And that powerful medicinal cave which was related to him became the property of Prabhāsa; it was under his control along with its attendants.
And below that, in the netherworld (pātāla), is the palace of Prabala,
where he has twelve principal wives, all beautifully adorned.
And various jewels and diverse weapons,
wish-fulfilling gems and a hundred thousand warriors, as well as horses.
All of that belongs to Prabhāsa, acquired by him in former times;
such is this Prabhāsa, and there is nothing at all wonderful about this.
Having thus heard this from the young sage, Sūryaprabha and the others, who were radiant with their vows,
set out at that very moment to reach the powerful palace located in the underworld, entering through its cavernous entrance.
Having entered there, seized his former wife, the wish-fulfilling gem, the horses, and the Asura warriors,
and having emerged with all their wealth taken, Prabhāsa alone gratified Sūryaprabha in an extraordinary manner.
Then Samayasunītha, accompanied by the radiant Sumeru and other kings and ministers,
having swiftly attained his desired success, that Sūryaprabha returned once more to his own military encampment.
There, among those lords of asuras, men, and others who had gone to their respective dwellings,
he spent the remainder of that night on a bed of kusha grass, having restrained himself once more for the initiation of battle.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Wave:
Then, in the morning, together with his armies, he [departed] from the penance grove of Sumeru.
Therefore, Sūryaprabha set out with the desire to conquer Śrutaśarman.
Having reached the vicinity of his residence on Mount Trikūṭa,
he encamped there after driving away that army with his own force.
And while he was staying there, together with Sumeru,
Maya, and the others, seated in the assembly hall, an envoy belonging to the Lord of Trikūṭa arrived.
Having arrived, he spoke thus to Sumeru, the lord of the sky-dwellers:
"The king, the father of Śrutaśarman, has sent this message to you."
"While you were far away, we never once performed the customary rites for you;
but today you have arrived within our domain along with your guests."
"Therefore, we shall now provide you with hospitality as is appropriate.
Having heard this message from his enemy, Sumeru replied to him:
"Excellent! You shall not find another guest worthy of being a vessel equal to us;
the fruit of hospitality will be realized in this very world, not in the next."
Thus, when Sumeru had said, "Let hospitality be offered," that messenger returned to his own lord exactly as he had come.
Then Sūryaprabha and the others, situated on the elevated ground,
beheld their own armies encamped separately.
Then Sunītha said to his father, Māyāsura:
"Declare to us here the distribution of the chariots and other equipment within our army."
Having said, "I shall do so; listen," and pointing with his finger, that omniscient lord of the Dānavas proceeded to speak as follows:
Subāhu, Nirghāta, Muṣṭika,
Gohara, as well as Pralamba, Pramātha, Kaṅkaṭa, and Piṅgala.
And these kings, Vasudatta and the others, are but half-charioteers (ardharatha),
as are Aṅkurin, Suviśāla, Daṇḍin, Bhūṣaṇa, and Somila.
Unmattaka, Devaśarman, the youth Pitṛśarman, and these others beginning with Haridatta—all of them are considered to be Pūrṇaratha. (SoKss 8.4.14)
Prakampana, Darpita, Kumbhīra, Mātṛpālita,
Mahābhaṭa, Sograbhaṭa, Vīrasvāmī, and Surādhara.
Bhaṇḍīra, Siṃhadatta, Guṇavarman, Sakīṭaka,
Bhīma, and Bhayaṃkara— all these are chariot-warriors of double strength.
Virocana, Vīrasena, Yajñasena, and then Khujjara; Indravarman, Śabaraka, Krūrakarman, and Nirāsaka.
"O son, these three charioteers— the prince Suśarman, Bāhuśālin, and this Viśākha Krodhana— would be three times [the strength of] these [others]."
And Pracaṇḍa— these princes, each possessing the fourfold qualities of a chariot-warrior,
were Juñjarī, Vīravarman, and Pravīravara.
Supratijña, Amarārāma, and Caṇḍadatta the fowler;
and also the three: Siṃhabhaṭa, Vyāghrabhaṭa, and Śatrubhaṭa.
These kings and princes are chariots possessing five qualities;
however, this prince Ugravarman would be a chariot possessing six qualities.
Rājaputra, Viśākha, Sutantu, Sugama,
and Narendraśarman— these are considered chariot-warriors possessing sevenfold qualities.
Furthermore, this son of King Sahasrāyu is a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha);
indeed, Śatānīka is the leader of a host of great chariot-warriors.
Subhāsa, Harṣa, and Vimala were the companions of Sūryaprabha;
also Mahābuddhi and the one named Acala, as well as Priyaṃkara and Śubhaṃkara.
These were Mahāratha, Yajñaruci, and Dharmaruci;
likewise Viśvaruci, Bhāsa, and Siddhārtha—these were the three.
The ministers of Sūryaprabha shall be leaders of hosts of great chariot-warriors;
Prahasta and Mahārtha shall be his leaders of hosts of atiratha warriors.
The two leaders of chariot-divisions were Prajñāḍhya and Sthirabuddhi;
likewise, there were Dānava, Sarvadamana, and Pramathana.
Dhūmaketu, Pravahaṇa, Vajrapañjara,
Kālacakra, and Marudvega— these are the chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors.
Prakampana, Siṃhanāda, Rathayūthapa, Atirathayūthapa, Mahāmāya, Kāmbalika, and this Kālakampanaka as well.
Rathāti,
Prahṛṣṭaroman, and Ceti— these four were also lords of the asuras;
they were the sovereigns over the sons who were commanders of hosts of atirathas.
And this general of the army, Prabhāsa, is equal to Sūryaprabha;
and this Śrīkuñjarakumāra is the son of Sumeru.
"These two are commanders of the hosts of great chariot-warriors;
these, along with other heroes in our army, are each surrounded by their own respective forces."
Although they are superior in number within the enemy army, they will not be sufficient against our forces once Maheśvara has bestowed his grace.
While the asura Maya was thus speaking to Sunītha,
another messenger arrived from the presence of Śrutaśarman’s father.
And he said: "The Lord of Trikūṭa speaks thus to you:
'This thing called battle is indeed a great festival for heroes.'"
"This is his perilous ground; therefore, let us depart from here and go to a region of vast extent called the village of Kalāpa."
Having heard this, Sunītha and the others, saying "So be it," all went with their armies and accompanied by Sūryaprabha to that village of Kalāpa.
Śrutaśarman and the others likewise set out for battle and arrived at that very place, surrounded by their Vidyādhara forces.
Seeing the elephants in Śrutaśarman’s army, Sūryaprabha and the others brought forth their own elephant force, mounted upon their celestial chariots.
Then Dāmodara, the best of the Vidyādharas, formed for Śrutaśarman’s army within the host a great needle-array (mahāsūcivyūha).
There, Śrutaśarman himself stood on one side with his ministers;
Dāmodara was at the front, and the other great chariot-warriors were elsewhere.
In the army of Sūryaprabha as well, Prabhāsa, the commander of the host,
formed the crescent-moon array (*ardhacandra-vyūha*), and he himself stood in its center.
Sakuñjarakumāra and Prahasta stood at his two corners,
while Sūryaprabha, Sunītha, and all the others remained behind him.
On Mount Sumeru and its vicinity, where the prince Suvāsava resided,
the musical instruments of war were sounded by both armies alike.
Meanwhile, the sky was filled with gods who had come to witness the battle, including Indra,
the world-protectors, and the celestial nymphs.
And there Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Universe, arrived accompanied by Pārvatī,
followed by the gods, the Gaṇas, the Bhūtas, and the Mothers.
And the Blessed Lord Brahmā arrived, accompanied by Sāvitrī and the others,
as well as the Vedas in embodied form, the Śāstras, and all the great ṛṣis.
And Lord Hari arrived, borne upon the chariot of the king of birds, holding his discus weapon, accompanied by goddesses such as Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and Jayā.
Kaśyapa also arrived with his wife, as did the Ādityas and the Vasus; the lords of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, as well as the Asuras headed by Prahlāda.
When the expanse of the sky was covered by them, a great battle with a terrible clashing of weapons broke out between those two armies.
Then, as the circle of the quarters was completely shrouded by a dense web of arrows,
flashes of fire and lightning were produced from the mutual friction of the shafts.
Rivers of blood flowed forth, filled with streams of gore from the multitudes of elephants and horses wounded by weapons, with the bodies of heroes serving as the crocodiles drifting upon them.
For the sake of the festival,
there was a battle between the heroes, the jackals, and the spirits, as they danced, leaped in the blood, and howled.
When the tumultuous battle had subsided and countless soldiers were slain,
the distinction between one's own army and the enemy's army could gradually be discerned.
And as the names of the heroic adversaries who had fought at Sumeru were heard one after another, beginning with Sūryaprabha and the others, [the army of Māra was overwhelmed].
Previously, there occurred a duel between King Subāhu and the lord of the Vidyādharas named Aṭṭahāsa.
As he was fighting for a very long time and pierced by arrows,
Aṭṭahāsa severed Subāhu’s head with a crescent-headed shaft.
Seeing Subāhu slain, Muṣṭika rushed forward in a rage;
he too fell, struck in the heart by an arrow from that [same] loud laughter.
When Muṣṭika was slain, the enraged king named Pralamba rushed forward with a loud roar and fought him with showers of arrows.
Aṭṭahāsa, too, having repeatedly struck that army and pierced it in its vital organs,
cast the hero Pralamba down upon the back of his chariot.
Seeing Pralamba slain, the king named Mohana rushed forward and struck Aṭṭahāsa with his arrows.
Then Aṭṭahāsa struck down Mohana, whose bow was severed, whose charioteer was slain,
and who had been struck by powerful blows.
Seeing those four slain by the skillful Aṭṭahāsa,
Śrutaśarman’s army, intent on victory, roared with joy.
Seeing that, Harṣa, the friend of Sūryaprabha, became enraged and,
together with his army, rushed toward Aṭṭahāsa and his troops.
Having warded off his arrows with his own arrows and having struck down his army,
he slew the charioteer and, after cutting through the bow along with its banner two or three times, [he prevailed].
When Harṣa split Aṭṭahāsa’s head with his arrows, the latter,
vomiting blood, fell from his chariot to the ground.
When Aṭṭahāsa was slain, such a commotion arose in that battle that in an instant those two armies were reduced to half their original strength.
Slain there, the horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers fell down;
yet at the front of the battle, only headless trunks (kabandhas) stood upright.
Then the lord of the Vidyādharas named Vikṛtadaṃṣṭra,
enraged by the death of Aṭṭahāsa, approached and overwhelmed him with arrows.
Harṣa also, having shaken off his arrows, struck down [the opponent] along with his banner and charioteer;
having destroyed the chariot and horses, he severed the head adorned with beautiful earrings.
But when the one with the deformed fangs was enraged, the Vidyādhara king known as Cakravāla rushed toward Harṣa in indignation.
Cakravāla slew Harṣa in battle, who had repeatedly had his bow broken,
was exhausted in combat, and whose other weapons were shattered.
Out of anger at that, King Pramātha approached and fought him;
he too was then slain by Cakravāla in the battle.
In the same manner, he then struck down the other four chief kings of the Cakravāla one by one in succession.
Kaṅkaṭa, Viśāla, Pracaṇḍa, and likewise Aṅkurin—
seeing that, the king named Nirghāta rushed toward him in fury.
Those two, Cakravāla and Nirghāta, fighting for a long time in succession,
eventually became foot-soldiers after their chariots had been pulverized by one another.
Both of them, wielding swords and discs and having encountered each other in a rage,
fell to the ground with their heads split in two by sword-strokes.
Seeing those two heroes defeated, even though both armies were despondent, Kālakampana, the lord of the Vidyādharas, came to the front of the battle.
And a prince named Prakampana rushed toward him;
there, in an instant, he was struck down by that Kālakampana.
When he had fallen, five other charioteers rushed toward him:
Jālika, Caṇḍadatta, Gopaka, and Somila as well.
And Pitṛśarman and all of them loosed their arrows at him;
but Kālakampana rendered even those five who were deprived of their chariots [powerless].
Piercing him simultaneously in the heart with five iron arrows, he struck him down;
because of that, the sky-dwellers cried out, while men and asuras were filled with despair.
Then four other chariots rushed toward him at once:
Unmattaka, Praśasta, Vilambaka, and Dhuraṃdhara.
That Kālakampana slew them all with ease;
likewise, he struck down six other charioteers who had rushed forward.
Tejikam, Geyikam, Vegilam, and likewise Śākhilam;
Bhadraṅkara and Daṇḍin—these great chariot-warriors possessed vast armies.
Furthermore, in battle, he slew another five combined avadhīs:
Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Kumbhīra, Vikaṭa, and Savi locana.
Seeing that slaughter wrought in battle by Kālakampana,
a prince named Sugaṇa rushed forward to face him.
He engaged in battle with him for as long as both remained equal,
until they both became deprived of their chariots, their horses and charioteers having been slain.
Then Kālakampana, moving on foot upon the ground, struck Sugana— who was also on foot— with a sword-fight.
And at that moment, as if distressed by witnessing this inconceivable battle between humans and Vidyādharas, the sun departed to its setting.
Not only was the battlefield filled with a flood of blood,
but even the sky turned crimson as it took on the hue of twilight.
Then, while the spirits together with the headless trunks were intent on the twilight dance,
those two armies, having ceased their battle, went to their respective camps.
On that day, three heroes were slain in the army of Śrutaśarman,
while thirty-three preeminent warriors were killed in the army of Sauryaprabha.
Due to that death of his kinsmen, friends, and others, Sūryaprabha was deeply distressed; he spent that night without the women of the inner apartments.
Remaining sleepless with his ministers, engaging in various conversations concerning battle,
he passed that night once more intent upon war.
And his wives, distressed by the loss of their kinsmen,
gathered together on that night, finding mutual comfort in one another's presence.
Even at a time for weeping, they engaged in various kinds of conversation;
for there is no moment for women in which their talk does not rely upon something other [than their immediate grief].
In the course of that conversation, a certain princess there said this:
"It is a marvel! How is it that today our noble son has slept without his consort?"
Having heard that, another spoke: "How can the noble son, who was so distressed today by the destruction of his own kin in battle, now take delight among women?"
Then another said:
"If he obtains a beautiful young maiden, he will forget that very sorrow right now."
Then the other said: "Do not say so; even though he was a libertine among women, nevertheless he would not have been such as this in this suffering."
While they were speaking thus, one among them said with astonishment:
"Tell me, why is our noble son so devoted to women?"
Even though he had taken many wives, one after another,
that prince was never satisfied as he continued to take new ones incessantly.
Having heard this, one among them, clever and named Manovatī, said:
"Listen to how kings come to have many favorites."
Due to differences in country, form, age, conduct, knowledge, and so forth, the qualities of excellent women are distinct; no single woman is endowed with all qualities.
Women born in regions such as Karṇāṭa, Lāṭa, Saurāṣṭra,
and Madhyadeśa delight [their lovers] with their own respective local customs.
Some of those beautiful women bear [the fruit] with faces resembling the autumnal moon; others bear it with breasts that are high, firm, and resemble golden jars.
Others with their hips resembling the throne of Smara,
and others with their remaining limbs, each enchanting through its own beauty.
One had limbs as fair as gold, another was dark as the *priyaṅgu* flower, and yet another was of a bright red hue;
at the mere sight of them, they captivated the eye.
One was fresh and lovely, another was in the full bloom of youth; one was radiant with the delight of maturity, resplendent with spreading grace.
One shines while laughing; another is charming even in anger;
one moves like an elephant, while another gleams like a swan.
One speaks as if sprinkling the ear with nectar;
another shines by her very nature as she gazes with the play of her eyebrows.
One woman is pleasing through her dancing; another shines with her singing;
and yet another beloved woman is radiant through her knowledge of playing the lute and other instruments.
One was skilled in external pleasures, another was fond of internal ones;
one was radiant with ornaments, while another was graced by her cleverness.
Another, skilled in capturing her husband’s heart, enjoys good fortune;
how much more could I say? For many other women possess yet other distinct virtues.
Thus, in this world, some excellent woman may possess a certain virtue,
but there are none in the three worlds who possess every virtue.
Therefore, those lords who have attained their rank by tasting various flavors,
even after taking one wife, always continue to take ever-new ones.
But the best of men never desire another's wife under any circumstances;
therefore, this fault would belong to our noble son, and not to us, for we are capable of enduring jealousy.
Thus were the wives of Sūryaprabha, beginning with Manovatī, addressed;
and others, such as Madanasenā and the rest, likewise spoke their stories in succession.
Then, beyond the hundreds [of men], those women—free from restraint and unimpeded—taught one another even the technical methods of sexual union.
Meeting in the course of conversation, their minds intent on the flow of talk, they said to each other: "Oh, there is nothing here that these women do not utter!"* 8.4.120 *SoKss_8,4.120*
Then, by some means, that long conversation of theirs came to an end, and that night gradually reached its close;
meanwhile, Sūryaprabha, who desired to conquer the enemy forces, was intent solely on observing the moment when the darkness would depart.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Sūryaprabha-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the fifth wave.
Then, at dawn, Sūryaprabha and his followers went to the battlefield,
and Śrutaśarman and his men likewise returned, fully armored and accompanied by their armies.
Furthermore, the gods together with Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, along with the asuras,
yakṣas, nāgas, and gandharvas, came to witness the battle.
Dāmodara formed a wheel-array (*cakravyūha*) against the army of Śrutaśarman,
and Prabhāsa formed a diamond-array (*vajravyūha*) against the army of Sūryaprabha.
Then the battle between those two armies commenced,
deafening the horizons with the sounds of trumpets and the shouts of great warriors.
"Heroes slain by the sword break through my mandala"—
as if thinking thus out of fear, the sun became shrouded within a mass of arrows.
Then, by the command of Sūryaprabha, Prabhāsa broke through the wheel-array formed by Dāmodara, which was difficult for anyone else to pierce, and entered.
And Dāmodara himself, having reached that breach in the formation, blocked it;
and Prabhāsa fought him there, alone upon a single chariot.
Then, seeing that he had entered alone, Sūryaprabha subsequently dispatched fifteen great chariot-warriors after him.
Prakampana, Dhūmaketu, Kālakampanaka,
as well as Mahāmāya, Marudvega, Prahasta, and Vajrapañjara.
Kālacakra, Pramathana, Siṃhanāda, Sakambala,
Vikaṭākṣa, Pravahaṇa, and that Kuñjarakumāraka.
And all those great chariot-warriors, having rushed toward that best of Asura lords whose hair stood on end with joy, went to the gate of the military formation.
In that regard, Dāmodara first displayed his own prowess,
in that he alone fought against those fifteen.
Seeing the sage Nārada standing by his side, Vāsava addressed him, saying:
"All these, beginning with Sūryaprabha, are likewise incarnations of the Asuras."
Śrutaśarman is a portion of me, and all these Vidyādharas are portions of the gods;
therefore, O Sage, this is by design a battle between the gods and the asuras.
And in that regard, behold: Hari is always the companion of the gods;
this Dāmodara is a portion of Him, and thus he fights here.
While Śakra was speaking thus,
fourteen great chariot-warriors arrived to assist this Dāmodara, the commander of the army.
Brahmagupta, Vāyubala, Yamadaṃṣṭra, Suroṣaṇa,
Roṣāvaroha, Atibala, Tejaḥprabha, and Dhuraṃdhara.
Kuberadatta, Varuṇaśarman, Kambalika, as well as Vīra, Duṣṭamadanaka, and both Dohana and Ārohaṇa. (SoKss 8.5.18)
Those fifteen heroes, accompanied by Dāmodara,
likewise held back those heroes belonging to Sūryaprabha who were fighting at the front of the battle array.
Then, duels broke out between them there one after another;
Prakampana engaged in a battle of missiles with Dāmodara.
Dhūmaketu fought together with Brahmadatta,
while Mahāmāya fought along with Atibala.
The Dānava Kālakampana fought with Tejaḥprabha,
and the great Asura Marudvega fought with Vāyubala.
Vajrapañjara fought together with Yamadaṃṣṭra, and Kālacakra, the supreme asura, fought together with Suroṣaṇa.
Pramathana waged war against Kuberadatta,
and the Daitya lord Siṃhanāda fought alongside Varuṇaśarman.
The Dānava Pravahaṇa engaged in battle with Duṣṭadamana,
his hair bristling with excitement and his face flushed with rage.
Vikaṭākṣa engaged in combat with Dhuraṃdhara,
and Kambalika fought alongside Kambalika.
And that young elephant,
Prahasta, was accompanied by Ārohaṇa, who was also known as Mahotpāta, and by Dohana.
While these duels between great chariot-warriors were thus taking place against one another at the front of the battle array, Sunītha spoke to Maya: SoKss_8,5.28 //
"Alas! These heroes of our chariots, though skilled in various modes of combat, have been hemmed in by these rival chariot-warriors; behold them as they enter the formation."
And Prabhāsa alone entered here first, without hesitation;
we do not know whose [victory] it will be, nor what exactly will happen here.
Having heard this, the young Suvāsakumāra said to him:
"Even all those in the three worlds, including gods, asuras, and humans, would not be sufficient [to satisfy you]."
How much more so for these sky-dwellers before this single radiance?
Therefore, how can such groundless doubt arise in you, even though you possess knowledge?
While this young sage was speaking thus,
the Vidyādhara Kālakampana advanced to face Prabhāsa in battle.
Then Prabhāsa said to him: "Ho there! You have indeed done us a great wrong;
today we shall see your prowess here."
Having said this, Prabhāsa loosed a volley of arrows upon him;
Kālakampana, for his part, covered him with sharp shafts.
Then those two, the Vidyādhara and the human, fought each other with a battle of missiles and counter-missiles, providing a marvel to the world.
Then Prabhāsa brought down the banner with one arrow and slew Kālakampana’s charioteer with a second.
With four [arrows] he cut down the four horses, and with one the bow;
with two he severed the hands, with two the arms, and with two each of the two ears.
And Prabhāsa, displaying marvelous swiftness, severed the head of his enemy with a single sharp-edged arrow.
Thus, with the fury arising from the many heroes previously slain, Prabhāsa seemed as if he were inflicting punishment upon Kālakampana.
And seeing that lord of the Vidyādharas slain by men and asuras,
the sky-dwellers immediately let out a cry and fell into despair.
Then the lord of Mount Kālañjara, named Vidyutprabha,
the sovereign of the Vidyādharas, rushed toward Prabhāsa in a fit of rage.
As he was fighting, Prabhāsa cut down his great banner and repeatedly severed his bow each time it was taken up.
Then, having risen into the sky by means of his illusory power, the ashamed Vidyutprabha, remaining concealed, rained down swords, maces, and other weapons upon Prabhāsa.
Prabhāsa, too, having warded off that succession of weapons with his own missiles,
illuminated that sky-dweller with the *prakāśana* weapon.
Having discharged the great Āgneya weapon, he caused it— blazing with its splendor like lightning— to fall from the sky onto the surface of the earth, burning it and depriving it of life.
Having seen that, Śrutaśarman spoke to those great chariot-warriors:
"Behold, by this man two leaders of hosts of great chariot-warriors have been slain."
"Therefore, why do you tolerate this? Let him be slain by you all acting together.
Hearing that, eight chariot-warriors, filled with rage, surrounded Prabhāsa.
There was a certain leader of chariot-divisions, a lord of the Vidyādharas renowned as Ūrdhvaroman, who dwelt upon the great mountain Kaṅkaṭaka.
The lord of the mountains that support the earth was named Vikrośana;
and the second was Mahāratha, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
And Indumālin, whose banner bears the emblem of the playful mountain,
is a hero, a lord of the host of *atiratha*s, and a sovereign of the *vidyādharas*.
And the fourth king, a dweller of the Malaya mountains known as Kākāṇḍaka, was a leader of chariot-divisions and the best among those who move through the sky.
The fifth was Niketādripati, named Darpavāha;
and the sixth was Dhūrtavahana, the lord of Añjanagiri by name.
These two are Vidyādharas, both leaders of hosts of Atirathas;
the seventh is King Gardabharatha on Mount Kumuda.
He who was named Varāhasvāmī, a leader of a host of great chariot-warriors, became the eighth [incarnation], Dundubhi, the mountain-like chariot, possessing excellent intelligence.
Having arrived with these eight [archers], Prabhāsa shook off the arrows released by them and simultaneously pierced all of them with his own shafts.
He struck the horses of one, and likewise the charioteer of another;
he cut down the banner of one, and severed the bow of another.
Having pierced Medhāvara squarely in the heart with four arrows,
he cast him down upon the surface of the earth, instantly deprived of life.
Then, while fighting others with his hair tied up in a knot,
he cut off the head of Ūrdhvaroman from afar with an añjalika arrow.
And having severed the necks of the remaining six with individual arrows,
Prabhāsa struck them down, leaving their horses and charioteers slain.
Then a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon his head,
while the asuras and kings were emboldened and the denizens of the celestial realms were cast into shadow.
Then four other great chariot-warriors, skilled archers, were dispatched there by Śrutaśarman; they besieged that Prabhāsa.
One was named Kācaraka, the lord of Mount Kuraṇḍaka;
the second was Diṇḍimālin, who resided on the Five Mountains.
Vibhāvasu was the third king on the mountain of Jayapura;
the fourth was named Dhavala, the ruler of Bhūmituṇḍaka.
Those supreme sky-dwellers, commanders of great chariot-divisions,
simultaneously released five hundred arrows each at Prabhāsa.
And Prabhāsa,
in turn, with effortless ease, struck down one by one their banner, their bow, and their charioteer.
With four arrows he struck down the horses, and with one he felled his head;
having thus finished each one with eight shafts, he let out a roar.
Then, by the command of Śrutaśarman, four other Vidyādharas likewise arrived at that battle to join Prabhāsa.

This is not a dance on a stage or similar performance that would cause shame to a man;

"If I should not attain this, what is the fruit of my life?

"We shall begin this undertaking on an auspicious day, just as you have instructed.

Then, while Guṇaśarman was teaching him the lute,

To the queen who had spoken thus, Guṇaśarman said:
"Do not speak in this way to me; for you are the wife of my master, and such [behavior] is not fitting."
"Someone like me would commit treason against his master; desist from this rashness!
To him who had spoken thus, the queen said to Guṇaśarman:
What is this fruitless beauty and your proficiency in the arts?
Why do you disregard me, such as I am, with cold indifference?
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman spoke to her with derision: "Well said! But what is the fruit of that beauty and of that cleverness?"
That which is not stained by infamy through the abduction of another's wife,
and that which would not lead to a fall into the ocean of hell in this world or the next.
When he had spoken thus, the queen, as if filled with anger, said to him:

"Therefore, having killed you, I shall die, insulted as I am.
Then Guṇaśarman said: "Let that indeed be so."
Better indeed is life for even a single moment bound by the fetters of Dharma, than a hundred million eons lived in violation of Dharma.
For me, who have committed no sin, death is praiseworthy and beyond reproach;

Having heard this, the queen spoke to him once again:

"This king does not overstep even my impossible command;

Therefore, what fear do you have? Who shall overcome you, and how?

Perceiving that the queen was speaking thus with her followers,

If you are so insistent, O Goddess, I shall do as you say;

Endure for some days; know my words to be true.
What purpose do I have in opposing you, which would result in the destruction of everything?
Having thus satisfied her with this intention and having had his word accepted by her,

Then, as the days passed, King Mahāsena went and besieged Somakeśvara, who was stationed in the fortress.

Then King Mahāsena said to Guṇaśarman:
"While we remain with one [of us] held captive, we have been besieged by another enemy."
Therefore, O hero, how can we fight now with insufficient forces against two? And if we do not fight while being besieged, how long shall we remain here?
When the king asked him, "In this crisis, what should we do?", Guṇaśarman, who was standing nearby, replied.
"Be steadfast; O God, I shall employ such means that we shall emerge from this peril, even by force of action."
Having thus comforted the king and applied the ointment of invisibility to his eyes,
he went at night to the camp of Vikramaśakti, remaining unseen.
Having entered into his presence and awakened him from sleep, he said:

"Having made peace with King Mahāsena, depart quickly;
otherwise, the destruction of you and your army here will be certain."
"Once you have dispatched a messenger, he will agree to a peace treaty with you;

"You are a devotee, and he looks after the welfare and security of his devotees.
Upon hearing this, King Vikramaśakti reflected thus.
This is certainly the truth; otherwise, how could anyone enter this place so difficult to penetrate? This is no deed worthy of a mortal.
Reflecting thus, he said to him: "I am blessed, O Lord, that you command me in this way;
I shall do exactly as commanded."
While the king was still speaking thus,
Guṇaśarman, instilling confidence in him, vanished by means of an ointment and departed from that place.
Having gone there, he reported what had been done to Mahāsena;
and he, embracing him around the neck, welcomed him as one who had bestowed both life and sovereignty.
In the morning, King Vikramaśakti dispatched a messenger and,

Mahāsena, having conquered that Somaka and obtained elephants and horses,

And while the king was staying there, Guṇaśarman protected him from a crocodile during a river bath, and from the venom of a snake's bite in the grove.

But Queen Aśokavatī, full of longing for Guṇaśarman,

But he did not accept that improper act under any circumstances;

Then Aśokavatī, having understood his resolve born of enmity,

"I shall inflict upon him punishment with my wealth and even my life; speak!

When Guṇaśarman was thus suspected of being that person,
the king rose from his seat and sat upon his shoulder.
And he said to the astonished members of the assembly, "Hear my case against Guṇaśarman," whereupon Guṇaśarman addressed him in reply.
I am your servant and you are my master; how can our legal proceeding be equal?
Sit upon the throne first, and then give your command as you wish.
Thus addressed by that steadfast man and exhorted by his ministers,
the king sat upon his throne once more and spoke again to those in the assembly:
O ministers, you already know that Guṇaśarman, having bypassed those who have held office by hereditary succession, has been made equal to himself.
Listen to me regarding how, through the coming and going of messengers,
he formed an alliance with the Lord of Gauḍa and intended to commit treachery.
Having said this, the lord of the earth described to them that which Aśokavatī had told him, having fabricated it falsely.
That objection he raised regarding the destruction of the self, which was falsely spoken by him,
was also refuted by that king after he had been expelled from the company of the wise.
Then Guṇaśarman said to him:
"O King, by whom was such an untruth reported to you? By whom was this wonderful sky-painting created?"
Upon hearing this, the king said: "O wicked man, if this is not true, how did you know that the poison was inside the vessel of sacrificial rice?"
When Guṇaśarman said, "Everything is known through wisdom," the other ministers spoke out of hatred for him, saying, "This is impossible."
"O King, it is not even fitting for you to speak without having investigated the truth;
a ruler who acts without deliberation is not praised by those who know statecraft."
While Guṇaśarman was speaking thus, the king rushed forward and,
shouting "You are audacious!", struck him with a blow from his dagger.
When that [first] blow was rendered futile by his skillful application of technique,
the other followers of the king struck at that hero.
And Guṇaśarman, having deceived them by means of mock combats, snatched away the small swords from all of them at once.
And he bound them together, entwining their locks of hair with one another,
having performed this by means of a manual technique with a lightness of hand learned through marvelous training.
And then he departed forcibly from that royal assembly,
and he slew about a hundred warriors who pursued him.
Then, having applied that invisibility ointment from the corner of his garment to his eyes,
he became invisible and departed from that place at that very moment.
Traveling toward the southern region, he thought on the road:
"Surely that foolish king was incited by that Aśokavatī."
Alas, women who are rejected after being loved are even worse than poison!
Alas, kings who perceive the truth are unfit to be served by the virtuous!
Reflecting thus, Guṇaśarman somehow reached a village, where he saw an excellent brahmin beneath a banyan tree.
Approaching him as he was teaching his disciples, he paid his respects;
and that Brahmin, having offered him hospitality, questioned him after a moment.
“O Brahmin, which branch of the Veda do you study? Let it be told.
Thereupon, Guṇaśarman replied to that Brahmin.
"O Brahmin, I study twelve branches:
two from the Sāmaveda, two from the Ṛgveda, seven from the Yajurveda, and one from the Atharvaveda."
Having heard that, the brahmin then said, "In that case, you are a god," and bowing low before him— whose excellence had been made known by his very appearance— he questioned him again.
"Tell me, what country and what lineage have been adorned by your birth?
What is your name, how was all this studied by you, or where did you learn it?"
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman said to him: "In the city of Ujjayinī, there was a certain son of a Brahmin named Ādityaśarman."
And while that boy was still a child, his father passed away;
his mother, together with her husband, entered the fire.
Then, while studying the Vedas, the sciences, and the arts, Ādityaśarman grew up in that city in his maternal uncle’s house.
When he had attained knowledge and was here engaged in the practice of recitation and vows,
friendship arose between him and a certain wandering mendicant.
That wandering mendicant, together with his friend Ādityaśarman,
went to the cemetery and performed a fire sacrifice for the sake of attaining mastery over a yakṣiṇī.
And there appeared before him a celestial maiden, seated in a golden chariot,
surrounded by excellent maidens and beautifully adorned.
With sweet words she spoke to him: "O Maskarin, I am a yakṣī named Vidyunmālā, and these other women here are also yakṣiṇīs."
Therefore, take one from among my retinue here according to your preference;
this alone shall be accomplished for you by means of this mantra practice.
For you have not fully understood the accomplishment of my mantra;
therefore, I am not yet perfected for you. Do not undergo further hardship in vain.
Having been addressed thus by that yakṣī, the wandering mendicant, after showing her due respect,
took one yakṣiṇī from among her retinue.
Then Vidyunmālā vanished; and Ādityaśarman questioned that yakṣiṇī who had been perfected by the wandering mendicant.
"Is there any yakṣiṇī superior to Vidyunmālā?
Having heard that, the yakṣiṇī replied to him, "There is, O handsome one."
Vidyunmālā, Candralekhā, and the third, Sulocanā—
these are the most excellent among the yakṣiṇīs, and among these, Sulocanā is the best.
Having spoken thus, the yakṣiṇī departed to return at the appointed time;
and the mendicant went with Ādityaśarman to her house.
There, every day, that Yakṣiṇī Kālopagā, being pleased with that renunciant, bestowed upon him the enjoyments he desired.
Once, Ādityaśarman asked through the mouth of a wandering mendicant:
"Who knows the ritual procedure for the mantra of Sulocanā?"
She too, right there in his presence, spoke thus to him:
"There is indeed a place named Tumbavana in the southern region."
There dwells one named Viṣṇugupta, a wandering mendicant who has made his home on the banks of the Veṇā; he is the foremost among venerable monks and knows that matter in full detail.
Having understood this from the words of the Yakṣiṇī,
Ādityaśarman, full of longing, went to that place accompanied by the wandering mendicant out of affection.
Having searched for him there in the proper manner and having approached that venerable one,
he devoted himself to service with devotion and attended upon him for three years.
And that wandering mendicant was attended by that perfected yakṣiṇī with superhuman services provided according to his needs.
Then that venerable one, being pleased, bestowed upon Ādityaśarman the requested mantra of Sulocanā, together with its ritual procedure.
Then Ādityaśarman, having received and mastered that mantra,
went to a secluded place and performed the fire-oblation in its entirety according to the prescribed rule.
Then, from that celestial chariot, the yakṣiṇī Sulocanā appeared,
her form bestowing wonder upon the world.
And she said to him: "Come, come! I am accomplished for you;
however, for six months my state as a maiden must not be removed by you."

If you wish to obtain from me a son who is a great hero, a vessel of supernatural power, endowed with auspicious marks, nearly omniscient, and unconquered— so it is said in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, 8.6.184.
Having said this, the Yakṣiṇī, taking Ādityaśarman— who had replied "So be it"— departed for Alakā by means of a celestial chariot.
And there Ādityaśarman remained for six months, constantly beholding her standing nearby while practicing the "sword-edge" vow.
Then the Lord of Wealth, being pleased, personally bestowed that Sulocanā upon Ādityaśarman according to a divine rite.
In that [city], I was born here as the son of that twice-born man;
and my father gave me the name Guṇaśarman on account of my virtuous qualities.
Then, right there, from the lord of the yakṣas named Maṇidhara,
I gradually acquired the Vedas, the sciences, and the arts.
Then once, Śakra came there to the presence of the Giver of Wealth;
and seeing him, whoever was sitting there stood up.
But my father, Ādityaśarman, at that moment,
due to the turn of fate and because his mind was elsewhere, did not rise up in agitation.
Then Śakra, enraged, cursed him: "Fie upon you, fool!
Go back to that very world of mortals; you are not fit to be here."
Then, having been entreated by that Sulocanā after prostrating before him, Śakra said: "In that case, let him not go to the world of mortals himself."
"Let this son go; for a son is said to be one's very self.
Having said, "Let not my word be in vain," Indra attained peace.
Then my father brought me to his own maternal uncle’s house in Ujjayinī and deposited me there; for that which is destined to be must come to pass.
There, by the power of destiny, friendship arose between me and the king who was present there.
Now hear from me everything that happened to me there; I shall tell it to you.
Having said this, he related the entire account from the beginning— what Aśokavatī had done and what the king had done, ending with the battle.
And he spoke to him again, "O Brahmin, having thus fled,
while traveling to another country, I saw you here on the road."
Having heard this, that brahmin said to Guṇaśarman:
"In that case, O Lord, I have become blessed by your arrival."
Therefore, come with me to my house for now; know me as Agnidatta by name, and this village is my royal grant—be at ease.
Having said this, Agnidatta led Guṇaśarman into his own opulent home,
which was filled with many cows, buffaloes, and horses.
There, he honored that guest with baths and ointments, with garments and ornaments, and with various kinds of food.
And he showed him his own daughter, named Sundarī, who could assume any form at will even by the gods, and who was so beautiful that one would desire her merely upon seeing her auspicious marks.
Guṇaśarman, too, having beheld her whose beauty was unequaled by any other,
said to Agnidatta, "She will have co-wives."
She has a mole on her nose, and because of its connection with that, I say:
there is also a second one on her chest; the wise know this to be the fruit of those two.
When he had spoken thus, her brother, with his father’s permission, opened her breast; as soon as he did so, he beheld a *tīlaka*.
Then Agnidatta, filled with wonder, said to Guṇaśarman:
"You are omniscient; these two *tilaka* marks of hers do not portend anything inauspicious."
For in this world, when a husband is prosperous, women generally become co-wives;
but how could a poor man support even one, let alone many? It would be a hardship.
Having heard that, Guṇaśarman replied to him: "O sir, what you say is true; for how could there be misfortune for one of such auspicious form as Sulakṣaṇā?"
Having spoken thus, being questioned in the course of conversation,
he explained to him the specific results for men and women regarding the *tilaka* and other marks on each individual limb.
And then, as soon as that Sundarī saw Guṇaśarman,
she was as eager to drink him in with her very eyes as a female cakora bird is for the moon.
Then Agnidatta said to Guṇaśarman in private:
"O noble one, I shall give this maiden Sundarī to you."
"Do not go to a foreign land; stay here in my house as you please.
Having heard these words of his, Guṇaśarman also spoke to him:
"True, if this were done, what happiness would not be mine?
But that [happiness] does not at all please me, for I am scorched by the fire of the king's insult."
The beloved, the rising moon, and the fifth note of the lute—
these things which delight those who are happy cause pain to those who are suffering.
And a wife who is naturally affectionate and devoted shall be free from infidelity;
yet, even if she is unwilling, she may become like Aśokavatī through the power of her father’s gift.
"Moreover, that city of Ujjayinī is near to this region;
having learned of this, that king might at some time cause me trouble."
Having wandered through those sacred fords and washed away the sins of my birth from this body, I shall cast it off and then become liberated.
To him who had spoken thus, Agnidatta replied with a smile:
"When even you are thus deluded, what can be said of another?"
Tell me, what loss can there be for you of pure intention from being ignorant or insulted?
For mud thrown into the sky falls back upon the head of the thrower.
That king shall soon reap the fruit of his lack of discernment;
for Fortune does not long serve one who is blinded by delusion and devoid of discrimination.
Furthermore, if you have developed a distaste for women upon seeing Aśokavatī, why do you not feel such confidence in them after seeing a virtuous woman? You yourself know the signs [of virtue].
Or, if Ujjayinī is near, I shall provide for you in such a way that no one at all will know you to be staying here.
Or if pilgrimage is dear to you, that is likewise praised by the wise for him in whom there is no success according to the rules in Vedic ritual. (SoK 8.6.224)
Otherwise, how could there be the accumulation of merit at home through rites for the gods, ancestors, and fire, as well as vows, recitations, and so forth, for one who wanders upon the noble path?
Using his arm as a pillow, sleeping on the ground, eating alms, solitary and without wealth—
even having attained equanimity like a sage, the traveler is not yet freed from the afflictions.
If you desire happiness from the abandonment of the body, this is your delusion;
for those who commit suicide suffer even greater misery hereafter.
Therefore, this delusion is unbecoming of you, who are both young and wise;
reflect upon it yourself, for my word must certainly be carried out by you.
"I shall have a large, beautiful, and secret underground chamber built for you here;
for after marrying Sundarī, there is indeed suffering in the next world for those who commit suicide."
Thus enlightened by Agnidatta, Guṇaśarman diligently accepted this with the words "So be it," and spoke to him.
"I have done as you requested; who would abandon a beautiful wife?
However, being an unfortunate man, I shall not marry this daughter of yours."
"I shall first propitiate some deity with great self-restraint,
so that I may repay the debt owed to that ungrateful king."
Delighted by those words, Agnidatta gave his consent;
and Guṇaśarman also spent that night there in comfort.
And on another day, Agnidatta had a secret underground chamber constructed there for his son's comfort,
resembling a dwelling in the underworld.
Remaining there, Guṇaśarman spoke privately to Agnidatta:
"Tell me here within, which deity should I worship with devotion and by what mantra?"
"I shall first propitiate the Giver of Boons through the practice of vows"—
to that steadfast one who had spoken thus, Agnidatta replied.
"I have a mantra of Svāmikumāra that was taught to me by my guru;
with it, propitiate that god, the commander-in-chief who is the destroyer of Tāraka."

He was the one for whose sake Kāma— though created by Śarva and born of mere thought— was sent by the gods oppressed by their enemies when they sought his birth, even though that Kāma had been previously burnt.
They proclaim his wondrous birth from Maheśvara, from the sacrificial fire-pit, from Agni, from the Śara forest, and from the Kṛttikās.
By him, as soon as he was born, the entire world was gladdened by his invincible splendor, and the invincible demon Tāraka was slain.
"Accept this mantra from me," he said,
and so Agnidatta gave that mantra to Guṇaśarman.
Thereupon, Guṇaśarman, firm in his vows and being attended upon by that Sundarī, propitiated Skanda while staying in an underground chamber.
Then, having become manifest before his very eyes, that six-faced god said to him:
"I am pleased with you; choose a boon, my son."
"O son, having become one whose treasury is inexhaustible and having conquered Mahāsena, you shall go forth unimpeded and rule over the earth."
Having thus granted him this additional boon, Skanda vanished;
and Guṇaśarman, too, became one who possessed an inexhaustible treasury.

Then, by means of his supernatural power suited to his own greatness, that virtuous man married Sundarī according to the prescribed rites— she who was the daughter of the Brahmin Agnidatta, whose love for him increased day by day, and who, beautiful as she was, appeared like the personification of the destined fulfillment of his purpose.
By virtue of the power arising from his inexhaustible treasury and stores, he assembled a vast army of elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers;
obstructing the earth with his forces, he marched toward Ujjayinī, where all the kings had gathered through their devotion to his generosity.
Having proclaimed that lack of virtue in Aśokavatī to her subjects and having defeated King Mahāsena in battle,
he stripped him of his kingdom and attained the sovereignty of the earth.

And having married other maidens as well, that emperor Guṇaśarman, his eyes never turning away even from the shores of the ocean of kings, enjoyed his desired pleasures for a long time together with Sundarī.
Thus, due to ignorance regarding the specific nature of persons, King Mahāsena suddenly met with calamity through his deluded intellect;
yet Guṇaśarman, being wise, relied solely upon fortitude as his companion and attained the highest prosperity.

Having thus heard this noble discourse from the mouth of his own minister Vītabhīti during the night, the heroic Sūryaprabha, desiring to cross the great ocean of battle, attained even greater enthusiasm and gradually fell asleep.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Sūryaprabhalambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Seventh Wave:
Then, having risen in the morning, Sūryaprabha, together with his ministers...
Accompanied by all his forces, including the Dānavas and others, he went to the field of battle.
And Śrutaśarman departed, surrounded by the forces of the Vidyādharas;
and all the gods, Asuras, and others returned once more to witness the spectacle.
Both those armies formed two crescent-shaped battle arrays,
and then a battle commenced between those two forces.
Even arrows, rushing forward with a whizzing sound and cutting one another down,
fought as if they were mounted on wings and possessed of great speed.
Emerging from their scabbards, long and yellowish-red with blood,
the flickering sword-blades shone like the tongues of Death.
Then that great lake of battle became a place for the destruction of royal swans, where the multitudes of wheels fell upon the lotus-faces of blooming heroes.
With the heads of heroes leaping up, falling down, and severed,
the battlefield shone like the ball-play of Kṛtānta, the God of Death.
On the field of battle, where the darkness of dust was washed away by the sprinkling of blood,
duels took place between the indignant great chariot-warriors.
There, Sūryaprabha had a battle with Śrutaśarman,
and Prabhāsa had a combat with Dāmodara.
Then Siddhārtha fought with Mahotpāta;
Prahasta fought with Brahmagupta, and Vītabhī with Saṃgama.
Prajñāḍhya fought with Candragupta, Priyaṃkara with Akrama,
and Sarvadamana with Atibala.
