That young prince fought with Dhurandhara;
the other great chariot-warriors likewise fought individually with their respective opponents.
There, Pūrṇa first repelled his arrows with his own;
then, having severed Siddhārtha’s bow, he struck down his horses along with the charioteer.
Deprived of his chariot, Siddhārtha also rushed forward in rage and crushed that chariot along with its horses using a great iron staff.
Then Siddhārtha, moving on foot, cast that opponent, who was also on foot,
down to the earth with a wrestling hold in a great upheaval.
And for as long as he desired to crush him, that sky-goer,
protected by his father Bhaga, rose up and departed from the battle.
Prahasta and Brahmagupta, having deprived each other of their chariots,
fought one another with various maneuvers and sword-combats.
And Prahasta, by means of a sequence of instruments, skillfully caused that Brahmagupta— whose skin had been sliced away by the sword— to fall to the surface of the earth.
Just as he desired to cut off the head of that fallen man,
he was restrained from afar by his father himself, Brahmā.
"You have come to protect the sons, not to witness the battle," having said this, all the Dānavas then mocked the gods.
Then Vītabhaya, having pierced Saṃkrama in the heart with the Pradyumna weapon, struck him down— his bow broken and his charioteer slain.
And Prajñāḍhya, being on foot due to the destruction of his two chariots, slew Candragupta—
who was also on foot— with a sword-fight, cutting off his head.
Then Candramas, enraged by the slaughter of his son, came in person and fought with Rajadhyaya; the battle between the two of them was equal.
And Priyaṃkara, being himself deprived of his chariot due to the destruction of his vehicle,
split Viratha in two with a single stroke of his sword as he advanced.
When the bow was severed,
Sarvadamana struck the exceedingly powerful [opponent] in the chest with a hurled goad, killing him effortlessly in battle.
Then that young elephant prince repeatedly deprived Dhurandhara of his chariot through a battle of missiles and counter-missiles.
And Vikramaśakti repeatedly presented him with a chariot;
and in that perilous situation, he protected him as well, warding off his weapons with his own weapons.
Then that young elephant, having run up in anger, suddenly hurled a massive rock onto the chariot of Vikramaśakti.
When his stride and power had failed and his chariot was crushed,
he then pulverized that leader of the team with that very same rock.
Although Sūryaprabha was engaged in combat with Śrutaśarman there,
out of anger over the slaying of Virocana, he killed Dama with a single arrow.
Out of anger at that, the two gods, the Aśvins, fell upon him with arrows for battle;
Sunītha received them, and a great battle took place between them.
And Sthirabuddhi, having displayed his prowess by striking with a spear in battle,
fought against the eight Vasus who were enraged by that killing.
And seeing Bhāsa deprived of his chariot by Mardana, Prabhāsa—
though already engaged in combat with Dāmodara— struck him down with a single arrow.
Having slain Tejaḥprabha in battle through a duel of missiles,
the Dānava Prakampana fought with Agni, who was enraged by that killing.
And when Dhūmaketu struck Yamadaṃṣṭra in battle,
a most terrible fight ensued with the enraged Yama.
Having ground together with a stone *siṃhadraṣṭa* and *suroṣaṇa*,
he [fought] in battle against Nirṛti, who was filled with indignation at his death.
Kālacakra also, with his wheel, split the force of the wind in two;
and out of anger, he fought against that blazing wind.
Assuming the forms of serpents, mountains, and trees, Mahāmāya, who brings about utter delusion,
destroyed the [palace] given by Kubera by assuming the forms of Tārkṣya, the thunderbolt, and fire.
Then Kubera, enraged, fought there with him;
likewise, the other gods also fought out of anger that their own portions were being destroyed.
And there, other various lords of the Vidyādharas were also struck down by those various men and Dānavas who sprang up at every step.
And meanwhile, there occurred between Prabhāsa and Dāmodara a battle terrifying with the mutual exchange of missiles and counter-missiles.
Then Dāmodara, his bow broken and his charioteer slain,
took up another bow and, grasping the reins himself, fought on.
And Indra asked the lotus-seated one, who was bestowing words of praise upon him:
"O Blessed One, why are you pleased with one who is declining?"
Then Brahmā said to him: "How is it that he is not satisfied with this man, who has been fighting with Prabhāsa for so long?"
Indeed, who but Dāmodara, a portion of Hari, could have performed this?
For even all the gods together were insignificant compared to Prabhāsa alone in battle.
He who was formerly the asura named Namuci, the crusher of the gods,
was born from that [merit] as the one called Prabala, who was composed of all kinds of jewels.
This very Prabhāsa has today become the invincible son of Bhāsa;
formerly, Bhāsa himself was the great asura Kālanemi.
Furthermore, having previously been Hiraṇyakaśipu, he became Kapiñjala;
and he who was the asura Sumuṇḍīka is now this Sūryaprabha.
And he who was formerly Hiraṇyākṣa is now this asura Sunītha;
and all these others, such as Prahasta and the rest, are likewise Daityas and Dānavas.
Those who were slain by you have been born again as these Asuras, such as Maya and others; for this very reason, they have taken refuge in their faction.
Behold Bali, whose bonds have been loosened through the power of the sacrifice to Rudra performed by Sūryaprabha and others; he has come here to see you.
Protecting his own word of truth, he remains in the netherworlds until the end of the period of your reign; after that, he will become a *cakravartin*.
These have now been taken under the protection of Tripurāri;
therefore, this is not the time for your victory—make peace, what is the use of seizing them?
While the lotus-seated one was thus addressing the lord of the gods,
Prabhāsa discharged the great Pāśupata weapon.
Seeing that all-devouring, fierce weapon had been unleashed,
Hari, out of affection for his son, discharged the Sudarśana discus.

Then there occurred a battle between those two who possessed identical forms and were masters of divine weapons— a conflict that threw the three worlds into a state of agitation, as if at the time of an untimely universal dissolution.
"Withdraw this weapon of yours until I withdraw mine.
Thus addressed by Hari, Prabhāsa then replied to him.
"A discharged weapon must not be in vain; let Dāmodara turn his back and leave the battle. Therefore, I shall withdraw this weapon."
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said: "In that case, honor me;
let there be no fruitlessness for either of us regarding the wheel."
Having heard these words of the thief, Prabhāsa, who knew the proper time, said:
"So be it; let this wheel of mine destroy your chariot."
When Hari had thus withdrawn Dāmodara from the battle, Prabhāsa withdrew his weapon; the discus then fell upon his own chariot.
Then, having mounted another chariot, he went into the presence of Sūryaprabha;
Dāmodara also then departed for the presence of Śrutaśarman.
And meanwhile, the duel between Śrutaśarman, who was arrogant because he was a portion of Vāsava,
and Sūryaprabha reached its ultimate limit.
Whatever weapon Śrutaśarman employed with great effort, Sūryaprabha countered each one in an instant with his own counter-weapons.
Whatever illusions were employed here by Śrutaśarman against him,
each one was destroyed by Sūryaprabha with a counter-illusion.
Then, out of extreme rage, Śrutaśarman discharged the Brahmā-missile;
the skillful Sūryaprabha also released the Pāśupata missile.
Having neutralized that Brahmā-weapon with that fierce great weapon,
Śrutaśarman was then overcome by Duṣpradharṣa.
At that time, Indra and the other world-protectors, filled with indignation, discharged supreme weapons such as the vajra from all sides.
But that Pāśupata weapon, having conquered all those other weapons as well,
blazed forth even more intensely with the intent to slay Śrutaśarman.
Then Sūryaprabha, having offered praise, made this request of that great weapon:
"Do not kill Śrutaśarman; bind him and hand him over."
Then, driven by the desire to conquer him, the gods equipped themselves for battle without exception, along with other asuras who had become mere spectators.
At that very moment, the attendant named Vīrabhadra, dispatched by Śambhu, arrived and delivered this command from him to Indra and the others: SoKss_8,7.72 //
"You have come here to look on; what course of action for battle is yours in this matter?
Furthermore, from the transgression of proper bounds, other improprieties may also arise."
Having heard this, the gods said: "We are being slain and have been slain;
all our sons are here. Therefore, how can we not fight?"
For the affection for a son is indeed difficult to abandon; therefore, a remedy must certainly be applied.
Since this [affection] must be directed toward those who destroy it according to one's ability, what is improper in this matter?
When the gods had spoken thus and Vīrabhadra had departed,
a great battle then commenced between the gods and the asuras.
Sunītha was equal to the Aśvins; Prajñāḍhya was with the Moon;
Sthirabuddhi was with the Vasus; and Kālacakra was with Vāyu.
Prakampana with Agni, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra with Nirṛti,
Prathamana with Varuṇa, and Dhūmaketu with Yama.
Then Mahāmāya fought with the Lord of Wealth using missiles and counter-missiles, as well as against the other gods.
At the end, whatever supreme weapon each deity discharged,
Hara destroyed that very weapon with a "hum" sound.
But Dhanada, with his mace raised, was restrained by Śarva with gentle words;
and those various gods, their weapons shattered, abandoned the battle and departed.
Then Śakra himself, out of anger, fought against Sūryaprabha;
he loosed a torrent of arrows upon him as well as various other weapons.
And Sūryaprabha, having effortlessly shaken off those weapons,
struck Indra with a hundred iron arrows drawn back to his ear.
Then the enraged lord of the gods seized his thunderbolt, and Rudra uttered the sound "huṃ"; thereupon, that thunderbolt was destroyed.
Then, when Śakra had retreated, Nārāyaṇa himself,
out of anger, fought Prabhāsa with millions of arrows having many points.
Unshaken, he fought equally with his own weapons against the other weapons;
and even though his horses were slain and he was deprived of his chariot, he mounted another chariot.
He fought without distinction against that enemy of the Daityas;
then the enraged god released his blazing discus.
Prabhāsa also, having consecrated it with mantras, released a divine sword;
and as those two weapons were clashing in combat, he beheld the discus.
As his sword was gradually failing him, Hara uttered the syllable "huṃ";
by that, both his sword and discus vanished from sight.
Then the Asuras rejoiced, while the gods despaired,
since Sūryaprabha had achieved victory and Śrutaśarman was bound.
Having offered praise, the gods then propitiated the bull-bannered Lord;
thereupon, the Lord of Ambikā, being pleased, commanded the gods as follows.
"Sūryaprabha, set aside what you have promised and choose another boon; O Lord, who is able to make otherwise that which has been promised by you?"
"But, O Lord, let that which was promised by us regarding this Śrutaśarman also come true; let there be neither falsehood nor the destruction of our lineage."
Having spoken thus to the gods who had ceased [speaking], the Blessed One commanded them:
"This shall come to pass when a reconciliation is made; and let there be such a reconciliation among you here."
"Let Śrutaśarman, together with his followers, pay homage to Sūryaprabha;
then we shall speak in such a way that it may be for the benefit of both."
Having accepted these words of the Lord, saying "So be it," the gods made Śrutaśarman bow down before Sūryaprabha.
Then, as those two had mutually abandoned their enmity and were locked in an embrace,
the gods and asuras, their own hostilities having subsided, established peace between them.
Then, while all the asuras and suras were listening,
the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke these words to Sūryaprabha:
"Bestow upon yourself the status of a universal monarch for the sake of the southern altar;
but for the sake of the northern altar, give that [status] to Śrutaśarman."
"O son, you shall before long obtain a fourfold sovereignty over all the *kiṃnaras* and other celestial beings who roam the heavens."
And when he has arrived, you should give even half of the sacrificial fee as a gift to Kuñjarakumāra, for he stands in a position of special distinction.
And those heroes who have been slain here in battle on both sides—
let them all indeed rise up alive with their limbs uninjured.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and all those who had been slain in battle rose up unhurt, as if awakened from sleep.
Then Sūryaprabha, the subduer of enemies, bearing the command of Śambhu upon his head,
went to a secluded and spacious stretch of ground.
Seated in his great hall, he personally had Śrutaśarman, who had arrived,
sit upon half of his own lion throne.
Their companions, Prabhāsa and the others, as well as Śrutaśarman’s companions,
Dāmodara and the others, sat down on both sides of those two.
Sunītha, Maya, and the other Dānavas sat down upon their respective seats, as did the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Then all the lords of the seven netherworlds, the chiefs of the Daityas and Dānavas headed by Prahlāda, arrived there in great joy.
And Śakra, accompanied by the world-protectors and others, with his preceptor at the head,
as well as the Vidyādhara Sumeru and that prince Suvāsakumāra.
Danu and all the other wives of Kaśyapa arrived,
as did the wives of Sūryaprabha, traveling in the celestial chariot Bhūtāsana.
When they had all sat down, having established mutual affection and proper conduct,
a friend named Siddhi, having offered [a seat], spoke these words according to their instruction:
"O gods and asuras! This goddess Danu says to you: 'Whatever joy and happiness we have in this assembly of affection,'" SoKss_8,7.112.
Therefore, tell me if you have ever experienced such a thing;
henceforth, you must not harbor mutual hostility that is so terrible in its suffering.
He was chosen for the sovereignty of heaven by his elder brothers, Hiraṇyākṣa and the others;
they have gone [to their own realms], and Śakra alone is now the eldest—what cause for opposition is there?
Therefore, dwell in mutual peace and happiness,
so that we may find contentment and the worlds may attain well-being.
Having thus heard the words of Danu from the mouth of Siddhi,
Bṛhaspati, looking toward Śakra, spoke to her.
There is no lingering enmity on the part of the gods toward the asuras,
provided that these asuras do not act deceitfully toward the gods.
When this had been said by the preceptor of the gods, Maya, the lord of the Dānavas, replied:
"If there were to be any transformation among the Asuras, how could Namuci not have given it?"
How could Prabala have surrendered to the gods his own body, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas, which grants life back to the dead, for the sake of Indra?
Having given the three worlds to Hari, how could Bali enter prison?
And how could he, whose body was made of iron, give his body to Viśvakarman?
Or how much more shall I say? Asuras are ever-present;
if they were not to be harassed by deceit, they would undergo no change at all.
When the asura Maya had spoken thus, Siddhi replied accordingly;
then the gods and asuras felt mutual joy, following with embraces around each other's necks.
Just then, a female doorkeeper named Jayā, sent by Bhavānī, arrived there;
she was honored by all and spoke as follows: "Sumeru is here."
"I have been sent to you by the Queen, and she has given this message to you:
'You have a daughter, a maiden named Kāmacūḍāmaṇi.'"
"Give her to Sūryaprabha quickly, for she is devoted to me.
Thus addressed by Jayā, Sumeru bowed low and replied to her.
"That which the Goddess commands me is indeed a supreme favor;
this very purpose was previously commanded to me by the God as well."
Thus addressed by Sumeru, Jayā said to Sūryaprabha:
"You must make her the presiding lady over all your wives."
"She shall be dear to you as well as to all those women you desire"; thus has the goddess Gaurī, being pleased, commanded even you today.
Having spoken thus, Jayā, honored by Sūryaprabha, vanished;
and on that very day, Sumeru quickly decided upon the auspicious moment for the marriage.
There he had an altar constructed with pillars and a floor made of excellent jewels, which,
due to the mass of their radiance, appeared as if covered by fire.
And he caused his daughter Kāmacūḍāmaṇi to be brought forth—
she whose loveliness was being drunk in by the restless eyes of gods and asuras.
"Umā was born from Himavat, and she was born from Sumeru"—
as if because of such equal beauty, they were united as one.
Then, having placed upon the altar that which was adorned with the auspicious marriage-thread and beautifully decorated,
he gave that Sumeru-like mountain to Sūryaprabha.
And then Sūryaprabha took the lotus-hand of Kāmacūḍāmaṇi, upon which bracelets had been bound by Danu and the others.
And at the first scattering of parched grain,
Jayā, sent by Bhavānī, arrived at that very moment and bestowed a divine, imperishable garland.
Then Sumeru also gave him priceless jewels and a divine,
excellent elephant born from Airāvaṇa.
And at the second scattering of parched grain, Jayā gave her the Ratnāvalī necklace;
by wearing it around her neck, neither death nor hunger and thirst cause her any affliction.
And Sumeru gave him a double store of jewels,
as well as an unsurpassed jewel among horses born from Uccaiḥśravas.
At the third scattering of parched grain, Jayā gave her a single-string necklace,
by which, when fastened around the neck, youth never at all diminishes.
And having distributed a heap of jewels three times the size of Mount Sumeru,
he gave him a divine pill that is effective for all accomplishments.
Then, when the wedding had been concluded, Sumeru addressed all the gods, asuras, vidyādharas, and divine mothers in this way:
"All of you must eat today in my house;
please show me your favor, for I join my palms upon my head."
While all of them were thus making their request to Sumeru and had not yet consented, Nandī arrived there.
He said to them as they bowed: "The Trident-bearer has commanded that you must eat at the house of Sumeru, for this is our domain."
"Once this food has been eaten, may there be for you eternal satisfaction.
Having heard this from Nandimukha, they all accepted it as true.
Then, immeasurable hosts dispatched by Śaṅkara arrived there,
presided over by Vināyaka, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and others.
And having prepared that altar for the meal, they seated those gods, celestial beings, asuras, and humans in due order.
And they presented to them foods prepared by magic, as well as those produced from the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) commanded by Śaṃkara, all originating from Mount Sumeru.
And Vīrabhadra, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgin, and the other gods stood before each [of them] individually, according to their merit, carrying out their every wish.
And at every step, there arose a divine concert, beautiful with the dancing of celestial women, while the *cāraṇa* bards sang in praise of his contentment.
And at the conclusion of the meal, Nandīśvara and the others gave to them all divine garlands, garments, and ornaments.
Having thus honored the gods and others, all the lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin, departed with all their attendants just as they had come.
Then all the gods and asuras, as well as those mothers of theirs, departed;
and Śrutaśarman and the others also took leave and went each to his own abode.
Sūryaprabha, together with his wife and accompanied by his friends and their wives,
traveled by means of a celestial chariot to that primordial grove of asceticism on Mount Sumeru.
And he dispatched his friend Harṣa to the kings to announce his own rise,
as well as to his brother Ratnaprabha.
And at the end of the day, he entered that bedchamber of Kāmacūḍāmaṇi’s bride, which contained a couch made of excellent jewels and was well-constructed.
There, by means of firm embraces and the biting of her lips,
he gradually caused her to abandon the modesty so easily found in a newlywed bride.
Together with her, he enjoyed a fresh, indescribable love-making, charming and sweet,
the likes of which had never been tasted by any other woman.
"Now let the dwelling of others be outside, but in my heart let there be only you alone"— with these words, he won her over.
Then, as he slept at the end of their dalliance, that night— and his sleep— gradually came to an end, bringing with it the pleasure of his beloved's embrace.
And at dawn, having risen and gone there, Sūryaprabha then gratified those first wives of his who were staying with him.
And while they were jesting with him, who was infatuated with his new bride, using sequences of words that were playful, indirect, sweet, affectionate, and charming; so too—
Having been announced by the doorkeeper,
the Vidyadhara named Suṣeṇa approached, prostrated himself, and addressed that skillful one.
"O Lord, I have been sent here by all the lords of the Vidyādharas, beginning with Trikūṭanātha; they thus address their request to Your Majesty."
"On the third day from the month of Ṛṣabha, your auspicious consecration shall take place;
let it be announced to all, and let preparations for this be made."
Having heard that, Sūryaprabha then replied to the messenger:
"Go and speak to the lord of Trikūṭa and the others in my name."
"May you yourselves undertake the endeavor and speak;
as for us, we stand here already fully prepared."
"We shall provide a formal greeting to all of them as is appropriate.
Having received this message, Suṣeṇa then departed.
And Sūryaprabha also [conversed] with each of his friends, beginning with Prabhāsa,
as well as with the gods, the sages beginning with Yājñavalkya, and likewise with the kings.
And he dispatched messengers individually to all the Vidyādharas and Asuras to invite them to his own great festival of consecration.
And he went alone by himself to Kailāsa, the most excellent of mountains,
making an effort to invite both Hara and Ambikā.
And as he ascended, he beheld that mountain, white with bright ashes,
worthy of being served by celestial sages and perfected beings, like a second Śaṅkara.
Having ascended more than half [the height], which was difficult to climb beyond that point,
he saw there a single door made of coral.
When he did not obtain entry there even though he was a perfected one,
he then praised the Moon-crested Lord with a one-pointed mind.
Then, having opened that door, the elephant-faced man said:
"Come, enter; the blessed Lord Heramba is pleased with you."
Then Sūryaprabha, having entered there with wonder,
sat down upon a surface of jyotīrasa stone that provided great comfort.
Resembling twelve suns, with a single tusk and the face of an elephant,
he has a protruding belly and three eyes, and holds a flaming axe and mallet.
Then he saw Vināyaka surrounded by hosts with the faces of various creatures; having prostrated at his feet, he paid him homage.
He too, delighted by the conqueror of obstacles, asked the reason for his arrival and said with affectionate words, "Ascend by this path."
Having mounted another chariot five yojanas long, Sūryaprabha saw another great gate made of ruby.
And not having gained entry even there, he,
with a single-minded heart, praised the god who wields the Pināka bow with a thousand names.
Then, having himself opened the door, that son of the prince,
who called himself Viśākha, spoke thus and led him inside.
And having entered, he saw there Skanda, possessing the brilliance of a blazing fire,
joined by his five sons who were like him, beginning with Śākha and Viśākha.
He was surrounded by millions of Gaṇeśas, who had bowed at his feet as soon as they were born, including those who were evil planets and those who were children.
When he was satisfied, the one born of the reeds (Kārttikeya) asked for the reason regarding the scripture,
and the path of ascent thereupon was pointed out to him.
In this manner, he [constructed] the other five jewel-gates in succession,
together with Bhairava, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, and Nandin.
Having passed through the successive gates guarded by Bhṛṅgin and his followers,
he reached the excellent crystal gate on the back of the mountain.
Then, praising the God of gods with devotion among the Rudras,
he was ushered in by one of them and beheld that abode of Śambhu, which surpassed even heaven.
It possessed winds carrying divine fragrances, trees always laden with flowers and fruit,
the music commenced by gandharvas, and the festive dances of apsarases.
There, upon a lion-throne made of crystal in one part,
he saw the three-eyed one, holding a trident in his hand, resembling clear crystal.
He has his tawny matted locks bound up and wears the beautiful crescent moon as a crest;
he is attended by the Blessed Lady Girijā standing at his side.
Filled with joy, Sūryaprabha beheld Maheśvara;
having approached, he fell at the feet of the Lord together with his consort.
Then, placing his hand on [his] back, the Blessed Lord Hara raised him up, seated him, and asked, "For what purpose have you come?"
"My consecration is imminent; therefore, I request your presence there, O Lord.
To him, Sūryaprabha replied:
Then Śambhu said to him: "In that case, why have you been so distressed?
Why, my son, was I not remembered for the sake of my presence right here?"
Having said, "Let it be so; I shall remain present," he, who is affectionate toward his devotees, summoned a certain Gaṇa standing nearby and commanded him.
"Go; lead him to Mount Ṛṣabha for the sake of his consecration, for that is the site of the great consecration for these universal monarchs."
Thus commanded by the Blessed One, that host circumambulated Īśāna and, bowing down, took Sūryaprabha onto their laps.
Having led him there, he established him on that Ṛṣabha mountain,
and by his own supernatural power, he vanished from that spot at that very moment.
And while Sūryaprabha remained there, his companions— Kāmacūḍāmaṇi and the others— arrived, along with their wives and the lords of the Vidyādharas.
The gods together with Indra, the asuras, the great ṛṣis beginning with Samaya,
Śrutaśarman, Sumeru, and that prince Suvāsaka.
And Sūryaprabha then honored them all as was appropriate;
and they, having been told the account of Rudra and the others, also congratulated him.
Then Prabhāsa and the others personally brought water from rivers, streams, oceans, and sacred fords, accompanied by various medicinal herbs, in jars made of jewels and gold.
At that moment, the Blessed Lord, the enemy of Tripura, arrived there accompanied by Gaurī,
his feet being saluted by gods, asuras, vidyādharas, kings, and great sages.

While all those gods, dānavas, and sky-dwellers resounded with the proclamation of "Auspicious Day," the sages consecrated Sūryaprabha with all the waters upon his lion throne in the sovereignty over the celestial beings.
The Asura Maya, composed of wisdom, being greatly delighted, bound upon him the turban and the crown;
and in the sky, accompanied by divine drums and preceded by the dances of excellent Apsarases, he sounded with musical instruments.
And that assembly of great seers, having consecrated her as Kāmacūḍāmaṇi,
appointed her as the appropriate Great Queen for Sūryaprabha.
Then, after the gods and asuras had departed, Sūryaprabha, the sovereign of the Vidyādharas, together with his kinsmen, friends, and companions,
celebrated a great consecration festival there.
After some days, having given half of his kingdom to Śrutaśarman as instructed by Hara,
he obtained other beloved wives and, together with his companions, long enjoyed the royal fortune of the sky-dwellers.
Thus, by the power of Hara’s grace, Sūryaprabha previously attained the status of a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas, even though he was a human being.
Having thus related this tale before the King of Vatsa, Vajraprabha, the foremost of the Vidyādharas, bowed to Naravāhanadatta and ascended into the sky.
And when he had departed, the hero Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by his queen Madanamañcukā,
remained in the palace of his father, the King of Vatsa, awaiting the attainment of the rank of Lord of the Vidyādharas.

Thus ends the seventh wave in the Sūryaprabha-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; and with this, the eighth lambaka, the Sūryaprabha-lambaka, is completed. Śrī.
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The ninth book, named Alaṃkāravatī.
This nectar of stories, it is said, was of old drawn forth from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the churning of the Mandara mountain of his love for the Daughter of the Mountain King.
Those who, having attained supernatural power through the removal of obstacles, forcibly savor [the nectar] and bear the burden of the gods upon this earth, do so by the grace of Bhava.
First Wave:
We pay homage to that Vināyaka, who, as he dances, causes even the mountains— dwarfed by the earth bent under the weight of Niśumbha— to bow down as if they themselves were prostrating.
Thus the son of the Lord of Vatsa, while dwelling in his father’s palace in Kauśāmbī,
was saluted at the very outset by the lords of the Vidyādharas.
Once, having gone out on a hunt, Naravāhanadatta,
accompanied by Gomukha and having dismissed his army, entered a vast forest.
There, his right eye throbbing, he was informed of the arrival of auspicious events;
he heard the sound of wailing mingled with the resonance of celestial lutes.
Having gone not very far along that path, he beheld a temple of Śiva consecrated by himself; and with his horses restrained, he entered it.
There he saw a celestial maiden playing the lute for the Lord of Gods,
surrounded by many excellent young women.
Beheld by him, she— whose cascading stream of radiance spread forth— suddenly agitated his heart,
like the form of the moon agitating the ocean.
She too, having gazed upon him with an eye that was fresh, tender, and charming,
became single-mindedly intent on him, forgetting her own natural grace and melody.
Then Gomukha, who knew the mind of Naravāhanadatta,
asked her companions, "Who is she, and whose daughter is she?"
And at that moment, a mature Vidyādharī, whose radiance was like gold and dawn, descended from the sky, resembling her in appearance.
Having descended, she sat down beside the maiden;
then the maiden also rose and fell at her feet.
"May you obtain as your husband, without obstacle, the sovereign lord of all Vidyādharas"—
thus did she, though mature, bestow this blessing upon the maiden.
Then Naravāhanadatta, having approached and bowed to that gentle Vidyādharī who had bestowed her blessing upon him, questioned her slowly.
"Mother, who is this maiden? Tell me, who is she?
Then that Vidyādharī said to him, "Listen, I shall tell you this."
On the mountain of Gaurī’s father, there is a city named Śrīsundarapura;
there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas known as Alaṃkāraśīla.
That king of noble virtues had a queen named Kāñcanaprabhā; and in due time, a son was born to him by her.
When Umā had prophesied in a dream, "He shall be devoted to the Dharma," his father then gave him the name Dharmashila.
When his son had gradually reached youth and was virtuous in character,
the king, having equipped him with the sciences, consecrated him as the crown prince.
Then, established in the position of crown prince, self-controlled, devoted solely to righteousness, and characterized by a virtuous nature, he delighted the subjects even more than his father had.
Then, Queen Kāñcanaprabhā, being pregnant with King Alaṃkāraśīla, gave birth to a daughter.
Then a divine voice proclaimed: "She shall become the daughter of Naravāhanadatta, the universal emperor, and his wife."
Then, having been given the name Alaṃkāravatī by her father,
that girl grew up in due course like the crescent of the moon.
In due time, having reached youth and acquired knowledge from her own father,
she prepared to wander with devotion through those various shrines of Śambhu.
At that time, his brother Dharmaśīla, though young and tranquil,
privately informed his father of his desire for the practice of adornment.
"Father, these pleasures, which perish in an instant, do not delight me;
for what is there in saṃsāra that is not ultimately bitter?"
And have you not likewise heard these words of the sage Vyāsa:
"All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall"?
"Unions end in separation, for life ends in death; therefore, my dear, what delight can there be for the wise in these transitory things?"
In the next world, neither enjoyments nor accumulations of wealth accompany one;
dharma alone is a kinsman, for it does not abandon one even for a single step.
Therefore, having gone to the forest, I shall practice supreme austerity,
so that I may attain that eternal, highest state.
When his son, who was virtuous by nature, had spoken thus, King Alaṃkāraśīla, deeply distressed and with eyes full of tears, then said to him:
"O son, what is this sudden delusion of mind in you who are still a child?
For it is when youth has been fully enjoyed that tranquility is desired by the virtuous."
For you, who have taken a wife and are righteously protecting the kingdom, this is the time to enjoy pleasures; it is not yet the time for dispassion.
Having heard these words of his father, Dharmaśīla replied again:
"In this matter, there is no restriction based on age regarding tranquility or its lack."
For even a child, if favored by the Lord, attains tranquility;
yet some base person, though old, does not reach peace.
I have no delight in sovereignty, nor in the possession of a wife;
this ascetic practice of propitiating Śiva is the very fruit of my life.
Seeing him speaking thus, who could not be turned back even by effort, his father Alaṃkāraśīla shed tears and spoke: SoKss_9,1.36 //
"If even you, my son, though young, possess such detachment as this, then I, who am old, have no [attachment]; shall I too take refuge in the forest?"
Having spoken thus, he went to the world of mortals and gave ten thousand loads of jewels and gold to poor brahmins.
Having returned to his own city, he said to his wife Kāñcanaprabhā:
"By my command, you must remain right here in your own city."
"O Alaṃkāravatī, this girl’s year is now complete;
there is an auspicious moment for her marriage on this very lunar day."
"I shall give her then to Naravāhanadatta;
he, as our son-in-law and a universal emperor (cakravartin), shall protect this city and us."
Having spoken thus, the king turned back his wife— who had sworn an oath— and,
together with his son, he retired to the forest while she, along with her children, continued to lament.
That virtuous wife, Kāñcanaprabhā, returned to her own city together with her daughter; for who indeed would transgress the command of her husband?
Then her daughter, Alaṃkāravatī, accompanied by her mother who followed out of affection,
wandered through many sacred shrines.
On one occasion, the knowledge known as Prajñapti said to her:
"Go yourself to the self-arisen sacred fields in Kaśmīra and worship them."
For you shall then obtain that husband Naravāhanadatta, the sole universal emperor of all the Vidyādhara lords, free from all obstacles.
Having been told this by Vidyā, Alaṃkāravatī went to Kaśmīra with her mother and worshipped Śambhu in those sacred fields.
In the field of Nandi, on Mount Mahādeva, on the Immortal Mountain (Amaraparvata), on the mountains of Sureśvarī, as well as in Vijaya and Kapaṭeśvara; SoKss_9,1.48 //
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Mountain-Daughter in these sacred fields and other places,
that daughter of the Vidyādhara king and her mother returned home.
"Know this maiden to be Alaṃkāravatī, O fortunate one;
and know me to be her mother, Kāñcanaprabhā."
And today she came to this temple of Śiva without even informing me;
therefore, having learned of it through the Prajñapti-vidyā, I have come here.
And from his very mouth I learned that you too have come here;
therefore, accept this daughter of mine, bestowed by the deity.
And in the morning, he was told by her father: "The day for the wedding has arrived;
therefore, my son, go today to Kauśāmbī, your own city."
And we two shall go from here; returning in the morning from the penance grove, that King Alaṃkāraśīla will himself give this daughter to you.
When she had spoken thus, both Alaṅkāravatī and Naravāhanadatta fell into a certain state of being.
Like two ruddy geese at the end of the day, whose eyes are filled with tears because they cannot endure even a single night's separation from one another, [the couple] drew near.
Seeing them both in such a state, Kāñcanaprabhā said:
"Why is there this lack of composure in you two at the separation of but a single night?"
The steadfast endure separation for a long time, even when its end is uncertain;
hear now the story of the noble Rāma and Queen Sītā.
King Daśaratha, the sovereign of Ayodhyā, had a son,
Rāma, who was formerly the eldest among Bharata, Śatrughna, and Lakṣmaṇa.
An emanation of Viṣṇu descended for the sake of destroying Rāvaṇa;
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and mistress of his life, became his wife.
By the decree of fate, he was sent to the forest by his father, who had transferred the sovereignty to Bharata,
together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
There, Rāvaṇa carried off his beloved Sītā by means of illusion,
and having slain Jaṭāyu on the way, he took her to the city of Laṅkā.
Then that Rama, separated from her, having won over Sugriva through the slaying of Valin and having dispatched Hanuman,
learned news of her.
Having gone to the ocean and built a bridge across it, and having slain Rāvaṇa,
he entrusted Laṅkā to Vibhīṣaṇa and brought back Sītā.
Then, while he was ruling the kingdom entrusted to Bharata from his forest retreat,
Sītā conceived a child in Ayodhyā.
Meanwhile, wandering at his own will with few attendants in order to observe the activities of the people there, the Lord saw a certain man.
Having seized his wife and casting her out from his own home, he [is censured] by the proclamation of her faults, saying, "She has gone to the house of another. (SoKs 9.1.67)
Sītā, though she dwelt in the house of a Rākṣasa, was not abandoned by Lord Rāma;
yet this man, who has gone to the home of his own kinsmen, abandons me—this is what makes him superior.
Thus King Rāma heard his wife speaking in that manner to her husband; distressed, he went into the inner apartments.
Fearing public reproach, he abandoned Sītā in the forest;
for a man of renown endures the suffering of separation rather than infamy.
And she, languid with pregnancy, by chance reached the hermitage of Vālmīki;
consoled by that seer, she was made to take up residence right there.
"Surely Sītā must be guilty; otherwise, how could she have been abandoned by her husband?
For it is from seeing her that this constant evil now transfers to us."
Out of compassion, Vālmīki banished her from the hermitage;
he thus dispelled the sin born of seeing her through his ascetic power.
"Therefore, let us go now to some other hermitage," so the other sages there deliberated at that time.
Having understood that, Vālmīki said to them, "O twice-born ones, there is no doubt in this matter; she has been seen by me through the power of my meditation to be pure."
Nevertheless, when they remained unconvinced, he then said:
"Venerable ones, purify me here in whatever manner you know to be right."
"Let the punishment of decapitation be carried out upon me for my impurity.
Hearing that, those sages there were moved with compassion and said:
In this great forest there is a sacred bathing place named Ṭīṭibhasaras;
for in ancient times, a certain female Ṭīṭibha bird was [abandoned] by her husband, who suspected her of being attached to another.
The virtuous woman, falsely defiled and left without refuge, cried out to the Earth and the World-Guardians; and for the sake of her purification, they were commissioned by them.
"Let this wife of Rāghava perform a purification for us there.
Having spoken thus, Jānaki went with them to that lake.
"If my mind has not turned toward anyone other than the Noble Son even in a dream, then, O Mother Earth, may I cross to the far shore of this lake!"
Having spoken thus, that virtuous woman entered the lake;
and the earth, having manifested itself, took her upon its lap and carried her to the other shore.
Then all those sages bowed down to that most virtuous woman,
and out of anger at her abandonment, they desired to curse Rāghava.
"You must not think inauspicious thoughts of my noble son;
you may curse me alone, O sinful ones—here is my salutation to you with joined palms."
Because that devoted wife Sītā thus restrained them,
those sages were pleased and bestowed upon her a blessing for sons.
Then, while staying there, she gave birth to a son in due time;
and that sage Vālmīki gave the name Lava to the infant.
Once, when she had gone to bathe taking the child with her, the sage saw that the hut was empty and thought: SoKss_9,1.87 //
"Having left the child behind, she has gone to bathe; where is that child?
Surely he has been carried off here by a beast of prey; therefore, I shall now create another."
Thinking, "Otherwise, Sītā will not maintain her life-breaths here after returning from her bath," he fashioned a sacred thread with *kuśa* grass and created a child.
The sage established him there in a manner similar to Lava;
and when Sītā arrived and saw the sage, she addressed him.
"This fool of mine stands here; how then could this other one exist, O Sage?
Having heard that, the Sage related what had occurred and said to her:
"O sinless one, you must accept this second son named Kuśa,
who was created by me with blades of kuśa grass through my own power."
Having been addressed thus by that sage, Sītā raised her two sons, Lava and Kuśa, there,
having performed for them the very same sacramental rites.
And even while they were still children, those two kṣatriya princes acquired the entire collection of divine weapons and all the sciences from the sage Vālmīki.
Once, having killed a deer from the hermitage,
they took its meat and made a plaything out of a clay image of Vālmīki.
Then that sage, distressed by this, being entreated by Queen Sītā,
prescribed such an expiation for those two princes.
"Let this Lava go to the lake of Kubera and fetch golden lotuses,
and let him quickly bring mandāra flowers from its garden."
"Let these two brothers both worship this linga;
by that means, this sin of theirs shall come to an end."
Upon hearing this, even though he was but a child, Lava went to Kailāsa;
he leapt onto the lake and the grove belonging to Kubera.
Having slain the yakṣas and taken the lotuses and flowers, he returned;
exhausted on the way, he rested at the foot of a tree.
In the meantime, while Rāma was searching for a man of auspicious marks for the human sacrifice,
Lakṣmaṇa came along that same path.
Having challenged Lava to battle and bewildered him with the *mohana* weapon,
he bound him according to the duty of a warrior and led him to the city of Ayodhyā.
And at that time, having comforted Sītā— who was distressed by the absence of Lava—
the wise Vālmīki spoke to Kuśa there in his own hermitage.
"Lava, my son, has been led away by Lakṣmaṇa after he had besieged Ayodhyā;
go and release him from that place once he has been conquered by these weapons."
Having spoken thus and been granted divine weapons by him, Kuśa then went and besieged the sacrificial ground at Ayodhyā, which was being defended by [Rāma].
There he also defeated Lakṣmaṇa, who had rushed forward for that purpose;
then Rāma approached him in battle with those great divine weapons.
Due to the power of Vālmīki, he was unable to conquer Kuśa with his missiles; therefore, with great effort, he asked him: "What is your purpose? Who are you?"
Then Kuśa said: "My elder brother was bound by Lakṣmaṇa and brought here;
I have come here for the purpose of releasing him."
"Janaki says that we two are Lavakuśa, the sons of Rama," he said,
and having spoken thus, he related their history.
Then Rāma, with tears in his eyes, having summoned both of them,
embraced them around the neck, saying, "I am that very same sinful Rāma."
Then, while the two heroes were praising Sītā and looking at those two children,
and while the citizens were gathered there, Rāma took hold of his two sons.
Then, having had Queen Sītā brought from the hermitage of Vālmīki,
he dwelt happily with her, having entrusted the burden of his responsibilities to his sons.
In this way, the steadfast endure such separation even for a long time;
why then, my two sons, can you two not endure it for even a single night?
Having spoken thus to Naravāhanadatta, who was eager to marry her daughter Alaṃkāravatī, Kāñcanaprabhā said:
Taking his daughter, Naravāhanadatta also departed through the air in the morning and went to Kauśāmbī, though he was despondent.
There, while he was sleepless at night, Gomukha spoke to him for his diversion:
"O King, listen; I shall relate to you this story of Pṛthvīrūpa."
There is a city named Pratiṣṭhāna in the southern region;
there lived a king of exceeding beauty, known by the name Pṛthvīrūpa.
Two ascetics, possessed of full knowledge, once approached him; beholding his wondrous form, they spoke thus to the king: SoKss_9,1.118 //
"O Lord, we two have wandered over the earth, yet we have never seen anywhere another man or woman who is equal to you in form. (SoKss_9.1.119)
However, on the island of Muktipura,
King Rūpadhara has a daughter named Rūpalatā, born of Queen Hemalatā.
This maiden is a match for you, and you alone are a match for her;
if a union were to take place between you two, it would be a great merit.
Thus, along with the words of the ascetic,
the arrows of Love entered through the path of his ears and lodged in the heart of that king.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa, filled with eagerness, commanded his own preeminent painter named Kumāridatta.
Taking my form as it has been duly painted upon the cloth,
go with these two monks to the island-city of Muktipura.
"There, by means of a stratagem, you must manifest my form to the king named Rūpadhara and likewise to his daughter, Rūpalatā."
See whether that king will give his daughter to me or not;
and having painted her, who is like a creeper of beauty, upon a canvas, you must bring her here.
Having spoken thus, the king sent that painter, along with the monks, to that island, having had his own form depicted upon a painted cloth.
Then those monks, the painters, set out by stages and reached a city named Patrapura on the shore of the ocean.
Then, having boarded a ship and traveled by way of the ocean path,
they reached that island of Muktipura in five days.
Thereupon, the painter went and hung his notice at the king’s gate, declaring:
"There is no other painter equal to me."
As soon as he learned of this, he was summoned by King Rūpadhara;
having entered the royal palace and bowed before him, he made this request:
"O Lord, having wandered the earth, I have not seen anyone equal to a painter.
Therefore, among gods, asuras, and mortals, whom shall I paint? Please command me."
Having heard that, the king summoned Rūpalatā before him and commanded him:
"Draw this daughter of mine and show it to her."
Then that painter, Kumāridatta, having painted a portrait of the princess exactly like her in appearance, showed it to her on a canvas.
Then King Rūpadhara, pleased and considering him to be wise,
questioned that painter with the desire to obtain him as a son-in-law.
"O Bhadra, you have wandered over the earth; tell me, if at any place you have seen a woman or even a man equal in beauty to my daughter."
Thus addressed by the king, that painter replied to him:
"I have never seen any woman or man equal to her."
"But there is a king in Pratiṣṭhāna named Pṛthvīrūpa;
he has been seen to be her equal, so if she were united with him, that would be excellent."
When he did not find a princess of equal form, then,
even though in the bloom of youth, he remained without a wife.
And as soon as I saw that king, so pleasing to the eye, O Lord,
I painted him correctly upon a cloth, out of curiosity for his form.
Having heard that, when the king asked, "Does that painting exist?",
the painter replied, "It exists," and showed him the canvas.
There, having seen that form of King Pṛthvīrūpa,
King Rūpadhara shook his head in wonder.
And he said: "We are blessed, for even we have seen this king here though only in a painting; homage to those who behold him in person! (SoKss 9.1.143)
Having heard these words of her father and having seen that king in the painting, Rūpalatā was filled with longing; she heard nothing else and saw nothing else.
Seeing his daughter thus deluded by Māra,
King Rūpadhara then spoke to that painter Kumāridatta.
There is no discrepancy between the painting and you, my daughter;
King Pṛthvīrūpa is a husband who is a perfect match for her.
Therefore, taking this painted cloth of my daughter, go today with haste and show it to King Pṛthvīrūpa, presenting my daughter to him.
And having related to him exactly what had occurred, if it pleases him,
then let him come here quickly to marry my daughter.
Having spoken thus and honored them with wealth, the king dismissed that painter, his own messenger, and the monk who had been staying with him.
Having gone there and crossed the ocean, those painters, messengers,
and mendicants all reached Pratiṣṭhāna, into the presence of King Pṛthvīrūpa.
Having presented a gift there, they reported to that king the message from Sarūpadhara regarding the task he had performed for him.
Then that painter showed her to the king—
his beloved Rūpalatā standing within the painting, whom Kumāridatta had given to him.
As the king gazed upon the lake of beauty that was her form, his vision became so submerged that he was unable to lift it up again.
For that king, chewing upon her who was composed of the flowing nectar of beauty,
did not reach satiety, his longing increasing ever more, like a cakora bird gazing at moonlight.
The venerable Creator spoke to that painter: "O friend, both the hand of the Creator by whom this form was fashioned and your own hand by which it has been painted are worthy of praise."
"I have accepted the word of that king who bears such a form:
'I shall go to the island-city of Muktipura and marry his daughter.'"
Having spoken thus and honored those painters and messenger-monks with wealth,
King Pṛthvīrūpa remained there gazing at the painted cloth.
Having spent that day in gardens and other such places, the king, afflicted by the pain of separation,
determined an auspicious moment and set out on his journey the following day.
He was accompanied by various elephants and horses, by vassal kings and princes,
by those envoys who bore his likeness, and by ascetics skilled in painting.
Mounting the royal elephant Maṅgalaghaṭa, the king traveled for several days and,
having reached the entrance of the Vindhya forest, stayed there in the evening.
On the second day, having mounted the elephant named Śatrumardana,
King Pṛthvīrūpa entered that forest.
Just as he was proceeding forward, he suddenly beheld his own vanguard army fleeing, yet turning back.
"What is this? he cried out in bewilderment; and at that very moment, the prince named Nirbhaya, mounted upon his elephant, approached him and addressed him thus: SoKss_9,1.163 //
A very large army of Bhills charged from before the gods;
in that battle, about fifty of our elephants were slain by those Bhills.
A thousand foot soldiers and three hundred horses,
along with two thousand of our own Bhilla warriors, were struck down.
For one Kabandha was seen in our army, and two in his;
consequently, our soldiers were broken, oppressed by his thunderbolt-like arrows.
Hearing that, King Pṛthvīrūpa, filled with rage,
rushed forward and struck down the army of the Bhillas, just as Arjuna did the Kauravas.
Then, while the other bandits were being slain by Nirbhaya and the others,
he severed the head of the Bhillas' army commander with a single broad-headed arrow.
With blood flowing from wounds inflicted by arrows, that elephant, the crusher of enemies,
resembled a mountain of collyrium with outpourings of mineral streams.
Then, when the entire army had returned after achieving victory and reassembled,
those Bhillas who remained after the slaughter fled and scattered in the ten directions.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa, having ceased his battle,
had his prowess extolled by the messenger Rūpadhara.
For the rest of his wounded army,
the victorious one stayed that day upon the shore of a lake in that very same forest region.
Then, having set out in the morning and traveling by stages,
the king reached that city of Patrapura situated on the shore of the ocean.
There I rested for one day, having been accorded appropriate hospitality by the local ruler named Udāracarita.
Having crossed the ocean in ships provided by him,
he reached that island of Muktipura in eight days.
Having understood that, the king, assuming his physical form, approached him with joy;
and those two monarchs met, embracing one another around the neck.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa entered that city together with him, as if being drunk in by the eyes of the city's women.
There, Queen Hemalatā and King Rūpadhara,
seeing that he was a suitable husband for their daughter, rejoiced.
Then King Pṛthvīrūpa remained there, honored by King Rūpadhara with courtly attentions appropriate for his own high status.
And on another day, when the auspicious moment had long been awaited, he joyfully took the hand of Rūpalatā upon ascending the altar at the appointed time.
As they beheld each other’s forms, the gaze of those two reached its full bloom, as if to say to their ears: "Truly, you have heard this before."
During the scattering of parched grain, the two of them, assuming human form, bestowed jewels in such a manner that he was regarded by the people as a mine of gems.
And when the marriage of his son was completed, he honored those ascetics who had performed the painting with garments and ornaments, and he honored all the others as well.
Then, staying in that city, King Pṛthvīrūpa,
together with his followers, partook of food and drink suitable for that island.
When the day had passed in dancing, singing, and other diversions, that king, filled with longing, entered at night the dwelling-chamber of Rūpalatā.
It was furnished with couches spread with jewels, adorned with jeweled pavements,
its expanse supported by jeweled pillars, and illuminated by jeweled lamps.
There, that youth enjoyed with her, who was like a creeper of beauty,
a festival of love-play at his will, multiplied by long-cherished desires.
Having fallen asleep from the exhaustion of lovemaking, he was awakened in the morning by bards and panegyrists chanting; having risen, he stood there like Indra in heaven.
Thus King Pṛthvīrūpa dwelt there for ten days on the island,
sporting with ever-new enjoyments provided by his father-in-law.
Then, on the eleventh day, joined by Rūpalatā and with the approval of the astrologers, the king set forth after performing the auspicious rites.
Accompanied by his father-in-law as far as the seashore, he,
together with his bride and his followers, boarded the ships.
Having crossed the ocean in eight days, when his forces had assembled on the shore and Udāracarita had reached the front, he went to Patrapura.
Having been thus entertained by that king and having rested there for some days, the lord of men, Pṛthvīrūpa, then departed from that place.
Having placed his beloved Rūpalatā upon the female elephant Jayamaṅgalā,
he himself mounted the elephant named Kalyāṇagiri.
Then, traveling by way of continuous stages, the king eventually reached his own city, Pratiṣṭhāna, where banners and flags were raised aloft.
There, upon seeing the creeper of his form, the women of the city instantly cast aside their pride in their own beauty, their eyes wide with wonder and unblinking.
Then, having entered the capital and celebrated a festival, King Pṛthvīrūpa gave villages and wealth to that painter.
And having honored those two ascetics with wealth as was appropriate, he likewise bestowed equal honors upon his vassals,
ministers, and princes.
Then that virtuous lord of the earth, accompanied by his beloved Rūpalatā, enjoyed the pleasures of the world of the living there.
Having told this story, the minister Gomukha,
eager for his master's pleasure, spoke again to the anxious Naravāhanadatta.
In this way, the wise endure both affliction and long separation;
how is it, O King, that you cannot endure even a single night?
"Tomorrow morning you shall indeed marry Alaṅkāravatī.
When Gomukha had spoken thus, someone who had arrived there at that very moment—
Marubhūti, the son of Yaugandharāyaṇa, said:
"Why do you not speak while remaining composed, having never experienced the torment of love?"
A man possesses fortitude, discernment, and even virtuous conduct only so long as he does not fall within the range of Kāma’s arrows.
Blessed are Sarasvatī, Skanda, and the Jina— these three in the world—
by whom Smara was cast away like a blade of grass caught at the edge of a cloth, having been shaken off.
Seeing Gomukha speaking thus in distress, Naravāhanadatta spoke to him in order to reassure him: SoKss_9,1.206 //
"Gomukha has spoken this appropriately to me for the sake of diversion;
for does one who is affectionate bestow words of praise upon the exhaustion of separation?"
Afflicted by separation, he was consoled by his kinsmen according to their ability;
beyond that, he knows only the god who possesses the peerless arrow.
Muttering such words and listening to various reports from his attendants,
Naravāhanadatta passed that night.
Then, having risen in the morning and performed his necessary duties,
he beheld a woman with a golden radiance descending from the sky.
She was accompanied by her husband Alaṃkāraśīla, her son Dharmaśīla,
and her own daughter Alaṃkāravatī.
And they all, having descended, approached his presence;
he greeted them and they greeted him, each as was appropriate.
And at that moment, thousands of other Vidyādharas, carrying loads of gold, jewels, and other treasures, descended there from the sky.
Having learned of this event, the King of Vatsa,
together with his ministers and his wife, arrived there, delighted by the excellence of his son.
Then, when the Lord of Vatsa had extended hospitality as was fitting,
King Alaṅkāraśīla spoke to him, bowing with affection.
"O King, this daughter of mine is Alaṅkāravatī;
as soon as she was born, she was thus prophesied by a voice arisen from the sky."
She is the wife of Naravāhanadatta, your son,
who shall become the future emperor (*cakravartin*) over all the lords of the Vidyādharas.
"Therefore, I give her to him, for today is an auspicious moment for their union;
it was for this purpose that I came here together with all of you."
Saying, "This is a great favor," the Lord of Vatsa rejoiced at these words of that King of the Vidyādharas.
Then, by the power of his own magic science, that lord of the Vidyādharas sprinkled the surface of the ground with water produced from the palm of his hand.
There arose an altar made of gold, covered with divine garments,
and an artificial chamber for the wedding festivities made of various jewels.
Then that virtuous King Alaṃkāraśīla said to Naravāhanadatta, "Arise! The auspicious hour has arrived; bathe."
Having led Alaṅkāravatī, who had bathed, was wearing her wedding ornaments,
and was dressed as a bride, to the altar, he joyfully gave his daughter to him in his mind.
At the scattering of parched grain into the fire, he, together with his son, bestowed thousands of loads of jewels, gold, garments, and ornaments, as well as celestial women, upon his daughter.
When the marriage was completed, having honored everyone and then taken his leave,
he departed with his wife and son just as he had come, like a cloud through the sky.
Then, seeing his son being thus attended by the prostrate kings of the sky-dwellers,
King Vatsarāja, like the sun about to rise, was filled with joy and extended that festival for a long time.

And that Naravāhanadatta, having obtained Alaṅkāravatī— who was delightful through her virtuous conduct and possessed of noble qualities— remained there as a connoisseur of her charms, just as a skilled poet remains devoted to the Goddess of Speech (Vāṇī), who is charming through her excellent meters and endowed with sublime attributes.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave:
Then the son of the Lord of Vatsa, united with Alaṃkāravatī, [set out].
There, in his father's house, Naravāhanadatta was with his new bride.
Delighted by the celestial dancing and singing of those female attendants,
he remained there enjoying the drinking hall together with his ministers.
And once, having come to him after being offered hospitality, his mother-in-law Kāñcanaprabhā, the mother of Alaṃkāravatī, spoke to him.
"Come to our home and behold that beautiful city of Pura;
take your delight there in the groves together with Alaṃkāravatī."
Having heard this and said "So be it," he informed his father; then, by his father's word, taking Vasantaka with him and accompanied by his wife and minister, [he departed].
Having ascended that excellent celestial chariot created by his mother-in-law through the power of her knowledge, he set out along the path of the sky.
Seated in his celestial chariot, looking down from the sky,
he beheld the earth as small as a mere patch of ground and the oceans as shallow as moats;
[and] together with his mother-in-law, his wife, and others, he gradually reached the Himalayas.
It resounded with the songs of kinnarīs and was made beautiful by the throngs of celestial nymphs.
Then, beholding many wonders there,
the youth Naravāhanadatta reached that city of Sundarapura.
It was adorned even on the Himavat with palaces made of gold and studded with jewels,
which created the illusion of being the peaks of Mount Sumeru.
Having descended from his celestial chariot, he entered that city,
which seemed to dance with its fluttering silken banners at the sight of its protector.
And having had the auspicious rites performed for him by his mother-in-law, he entered the royal capital accompanied by Alaṃkāravatī and his friend Vasantaka.
There, on that day, the virtuous man dwelt in his father-in-law’s house like a resident of heaven, enjoying divine pleasures produced by the power of his mother-in-law.
And on another day, her mother-in-law Kāñcanaprabhā said to him:
"In this city there is the Lord Svayambhū, the Master of Umā."
When seen or worshipped, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
there, the father of Alaṃkāravatī constructed a great park.
A sacred ford named Gaṅgāsaras, true to its name, has been brought down;
go there today to worship that deity and to enjoy yourselves.
Thus addressed by his mother-in-law, Naravāhanadatta went with his followers to Śarva’s garden, accompanied by Alaṅkāravatī.
It was lovely with trees whose trunks were of gold, delightful with branches of jewels, possessing clusters of pearls for flowers and coral for sprouts.
Having bathed there in the lake of the Gaṅgā and worshipped the Lord of Umā,
he wandered among the ponds with jeweled steps and golden lotuses.
On their delightful banks and in dwellings formed by wish-fulfilling creepers,
he sported together with Alaṃkāravatī and his retinue.
And there he delighted in divine drinking parties and music, as well as in clever jests made by Marubhūti out of his natural straightforwardness.
Thus Naravāhanadatta dwelt for a full month, sporting in the garden grounds through the assistance of his mother-in-law’s magical sciences.
Then, honored with garments and ornaments befitting a god, he,
together with his bride, his ministers, and Kāñcanaprabhā, [departed].
Accompanied by his followers and his bride, he arrived in that very celestial chariot at Kauśāmbī, providing a festival for the eyes of his father.
There, in the presence of Vāsavadattā and the King of Vatsa,
her mother Kāñcanaprabhā spoke to Alaṃkāravatī.
"You must never, out of jealousy or anger, cause suffering to your husband;
for separation born of such sin, my daughter, brings about intense remorse."
"Because my husband was previously made to suffer by me out of envy,
I am now consumed by remorse since he has departed for the forest."
Having spoken thus and embraced her, Kāñcanaprabhā, her eyes choked with tears, flew up into the sky and departed for her own city.
Then, when that day had passed, Naravāhanadatta, having performed his customary morning rites, remained there accompanied by his ministers.
As soon as she had entered the presence of Alaṃkāravatī, one of those wanton women, trembling with fear, said: "O Queen, protect me! Protect me! (SoKss 9.2.31)
"For this brahmin has come to kill me and stands outside;
out of fear of him, I have entered here, fleeing and seeking refuge."
"Do not fear; tell me what has happened. Who is this, and who seeks to kill you?
Thus questioned, she began to speak once more.
"O Lord, in this very city there was one named Aśokamālā,
born of a Kṣatriya father called Balasena."
Formerly, while I was still a maiden, I was requested by my father from a wealthy brahmin named Haṭhaśarman, who was greedy for my beauty.
"I do not desire this man of hideous form and terrible countenance as my husband;
I said to my father, 'I shall not be given to him in marriage.'"
Having heard that, Haṭhaśarman nevertheless performed a fast unto death at his father’s house until she was given to him by that man who feared her execution.
Then that twice-born man took me away to be married, even though I did not wish it;
and I, having abandoned him, went to another, the son of a kṣatriya.
Thus overcome by Haṭhaśarman through his arrogance regarding wealth and other means,
I, accompanied by that second Kṣatriya prince Dhanavat, took refuge [with him].
That man went there at night and set his house on fire with that fire;
then, having been released by him, I went to a third kṣatriya.
His house, too, was set on fire by that twice-born man at night;
consequently, I was abandoned by him as well and fell into a state of utter desolation.
Then, fearing that Haṭhaśarman, the twice-born, who was intent on killing her, would not let go of even a single step from her, she fled like a doe from a jackal.
Right here, I have taken refuge in the state of a maidservant to your servant, the powerful Prince Vīraśarman, who is a worthy protector.
Having learned of that, Haṭhaśarman— despondent due to his loss of hope for me, tormented by separation,
and reduced to mere skin and bone— was restrained.
O Queen, that prince Vīraśarman, who had set out here for my protection and to bind him, was restrained by me.
Today, by chance, seeing me gone out, that Haṭhaśarman, with sword drawn, has rushed from here in order to kill me. (SoKss 9.2.46)
Therefore, having fled here, I was admitted by the doorkeeper who was moist with compassion; she opened the door for me to enter, and I know that he remained outside.
When she had spoken thus,
Naravāhanadatta summoned that Brahmin Haṭhaśarman from his presence.
He saw him, distorted with rage, gazing at that garland of *aśoka* flowers with a blazing eye,
a curved knife in his hand, and the joints of his limbs trembling with fury.
And he said to him: "O base Brahmin, you kill women and you burn them as well;
for what purpose do you commit such sinful deeds by entering the houses of others?"
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "This woman is my lawful wife;
having abandoned me, she has gone elsewhere—how could I endure that?"
When he had spoken thus, Aśokamālā was distressed and then said to him:
"O world-protectors, tell me this: why [is this so] when you yourselves are witnesses?"
"Though unwilling, I was forcibly led here and married by him;
why did I not say then, 'I will not live in your house'? (SoKss 9.2.53)
When she had spoken thus, a divine voice there proclaimed:
"Just as this Aśokamālā speaks, so indeed is it true."
And she is not human; hear this truth concerning her:
there is a hero, a lord of the Vidyādharas named Aśokakara.
To that sonless man, by the power of fate, a single daughter was born;
named Aśokamālā, she grew up in her father’s house.
And she, being in the prime of youth and offered by him who sought a kinsman for her,
desired no husband at all due to her excessive pride in her own beauty.
Enraged by her persistence, her father gave her this curse:
"Go to the human state; and here, your name shall be your own."
And there, a deformed Brahmin will forcibly marry you;
having abandoned him out of fear of him, you will successively obtain three husbands.
Afflicted even by that, you will be taken as a slave;
though the prince is more powerful, he will not turn back at all.
And when he saw her and ran toward her, desiring to kill her, she fled;
she entered the royal palace, [thinking], "You shall be released from this curse."
Thus, that Vidyādharī Yaśokamālā, who was formerly cursed by her father,
has now been born here as a human being under that very same name.
"Now that he has been born, this end of the curse has arrived;
go now to his Vidyādhara abode, and staying there, she shall enter her own body."
Then, accompanied by her chosen husband, the Vidyādhara king named Abhiruci, she will enjoy herself, remembering the curse.
Having spoken thus, at that very moment she too, Aśokamālā, suddenly ceased speaking and fell to the ground lifeless.
And having seen her, Alaṃkāravatī, her eyes filled with tears,
while Naravāhanadatta stood by her side.
But that brahmin Haṭhaśarman, though overwhelmed by grief and blinded by passion, even as he lamented,
suddenly became one whose face blossomed with joy.
When asked by everyone, "What is this?", that brahmin said:
"I have remembered my former birth; listen as I tell it."
On the Himālaya mountain there is an excellent city named Madanapura;
there dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Pralambabhuja.
O Lord, a son named Sthūlabhuja was born to him;
and that noble prince gradually reached the prime of youth.
Then the lord of the Vidyādharas named Surabhivatsa himself came to his house with his daughter and spoke to that Pralambabhuja:
"This daughter named Surabhidattā has been given by me today to your grandson Sthūlabhuja; let that virtuous man take her as his wife."
Having heard that and immediately acting upon it, he, whose arms were long, summoned his own son and communicated this matter to him.
Then his son Sthūlabhuja said to him out of pride in his own beauty: "Father, I will not marry her; for she is merely mediocre in appearance. (SoKss_9,2.74)
"O son, why this excessive indignation? For she is of noble lineage and worthy of respect;
she was given by my father and accepted by me for your sake—do not act otherwise."
Though addressed thus again by his father, Sthūlabhuja did not do that which was commanded; thereupon, his father, filled with anger, cursed him.
Due to the fault of identifying with form, descend into the human realm by means of this [body];
and there you shall become deformed, with a hideous face.
Having forcibly obtained as your wife the one named Aśokamālā, who had fallen [from heaven] due to a curse,
you were abandoned by her against her will, and thus you have experienced the suffering of separation.
And for the sake of her who is attached to another, you— emaciated by grief and deluded by passion— will commit a sin such as setting fire to [her] and so forth.
Having been thus addressed with a curse, the virtuous Surabhidattā then, weeping, clung to the feet of that Pralambabhuja and entreated him.
"Grant me this same curse as well; let our destinies be equal.
Let not my husband alone suffer distress on account of my transgression."

When she had spoken thus, the long-armed one, being pleased, comforted that virtuous woman and declared this end to the curse for his son: "O lady of beautiful hips, when your son, having become a king, shall behold you with his own eyes while you are in the form of a mare, then he shall release you from this curse. (SoKss_9,2.82)
As soon as Aśokamālā’s release from the curse occurs, he too,
remembering his former birth, will be liberated from this curse.
Having regained his own body and remembering the curse, he will soon marry you here; free from egoism and united with you, he shall be happy.
Having been addressed thus by him, that virtuous woman somehow regained her composure;
and know me to be Sthūlabhuja, fallen here from my celestial state due to a curse.
"I have seen that this great suffering of men arises from the fault of egoism;
whether the unseen [result] is perceived or not, how could there be any well-being for those possessed by egoism?"
"Today that curse of mine has been exhausted," saying this and casting off that body,
Haṭhaśarman became a young Vidyādhara.
And having taken the body of Aśokamālā, he cast it into the Gaṅgā while remaining invisible through the power of his knowledge, out of compassion.
And with those waters brought forth by the power of his knowledge, he instantly and thoroughly washed that bedchamber of Alaṃkāravatī on all sides.
And having bowed to Naravāhanadatta, his future lord,
he flew up from there into the sky and departed to accomplish his own purpose.
Then, while everyone was filled with wonder, Gomukha, in the course of conversation, told this story connected with Anaṅgarati.
On this earth there was a city truly named Śūrapura;
there lived a king called Mahāvarāha, who was exceedingly haughty.
From the propitiation of the goddess Gaurī, a daughter named Anaṅgarati was born to that king— who had no other offspring— to his queen Padmarati.
In time, having reached the prime of youth and being proud of her beauty,
she did not desire any husband, even though kings were entreating her.
"He who is brave, handsome, and possesses excellent singular discernment—
to him I must give myself," she said with firm resolve.
Then four heroes arrived there from the southern region,
having heard the news and seeking him, for they were endowed with the very qualities he desired.
When they had been announced by the doorkeepers and had entered, King Mahāvarāha questioned them in the presence of Anaṅgarati.
"What is your name, whose are you, and what is your birth and consciousness?
Having heard these words of the king, one among them addressed him:
"I am a Śūdra named Pañcapaṭṭika; I possess knowledge, for I weave five pairs of cloth strips every day. (SoKss 9.2.99)
Of these, I give one to a brahmin and bestow the second upon the Supreme Lord; the third I keep for myself.
"If my fourth wife were to exist, I would give that [wealth] to her;
by selling my own bodily sustenance, I shall provide for her with the fifth."
Then the second one also declared: "I am known as Bhāṣājña;
I am a Vaiśya who understands the cries of all beasts and birds."
Then the third spoke: "I am a Kṣatriya named Khaḍgadhara; I shall be conquered by sword-fight alone, and not by any other means."
And the fourth said, "I am a preeminent brahmin named Jīvadatta;
by means of the lore obtained through the grace of Gaurī, I restore dead women to life."
When they had spoken thus, the remaining three— the Śūdra, the Vaiśya, and the Kṣatriya—
each praised their own form, heroism, and strength.
The Brahmin praised his strength and heroism, excluding his physical form;
then King Mahāvarāha spoke to his own steward.
"Take them all now and let them rest in your own home.
Having heard that, the steward said, "So be it," and led them into the house.
Then that king said to his daughter Anaṅgarati:
"My daughter, which of these four heroes is pleasing to you?"
Having heard this, Anaṅgarati then said to her father:
"O father, not one among these four is pleasing to me."
If a Śūdra and a weaver are made into one, what is the use of his qualities? And if a Vaiśya is the second, what is the use of his knowledge of birds and the like?
Being a Kṣatriya woman, how could I give myself to those two?
A third [husband] who is my equal in caste, a virtuous Kṣatriya, would be appropriate for me.
But he is a servant who lives by his labor, a poor man who sells his very life;
how could I, being the daughter of a lord of the earth, become his wife?
Even the fourth Brāhmaṇa, Jīvadatta, is not approved by me;
he is deformed, engaged in improper occupations, fallen, and devoid of the Vedas.
It is fitting that he should punish you; why indeed do you give me to him?
For you, my dear, are the king and protector of the dharma of the social classes and stages of life.
A king who is a hero in righteousness is praised more than one who is a hero with the sword;
a hero in righteousness would be the lord of thousands of heroes with the sword.
Having dismissed his daughter, who had spoken thus,
that king rose from her presence to attend to his bath and other duties.
And on the second day, those four heroes, having departed from the house of the steward, wandered through that city full of curiosity.
And at that moment, a rogue elephant named Padmakavala,
having broken its hitching post, emerged from the stable in a state of rut, crushing the people.
Seeing those heroes, that great elephant also rushed forward to slay them;
and they too, with weapons raised, ran toward him.
Then the Kṣatriya among them named Khaḍgadhara,
having warded off those other three, alone charged toward that elephant.
And with a single blow, as effortless as one would pluck a lotus stalk, he lopped off the trunk of that roaring elephant as it was extended forward.
Emerging from the midst of his foot and displaying his agility,
he delivered a second blow to the back of that elephant.
And with the third [arrow], he cut off both of his feet;
then, letting out a cry, the elephant fell down and died.
Seeing that prowess of his, all the people were amazed;
and King Mahāvarāha, having learned of it, was filled with wonder.
On another day, that king set out for the hunt mounted upon an elephant;
those four heroes, Khaḍgadhara and the others, also followed him.
There, while the king was slaying tigers, deer, and boars along with his army,
lions rushed forward in a rage upon hearing the trumpeting of the elephants.
Then, as a single lion was charging at him, he, wielding a sword,
cut it in two with a single stroke of his sharp blade.
And seizing the second one with his left hand,
he struck it against the ground and rendered the lion lifeless.
Bhāṣājña, Jīvadatta, and Pañcapaṭṭika likewise each struck a single lion upon the ground.
In this manner, as the king looked on,
many lions, tigers, and other beasts were slain with ease by those heroes moving on foot.
Then, filled with wonder and satisfaction after his hunt, that king entered his own city; those heroes also went to the house of the steward.
And that king, having entered the inner apartments, although exhausted,
had his daughter Anaṅgarati summoned to that very spot at that moment.
Having related to her, who was greatly amazed, the prowess of each one of those heroes as he had observed it during the hunt, he spoke to her.
