If both [the bridegroom and the groom] possess knowledge of the five treatises and the science of grammar, yet the Brahmin Jīvadatta is devoid of beauty and performs improper acts; SoKss_9,2.134.
What fault is there in that Kṣatriya, the wielder of the sword,
who is of perfect proportions and handsome form, and endowed with strength and prowess?
He who killed such an elephant and crushed it upon the ground, and who,
seizing lions by their feet, struck others down with his sword.
If it is argued that he is at fault because he is poor and a servant, [I reply:
in an instant I shall make him the Lord to be served by others. (SoKs 9.2.137)
"Choose a husband, daughter, if one pleases you," her father said to her; thus addressed by him, Anaṅgarati spoke to him.
"Therefore, once all those heroes have been brought here by you, let the astrologer be questioned for now; let us see what he says."
Thus addressed by her, the king summoned those heroes there and, with great persistence,
personally questioned the astrologer in their presence.
Behold, among these, with whom does she have mutual compatibility? And when will her auspicious moment for marriage occur?

Having heard that, and having been asked about the lunar mansions, that best of astrologers calculated for a long time and then addressed the king: SoKss_9,2.142: "Having heard that, and having been asked about the lunar mansions, that best of astrologers calculated for a long time and then addressed the king."
"If you will not be angry with me, O Lord, I shall clearly explain this:
there is not even a single point of compatibility between your daughter and these [suitors]."
"And there is no marriage for her here, because she has fallen here due to a curse;
she is a Vidyādharī, and that curse of hers will terminate after three months."
Therefore, let these people wait here for three months;
if she has not gone to her own world by then, this will come to pass.
All those heroes there placed their trust in these words of the astrologer and remained there for a period of three months.
When three months had passed, the king summoned those heroes, that astrologer,
and Anaṅgarati to his own presence.
Seeing that his daughter had suddenly become exceedingly beautiful, the king rejoiced,
while the astrologer considered her to have reached the proper time [for marriage].
"Now tell me what is appropriate, for those three months have indeed passed," thus the king questioned that calculator.
Then, remembering her own birth, Sānaṅgarati covered her face with her upper garment and abandoned that human body.
While the king himself was wondering, "How has she come to rest thus?
and was about to lift her veil, he beheld that she was dead.
With her bee-like eyes rolling back and her lotus-face discolored,
she was like a lotus plant struck by frost, deprived of the sweet sound of its swans.
Then, struck instantly by that thunderbolt of grief,
the king fell motionless upon the earth, fainting from the loss of his own wings.
Queen Padmarati also fell into a state of delusion and went [to the ground],
her ornaments and flowers fallen away, like a cluster of blossoms on a tree broken by an elephant.
While the attendants raised cries of lamentation and those heroes were in distress,
the king regained consciousness in an instant and spoke to Jīvadatta.
They have no power here; now let it be your turn.
You have promised: "I shall revive a woman who is dead."
"If you possess the power of knowledge, then restore my daughter to life;
once she has regained her life, O Brahmin, I shall give her to you alone."
Having heard these words of the king, Jīvadatta sprinkled the princess with consecrated waters and recited this noble verse: SoKss_9,2.158 //
O Cāmuṇḍā, who laughs with loud, piercing laughter, who is adorned with a garland of skulls, and who is difficult to behold; O Vikarālā, quickly grant me your assistance!
When, despite such efforts made by him, that young girl did not regain her life, Jīvadatta, despondent, then said:
"Even though the lore was bestowed upon me by Vindhyavāsinī, it has gone forth fruitless.
Therefore, what is the use of this life of mine, which is now a source of ridicule?"
Having said this, just as Jīvadatta proceeded to cut off his own head with a great sword, a voice arose from the sky:
"O Jīvadatta, do not act rashly; listen now!
This is a virtuous daughter of the Vidyādharas named Anaṅgaprabhā."
Having attained human form for this long a time due to the curse of her parents,
she has now abandoned this body and gone to her own world, having resumed her natural form.
Therefore, go once more to Vindhyavāsinī herself and propitiate her;
through her grace, you shall regain this virtuous Vidyādharī.
"And this place of divine enjoyment is not to be grieved for by the king, nor by you either.
Having spoken thus according to the truth, that divine voice ceased.
Then, having performed the consecration rites for his daughter, the king abandoned his grief;
and those other three heroes, along with their wives, departed as they had come.
Jīvadatta, having conceived hope, went to that goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains and propitiated her with ascetic penance; she, too, commanded him in a dream.
"I am pleased with you; arise and listen, for I shall tell you this:
there is a city named Vīrapura on the Snowy Mountain."
There lived a sovereign of the Vidyādharas named Samara;
by him, through Queen Anaṅgavatī, a daughter named Anaṅgaprabhā was born.
When she, arrogant with her beauty and youth, did not desire any husband,
then her parents, enraged by that most obstinate act, cursed her.
Go to the human realm; even there you will not obtain the happiness of a husband.
Like a sixteen-year-old maiden, having abandoned that body here, you shall depart.
"Your husband shall become a mortal and deformed, yet he will be one perfected in the sword;
having fallen into the state of a mortal due to a curse arising from his desire for a sage’s daughter."
Even though you do not wish it, he will lead you to the world of mortals;
there, a separation from him will occur for you, as you have been led elsewhere.
In a previous birth, he indeed abducted eight wives belonging to others;
therefore, he will experience suffering worthy of being endured for eight lifetimes.
And in this single birth, you— though made a human being— will experience suffering through the loss of your sciences, as if they were births lost in previous lives.
For association with anyone who is most wicked indeed brings a share of that person's sin;
yet, for women, union with a sinful husband brings an equal share of sin.
Having lost your memory, you shall obtain many human husbands here,
because you harbored a stubborn attachment born of hatred toward the husband chosen by you.
"That celestial being Madanaprabha who entreated you,
having become a human king, shall at the end be your husband."
Then, released from the curse, you will return to your own world and regain that very husband who is worthy of you, though he has become a sky-dweller.
Thus, having been cursed by her father and become Anaṅgarati on earth,
she has today returned to the presence of her parents and become Anaṅgaprabhā once again.
Therefore, having gone to Vīrapura and defeated her father in battle—
even though he is a man of noble lineage and well-protected— win her back.
"Take this sword, by which, held in your hand,
you shall have the power to move through the sky and shall become invincible."
Having spoken thus and surrendered her sword, the goddess vanished from his sight;
and he awoke and beheld the divine sword lying in his hand.
Then, having risen with a joyful heart, Jīvadatta bowed to the Mother;
all the exhaustion of his ascetic toil was stilled by being nourished with the nectar of her grace.
With sword in hand, he leaped into the sky and, after circling the Himalayas,
reached that battle where the lord of the sky-dwellers stood at Vīrapura.
Having married that Anaṅgaprabhā, who was bestowed upon him there by the victor in battle, he enjoyed divine excellence in sensual pleasure.
Having stayed there for some time, Jīvadatta spoke thus to his father-in-law Samara and to his beloved Anaṅgaprabhā.
"Let us go to the world of men; I am longing for it, for even a lowly birthplace is most dear to living beings. (SoKss 9.2.189)
Having heard these words of his, the father-in-law consented;
but Anaṅgaprabhā, understanding the situation, reluctantly gave her permission.
Then Jīvadatta, together with that Anaṅgaprabhā whom he held in his embrace, descended from the sky to the world of mortals.
Seeing a single beautiful mountain there, Anaṅgaprabhā said to him, "I am weary; let us rest here quickly."
Then, saying "So be it," he descended right there with her and,
through the power of those various vidyās, partook of food, drink, and other necessities.
Then, impelled by destiny, Jīvadatta said to Anaṅgaprabhā:
"My dear, please sing something sweet for me."
Having heard that, she began with devotion a hymn of praise to Dhūrjaṭi;
then, by the sound of that singing, the brahmin fell asleep.
Meanwhile, a king named Harivara, exhausted from hunting and longing for the water of a mountain stream, reportedly arrived by that very path.
Drawn by that sound of singing which he heard, like a deer,
he abandoned his chariot and rushed there all alone.
Having previously been foretold by auspicious omens, that king beheld Anaṅgaprabhā,
who was truly like the radiance of the God of Love himself.
Then, by means of her song and form, she brought him to a state of agitation;
Madana pierced his heart at will with his arrows.
Seeing that fortunate man, Anaṅgaprabhā suddenly fell within the range of the Flower-Bowed God's influence and reflected for a moment:
"Who is this? What is this one whose flower-bow has been cast aside? Is it the Mind-born [God of Love], or is it the embodied grace of Śarva, who is pleased by my song?"
Having reflected thus, she, infatuated by passion, asked him:
"Who are you, and how have you come to this forest? Please tell me."
Then he related everything to her exactly as it had happened;
the king then asked her, "Who are you, O beautiful one? Tell me."
And when he asked her, "O lotus-faced one, who is this person lying here asleep?",
she replied to him briefly:
"I am a Vidyādharī, and this man here is my husband, who has attained mastery over the sword;
as soon as I saw you, I have now become filled with love for you."
Therefore, come, let us go quickly to your city;
before he awakens, I shall explain it to you in detail there.
Having heard these words and assenting with "So be it," King Harivara experienced a joy equal to the attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds.
"Taking this king upon my lap, I shall fly up into the sky with speed," thus Anaṅgaprabhā thought within herself in great haste.
And at that moment, she lost her magic power through that betrayal of her husband;
remembering her father’s curse, she suddenly fell into despair.
Having seen that and asked the reason, the king said to her:
"This is not the time for despondency; this husband of yours will wake up."
"O beloved, you ought not to grieve over this matter which is dependent on fate;
for who can overstep the shadow of their own head or the course of destiny?"
Saying, "Come, let us go," that best of monkeys, the king of the Cakras, whose words she trusted, quickly took Anaṅgaprabhā onto his lap.
Then, as delighted as if he had found a treasure, the king went swiftly from there and,
cheered by his attendants, mounted his own chariot.
Mounted upon that delightful chariot, which moved as swiftly as thought, he reached his own city, bestowing joy upon the people.
Then King Harivara, together with that Anaṅgaprabhā, dwelt in divine bliss upon that mountain marked with his own name.
Anaṅgaprabhā also remained right there, enamored of him;
deluded by the curse, she had forgotten her entire innate power.
In the meantime, on that mountain, Jīvadatta not only woke up, but he did not see Anaṅgaprabhā, nor even his own sword.
"Where is that Anaṅgaprabhā? Alas! Where is that sword as well?
Has she gone away having stolen it, or have both of them been carried off by someone?"
Thus, bewildered and producing many discursive thoughts for three days,
he searched that mountain while being consumed by the fire of passion.
Then, descending and searching through the forests for ten days,
he wandered about, yet he did not see even a footprint of hers anywhere.
"Alas, O cruel Fate! Why was my beloved Anaṅgaprabhā, though given to me with great difficulty, snatched away by you along with the power of the sword?"
Lamenting thus, fasting, and wandering, he eventually reached a certain village; there he entered a wealthy house belonging to a brahmin.
There, his fortunate wife, named Priyadattā, dressed in fine garments, seated him upon a throne and quickly commanded her own maidservants.
"Quickly wash the feet of Jīvadatta,
for today is the thirteenth day of his fasting due to separation."
Having heard that, Jīvadatta was astonished and reflected within himself:
"Has Anaṅgaprabhā arrived here? Or is she perhaps a yoginī?"
Reflecting thus, having washed his feet and consumed the food she had given him,
he bowed down and, out of great distress, questioned Priyadattā.
"Tell me one thing, O blameless lady: how do you know my history?
And tell me this second thing as well: where have my two beloved swords gone?"
Having heard that, the devoted wife Priyadattā said to him:
"No one other than my husband sets foot in my heart, even in a dream."
I regard other men as equal to my own sons and brothers;
and never does a guest depart from my house without having been honored.
By its power, I know the past, the present, and the future;
and that Anaṅgaprabhā has been taken away by your king Harivara.
While you were asleep, by the power of destiny, he who dwelt in the city named after himself approached along that path, drawn by your song.
And she cannot be won by you through force, for that king is possessed of great power;
moreover, having abandoned him, that unchaste woman will go elsewhere.
And the goddess gave him a sword; having performed the rites for its acquisition, when she was carried off, he went into the very presence of the goddess because of his divine nature.
Furthermore, O Queen, how have you forgotten that which was foretold to you in a dream during the description of the curse of Anaṅgaprabhā?
Therefore, why do you harbor this futile delusion regarding what is destined to be?
Abandon this pursuit of evil, which brings such intense suffering again and again.
Or what use have you now for that sinful woman who was once devoted to you,
O brother, but has become a human being and lost her magical powers through her malice toward you?
Thus addressed by that virtuous woman, Jīvadatta— having abandoned his longing for Anaṅgaprabhā and having turned his soul away from her fickleness— spoke to her.
"O Mother, by your truthful words my delusion has been stilled;
for who indeed would not find that association with you leads to their own welfare?"
"This suffering has befallen me due to the power of past sins;
therefore, casting aside all envy, I shall go to sacred fords (tīrthas) to wash them away."
"What need have I for enmity with others on account of Anaṅgaprabhā?
For by one who has conquered anger, this entire world is conquered."
While he was still speaking thus, the virtuous husband of Priyadattā, who was fond of guests, arrived at her house.
Having been made to abandon his sorrow there by that king who had offered him hospitality,
he rested and then set out on a pilgrimage after taking leave of them both.
Then, subsisting on roots and fruits, he wandered in due course over all the sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the earth, enduring the hardships of many wildernesses.
And that deluded seeker went to that very goddess Vindhyavāsinī;
there he performed intense penance, fasting and lying upon a bed of kusha grass.
And Ambikā, pleased by his asceticism, spoke thus to him in person:
"Arise, my son; for you four are indeed my own attendants."
The three [deities] are Pañcamūla, Caturvaktra, and Mahodaramukha;
you are the fourth, known as Vikaṭavadana, the supreme sequence.
Once, you all went to the sandy bank of the Gaṅgā to sport;
there, you saw a certain daughter of a sage bathing.
Cāpalekhā, the daughter of the sage named Kapilajaṭa,
was sought in marriage by all of you, who were overcome with passion for her.
When she said, "I am a maiden; let me go," those other three remained silent, but she was seized by the arm by force.
And she cried out, "O father! O father! Save me!
Hearing that, the enraged sage who was nearby came there.
Seeing him, she was released by you; thereupon he cursed you all, saying:
"O most wicked ones, may you all enter a human womb at that very moment!"
Then, being entreated, that sage declared to you the end of the curse thus:
"When the princess Anaṅgaprabhā is sought after by you."
They will go to the world of the Vidyādharas, and then these three shall be liberated;
however, you, having obtained her once she has become a Vidyādharī, will cause her to be lost again.
Then, O you of hideous countenance, you shall encounter great calamity;
and after propitiating the Goddess for a long time, you will be released from this curse.
"Since you have touched the hand of this woman, who is like a streak of wantonness,
you possess much sin arising from the theft of another's wife."
Thus, you who were my attendants and were cursed by that great seer,
have now been born as four preeminent heroes in the southern region.
Those two who were the commanders of the five companies, and he who was the bearer of the sword—
those three were your friends, and you, Jīvadattaka, were the fourth.
And those three, having departed for their own abode while Anaṅgarati was traveling,
returned here and were released from the curse by my grace.
"I have been propitiated by you today, and the end of your curse has arrived.
Therefore, having taken up this *dhāraṇī* of Agni, cast off your body."
"O burn away that sin which would have been experienced over eight lifetimes by this single [act]!
Having said this and bestowed the dhāraṇā, the Goddess vanished from his sight.
Having burned away his mortal body and his sin through that very concentration (dhāraṇā),
Jīvadatta was finally released from the curse and became an eminent Gaṇa.
Alas! Even for the gods, such is the affliction arising from union with another's wife; what then will be the fate of others because of it?
And at that time, in that city of Harivara, Sānaṅgaprabhā attained the position of chief among the women of King Harivara’s harem.
And that king remained day and night with his mind one-pointedly fixed upon him,
having entrusted the great burden of the kingdom to his minister named Sumantra.
Once, a new dance master named Labdhavara came from the Middle Country into the presence of that king.
Having observed his skill in instrumental music and dance,
that king honored him and appointed him as the master of dance for the women of the inner apartments.
By him, Anaṅgaprabhā was brought to such excellence in dancing that even while she was dancing, she became an object of envy for her co-wives.
And then, due to living together with him and her delight in the practice of dance,
that Anaṅgaprabhā became enamored of the master of dramatic arts.
And behold! Drawn by her beauty and her dancing, even that master of the dramatic art slowly began to dance something else entirely out of desire.
And once, in a secluded dance hall, that Anaṅgaprabhā,
longing for sexual union, approached that master of dance by force.
And at the end of their union, she, filled with intense passion, said to him:
"Without you, I shall not be able to endure remaining even for a moment."
"King Harivara, having learned of this, will certainly not tolerate it;
therefore come, let us go elsewhere where the king does not know."
"You possess wealth such as gold, horses, and camels, which was given to you by the king who was pleased with your dance; and I possess my own ornaments."
"Let us go there quickly; we shall stay where we are free from fear.
Delighted, the dance master approved those words of his.
Then, having assumed the dress of a man, Anaṅgaprabhā went to the house of a dance teacher together with a single very affectionate female servant.
Then she set out on horseback together with him, who was seeking wealth and had placed it upon the back of a camel, and who was a teacher of dance.
Having first abandoned the fortune of the Vidyādharas and then the royal splendor, she took refuge in the supernatural power of a Cāraṇa; fie upon the fickle mind of women!
And having gone with that master of dance,
Anaṅgaprabhā reached a distant city named Viyogapura.
There she remained happily with him, and he too,
the leader of the actors, considered his own name "Attainer-of-the-Blessing" to be truly realized through her.
And when King Harivara learned that his beloved Anaṅgaprabhā had gone away somewhere, he became intent on abandoning his body out of grief.
Then the minister Sumantra spoke to the king, comforting him:
"O Lord, what is it that you do not know? Consider that for yourself."
O Lord, having abandoned her husband Khaḍgavidyādhara as soon as she saw you,
how could there be any constancy in her even toward you?
Taking up some small trifle, she departed, indifferent to the excellent object,
like one who, out of a fondness for the sight of grass, mistakes a blade of grass for a jewel.
"She has surely been taken away by the master of dance, for he is not to be seen;
and it was heard that the two of them were staying in the music hall this morning."
Therefore, O King, tell me: why do you persist in this attachment even though you know her nature?
For a wanton woman is like the twilight, momentarily passionate toward everyone.
Having been addressed thus by the minister, the king then fell into reflection and thought: "Aha! Truly has this been said to me by this wise man."
For a courtesan is indeed like the condition of worldly existence: ultimately devoid of charm, miserable, changing at every moment, and characterized by impermanent associations.
A wise man does not fall into women or into rivers that plunge one down, which display their waves even as they drown what has fallen into them.
Those who are unperturbed in calamities, free from pride even in prosperity, and undaunted in their duties—they are the steadfast; by them the world is conquered.
Having reflected thus and abandoned his grief at the word of his minister,
King Harivara established contentment with his own wife alone.
That Anaṅgaprabhā also remained for some time in that city named Viyogapura, accompanied by her dance teacher.
Just then, by fate, that teacher of dance also formed an association there with a young gambler named Sudarśana.
Thereupon, Sudarśana, having lost his entire fortune at dice, was soon appointed by him as a master of dance in the presence of Anaṅgaprabhā.
Then Anaṅgaprabhā, as if devoid of splendor due to his anger,
abandoned him and forcibly took Sudarśana alone as her husband.
Then that teacher of dance, having lost his wife and wealth and being without shelter,
went to the bank of the Gaṅgā with matted hair tied up out of world-weariness to practice asceticism.
That Anaṅgaprabhā, having united with that gambler Sudarśana,
remained right there, ever-newly enamored.
And once, while his wife was away, that Sudarśana entered [his home] at night and had all his possessions stolen by thieves.
Then, seeing Anaṅgaprabhā distressed and full of regret due to her lack of wealth, Sudarśana said this to her:
"I have a wealthy friend named Hiraṇyagupta;
come today, let us seek some debt from him."
Having spoken thus, his mind struck by fate,
he went with her and begged that preeminent merchant, Hiraṇyagupta, for a debt.
And when he saw Anaṅgaprabhā, and she saw him as well,
both of them then became filled with mutual longing.
And that merchant spoke thus with respect to Sudarśana:
"I shall give you gold tomorrow morning; for now, let it be eaten right here today."
Having heard that and perceiving a different state of mind in those two, Sudarśana said: "I am not fit for food today."
Then the merchant leader said: "In that case, my friend, let your wife eat first among us, for she has come to our home."
Having been addressed thus by him, even though he was a gambler, he became silent; and the merchant, accompanied by Anaṅgaprabhā, went into his inner apartments.
There, in that circle, he experienced the satisfaction of food, drink, and other pleasures together with her,
who had appeared unexpectedly and was radiant with the playfulness of intoxication.
Sudarśana,
standing outside while waiting for her departure, was then addressed by her servants who had been incited by her.
Having eaten, she went home; as she was departing, you did not see her. Why do you still remain here? You should go.
Remaining inside, saying, "I will not come out,
nor shall I go," he was driven away by those servants after they had struck him with blows from their feet.
Then Sudarśana, having gone there, reflected in his distress:
"How is it that my wife has been carried off by this merchant, even though he was my friend?"
"Is it that the fruit of my own evil deed has come upon me right here, such that what was done by me for another has been done to me by another? ||| SoKss_9,2.311 |||
"Why am I angry with another for that? That which deserves my anger is my own karma;
I shall cut that away so that there may be no further defeat for me."
Having reflected thus, the gambler abandoned his anger, went to Badarikāśrama,
and there performed ascetic penance that cuts through worldly existence.
And having obtained that beloved merchant as her husband, who surpassed all in beauty,
Anaṅgaprabhā took her delight with him, like a female bee that has moved from flower to flower.
Gradually, she became the mistress— possessed of deep affection even for his life as well as his wealth— of that merchant of vast fortune.
And King Vīrabāhu, although he learned that Ekasundarī was staying there, did not carry her off, as he protected the boundaries of righteousness.
And through those daily expenditures, he became a merchant whose wealth was diminishing;
for prosperity withers like a noblewoman in a household presided over by a harlot.
Then, having gathered his wares, that merchant Hiraṇyagupta set out for trade toward the island known as Suvarṇabhūmi.
And out of fear of separation, taking Anaṅgaprabhā with him,
he traveled along the road and eventually reached the city of Sāgarapura.
There, in a city near the ocean, he met a certain chief of fishermen named Sāgaravīra, who was a resident of that place.
Then, having gone to the shore of the ocean together with that sea-farer, he,
accompanied by his beloved, boarded the vessel offered to him.
Then,
as that merchant Sāgaravīra traveled upon the ocean by means of his ship, some days passed.
One day, a fierce dark cloud, resembling the time of universal destruction and terrifying with its lightning-eyes, arrived.
Struck by a powerful wind with thick, torrential rain,
the ship then began to sink amidst the waves.
While his attendants raised cries of lamentation as if for their own cherished desires,
and while the ship was sinking, he fastened his upper garment around his waist.
The merchant Hiranyagupta, not seeing the face of Anaṅgaprabhā, cried out, "Alas, my beloved! Where are you? and threw himself into the ocean.
Having gone forth with his arms outstretched, he reached by chance a certain merchant vessel; seizing it, he climbed aboard.
Then Anaṅgaprabhā was instantly hoisted by that Sāgaravīra onto a pile of planks bound together with ropes.
Having himself climbed up right there, he comforted her as she was terrified;
swimming across the ocean, he went along splashing the water with his arms.
In an instant, when the ship was shattered, the sky became cloudless;
the ocean became as still as the Sage whose anger had been pacified.
Having boarded the ship propelled by the wind, that merchant Hiraṇyagupta then reached the shore of the ocean after five days, by the power of fate.
Then, having descended to the bank, he was distressed by the pain of separation from his beloved;
and he realized that the workings of destiny were beyond remedy.
Having slowly returned to his own city, Hiraṇyagupta, firm in his resolve, maintained his fortitude; having acquired wealth once again, he lived in perfect contentment.
But that Anaṅgaprabhā, seated upon a plank,
was brought by that Sāgaravīra to the shore of the ocean in a single day— how wonderful!
There, having been comforted by that lord of merchants, she was led by him to his own residence,
the city named Sāgarapura.
There, he beheld a hero who possessed a splendor equal to that of Rājasena, who had bestowed his life upon him,
who was in the prime of youth, handsome, and obedient to his commands.
Anangaprabha chose that very fisherman as her husband;
for a woman whose conduct is unshakable does not look toward the ups and downs of life.
Then she lived with that fisherman chief in his house,
enjoying the prosperity bestowed upon her by him.
Once, from the top of that palace, she saw by way of that street a handsome young son of a kṣatriya named Vijayavarman passing along.
Lusting after his beauty, she descended, approached him, and said:
"Love me, your devoted one, for my heart has been captivated by the sight of you."
And he, having rejoiced and being thrilled, took her— who was like one fallen from the sky—
and went to his own home with her, who was the most beautiful woman in the three worlds.
Then Sāgaravīra, having learned that his beloved had gone somewhere,
abandoned everything and, intending to cast off his body, went to the celestial river through ascetic penance.
How could it be that he did not experience such suffering when he went there?
Where is the state of being a fisherman, and where is union with such a Vidyādharī?
And that Anaṅgaprabhā remained right there in that city with Vijayavarman, living at ease and without restraint.
Then once,
King Sāgaravarman, having mounted his female elephant, went out from there to wander through the city.
Beholding that city he had built and named after his own name,
the king traveled by that same path to where the house of Vijayavarman was located.
And having learned that the king was approaching, out of curiosity to see him,
Anaṅgaprabhā then ascended to the roof of the palace.
As soon as she saw the king, she fell under his power;
thus, she spoke impetuously to the elephant-driver seated upon the royal elephant:
"O elephant-rider, I have never mounted an elephant before;
therefore, let me mount here and see how much pleasure there is. (SoKss 9.2.349)
Having heard that while the driver was looking at the king’s face,
the king beheld her, like the splendor of the moon fallen from the sky.
And drinking her in with an insatiable eye like a cakora bird,
the king, his hopes fixed upon regaining her, said to the elephant-driver:
"Bring the female elephant near and fulfill her desire;
place this moon-faced woman upon it without delay."
When the king had spoken thus, that elephant-keeper brought the female elephant there at that very moment, beneath the palace.
Seeing that she had come near King Sāgaravarman,
Anaṅgaprabhā threw herself onto his lap.
Where did that hatred for her husband first arise, and what is this insatiability toward husbands?
Alas! By her father’s curse, a most perverse reversal has been revealed.
As if terrified of falling, she clasped the king by the neck;
his limbs drenched by the nectar of her touch, he too attained supreme joy.
Having taken her— who had surrendered herself through reasoning and was longing for a kiss—
he, the king, departed quickly for his own palace.
Thereupon, having brought that celestial woman— who had related her story—
into his inner apartments, the king made her his chief queen at that very moment.
Having realized that she had been carried off by the king,
Vijayavarman then approached the royal guards outside and fought them, as one warrior might face another.
And there in battle, he cast off his body without turning his back;
for heroes do not endure defeat on account of a woman.
"What is the use of this wretched woman to you? Enjoy us instead, O Nandin!"—as if thus entreated by the celestial women, he was led back to the abode of the gods.
And Anaṅgaprabhā, like a river finding its steadiness in the ocean, fixed her steadfastness upon that king Sāgaravarman, never turning to another.
By the power of destiny, she considered her purpose fulfilled through him as her husband;
he too believed that the fruit of his birth had been attained by her as his wife.
And after some days, that Queen Anaṅgaprabhā conceived a child by King Sāgaravarman, and in due time she gave birth to a son.
Having performed the grand festival for the birth of his noble son, the king, his father, gave that infant the name Samudravarman.
And when he had gradually attained growth, possessed of virtues, and reached youth,
the king consecrated that son, who was endowed with powerful arms, as the crown prince.
Then, for the sake of his son Samaravarman’s marriage,
he brought home the king’s daughter named Kamalavatī.
And that king, won over by his virtues, bestowed his own kingdom upon his son Samudravarman, who had already been married.
Having obtained that kingdom, the energetic Samudravarman, who knew the dharma of the kṣatriyas, bowed down to his father and addressed him thus:
"Grant me leave, father; I am going forth to conquer the quarters.
A lord of the earth who does not desire conquest is as contemptible as a eunuch is to a woman."
For kings in this world, that prosperity which is acquired by conquering foreign kingdoms through the strength of one's own arms is righteous and brings renown.
O Father, what sovereignty can those base men possess who exist only for the sake of oppression?
Like greedy cats, they devour their own offspring.
When he had spoken thus, he was told by his father Sāgaravarman: "Son, your kingdom is new; therefore, for the time being, you must govern it."
For one who rules his subjects with righteousness, there is neither demerit nor ill-repute;
and for kings, it is not fitting to engage in conflict without first considering their own power.
"My child, although you are a hero and your army is vast, nevertheless there can be no certainty at all; for the glory of victory in battle is fickle."
Although addressed with these and other words by his father,
the resplendent Samudravarman took leave of him with great effort and departed with the desire to conquer the quarters.
And having gradually conquered the directions and brought the kings under his control,
he returned to his own city, having obtained elephants, horses, gold, and other riches.
There, bowing down before his parents who were deeply gratified, he honored their feet with great jewels originating from various lands.
And by his command, that one of great renown bestowed upon the brahmins great gifts consisting of elephants, horses, gold, and jewels.
Then he rained down wealth upon those who sought it and upon his servants;
so that here, the single word "poor" remained devoid of its actual meaning.
Having witnessed that greatness of his son and his own state of having accomplished all that was to be done,
King Sāgaravarman, united with Anaṅgaprabhā, felt he had achieved his purpose.
Having passed those days in celebration, the king spoke to his son Samudravarman in the presence of his ministers:
"O son, that which was to be done by me has been accomplished in this birth:
the happiness of sovereignty has been enjoyed, and no defeat from enemies has been seen."
"You have been seen with your empire attained; what else remains for me to obtain?
Therefore, as long as this body of mine endures, I shall resort to a sacred ford (tīrtha)."
"Look! This old age whispers into my very ear as if to say: 'While this body is perishable, why do you still remain at home?'"
Having spoken thus, although his son was unwilling, the virtuous King Sāgaravarman then departed for Prayāga together with his beloved wife.
Having followed his father and returned to his own city,
Samudravarman ruled that kingdom according to the prescribed law.
King Sāgaravarman, accompanied by Anaṅgaprabhā,
gratified the bull-bannered god at Prayāga through his ascetic penance.
At the end of the night, the Enemy of Tripura spoke thus to him in a dream:
"I am pleased with you and your wife because of your asceticism; therefore, hear this."
"This Anaṅgaprabhā and you—both of you are Vidyādharas;
at dawn, my son, you shall both go to your own world upon the expiration of the curse."
Having heard that, the king and Aṅgaprabhā woke up;
having seen such a dream, they then spoke to one another.
Then, filled with joy, Anaṅgaprabhā said to that king:
"Noble son, I have now remembered my entire previous birth."
I am the daughter of the lord of the Vidyādharas, Samara;
my name is Anaṅgaprabhā, and I dwell in the city called Vīrapura.
Having come here due to my father’s curse, I became a human through the loss of my magic power; thus, I forgot my own nature as a Vidyādharī.
And just as she said, "Now I have awakened," her father, Samara, descended from heaven at that moment.
Having been saluted there by King Sāgaravarman,
he spoke to his daughter Anaṅgaprabhā, who had fallen at his feet.
"Come, daughter, take these spells; that curse of yours has passed away.
For the suffering of eight births has been experienced by you in a single birth."
Having said this, she took him onto her lap and bestowed the sciences upon him once more;
then she addressed King Sāgaravarman.
"You are the sovereign of the Vidyādharas named Madanaprabha, and I am Samara by name; Anaṅgaprabhā is my daughter."
Though she was to be given away, she was previously solicited by various suitors;
yet, proud of her beauty, she did not desire any one of them as her husband.
Then she was requested by you with equal qualities and great intensity;
yet, due to the turn of fate, you were not accepted by her at that time.
Because of this, I gave her a curse so that she might come to the world of mortals;
for, filled with passion, I thought, "May she become my wife even in the mortal world."
Having formed a resolve and meditated in your heart upon the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, the bestower of boons,
you then abandoned your own body through yoga and became a Vidyādharī.
"Therefore, you were born as a human, and she too was born as your wife;
now come together with her to your own world, for you two are joined as one."
Thus addressed by Samara, Sāgaravarman— having remembered his former birth— cast off that body in the waters of Prayāga and immediately became Madanaprabha.
Furthermore, having attained that science, she suddenly shone forth as another being, a Vidyādharī, with that very same body, radiant with the brilliance of the god of love.
Then Madanaprabha was filled with joy, as was Anaṅgaprabhā; both of them felt a deep passion that blossomed from gazing upon each other’s divine forms.
Along with the illustrious Samara, lord of the sky-dwellers, they all flew up into the air and went together to Vīrapura—that city of the Vidyādharas.
There, in accordance with the prescribed rites, he gave his daughter Anaṅgaprabhā to Madanaprabha, the king of the sky-dwellers;
and then Madanaprabha departed for his own city together with her, who was now freed from her curse and filled with joy, and there he lived happily.
Thus, by the power of the ripening of their own misconduct, divine beings fall through a curse and descend into the world of men;
having experienced the fruit appropriate to that state, they return again to their own destination by virtue of their previously acquired merit.
Having heard this story from his minister Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta, together with Alaṅkāravatī, was delighted; and then he performed his daily duties.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave.
Then, on another day, his friend who was staying by the side of Alaṃkāravatī—
Marubhūti addressed Naravāhanadatta as follows:
"Look, look, O King! This wretched traveler of yours is clad in a single piece of leather, matted-haired, emaciated, and grey."
Day and night, from the lion-gate, whether in cold or even in heat, he does not stir at all; why then do you still not show him favor?
For a gift given at the right time, even if small, is excellent; what is the use of much given at the wrong time?
Therefore, show him mercy as long as he does not die.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "What Marubhūti has said is well spoken;
however, O Prince, there is no fault whatsoever here on your part."
For as long as the destruction of the obstructing evil has not occurred, so long even one engaged in giving is unable to give; he is not the master [of his own action].
But when evil has been completely exhausted, even though he is restrained with effort, the Lord surely grants [the result]; for this is indeed dependent upon karma.
And likewise, O King, I shall relate to you this story of King Lakṣadatta and the mendicant Labdhadatta; listen.
On the surface of the earth there was a city named Lakṣapura;
there lived a king called Lakṣadatta, the foremost among the generous.
It is said that he did not know how to give less than a hundred thousand to a petitioner;
however, whatever he spoke of, he gave five hundred thousand of that to him.
He was pleased with him and, moreover, bestowed upon him freedom from poverty;
for this reason, he became known by the name Lakṣadatta.
A certain traveler named Labdhadatta stood at his gate day and night,
wearing only a piece of leather around his waist and a rag as a garment.
With his matted locks bound, he did not move from that spot quickly, whether in cold rain or in the heat of summer; and the king beheld him.
Thus, as he remained there for a long time living in affliction,
that king, although he was a donor and possessed of compassion, gave him nothing at all.
Then once, that king went to a forest for hunting;
and that mendicant, carrying his staff, followed after him.
There, as he—accompanied by his army, mounted on a vehicle, and armed with a bow—slew tigers, boars, and deer with a rain of arrows; ||| SoKss_9,3.16 |||
Traveling on foot ahead, that solitary pilgrim struck down many boars and deer with nothing but his staff.
Having witnessed his marvelous prowess, that king thought to himself, "What a hero this man is! yet he gave him nothing at all.
Having finished his hunt, the king entered the city for his own pleasure;
and that traveler remained as before at the main gate.
Once, King Lakṣadatta went forth to conquer a kinsman living within the same boundary; and a great battle took place with him.
In that battle, before the king, that kārpaṭika slew many enemies with blows from the tips of his sturdy khadira staffs.
And King Jitaśatru returned to his own city;
yet, having witnessed his prowess, he did not grant him anything at all.
In this way, five years passed for that pilgrim named Labdhadatta as he remained there, subsisting on wood.
When the sixth [son] had been born, King Lakṣadatta, having seen him one day by the turn of fate, was moved by compassion and reflected:
"Even now, I have not given anything to him who has suffered for so long;
therefore, by some artifice, having given him something, let me see what he does."
Has the destruction of his evil karma occurred for this wretched man, or not?
Does Fortune still withhold even a sight of herself from him today, or not?
Having reflected thus, the king entered his treasury of his own accord and fashioned a citron filled with jewels, like a small casket.
Having arranged the entire assembly hall outside, he had it prepared;
and there all the citizens, vassals, and ministers entered.
And as that kārpaṭika entered into their midst, the king himself said to him in an affectionate voice, "Come here, close to me."
Then, having heard this, Labdhadatta, the pilgrim, filled with great joy,
approached the presence of the king and sat down before him.
Then the king said to him, "Recite some well-spoken verse.
Having heard that, the kārpaṭika then recited this Āryā verse: SoKss_9,3.31 //
This collection of waves fills the ocean, which is already full;
but for one who lacks wealth, prosperity does not even come within the range of his vision.
Having heard this and having had it recited again, the king was delighted and gave him that citron fruit filled with excellent jewels.
But for him with whom this king is pleased, poverty is cut away;
yet pitiable is this mendicant who, having been summoned, is thus treated with such respect.
"This citron was given by this king out of satisfaction;
for even the wish-fulfilling tree, for those who lack merit, generally turns into a mere palāśa."
Thus, having seen that, they were all despondent at that improper occasion;
because they did not know the ultimate truth, they spoke to one another according to their own inclinations.
Taking a citron, that kārpaṭika departed; and as he was going along, dejected, a certain monk came before him.
That man named Rājabandin gave him the garment and took from that traveler a beautiful citron.
Having entered, that monk presented the fruit to the king;
and the king, having recognized it, questioned the ascetic.
"Venerable sir, from where did you obtain this citron?
Thereupon, he pointed out to him that traveler who had given it to him.
Then the king became both despondent and amazed, thinking: "Alas!
Even today his evil karma has not yet been exhausted."
Having accepted that citron, King Lakṣadatta rose from his seat in an instant and performed his daily duties.
That pilgrim also went and remained at the main gate;
having sold his garment, he sat there provided with food, drink, and other necessities.
On the second day, the king performed that entire ceremony in the same manner;
and all the citizens entered there once again.
Then, having seen that traveler enter,
the king likewise called him again and seated him near him.
And having taught that same noble lady once more out of favor,
he gave him that very citron, which was a hidden jewel.
"Aha! On the second day, this lord is pleased with him in vain;
what could this possibly mean?"—thus did they all reflect there, filled with wonder.
And that kārpaṭika, filled with joy, having laughed at that result and considering the king’s favor to have borne fruit, went outside.
Just then, a certain official in charge of the realm came before him,
desiring to enter the assembly hall and see the lord of the earth.
Seeing that citron, he then requested it from the traveler;
observing the omen, he took it, giving the traveler a pair of garments in return.
Having entered the royal court, he bowed at the king's feet and first presented that citron to the king, and then his other own gifts.
Having understood that result, the king, the lord of the realm, asked him, "From where did you obtain this? and he replied, "From the kārpaṭika."
"Alas! Even now Lakṣmī does not grant him her sight here.
Thinking thus within himself, the king then became deeply despondent.
Taking that mātuluṅga fruit, he rose from his place;
then that kārpaṭika, having obtained a pair of garments, went to the marketplace.
Having sold one garment, he provided himself with food, drink, and other necessities;
and having cut the second into two, he made two garments for himself.
Then on the third day as well, that king held a general assembly in the same manner,
and all the people entered once again.
When he had entered and taken that citron, the king likewise summoned that noble lady once more, had her recite it, and gave it to him.
Then, while everyone was filled with wonder, that kārpaṭika went outside and gave that citron to the king’s mistress.
Like a moving creeper upon the tree of royal honor,
she gave him gold as if it were a flower indicating the fruit to come.
Having sold that [jewel], the pilgrim remained there happily on that very day;
at that time, the courtesan also entered the presence of the king.
And he presented him with that large, beautiful citron;
having recognized it, he then asked her how she had obtained it.
Then she said, "This was given to me by a pauper.
Hearing that, the king reflected: "Even now he has not been looked upon by Fortune."
One of little merit does not realize that my grace is never fruitless;
for it is to me alone that these great jewels repeatedly come, alas! SoKss_9,3.63.
Having meditated thus, taken it, and placed it so that it was protected,
the king rose and performed his daily rites.
And on the fourth day, the king held his court in that same manner;
it was filled with all the vassal lords, ministers, and others.
Then, when that traveler had arrived there once more, the king seated him before him as before and made him recite the Āryā verse.
And he gave him that citron, which was quickly released;
having reached halfway toward his hand, it fell to the ground and split in two.
And from that [stūpa], as its covering and joints were broken open, many highly precious jewels emerged, illuminating that assembly hall.
Having seen them, they all said: "For us who did not know the ultimate truth, there was a false delusion for three days; yet such is the grace of the Lord."
Having heard this, the king said: "By this stratagem, I have indeed tested whether or not Śrī grants him her vision."
The end of his evil was not reached for three days, but today it has been reached;
by that very fact, Lakṣmī has now granted him her vision.
Having said this, the lord gave him those jewels, villages, elephants, horses, and gold,
and made that traveler his vassal.
Then, while the people were offering praises, he rose from the assembly hall to bathe;
and that traveler, having achieved his purpose, went to his own dwelling.
In this way, as long as the end of one's evil deeds has not occurred,
the favor of a master cannot be obtained by a servant, even through hundreds of hardships endured.
Having related this story, that chief minister Gomukha spoke again to his lord, Naravāhanadatta.
Therefore, O King, I know that surely the destruction of this mendicant's evil karma has not yet occurred, since you do not show him favor.
Having heard these words of Gomukha and exclaiming, "Ah, well said!",
he [the king] addressed that attendant named Kārpaṭika.
The son of the Lord of Vatsa immediately bestowed a multitude of villages,
elephants, horses, ten million gold pieces, and excellent garments and ornaments.
At that very moment, that successful traveler became like a king;
for when a master is grateful and has a virtuous retinue, how can service not bear fruit?
While he was staying there in this manner,
a young brahmin from the south came to serve Naravāhanadatta.
And that hero named Pralambabāhu addressed him:
"O Lord, drawn by your fame, I have come to take refuge at your feet."
I do not move even a single step from the foot of the God,
whether he travels on the ground by elephant, horse, or chariot, or again in the sky.
"Since it is heard that the lordship of the Vidyādharas will belong to my master in the future,
let a hundred pieces of gold be given to me daily for my livelihood."
When he had spoken thus,
Naravāhanadatta bestowed that means of livelihood upon that brahmin of incomparable splendor.
In connection with that, Gomukha said: "O King, the attendants of kings are indeed of such a nature; therefore, let this story be heard."
In this world there is a great and excellent city named Vikramapura;
there, in former times, there was a king called Vikramatuṅga.
Sharpness resided in the sword of that ruler of policy, not in his staff;
he was constantly devoted to dharma, but never to women, hunting, and the like.
And during that king’s reign, there was a falling away from virtue among the dust of the families, a lack of discrimination regarding arrows, and a failure of cattle-herders in their pens.
Once, a brave Brahmin named Vīravara, a hero born in the land of Mālava and possessed of handsome form, came before the king for the purpose of service.
He had a wife named Dharmavatī, a daughter named Vīravatī, and a son named Sattvavara; these three were his retinue at home.
Furthermore, there is a waist-belt for service and another triad:
a small sword at the waist, a shield in one hand, and a beautiful mirror in the other.
With only this much retinue,
he requested from that king five hundred dīnāras every day for his livelihood.
And the king granted that livelihood to him,
whose power had been observed, thinking, "I shall first observe his excellence."
And afterwards, the king gave him spies to find out:
"What would this two-armed man do with so many dinars?"
And that Vīravara gave a hundred of those dinars every day from his own hand for the sake of food and other needs for his wife.

With a hundred [pieces of gold], he used to purchase garments, garlands, and other offerings; furthermore, having bathed, he set aside another hundred for the purpose of worshipping Hari, Hara, and the other deities.
He gave another two hundred to the twice-born, the wretched, and others;
in this manner, he constantly distributed even those five hundred.
He remained at the lion-gate of that king until midday;
having performed his daily rites and so forth, he returned and stayed there once again for the night.
The spies constantly reported this daily conduct to that king;
thereupon, being pleased, he dismissed those spies.
That Vīravara also remained day and night at the king’s main gate,
bearing his weapon, except for the time set aside for bathing and other such duties.
Then, as if wishing to conquer that Vīravara,
the arrival of the clouds came forth, fierce with thunder and unable to endure the prowess of heroes.
Then, while the cloud rained down a terrible volley of arrow-like torrents,
that Vīravara did not stir from the lion-gate, remaining as immovable as a pillar.
And King Vikramatuṅga, having always watched him from the palace,
climbed that palace again at night, desiring to know [his secret].
Standing at the main gate, he called out from above, "Who is there?
Hearing that, I replied, "I am standing here," and Vīravara said the same.
"Aha! This Great Being deserves a most exalted station, he who does not leave the lion-gate while such rain as this is falling from the clouds."
While the king was thus reflecting after hearing this,
he heard from afar the piteous weeping of a woman.
"There is no one suffering in my kingdom; who then is this that weeps?
Having reflected thus, the king then spoke to Vīravara.
"O Vīravara, listen; some woman is weeping there in the distance.
Go there and investigate who she is and what her suffering is."
Having heard that, Vīravara said, "So be it," and then set out from there to go,
shaking his hand and with his sword-belt fastened.
Seeing him set out when such a cloud was flashing with lightning, and when the space between heaven and earth was obstructed by the falling torrent of rain, he was filled with wonder.
And that king, full of compassion, descended from the palace and set out behind him, sword in hand, unobserved.
Following the sound of weeping, Vīravara, accompanied by the king who had followed him in secret,
went outside the city and reached a certain lake.
"Alas, my lord! Alas, compassionate one! Alas, hero! How shall I live, abandoned by you?"—thus he saw that woman weeping in their midst.
When she was asked by him, "Who are you that grieves, and who is your protector? she replied, "O Vīravara, know me to be this Earth, your mother."
"King Vikramatuṅga is now my righteous lord;
it is certain that his death will occur on the third day."
"O son, how could such a husband ever be mine again?
Therefore, being deeply distressed, I grieve for him and for myself."
For with divine vision I behold what is to come, both auspicious and inauspicious,
just as the young son of a god Suprabha beheld while staying in the third heaven.
For he, possessing divine vision, foresaw his impending fall from heaven due to the exhaustion of his merit,
as well as his own rebirth within the womb of a sow after seven days.
Then, reflecting upon the suffering of dwelling within the womb of a sow,
that son of the gods lamented for those divine enjoyments along with himself.
"Alas, heaven! Alas, O apsarases! Alas, the bower-lattices of the Nandana grove!
Alas, how shall I dwell thereafter in the womb of a sow, amidst the mire?"
Hearing him lamenting in this way and more, the Lord of the Gods approached and questioned him; he, in turn, described to him the cause of his own sorrow.
Then Śakra said to him: "There is a means for you in this matter; listen.
Chanting 'Vrajoṃ Namaḥ Śivāya,' take refuge in the Lord."
Having gone to him for refuge and abandoned evil, you will attain merit;
by means of which you shall not enter the womb of a boar, nor fall from the heavenly realms.
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, Suprabha then said, "So be it," and having uttered "Obeisance to Śiva," he took refuge in Śambhu.
Absorbed in that [meditation] for six days, by virtue of its grace,
he was not only cast into the womb of a sow, but ascended even above heaven.
And on the seventh day, Śatakratu saw him there in heaven;
as he looked further, he saw that he had gone to another world.
Just as that radiant one grieved upon seeing the impending calamity,
so too do I grieve upon seeing the impending death of the king.
When Bhūmi had spoken thus, Vīravara said to her:
"Mother, just as there was a means for Suprabha through the words of Śakra..."
When Vīravara said, "In that case, if there is a means for this king's protection,
let it be told," the Earth spoke to him.
"There is but one means in this matter, and it is entirely within your own power.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin Vīravara spoke joyfully:
Then speak quickly, O Goddess, if there may be welfare for my Lord;
whether by my life or by my sons and wife, that birth shall be fruitful for me.
When he had spoken thus, the Earth said to that Vīravara:
"There is here, near the royal palace, this Goddess Caṇḍikā."
If you offer that best of beings as a sacrifice for her sake, then this king will live; there is no other means whatsoever.
Having heard these words of the Earth, the steadfast Vīravara then said, "O Goddess, I am going; I shall do this right now."
"Who else is as devoted to his master's welfare as you? May it be well with you;
go! Having said this, the Earth vanished; and the king, following after her, heard everything.
Then, while King Vikramatuṅga followed her in disguise,
Vīravara quickly went to his own home that very night.
There, having awakened his wife Dharmavatī, he told her that,
at the word of the Earth, their own son must be offered for the sake of the king.
Having heard that, she said: "The welfare of my master must certainly be accomplished;
therefore, you should inform his sons today and tell them this."
Then, having awakened that boy, Vīravara told him everything that had been said by the Earth for the sake of the king, ending with the matter of the sacrifice.
Having heard that, the boy named Yathārthākhyo, the best of beings, replied:
"Father, am I not a man of merit whose life has been dedicated to the service of my lord?"
I have eaten that food which I must also purify;
therefore, take me and offer me as a sacrifice for her sake.
To that best of beings, the excellent hero, who had spoken thus, the child replied without hesitation: "You have truly been born from my very marrow."
Having heard this while standing outside, King Vikramatuṅga thought: "Aha! All these people possess equal courage."
Then Vīravara placed his son Sattvavara upon his shoulder,
and his wife Dharmavatī placed her daughter Vīravatī upon his back.
Having taken [the child], those two went that night to the temple of Caṇḍikā;
and King Vikramatuṅga followed behind them, remaining concealed.

Then, having been brought down from his father's shoulder, that best of beings, though but a child, bowed to the goddess and, being a mass of fortitude, made this request: SoKss_9,3.146: "Then, having been brought down from his father's shoulder, that best of beings, though but a child, bowed to the goddess and, being a mass of fortitude, made this request."
"O Queen, let our lord live by the sacrifice of my head;
let King Vikramatuṅga rule here over the earth free from thorns."
When he had spoken thus, Vīravara exclaimed, "Excellent, my son! and drawing his sword from its scabbard, he severed his son's head with the palm of his hand.
And Caṇḍikādevī gave [the child] to the king, saying, "May it be for your welfare!
Indeed, those devoted to their master have no longing for a son or even for themselves."
"Excellent, O best of heroes! You have restored the life of your master, even at the cost of your own son's life"—such was the voice heard then from the sky.
And while the king, filled with great amazement, was seeing and hearing all of this,
the young Vīravatī, daughter of his brother Vīravara, [was there].
Approaching the head of the slain man, she embraced it and kissed it;
then, crying out "Alas, brother!", her heart burst and she perished.
Then, seeing even her daughter dead, the virtuous wife Dharmavatī spoke with dejection to Vīravara, joining her palms in reverence: SoKss_9,3.153 //
"I have already ensured the king's welfare; now grant me your permission so that I may enter the fire, taking with me my two deceased children."
"Since even this child, though ignorant, has died here from grief for her brother,
what beauty is there in life for me now that both my children are lost?"
To her who was speaking thus with certainty, Vīravara said:
"Do so; what more can I say now, O blameless one?"
"In this saṃsāra, which consists solely of grief for your offspring, is there any happiness for you? Wait therefore while I prepare a funeral pyre for you."
Having said this, those who remained there constructed a funeral pyre from the timber used for the construction of the Goddess’s temple;
upon it they placed the corpses of their children and set it ablaze with the fire of lamps.
Then his wife Dharmavatī, having bowed at his feet, said:
"O noble son, may you be my husband even in another birth."
Saying, "May it be well with the king," the virtuous woman cast herself into that funeral pyre,
thick with masses of flames, as if into the play of a cool lake.
And King Vikramatuṅga, having seen this while remaining hidden, was overcome with anxious thought: "By what means might I become free from my debt to these people?"
Then Vīravara, firm of mind, reflected:
"My master’s business has been accomplished; for indeed, a divine voice was heard directly."
Now that lump of food has been eaten by my Lord and is completely digested;
having spent everything desired, the family must now be supported by me. (SoK 9.3.163)
Life indeed shines forth only by supporting oneself alone;
so why should I not honor this Mother Ambika even by the sacrifice of my own self?
Thus Vīravara, being firmly established in his resolve toward the virtuous, first propitiated that goddess Caṇḍikā, the bestower of boons, with a hymn of praise.
O Maheśvarī, salutations to you, the bestower of fearlessness to those who bow before you; lift me up, for I have come to you for refuge, sinking deep in the mire of saṃsāra.
You are the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) of all beings; by you this world is set in motion.
At the beginning of creation, having arisen from yourself, you were beheld by Śambhu himself.
Blazing and illuminating the entire universe with a brilliance difficult to behold,
she appeared like a row of ten million fierce, untimely suns risen at once.
The intermediate quarters were covered by the circle of her arms,
which bore swords, shields, bows, arrows, spears, and other weapons.
And you have been praised by that very god, the wielder of the trident, thus:
"Homage to you, O Caṇḍī, Cāmuṇḍā, Maṅgalā, Tripurā, Jayā! (SoKss 9.3.170)
O Ekānaṃśā, Śivā, Durgā, Nārāyaṇī, Sarasvatī, Bhadrakālī, Mahālakṣmī, Siddhā, and Ruruvidāriṇī! SoKss_9,3.171 //
You are Gāyatrī, the Great Queen; you are Revatī, the dweller of the Vindhya mountains;
you are Umā and Kātyāyanī, the dweller on Mount Śarva.
O Goddess, having heard you being praised by Hara with such names as these, Skanda, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and the others likewise offered hymns of praise to you.
And while praising you, O Blessed One, the immortals, sages,
and men have obtained and continue to obtain their desired wishes, even exceeding them.
Therefore, be gracious to me, O Giver of Boons;
accept even this worship consisting of the offering of my own body, so that there may be welfare for my lord, the king.
Having spoken thus, just as he desired to cut off his own head,
an incorporeal voice arose from the expanse of the sky.
"Do not act rashly, my son; for I am well-pleased with this very courage of yours. Therefore, ask of me whatever boon you desire."
Having heard that, Vīravara said: "If you are pleased, O Queen, then let King Vikramatuṅga live for another hundred years."
When he requested the boon, "May my wife and children live," a voice arose from the sky, saying once more, "So be it."
At that very moment, all three— Dharmavatī, Sattvavara, and Vīravatī— rose up alive with their bodies uninjured.
Then Vīravara, delighted by the awakening [of his sons] through the favor of the goddess,
led them all to his own home and went once again to the king’s gate.
And King Vikramatuṅga, seeing that, was delighted and amazed;
he went back and ascended that palace unobserved.
Standing at the main gate, he asked from above, "Who is there?
Hearing that, Vīravara, who was stationed below, replied to him.
I remained there, having dismounted from my vehicle to look for that woman;
yet she, like a goddess, vanished from my sight as soon as I saw her.
Having heard this entire account and witnessed that most extraordinary marvel,
King Vikramatuṅga reflected alone during the night:
"Oh! What an unprecedented and extraordinary person this is!
Alas, he performs such praiseworthy deeds yet does not speak of them."
Though deep, vast, and a great being, the ocean does not rival this mountain,
even when it is buffeted by the touch of mighty winds.
What recompense could I possibly offer to him who, in my absence during the night, gave up his own life by sacrificing his son and wife?
Reflecting on these and other matters, the king descended from the palace,
entered the inner apartments, and passed that night with a smile.
And in the morning, while that great hero Vīravara stood in that place,
he related to him the wonderful account of his deeds during the night.
Then, while that best of heroes was being praised by all,
the lord of men fastened the turban upon him and his son as well.
He gave many territories, horses, jewels, and elephants,
as well as ten crores of gold and a sixtyfold livelihood.
At that very moment, the brahmin Vīravara became like a king;
with a raised parasol, he and his entire family attained their purpose.
Having thus told this story and bringing the present matter to a conclusion,
the minister Gomukha spoke again to Naravāhanadatta.
Thus, O King, by the power of merit, some servants who are peerless heroes among kings meet;
those beings of noble character, having cast aside regard for their own bodies and so forth for the sake of their master, conquer both worlds. (SoKss 9,3.195)
"Therefore, O Lord, this foremost of the twice-born, your servant, is seen to be exactly such as that:
newly arrived, preeminent in the quality of courage, with long arms and a form of steady grace."
Thus, having heard from his own minister Gomukha, who possessed noble character and vast intelligence,
Prince Naravāhanadatta experienced unsurpassed satisfaction in his heart.
Thus ends the third wave in the Alaṃkāravatī book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Wave:
While he was thus dwelling there in the house of his father, the King of Vatsa...
He was attended by his devoted ministers, Gomukha and the others.
And while he was dwelling there, Queen Alaṃkāravatī, who was devoted to him,
had her jealousy stolen away by that intense love which could not endure any obstacle to his honor.
Then, on one occasion, Naravāhanadatta mounted his chariot and went to a deer-park, with Gomukha following behind him.
And while that heroic brahmin with long arms went ahead as his guide,
he engaged in the sport of hunting there together with his followers.
Even as the chariots and horses were galloping with all their might, he,
with his long arms, overcame their speed and went ahead of them.
Standing in his chariot, he struck lions, tigers, and other beasts with arrows;
but Pralambabāhu, moving on foot, slew them with his sword.
And Naravāhanadatta, seeing that brahmin again and again, was filled with wonder, thinking, "Oh, what courage! Oh, what speed of leg!"
Having finished his hunt and being thoroughly exhausted, he, along with his charioteer and Gomukha,
[rested] while that great warrior Pralambabāhu was leading the way.
Mounted on his chariot and overcome by thirst,
the son of the Lord of Vatsa entered another great forest far away in his search for water.
There he reached a great, divine lake filled with blossoming golden lotuses,
like a second sky descended to earth, abounding with many solar discs.
There, having bathed and drunk water, and having performed his ablutions and other rites along with his followers,
he beheld from afar four men in one part of that place.
They were of divine form, wearing divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments,
as they gathered golden lotuses from that lake.
Out of curiosity he approached them, and when questioned by them, "Who are you?",
he related his lineage, his name, and his own life story to them.
Delighted by this vision, they said to him as he questioned them:
"In the midst of the great ocean, there is a vast and glorious, preeminent island."
There is a place renowned in the world as Nārikela-dvīpa, beautiful to behold;
there are four mountains there whose grounds are like the sky.
Maināka, Vṛṣabha, Cakra, and Balāhaka—these are the four remembered;
we four dwell upon those four.
One of us is named Rūpasiddhi, who assumes various forms;
the other is Pramāṇasiddhi, who perceives both the large and the subtle.
The third is Jñānasiddhi, who knows the past, present, and future;
the fourth is Devasiddhi, who possesses the accomplishments of all deities.
"Taking these golden lotuses,
we shall now go to Śvetadvīpa to worship the Lord of Śrī, the God."
For we are all his devotees, and by his grace we possess sovereignty over those respective mountains, as well as perfections and riches.
Therefore come, let us show you the Lord Hari in Śvetadvīpa;
we shall carry you through the air, friend, if it pleases you.
When those sons of the gods had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta agreed, saying "So be it," and there he found water, fruit, and other provisions at his disposal.
Having established Gomukha and the others on Śvetadvīpa, he traveled through the air;
then, from among them, he was taken onto his own lap by Devasiddhi.
Having descended there from the sky and approached from afar,
he saw him standing by the side, with the daughter of the ocean nearby and the Earth at his feet.
He was being served by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in embodied forms,
and was being praised with devotion in song by Gandharvas such as Nārada and others.
Hari, who was being prostrated to by gods, siddhas, and likewise by vidyādharas,
with Garuḍa seated before him and resting upon the couch of Śeṣa.
He saw that he had been brought there by those four sons of gods;
for whose prosperity could the company of the virtuous not be a cause?
Then Naravāhanadatta, with palms joined in reverence, praised that Lord who had been honored by the sons of gods and extolled by Kaśyapa and others.
Homage be to you, O Blessed One,
the wish-fulfilling tree for devotees, whose body is embraced by the wish-granting creeper of Lakṣmī, the bestower of all desires.
Homage to you, the divine swan, who dwells in the lake of the heart,
whose sound is ever-arising, and who roams in the supreme ether.
Homage to you, who transcend all, who abide within the heart of all,
whose form surpasses all qualities, and whose embodiment is the perfection of the six sovereign attributes.
Brahmā, rising from his own meditation within the lotus of your navel with a soft sound, though he possesses many feet born of that [lotus], acts as if he has only six. (SoK 9.4.32)
With the earth as your feet and the heavens as your head, with the quarters as your ears and the sun and moon as your eyes,
you are praised by the wise as some ineffable Puruṣa whose belly contains the entire cosmic egg.
O Lord, from you, the treasury of light, this multitude of beings unfolds,
like a mass of sparks from a blazing fire.
And again, at the arrival of dissolution, he enters into you alone,
like a multitude of embodied beings entering a great dwelling-tree at the end of the day.
Exulting, you create these lords of the world as your own partial manifestations,
just as the ocean, agitated by its endless tides, produces waves.
Though possessing all forms, you are formless; though the creator of all, you are inactive;
though the support of all, you are without support—who can truly comprehend your reality?
The gods have attained various supernatural powers (ṛddhi) by being gazed upon by your gracious eyes;
therefore, be gracious, look upon me who have sought refuge, and look with a compassionate glance.
Seeing Naravāhanadatta having thus offered praise, Hari, with a gracious eye, addressed Nārada.
"Go! Those excellent apsarases who were born from the Ocean of Milk and were formerly deposited by me as a trust—those who were established by me for Śakra—are yours."
Therefore, O great sage, having searched for them at my word and placed them all upon that chariot, you must bring them here with haste.
Having been thus addressed by Hari, Nārada went and said "So be it" to them;
then, together with Mātali, he brought those Apsarases from Śakra by means of that chariot.
Then, when those apsarases had been presented by him with a bow,
the Blessed One gave instructions to that son of the King of Vatsa.
"O Naravāhanadatta, these Apsarases are given by me to you,
who shall become the future emperor of the Vidyādhara lords."
"You are the fitting husband for these women, and they are the fitting wives for you;
for you have been fashioned by the Enemy of Tripura as an incarnation of Kāmadeva."
Having heard that, while the son of the Lord of Vatsa lay prostrate at his feet, Hari, delighted by the favor he had received, commanded Mātali: SoKss_9,4.46 //
"Let this Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by you and the Apsarases,
be taken to his own home by whatever path he desires."
When the Blessed One had thus instructed him, Naravāhanadatta, together with the Apsaras, bowed to him and [ascended] that chariot with Mātali as its driver.
Having ascended together with those sons of the gods who had extended invitations,
and being envied by the gods themselves, he went to the island of Nārikela.
There, the successful one was honored by those four divine beings, beginning with Rūpasiddhi, together with Śakra’s charioteer.
On those mountains where he resided, beginning with Maināka and Vṛṣabha,
he took delight in succession with those very Apsarases, in places that rivaled heaven itself.
And full of curiosity, he wandered through the grounds of those garden groves, where various trees were in full bloom with the arrival of the honey-months.
Behold these clusters of blossoms on the trees, which seem to gaze upon their beloved Spring as he approaches with their wide-open eyes of full-blown flowers.
"May we not suffer here in our birthplace from the heat of the sun's rays"—
as if thinking thus, behold the lake covered with blossoming lotuses.
Behold how bees, even upon approaching the radiant *karṇikāra* flower that lacks fragrance,
abandon it as base beings forsake a wealthy man.
Behold here how the concert of the king of seasons is being performed by the songs of the kinnarīs, the warbling of the cuckoos,
and the humming of the bees.
Saying these and other words, those sons of the gods showed their own series of groves to that Naravāhanadatta.
In those cities as well, the son of the Lord of Vatsa took his pleasure, beholding the festive songs and dances of the citizens who were dancing unrestrainedly during the spring festival.
Accompanied by the Apsarases, he enjoyed there the pleasures cherished by the immortals;
for wherever those of meritorious deeds go, their splendors precede them.
Having remained thus for three or four days, Naravāhanadatta spoke to those sons of the gods, his friends:
"I am going to my own city, eager for a sight of my father;
therefore, you too, having reached that city, fulfill your purpose by seeing him."
Having heard that, they said: "The essence of her city has been seen by you;
what else remains? We should be remembered by you as those who have attained knowledge."
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta was released by them; and when the chariot equal to Indra’s had been brought forward, he addressed Mātali.
"By that path where Gomukha and the others are staying on the shore of the divine lake, lead me to the city of Kauśāmbī."
Then, having been told "So be it" by him, he ascended that chariot together with the apsaras and reached that lake; there he saw Gomukha and the others.
"Return quickly by your own way; I shall tell you everything at home.
Having said this to them, he departed for Kauśāmbī in the chariot of Śakra.
Having descended there from the sky and dismissed Mātali after he had been honored,
he entered his own palace accompanied by those celestial nymphs.
Having stationed them there, he went to the King of Vatsa,
who was delighted by his arrival, and prostrated at the feet of his father.
And they too, their eyes satiated with the sight of him, greeted both his mother Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī in the same way.
And at that moment, Gomukha, mounted on his chariot along with his charioteer,
arrived there together with that brahmin Pralambabāhu.
Then, while the circle of ministers was present, Naravāhanadatta, being questioned by his father, related that most wonderful account of his own adventures.
The Lord grants that person association with spiritual friends,
for he desires to bestow his favor upon one who has performed virtuous deeds.
While everyone was thus praising him, King Vatsarāja,
being well-pleased, then celebrated the festival of his son’s reception of Acyuta’s grace.
And together with his wife, he beheld those apsarases, who had been obtained through the grace of Hari, brought by Gomukha to prostrate themselves at his feet as daughters-in-law.
Devarūpā, Devarati, Devamālā,
and likewise Devapriyā as the fourth— these were the names asked of by the maidservants.
Where am I, and where are the apsarases? By good fortune, I have been made a city of heaven upon the earth by Prince Naravāhanadatta.
Thus, as if scattering vermilion in celebration,
Kauśāmbī was seen at that time with its fluttering red banners spread wide.
And Naravāhanadatta, having brought a festival of joy to the eyes of his parents,
honored his other wives who were looking out for him on the road.
For four days, they delighted him— though they themselves were made thin as if by four years— by describing their various pangs of separation.
