And Gomukha described the heroic slaying of lions and other beasts by Pralambabāhu while he was protecting the chariot horses during his forest dwelling.
Thus he listened to unrestrained conversations that were pleasant to the ear,
and he gazed upon the forms of beautiful women, which were nectar for his eyes.
And there Naravāhanadatta dwelt happily for that time, accompanied by his ministers, performing endearments and drinking honey-wines.
Once, while staying with his friends in the inner apartments of Laṅkāravatī, he heard from outside the tumultuous sound of musical instruments.
Then he spoke to his own general, Hariśikha:
"From where could this great sound of trumpets come here so suddenly?"
Having heard this, Hariśikha immediately went out and then re-entered; in that very moment, he addressed his lord, the son of Vatsarāja.
There is a merchant named Rudra here in this city;
he went from here to Suvarṇadvīpa for the purpose of trade.
The accumulation of wealth belonging to him as he was returning, though already attained,
sank and went to destruction when his ship was wrecked in the ocean.
O Lord, having crossed the ocean by himself alone while still alive,
he has reached here today on the sixth day and arrived at his own home.
While he remained here in distress for some days,
by chance, a great treasure was discovered by him from his own pleasure garden.
The Lord of Vatsa learned of this from the mouths of those born of his own lineage;
then, having arrived that very day, he informed the sovereign of the matter through that merchant.
"I have obtained four crores of gold along with a multitude of jewels;
if Your Majesty commands, I shall offer them."
Seeing you robbed by the reservoir and distressed, who with a non-dull heart would rob you again, whom the Creator has already shared out of compassion?
"Go and enjoy at your pleasure the wealth obtained from your own land," thus was that merchant commanded by the Lord of Vatsa.
Having prostrated at the feet of the king, that merchant, overflowing with joy,
went to his own home accompanied by his followers while sounding musical instruments.
Having thus heard Hariśikha describe the righteousness of his father,
Naravāhanadatta, filled with wonder, spoke to his own ministers.
If he first acquires wealth and immediately thereafter gives it away, what is the wonder?
Fate seems to play with men through their rise and fall.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "Such indeed is the course of destiny;
listen now to this story of Samudraśūra."
Formerly, there was a city belonging to King Harṣavarman,
prosperous by name of Harṣapura, whose subjects were made happy by excellent governance.
In that city there was a great merchant named Samudraśūra,
of noble birth, righteous, firm in character, and a lord of vast wealth.
Once, while traveling for the sake of trade to Suvarṇadvīpa,
he reached the shore of the great ocean and boarded a ship.
As he was traveling on that path toward the ocean when only a small portion remained,
a terrible cloud arose and a wind agitated the sea.
When his ship was tossed by the force of the wind and struck by sea-monsters,
the merchant, having broken it, fastened his belt and leaped into the ocean.
And for as long as the hero crosses over there for a moment by flailing his arms,
so long he reaches a man who has been dead for a long time and is driven by the wind.
And once he had mounted it, with the water cast aside by his arms,
he was carried to Suvarṇadvīpa by a favorable wind, as if by the Creator himself.
Having stepped onto the shore from that [boat],
he beheld a cloth with a knot tied at the waist, which had been fastened by that deceased man.
As soon as he unfastened and looked at that cloth-bag from his waist,
he found within it a divine necklace, rich with jewels.
Seeing that priceless object and taking it, he was satisfied after bathing;
for he considered the wealth lost at sea to be as a blade of grass before him.
Then, having traveled by stages, he reached the city named Kalaśapura;
with a staff held in his hand, he entered a certain temple.
There, seated in the shade and utterly exhausted by his strenuous exertion in the water,
he gradually succumbed to sleep, bewildered by fate.
While he was sleeping there, the city guards arrived unexpectedly and saw Kaṇṭhaka standing by his side, unheeded.
"This is that Kaṇṭhaka; he was snatched from the neck of the princess Cakrasenā right here. Surely this man is that very thief."
Having spoken thus, those merchants woke him up and led the merchant to the royal palace;
there, questioned by the king himself, he related everything exactly as it had happened.
"This man is a thief; look at this thorn!"—so saying, as the king extended him [toward the executioners] and addressed the members of the court: (SoKss 9.4.113)
Seeing that radiant light, a vulture swooped down from the sky with great speed,
seized Kaṇṭhaka by the neck, and departed for some unknown place out of sight.
Then, as the merchant cried out in extreme distress for the protection of Śiva, while the king had ordered his execution in a fit of rage, a voice was heard from heaven: "O Bhārata! (SoKss_9.4.115)
"O King, do not slay this man; he is a virtuous merchant named Samudraśūra who has come from the city of Harṣapura to your realm."
The thief by whom Kaṇṭhaka had been led away, overwhelmed with fear and fleeing, fell at night into the water near the city wall and died.
But this merchant, having reached and boarded the body of that thief,
crossed the ocean with his ship wrecked and has now arrived here.
And at that time, Kaṇṭhaka was recovered by this merchant from the knot of the cloth tied around his waist; he had not been taken away from the house by him.
"Therefore, O King, release this righteous merchant who is not a thief;
honor him and send him on his way. Having spoken thus, the voice fell silent.
Having heard this, the king was satisfied; he spared the merchant from execution, honored Samudraśūra with wealth, and sent him on his way.
And that merchant, having acquired wealth and purchased his wares, crossed the ocean by ship as he was returning to his own country, though it was once again terrifying.
And having crossed the ocean, he then proceeded with a caravan and reached a forest one day at the close of the day.
When that caravan had halted there at night, while he was keeping watch,
an invincible army of thieves fell upon Samudraśūra.
While the caravan was being slaughtered by her, Samudraśūra abandoned his goods and fled; he climbed up a banyan tree and remained there unobserved.
When the band of thieves had departed with all his wealth taken, he, overwhelmed by fear and afflicted by grief, spent that night right there under the tree.
In the morning, that fortunate man, casting his gaze upon the top of that tree,
saw something shimmering amidst the leaves like the light of a lamp.
Having climbed up there out of wonder, he beheld a vulture’s nest containing a collection of brilliant and priceless jewel ornaments.
From that [pile], he took all of it;
among it, he found the neck-bone—the very one he had obtained on the Golden Island, which the vulture had carried off.
Then, having obtained immeasurable wealth, he descended from the banyan tree and,
traveling joyfully, eventually reached his own city of Harṣapura.
Then the merchant Samudraśūra, his desire for other wealth gone, remained there with his kinsmen, rejoicing according to his wish.
His falling into the ocean is the loss of that wealth;
his crossing over from there is the recovery of Kaṇṭhaka; and his subsequent departure is the loss of him as well.
That was the attainment of a state of being unjustly condemned;
that was the gain from the Lord of the Island out of mere pleasure at that very moment; and that was the crossing of the ocean once again.
Then there was the total loss of everything due to meeting bandits on the road,
and at the end, for that merchant, the recovery of wealth from the top of a tree.
Thus, O Lord, such is the wondrous activity of Fate:
even a doer of good deeds must experience suffering before attaining happiness.
Having heard this from Gomukha, Naravāhanadatta accepted it with faith, rose up, and performed his daily duties there, beginning with his bath.
On another day,
a young attendant named Śūra, who was known as Samaratuṅga, approached the prince while he was in the assembly hall and addressed him.
"O King, my kingdom has been destroyed by my own kinsman, Vīrajit and his three other sons, who have rained down a shower of battle."
"Therefore, having gone there, I shall bind even those five and bring them here;
let this be known to my lord. Having said this, he went there.
Perceiving that he had few troops while those others had vast armies,
the son of the Lord of Vatsa commanded his own forces to follow him.
Without even seizing them, that proud man went forth and, having conquered all five enemies in battle with his own two arms, he bound them and brought them back together.
Then, having honored that victorious hero as he approached,
the lord Naravāhanadatta praised his own servant.
Having conquered these five enemies— who have invaded their objects, who possess strength, and who are like the senses— by means of this [mind], the goal of human endeavor has been accomplished.
Having heard that, Gomukha said: "O King, if you have not heard such a story of King Camarabāla, then listen; I shall tell it to you."
There was a city called Hastināpura,
and there lived a king named Cāmaravāla, who possessed great wealth, strong fortresses, and a powerful army.

His neighboring kings, such as Samarabāla and others, who were born of his own lineage, gathered together and reflected thus: SoKss_9,4.146: "His neighboring kings, such as Samarabāla and others, who were born of his own lineage, gathered together and reflected thus:"
"This yak-tailed one constantly harasses each of us individually;
therefore, let all of us join together and bring about his defeat."
Having thus deliberated, these five kings, desiring to go forth for victory over him, asked the astrologer in private for an auspicious time of departure.
Not seeing an auspicious moment and observing ill omens, the astrologer said: "There is no favorable moment for you in this year."
In whatever way you may go, victory will not be yours;
what is the use of your persistence here, when you see his prosperity?
Wealth indeed has enjoyment as its fruit, and that [enjoyment] is even greater for you;
if you have not heard it, then let this story of two merchants be heard here.
In ancient times, there was here a city named Kautukapura;
in that city lived a king named Bahusuvarṇaka, whose name was truly significant.
He had a young Kṣatriya servant named Yaśovarman;
although the king was a giver, he never gave anything to him at any time.
And whenever that king entreated him with such distress,
he would show him the sun and speak to him thus on each occasion.
"I wish to give to you; why then does this Blessed One not wish to give to you? What shall I do? Tell me. (SoKss 9.4.155)
Then, while he remained there in distress, waiting for an opportunity,
the time of a solar eclipse arrived.
At that time, his constant servant Yaśovarman went and addressed the king, who was then engaged in extensive and great acts of charity.
"O Lord, this sun, who does not give to you, has been seized by his enemy today; therefore, grant me whatever little I request."
Having heard that and having laughed, the lord of the earth, who had bestowed his gifts,
gave him garments, gold, and other riches consisting of much gold.
When that fuel had been consumed,
Yaśovarman, distressed and having lost his wife, went to the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas to offer himself as a gift to the Lord.
"What is the use of this body of mine, which is as good as dead though it still breathes?
I shall cast it away before the Goddess and obtain the boon I desire."
Thus, lying upon a bed of darbha grass before the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas, he,
with his mind fixed on her and abstaining from food, performed great austerities.
And in a dream, that goddess commanded him: "I am pleased with you, my son.
Shall I grant you the glory of wealth, or shall I grant you the glory of enjoyments? Tell me."
Having heard that, Yaśovarman replied to the queen:
"I do not perceive any subtle distinction between the splendors of these two."
Then the queen said to him: "In that case, you have two merchants in your own country, Bhogavarman and Arthavarman."
"Go and behold the splendor of those two; then, having returned, let that which is suitable for you and which pleases you be requested from them."
Having heard this and being awakened, Yaśovarman broke his fast in the morning and then departed for his own country, filled with curiosity.
There he first went to the house of Arthavarman,
whose wealth had been acquired through transactions involving countless gold, jewels, and other riches.
Beholding that prosperity of his, he approached him in the proper manner;
and having been offered hospitality by him, he was invited to a meal.
Then, by the side of that Arthavarman, he ate food suitable for a guest— accompanied by ghee, meat, and condiments.
But Arthavarman ate barley meal mixed with half a *pala* of ghee,
along with a small amount of cooked rice and a tiny portion of meat curry.
"Caravan leader, why do you eat only this much? Thus questioned with curiosity by Yaśovarman, the merchant spoke as follows:
Today, out of deference to you, I have eaten a small amount of food with meat as a condiment; I have consumed half a pala of ghee and some barley meal.
But I always eat only a karṣa of ghee and plain roasted flour;
more than this does not digest at all in my stomach, which has a weak fire.
Having heard that, Yaśovarman, feeling uncertain,
inwardly reviled the fortune of Arthavarman as being fruitless.
Then, at the arrival of night, the merchant Arthavarman again brought food and milk for the sake of that Yaśovarman.
And Yaśovarman enjoyed that further according to his desire;
meanwhile, Atharvān also then drank one *pala* of Kīra.
And right there in that same place, having spread out their beds,
both Yaśovarman and Arthavarman gradually fell asleep.
And at midnight, Yaśovarman unexpectedly saw in a dream terrifying men with staffs in their hands entering there.
"Shame on you! You have consumed an excessive karṣa of ghee; why did you eat meat and rice today, and drink a pala of milk? (SoK 9.4.180)
Thus speaking in anger, those men dragged Arthavarman by the feet and beat him all over with clubs.
They drew out from his belly all that he had eaten— ghee, a karṣa of milk, meat, and rice— as well as whatever else was in excess.
Having seen that, as Yaśovarman woke up and looked around,
the spear of the awakened Arthavarman came toward him.
Then, while being massaged by his attendants,
Arthavarman cried out and vomited up even more than what he had eaten.
When the pain had subsided, Yaśovarman then reflected:
"Fie, fie upon this wealth and glory, for whose enjoyment such a thing as this exists!"
"May this [world] be rendered desolate by such a lack of prosperity"—
thinking thus within himself, he passed that night there.
In the morning, having taken leave of Arthavarman,
Yaśovarman then went to the house of that merchant Bhogavarman.
He approached him there according to custom, and having been shown hospitality by him as well, he was invited by the merchant to take a meal that very day.
And that merchant saw no accumulation of wealth belonging to him;
yet he saw a beautiful house, as well as garments and ornaments.
Then, while Yaśovarman remained there,
that merchant Bhogavarman proceeded to conduct his own customary business.
Taking a vessel from one person, he gave it to another at that very moment;
even without his own wealth, he produced dinars from the earth.
He quickly placed those dinars in the hand of his servant,
so that she might provide various foods and drinks for his wife.
And in an instant, a certain friend named Icchābharaṇa approached Bhogavarman with great haste and said to him:
"The meal is ready for us; arise, come, let us eat! For other friends have gathered and are standing here waiting for you. (SoKss 9.4.194)
To him who was saying, "I will not come today, for this guest is staying with me," that friend spoke to him once again.
"Then let this guest also come along with you.
Is he not also our friend? Arise quickly!"
Thus, out of persistence, Bhogavarman was led by that friend;
having gone together with Yaśovarman, he enjoyed excellent food.
Having drunk his wine and returned home in the evening,
that Yaśovarman again partook of various kinds of food and drink.
When night had arrived, he asked his own attendants:
"Is there enough *saraka* for us tonight, or not?"
"Master, there is none," he said; the merchant then went to his bed, saying, "How shall we drink water today during the latter part of the night?"
Then Yaśovarman, having fallen asleep by his side, saw in a dream two or three men entering there, and others behind them.
"Why was the sake of the latter part of the night not considered by you today for the sake of Bhogavarman’s drink? Where have you been staying, O deceivers? (SoKss 9.4.202)
Thus, those men who entered later, carrying staffs in their hands,
struck with blows from their staffs out of anger those who had entered earlier.
Saying, "This is our one transgression; may it be forgiven," those men who had been struck by the staff and others departed from there.
Then Yaśovarman, having seen that, woke up and reflected:
"The arrival of Bhogavarman’s wealth and glory is beyond thought and is truly praiseworthy."
"Though she is prosperous, she is devoid of enjoyments; she is not the wealth of Arthavarman's purpose.
As he was thinking thus, the night passed away.
And in the morning, having taken leave of that excellent merchant, Yaśovarman then went once more to the feet of the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas.
While established in austerity, he chose from those two previously mentioned forms of Śrī the one seen in his dream—
the Śrī of enjoyment— and she granted it to him there.
Then Yaśovarman, having returned home by the grace of the Goddess,
lived happily with a splendor of enjoyments that came upon him unexpectedly.
Thus, even a very small fortune endowed with enjoyments is better;
however, a vast fortune devoid of enjoyments is useless.
Is it because of King Camarabāla’s wealth in miserliness that you suffer?
Do you not observe your own prosperity, which is rich in both giving and enjoyment?
Therefore, an attack against him is not auspicious for you;
there is no favorable moment for an expedition, nor is victory even visible.
Although addressed thus by that astrologer, those five kings,
unable to endure King Camaravāla, set out toward him.
Having learned that they had reached the border, King Camaravāla, intending to set out for battle,
first bathed and worshipped Hara.
And he praised him appropriately with auspicious names that destroy sins and grant all desires— names fixed upon sixty-eight supreme states.
"O King, fight without hesitation; you shall conquer your enemies in battle"—thus he then heard a voice arising from the sky.
Then, filled with joy and having equipped himself, King Camaravāla, accompanied by his own forces, went forth to battle the enemies before him.
In the army of his enemies, there were thirty thousand elephants, three hundred thousand horses, and ten million foot soldiers.
In his own army, there were twenty lakhs of foot soldiers;
there were also ten thousand elephants and one lakh of horses.
When the great battle between those two armies had commenced, the gatekeeper named Vīra— whose name was true to his character— advanced at their head.
That king himself, with his yak-tail fan,
entered that field of battle just as the Blessed One, the Great Boar, entered the great ocean.
And though his army was small, he crushed that great enemy force in such a way that there were heaps of horses, elephants, and foot soldiers.
Having run toward that army of warriors who had come before him,
he struck the king with a spear, dragged him with a noose, and bound him.
Then, having likewise dragged out the second king, Samaraśūra, who had been struck in the heart by an arrow, he bound him with that very same noose.
And there, his doorkeeper named Vīra captured the king named Samarajita and brought him before him.
The commander Devabala brought and presented before him King Pratāpacandra, the fourth, who had been struck by an arrow.
Then, having seen that, the fifth king named Pratāpasena rushed in battle toward King Camaravāla out of anger.
Having shaken off those arrows and pierced him with a shower of his own shafts,
King Camaravāla struck him in the forehead with three swift arrows.
Then, like Time itself, he drew him in by means of a noose cast around his neck and brought him under his control, as he reeled from the blow of the arrow.
Thus, when those five had been thoroughly bound by the king, the remaining armies fled toward their respective directions.
Immeasurable gold, jewels, and the like, as well as many female attendants,
were obtained by King Camaravāla from those other rulers.
And in their midst was the great queen, renowned as Yaśolekhā,
that most excellent of women, who had been obtained by King Pratāpasena.
Then, having entered the city, he bound the turbans upon Vīradeva and Balasena, the chamberlain and the commander-in-chief, and filled them with jewels.
That king made Yaśolekhā, the chief queen of Pratāpasena, his own consort, because she had been won through the duty of a Kṣatriya.
Thinking, "I was won by his arm," that fickle woman tolerated him;
for those who have set out upon the path of delusion through desire, their latent impression of dharma is mottled.
And on that day, being entreated by Queen Yaśolekhā,
King Camaravāla released all five of those bound monarchs.
Having honored Pratāpasena and the others, who were bowed down and had received his instruction,
he released them and sent them forth to their own kingdoms.
Then that lord of the Camaravāla realm ruled for a long time his own prosperous kingdom, now free of thorns and with its enemies conquered;
and he took delight with that Yaśolekhā, whose beauty and loveliness surpassed even those of the finest apsarases, and who was a banner of victory over his foes.

In this way, even alone, a steadfast man— whose courage is peerless and who has shattered the fever of their core pride and arrogance— conquers at the head of battle even many enemies who have rushed forward impetuously, who are agitated by hatred, and who disregard the distinction between self and other.
Having heard this meaningful tale told by Gomukha and having offered praise,
Naravāhanadatta then performed his daily duties, beginning with his bath.
Accompanied by his women, he spent that night likewise singing himself out of a passion for music;
meanwhile, Sarasvatī, stationed in the sky, bestowed upon him the boon of long-standing intimacy with his beloveds.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fifth Wave.
Then, on another day, while he was staying in the residence of Alaṃkāravatī—
He [spoke] to that Naravāhanadatta in the presence of all the ministers.
Then the servant of Marubhūti, the uterine brother of the chamberlain who protected that inner apartment, approached and made this representation: SoKss_9,5.2 //
"O Lord, I have performed service for Marubhūti for two years;
food and clothing were provided by him to me and my wife."
"Furthermore, fifty dīnāras were promised by him to me every year; he does not give those to me."
While he was searching for this very foot, I was struck by it;
consequently, I have now been seated here at your lion-gate.
"If the Lord does not grant me this even as I reflect upon it, I shall enter the fire; what more need I say? For he is my master."
When he had finished speaking, Marubhūti said:
"I ought to give him dinars, but at present I have none."
When his minister Marubhūti had spoken thus while everyone was laughing,
Naravāhanadatta addressed him:
"Why is there such foolishness in you? This intellect of yours is not superior.
Arise and give him a hundred dinars without delay!"
Having heard these words of his master, Marubhūti was filled with shame;
he immediately brought that [money] and gave those hundred dīnāras to him.
Then Gomukha spoke there: "O Lord, the creation of Prajāpati has such diverse mental dispositions that Marubhūtika should not be censured."
Have you not heard here this story of the long-suffering king Prasaṅga and his servant? SoKss_9,5.12 //
Long ago, there was a king named Ciradāta, the lord of Cirapura;
though he himself was a good man, his retinue was exceedingly wicked.
It is said that a servant named Prasaṅga, having arrived from another country,
became an attendant to that king along with two friends.
As he performed service for five years,
that king gave him nothing at all, even on occasions such as festivals.
And he did not obtain an opportunity to inform his lord because of the wickedness of his attendants, who were constantly inciting him.
Once, the young son of that king passed away;
seeing him in distress, all the attendants gathered around him.
And in the midst of that, out of sheer grief, that servant named Prasaṅga,
even though being restrained by his two friends, addressed the king.
"O King, we have been your servants for a long time, yet nothing has been given to us by you; nevertheless, we remain here with the hope that you might grant it to your son."
"If you do not give it, then your son will give it to us;
but if he too is taken away by fate, what can we do in this matter now?"
Having said, "Let us go," he fell at the king's feet;
then, accompanied by his two friends, he departed from that presence.
"Aha! These servants of mine are so firmly attached even to my son;
therefore, I must not abandon them. Having reflected thus at that very moment—
The king summoned those who were habitually addicted to such vices and satisfied them with wealth in such a way that poverty never again touched them.
"O King, such diverse natures are seen among embodied beings;
at what time that king gave [gifts], at that time he did not give them when it was the wrong time."
Having spoken thus, that Gomukha, skilled in the narration of stories,
further related this tale at the command of the daughter of the Lord of Vatsa.
Formerly, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, there was an excellent city named Kanakapura, whose citizens were purified by its waters and which was delightful due to good governance.
Where the binding of the poet’s words was seen as a break upon the ears, and the breaking of women’s tresses was seen as a threshing-floor during the harvest of grain. (SoK 9.5.27)
There, from Priyadarśana, the son of Vāsuki,
the lord of nāgas, a man of great renown was born to the princess named Yaśodharā.
In former times, there was a king named Kanakavarṣa in that city;
though he bore the entire burden of the earth, he was adorned with every virtue.
He was greedy for fame, not for wealth; he was afraid of sin, not of enemies;
and he was a fool regarding the slander of others, not regarding the sacred scriptures.
In that great-souled one, there was little anger and much grace;
in that firm-minded one, his fist was clenched only upon the bow, never in the act of giving.
By him, who protects the entire world with such an exceedingly wonderful form,
even the host of women was made distressed by the affliction of Māra merely upon being seen.
Once, during the autumn season, when the heat had subsided and the elephants were in rut,
amidst a retinue of royal swans, while the subjects were filled with festive joy—
To sport with one whose virtues were equal to his own, he entered a painted palace,
cooled by breezes carrying the fragrance of drawn-out lotuses.
While he was thus gazing upon and praising that painting,
the doorkeeper entered and addressed the king.
"O Lord, an unprecedented painter has arrived here from Vidarbha,
proclaiming himself to be peerless in the art of painting."
And by that man named Roladeva, having painted this deity here at the lion-gate,
a proclamation was indeed hung today.
Upon hearing this, the king respectfully ordered his attendant to fetch him;
the doorkeeper went and brought the painter back in an instant.
Having entered, he saw there in private that King Kanakavarṣa standing amidst the playful display of viewing the paintings.
His body’s weight was supported by the bosoms of beautiful women,
and he held a roll of betel leaf with his hand playfully raised.
Having bowed and sat down before the king, who had shown him due respect,
that painter Roladeva addressed him slowly.
"O Lord, this notice was hung by me out of a desire to see your lotus feet;
it did not grant me knowledge. This of mine should be forgiven."
"O Lord, let it be commanded: what form should I paint here on this canvas? May this effort of mine in training in the arts bear fruit."
When the painter had spoken thus, the king said to him:
"Teacher, paint whatever you please."
"We delight your eyes; what delusion could there be regarding your skill?"—when the king had spoken thus, those standing by his side replied.
"Let the king himself be painted; what is the use of other misshapen forms?
Hearing this, the painter was pleased and painted that king.
With a prominent bridge of the nose, long and reddish eyes,
a broad forehead, and dark, curled locks of hair.
With his broad chest adorned by the scars of arrows and other wounds,
and with his pair of arms— shapely like the trunks of world-elephants— captivating to behold.
With his waist, which could be measured by a single fist, he was like a young lion cub who had been presented as a tribute after being conquered by his prowess.
And with a pair of thighs resembling the girth-ropes of the elephant of youth,
and with a beautiful pair of feet resembling the tender sprouts of the *aśoka* tree.
Upon seeing the king depicted in a form so perfectly suited to his own,
everyone then offered words of praise to that painter.
And we do not wish to see that Lord alone, who has cursed the world,
here upon this painted wall while these others are depicted alongside him.
"O Preceptor, having carefully considered one among these queens who is suitable, paint her here by my side; may it be a full feast for our eyes."
Having heard that and looked there, the painter said:
"Even among these many women, there is not one who is equal to the king."
And I know that on this very earth there is no woman equal to her in beauty;
there is one princess—listen, and I shall tell you of her.
In Vidarbha there is a glorious city named Kuṇḍina,
and there dwells a lord of the earth renowned as Devaśakti.
He had a queen named Anantavatī, dearer to him than his own life;
by her he had a daughter born, Madanasundarī by name.
Who like me would dare to describe her form with this single tongue? Nevertheless, I shall say this much.
Having created her, I believe that even the Creator, though his desire was already fulfilled by the taste of that creation,
would not know how to create another of such form even in the course of many ages.
On this earth, there was a princess who was the equal of King Saika in beauty, grace, and modesty, as well as in age and lineage.
While staying there, I once sent a maidservant and was summoned;
I went to the inner apartments of that princess.
There I saw her, anointed with moist sandalwood paste,
wearing a necklace of lotus stalks, tossing about upon a bed of lotus leaves.
Fanned by her companions with palm leaves,
she was pale and emaciated, displaying the manifest signs of the fever of love.
"O friends, what has been achieved by you with these sandalwood ointments and breezes from plantain leaves? What is the use of this fruitless exertion of yours?"
For these [objects], though cool, burn me who am of little merit,
even as they thus restrain their friends who are busily engaged in consoling them.
Beholding her in that condition, my mind agitated by thoughts concerning her,
I offered my salutations and sat down before her.
"Preceptor, having painted such a likeness, give me the payment," he said,
holding the brush in a trembling hand.
Slowly drawing on the ground, the princess showed him that she had been sketching a certain youth, more handsome than anyone else.
Having painted that beautiful form, O Lord, I thought:
"It is Kāma himself who has been depicted by me here in person."
"But since your bow is made of flowers and it was not drawn by him, I know that this is not Kāma; he must be some youth of that same form."
Surely he must have been seen by her somewhere, or perhaps even heard of;
for this manifestation of passion in her has this very thing as its cause.
Therefore, I must depart from here, for this king wields a terrible rod of punishment;
if his father Devaśakti were to learn of this, he would not tolerate it on my account.
Having reflected thus, I bowed to that princess Madanasundarī and departed from there,
honored by her.
And in this matter, O Great King, I have heard from my attendants as they spoke privately among themselves how she felt affection for you upon hearing of you.
Then, taking that princess who had been secretly painted upon a canvas,
I have come quickly to the feet of your majesty.
And having seen the King’s appearance, my doubt has been dispelled;
it was the King himself whom she depicted in the painting with my own hand.
"And because she cannot be depicted even once as truly similar [to the original],
I shall not paint her by the side of the God in the picture, however much she may resemble him."
When Roladeva had spoken thus, the king said to him:
"In that case, let her who is depicted on that painted cloth be shown by you."
Then, having pulled it out from the bag, he showed the painting to the king—
the Madanasundarī depicted within that picture.
King Kanakavarṣa, too,
upon beholding her even in that painted form with her wondrous beauty, immediately fell under the sway of love.
And having rewarded that painter with much gold,
the king, taking the portrait of his beloved, entered the inner apartments.
There, his eyes satiated by the sight of her form and beauty,
he stood with all other activities abandoned, his mind entirely absorbed in her alone.
Finding his opportunity, he harassed him, striking him with arrows,
like the god of love who, provoked by rivalry over beauty, assails one who has stolen his steadfastness.
The very same passion of love that was bestowed upon women by him, who were greedy for his beauty,
has now, as it were, borne fruit for that king in a hundred branches.
Then, after some days, having become thin and pale from separation,
he disclosed his inner thoughts to his trusted ministers who questioned him.
And having consulted with them, he dispatched a messenger to King Devaśakti to request the hand of the maiden Madanasundarī.
He was named Saṃgamasvāmin; he knew the proper time, understood what ought to be done, was a learned Brahmin of noble birth, and spoke with sweet and dignified speech.
Having traveled with a most magnificent retinue, that brahmin Saṃgamasvāmin entered the city of Kuṇḍina in Vidarbha.
There he beheld King Devaśakti as he truly was;
for the sake of his master, he requested the king's daughter from him.
"I must first give her to another, for he is a suitable match;
King Kanakavarṣa, like one of us, even now requests her hand."
Having deliberated, "I shall give this one to him," he too,
through the power of the gods, placed his faith in the words of Saṃgamasvāmin.
And that lord of the earth showed him the wondrous dance of his daughter Madanasundarī, as if it were her very form.
Then the king, having promised to give him his daughter, honored Saṃgamasvāmin— who was delighted by that sight— and sent him on his way.
"Having determined an auspicious moment, please come here for the sake of the marriage"; having thus instructed him, he dispatched a return messenger along with him.
Then Saṃgamasvāmin, accompanied by his counter-ambassador,
arrived and reported to King Kanakavarṣa that the mission had been accomplished.
Then, having determined an auspicious moment and honored that counter-messenger,
he repeatedly ascertained that Madanasundarī was indeed enamored.
For the sake of that marriage, King Kanakavarṣa, possessing irresistible valor and a mind free from hesitation, set out for that city of Kuṇḍina.

Mounted upon an Ashoka creeper, he struck down the lions and other beasts dwelling in the remote forests— creatures that snatch away the lives of living beings— just as he would have slain the Śabara tribesmen.
Having reached the city of Vidarbha, he entered that city of Kuṇḍina,
accompanied by King Devaśakti who had gone out ahead of him.
There, providing a festival for the eyes of the city's matrons,
he entered the royal palace where the preparations for the wedding were being readied.
There he rested for that day with his retinue,
gratified by the noble conduct shown to him by King Devaśakti.
On another day, Devaśakti gave that daughter Madanasundarī to him, together with his entire property, leaving only the kingdom behind.
Having stayed there for seven days, King Kanakavarṣa then returned to his own city together with that new bride.
When he, who bestows joy upon the world, arrived united with his beloved,
that city was filled with celebration like the sky when the moon is accompanied by the moonlight.
Then Madanasundarī became dearer than life to that king,
even though he had a vast harem, just as Rukmiṇī was to Acyuta.
With their eyes fixed upon one another’s faces,
those two, husband and wife, remained as if nailed down by the arrows of Love, which possessed beautiful lashes.
And once there arrived here the lion of spring, with its rows of blossoming filaments,
shattering the elephant-like pride of haughty women.
The spring season prepared the blossoming mango creepers as bow-strings for the flower-arrowed god of love,
whose bowstring was a row of bees clinging to the tips of the flowers.
And the Malaya breeze blew, shaking the minds of the women of the travelers like groves of trees, inflaming their passion.
The fullness of rivers, the blossoms of trees, and the digits of the moon return once more when diminished; but the youth of embodied beings does not.
"O you who have abandoned pride and quarrels, rejoice together with your beloveds!"—
thus, as it were, did the cuckoos address the people with their sweet songs.
And at that time, King Kanakavarṣa entered the Madhu garden to enjoy himself there together with all his harem women.
He robbed the *aśoka* trees of their splendor with the red garments of his attendants,
and he silenced the songs of the beautiful women with the cries of cuckoos and bees.
There, that king, together with Queen Madanasundarī and his harem,
sported in activities such as gathering flowers.
Having stayed there for a very long time, the king descended into the Godāvarī to bathe and engaged in water-sports together with the members of his harem.
With their faces they were lotuses, with their eyes blue water-lilies,
with their breasts pairs of *cakravāka* birds, and with their hips sandy banks.
Having conquered that river, her women agitated its depths,
displaying the frown of indignation through their tossing waves.
At that time, his mind took delight in those women of Kanakavarṣa, whose graceful movements of their limbs were revealed by garments shifting as they moved through the water.
And he struck the queen once with water from his hand upon her pair of breasts, which resembled two golden jars, as her garment had slipped away.
Seeing that, Madanasundarī became angry with her out of jealousy; as if agitated, she said: "How much can a river be disturbed? (SoKss 9.5.120)
Having emerged from the water, she departed for her own palace in anger, wearing another garment and recounting her beloved’s offense to her friends.
Then, having understood her intention, King Kanakavarṣa abandoned his water-sport and went to her dwelling.
Though he was being forbidden there even by the parrots staying in their cages,
he entered in anger and saw the queen within, afflicted by grief.
With her lotus-like face resting dejectedly upon the palm of her left hand,
she was drenched by falling teardrops resembling clear pearls.
If separation cannot be endured, then pride should be avoided by you; O heart, if separation can be endured, then pride alone should be increased by you.
"If separation cannot be endured, then pride must be abandoned by you, even for the sake of happiness; O heart, if separation can be endured, then pride alone must be increased by you.
Having understood this skillfully, remain hanging on with a single thread of hope.
Having drunk what was given by a fool and having settled in the middle [of the night], you will surely perish.
"Knowing this, stand skillfully, grasping one side while placing your feet on both banks; if you fall into the middle, you will certainly perish"—
reciting this verse from the *Dvipadī* in a voice choked with tears, she spoke.
With a voice that captivated with the luster of emerging rays of teeth, yet charmingly accented with Apabhraṃśa.
And beholding her in such a state, beautiful even in her anger,
that king approached her both with shame and with fear.
Then, embracing her as she turned her face away with words tender with affection, he began to propitiate her with humble entreaties.
And he fell at her feet, censuring himself as a sinner, while his retinue was made to feel ashamed by his indirect speech.
Then, as if sprinkling him with tears fallen from her own grief,
she clung to the neck of the lord of the earth and was reconciled.
Then, having spent that day with her— whose anger had been appeased by his devotion— the king, delighted,
enjoyed sexual pleasure with her and fell asleep at night.
While asleep, he suddenly saw in a dream that a single-string necklace had been taken from his neck and the crest-jewel from his head by a woman of distorted appearance.
Then he also saw a vetāla with a body composed of the limbs of various creatures;
and as that vetāla engaged him in a wrestling match, he threw him down to the ground.
Seated upon his back, the king was carried through the air like a bird taking flight by that vetāla,
and he was then cast into the ocean.
Then, having somehow emerged, he saw that the single-stringed pearl necklace was around his neck and that crest-jewel remained on his head as it had been before.
Having seen this, the king woke up and, at dawn, questioned the mendicant who had come from his previous acquaintance about the fruit of his dream:
"It is not that something unpleasant should be said; rather, why should I not speak when I have been asked?"
"That single-string necklace which was seen by you, and likewise the crest-jewel that was taken—
this shall be your separation from the queen and from your son."
And when the single-string pearl necklace is obtained by you after crossing the ocean,
then at the end of your suffering, there will also be that reunion with the princess.
When the mendicant had spoken thus, the king reflected and said:
"I do not yet have a son; let him first be born."
Then, from a reciter of the Rāmāyaṇa who had arrived, he heard about King Daśaratha,
who had undergone great hardships for the sake of his son.
When the Kṣapaṇaka had departed, King Kanakavarṣa, his mind preoccupied with the thought of obtaining a son born from him, passed that day in dejection.
And one night, while lying alone in bed and suddenly awake,
he saw a woman who had entered inside even though the door was not opened.
Disciplined and gentle in appearance, she spoke to the lord of the earth, who had risen in wonder and offered his salutation, after she had bestowed her blessing upon him.
"Son, know me to be the daughter of Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas;
I am your father’s elder sister, known by the name Ratnaprabhā."
For the sake of protecting you, I have always dwelt near you while remaining unseen;
today, seeing you filled with anxiety, I have revealed my true self to you.
"I cannot bear to see your distress; therefore, tell me the cause.
Thus addressed by his father's sister, the king spoke to her.
"I am blessed, O Mother, that you show such grace toward me;
know also that my lack of peace is caused by the fact that no son has been born to me."
O Mother, if even royal sages such as Daśaratha and others sought that place in ancient times for the sake of heaven, how could those like me not desire it?
Having heard these words of King Kanakavarṣa,
the Nāga maiden Ratnaprabhā spoke to her brother’s son.
"In that case, my son, I shall tell you one means; perform it!
Go and entreat Svāmikumāra for this purpose."
"You shall endure the unbearable Kumāradhārā falling upon your head as an obstacle,
once it has entered within your body through my power."
"Having overcome the multitude of obstacles, you shall obtain whatever else you desire.
Having spoken thus, the Nāga woman vanished; the king, filled with joy, passed the night.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers in the morning out of a desire for a son,
that king went to the feet of Svāmikumāra.
There he performed intense austerities in order to propitiate that Lord,
his strength being offered by the Nāgī who had entered within his body.
Then, like a thunderbolt, that stream of water from the prince began to fall incessantly upon the king's head.
But that novice, by the power of the nāginī within his body, [overcame] her;
then Guha dispatched Heramba to create an obstacle for him.
And there Heramba created a great poison in the midst of the stream;
it was an exceedingly fierce serpent, yet he did not tremble even because of that.
Then Vināyaka himself, invincible even by the gods, approached and proceeded to strike his chest with the blows of his tusks.
Considering that god invincible, King Kanakavarṣa then proceeded to honor him with hymns of praise, enduring all the hardships involved.
Homage to you, O Vighneśa, whose form is like a jar that is a treasure-trove for the accomplishment of all aims— O Lambodara, adorned with serpents!
Victory to you, O Elephant-faced One, who causes even Brahmā to tremble by shaking his lotus-throne with the playful strike of your upraised trunk!
Even for the lords of the gods, asuras, and sages, there are no spiritual accomplishments if you,
the sole refuge of the world and beloved of Śaṅkara, are not satisfied.
Ghaṭodara, Śūrpakarṇa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Madotkaṭa,
Pāśahasta, Ambarīṣa, Jambaka, and Triśikhāyudha.
Thus did the supreme gods praise you with sixty-eight names that destroy evil, each fixed to its corresponding station.
O Lord, for one who remembers and praises you, fear born of battle,
royal families, gambling, thieves, fire, wild beasts, and so forth, perishes.
Thus, with these words of praise and many others of various kinds,
King Kanakavarṣa worshipped that Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara).
"I am pleased; I shall not create obstacles for you. Obtain a son," said Vighnajit to that king, and having spoken thus, he vanished on the spot.
Then the Lord Kumāra said to that king who was bearing the stream of water:
"O steadfast one, I am pleased with you; ask for a boon."
Having heard that, the king was delighted and petitioned the god:
"O Lord, by your grace, let a son be born to me."
"Let it be so; you shall have a son born from a portion of my host, O lord of the earth, and he shall be named Hiraṇyavarṣa."
Having spoken thus, the one whose vehicle is peacocks (Indra), desiring to show him special favor, invited the king to enter within the inner sanctum.
Therefore, that nāgī emerged invisibly from the body of the king;
for women, fearing a curse, do not enter the prince’s quarters.
Then Kanakavarṣa, by his own human splendor,
entered the inner chamber of that god Pāvaka.
Seeing that king deprived of his former splendor because he was no longer sustained by the Naga's power, the god also wondered, "What could this be?"
Having learned that his severe vow had been carried out under the pretext of the power of the Nāga women,
Guha, incensed by that [Nāga]’s resolve, cursed the king.
"O Durdānta, because you have practiced deceit, you shall suffer separation from your newborn son and from the Great Queen."
Having heard this curse, as terrible as a thunderbolt, that king,
a great poet, cast off his delusion and praised the god with well-spoken hymns.
Then Ṣaṇmukha, delighted by those well-spoken words, addressed him:
"O King, I am pleased with your eloquent verses; I shall tell you that end to your curse."
For one year you shall suffer separation from your wife and son;
thereafter, being freed from the three types of untimely death, you shall regain them.
Having spoken thus, when the Six-faced One had ceased speaking,
the king, having bowed to him and being satiated by the nectar of his grace, returned to his own city.
There, from that Queen Madanasundarī, a son was born in due course, like a flow of nectar from the moon amidst its moonlight.
Then, having beheld the face of their son, both the king and the queen were so overwhelmed by excessive joy that they could not contain it within themselves.
At that time, raining down wealth, the king held a festival,
bringing his own name, "Golden Shower" (*kanakavarṣa*), to its literal truth upon the earth.
When five nights had passed and on the sixth night,
while the protective rites were being performed there in the birth-chamber, a cloud arrived unexpectedly.
As he gradually attained growth there, he covered the sky,
just as a neglected enemy might seize the kingdom of a negligent king.
Then, like a rutting elephant intoxicated by wind, uprooting trees with its torrential spray, it began to charge forward.
At that moment, having flung open the bolted door,
a certain terrifying woman with a dagger in her hand entered that birth-chamber.
Having snatched away her son, whose face was pressed against Madanasundarī’s breasts,
she fled from the queen, utterly bewildering the attendants.
"Alas, alas! My son has been carried off by a rākṣasī!"—thus crying out in distress, the queen pursued that woman even through the darkness.
And having gone there, that woman fell into the lake along with her child;
the queen also followed after them, falling in that very place out of longing for her offspring.
In an instant the cloud withdrew and the night came to an end;
and the wailing of the attendants was heard in the birth-chamber.
Then King Kanakavarṣa, having heard that and arrived at the birth-chamber,
fell into a swoon upon seeing it empty of his beloved son.
Having regained his composure, he lamented, "O Queen! O dear little son!
and then remembered that curse which had its limit set for one year.
"O Blessed One, why was this boon granted by you to me, one of such little merit, when it is beset by a curse? O Skanda, it is like nectar mixed with poison."
Alas! How shall I pass this year, which seems like a thousand ages, without the goddess Madanasundarī, who was dearer to me than my own life?
Thus lamenting, the king, though being consoled by his ministers who were informed of the events,
could not regain his composure regarding the queen who had passed away.
And gradually, helpless under the impulse of passion, he departed from the city;
wandering about with his mind distraught, he entered the Vindhya forest.
There, he beheld the beauty of his beloved’s eyes through the eyes of young does,
and the splendor of the mass of her braided hair through the clusters of yak-tail tufts.
As he recalled those elephants and their female mates, whose gait had become sluggish with passion, the fire of his love blazed up even more intensely.
Wandering on, exhausted by the heat of thirst, he reached the foot of the Vindhya mountains;
having drunk the water of a mountain torrent, he sat down at the root of a tree.
Then, roaring like a loud laugh from the mouth of the Vindhya cave,
a maned lion emerged and sprang forward to kill him.
At that very moment, a certain Vidyadhara descended from the sky and, swooping down with speed,
split that lion in two with a blow of his sword.
Approaching the king, that sky-goer asked him:
"O King Kanakavarṣa, how have you come to this land?"
Having heard that, the king regained his memory and replied to him:
"How do you know me, who am consumed by the fire of separation?"
Then the Vidyadhara said: "Formerly, having become a renunciant, I lived in your city as a human being named Bandhumitra."
"Since you have rendered assistance here at my request through your service,
I have attained the state of a Vidyādhara by means of the accomplishment of the heroic Vetāla."
Recognizing you for that reason, so as to perform a service for you,
I slew this lion upon seeing it intent on killing you.
To him who was saying, "Today I have become Bandhuprabha by name," King Kanakavarṣa, feeling born affection, spoke to him:
Ah, I remember that friendship which was cultivated by you here;
therefore, tell me, when will the reunion with my wife and son take place?
Having heard these words of his and having understood them through the power of his magic science,
that Vidyādhara Bandhuprabha spoke to the king:
"By the grace of Vindhyavāsinī, you shall obtain a wife and a son;
therefore, go there for the sake of success, while I depart for my own world."
When he had spoken thus and departed into the sky, King Kanakavarṣa, having regained his composure, slowly set out to see that goddess dwelling in the Vindhya mountains.
As that king was traveling along the road, a great wild elephant with its head shaking, intoxicated and with its trunk extended, charged toward him.
Seeing that, the king fled by way of the chasm;
as he pursued him, the elephant perished from falling into the abyss.
Then that king, exhausted by the fatigue and toil of the journey, as he proceeded by degrees,
reached a great lake abounding in tall white lotuses.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, and having eaten the lotus stalks,
he rested at the foot of a tree and was for a moment overcome by sleep.
Just then, some Śabaras returning from a hunt came along that path and saw the king, endowed with auspicious marks, lying fast asleep.
And having bound him for the purpose of an offering to the goddess, they took him at that very moment to the presence of their own Śabara king named Muktāphala.
That lord of the Śabaras, having observed him to be praiseworthy,
led the king to the abode of the Goddess who dwells in the Vindhyas in order to make him a sacrificial victim.
As soon as he saw the goddess and bowed before her,
by her grace and through the favor of Skanda, the king’s bonds were loosened.
Beholding that wonder and considering it to be the goddess's favor toward him,
the lord of the Śabaras released the king from execution.
Thus, for Kanakavarṣa, who had escaped from his third untimely death,
that year of the curse came to an end.
And at that moment, his paternal aunt, that Nāga woman, arrived there taking Queen Madanasundarī along with her son.
And he said to him: "O King, having learned of the curse of Kumāra, I have taken these two to my own abode and protected them by employing appropriate means."
Therefore, O Kanakavarṣa, accept these two, your own dear son and daughter;
enjoy this sovereignty over the earth, for your curse has now been exhausted.
Having spoken thus, the nāga woman vanished from before the king as he bowed;
the king, for his part, regarded the arrival of his wife and son as if it were a dream.
Then, as the king and queen finally embraced one another after a long time,
the pain of their separation dissolved along with their tears of joy.
Then, having learned that the lord Kanakavarṣa was the sovereign of the earth,
that Śabarendra Muktāphala fell at his feet.
Having asked for his forgiveness and led him into his own village,
he attended upon him and his wife and children with various services appropriate for himself.
Then, remaining there, the king had his father-in-law, King Devaśakti, and his own army summoned from his city by means of messengers.
Then King Kanakavarṣa, having placed his beloved wife Asthitakareṇukā and their son— named Hiraṇyavarṣa as ordained by the six-faced god (Kārttikeya)—
before him, set out from the residence of his father-in-law, accompanied by them.
And after a few days, he reached his father-in-law’s home situated in the Vidarbha region, that city named Kuṇḍina;
there, honored by his father-in-law, he dwelt for some days in that prosperous place, accompanied by his son, his wife, and his army.
Then, setting out slowly from there, he reached his own city of Kanakapura,
as if being drunk in by the eyes of the city's women who had long been longing for him.
And that king, accompanied by his son and joined by Madanasundarī,
entered the capital like a festival incarnate, endowed with the splendor of joy.
Having consecrated her and bound the ceremonial turban upon her head, he, honoring his subjects on this auspicious occasion, made Madanasundarī the chief of the entire harem.

Together with that queen and his son, King Kanakavarṣa held perpetual festivals; no longer suffering the pain of separation from those he had not seen before, he then ruled this earth, bounded by its four oceans, free from all thorns.
Having heard this charming story there from his chief minister Gomukha,
Prince Naravāhanadatta, together with Alaṅkāravatī, was greatly delighted.
Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Alaṃkāravatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Sixth Wave.
Then he, accompanied by his beloved, was delighted by the story told by Gomukha.
Having seen Marubhūti with a look of angry agitation out of jealousy toward him.
Naravāhanadatta addressed him, seeking to win him over:
"Marubhūti, why do you not also tell one story?"
Then, having said with a contented heart, "Very well, I shall tell it," Marubhūti proceeded to relate this story.
O King, in the past, in the city named Kamalapura, there was an excellent Brahmin belonging to King Kamalavarman known as Candrasvāmin.
To him was born a wife named Devamati, who was like a third goddess between Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, radiant with modesty, and equal in virtue to Sumati.
In her, the wife of that brahmin, was born a son endowed with auspicious marks; as soon as he was born, this voice arose from the sky: SoKss_9,6.6 //
"You must give birth to a son named Candrasvāmī;
for having become king, he shall protect the earth for a long time."
Having heard these divine words,
he held a celebratory festival and gave that very protector of the earth the name Candrasvāmin-suta.
And in due course, that protector of the earth grew up and was made to master the knowledge of weapons and missiles; he was trained equally in all branches of learning.
And at that very time, Candrasvāmin’s wife Devamati gave birth once more to a daughter, beautiful in every limb.
And she, named Candravatī, and that king—
those two brothers grew up in the palace of their father in due course.
Then, because the crops had been scorched by the rays of the sun, a calamity of famine caused by drought arose in that region.
And because of that fault, the king here began to act like a thief;
having abandoned the path of the righteous, he extracted wealth from his subjects through unrighteousness.
"Come, let us go from this city to my father's house;
for these two children might at some point perish here."
Having heard that, Candrasvāmin said to his wife:
"Do not do this; it is a great sin to flee from one's home during a famine."
"Therefore, taking these two children to their father's house, I shall place them there; you remain here, and I will return quickly."
Having spoken thus and established her in the house, she having replied "So be it," Candrasvāmin took those two children of his own and [departed] with his wife.
Then he set out from the city for his father’s house with both the protector of the earth and that maiden Candravatī, his wife.
Proceeding gradually, after three or four days he reached a great forest,
where the sands were scorched by the rays of the sun and the trees were withered and sparse.
Having left those two children there while they were overcome by thirst,
Candrasvāmin went far away to search for water for their sake.
Then, at the very front of that [procession], the lord of the Śabaras named Siṃhadaṃṣṭra arrived with his followers, having set out for some purpose somewhere.
Having seen him, and having understood that he was a hunter seeking water without even asking,
he made a sign and said to his servants, "Take this man and let him obtain water."
Having heard that, two or three of his servants, who had grasped his true intention,
led the upright Candrasvāmin to the village and bound him.
Realizing that he had bound himself for the sake of being offered as a human sacrifice to them,
Candrasvāmin grieved for his two children who had gone into the forest.
"Alas, O protector of the earth! Alas, dear Candravatī! How is it that I have abandoned you both in this trackless forest, leaving you as mere prey for lions and tigers?"
"My life has been destroyed by thieves, and I have no refuge," the Brahmin cried out, and in his distress, he beheld the sun in the sky.
"Alas! Abandoning this delusion, I shall take refuge in my own Lord.
Having reflected thus, the twice-born man began to praise the Sun.
Salutations to you, O All-pervading One, the Light who rests in the supreme ether,
who dispels both internal and external darkness.
You are Viṣṇu, pervading the three worlds; you are Śiva, the treasury of all that is auspicious;
stirring the sleeping universe into motion, you are the supreme Lord of Creatures.
"May these two, fire and moon, shine forth;
thus, as if out of compassion, you withdraw your own splendor within yourself during the night."
Even the *rākṣasas* flee and the bandits do not prevail;
the virtuous rejoice when you, O Radiant One, have risen.
O sole lamp of the three worlds, protect me who have come to you for refuge;
dispel this darkness of suffering for me and show compassion.
As this brahmin Candrasvāmin was thus praising the Sun with devotion through these and other verses, a voice issued forth from the sky:
"I am pleased with you, Candrasvāmin; you shall not suffer death.
And by my grace, there shall be a reunion for you with your sons and others."
Thus addressed by the divine voice,
Candrasvāmin remained there while still in the womb, having been provided with baths and food by the Śabara.
And at that moment, the protector of the earth was accompanied by his sister as they went to the forest;
with his father not yet arrived, he was distressed by lamentation and apprehensive of misfortune.
A great caravan leader named Sārthadharo, who had arrived by that same path, saw him and asked about his circumstances.
Having comforted him out of compassion and seeing that the child possessed auspicious marks,
the caravan leader then led him, accompanied by his sister, to his own country.
There, even in his childhood, that protector of the earth was devoted to the fire-rituals,
while the merchant looked on from his house out of affection for his son.
Once, the king’s minister came along that same path for the sake of a matter concerning one named Tārādharmā, a resident of Tārāpura.
The best of the twice-born, Anantasvāmin, entered the house of that merchant leader together with his elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers.
Having rested there and seen that protector of the earth of auspicious appearance,
who was devoted to the recitation of mantras and fire-rituals, he questioned him about his circumstances.
Realizing that he was childless, the minister,
desiring offspring, requested from the caravan leader Savarṇa both his daughter and her sister.
Then, having taken those two children given by that merchant,
Anantasvāmin went to Tārāpura with the caravan leader.
There, that protector of the earth, having been adopted as a son by the minister,
remained in his residence, which was filled with the abundant wealth of his magical sciences.
In the meantime, Siṃhadaṃṣṭra, the lord of the Bhillas, approached Candrasvāmin while he was still bound and spoke to him in that village.
O Brahmin, I was thus commanded by the divine Sun in a dream:
"Having honored him, you must release him; he is not to be killed by me. (SoKss 9.6.48)
Having said, "Therefore, rise and go as you wish," he released him,
having provided him with pearls and musk and arranged a forest escort for his journey.
Then, having been released from there, Candrasvāmin,
unable to find his son Mahīpāla in the forest, searched for him along with his younger brother.
Wandering along the shore of the ocean, he reached a city named Jalapura and,
having become a guest, entered the house of a certain brahmin.
There, after they had finished eating, that brahmin householder, on the occasion of conversation, spoke to Candrasvāmin regarding his own life story as it had been related.
In days past, a merchant named Kanakavarman arrived here;
by him was found in the forest a young Brahmin accompanied by his sister.
Having taken those two most excellent boys with him, he departed from here;
however, he did not mention their names on the great island of Nārikela.
Hearing that, thinking to himself, "Those two must surely be my own [sons]," Candrasvāmin made up his mind to go to that excellent island.
Having spent the night and searched for him, he formed an alliance with the merchant Viṣṇuvarman,
who was about to depart for the island of Nārikela.
And having embarked on that very ship together with him,
Candrasvāmin went by way of the ocean to that island out of affection for his son.
There, the merchants residing there said to him as he asked:
"A merchant named Kanakavarman certainly did come here."
Having taken the two sons of the brahmin upon reaching the Surūpā forest,
he has now departed from here for Kaṭāha Island accompanied by them.
Having heard that, the brahmin then went with the merchant Dānavarman, who was traveling by ship, to the island of Kaṭāha.
There too, that twice-born man heard that the merchant Kanakavarman had departed from that island for the island known as Karpūra.
Thus, traveling in succession to Karpūradvīpa, Suvarṇadvīpa, and Siṃhala along with merchants, he still did not find that merchant.
From the Siṃhalas, however, he heard that his own merchant had gone to the country of Kanakavarman, to the city named Citrakūṭa.
Then, having crossed the ocean by means of that ship, Candrasvāmin went together with a merchant named Koṭīśvara to Citrakūṭa.
There he encountered that merchant Kanakavarman,
and eager for news of his children, he related his entire story to him.
Then Kanakavarman, having learned of his distress, showed him those two children whom he had found and brought from the forest.
And as long as Candrasvāmin gazed upon those two boys, they were not his own at all; they were simply two others.
Then, afflicted by grief and despairing, he lamented with tears:
"Alas! Though I have wandered so far, neither a son nor a daughter has been found by me."
Like a wicked master, the Creator showed me hope but did not fulfill it;
and by that evil-souled one, I have been led astray in vain from afar to even further distance.
Lamenting in this manner, Candrasvāmin was gradually consoled by the merchant Kanakavarman; then, still grieving, he spoke.
If, while wandering the earth, I do not find those two sons of mine within a year,
then I shall abandon this body through asceticism on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
To him who had spoken thus, a certain wise man standing there replied:
"Go; by the grace of Nārāyaṇī, you shall surely regain those two sons."
Having heard that, his heart filled with joy as he recalled the favor of the Sun-god,
Candrasvāmin was honored by the merchants and departed from that city.
Then, gathering up agrahāras, villages, and cities,
he wandered and one evening reached a forest filled with many tall trees.
There, having subsisted on fruits and water to pass the night,
he climbed a tree and remained there, fearing lions, tigers, and other wild beasts.
And there, sleepless in the middle of the night, he saw beneath a tree the great assembly of Mothers gathered together, headed by Nārāyaṇī.
Having gathered various kinds of offerings suitable for himself,
he was indeed awaiting the arrival of the god Bhairava.
And there the mothers asked Nārāyaṇī, "O Goddess, why is he delaying today? She laughed, but did not speak.
And when she was questioned by them with great persistence, she replied to them:
"Friends, although this brings me shame, I shall nevertheless speak."
In this city of Surapura, there is a king named Surasena;
he has a daughter named Vidyādharī, renowned for her beauty.
And by him, for her who was to be given in marriage, there had been heard of a son of King Vimala named Prabhākara, who was equal to her in beauty.
While he was wishing to give her to that king, it was heard by Vimala that this daughter of his was a worthy match for his own son.
Then Vimala requested that daughter of Surasena from him through a messenger for the sake of his son.
Out of regard for the fulfillment of his expectations, Surasena gave that daughter to his son Prabhākara according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having reached her father-in-law’s city named Vimalapura,
that Vidyādharī went with her husband to their bedchamber at night.
There, while she was longing for him, she gazed at her husband Prabhākara as he slept without sexual union; yet, looking closely, she saw that he was not a man.
"Alas, I am ruined! How have I obtained a eunuch as my husband?
Thus grieving in her heart, the princess spent that night.
"How was I given away by you to a eunuch without your having investigated?
Having written this letter, she then dispatched it to her father.
"Having read the letter, my father became enraged at Vimala, thinking, 'I have been deceived by Vimala through a ruse.'"
"Enjoy the fruit of that daughter whom you had me give to your son under a pretext; behold, I am coming to kill you!"
Thus that king Surasena, overflowing with power, sent this message by his own hand to King Vimala.
And Vimala, having understood the meaning of that letter together with his ministers, reflected upon it; yet, regarding that invincible [enemy], he did not perceive any means [to overcome him].
Then the minister named Piṅgadatta said to Vimala:
"There is but one remedy for this; O King, employ it for your own welfare."
There is a yakṣa named Sthūlaśiras, and I know his mantra and the method of propitiation by which he grants desired boons.
Having propitiated the Yakṣa with that mantra you have taken up, now request a *liṅga* for the sake of a son; let the conflict be pacified immediately.
Having been addressed thus by the minister, the king took that mantra from him;
and for the sake of a son, having propitiated the Yakṣa, he requested a *liṅga* from him.
When the Yakṣa had now bestowed the male organ upon him,
his son became the man Prabhākara, while the Yakṣa himself became a neuter.
But that Vidyādharī, having seen that man Prabhākara and having obtained the pleasure of sexual union with him as her husband, reflected:
"I was deluded by the fault of intoxication; my husband is not a eunuch.
He is indeed a fortunate man; one should not entertain any other thought in this matter."
Having reflected thus and written this very matter, she, feeling ashamed, sent the letter again to her father; and by that means, he attained tranquility.
Having learned this account today, the enraged Bhairava summoned Sthūlaśiras and cursed that Guhyaka.
Since you have resorted to the state of a eunuch by abandoning your gender, therefore remain a eunuch for as long as you live; let that Prabhākara be a man.
Thus, having become a eunuch, that Guhyaka now partakes in suffering;
whereas Prabhākara, having become a man, enjoys the happiness of worldly pleasures.
"Because of this business today, there has been a slight delay in the arrival of Your Majesty;
know that he will arrive very soon."
While the goddess Nārāyaṇī was thus speaking to the Mothers,
the god Bhairava, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), arrived there.
Honored by all those Mothers with various offerings,
he danced for a moment with the *tāṇḍava* and sported in the company of the Yoginīs.
And as Candrasvāmin was looking from the top of the tree at all of that,
he saw a single maidservant of Nārāyaṇī, and she too beheld him.
And by fate, those two became filled with mutual longing;
and the goddess Nārāyaṇī perceived them to have become so.
Then, after Bhairava had departed along with his mother,
Nārāyaṇī lingered there and called out to Candrasvāmin, who was perched upon the tree.
Then, after he and her own maidservant had dismounted and arrived, she asked them both: "Do you have any mutual desire for one another?"
When they had thus informed her that she was indeed a queen,
she, the queen, having cast off her anger, spoke to that Candrasvāmin:
"I am satisfied by the truth you have spoken; I do not curse you both.
I give this maidservant to you; may you two be at peace."
Having heard that, the brahmin said: "O Goddess, even though the mind is fickle, I restrain it; nevertheless, I shall not touch another's wife."
"The nature of the mind is indeed this [fluctuation], but physical evil must be guarded against"—
to that wise Brahmin who had spoken thus, the goddess replied:
"I am pleased with you, and this is your boon: you shall soon obtain sons and other blessings.
And take from me this unfading lotus, which destroys poison and other evils."
Having spoken thus and having given the *nīraja* flower to the brahmin Candrasvāmin,
the goddess Nārāyaṇī, together with her eternal handmaidens, vanished from his sight.
Having obtained the lotus, he set out from there when the night had ended;
wandering about, the brahmin reached that city of Tārāpura.
There, his son Mahīpāla and his daughter remained in the house of that minister, the Brahmin Anantasvāmin.
Having gone there, desiring food from that very minister, he recited his lesson at the door; and hearing of that dear guest, [the minister] came out.
And that minister, having been announced by the doorkeepers and ushered inside,
invited the learned man to a meal as soon as he saw him.
Then, having been invited and hearing that there was a sin-removing lake there,
Candrasvāmin went to bathe in the one known as Anantahrada.
Then, as that twice-born man was returning after bathing, he heard from all sides throughout that city a cry of "Alas! Woe! (hā kaṣṭam).
When he asked the cause of that, the people said this to him:
"There stands here a young Brahmin named Mahīpāla."
He was found in the forest by Sārthadhara, the caravan leader;
Sulakṣaṇa, having seen him, requested him [to stay] along with his sister.
That minister was brought here with great effort by Anantasvāmin;
having been adopted as a son by him who had no son, he became his beloved.
"He who was the virtuous protector of King Tārāvarman and of this kingdom has today been bitten by a black snake; therefore, there is a cry of 'Alas! Alas! in the city."
Having heard this, Candrasvāmin, thinking to himself, "This is indeed that very son of mine," went quickly to the minister’s house.
There, seeing him surrounded by everyone and recognizing him as his son,
he rejoiced, holding in his hand the blue lotus of antidote given by the goddess.
And he offered that blue lotus to the king’s nose; at that very moment, by its fragrance, the king became free from poison.
The protector of the earth rose up, yet he remained as if still possessed by sleep;
and all the people in the city, together with the king, held a festival there.
And then Candrasvāmin,
being honored with wealth by Anantasvāmin, the citizens, and the king, was regarded as some portion of a god.
And there, honored in the minister’s residence, he remained at ease,
beholding his son Mahīpāla and his daughter Candravatī.
Even though they had recognized one another, all three remained silent;
for wise men who have regard for their duty do not manifest themselves at an improper time.
Then King Tārāvarman, inwardly gratified by his virtues,
gave his daughter named Bandhumatī to that protector of the earth.
Having given him half of his own kingdom,
that king— who had no other son— then entrusted the entire burden of sovereignty to him and lived happily.
Having obtained the kingdom, Mahīpāla also proclaimed his father as his own; having established his younger sister in her place, he remained there at ease.
Once his father, Candrasvāmin, spoke to him privately:
"Come, let us go to our own country in order to bring back your mother."
"Knowing you to be established in sovereignty, how could she have forgotten me because of him?
Thus, her son having suffered for so long, she might one day curse in her anger.
One who has been cursed by his mother and father never enjoys happiness;
in this regard, listen to this ancient story concerning the son of a merchant.
In the city named Dhavala, there was a merchant’s son named Cakra;
against the wishes of his parents, he went to Suvarṇadvīpa for the sake of trade.
Then, having acquired great wealth over five years,
he boarded a ship filled with jewels as he set out upon the ocean.
When but little remained of the ocean to be traversed,
a cloud arose, roaring and agitated by the force of great winds and rain.
As if thinking, "Why has he come here to despise his parents?",
the great waves broke his carriage in anger.
Some staying there were carried away by the waters; some were devoured by sea-monsters;
but Cakra, by the power of his life-force, was drawn out and cast onto the shore by the waves.
Remaining there, exhausted as if in a dream, that merchant’s son saw a certain man of fierce and dark appearance with a noose in his hand.
Then, having been lifted up by that man seated upon the lion-throne, the wheel, encircled by nooses, was carried far away to the assembly hall where he stood.
By his command, while he remained seated on his throne, that young merchant was led away by the same warder and confined within an iron house.
There he beheld a man being tormented within by a wheel that revolved incessantly upon his head with a glowing iron disc.
"Who are you? By what evil deed has this happened to you? Alas, how did this come to be?
Thus he questioned that wheel, and it replied to him in this way:
"I am a merchant’s son named Khaḍga; because I did not carry out the words of my parents, they became enraged and cursed me in their anger."
"O you of evil conduct, since you cause us pain with [your body] glowing like a heated iron wheel placed upon our heads, such shall be your own suffering."
Having spoken thus, they both ceased; then they said to me as I was weeping:
"Do not weep; let such suffering be yours for only one month."
Having heard that, I spent that day in grief, reclining upon my bed;
then at night, as if in a dream, I beheld a terrifying man who had arrived.
Therefore, having seized me by force, I was cast into this iron house,
and this flaming wheel has been placed upon my head and is spinning.
"Thus was this curse from my father; because of it, O Prāṇa, my life-breaths do not depart.
That month has now been completed, yet even so, I am not released."
To Khaḍga, who had spoken thus, Cakra replied with compassion:
"Even by me, while traveling abroad for the sake of wealth, the word of my parents was not heeded."
"Your acquired wealth shall perish," they both cursed me;
because of that, all my wealth earned from other islands was lost in the ocean.
