This is the very same situation elsewhere; what is the use of my life?
Give this wheel upon my head, and let your curse pass away from you.
Even as he was speaking thus, a divine voice was heard there:
"You have been released from the sword; place this wheel upon the head of Cakra."
Having heard that, at the very moment he placed the discus upon the head of the wheel,
that sword was carried away by some invisible being to the house of his father.
There he remained, never transgressing the commands of his parents;
then Cakrī, having placed the wheel upon his head, spoke thus to him.
"May others who are sinful also be liberated from their transgressions on this earth;
until my own sins are exhausted, may this wheel revolve upon my head."
When he of firm resolve had spoken thus, the gods stationed in the sky,
raining down a shower of flowers, were deeply gratified and spoke as follows:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Being! By this compassion, you have pacified your evil;
go, and your wealth shall become inexhaustible."
When the gods had spoken thus, that iron wheel of his instantly vanished from the head of the Discus and went somewhere out of sight.
Likewise, one young Vidyadhara arrived from the sky and,
having been sent by a pleased Indra, presented him with a highly precious collection of jewels.
Placing that wheel upon his hip, he brought it to his own city named Dhavala and departed just as he had come.
Then Cakra, having reached his parents' presence and gladdened his kinsmen,
remained there after recounting his adventures, never having fallen away from the Dharma.
Having thus addressed the protector of the earth, Candrasvāmin spoke again:
"O son, such is the fruit of sin: the provocation of one's mother and father."
Devotion to them is indeed like a wish-fulfilling cow; in this regard, listen to this story:
in former times, there was a certain sage who wandered in the forest and practiced great austerities.
Once, while he was seated in the shade of a tree, a crane dropped its excrement upon him;
he then looked up in anger and saw it.
Right there, he saw that crane reduced to ashes;
thereafter, that sage became possessed by pride in the power of his asceticism.
Once, having entered a certain brahmin’s house in a city, that sage requested alms from the housewife there.
"Wait a moment until I have finished my service to my husband," said that devoted wife to him.
Then, smiling at him as he gazed upon her with an angry look, she said:
"O sage, I am not a crane; let this be forgiven."
Having heard this, that sage sat down there in wonder, reflecting, "How indeed was this known by her?"
Then, having performed the fire-rituals and other duties, that virtuous woman attended to her husband there; then, taking alms, she approached the presence of that sage.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, the sage said to that virtuous woman:
"How was it that you learned the story of the crane, even though it was beyond my perception?"
"Tell me first that you have been recognized [as a sage], and then I shall accept alms from you.
To the seer who had spoken thus, she, whose deity was her husband, replied:
I know no duty whatsoever superior to devotion to my husband;
by his grace, therefore, I possess such power of higher knowledge.
Moreover, go there and see the one known as Dharmavyādha, who lives by the sale of meat; from that, you will attain the highest good, free from egoism.
Thus addressed by that devoted wife, the sage,
having accepted her portion of hospitality, bowed to her and departed from there.
On another day, that sage, having sought out the hunter Dharmavyādha there,
approached him as he stood in his shop selling meat.
And as soon as Dharmavyādha saw that sage, he addressed him:
"O Brahmin, have you been sent here by that devoted wife?"
Having heard that, the sage Dharmavyādha was amazed and said to him:
"How is it that you, being a seller of meat, possess such knowledge?"
To the seer who had spoken thus, the Dharma-fowler replied:
"I am devoted to my mother and father; they are my sole refuge."
"When those two have bathed, I bathe; when they have eaten, I eat;
when they have lain down, I lie down. By that means, my knowledge is of such a kind."
And for my livelihood, I sell the meat of deer and other animals killed by others, solely for the sake of my subsistence; being devoted to my own duty, I do not sell out of greed for wealth.
"O Sage, neither I nor that devoted wife create the egoism that obstructs knowledge; therefore, our knowledge remains unimpeded."
Therefore, you too, having abandoned egoism and observing the vow of a sage for the sake of purification,
practice your own duty, by which you will swiftly attain the supreme light.
Having been thus instructed by the Dharma-hunter, the sage went to his home,
witnessed his conduct, and departed for the forest satisfied.
Through his instruction, he attained perfection, and those two also achieved success by practicing that dharma under the virtuous hunter.
Such is the power of devotion toward one's husband, father, and mother.
Therefore, come and honor that mother who is eager for your sight.
Thus addressed by his father Candrasvāmin, O protector of the earth,
Mahīpāla resolved to go to his own country out of deference to his mother.
Having reported all of that to his father-in-law Ananta, the father of his dharma,
he then departed at night with his friend, his burden having been taken up by him.
Having gradually reached his own country, he delighted his mother with the sight of him,
just as the spring delights the female cuckoo.
For some time the protector of the earth remained there, honored by his kinsmen,
together with his mother and his father, who related the news of what had occurred.
Meanwhile, in that city of Tārāpura, his wife, the princess Bandhumatī,
who had been sleeping soundly within her inner apartments, woke up at the end of the night.
And having realized that her husband had gone somewhere, she, distressed by separation,
found no pleasure anywhere, whether in palaces, gardens, or other such places.
With her tears forming a double stream as she wept intensely,
she was entirely consumed by lamentation, longing for the comfort of death.
"I am going on some business; I shall return quickly"—having said this to me of his own accord, he departed. Therefore, my daughter, do not grieve.
Then, having been approached and comforted by the minister Anantasvāmin with words that pointed toward hope, she regained her fortitude after much difficulty.
Thereafter, in order to learn news of her husband, she constantly honored with gifts those eminent brahmins who had arrived from other lands.
She asked that wretched brahmin named Saṃgamadatta,
who had come for alms, about news of her husband, after telling him her own name and identifying marks.
Then that brahmin said to her: "I have never seen anyone like this;
nevertheless, O Queen, you should not feel any anxiety in this matter."
Through auspicious deeds, the union with one's beloved is attained after a long time;
likewise, listen as I relate the marvel that was witnessed by me.
While wandering among sacred fords, I reached Lake Mānasa on the Himālaya;
there, I beheld within it a palace made of jewels, like a mirror.
Then, suddenly emerging from the house with a sword in hand,
a man accompanied by a host of celestial women ascended to the bank of the lake.
There in the garden, he sported with the women in a drinking revelry;
and I, watching from afar with curiosity, remained unobserved.
Just then, another fortunate man arrived there from somewhere;
and when he met with me, I told him exactly what I had seen.

And out of curiosity, he pointed out from afar that man accompanied by his wife; as soon as he saw him, he related his own story to me in this way: SoKss_9,6.211: "And out of curiosity, he pointed out from afar that man accompanied by his wife; as soon as he saw him, he related his own story to me in this way."
"In the city named Tribhuvana, I was a king called Tribhuvana.
There, a certain Pāśupata performed service for me for a very long time. When he was asked privately the reason for his mastery over the sword and the dagger..."
He requested me as his companion, and that was accepted by me.
Then, having gone with me to the forest at night, that Pāśupata revealed the opening by means of fire oblations and other rites, and said to me:
"O hero, enter first; having obtained the sword, you should cause me to enter as well. Having emerged, make a pact with me regarding this matter."
Having been addressed thus by him, I quickly made a pact with him,
entered the opening, and reached a house made of jewels.
Then, having emerged, a certain preeminent daughter of the asuras led me inside with affection and gave me a sword there.
"This sword, which bestows all accomplishments and grants the power of flight, must be protected," she said; having spoken thus, I dwelt there together with her.
Then, remembering this, I went out sword in hand through the opening and made that Pāśupata enter that asura palace.
There, I sat together with that first one and her retinue;
he too sat together with the second asura maiden.
Once, while I had taken up a drink, that Pāśupata, through a ruse,
snatched the sword lying at my side and placed it in his own hand.
When that [sword] was held in his hand, he attained great supernatural power;
having seized me by the hand, he dragged me out from the cave and cast me outside.
Then, for twelve years, he was searched for at the openings of the fish's caves, thinking, "Perhaps I might find him once he has emerged."
"There is that rogue, now fallen here today within the range of my vision,
sporting with this very daughter of the asuras who belongs to me."
O Goddess, while that king Tribhuvana was thus speaking to me,
that Pāśupata there fell asleep from the effects of drinking.
Having gone to the side of that sleeping man, he seized his sword;
by means of it, the king further attained divine power.
Then, having awakened that Pāśupata with a kick to the foot,
the hero rebuked him for his transgression, yet he did not kill him again.
And he entered the city of the asuras together with her and her retinue,
having obtained that asura maiden as his own personal accomplishment (siddhi).
And that Pāśupata, having fallen from his supernatural powers, fell into great misery;
for those who are ungrateful certainly fall, even if they have long achieved their goals.

I obtained a jeweled bracelet from the gate of the royal palace;
having extracted a single jewel from it, I then sold it. (SoKss 10.1.9)
And that was given by me to the merchant Hiraṇyagupta for a price of one hundred thousand dīnāras; because of that, I am now living in comfort today.
Having said this, he showed me the bracelet marked with the king's name;
therefore, O Lord, I have today made this request to my master.
Having heard this, the Lord of Vatsa had both of them brought there:
the porter with the bracelet, and that merchant with the jewel.
"Ah! I remember; this slipped from my wrist during my wandering through the city," the king said himself upon seeing that bracelet.
"Having obtained this bracelet engraved with the king's name, what have you done with it?"—
thus questioned by the courtiers, the porter then spoke in the presence of the king.
"How could I, who live by carrying burdens, know the syllables of a king's name? Having obtained this, I accepted it while consumed by the suffering of poverty. (SoKss_10.1.15)
When he had spoken thus, the merchant, having been challenged for the sake of the jewel, said:
"I purchased this jewel by force at its price in the marketplace."
And he possesses no royal insignia; thus it is said that he is made of that [wood].
However, for five thousand [pieces of gold], it was brought by him, and it remains supreme.
[In another manuscript, the reading is "tad ayam ucyate" (then this is said).
Having heard these words of Hiraṇyagupta, Yaugandharāyaṇa, remaining there, said: "There is no fault here belonging to anyone. (SoKss 10.1.18)
Tell me, what can be said of a poor man who is illiterate and a porter?
Out of poverty he commits theft; and once obtained, by whom has it ever been relinquished?
"Even a merchant who purchases a jewel for its price is not to be blamed";
at that time, the Lord of Vatsa placed his trust in these words of the great minister.
Having given five thousand [pieces of gold] spent by the porter,
he took from that merchant Hiraṇyagupta the jewel belonging to himself.
Having taken back his own bracelet, which had been released and was now heavy with its value,
and having enjoyed five thousand [pieces of gold], he too returned home free from fear.
Thinking, "This man is a treacherous sinner," and hating him within his heart,
the king summoned that merchant Ratnadatta for the sake of the matter at hand.
When they had departed, Vasantaka, who was walking ahead of the king, said:
"Alas! For those cursed by fate, even when wealth is attained, it flees away."
The story of this porter’s auspicious jar came to pass;
for instance, there was once a certain man in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the past.
Named Śubhadatta, he would daily bring a load of wood from the forest and, by selling it, supported his family.
And once, having come to a distant forest by chance,
he beheld four yakṣas standing there, adorned with divine ornaments and garments.

Seeing him terrified, all those yakṣas questioned him with affection about the facts as they were; and having understood that he was poor, compassion arose within them, and they spoke: SoKss_10,1.28 //
"Stay here in our presence, O good man; be our laborer.
We shall provide for you the maintenance of a household without hardship."
Having been addressed thus by them, Śubhadatta agreed, saying "So be it," in their presence,
and he performed for them the entirety of service, beginning with bathing.
When the mealtime had arrived, those yakṣas said to him:
"Give us food from this auspicious jar."
While he was lingering there, having seen that the jar was empty within,
those Guhyakas, with smiling faces, spoke to him once more.
"Śubhadatta, you do not know this: cast your hand into the interior of the jar;
you shall obtain everything as you desire, for this jar is indeed a granter of all wishes."
Having heard that, as soon as he thrust his hand inside the jar, he saw whatever food, drink, and other desired things he wished for. Śubhadatta gave these to them, and then he himself ate from it.
Thus attending upon the yakṣas daily with devotion and fear,
Śubhadatta remained in their presence, distressed by anxiety for his family.
And that family, afflicted by suffering, was comforted by the Guhyakas through the instruction of a dream;
by their grace, they then began to rejoice, and so did he.
Within just a month, those yakṣas said to Śubhadatta:
"We are pleased with this devotion of yours; tell us something, and we shall give it to you."
Having heard that, he said to them: "If you are truly satisfied, then let this auspicious jar be given to me by you."
Then those yakṣas said to him: "You will not be able to protect this;
for he flees at the first sign of defeat. Therefore, choose another boon."
Although he was addressed thus by those yakṣas, when Śubhadatta did not desire another boon, they then gave him that auspicious jar.
Then, having bowed to them with joy, Śubhadatta took that jar and, his kinsmen filled with delight, reached his own home with speed.
Having obtained food and other provisions from that pot and placed them there,
he ate together with his kinsmen, keeping them in other vessels for the sake of concealment.

Having been freed from his burden and enjoying pleasures, he was once questioned by his kinsmen while intoxicated with drink: "Whence comes this splendor of yours regarding enjoyments? (SoKss 10.1.44)
Clearly speaking thus like a fool, he took the jar that grants all desires upon his shoulder and, alas, began to dance.
And as he was dancing, his gait faltering from the excess of his intoxication,
that auspicious jar fell from his shoulder and shattered into pieces upon the ground.
At that very moment, having become whole again, he departed as he had come;
and Śubhadatta, filled with despair, returned to his former state.
Thus, those whose intellects are struck by the influence of the faults of drinking and so forth are incapable of protecting even that which they have already fully attained. (SoK 10.1.48)
Having heard this humorous tale of the auspicious jar from Vasantaka,
the Lord of Vatsa rose and performed his daily duties, such as bathing and eating.
Naravāhanadatta, too, having bathed and eaten in the presence of his father,
went at the end of the day to his own palace together with his friends.
There, at night, while he lay upon his bed sleepless, Marubhūtika spoke to him as these ministers listened.
"O King, I know that you did not summon the women of the inner apartments out of a desire for the company of a slave-girl;
she too was not summoned. Therefore, there is no sleep for you today."
Why then, even knowing this, do you still feel attachment for courtesans? For they possess no true affection; listen therefore to this story.
In this world, there is a great and prosperous city named Citrakūṭa;
there lived a merchant, a master of great wealth, known by the name Ratnavarman.
From the worship of Īśvara, one son was born to him;
therefore, he gave that son the name Īśvaravarman.
And seeing that he had completed his studies and was approaching youth, Ratnavarman, the chief merchant who had an only son, reflected: SoKss_10,1.56 //
In this world, the Creator fashioned the courtesan as a visible snare for the wealthy who are blinded by youth—a snare that carries away both their wealth and their lives. (SoKss 10.1.57)
Therefore, I entrust this son to a certain courtesan so that,
through training in the guise of a prostitute, he may not be deceived by them.
Having reflected thus, he went together with his son, Īśvaravarman,
to the house of a procuress named Yamajihvā.
There he saw that procuress, who had a thick jaw, long teeth, and a crooked nose, as she was instructing her daughter.
"O daughter, everyone is honored by wealth, and a courtesan especially so; yet that wealth does not belong to one who is full of passion. Therefore, a courtesan should abandon passion."
For passion is the foremost messenger of the faults; like a well-trained actress, a courtesan displays that [passion] falsely during both the morning and evening twilights.
By that means she should first win his affection; then, once he is attached, she should milk him for wealth.
Having extracted the wealth, she should eventually abandon him, but she should retrieve it again once her purpose is achieved.
He who is equal toward the young, the infant, the old, the deformed, and the beautiful—
like a sage, that courtesan attains the supreme goal as taught in the sacred scriptures.
While his daughter was speaking thus, Ratnavarman approached that procuress; having been offered hospitality by her, he sat down together with her.
And she said to her, "Noble lady, let this son of mine be instructed by you in the arts of courtesans, so that he may attain proficiency. (SoKss 10.1.66)
"And I shall give you a thousand dīnāras as your ransom.
Having heard that, she accepted his wish, saying, "So be it."
Then, having distributed the dinars and entrusted his son to her,
Ratnavarman went home with that Īśvaravarman.
Then Īśvaravarman, having learned the arts in the house of Yamajihva within a single year, went to the home of his father.
And having reached his sixteenth year, he said to his father: "For from wealth come both dharma and desire; from wealth comes honor, and from wealth comes fame."
When he had spoken thus, his father, full of joy, believed him and saying "So be it," gave him the merchandise consisting of five crores of wealth.
Then, taking that [wealth], the merchant’s son Īśvaravarman set out on an auspicious day with his caravan,
desiring to reach Suvarṇadvīpa.
Traveling by stages, he reached a city named Kāñcanapura on the way;
there he stayed in a garden situated near the outskirts.
Having bathed, eaten, and anointed himself, that youth entered this city and went to a temple to see a spectacle.
There he saw a dancer named Sundarī,
dancing like a wave from the ocean of beauty tossed up by the wind of youth.
As soon as he saw her, his mind became fixed solely upon her;
it was as if the instructions of the angry procuress had vanished far away from him.
At the conclusion of the dance, he sent his companion and requested her;
and she, bowing low and realizing "I am blessed," gave her consent.
Having stationed skillful guards over his own residence to protect the goods,
Īśvaravarman went to the dwelling of that Sundarī.
His mother, named Makarakaṭī, honored him as he arrived with various domestic rites appropriate for that occasion.
And at the arrival of night, he was led by her into a bedchamber with a canopy of shimmering jewels, wherein a couch had been prepared for him to lie upon.
There he took delight with that beautiful Sundarī,
who was skilled in various arts, in dance, and in amorous play, as she gave her consent.
Seeing her displaying such intense passion and not departing from his side,
he was unable to leave that place on the second day.
And on those two days, that young merchant gave twenty-five lakhs of gold, jewels, and other riches to Sundarī.
"I have acquired abundant wealth, but I have not found one such as you.
If I have indeed found him, what shall I do with wealth?"

When Sundarī did not accept him because of his attachment to falsehoods, her mother Makarakaṭī, who had but one child, spoke to her thus: SoKss_10,1.85: "When Sundarī did not accept him because of his attachment to falsehoods, her mother Makarakaṭī, who had but one child, spoke to her thus:"
"Now, whatever belongs to us is his own property;
having placed it among those [other goods], let it be taken, daughter—what harm is there in that?"
Thus addressed by her mother, Sundarī accepted that [proposal] as if with great reluctance;
and the foolish Īśvaravarman believed her to be truly devoted to him.
Then, as his heart was captivated by her beauty, dancing, and singing,
two months passed for that merchant while he remained there.
And he gave two crores to that Sundarī one after the other;
then his friend, named Arthadatta, approached him and spoke to him privately.
"Friend, has that instruction from the procuress, though acquired by you with such effort,
gone to waste at this critical moment— just like the science of weapons to one who is a coward?"
That you perceive sincerity in this love for a courtesan—is water ever truly present in the mirages of the desert? (SoKss 10.1.91)
All of that will be exhausted before your wealth here is spent;
therefore, let us depart while we still have it, for once you are aware of this, your father will not forgive it.
Thus addressed by that friend, the merchant’s son replied:
"It is true that there is no trust in courtesans, yet Sundarī was not like them."
"For if she does not see me for even a moment, my friend, she will give up her life;
therefore, go and awaken her, if you must depart by all means."
Having been addressed thus by him, Arthadatta then spoke to Sundarī in the very presence of her mother, Makarakaṭī.
Your affection for Īśvaravarman is indeed extraordinary;
yet, you must now certainly go to Suvarṇadvīpa for the sake of trade.
"Therefore, she will obtain that fortune by which, having come into your presence, she shall remain happily for as long as time permits; grant your consent to this, my friend."
Having heard that, her eyes filled with tears and gazing at the face of Īśvaravarman, Sundarī, overcome with despondency, addressed him:
"You should know: who speaks without regard for the end? Who can trust anyone? Therefore, enough! Let Fate do with me as it will."
Having heard that, his mother said to her: "Do not grieve; let there be fortitude in you.
This beloved Siddhārtha of yours will surely come; he will not abandon you."
Thus, having consoled him, his mother, acting in concert with her accomplices,
had a net laid secretly over a well at the entrance of the road.
Then Īśvaravarman’s mind became fixed upon her like one on a swing,
and Sundarī, as if out of grief, took only very little food and drink.
She took no delight in singing, instrumental music, or dancing;
she was consoled by Īśvaravarman with various expressions of affection.
Then, on the day appointed by his friend, Īśvaravarman set out from Sundarī’s residence,
having had the auspicious rites performed for him by the procuress.
Then Sundarī, with her mother, followed him weeping,
as far as the well outside the city that was enclosed by a lattice-work.
Then, as he was turning back and approaching Sundarī,
she threw herself into a well onto the surface of a net.
Then, a great cry of "Alas, alas! O mistress! O daughter!
was heard there from the female slaves, the circle of servants, and her mother.
Having turned back with his friend, that merchant’s son,
realizing that his beloved had cast her body into the well, fell into a swoon for a moment.
Then, lamenting with cries of distress, Makarakaṭī caused her affectionate servants, who were in league with her, to descend into that well.
"By good fortune he lives! By good fortune he lives! saying this, they drew Sundarī out from the well by means of ropes.
Having been cast out, she made herself appear as if dead and offered herself up;
when the merchant’s son returned, she slowly began to converse with him.
Having taken up his beloved, who was now comforted, Īśvaravarman returned to that very house, joyful and accompanied by his followers.
Having ascertained that the proof of Sundarī’s love was the fruit of his birth,
and considering her attainment alone to be his goal, he abandoned once again the intention of setting out on his journey.
Then his friend Arthadatta, having established himself there once more, said to him:
"Friend, why have you destroyed yourself through delusion?"
Let there be no confidence in Sundarī’s affection that might lead you to fall into a well;
for the deceptive schemes of a procuress are inconceivable, even to Fate itself.
Having squandered your father’s wealth, what will you say, or where will you go?
Therefore, depart from here this very day, if your mind is set on what is auspicious.
Disregarding these words of his friend, that young merchant spent another thirty million there in a single month.
Then, his wealth having been seized and the half-moon brand being placed upon him, Sundarī was expelled from her house by that procuress Makarakaṭī.
And Arthadatta and the others, having gone quickly to their own city,
related everything exactly as it had happened to his father.
When his father Ratnavarman learned of this, he became deeply distressed;
that lord of merchants went to the procuress Yamajihvā and said to her: SoKss_10,1.120
"Having paid such a price, you have taught my son this;
Makarakaṭī has easily stripped him of all his possessions."
Having said this, he described that account of his son to her;
then she, the old procuress, spoke to Yamajihvā.
"Bring your son here; I shall act in such a way that he will seize all the property of that Makarakaṭī."
When she had thus made her promise, the procuress Yamajihvā immediately dispatched a messenger with a gift of wealth as a preliminary offering.
Then Ratnavarman dispatched his well-wishing friend Arthadatta in order to bring back that son.
Having gone to that city of Kāñcanapura,
Arthadatta related that entire message to Īśvaravarman.
Furthermore, he said to that friend: "Indeed, you did not follow my word;
therefore, today the true nature of courtesans has been seen by you with your own eyes."
Having given five crores, you have obtained but a half-moon;
what wise man would desire affection from courtesans, any more than from grains of sand?
Or what do you say? Is this the nature of things—that a man who is so clever and heroic shall be a partaker of prosperity?
As long as he does not fall into the lapses of amorous dalliance with women,
come now to your father’s side and appease his wrath.
Having said this, he was quickly led by Arthadatta;
after being consoled, Īśvaravarman approached his father’s side.
And his father, out of affection for their only son, consoled him and led him once again into the presence of the procuress Yamajihvā.
Being questioned by her on this matter, he related through the mouth of Arthadatta his own history,
ending with his fall into Sundarī’s well and the loss of his wealth.
Then Yamajihvā said: "I alone am the offender, since, having forgotten it, I did not instruct him in this illusion."
For Makarakaṭī had indeed cast a net inside the well;
Sundarī threw her body onto its back and did not die.
Having said, "There is a remedy for this," that procuress also had her own monkey named Āla brought by her female servants.
Having first given him her own thousand dīnāras, she said to him, "Swallow it!
Then he, being thus instructed, swallowed it.
"Give twenty sons to him; give twenty-five to him;
sixty to him and a hundred to him"—thus [he speaks] in various instances of expenditure.
Though being made to pay, that monkey gave up the dinars he had swallowed by that Yamajihvā, disgorging them again and again in that very same manner.
Having demonstrated this skillful means, Yamajihvā spoke again:
"O Īśvaravarman, take this young monkey."
"Furthermore, going day by day to that house of Sundarī as before,
seek out those [jewels] which have been thus secretly swallowed from this [treasury] for expenditure."
Having seen him who resembles a wish-fulfilling gem and is adorned with a garland of sītā flowers, Sundarī will offer all her possessions and, having made her request, take back that one monkey.
Having taken that wealth and given her the expenses for two days already consumed,
you should then depart from her presence without delay.
Having said this, Yamajihvā gave that monkey as a gift to Īśvaravarman,
along with a chest containing twenty million [gold pieces].
Having taken that, he set out once more for that city of Kāñcanapura;
and having dispatched a foremost messenger, he entered Sundarī’s house.
Sundarī welcomed him, along with his friends, with embraces around the neck and other gestures of affection, as if he were her very life-force and the essence of all means to achieve her goal.
Then, in a moment, while that trustworthy Īśvaravarman was present,
he said to Arthadatta, "Go and bring Āla."
Saying "So be it," he went and brought the monkey;
once the monkey had swallowed the previous thousand dinars, he spoke to him:
"O son Āla, give today three hundred dīnāras for the sake of food and drink,
and one hundred for the expense of betel and other such items."
Give one hundred [offerings] to Makarakaṭī and to Ambā among the twice-born;
give the remainder of the thousand, starting from the first, to Sundarī.
Thus addressed by Īśvaravarman, that monkey,
having repeatedly disgorged those dinars he had previously swallowed, gave them for their expenses exactly as instructed.
In this manner, by this reasoning, Ālo is constantly made to pay dināras for as long as Īśvaravarman lives— at the rate of merely one per fortnight— for the expenses of his maintenance.
At that moment, Makarakaṭī and Sundarī thought:
"Aha! This wish-fulfilling gem has been attained by him who assumes the form of a monkey."
"He who gives a thousand dinars day after day—
if he has given this to us, our heart's desires are fulfilled."
Having reflected thus, together with his mother, he entreated Sundarīśvaravarman in a secluded place while the king was resting after his meal.

"That is my father's entire fortune, and it is not proper to give that away"—
to him who had spoken thus, Sundarī spoke again.
"I shall give five crores; let this object be given.
Then Īśvaravarman, having made his decision, spoke to him.
Even if you were to give me all your possessions or this entire city, it would still not be right to give him away; why then speak of millions?
Having heard this, Sundarī said: "I shall give you my all;
give this monkey to me, even if my mother should be angry with me."
Having said this, Sundarī grasped the feet of Īśvaravarman;
then Arthadatta and the others said, "Let whatever is to be given be given."
Then Īśvaravarman agreed to give her to him in that manner;
and he spent that day with Sundarī, who was filled with joy.
In the morning, he gave that monkey to Sundarī, who had requested it,
after she had swallowed two thousand hidden gold coins (dīnāra) within its mouth.
Taking her entire fortune, which was the whole of her household wealth, at that very moment,
he departed quickly from there and went to Suvarṇadvīpa for trade.
And for two days, that monkey Ālo gave a thousand dīnāras each to Sundarī, whose face was filled with joy, when she had requested them.
On the third day, when he was repeatedly entreated with affection but still gave nothing at all, Sundarī struck him with her fist.
Struck thus, the monkey rose up in a rage and, with his teeth and claws,
tore open the faces of both Sundarī and her mother as they were striking him.
Then his mother, her face dripping with blood, struck him in anger with clubs; by that, the boy died there.
Seeing him dead and perceiving that all her possessions were lost, Sundarī was filled with grief; together with her mother, she prepared to give up her life.
Having made a net of Makarakaṭī’s hair, by which his wealth was taken away,
that wise man has today used her as a hook to seize her entire fortune.
"She recognized the net woven by another, but not her own.
Thus spoke the people there, laughing, having learned the true circumstances of the matter.
Then that Sundarī, her purpose frustrated and her face torn, was with great difficulty turned away from suicide by her kinsmen along with her mother.
And having acquired abundant wealth from Svarṇadvīpa,
Īśvaravarman soon returned from there to his father’s house at Citrakūṭa.
Seeing that his son had returned with immeasurable wealth acquired, his father Ratnavarman honored the procuress Yamajihvā with money and held a grand festival.
Having realized the peerless nature of illusion, Īśvaravarman’s mind became dispassionate toward the company of wanton women;
thereafter, he took a wife and lived there in his own home.
Thus, O Lord of Men, not even a fragment of truthful speech ever dwells in the heart of a woman without deceit;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should never take pleasure in them, for they are always like empty forests whose journey can only be accomplished by means of a caravan.
Having heard this story of Ālajālaka exactly as it was from the mouth of Marubhūti,
Naravāhanadatta, together with Gomukha and the others, believed it and laughed.
Thus ends the first wave in the Śaktiyaśas book of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The second wave begins:
When Marubhūti had thus related the true nature of courtesans, [the King said:]...
The wise Gomukha likewise related the story of Kumudikā.
In Pratiṣṭhāna there was a lord of the earth named Vikramasiṃha,
who by his very name was made significant by fate, for he was like a lion in his prowess.
The beloved of that Lord was the auspicious river Nandinī,
and his goddess Alaṅkāratanu was known as Śaśilekhā.
Once, while he was staying in his own city, five or six kinsmen gathered together, came to his house, and surrounded the king.
Mahābhaṭa, Vīrabāhu, Subāhu, Subhaṭa,
and King Pratāpāditya— all of these were also possessed of great strength.
Having rejected conciliation and the other [stratagems] toward them, King Vikramasiṃha sent his own minister and set out for battle against them.
When the clash of weapons had begun between the two armies, that king,
mounted upon an elephant out of pride in his valor, entered the battle himself.
Seeing him with his bow as his companion, shattering the army of his enemies,
the five kings, led by Mahābhaṭa, rushed forward together.
And as that entire force rushed forward together with equal might,
it was shattered by the incomparable strength of Vikrama-siṃha.
Then the minister named Anantaguṇa, standing by his side, said to him:
"Our army has been broken; for now, there is no victory here."
Having cast us aside, you have entered into this powerful conflict;
therefore, for the sake of your own welfare, now act upon these words of mine.
"Descend from this elephant and mount a horse;
come, let us go to another realm, so that you may live and conquer your enemies again."
Thus, at the word of his minister, he dismounted from the elephant of his own accord and,
mounting a horse, went out again with him and his young children.
And King Vikramasiṃha, disguised in this attire, went together with that minister, step by step, toward the city of Ujjayinī.
Accompanied by his minister, he entered the residence of that courtesan named Kumudikā, who was renowned for her abundant wealth.
Seeing him arrive at her house unexpectedly, she too thought:
"This is some extraordinary man who has come to my home."
"By his splendor and his marks, it is indicated that he is a great king;
if such a one as this were to accept me, then my desire would be fulfilled."
Having reflected thus, Kumudikā rose up, greeted him with a welcome, and offered great hospitality to the king.
And when the king had rested, after a short while she said to him:
"I am blessed today; my past merit has borne fruit for me."
"Since my home has been purified by Your Majesty coming here in person,
I have become your purchased slave through this very favor."
The hundred elephants I possess, the twenty thousand horses,
and the palace filled with jewels— all this is now at your disposal.
Having spoken thus, Kumudikā attended upon the king and his ministers with costly services such as bathing and other comforts.
Then, having entrusted his own daughter to her there,
King Vikramasiṃha remained at ease in that palace together with her, though he was weary.
He enjoyed her wealth and gave it away to supplicants;
yet she showed no sign of resentment toward him, for she was truly content.
Then, as the king was pleased, thinking, "Ah, she is devoted to me," that minister Anantaguṇa, who stood by him, spoke to him in private:
"O King, courtesans possess no true sincerity at all;
yet Kumudikā shows you devotion—of that I know not the cause."
Having heard these words of his, the king said to him:
"Do not speak thus; Kumudikā would give up even her life for my sake."
"If you do not believe me, I shall show you proof," having said this,
the king devised this ruse with his own minister.
Gradually emaciating his body, restricting his drink and eating little,
he made himself appear as if dead, motionless with his limbs sprawled out.
Then, having placed him upon a litter, his attendants led him to the cremation ground while they grieved, feigning sorrow for him who possessed infinite virtues.
And she, Śokākumudikā, though being restrained by her kinsmen,
came and ascended the funeral pyre together with him.
As long as the fire did not yet blaze up,
the King, perceiving that Kumudikā had arrived, rose from his seat with a yawn.
"By good fortune, by good fortune, he has been restored to life here!"— saying this,
they all joyfully led him, together with Kumudikā, to their own home.
Then, when the festival had been celebrated, the king approached his minister in private and said to him, "Has her affection been observed?"
Then that minister said to him: "Even so, I do not believe this;
there must certainly be a reason for it here, so let us investigate the matter to reach a certainty."
"Let him reveal himself to her, by whom this strength and the other strength of our allies have been bestowed; having obtained it, let us slay the enemies in battle."
While the minister was speaking thus, that spy sent secretly arrived there once more; and when questioned, he spoke as follows:
The realm was overrun by enemies, but Queen Śaśilekhā, hearing from the people that the king had perished, falsely, entered the fire.
Having heard these words of the spy, the king, then struck by the thunderbolt of grief, lamented: "Alas, my queen! Alas, the virtuous one! and so forth.
Then, having gradually come to understand the truth of the matter, Kumudikā approached King Vikramasiṃha, comforted him, and spoke to the monarch:
Why was this not commanded by Your Majesty even earlier? Why now, as well, do you say:
"Let the suppression of the enemy be carried out with my wealth and my forces"?
Having been addressed thus by her, the king increased his forces with that wealth and went into the presence of a powerful neighboring king who was his ally.
Having gone there with those forces and his own troops,
he slew those five enemy kings in battle and obtained their kingdoms as well.
Then, being pleased, he said to Kumudikā who stood beside him:
"I am gratified with you; tell me, what desired thing shall I do for you?"
Then Kumudikā said: "If you are truly pleased, O Lord, then please extract this one thorn from my heart that has remained there for a long time."
"In Ujjayinī, there is a dear friend of mine, the son of a brahmin named Śrīdhara, who has been imprisoned by the king for a minor offense; release him from that."
"O Lord, having seen you with your supreme royal marks, which portend future prosperity,
I have served you with devotion, knowing you to be capable of accomplishing this task."
Due to the despair of not attaining my desired goal, I even ascended your funeral pyre,
considering life to be fruitless without that young son of a brahmin.
When she had spoken thus, the king said to that playful woman:
"I shall accomplish this for you; be steadfast, O fair-faced one."
Having spoken thus and recalling the words of the minister, he reflected:
"Truly, the lack of integrity in courtesans was described by me to Anantaguṇa."
"Therefore, this wretched desire of Varāha must be fulfilled by me";
having thus resolved, he went to Ujjayinī accompanied by his army.
Having released Śrīdhara and given him much wealth,
he established Kumudikā there in a state of well-being through union with her beloved.
And having returned to his own city, Vikramasiṃha, not transgressing the counsel of his ministers, gradually enjoyed the entire earth.
"Thus is the heart of courtesans— unknowable and unfathomable.
When Gomukha had finished telling this story in the presence of Naravāhanadatta, Tapantaka then spoke.
"O King, one should never place trust in women, for they are all fickle;
even those who are mature are not to be relied upon, always being like courtesans."
Listen as I relate a wonder that I myself beheld right here:
there was once, in this very city of merchants, a man named Balavarman.
Candraśrī was his wife, and she, from the front of a window,
saw a certain merchant’s son named Bhavyaśīlahara.
Having had him brought to her friend’s house, she, overcome by passion, enjoyed herself with him at that very moment through her friend’s mouth, remaining unobserved.
And every day, as she enjoyed herself with him in that manner,
she was recognized by all the servants and kinsmen as being attached to him.
But her husband Balavarman did not know her to be unchaste;
for generally, a person blinded by affection does not perceive the wickedness of his wife.
Then a fever with burning sensations arose for that Valavarman;
by means of it, the merchant gradually reached his final state.
Even while he was in that state, his wife went day after day to the house of her friend, into the presence of that paramour.
While she remained right there, her husband died on another day;
having learned of this, she quickly took leave of that lover and departed.
Firmly resolved, she ascended that funeral pyre together with her husband,
despite being restrained by her kinsmen who were well-acquainted with her virtuous character and grieved for her.
Thus, indeed, the course of a woman's mind is difficult to fathom;
they form attachments with others and yet die without their husband.
When Tapantaka had spoken thus, Hariśikha replied in due course:
"Have you not heard what happened to Devadāsa in this very case?"
In former times, there was a householder in that village named Devadāsa;
his wife was named Duḥśīlā, a name that truly accorded with her character.
The neighbors discovered that she was attached to another man;
one day, that Devadāsa went to the royal court on business.
And at that moment, his wife,
desiring his death, brought that other man up and placed him on the upper floor of the house.
Then, when her own husband Devadāsa had returned and was lying asleep after having been enjoyed by that lover during the night, she had him killed.
Having dismissed that paramour and remained silent until the end of the night,
she went out at dawn and cried out, "My husband has been killed by thieves!"
Then his kinsmen, having arrived there and seen him, said:
"Since he was killed by thieves, why has nothing at all been taken from here by them?"
Having said this, they then questioned the boy standing there, their own son:
"By whom was your father killed? Thereupon, he spoke clearly.
One day, some youth climbed up onto the roof;
at night, having descended, he killed my father even as I was looking on.
"But first my mother took me from my father's side and rose up"—
when the child said this, his wife’s paramour realized that he had been killed.
His kinsmen searched for and killed that paramour of his at that very moment;
they then took charge of the child and that woman of ill-repute, and banished them both.
"Thus, a woman who is a female serpent with a heart colored by another kills without a doubt.
When Hariśikha had spoken thus, Gomukha replied once more:
What need is there for anything else that has occurred here? Listen now to this laughable account concerning Vajrasāra, the servant of the King of Vatsa.
The beautiful Mālavī, born in Mālava, became the wife of that heroic and handsome Vajrasāra, dearer to him than his own body.
Once, his father-in-law, the King of Mālava, accompanied by his sons, came in person with great eagerness to extend an invitation to him and his wife.
Then Vajrasāra, having honored him and reported it to the king,
went with his wife to Mālava, invited by the king to accompany him.
Having rested for just one month there in his father-in-law's house,
he returned here for the sake of serving the king, while his wife remained there.
Then, after some days had passed, a friend named Krodhana approached Vajrasāra and suddenly spoke to him thus:
Having abandoned your wife at her father’s house, why did you destroy your own home? For there, that sinful woman indeed committed adultery with other men.
"Having arrived there today, this was told to me by a trustworthy person.
Therefore, do not consider it to be false; seize her and carry off another."
Having spoken thus, when Krodhana had departed, Vajrasāra stood for a moment like one bewildered and thought: "I suspect this may indeed be true."
"Even though the messenger was sent, she did not come; how could this be?
Therefore, I shall go myself to bring her back and see what will happen."
Having thus resolved, he went to Mālava, took leave of his two parents-in-law,
and set out from there taking his wife with him.
Having traveled a long distance, he, having skillfully deceived his followers,
entered a dense forest by a wrong path, taking his wife with him.
Having seated her there in the middle of a secluded place, he said to her:
"I have heard from trustworthy people that you are attached to another man."
"Since you did not come when you were summoned by me while I remained right here,
tell the truth, or else I shall inflict punishment upon you."
Having heard that, she said to him: "If this is your resolve, then why do you ask me? Do as you please with me."
Having heard her words thus with contempt, Vajrasāra, out of anger, bound her to a tree with creepers and beat her.
As she was taking away her garment,
the lustful fool gazed at her nakedness, and a desire for sexual pleasure arose within him.
Then, having settled her down and bound her, he embraced her to dally with her;
but she did not desire him, and though entreated by him, she spoke: SoKss_10,2.96 //
"Just as I was bound and beaten with creepers by you, so too do I wish it were otherwise if I were to strike you; not otherwise."
"So be it," he agreed, deluded by his passion;
for strange indeed was that one of diamond-like essence who had been reduced to the state of a blade of straw by the god of love.
Then she bound him, with his hands and feet, firmly to a tree;
and while he was thus bound, she cut off his ears and nose with that very same weapon.
Having taken his weapons and garments and having dressed herself,
that wicked woman then departed as she pleased, assuming the appearance of a man.
But Vajrasāra remained there, his ears and nose severed,
with a stream of blood flowing from him and his face bowed down by shame.
Then a certain physician, who had come there into the forest for the sake of medicinal herbs, saw him; out of compassion, that virtuous man released him and led him to his own home.
There he was comforted by him, and slowly returned to his own home;
yet Vajrasāra, not finding her, did not find that wicked wife.
And he related that entire account to Krodhana,
who in turn recounted it all before the King of Vatsa.
"This man, devoid of manliness and indignation, has become a woman; surely his male attire was taken away by his wife, and a fitting punishment was meted out."
Thus, although he was mocked by everyone in the royal court,
Vajrasāra remained right there with a mind as firm as adamant.
When Gomukha had thus said, "O King, who can place their trust in women?",
Marubhūtika spoke once more.
"The minds of women are unstable; hear now a story regarding this as well.
Formerly, there was a king named Siṃhabala in the southern region."
And he had as his wife, the beloved of all the women in the inner apartments, one named Kalyāṇavatī, the daughter of a feudatory ruler of Mālava.
Once, while that king was ruling his own kingdom together with her,
he was expelled from the country by powerful kinsmen who had united against him.
Accompanied by his queen, armed and with a small retinue, the king then set out in secret for Mālava, the residence of his father-in-law.
And as he was traveling on the road through the forest, a lion charging toward him from the front,
he effortlessly split it in two with a blow of his sword.
And as a forest elephant approached, trumpeting and wheeling in circles,
he struck it down with his sword so that its trunk and feet were severed, causing it to cease its cries.
Then, alone, he strode through the forest like an elephant crushing a lotus pond, trampling the fresh mud-born flowers as a band of thieves might crush them.
Having thus traversed the road and beheld her of most wondrous prowess, he,
that ocean of courage, reached Mālava and spoke to his own queen:
"O Queen, you must not speak of this conduct on my part while we are in my father's house;
for this is a source of shame, what praise indeed can there be for the prowess of a Kṣatriya?"
Having said this, he entered his father's house together with her;
and when questioned by him in great agitation, he related his own story.
Honored by that very father-in-law and provided with elephants and horses,
he went into the presence of the exceedingly powerful king named Gajānīka.
But his wife Kalyāṇavatī, the queen, he left right there in her father’s house, as he was intent on victory over his enemies.
When he had departed and some days had passed,
on one occasion that queen, standing at the window, beheld a certain man.
The moment he was seen in his form, he captivated her heart;
and being drawn by the god of love, she reflected at that very instant:
"I know, noble son, that another may be handsome but not heroic;
nevertheless, alas, my mind runs toward this man."
Thinking, "I shall devote myself to him this very day," she then disclosed that intention of hers to her friend, who was a keeper of secrets.
Having had him brought by that same woman at night, she caused him to enter that harsh inner apartment, drawn up by ropes through the path of the window.
Having entered there, that man was unable to sit upon her couch by his own power; he sat down instead on a separate seat.
Seeing this, while the king was despondent, thinking, "Alas, this man is base," the queen arrived there at that very moment, as a serpent was gliding above.
Seeing him, that man there suddenly rose up in fear,
took up his bow, and struck the serpent with an arrow.
And as he fell from that ruin, the coward threw him out through the window; having escaped that danger, he danced with joy.
Seeing him dancing, Kalyāṇavatī was deeply distressed and thought: "Fie, fie! What is the use of this cowardly and base man of mine?"
As soon as she saw that she was indifferent [to him], her friend, who knew her mind, quickly went out, entered there, and spoke with great agitation: SoKss_10,2.130 //
"O Queen, your father has arrived;
let this youth now go quickly to his own home by the very same path by which he came."
When she had spoken thus, he went out through the window by means of a rope;
overcome with fear, he fell, yet by fate he did not meet his death.
When he had departed, that Kalyāṇavatī said to her friend:
"Friend, you have done very well; since this low fellow has been turned out by you."
"You have understood my heart; indeed, my mind is pained.
Out of shame, my husband conceals the fact that he has struck down tigers, lions, and other beasts."
But this one, having killed a serpent, dances with a base spirit;
having abandoned such a person as that, what delight can I find in this common man?
"Fie on me, whose mind is so unsteady! Or rather, fie on women, who, like flies, abandon camphor and run toward impurity."
Thus, having felt remorse, that queen spent the night and remained there in her father’s house, awaiting her husband.
Meanwhile, Siṃhabala, having been granted the strength of an elephant division by the king,
went and slew those five wicked kinsmen.
Then, having regained his own kingdom and brought back his wife from his father's house,
and having gratified his father-in-law with floods of wealth, he ruled the earth free from thorns for a very long time.

"Thus, O King, even among noble women who possess discernment, the mind—fickle though it may be—runs hither and thither toward a hero, a fortunate man, or a virtuous lord; yet women of pure character are rare indeed."
Having heard this story told by Marubhūti, Naravāhanadatta, the son of the King of Vatsa, spent that night sleeping soundly.
Thus ends the second wave in the Śaktiyaśas book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave.
Then, in the morning, having performed his necessary duties, he [the king] together with his ministers—
Naravāhanadatta went to his own garden to enjoy himself.
Remaining there, he first beheld a mass of light even beyond the sky,
and then he saw many Vidyādharīs descending.
And in the midst of those radiant women, he beheld a certain maiden who captivated the eyes, like a digit of the cool-rayed moon among the stars.
Her face was like a blooming lotus, her tremulous eyes were like bees,
her gait was like that of a graceful swan, and she possessed the fragrance of a flowing blue lotus.
Her waist was adorned with the three folds of skin like a creeper that steals the beauty of waves; she was like the presiding deity of the splendor of a pond in the garden of the God of Love.
And upon seeing her, who was the reviver of his love,
that prince was agitated with longing, like the ocean at the sight of the moon’s form.
"Oh, what an indescribable variety in the beautiful creation of the Creator!
praising thus, he approached her accompanied by his ministers.
And as she gazed at him with a sidelong glance moist with love, he gradually asked her: "Who are you, O blessed lady, and what is the purpose of your coming here?"
Having heard that, the maiden said: "Listen, I shall tell you this:
there is a golden city named Kāñcanaśṛṅga on the Himālaya."
There dwells a lord of the Vidyādharas named Sphaṭikayaśas,
who is righteous and compassionate toward the wretched, the destitute, and those who have come to him for refuge.
Know that I am this daughter of his, named Śaktiyaśas, born of Queen Hemaprabhā and produced through the grace of Gaurī.
I, who was my father’s beloved as his own life and the youngest of five brothers,
then propitiated Pārvatī with vows and hymns at his command.
Satisfied, she granted me all the sciences and commanded me thus:
"Daughter, the power of your science shall be tenfold that of your father."
And Naravāhanadatta, the son of the King of Vatsa and the future emperor of the sky-dwellers, shall be your husband.
Having spoken thus, the wife of Śarva vanished from my sight;
and by her grace, having acquired the power of knowledge, I have gradually attained youth.
And that goddess, having granted me her vision during the night, commanded me today:
"Daughter, you must go in the morning and behold your own husband."
"You must indeed come here this very month, for your father,
with his mind fixed on this intention, will arrange the marriage."
Having spoken thus, that goddess vanished and the night passed away;
then, O noble son, she has come here to see you.
Having said, "Therefore, I shall depart now," Śaktiyaśas, together with her circle of female companions, leapt into the sky and went to her father’s city.
And Naravāhanadatta, eager for that marriage,
entered the inner apartments dejected, perceiving the month as being like an eon.
Seeing him there despondent, Gomukha then said to him:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you a story for your amusement."
In ancient times there was a city known by the name Kāñcanapurī,
and in it there was a great lord of the earth named Sumanas.
By him, who had traversed difficult terrain and wildernesses,
even such enemies were rendered as mere curiosities by his resplendent majesty.
Once, when he was seated in the assembly hall, the doorkeeper informed him:
"Your Majesty, there is a daughter of the Niṣāda chief named Muktālatā."
Taking the parrot held in a cage, she stood outside at the gate,
accompanied by her brother Vīraprabha, desiring to see the King.
When the king said, "Let her enter," that Bhilla maiden entered the courtyard of the royal assembly hall by the command of the doorkeeper.
"Is she not human? Surely she is some celestial woman!"—thus everyone thought there, having beheld her wondrous form.
And having bowed to the king, she then addressed him thus:
"Your Majesty, this parrot named Śāstragañja is a master of the four Vedas."
"A poet, proficient in all branches of knowledge and the arts, has been brought here today for the sake of the Lord's service; let him be accepted."
Having been thus presented by her and taken by the doorkeeper out of curiosity,
the parrot was led before the king and recited this verse.
"O King, this is always fitting that he, with his face darkened by smoke, is kindled by the god [Fire] through the gusts of breath from the wives of his enemies separated from their lovers;
but this is truly a marvel—that by the floods of the water of tears from their humiliation, the great fire of his majesty blazes forth here in the ten directions."
Having thus recited and explained it, Śuka spoke again:
"What is the object of knowledge? From which scripture do you speak? Let it be commanded."
Then, while the king was utterly amazed, the minister said this to him:
"O Lord, I suspect that this is some ancient seer who has been turned into a parrot by a curse."
"When the minister said, 'One who remembers his past lives recalls what was studied previously through the power of the Dharma,' the king then questioned that parrot."
"I am curious, my good sir; tell me your own story: where was your birth?
How did you come to possess such knowledge of the scriptures while in the form of a parrot? And who indeed are you?"
Then, shedding tears, that parrot spoke slowly:
"Even though this should not be told, listen; I shall speak at your command."
O King, near the Himalayas there is a single *rohiṇī* tree,
like the Veda itself, with many branches spreading through the quarters and providing refuge for birds.
In that place, a certain parrot took up residence and lived together with a female parrot;
from her, I was born as a result of the connection of my past misdeeds.
And as soon as I was born, my mother, that female parrot, passed away;
but my father, though old, placed me within his wings and raised me.
Eating the remains of fruits brought by nearby parrots and offering some to me, my father remained there.
Once, a terrifying army of Bhils arrived there for the sake of hunting, making the mountain peaks resound with the blare of trumpets.
Her eyes like those of a terrified black antelope, her garment disarrayed by the dust,
and the mass of her braided hair loosened as the *camarī* yak-tail fans surged in her agitation.
Suddenly that great forest became as if agitated by flight,
as the hosts of Pulindas ran about to slaughter various living beings.
Having spent the day sporting like the God of Death on the hunting grounds,
that army of Śabaras returned, carrying loads of raw flesh.
But there, an old Śabara who had not obtained any meat saw a tree in the evening; being hungry, he approached it.
And having climbed there, he quickly dragged parrots and other birds from their nests one after another, and killing them, he threw them onto the ground.
Seeing him approaching nearby, resembling a servant of Yama, I cowered in fear and slowly hid within my father's wing.
Then that sinner, having reached our nest, dragged my father out by force,
wrung his neck, killed him, and threw him down at the foot of the tree.
And I, having fallen along with my father from the edge of that wing,
emerged and entered slowly and fearfully into the midst of the grass and leaves.
Then, having descended, that Bhilla roasted and ate some parrots in the fire;
taking others, the wicked man went to his own village.
Then, my fears stilled, I passed that night which was long with sorrow;
at dawn, when the sun, the eye of the world, had mostly risen.
My wings obstructing my progress, I moved along with frequent stumbles;
afflicted by thirst, I reached the shore of a lotus pond situated nearby.
There I saw the sage named Marīci, who had performed his ablutions and was seated upon that sandy bank, appearing like my own past merit personified.
Seeing me, the sage comforted me with drops of water from his mouth; out of compassion, he placed me in a leaf-cup and carried me to the hermitage.
Seeing me there, the patriarch Pulastya reportedly laughed;
questioned by the other sages regarding this, he, possessing divine vision, spoke.
"Seeing this parrot of a curse, I laughed out of sorrow;
and having performed my daily rites, I shall relate to you this connected story."
"By hearing this, he shall remember his birth and his previous life.
Having said this, the seer Pulastya rose from his daily ritual.
And when he had performed his daily rites, being requested again by the sages,
that great sage related this story concerning me.
In the city of Ratnākara, there was a king named Jyotiṣprabha,
who ruled the earth as far as the ocean with his powerful command.
To him was born a son by his queen named Harṣavatī, produced by the grace of the Lord of Gaurī, who was pleased by his intense asceticism.
Because the queen had seen the Soma enter her mouth in a dream,
the king gave his son the name Somaprabha.
And that prince Somaprabha gradually grew, spreading through his nectar-like virtues a festival for the eyes of all creatures.
Seeing that he was a hero capable of bearing the burden of sovereignty, young, and beloved by nature,
his father Jyotiṣprabha joyfully consecrated him as the crown prince.
He appointed his own minister’s son, named Priyaṅkara, who possessed excellent qualities, to the office of minister for him, the one known as Prabhākara.
At that moment, Mātali, having taken a divine horse from the sky,
descended and, approaching Somaprabha, addressed him.
"You are a Vidyādhara, a friend of Śakra, who has descended here;
by him was born the one named Aśvaśravas, the son of Uccaiḥśravas."
"O King, out of our former affection, this supreme horse has been sent to you;
mounted upon him here, you shall become invincible to your enemies."
Having spoken thus and given that jewel of a horse to Somaprabha,
he— having received worship— flew up into the sky and departed as the charioteer of Vāsava.
Then, having spent that day in the delightful festivities,
on the following day Somaprabha spoke to his father, the king:
"Father, this is not the duty of a Kṣatriya, namely, to lack the desire for victory.
Therefore, give me your command so that I may set out for the conquest of the quarters."
Hearing that, his father was pleased and replied, "So be it," and Jyotiṣprabha made the necessary arrangements for his journey.

Then, having prostrated before his father, on an auspicious day marked by the moon’s brilliance, Somaprabha set out for the conquest of the quarters accompanied by his forces, mounted upon Indra’s horse.
With that jewel of a horse, he conquered the lords of the earth in all directions;
and he of irresistible prowess extracted treasures from them.
He bent his own bow and the heads of his enemies simultaneously;
yet while that bow attained loftiness, the heads of those enemies did not.
Then, having accomplished his task, as he was returning on the road near the Himalayas,
he encamped his army and engaged in a hunt within the forest.
By chance, he saw there a *kiṃnara* adorned with excellent jewels; and with that horse given by Śakra, he galloped after him to catch him.
That *kiṃnara*, having entered a mountain cave, vanished from sight;
Somaprabha, however, was carried a very great distance by that horse.
