That powder smeared the lips and beard of that evil-minded man,
while the faces of the people there turned white with laughter.
"O Lord, you have heard of the one who eats salt; now hear of the cow-milker.
There was a certain foolish villager, and he had a single cow."
And that cow of his gave a hundred palas of milk to him every day;
once, it happened that a festival was approaching for him.
"I shall drink her abundant milk just once during the festival"—
thinking thus, that fool did not even milk the cow for a single month.
And as soon as he, having reached the festival, milked her, all the milk was gone;
it had been cut off for him, yet the laughter of the world remained unceasing.
The fool who milked the cow has been heard of; now hear of these two others. There was a certain man with a bald head that resembled a copper pot. (SoK 10.5.48)
A certain young man, hungry and having come along the road carrying wood-apples, saw him seated at the foot of a tree.
He struck him on the head with a wood-apple for sport;
though he was bald, he endured it and said nothing to him.
Then he struck him on the head with all the other wood-apples one by one;
yet he remained silent even as blood flowed.
And that foolish youth, exhausted by hunger and deprived of wood-apples— those fruits crushed by his own play in the fruitlessness of his youth— then departed from there.
Saying, "Why should I not endure blows for the sake of sweet wood-apples?",
that bald-headed fool, with blood trickling from his head, went home.
Seeing his head encircled by that blood as if by a turban bound for the empire of a fool, who there did not laugh?
Thus, those of little intelligence fall into the state of being ridiculed by the gods in this world;
they do not achieve their goals, whereas those of great intelligence are honored.
Having heard these stories of charming laughter from Gomukha,
Naravāhanadatta rose and performed his daily rites.
Then, at the onset of night, being urged by him who was full of longing,
Gomukha related this story concerning the perfection of wisdom.
In a certain region of the forest, there was a great silk-cotton tree;
a crow named Laghupāti made his home there and lived in it.
Once, while staying in his own nest, he saw a fierce man arrive there beneath the tree, carrying a net in his hand and holding a club.
Then, as soon as he looked,
the crow spread his net across the ground and scattered grains there, while the man remained hidden.
And at that moment, the lord of pigeons named Citragrīva, wandering through the sky,
arrived there surrounded by hundreds of pigeons.
Seeing that heap of rice, he fell into the net out of a desire for food;
together with his retinue, he became bound by the multitude of snares.
Seeing that, Citragrīva said to all his followers:
"Seizing the net with your beaks, fly up into the sky with speed!"
Then, saying "So be it," they all took up the net and, terrified, began to fly swiftly through the sky as pigeons.
Rising up with his gaze directed upward, the distressed hunter turned back; then Citragrīva, free from fear, spoke to those who were following him.
"Let us go quickly to our friend, the mouse Hiraṇya;
he will cut these snares and set us free."
Having said this, he went with his followers, those who were drawing in the net,
and reaching the entrance of the mouse's hole, he descended from the sky.
"O Hiraṇya, come out! I, Citragrīva, have arrived," thus did the king of pigeons call out to that mouse there.
Having heard this and seeing his friend approaching by way of the entrance,
the mouse emerged from that hundred-mouthed hole.
Approaching and inquiring after his welfare, that mouse,
his friend, also hurriedly cut the snares of the king of pigeons and his followers.
Having addressed the mouse with affectionate words,
Citragrīva, his bonds severed, flew up into the sky and departed together with his followers.

Having observed that [the mongoose] had entered the hole, the swift-flying crow followed him there, came to the entrance of the hole, and spoke to the mouse: *anvāgataḥ sa kāko 'tra laghupātī vilokya tat | bilapraviṣṭaṃ taddvāram āgatyovāca mūṣakam ||* (SoKss 10.5.72)
"I am a crow, swift of flight; having seen you who are so affectionate toward friends, I choose you as a friend—one capable of rescuing me from such a calamity."
Having heard that and seen the crow from within, the mouse said to him: "Go away! What friendship can there be between prey and predator?"
Then that crow said: "Peace! If you were eaten by me, my satisfaction would last but a moment; but in a friend, there is the constant protection of life."
Having spoken thus and made a solemn oath,
the crow, having been reassured by him, formed a friendship with the mouse who had emerged.
The rat brought lumps of meat, and he also brought grains of rice;
eating together in one place, the two of them lived happily. (SoK 10.5.77)
And once that crow said to his friend, the mouse:
"Friend, not far from here, in the middle of the forest, there is a river."
"In that place there is a friend of mine, a tortoise named Mantharaka;
for his sake I am going to that location, where food consisting of meat is easily obtained."
"Food is obtained here only with great difficulty, and I am constantly in fear of hunters.
To the crow who had spoken thus, the mouse replied: SoKss_10,5.80 //
"In that case, let us dwell together; take me there as well.
For I too have this world-weariness here, and I shall speak of it to you right there."
Taking Hiraṇyaka while he was speaking thus with his beak,
Laghupāti flew through the sky and went to the bank of the forest river.
Having gathered there together with the tortoise and his friend Mantharaka,
who had offered him hospitality, he remained there accompanied by the mouse.
And in the course of their conversation, the crow related to that tortoise the reason for his arrival,
including the account of his friendship with Hiraṇya.
Then that tortoise, having made the mouse his friend as praised by the crow, asked him the reason for his weariness and desire to leave his country.
Then Hiraṇya, while both the crow and the tortoise were listening, related this story of his own life.
Dwelling there in a great cave situated near the city, I brought the horse from the royal palace and tethered it there at night.
Seeing me endowed with vigor by that visible necklace and capable of procuring food, the mice surrounded me.
In the meantime, there was a certain wandering mendicant near our cave who had built a small hut and subsisted on various kinds of alms-food.
Having hung the alms-bowl containing the remnants of his meal upon a peg at night, he would set it aside out of a desire to eat in the morning.
And while he was sleeping there, I entered inside through a hole, gave him a leap upward, and carried him off entirely, O night-walker.
Once, another mendicant friend came there to him;
after they had finished eating, he engaged in conversation with him during the night.
Just as I set about taking the food, that mendicant,
lending an ear, repeatedly struck his small gong.
"How did you tear it off? What are you doing with this?"—thus questioned by that visiting mendicant, the monk said to him:
"Here, this mouse has arisen as my enemy; for it always leaps from here and carries away my food, even though it is far off."
"I am frightening him by shaking this worn-out food bowl," said that other wandering mendicant to the monk who had spoken thus.
This greed of living beings leads to their ruin; hear now the story regarding this matter.
Once, while wandering among sacred fords, I reached a certain city.
And there, for the sake of one brahmin’s residence, I entered a house; while I was staying there, that brahmin spoke to his wife.
"Today, on this festival day, cook kṛsara for the sake of the brahmins.
She said to him, "How can you have this, being as destitute as you are?"
Then that brahmin said to her: "My dear, even when there is a need for accumulation, one should not have a mind excessively intent on hoarding; listen to this story in this regard."
Having hunted in a certain forest and fixed his arrow in the notch,
the hunter, taking up meat upon his bow, ran after a boar.
Struck by that very arrow and wounded by the spear, he perished;
and the jackal saw this from a distance.
And he, having arrived, though afflicted by hunger, desiring to make a store,
did not eat even a little of the abundant meat of the boar and the hunter.
He set out to eat that which was placed upon the bow;
at that very moment, pierced by an arrow from a moving machine, he died.
"Therefore, you should not accumulate too much," said that twice-born man to his wife; she agreed to this and cast the sesame seeds out in the sun.
Once she had entered the house, a dog defiled those [beans] by eating them;
consequently, no one would take these kṛsara beans even for a price or otherwise.
"Thus, greed is not for the sake of enjoyment, but leads only to affliction.
Having said this, that wandering mendicant who had arrived there spoke again:
"If you have a spade, give it to me so that today I may skillfully ward off this calamity arising from the mouse."
Having heard that, the wandering mendicant living there gave him a small spade;
and I, remaining concealed, having seen this, entered the cave.
Then,
having seen the hole where I was moving, that rogue wandering mendicant began to dig with that spade.
And while I was intent on fleeing, he dug gradually until he reached that necklace of mine and another collection [of jewels] lying there.
"By this splendor, such strength as that arose in his body," he said to that resident monk while I was listening.
Having taken all my possessions and placed the necklace upon his head,
those two wandering mendicants, joyful as guests and residents alike, went to sleep.
While those two were fast asleep, that wandering mendicant Sthāyin woke up and struck me on the head with a staff as I returned to seize him.
Wounded by that, I did not die by fate, but entered a cave;
moreover, I no longer possessed the strength for the exertion of fetching food.
For youth is indeed the wealth of men, and its absence is old age;
by it, one's vigor, strength, beauty, and even enthusiasm decline.
Then, seeing that I was intent on supporting myself alone,
that entire retinue of mice departed, leaving me behind.
Servants abandon a master who provides no livelihood, bees a tree that bears no flowers, and swans a lake devoid of water—even if they have dwelt there for a long time. (Sūtra-kṛtāṅga 10.5.118)
Thus, having been long distressed there, O best of tortoises, I have come to your side after finding this swift-flying friend.
When Hiraṇyaka had spoken thus, the tortoise Mantharaka replied:
"This is your own place; therefore, do not lose heart regarding your friend."
For the virtuous there is no foreign land; for the contented there is no unhappiness;
for the steadfast there is no misfortune; and for the industrious there is nothing unattainable.
Even as the tortoise was speaking thus, a deer named Citrāṅga,
terrified by a hunter, arrived at that forest from afar.
Having seen him, and seeing that the hunter had subsequently departed,
the tortoise and the others formed a friendship with him as he was comforted.
Then the crow, the tortoise, the deer, and the mouse lived there together as friends, equally happy through their mutual service to one another.
Once, having climbed a tree in that forest, Laghupāti watched for Citrāṅga, who had been away for a long time.
And he saw Citrāṅga on the riverbank, bound by a tethering rope; having dismounted from his horse, he spoke this to the mouse and the tortoise: SoKss_10,5.126
Then, having deliberated and seized that mouse Hiraṇyaka with his beak,
Laghupāti brought him into the presence of Citrāṅga.
And the mouse Hiraṇyaka, having comforted that deer who was distressed by his bonds,
released him in an instant, having severed the snare with his teeth.
Then Mantharaka, the turtle, having approached by way of the middle of the river,
climbed onto the bank near them, he who was dear to his friends.
At that very moment, a hunter who had set the snare arrived from somewhere;
while the deer and other animals fled, he caught and seized the tortoise.
And having thrown him into the net, while he was departing surrounded by the lost deer,
the wicked [hunter] heard this from the words of the far-sighted mouse.
The deer then went a short distance away and lay down as if dead;
meanwhile, the crow remained upon its head, as if pecking at its eyes.
Seeing that, the hunter, thinking the deer was dead and had been caught,
set the tortoise down on the bank of the river and proceeded to go away.
Seeing him gone, the mouse approached and cut the net of the tortoise; released by that means, he fell into the river.
The deer, seeing the hunter draw near, rose up and fled with his tortoise;
the crow also climbed a tree.
Having arrived there, the hunter, failing to catch the tortoise which had escaped by severing its bonds and being deprived of both [the net and the water], went home grieving for his ill fortune.
Then the tortoise and the others gathered together there in joy; and the deer, being full of affection, spoke thus to the tortoise and the rest: SoKss_10,5.137 //
I am fortunate that I have obtained you as friends, who,
disregarding their own lives, have thus rescued me from death today.
Thus praised by that deer,
the crow, the tortoise, and the mouse dwelt there together with him, happy in their mutual affection.
In this way, even animals accomplish their desired ends through wisdom;
they likewise do not abandon a friend in times of distress, even at the cost of their own lives.
Thus, attachment to friends is superior to that toward women;
they declare this because [attachment to women] is the basis for envy. Listen, therefore, to a story concerning this.
O Lord, in a certain city there lived a certain envious man;
he had a beloved wife who was endowed with great beauty.
Lacking trust, he never left her alone;
for he feared the ruin of her virtue even from those depicted in paintings.
Then, on one occasion, due to some necessary business, that man set out for another region, taking his wife with him.
Seeing ahead on the road a forest infested with snakes, he, out of fear of them,
left her in the house of an elderly village Brahmin and went on his way.
While she was staying there, he saw her coming along the path with a certain bold young Bhilla; she then departed from that place with him.
Possessed by him, she wandered at will through that village,
her jealousy toward her husband departed like a river whose dam has been broken.
Meanwhile, having finished his business, the husband returned and requested that wife from the village-dwelling brahmin; that brahmin then spoke to him.
"I do not know where she has gone; I know only this much:
the Bhillas came here, and she must have been carried off by them."
Go quickly from here to that village nearby;
there you will find your wife, so do not entertain any other thought.
Having been addressed thus by him, weeping and censuring his own perverted intellect,
he went to that Bhilla village and saw his wife there.
Seeing him, that wicked woman approached him and, being afraid, then said:
"It is not my fault; I was brought here by force by a Bhilla."
"Come, let us go there before anyone sees us.
To her husband, who spoke thus and was blinded by passion, she replied:
This is the time for the arrival of that Bhilla who goes hunting;
having pursued us, he will certainly kill both you and me.
"Having entered this cave, remain hidden for now;
and having killed him while he sleeps at night, we two shall depart from here without fear."
Thus addressed by that deceitful woman, he entered that cave;
for what room is there for discernment in the heart of one whose mind is blinded by desire?
Then that wicked woman showed him, who had been brought inside the house due to his addiction,
to the Bhilla when he arrived at the end of the day.
And that powerful Bhillas of cruel deeds, having dragged him out,
bound him very firmly to a tree in the morning for the purpose of an offering to the goddess.
And having eaten, while he was watching, he enjoyed the pleasure of sexual union with his wife during the night and fell asleep together with her.
Seeing him asleep, that envious man, bound to the tree,
worshipped Caṇḍī with hymns of praise and, afflicted by distress, went to her for refuge.
Manifesting herself, she granted him that boon by which,
with that very sword, he severed the head of the Bhilla, whose bonds had already slipped loose.
"Now come! This wicked man has been slain by me," he said, awakening his wife; she too rose up, deeply distressed.
Having taken the head of that Bhilla unnoticed during the night,
that wicked woman then set out together with her husband.
And having reached the city in the morning, showing him that head there, she cried out, attacking her husband: "My husband has been killed by this man!"
Then, accompanied by him, he was led before the king by the city guards;
questioned there concerning what had occurred, the envious man described it exactly as it had happened.
Then the king, having investigated the truth, had the ears and nose of that wicked woman cut off; he released her husband and set him free.
Released and freed from the grip of affection for his wicked wife, he went to his own home;
for such, O King, does a woman act when constrained by jealousy.
For jealousy alone teaches women an excessive attachment to men;
therefore, a wise man should protect a woman by never revealing her jealousy.
A secret must not be disclosed to women in any way whatsoever by a man desiring his own welfare; in this regard, let this story be heard.
A certain nāga, out of fear of Vainateya, had fled to some courtesan’s house on earth, having assumed a human form.
The courtesan also took a fee of five hundred elephants;
and by his own power, that Naga gave them to her every day.
“From where have you come day after day with so many elephants? Tell me, who are you?
Thus the playful woman then questioned him persistently.
"Do not speak to anyone; out of fear of Tārkṣya, I remain here thus," he said, for even he, deluded by Māra, claimed, "I am a nāga."
Then that courtesan told her secret to a procuress;
subsequently, Tārkṣya, searching the world, arrived there in human form.
Approaching that procuress, she said to her: "Noble lady, I shall stay today in your daughter's house; let my lodging fee be taken."
"Here a nāga dwells eternally, providing [the food for] five hundred elephants; so why pay a daily fee? Thus even the procuress spoke to him.
Then Garuḍa, perceiving that the nāga was staying there,
entered the house of the woman at the gate in the guise of a guest.
There, beholding that naga situated upon the roof of the palace,
he revealed himself, leaped up, struck him, and devoured him.
"Therefore, a wise man should not speak of secrets without restraint to women.
Having said this, Gomukha began to recount another story of a fool.
Who was that bald man with a head resembling a copper pot? He was a fool, yet he possessed wealth in this world and felt ashamed of being without hair.
Then a certain rogue, a parasite, approached him and said:
"There is a physician who knows the medicine for producing hair."
Having heard this, he said to him: "If you will command me, then I shall give wealth to you and to that physician."
When he had spoken thus, that rogue, having enjoyed the wealth of the simple man for some time, brought him a fraudulent physician.
Having lived off that bald-headed man for a long time, the physician finally removed his turban, bound it around his own head, and showed it to the foolish woman.
Even upon seeing that, being devoid of reflection, that dull-witted man requested medicine from the physician for the sake of his hair; then the physician said to him:
"How can a bald man himself produce hair for another?"—
thus, O fool, have I shown you my own hairless head.
"Nevertheless, you will not understand at all," the physician said, and departing with the words "Fie on you! he went away.
Thus, O King, rogues always play with those of dull intellect.
Thus has been heard the story of one deluded by hair; now let the story of one deluded by oil be heard: there was a certain man who was the servant of a certain learned man.
Once, sent by that master to a merchant to fetch oil,
he took some oil from him into his bowl.
Then, as he was returning carrying a bowl of oil, he was told by a certain friend: "Guard this bowl of oil; it is leaking downward."
Having heard that, the fool turned the vessel over to look beneath;
by doing so, all that oil fell from it onto the ground.
Having realized this, he was laughed at by the world and expelled from his master's house;
therefore, for a deluded person, one's own intelligence is better than following instruction.
Listen to the story of the fool who was deluded by oil and the one deluded by bones;
there was a certain foolish man whose wife was unchaste.
Once, when her husband had gone to another country on business,
she [instructed] her own trusted female servant in the house, having given her instructions regarding her duties.
Having established Ananyadāsī in her position and departed from there, she then went to the house of her paramour, desiring unrestrained pleasure.
Then, as her husband arrived, she stood with her training intact, her voice choked with tears, and said to him like a servant-woman: "Your wife has died and has been cremated."
Having said this, she led him to the cemetery and showed him the bones from another funeral pyre; taking them up, he wept.
Having performed the water libations at sacred fords and having cast those bones [into the water],
that fool proceeded with the funeral rites (śrāddha) for his wife.
And by that very same female servant who had brought him, saying "O good Brahmin," he made that very man his wife's paramour a Brahmin invited to the *śrāddha*.
Having approached there together with that Upapati, his wife,
dressed in magnificent attire, ate choice food month after month.
O Lord, by the power of the dharma of a virtuous wife, your wife has come from the other world in person and now eats together with the brahmin.
Just as that female servant spoke to her husband,
so did that crest-jewel of fools carry out everything accordingly.
In this way, those of simple disposition are deceived with ease by wicked women;
you have heard the story of Asthimugdha—now let the tale of the Caṇḍāla girl be heard by you.
There was a certain beautiful and charming Caṇḍāla girl who formed a resolution in her heart to obtain a universal monarch as her husband.
Once, seeing the king who had come out for a stroll through the city— the most excellent of men— she proceeded to follow him with the thought that he was her husband.
Just then, a sage came along that path; having bowed at his feet while still mounted upon his elephant, the king departed for his own palace.
Having seen that and reflecting upon this supreme sage even more than the king,
the Caṇḍāla girl abandoned the king and followed the sage.
That sage, as he was proceeding, saw an empty temple of Śiva before him;
placing his knees upon the ground there and bowing to Śiva, he departed from that place.

Seeing that and considering Śiva to be even more excellent than the sage, that woman of the lowest caste abandoned the sage with the thought that he was her husband, and took refuge right there in the God.
And in that very moment, a dog entered there, climbed onto the throne of the deity,
and lifting up its leg, did what was appropriate for its kind.
Seeing that, the woman of the lowest caste, perceiving that dog to be the supreme deity,
followed after him as he went, abandoning the god out of a desire for a husband.
And the dog, having arrived at the Caṇḍāla’s house,
rolled affectionately at the feet of a certain familiar young Caṇḍāla.
Then, beholding him and considering the son of a Caṇḍāla to be the best of dogs,
that low-born woman, content with her own kind, chose him alone as her husband.
Thus, the dull-witted, having set foot upon the wrong path, fall far from their own proper station;
and in this way, a king becomes a fool—now hear further in brief.
There was once a certain foolish king who, though possessing a treasury, was miserly; one day, his well-wishing ministers spoke to him thus:
In this world and the next, generosity removes the miserable destinies;
therefore, give that gift, for both lifespans and riches are fragile.
Having heard that, the king said: "I shall give that gift only if, upon dying, I see myself fallen into an evil rebirth."
Then those ministers sat in silence, inwardly laughing:
"In this way, the fool does not abandon his wealth until he is abandoned by his wealth."
"O King, you have heard of Rājabhaṭa; now hear of two friends in the interval. There was a lord of the earth named Candrāpīḍa in Kānyakubja."
And he had a certain servant named Dhavalamukha,
who would always enter the house after having eaten and drunk outside.

Once, when asked by his wife, "From where do you always come back so full of food and drink?", Dhavalamukha replied to her in this way: SoKss_10,5.221: "I have been eating the flesh of those who, having eaten and drunk themselves, have gone to sleep. SoKss_10,5.222: "And I have been drinking the wine that they drank. SoKss_10,5.223: "And I have been wearing the garments that they wore. SoKss_10,5.224: "And I have been sleeping upon the beds that they slept upon. SoKss_10,5.225: "Thus, O lady with beautiful hips, I am always satisfied. SoKss_10,5.226: "But I am not able to give you anything; for I am a thief who steals from others. SoKss_10,5.227: "Therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall go elsewhere; for I cannot remain here. "O beautiful one, having constantly eaten and drunk at the side of my friend,
I always return to him, for I have two friends in this world."
One was named Kalyāṇavarman, who provided assistance with food and other necessities;
the second was Vīrabāhu, who assisted even with his own life.
Having heard this from his wife, Dhavalamukha said:
"Show me those two friends of mine. (SoKss 10.5.224)
Then, accompanied by him, he went to the house of Kalyāṇavarman; and he too attended upon him with costly services.
On another day, he went into the presence of Vīrabāhu accompanied by his wife;
and he, being occupied with dice, offered him a welcome and then dismissed him.
Then his wife, full of curiosity, said to Dhavalamukha:
"Kalyāṇavarman performed a great act of hospitality for you."
"Only a mere welcome was offered by Vīrabāhu to you;
O noble son, how then can you consider that man to be a superior friend?"
Having heard that, he said: "Go and tell them both in turn that our king has suddenly become angry; then you will know for yourself."
Having been told this by him, she went at once and said "So be it" to Kalyāṇavarman; and as soon as he heard her, he spoke to her.
"I am a merchant's son; tell me, what shall I do for the king?
Having been addressed thus by him, she then went into the presence of Vīrabāhu.
He likewise reported the king’s wrath toward his master;
upon hearing this, he came running, seizing his sword and shield.
Dissuaded from his anger by his ministers,
that king then sent Vīrabāhu home with the words, "Go to him," O Dhavalamukha.
"In this way, O slender one, there was an interval between these two friends of mine.
Having been addressed thus by Dhavalamukha, his wife was then satisfied.
Thus, one is a friend by way of metaphor, while another is so in reality;
for even though they are equal in their quality of being oily, oil is simply oil and ghee is ghee.
Having thus related this story,
the minister Gomukha again told other charming tales in succession to Naravāhanadatta.

"Do not do so; you must not place your trust in this deceitful man.

"Since she, though trusted by me, is wicked and has fled after stealing my wealth—

"Shall I suddenly bring this unchaste woman into my house?
Thus reflected Dhanadeva upon reaching his own country.

For a leather bag is suspended there by a rope through a window;

And this state of affairs became known throughout this entire city;

As long as he had no desire for dalliance because he perceived those faults,

I always enjoy the company of the young wife of the village headman;

Having heard this from Gopāla and restraining his inner anger,

"If that is so, I am your guest here; give me this garment of yours, so that today I may go there just like you, for I have a great curiosity."

And under the impression that it was me, he summoned her and gave her his own woman's clothing;

When the cowherd had spoken thus,

Even toward one who is base and nearby, wicked women feel passion;

He, though afflicted with leprosy, replied to him, "I am Kāmadeva."
"What delusion is this? You are Kāmadeva; it is your own beauty that proclaims it to you.

In this case, a rogue named Śaśin,
having deposited his wife— who had been given to him as a sole attendant— in an underground chamber, departed for another country out of jealousy.
By the power of destiny, my wife saw me here,
and her heart instantly drawn by passion, she surrendered herself to me.
Together with her, I constantly take my pleasure night after night;

curiosity has arisen in me regarding her, having heard about her from you."
Therefore, this very night, I shall enter there out of devotion to you;

Having been addressed thus by that Śaśin, the leper spoke to him:

"Stay here, wrapping your hands and feet with your garment as I am,

There, having ascertained for certain by the touch of her limbs that she grieving in the darkness was indeed his own wife, the Moon attained a state of world-weariness.
Then, while she was fast asleep, he went out unobserved and approached Dhanadeva and Rudrasoma.
Having related his own life story to them, he spoke in distress:
"Alas! Fie upon those things that fall into low places, which are fickle, yet appear delightful from afar!"
Women as difficult to guard as rivers flowing into a chasm cannot be restrained;
for even though she dwells in an underground chamber, this wife of mine has gone to a leper.
Saying, "Therefore, even for me the forest is better; fie on the household life," he spent that night together with the merchant, who shared his sorrow.
In the morning, all three set out together toward the forest;
at the end of the day, they reached a tree by the roadside near the edge of a pond.
Having eaten and drunk, they climbed that tree at night and remained there;
they saw a traveler who had come and fallen asleep beneath the tree.
And in an instant, they saw another man emerge from the middle of the pond,
vomiting up a bed with women upon it.
Having enjoyed that woman, he fell asleep upon his bed;
and as soon as she saw him, the woman rose and united with a traveler.
When asked by him at the end of their dalliance, "Who are you two?", she replied:
"This is a nāga; I am his wife, a nāga maiden."
And let there be no fear for you, because ninety-nine travelers have already been consumed by me;

As she was speaking thus,
that serpent woke up by chance, bit the traveler, and having emitted flames from his mouth, reduced them both to ashes.
Where women cannot be guarded even when confined within the body, what talk can there be of guarding them in a house? Fie, fie upon them!
When Nāga had thus departed for the pond, those three— Śaśin and the others— having spent the night conversing, went to the forest contented.
In that [state], with minds stilled by the practice of the four meditations— loving-kindness and the rest— complete and undivided, their intellects rightly disciplined and gentle toward all beings,
those three also attained accomplishment in the samādhi of incomparable supreme bliss and, having exhausted all darkness, gradually reached liberation.
But their wives, who had fallen into a miserable state produced by the ripening of their own sins—
wicked women fallen from both worlds— perished very soon indeed.
Thus, passion born of delusion brings suffering to no one more than toward women; yet for those who maintain detachment even toward them, dispassion leads to liberation.
Thus, having heard for a long time from his minister Gomukha this diversion of stories while longing for a reunion with Śaktiyaśas, the son of the King of Vatsa finally and slowly fell asleep.
Thus ends the eighth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Ninth Wave.
Then, on another day, once again entertaining her during this night as before, [he said:]
Gomukha told a story to Naravāhanadatta.
In a certain city, there was the son of a wealthy merchant, born from a portion of a Bodhisattva, who was compassionate even toward the dead.
His father, being infatuated with another’s wife and incited by her, banished him;

But leaving behind his younger brother— who was coming along as a companion, who had likewise been rejected by his father,

Traveling along that path for seven days, he sustained his wife—who was exhausted by hunger and thirst—with his own flesh and blood; yet she, being wicked, ate those very things.
On the eighth day, he reached a mountain forest resounding with the voices of river waves, where the trees bore excellent fruit and provided good shade, and the meadows were lush and green.
There, having comforted his weary wife with roots, fruits, and water,
he descended to a mountain river garlanded with waves in order to bathe.
And there he saw a man whose four limbs— both hands and feet— had been severed,
being carried away by the flood of water and longing for protection.
Then, although exhausted by many fasts, that compassionate Great Being plunged into the river and rescued that man.
"Brother, who did this to you? asked the compassionate one.
Having brought that mangled man to dry land, he questioned him, and the man replied: SoKss_10,9.11 //
"With my hands and feet cut off, I was cast into a river by my enemies who wished to bring about my death through suffering; yet I was rescued from there by you."
When he had spoken thus, the Great Being, having understood him, applied a bandage to his wound, provided him with food, and performed his own bathing and other personal needs.
Then, subsisting on roots and fruits, that son of a merchant— an incarnation of a Bodhisattva— remained in that forest together with his wife, practicing austerities.
Once, while he had gone out for the sake of fruits and roots,
his wife, afflicted by passion, dallied with that Ruṇḍa whose wounds were still healing.
Having consulted with him, that wicked woman, desiring the death of her husband,

Having heard that, he said, "So be it," and there in the pit, having prepared a medicine,

Having led him to a place far, far away, and having protected him well,

Then, having ascended to dry land and reflecting upon the behavior of women, he,

Whomever the auspicious elephant, while being led through the streets by the citizens,

Delighted by his courage, the elephant wandered about like the Creator himself and, approaching him,

Having obtained the kingdom, he delighted in compassion, sympathetic joy, and patience,

His wife, too, being fearless and believing him to have been carried away by the river, wandered here and there with her lover,
the maimed man, mounted upon her back.
"This husband of mine has his feet and hands cut off by an enemy; I am a devoted wife who sustains him by begging. Therefore, give me alms."
Thus, begging from village to village and town to town,

In that very manner, as she wandered here begging for alms,

having recognized from afar that she was a devoted wife, he questioned her: "Who is this woman of such devotion?"
"O Goddess, I am a devoted wife"— not realizing this,
that sinful woman spoke thus to her husband, who was surrounded by the majesty of royal splendor.
Then that king, who was a portion of a Bodhisattva, said to her with a smile:
"Your devotion to your husband has been witnessed by me through this very fruit."
That human rakshasi, who was not even willing to accept her own blood and flesh when offered by her husband with his own uncut hand, [now acts otherwise].
Alas, how is it that she, who was always taking away my blood and flesh,
has now been accepted and made a vehicle by this mangled and mutilated man?
"Who indeed was that blameless husband of yours who was cast into the river?
By that deed you carry this mangled man and now bear him."
Having thus recognized her husband with his conduct revealed,
she then became, as if out of fear, like one swooning, like one painted in a picture, and like one dead.
"What is this? Tell us, O Lord!"—thus questioned by his ministers who were full of curiosity, the king then described everything to them exactly as it had happened.
Then, having learned that she was the wife of another, they cut off her ears and nose,
branded her with a mark, and banished her from the country along with her husband.
Then Fate displayed a fitting union: the maimed Bodhisattva with his severed nose joined with the royal splendor of a king.
Thus, the course of women's minds is indeed as difficult to discern as that of fate— which is beyond deliberation and ever-inclined toward the base.
Thus, for those who have not abandoned ethical discipline, who possess compassion for sentient beings, and who have conquered anger,
prosperity comes of its own accord and unexpectedly, as if out of satisfaction.
Having thus told this story, the minister Gomukha once again related this tale to Naravāhanadatta.
Somewhere in a forest, there was a certain portion of a bodhisattva who had built a hut;
with a heart single-mindedly devoted to compassion, that great being was practicing austerities.
There, rescuing living beings who were in distress as well as *piśācas*,
he satisfied others with water and food through his own supernatural power.
Once, while wandering in this forest region for the sake of helping others,
he saw a great well and cast his gaze into its depths.
And at that moment, a woman standing within it saw him and spoke aloud:
"O Great-souled One, I am a woman; [those were] a lion, a golden-crested bird, and a [golden] horse."
"And we four, including the serpent, have fallen here into this well during the night; therefore, out of compassion, deliver us from this suffering."
Having heard this, he said to those women: "If you three have fallen here blinded by darkness, how did the bird fall here?"
"Likewise, this one has also fallen and is bound by the net of hunters," that woman replied to the Great Being.
Then, as he desired to lift them up by the power of his asceticism, he was unable to lift them; rather, his spiritual success began to decline.
"This woman is surely wicked, for my success has been destroyed simply by conversing with her;
therefore, I shall now employ another stratagem."
Having reflected thus, the Great Being, while they were offering praise, drew them all out from the well using a rope made of grass.
Filled with wonder, he questioned the lion, the bird, and the serpent:
"How is it that your speech is articulate? Tell me, what is the story?"
Then the lion said: "We are those who remember our former births and possess clear speech;
we were mutual oppressors, so hear our story in due order."
Having said this, the lion began to relate his own story:
"On the Snowy Mountain, there is a preeminent city named Vaidūryaśṛṅga."
There was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Padmavega,
and a son named Vajravega was born to him.
Living in the world of the Vidyādharas, that Vajravega, arrogant and intoxicated by his own heroism, engaged in conflict with whomever he encountered.
When he disregarded the words of his father who was forbidding him,
his father then cursed him, saying, "Fall into the world of mortals!"
Then Vajravega, his pride destroyed, fallen from his knowledge, and struck by the curse, wept and begged his father for an end to that curse.
Then his father, Padmavega, having reflected for a moment, said:
"Having become the son of a Brahmin on earth, you have once again displayed such pride."
Then, due to your father’s curse, you will become a lion and fall into a well;
however, some great being, out of compassion, will rescue you.
"By performing a service for him in times of distress,
you shall be released from this curse," his father thus ordained the end of his curse.
Now, here in Mālava, this Vajravega was born as the son named Devaghoṣa to the brahmin named Haraghoṣa.
There too, out of pride in his heroism, he created enmity with many;
and his father said to him, "Do not create enmity with many."
Not doing as he was told, his father, arrogant in his own prowess, cursed him in anger: "O evil-minded one, become a lion this very moment!"
Thus, by the curse of his father, Devaghoṣa was once again born here in this forest as a lion, having been an incarnation of a Vidyādhara.
Know me to be this very lion; wandering by chance at night, I have today fallen into this well and have been rescued by you, O Great Being.
Therefore, I shall depart for now; and whenever you may fall into distress anywhere, you should remember me, and by performing a service for you, I shall release myself from my own curse.
When the lion had departed after speaking thus, that bird Suvarṇacūḍa was questioned by the Bodhisattva and then related his own story.
On the Himalayas there was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Vajradaṃṣṭra;
five daughters were born to him in succession from his queen.
Then, having propitiated Hara through ascetic penance,
that king obtained a son named Rajatadamshtra, who was dearer to him than life itself.
Through that father’s affection, the boy Rajatadamstra was granted the sciences; even as a child, he grew there, a festival for the eyes of his kinsmen.
Once, he beheld his elder sister, Somaprabhā by name,
playing the piñjaraka lute before the goddess Gaurī.
"Give me your yellow lute; I too shall play upon it," he then requested of her, out of childishness and persistence.
When she herself, out of fickleness, offered that sound and other things to him,
he snatched them away from her and flew up into the sky like a bird.
Then his sister cursed him:
"Since you flew away after forcibly seizing my piñjaraka bird, you shall become a golden-crested bird."
Having heard that, Rajatadamṣṭra approached him while prostrate at his feet and, being entreated by him,
his sister told him the end of the curse.
When you have become a bird and fall into a blind well, O fool,
someone filled with compassion will then rescue you.
"By performing a service for him, you shall cross over this curse";
having been told this by her, his brother Svarṇacūla was born as a bird.
"I am that very bird with the golden crest who fell into this pit at night;
having been rescued here by you, I shall now depart."
"Remember me when you are in distress, for I have indeed rendered you a service;
I shall release you from the curse," having said this, the bird also departed from there.
Then, questioned by that Bodhisattva, the serpent related his own story to that great-souled one.
Long ago, I was a young ascetic in the hermitage of Kaśyapa;
there I had a single friend, the son of a sage.
And once, when my friend had descended into this lake to bathe,
I, standing on the bank, saw a three-hooded serpent approaching.
In order to frighten that friend of mine in jest,
I bound that serpent by the power of mantras at the edge of the bank in his presence.
Having bathed in an instant, my friend reached the bank; seeing that great serpent unexpectedly, he was terrified and fell into a state of confusion.
Then, having perceived through meditation that my attempt to terrify him had finally brought him consolation after a long time, he, though my friend, rebuked me in anger.
"Go! Become a great three-hooded serpent right now!
Thus addressed, the son of the seer then told me the end of his curse.
When you have fallen into the well and become like a serpent, he who shall rescue you—
if you perform a service for him at that opportune moment, you will be released from the curse.
Having spoken thus, when he had departed, I became a serpent;
and today I have been pulled out of the well by you, so now I am going.
"Once you have remembered and rendered service to the shrine, you shall be released from your own curse.
Having said this, the serpent departed, and the woman described her own history.
"I am the wife of a son of the kṣatriya caste, an attendant of the king—
brave, generous, young, handsome, and proud."
"Even though I, a sinful woman, had ceased my attachment to other men,
my husband, having learned of that, set his mind upon punishing me."
Having learned of this from the mouth of my friend, I fled at once;
having entered this forest at night, I was rescued by you after falling into a well.
"By your grace, I shall now go somewhere and live;
may that day come for me when I can perform a service in return for you."
Having spoken thus to the Bodhisattva, that unchaste woman departed from his presence and went to the city of the king named Gotravardhana.
Having established an acquaintance with his retinue,
she remained there in the service of the king’s chief queen, assuming the status of a maidservant.
Because of that conversation with the woman, even for that bodhisattva,

Then, exhausted by hunger and thirst, he first remembered that lion; and the lion, having arrived as soon as he was thought of, provided for his sustenance with the flesh of deer.

Having spoken thus, he abandoned his lion-form, became a Vidyādhara once more,

Then that portion of the Bodhisattva, distressed for lack of livelihood, again remembered Khaga;

Having been informed of his distress by him, that bird went and returned in an instant,

And he said: "By this means, your livelihood shall be eternal;
and for me, the end of the curse has come. May it be well with you; I shall now depart."
Having spoken thus, he too became a young Vidyādhara and,
traveling through the sky to his own world, obtained the kingdom from his father.
Wandering about to sell those jewels, the Bodhisattva reached that city where the woman who had been pulled from the well was staying.
There, having placed those ornaments in the secluded house of a certain elderly Brahmin woman, he went to the marketplace.
At that moment, he saw that very woman being pulled up from the well in the forest as she was coming toward him; she too beheld him.
When they had conversed with one another, that woman then, in the course of their talk,
informed him that she was situated by the side of the king’s chief queen.
Questioned by her regarding his own history,
that upright man related to her how he had obtained those jeweled ornaments from the bird with the golden crest.
Having taken the jewelry, she showed it in the house of the old woman;
that deceitful woman also went and reported it to the queen, her own mistress.
And while that queen was looking on, a bird with a golden crest deceitfully carried off her jewelry box from within the palace.
And having learned from the mouth of that woman— she who had known what was to be known— that he had arrived at her own city, the queen informed the king.
The king also had that Bodhisattva, who had been shown by that wicked woman,
brought from his house by his servants after having him bound along with his ornaments.
Having questioned him about his story and considering his words to be true,
he took him prisoner along with his ornaments and had him bound.
While staying there in captivity, the Bodhisattva remembered that serpent;
and he, too, approached him as one who had entered the state of a seer’s son.
Having seen him and being asked about his purpose, the serpent spoke to the virtuous man:
"I shall go and coil myself around this lord of the earth from his feet to the top of his head."
"And I shall not release him until you have come here and said to me, 'I will release the king from the serpent'; and you must say these words right here."
"When you have arrived, I shall release the king from here by your word;
and once released by me, this king will bestow half of his own kingdom upon you."
Having spoken thus, that serpent went and coiled itself around the king, remaining there with its three hoods spread over his head.
Then, while the people were crying out, "Alas, alas! The king has been bitten by a snake!
the Bodhisattva said, "I shall protect the king from the serpent."
When his attendants, who were learned in the scriptures, informed him of those words,
the king, seized by the serpent, had the Bodhisattva summoned and spoke to him.
"If you release me from this serpent,
I shall give half of my kingdom to you, as well as these ministers of mine who stand here between us."
Having heard that and being told "So be it" by the ministers, he said to the serpent: "O portion of a Bodhisattva, release the king immediately!"
Then, released by that serpent, the king gave half his kingdom to that Bodhisattva; and he, too, became healthy in an instant.
And the serpent, his curse having been exhausted, became a young son of a sage;
having related the account to the assembly, he departed for his own hermitage.
Thus, for those of virtuous nature, certainty leads only to what is auspicious;
likewise, transgression leads to suffering even for the great.
Even the benefit of saving their lives touches upon the destruction of trust in women; what more need be said of them?
Having told this story, Gomukha said to the son of the King of Vatsa: "I shall tell you more; listen again to these charming tales."
There was once a certain dull-witted monk in a certain monastery;
while wandering one day along a street, he was bitten on the knee by a dog.
Bitten by a dog, he returned to his own monastery and reflected:
"Each one here will ask me, 'What happened to your knee? (SoKss 10.9.133)
"In this way, for how much longer shall I continue to convince them?
Therefore, I shall employ a means here to awaken everyone all at once."
Having reflected thus, that foolish monk quickly climbed atop the monastery, took up his staff with its knotted end, and struck it.
Having heard him say, "Why do you play the lute at this unseasonable time and without cause?", the monks then gathered together in astonishment and questioned him.
"A dog has bitten my knee; I tell you this only when asked by each one of you individually. It is in this way that you have been assembled by me. (SoKss 10.9.137)
"Therefore, all of you understand this;
see my knee," he said to those monks, pointing out his knee that had been bitten by a dog.
Then all those monks laughed heartily, pressing their sides together,
saying, "How much has he done, and yet how great is this outburst of passion!"
O fool, listen to this account of a *mūrkha-ṣṭakkva-mūrkha* ascetic:
there was once a certain miserly man somewhere who was both a fool and a *ṣṭakkva*, yet possessed great wealth.
In that assembly, he always ate barley meal devoid of salt;
he never once perceived the taste of any other food.
Once, impelled by the Creator, he said to his own wife:
"Faith has arisen in me toward the milk-tree; cook it for me today."
"So be it," she replied; then his wife cooked the milk-based dish, while that *ṭakka* remained hidden inside, having retired to his bed.
Seeing him, [the thief thought], "May no guest come here to me"; at that moment, a certain friend of his, a rogue named Ṭakka, arrived there.
"Where is your husband? he asked her, his wife; she, however, gave him no answer and entered her husband's presence.
Having related the arrival of his friend, he said to that wife:
"Sit here weeping and remain holding my feet."
And you should say to my friend, "My husband has died";
then, once he has departed, we two may enjoy the milk-yielding cow in comfort.
When she had been told this by him and began to weep,
her friend entered and asked her, "What is this?"
"Look, my husband has died," she said; at this, he reflected:
"Where have I ever seen her cooking so happily, with such an abundance of milk?"
"How is it that this husband of mine has just now perished without any illness?
Surely, having seen me as a guest, these two have fabricated this falsehood."
Thinking, "Therefore, I must not go," that rogue sat down and remained there, crying out, "Alas, friend! Alas, friend!"
Hearing his cries, his kinsmen entered the cemetery and prepared to take that fool, who lay there like a corpse, to the *ṭakka* (cremation ground).
"Arise, before you are led away by these kinsmen and cremated," his wife then whispered into his ear.
"Not so! This rogue Ṭakka wishes to devour my Kṣīriṇī.
I shall not rise; even if he comes for me, I will remain dead."
"For even a handful of food is more precious than life itself for those such as I," that fool replied to his wife in private.
Then, led away by that evil friend and his own kinsmen,
though being burned, he remained motionless and uttered no word until death.
Thus that fool gave up his life, yet he did not [protect] the milch cow;
and he consumed her wealth, acquired through hardship, while others enjoyed it with ease.
The miser has been heard of; now let these "ghosts of cats" be heard.
In Ujjayinī, there was once a certain foolish teacher in a monastery.
There, he could not sleep at night due to the harassment of mice;
distressed by this, he described it to a certain friend.
"Bring a cat and place it here; it will eat the mice.
Thus that brahmin friend spoke to his teacher.
"What kind of cat is it, where does it stay? I have never seen one before," said the teacher; to him, his friend replied once more:
His eyes are glassy, his complexion is tawny and grey, and he has a hairy skin upon his back; he wanders here in the streets.
"Search for him by these identifying marks and bring him here quickly;
he is my friend Mārjāra. Having said this, the king's friend departed for his home.
Then that dull-witted preceptor said to his own disciples:
"While you were standing here, you have surely heard the signs [of recognition]."
"Search for that cat here somewhere in the streets.
"So be it," said those disciples, and they went there, wandering here and there.
Nevertheless, they did not see that cat at all;
then, they beheld a certain young brahmin coming out from the mouth of the street.
He had glass beads on his pair of eyes, was ash-brown in complexion,
and wore upon his back a hairy deer-skin.
"Having seen him, they said, 'This is that very cat who has been found by us, just as we were told,' and having seized him, they led him into the presence of their teacher."
The preceptor, too, having observed that he possessed the appropriate characteristics of a cat as described by Maitra,
placed him there inside the monastery at night.
Hearing the name "Mārjāra" given to himself by those foolish men, that dull-witted boy thought, "Surely there is a cat here."
And that foolish boy was the pupil of that brahmin by whom those characteristics of a cat had been told out of friendship to his preceptor.
In the morning, that brahmin arrived there and, seeing the boy inside,
asked the students in alarm, "By whom was he brought here?"
"This cat was recognized by us as being you, O Śruta,
and has been brought here," said the foolish teacher and his disciples.
Then, laughing, that brahmin said: "O fools, where is a human being, and where is this animal, a cat, four-legged and possessing a tail?"
Having heard that, those dull-witted men released the boy and said,
"In that case, let us search for and bring back another cat just like that one."
When they had spoken thus, the people there laughed at those fools;
for to whom in this world does ignorance not become a cause for ridicule?
The story of the Cat-Demon has been told; now hear these others as well.
In a certain monastery, there was a foolish man who was the leader of many fools.
Once, while being recited by someone, he heard from a treatise on dharma that there is very great fruit for the maker of a pond in the world beyond.
Then, having filled it with wealth, he had a vast pond dug, full of water,
not far from his own monastery.
Once, that leader of fools went to see that pond and beheld its sandy banks uprooted by someone.
Having returned in the same manner on another day, he saw that the bank of that pond had been excavated elsewhere, and filled with agitation, he reflected:
"Starting from dawn, I shall remain right here for the day;
I will see who does this," he reflected, and set out in the morning.
On another day, when he arrived and was staying there,
he saw a bull descending from the sky and digging into the bank with its two horns.
"This bull is divine; why then should I not go to heaven with him?
Thinking thus, he approached the bull and seized its tail with both hands.
Then, having swiftly lifted up that Bhūta who was clinging to the tip of his tail,
the Blessed Lord Bull carried him in an instant to his own abode, Kailāsa.
There, having obtained divine foods such as sweetmeats and the like,
that Bhauta lived happily for some days while enjoying them.
Seeing that great bull making its way back and forth, he—the foremost of the materialists, deluded by fate—thought to himself: SoKss_10.9.187.
"I shall go, clinging to the tip of the bull's tail; I will see my kinsmen, and having told them of this marvel, I shall return here once again."
Having reflected thus, he once approached the bull as it was walking along; seizing its tail, that being went down to the surface of the earth.
Then, having arrived at the monastery, he was embraced by the other novices who were staying there;
when they asked him, "Where have you been?", he related his own account to them.
Then all those who had heard the marvels were filled with fear and entreated him:
"Be gracious; take us there as well and feed us with the sweetmeats."
Having heard that, he said "So be it," and after uttering these words, on the following day he led them to the edge of the pond; and there the bull arrived.
The chief one seized his tail with both hands;
another seized his feet, and yet another seized those as well.
While those monks, clinging to one another's feet, had managed to construct a chain,
the bull suddenly leapt into the sky with great speed.
And as that bull walked along with its tail held up by a ghost, another ghost,
acting as a deity, then questioned that chief ghost.
"Tell us now, O Śraddhā: how is it that you so easily obtain what you desire in heaven? And what quantity of sweetmeats have you consumed?"
Then, having lost his composure and released the tail of the bull,
the leader of the Bhūtas joined his two hands together in the shape of a lotus.
As soon as he replied to them, "They are of such a size," they all—
both he and the others— fell from the sky and perished.
The bull set out for Kailāsa, and the people laughed upon seeing him;
thus, an action consisting of answering the questions of a fool leads only to fault when devoid of reflection.
You have heard of those fools who travel by air; now hear of another fool as well:
a certain fool, while traveling along a path, forgot the way.
And as he was asking people for the way, they said to him: "Go by the upper path over the tree standing on the riverbank. *Sūtrakṛtāṅga* 10.9.201.
Then that fool-minded man went to the back of that tree and climbed up, thinking,
"The people pointed out the path to me by way of this back."
As he crawled upon its back, the branch at its edge bent under his weight; though he exerted himself, he did not fall, having clung to it.
While he remained there, supported by her, an elephant came along that path;
with its rider seated upon it, the beast drank the water of the river.
Seeing him, that terrified man hanging from the tip of a tree branch spoke in a piteous voice to the elephant rider: "O Great-souled One, take me!"
And the elephant-riders,
letting go of their hooks, seized that fool by his two feet with both hands in order to pull him down from the tree.
And as soon as the elephant had gone out and departed, that elephant-driver clung to the feet of that terrified man who was hanging from the top of a tree.
Then that fool, urging him on, said to the elephant rider:
"If you know anything, sing it quickly."
One might perhaps rescue us from here if people, having heard of us, were to come;
otherwise, this river will carry us away as we fall down below.
Thus addressed, that elephant-ridder sang so sweetly that even the fool there attained the highest satisfaction.
Uttering words of praise, that fool forgot himself and, letting go of his branch,
began with both hands to snap his fingers.
At that very moment, having fallen along with his elephant rider, he perished in the river; for to whom can association with fools bring happiness?
Having thus related this story once more to the son of the Lord of Vatsa,
Gomukha told him this tale of Hiraṇyākṣa.
In this region within the lap of the Himalayas, there is a land that is the crest-jewel of the earth,
known as Kaśmīra, the abode of sciences and of Dharma.
There, the capital city named Hiraṇyapura arose,
and a king known as Kanakākṣa reigned there.
To that king, by his queen Ratnaprabhā, a son named Hiraṇyākṣa was born, produced through the propitiation of Śaṅkara.
Once, while playing with a ball,
the prince struck an ascetic woman who was coming along the path with a deceptive throw of the ball.
That female ascetic, a mistress of yoga who had conquered anger, smiled at the prince and spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa with her distorted face.
If such pride as this arises in you because of your own youth and other qualities,
then what would it be like if you were to obtain Mṛgāṅkalekhā as your wife?
Having heard that and having asked her for forgiveness, the prince asked:
"O Blessed One, please tell me, to whom does this name Mṛgāṅkalekhā belong?"
Then she said to him: "There is a highly renowned lord of the Vidyādharas on Himavat, the king of mountains, known as Śaśitejas."
He has a daughter, an excellent maiden named Mṛgāṅkalekhā,
who by her beauty causes the lords of the celestial beings to open their eyes at night.
"She is a suitable wife for you, and you are a fitting husband for her. Having been addressed thus by the perfected female ascetic, Hiraṇyākṣa said to her:
"How then may I attain that [state] in the Blessed One? Please tell me.
Having heard that, the Mistress of Yoga spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having gone there, I shall ascertain his intention through the narration of your story;
then, having returned, I myself will lead you from here to that place.
"There is here a deity named Amareśa;
you shall reach his shrine tomorrow morning, for I go there daily to worship him."
Having spoken thus, that female ascetic departed through the sky by means of her own supernatural power toward the Snowy Mountain, to the presence of Mṛgāṅkalekhā.
There, she skillfully praised the virtues of Hiraṇyākṣa to her,
in such a way that the celestial maiden spoke to her with great eagerness.
O Blessed One, if I do not obtain such a husband,
what is the use of this fruitless life of mine?
Thus, her passion having been aroused by that conversation, Mṛgāṅkalekhā spent the day with the female ascetic and dwelt with her through the night.
Meanwhile, Hiraṇyākṣa, having spent his day in those reflections, fell asleep; at the end of the night, Gaurī somehow spoke to him in a dream.
Having been a Vidyādhara, you have attained the state of a mortal due to a sage’s curse;
from this, you shall be liberated by the touch of this female ascetic’s hand.
"And then you shall quickly marry Mṛgāṅkalekhā;
you need not worry about that, for she was indeed your wife in a previous life."
Having thus instructed him, the goddess vanished from his sight;
and he too, waking up and rising in the morning, performed the auspicious rites beginning with his bath.
Then, having bowed to him, she went and stood before the Lord of Men at the place where the rendezvous had been arranged for him by that female ascetic.
In the meantime, Gaurī commanded Mṛgāṅkalekhā— who had somehow fallen asleep in her own palace— in a dream:
Hiraṇyākṣa, whose curse has been exhausted and who has become a Vidyādhara once again, will regain his wife through the touch of the ascetic’s hand; enough with your grief.
When the goddess had spoken thus and vanished, Mṛgāṅkalekhā woke up in the morning and related that dream to the female ascetic.
Having heard that, the perfected female ascetic came to the world of mortals and addressed Hiraṇyākṣa as he stood in the sacred field of Amareśa.
Saying, "Come, my son, to the world of the Vidyādharas," she took him by the hand as he bowed,
and lifting him onto her arm, she flew up into the sky.
Then that lord of the Vidyādharas, having become Hiraṇyākṣa,
remembered his birth as an ascetic woman due to the exhaustion of his curse and spoke to her.
Know me to be this one, born in the city named Vajrakūṭa on the Himālaya mountains,
the king of the Vidyādharas by the name of Amṛtatejas.
Thus, O Sage, having received a curse from that seer long ago due to my transgression and anger,
I entered a mortal womb with the condition that it should end through the touch of your hand.
"She who was my wife when I was cursed, and who abandoned her body out of grief—
she has now been born as Mṛgāṅkalekhā, my former beloved."
And now, having gone with you, I shall obtain her;
for today that curse of mine has been pacified, purified by the touch of your hand.
Speaking thus,
that lord of sky-dwellers, possessing the splendor of nectar, went through the air with that female ascetic to the Himalaya mountain.
There he saw Mṛgāṅkalekhā staying in the garden;
she too saw him approaching, as he had been announced to her by the female ascetic.
Having first entered each other's minds by way of the path of hearing,
those two wondrously entered again through the path of sight, even without departing.
"In order to accomplish the marriage, let this be told by you to your father," said Mṛgāṅkalekhā there to that mature female ascetic.
Then, her face bowed with shame, she went to her father and immediately informed him of everything through the mouth of her friend.
In a dream, that father of his, the lord of the sky-dwellers, was instructed by Ambikā;
having honored Amṛtatejas, he brought him to his own abode.
And he gave Mṛgāṅkalekhā to him according to the prescribed rites;
having performed the marriage, he returned to his own city, Vajrakūṭa.
There, having regained his own kingdom along with his wife, that Amṛtatejas brought back his own father, who had been brought there by the perfected female ascetic because of his mortal nature.
Having worshipped Kanakākṣa with offerings and brought him down to the earth,
he enjoyed that prosperity for a long time together with Mṛgāṅkalekhā.
Thus, whatever is destined for a living being in this world by the dictates of past karma,
that he obtains without effort, even if it be unattainable, as it falls right before him.
Having thus heard at night on his couch the story told by Gomukha concerning Śaktiyaśas, Naravāhanadatta, longing for her, fell asleep.
Thus ends the ninth wave in the *Śaktiyaśas* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Tenth Wave.
Then, on another day, at night once more, for the sake of diversion, that Gomukha—
He related this story to Naravāhanadatta.
Long ago, a certain great sage dwelt in the Śaiva holy site named Dhāreśvara, being attended by many disciples.
He said to his disciples: "If anyone among you has ever seen or heard of anything unprecedented, let it be reported."
When that sage had spoken thus, one disciple said to him:
"I shall relate what I have heard, which is unprecedented; let it be heard."
In Kaśmīra there is a great Śaiva sacred field called Vijaya;
there lived a certain wandering mendicant who was full of pride in his learning.
Wishing, "May I be victorious everywhere," he bowed to Śambhu and set out for Pāṭaliputra to debate, the wandering mendicant.
And as he went along the road, passing through forests, rivers, and mountains, he reached a wilderness; exhausted, he rested at the foot of a tree.
And in an instant, in that cool pool, he saw a righteous man arrive, dusty from the long journey, with a staff and a water-pot in his hands.
Seated there, he was asked by that wandering mendicant, "Where are you from? Where are you going? and the righteous man spoke to him thus:
"Friend, I have come from Pāṭaliputra, the field of learning;
I am going to Kaśmīra to defeat the scholars there in debate."
Having heard these words of the righteous man, that wandering mendicant reflected:
"If this single inhabitant of Pāṭaliputra has not been conquered by me here," soKss_10,10.11 //
"Having gone there, how shall I defeat so many others?"—having reflected thus, that wandering mendicant insulted the righteous man and said: SoKss_10,10.12.
"Tell me, O righteous one, why is this conduct of yours so contrary?
Where is the righteous seeker of liberation, and where is this disputant afflicted by calamity?"
Bound by the pride of debate, you desire liberation from saṃsāra;
you seek to quench heat with fire and destroy cold with frost.
O fool, you wish to cross the great ocean with a boat made of stone;
you strive to extinguish a fire blazing with wind.

Brahmin conduct is known as patience; the conduct of a kṣatriya is the protection of those who have sought refuge; the conduct of one seeking liberation is tranquility; and quarreling is said to be the conduct of rākṣasas.
Therefore, one who desires liberation must be peaceful and self-controlled,
having cast off the suffering of dualities and fearing the afflictions of saṃsāra.
Therefore, with the axe of tranquility, cut down this tree of existence;
but do not provide it with the watering of pride in speculative theories.
Having been addressed thus by him, the righteous man was deeply satisfied;
bowing to him and saying, "You are my guru," he departed as he had come.
Standing right there at the foot of the tree, laughing as he wandered about, he heard from within it the conversation of a yakṣa sporting with his wife.
And as long as that mendicant was lending his ear,
the yakṣa there struck his wife with a garland of flowers in jest.
Then that deceitful woman, having falsely made herself appear as if dead, remained there;
and her retinue suddenly broke out into loud lamentation.
After a long time, as if her life had returned, she opened her eyes;
then her husband, the Yakṣa, asked her: "What have you seen?"
Then she spoke falsely: "When I was struck by you with a garland, I saw a dark man arrive."
Holding a noose in his hand, with blazing eyes, tall in stature, and with hair standing erect on his head;
terrifying, he darkened the horizons with his own shadow.
Led by that wicked man, I went to the abode of Yama;
however, I was released there by the officials who restrained him.
When the yakṣiṇī had spoken thus, the yakṣa said to her with a laugh:
"Aha! Without the power of illusion (indrajāla), no such conduct exists among women."
"What is death? A blow from a flower! What is returning from the abode of Yama?
O fool, you have merely imitated the story of the women of Pāṭaliputra."
For in that city there was a king named Siṃhākṣa;
his wives were the wives of the minister, the general, the chaplain, and the physician.
Once, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight,
he took [his companions] with him and went to see the Sarasvatī river, which had been made to have a protector in that region.

"Give us medicine for those who are afflicted by disease and miserable, so that we may be freed from illness; show compassion for those who are suffering."
This world of living beings is as restless as the waves of the ocean, as fleeting as a flash of lightning, yet beautiful for a moment like the occasion of a journey or a festival.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the essence is compassion toward the wretched and generosity toward the destitute; where does a person of virtue not live?

What is the use of giving for one who is wealthy? What is the use of food for one who is well-fed? What is the use of sandalwood paste for one who is cold? What is the use of wealth when winter has arrived?
"Therefore, rescue us, miserable ones, from this calamity!"—
when they were addressed thus by those who were diseased, the king's wives and others replied:
"These miserable, diseased people speak quite rightly;
therefore, we must provide medical treatment for them even at the cost of our entire possessions."
Having thus conversed with one another and honored the queen,
the women led those who were ill back to their own respective homes.
Having urged their husbands, they had those great beings treated with potent medicines,
yet they did not rise from their side.
And through living together with those very beings whose passion had been aroused,
they entered into saṃsāra in such a way that they perceived it as being composed entirely of that.
"Where are these wretched, diseased husbands, and where are kings and the like?"—
thus did their minds, blinded by passion, fail to reflect.
And then their husbands saw them marked with nail and tooth wounds produced by sexual union with an impossible sick man.
And those [ministers], headed by the king’s counselors and generals,
being alert and filled with doubt, then spoke to one another.
Then the king said to the others, "You all stay here for now;
today I shall first question my own wife with skillful means."
Having spoken thus and dismissed them, the king went to his private chamber and,
displaying both affection and fear, questioned his wife.
"By whom has this lower lip of yours been bitten? By whom have your breasts been wounded with fingernails?
If you speak the truth, it will be well for you; otherwise, it shall not be so."
Having been addressed thus by that king, the queen spoke what was feigned:
"I shall speak even that which should not be said; listen now to this wonder."
From this painted wall, at night, a man bearing a discus and a mace emerges and enjoys me; in the morning, he dissolves right back into it.

To that king, by his queen named Ratnarekhā,

And when that Vidyādharī had descended due to the curse, she then sported on a swing, owing to the residual impression of her former practice of traveling through the sky.

Because of that slight of honor, the princess, seeking the forest,
went out to the grove under the pretext of visiting a monastery.
While her attendants were intoxicated with drink, she moved about there;
then, entering a thicket of trees, she passed out of their range of vision.
Having gone alone to a distant forest and constructed a hut,
she remained there subsisting on fruits and roots, intent upon the propitiation of Hara.
Her father, the king, having learned that she had gone away from there to some unknown place,

After a long time, his suffering having somewhat diminished,

Wandering by chance, he reached that very distant forest region where his daughter Hemaprabhā remained engaged in ascetic penance.

She too, seeing him, rose up and suddenly grasped his feet; her father embraced her and, with tears, placed her upon his lap.
Having seen each other after a long time, they both wept there;
indeed, even the deer in that forest were moved to tears.
Then, having gradually comforted her, the king said to his daughter:
"Daughter, having abandoned royal splendor, what is this that you have done?"
"Come, therefore, to your mother's side; abandon this forest dwelling.

"I am impelled by destiny alone; what power do I have here, my dear?

Because she did not waver from that resolve even as she spoke thus,
the king had a palace constructed for her right there in that forest.
And having gone to his own capital,
he sent daily cooked foods and wealth for the purpose of honoring her as a guest.
And there, Hemaprabhā remained constantly honoring guests with those riches and foods, while she herself subsisted on fruits and roots.
And once, a certain female ascetic, who had observed the vow of celibacy from her youth, arrived at that hermitage while wandering about, seeking the princess.
Having been honored by Hemaprabhā, she asked about the reason for her renunciation during the course of their conversation, and Bālapravrajikā replied:
While massaging my father's feet as a maiden,

When the female ascetic had spoken thus, Hemaprabhā,

Thus, listening in succession to these stories narrated by Gomukha, King Naravāhanadatta—

Be gracious, for you are indeed a wish-fulfilling tree for the petition of all goals;

Thus entreated by Ruciradeva for the sake of the horse-essence,

Having mounted the wind-chariot brought by him at that very moment,

Thus, being gazed upon by the city women with eyes wide and tremulous with intoxication,

There, the prince beheld the temple of Kāmadeva, established by his ancestors, which consisted entirely of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
