There is a city named Lampā, which is like a garland upon the crown of the earth;
in it there lived a wealthy and great merchant named Kusumasāra.
O delight of the Lord of Vatsa, I am his only son, named Candrasāra, earned through the propitiation of Śaṅkara by him whose sole abode is Dharma.
Once, having gone with my friends to witness a festival for the gods,
I saw there other wealthy men giving to those who asked for alms.
Then, through my faith in giving, the desire to acquire wealth arose in me;
for I was not satisfied even with the great fortune acquired by my father.
Therefore, in order to go to another continent by way of the ocean,
I boarded a ship filled with various jewels.
And impelled by a favorable wind as if by destiny itself,
that ship of mine reached that island in just a few days.
There, perceiving me to be unfamiliar with the trade of precious gems and suspecting me of being motivated by greed for wealth, the king had me bound and cast into prison.
In that house, which resembled a hell, I remained for a time among those who were like hungry ghosts (pretas), crying out in distress and tormented by hunger and thirst due to their evil deeds.

At that time, a great merchant named Mahīdhara, a resident of that city and one well-acquainted with our family, made this request to the king on my behalf: SoKss_11,1.44: "At that time, a great merchant named Mahīdhara, a resident of that city and one well-acquainted with our family, made this request to the king on my behalf."
"O King, this son of a merchant from Lampā has imprisoned this blameless man; therefore, this act brings him infamy."
Having been thus instructed by him, the king released me from my bonds, brought me into his presence, and honored me with great respect.
Then, by the favor of the king and through the support of that friend,
I lived there happily, conducting extensive business affairs.
Once, during a festival at the Madhu garden,
I beheld the excellent daughter of the merchant named Śikhara.
Then, as if by a wave from the ocean of Kandarpa’s pride, she was carried away;
having gone there, I requested her from her father.
Having reflected within himself for a moment, his father said to me:
"It is not appropriate to give her to you directly; I have a reason for this."
Therefore, I am sending her to my maternal grandfather in Siṃhaladvīpa; go there and marry her once she has been requested by you.
"I shall instruct you there in such a way that this will succeed for you.
Having said this and honored me, Śikhara sent me home.
And on another day, having placed that maiden along with her attendants upon a ship,
he dispatched her by way of the sea toward Siṃhala.
Just as I was eager to go there,
this news arose from that place, as fierce as a stroke of lightning.
The ship by which the daughter of Śikhara had gone sank in the ocean, and not even a single person emerged from it.
When that news was lost, my fortitude shattered and my ship tossed about,
I immediately fell into a shoreless ocean of grief.
And while being comforted by the elders, yet drawing my mind away with hopes [for home],
I made the firm resolve to seek knowledge, setting my intent upon going to that island.
Then, although I was beloved by the king and well-provided with various means of wealth,
I embarked upon a ship in the ocean and began to set out.
And as I was going, a great roar arose; suddenly there appeared before me a terrifying thief of clouds, discharging showers like a volley of arrows.
Then, by that opposing wind, acting with even greater force according to its own law,
my ship was tossed up again and again and finally shattered.
When my attendants and wealth had been swallowed by the ocean through the power of fate,
I, having fallen in, obtained a single great log.
By that arm of the Creator, as if suddenly extended,
I was slowly brought to the shore of the ocean by the force of the wind.
Having climbed up there, afflicted by suffering and reproaching fate without hesitation,
I obtained a tiny fragment of gold that had fallen and remained on the edge of the bank.
Having sold that [money] here in a nearby village and taken food and other necessities,
I purchased a pair of garments and somewhat relieved the fatigue of traveling by sea.
Then, wandering about without knowing the direction and separated from my beloved,
I beheld a land filled with sand-shrines of Śiva.
While wandering through that grove of hermit-maidens, I saw on one side a girl who, though dressed in forest attire, was radiant and intent upon the worship of the Linga.
"Aha! This is someone very much like my beloved; could it be she herself?
Or from where has this come, for such good fortune as that no longer exists for me?"
While I was reflecting thus, my right eye, throbbing repeatedly with joy, spoke to me as if saying, "It is she indeed."
"O slender one, you are worthy of dwelling in a palace; tell me, what are you doing here in this forest?
When she was thus questioned by me, she said nothing at all.
Then, out of fear of the sage’s curse, I took refuge within a thicket of creepers and remained there, gazing at her with eyes that could not be satiated.
Having performed her worship, she turned toward me repeatedly with affection; looking at me and reflecting for a moment, she then departed slowly from that place.
When she had passed from the range of my vision, I, blinded by darkness, beheld the quarters of the sky; a certain indescribable state came over me, resembling that of an owl at night.

In an instant, she beheld the daughter of the sage Mataṅga, who had arrived unexpectedly, whose splendor was like the radiance of the sun, and who had observed the vow of celibacy from her very childhood.
I beheld her, named Yamunā, whose body was emaciated by asceticism, who possessed divine vision, and whose appearance was auspicious— she appeared to me like Fortitude incarnate.
She said to me, "Candrasāra, summoning fortitude, listen:
there is a great merchant named Śikhara on another island."

When a daughter had been born in Rūpavatī, it is said that a wise monk named Jinarakṣita spoke to her friend: SoKss_11.1.76: "When a daughter had been born in Rūpavatī, it is said that a wise monk named Jinarakṣita spoke to her friend."
"You yourself must not give away this girl, for she has another mother;
there would be fault in your giving her yourself, whereas such a beneficial course has been ordained."
Having been thus addressed by the monk, the merchant then desired to give his daughter— who was to be bestowed upon you— to that monk's maternal grandfather, as she had sought you out.
Therefore, sent by her father on a ship to Siṃhaladvīpa to be with her maternal grandfather, she fell into the ocean when the vessel was wrecked.
And as if brought by the force of her own life-span,
that merchant’s daughter was cast upon the shore by the ocean, as if by a great wave of destiny.
At that time, my father, the venerable sage Mataṅga,
came to the ocean with his disciples to bathe and saw her, who was like one dead.
That compassionate one, having comforted her, led her to his own hermitage and entrusted her to me, saying, "O Yamunā, she is to be protected by you."
"This girl has reached the shore (velā)," thought that great sage;
thus he gave the name Velā to the girl, who was beloved by the company of sages.
And because of that affection, my mind—though filled with compassion free from worldly passion and though repelled by the holy life—is today tormented by saṃsāra; alas! SoKss_11,1.84.
And my mind, O Candrasāra, is pained as it beholds her again and again— her, who has not yet taken a husband and who shines with the beauty of fresh youth.
"And she was your wife in a previous birth; having learned that you had come here, O son, I have arrived in your presence through the power of my vow."
Therefore, come and accept this time granted by us;
let the hardship you have endured now bear fruit for both of you.
Thus consoling me with words like a rain from a cloudless sky,
the blessed Yamunā led me to the hermitage of my father, Mataṅga.
And having been informed by her, the sage Mataṅga there gave her to me, like the fulfillment of a kingdom of one's desires incarnate in form.
Then, staying there happily with her at that time,
I once engaged in water-sports with her in the waters of a lake.
Not seeing the boundary, I cast water even beyond it;
thus, while he was engaged in his bath, the sage Mataṅga was drenched by me here.
Enraged by that, he cast a curse upon me and my wife:
"O sinners, a separation shall come to you two, husband and wife."
Then, entreated by that Velā, who clung to his feet with a piteous voice,
the sage meditated and ordained an end to our curse.
The powerful Jetṛ, who by the speed of his elephant could [overcome] a pair of excellent horses,
[will become] that Naravāhanadatta, the future lord of the Vidyādharas.
O Candrasāra, when you behold the son of the Lord of Vatsa from afar,
you shall then be reunited with this wife due to the cessation of your curse.
Having spoken thus, that sage Mataṅga, having performed his ritual acts such as bathing,
went through the sky to Śvetadvīpa in order to behold Hari.
That mango tree which was formerly seized from the tip of Dhūrjaṭi’s foot by a Vidyādhara, and which was later taken by me in my childhood; ||| 11.97 ||
"This very [place], filled with excellent jewels, is now given by me to you along with your wife"; having said this, Yamunā also departed from that very spot.
Then, having found my beloved, I grew weary of dwelling in the forest;
out of fear of separation, I became eager to return to my own country.
Then, having set out to travel and reached the shore of the ocean,
I boarded a merchant vessel and placed my wife on board first.
Just as I myself was wishing to board it, the wind,
due to the sage’s curse, carried that boat, my friend, far away from me.
Even delusion, having fallen upon me whose wife had been carried off by the thief,
seized the consciousness of my distraught self as if it had found a vulnerable opening.
Then a certain ascetic, having arrived there and seeing me unconscious,
compassionately comforted me and slowly led me to his hermitage.
Having questioned him there about what had occurred and having heard of the manifestation of the curse,
and having understood that the curse was limited by a specific duration, he established for me a bond of steadfastness.
Then, having reached a preeminent merchant who had survived a shipwreck at sea,
we met with him as our companion while continuing our search for that beloved one once more.
With the hope that the curse might end, I took hold of his hand and traversed various difficult regions and many days.
And gradually reaching the city of Vaiśākha, I heard this:
"The crest-jewel of the noble lineage of the Lord of Vatsa has arrived here."
And when you were seen from afar with the elephant and having conquered the pair of horses,
that burden of the curse was cast off by me, whose inner self had become light.
And in an instant, I beheld my beloved here, having arrived before me,
brought by those virtuous merchants on that very ship at the [proper] time.
Then, by your grace, I met her as she held a magnificent jewel in her hand that had been given by Yamunā, and I crossed over the great ocean of the curse.
Therefore, I have come to pay homage to you as the daughter of the King of Vatsa;
now, united with my beloved, I shall go in peace to my own country.

When that merchant Candrasāra had thus related his own story and departed having achieved his purpose, Ruciradeva— delighted by the greatness he had witnessed— bowed deeply and became exceedingly humble before this son of the King of Vatsa.

And adopting a formal courtesy, he gave his own sister Jayendrasenā—who had been intended for him since long ago and was most worthy of him—to that man who had been captivated by his devotion; she was immediately provided with a pair of excellent female and male elephants and horses.
And taking that bride along with the horses and the mares,
Naravāhanadatta took leave of Ruciradeva and returned to his own city of Kauśāmbī.
And there he dwelt, sporting together with her, the Queen of the Lord of Vatsa,
as well as with his other queens, such as Madanamañcukā and the rest, living in happiness.
Thus ends the first wave in the Velālambaka of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
This eleventh book, the Velālambaka, is now complete. Śrī!
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The twelfth book, named Śaśāṅkavatī.
Long ago, it is said, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, stirred by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Those who, having attained supernatural power through the removal of obstacles, forcibly savor [the nectar] and bear the divine burden upon earth, do so by the grace of Bhava.
May Gaṇapati protect you, raising his trunk like a pillar of fame that destroys all obstacles—
We bow to the Supreme Hara, who is free from passion yet skilled in the artful arrangement of intense passion,
and who is the painter of the wondrously diverse creation of ever-new marvels.
Victory belongs to the arrows of the God of Love; for even when these, though made of flowers, fall here, even diamonds and other such weapons become blunted for those who bear them.
Thus, having obtained each of those wives,
Naravāhanadatta, the son of the Lord of Vatsa, remained there in Kauśāmbī.
Although he had many wives, he regarded that first wife, Madanamañcukā,
as dearer than his own life, just as Mādhava regarded Rukmiṇī.
And once at night, in a dream, he saw himself being carried away through the sky by some divine maiden.
And having awakened on the peak of the great mountain among shady trees,
he saw himself standing upon a slab of sapphire stone.
And at night, he beheld that maiden standing by his side, illuminating the forest like a universal enchantment-elixir belonging to the God of Love.
Thinking, "I have been brought here by her," and having looked at her,
he made her desire falter with shame and feigned sleep.
Then that rogue, as if prattling and desiring to test her, said this:
"Where are you? Come and embrace me, my dear Madanamañcukā!"
Upon hearing that, she forgot her modesty and, casting off all restraint out of shamelessness,
she assumed the form of her beloved and embraced him.
Then, opening his eyes and seeing her in the form of his beloved, he said with a smile, "Oh, what wonderful insight! and took her by the neck.
Then, casting aside her shame and revealing her true form, she said to him:
"Noble son, accept me now as one who has chosen you of her own accord."
When she had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta then married that maiden there according to the Gāndharva rite.
Having spent that night there with her in the proper manner,
he spoke to his beloved in the morning, using a clever pretext out of a desire to learn about her family.
"O beloved, listen; I shall tell you this unprecedented story.
Once, there was a sage named Brahmasiddhi in a certain penance grove."
And near the hermitage of that true sage who had attained perfection in yoga,
there lived an old female jackal who had made her dwelling in a cave.
On a rainy day, when she had gone out for food while fasting,
a wild elephant— driven mad by the separation from his mate— came to kill her.
Seeing that, the compassionate sage, possessing wisdom, transformed that female jackal into a female elephant for the sake of bestowing grace upon both of them.
Then that elephant, seeing the female elephant and having his agitation stilled, became devoted to her; she, too, was released from death.
Then, while wandering with her, that elephant once entered a lake choked with autumn mud in order to fetch a lotus for her sake.
Today, stuck there in the mire, he was unable to move;
he stood like a mountain whose wings have been shattered by the thunderbolt, fallen and motionless.
Seeing him thus dejected, that female jackal-elephant immediately sought refuge with another elephant and departed from there.
And at that moment, his own female elephant, who had been separated from him earlier,
arrived at that place by the power of fate while searching for her mate.
As soon as that noble-born woman saw her husband swallowed by the mud,
she then entered that very same lake-mud to follow after him.
At that time, the sage Brahmasiddhi, accompanied by his disciples, arrived by that very path; upon seeing him, he was filled with compassion.
And that one of great asceticism, by means of his disciples whose strength was produced through boons, raised up those two elephants under his control from within the mud of the lake.
Then, when that sage had departed, the couple— the female elephant and the bull elephant—
having escaped from death and separation, wandered about as they pleased.
Thus, even animals of noble birth, when in distress, do not abandon their lord or friend; rather, they rescue them from that very danger.
But for those born of low birth,
who are fickle-minded, neither affection nor love ever touches their hearts, even at any time.
Having heard this from the daughter of the Lord of Vatsa, that divine maiden said to him:
"It is exactly so; there is no doubt in this matter."
And your intention has been understood by me as you speak thus;
therefore, O noble son, listen now to this story from me as well.
In Kānyakubja, there was a most excellent brahmin named Śūradatta,
who was honored by King Bāhuśakti as the lord of a hundred villages.
He had a wife named Vasumatī, who regarded her husband as a deity;
through her, he begot a noble son named Vāmadatta.
Before long, Vāmadatta, who was dear to his father, became proficient in all branches of knowledge and married a wife named Śaśiprabhā.
In due course, when his father had gone to heaven followed by his wife,
he entered into the life of a householder together with that wife.
And she became his wife, acting according to her own will without his knowledge; by some chance, she had obtained through fate the mastery of the *siddhi* of a *śākinī*.
Once, while he was staying in the king's camp for the purpose of serving the monarch,
his own paternal uncle came from home and spoke to him in private:
"O son, our lineage is ruined, since your wife was seen by me in union with the very buffalo-herder who belongs to you."
Having heard this from his paternal uncle and having settled him in the camp,
Vāmadatta returned to his own home, accompanied only by his sword.
While he remained there in concealment, the buffalo-herder entered the flower garden at night and arrived right there.
In an instant, his wife, eager for union with him, approached the buffalo-herder there,
carrying various kinds of food in her hands.
Then, after he had finished eating, she departed with him toward Śāsana;
seeing this, Vāmadatta ran after them with his weapon raised.
As he said, "O you two sinners, where are you going?", his wife saw him, stood up, and saying, "Shame on you, wretch!", she threw dust in his face.
Then that man, Vāmadatta, quickly became a buffalo;
yet his memory was not lost even in that state.
Then that deceitful wife, having cast him into the midst of the buffaloes, had him beaten with clubs by the buffalo-herder.
At that very moment, that cruel woman sold him, rendered helpless by his animal state, to a certain merchant who was seeking a buffalo.
Then, having been made to bear that burden and oppressed by his condition as a buffalo,
Vāmadatta was led to a village near the Ganges.
In his house, his wife—though of very wicked conduct—was unexpectedly like a female serpent that has entered the interior of a thicket; for whose happiness could she be?
While he was thus reflecting there, weeping and deeply distressed,
his body reduced to mere bones through the exhaustion of his burden, a certain yoginī beheld him.
Having understood that entire account through her knowledge, she, overwhelmed with compassion,
sprinkled him with consecrated water and liberated him from his state as a buffalo.
Having brought him, who had assumed human form, to her own home,
she gave him her daughter, a maiden named Kāntimatī.
"Having struck that first mare, Durbhāryā, with these, make her [your own]," he said,
and gave him consecrated mustard seeds.
Then Vāmadatta, taking that beautiful new wife along with the mustard seeds, returned to his own home.
Having killed that buffalo-herder and having performed [the rite] there with mustard seeds,
he turned that first wife, Vaḍavā, into one bound to a stable.
And having given her seven blows with a club every day, he,
bound by his vow, took his meal for the sake of purging their enmity.
While Vāmadatta was thus dwelling there together with his lovely wife Kāntimatī, a certain guest arrived at his house.
And when he had begun to eat,
Vāmadatta, remembering the blow from the stick dealt by his wicked wife, quickly went out without eating.
And having given blows with a staff to her who was in the form of a mare,
he entered there regularly and enjoyed himself, his heart filled with satisfaction.
Then the guest, filled with wonder and curiosity, asked him:
"Where did you go in such agitation, having abandoned your meal?"
Then Vāmadatta told him his own story from the very beginning; and then he, too, related his own account to him.
What is the use of this persistent obsession by which your state as a human has been stolen?
Propitiate that very mother-in-law of yours and achieve some degree of excellence.
Having been addressed thus by that guest, Vāmadatta said, "So be it," and having honored the guest with faith, he dismissed him in the morning.
Then, seeing that his mother-in-law, a perfected yoginī, had arrived at his house unexpectedly, he, desiring her favor, honored her and earnestly made this request:
Then Yogeśvarī, according to the prescribed rite, taught him the Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī vidyā, preceded by initiation, together with his wife.
Then, having gone to Śrīparvata, he mastered that vidyā;
and once it was perfected, she appeared in person and gave him an excellent sword.
And having obtained the sword, that accomplished Vāmadatta, the best of the Vidyādharas, became united with his wife Kāntimatī.
Then, on the peak of the Malaya mountain known as Rajatakūṭa,
he established an excellent city by the power of his own supernatural attainments.
Then, in due course, a daughter named Lalitalocanā was born there to that lord of the Vidyādharas by his wife.
As soon as she was born, it was prophesied by a voice arising from the sky that she would become the wife of a noble universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
"Know me, noble son, to be one who has realized the truth through my own knowledge;
I am devoted to you and have brought you here to this, my own Malaya mountain."
Having learned that she was a Vidyādharī born of such a lineage,
Naravāhanadatta then held his wife Lalitalocanā in high esteem, his heart filled with joy.
And he remained there with her; meanwhile, Vatsarāja and the others learned of his situation through the power of Ratnaprabhā’s magic science.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave:
Then, having obtained that beautiful-eyed woman as his new wife...
That Naravāhanadatta was on that Malaya mountain.
He sported with her in various forest regions, which were beautiful with trees in full bloom and fortunate with the onset of spring.
And in a certain forest, while his beloved was wandering out of sight into the thicket in the course of gathering flowers for play, [he remained behind].
As he was wandering along, he beheld a great lake of clear water,
which, with the flowers fallen from the trees on its banks, resembled the sky filled with stars.
"As long as that beloved does not arrive while gathering flowers,
so long shall I bathe in this lake and sit for a moment on its shore."
Having reflected thus, he bathed, performed his worship of the gods,
and sat there upon a stone slab shaded by a sandalwood tree.
Staying there, he beheld the gait of the royal swans, which resembled her own,
and heard the warbling of the cuckoos in the mango groves, which was like her voice.
And beholding the eyes of the does, which resembled her own eyes,
he remembered his beloved Madanamañcukā, who was far away.
As soon as he remembered her, he was tormented by the fire of desire and fainted;
at that very moment, a certain eminent sage arrived there to bathe.
Seeing him in that state, the one named Piśaṅgajaṭa sprinkled him with sandalwood waters that were like the touch of his own beloved.
Then that sage, possessing divine vision, spoke to him as he had awakened and bowed:
"My son, you shall attain whatever you desire; maintain your fortitude."
Therefore, everything will be attained; likewise, come to my hermitage and hear from me the story of Mṛgāṅkadatta, if it has not already been heard by you.
Having said this, the sage bathed and led Naravāhanadatta to his own hermitage, and there he quickly performed his daily religious rites.
Having offered him hospitality with fruits and having himself eaten there,
that Piṅgalajaṭa proceeded to relate a story to him.
There is a city named Ayodhyā, renowned throughout the three worlds;
in it there formerly lived a sovereign of the earth named Amaradatta.
To him, whose splendor was exceedingly radiant, there was a wife named Surataprabhā, who was eternally devoted to him alone, just as Svāhā is to Agni.
To him was born a son named Mṛgāṅkadatta, who,
like his own bow, was bent by a string that had reached its highest excellence.
And that prince had ten ministers of his own:
Pracaṇḍaśakti, Sthūlabāhu, and Vikramakesarī.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Meghabala, and Bhīmaparākrama, as well as Vimalabuddhi, Vyāghrasena, and Guṇākara. SoKss_12,2.19 //
And the tenth is named Vicitrakatha;
they are all of noble lineage, young, heroic, wise, and seekers of their master's welfare.
While staying happily with them in his father’s house,
Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta had not yet obtained a suitable wife.
And once, when they were alone, a minister named Bhīmaparākrama said to him:
"Listen, O King, to what happened to me today during the night."
Today, while sleeping in my palace, I woke up unexpectedly in the night and saw a lion with claws as sharp as thunderbolts charging toward me.
When I rose up with my sword drawn,
that lion then set out to flee, and I pursued him with speed.
Having gone to the other side of the river, he extended his tongue toward me;
I, however, cut off that long tongue of his with my knife.
As soon as I had crossed that river by means of that very embankment-earth,
that great lion became transformed into a deformed man.
When asked by me, "Who are you?", that man replied:
"I am a Vetāla, O hero; I have been gratified by your courage."
Having heard that, I asked him: "If it is so, then tell me this:
who will become the wife of my lord Mṛgāṅkadatta?"
Having heard these words of mine, the vetāla then said:
"In this city of Ujjayinī, there is a king known as Karmasena."
That king has a daughter who surpasses the Apsarases in loveliness;
she is like a treasury of beauty created by Prajāpati himself.
She shall become his wife, named Śaśāṅkavatī;
and by obtaining her, your master will rule over the kingdom of the earth.
Having said this, that Vetāla vanished from my sight, and I likewise returned home; such, O Lord, was what occurred to me during the night.
Having heard this from Bhīmaparākrama, Mṛgāṅkadatta summoned all his own ministers and had it recited to them.
And he said to them, "Listen to what was seen by me in a dream:
I know that we have all entered a certain great forest."
There, thirsty from the journey and seeking water, we reached it with difficulty;
yet we were blocked by five men armed with weapons who rose up against us.
Having killed them, we desired to drink again as long as we were afflicted by thirst;
yet there we saw neither those men nor that water.
Then, having reached a state of great distress, we beheld Maheśvara approaching, mounted upon his bull, unexpectedly radiant as the moon.
As we bowed before him, he let fall a single drop of tear from his right eye upon the ground;
there it became the ocean.
Therefore, having tied that auspicious pearl necklace which I had obtained around my neck,
I drank that ocean from a human skull smeared with blood.
And at that very moment I awoke, and the night had passed;
thus was the wondrous dream reported by Mṛgāṅkadatta.
While the others were rejoicing, the minister Vimalabuddhi said to him:
"O King, you are fortunate, for Hara has thus bestowed his grace upon you."
"Because you obtained a string of pearls in a dream and drank the ocean,
you will certainly enjoy the earth after winning Śaśāṅkavatī."
When Vimalabuddhi had said, "Others, however, lead somewhat to affliction," Mṛgāṅkadatta then spoke again to those ministers.
Just as the fruit of my dream, and just as Bhīmaparākrama has heard this from the vetāla here, so too shall it come to pass.
Nevertheless, by the power of my wisdom, that daughter Śaśāṅkavatī shall be won by me from Karmasena, who relies on the strength of his army and the security of his fortress.
And the power of wisdom is the primary means for accomplishing all tasks;
likewise, listen to this story which I shall relate to you.
In Magadha there was a king named Bhadrabāhu;
he had a minister called Mantragupta, the best among the wise.
Once, that king spoke privately to his own minister:
"The daughter of the King of Vārāṇasī is named Anaṅgalīlā."
There is a woman who is the beauty of the three worlds belonging to Dharmagopa;
though I have requested her, that king does not grant her to me out of hatred.
And by the power of that elephant Bhadradanta, he is difficult to conquer;
furthermore, I have no desire to live without his daughter.
"Therefore, my friend, there is no remedy for this; tell me, what should be done?
When the king had spoken thus, the minister replied to him:
"O King, is success achieved through valor alone and not through intelligence?
Therefore, enough with this anxiety; by my own wit, I shall accomplish this for you."
Having spoken thus to the king, on the following day, the minister, accompanied by five or seven attendants and wearing the garb of a Mahāvratika ascetic, went to Vārāṇasī.
There, those disciples in disguise proclaimed everywhere to the people who had gathered, bowing low in devotion, "This one is a perfected master."
And once, while wandering at night with his followers in order to discover the facts of the matter, he saw from afar a woman who had come out from her house.
The wife of Hastipāla, her gait hurried by fear,
was being led away somewhere by three or four armed men.
"Surely she has risen and departed; let us see where she goes.
Having reflected thus, he followed her at his ease along with his attendants.
Having gone there, she entered that house;
but having seen it from afar, he returned at once to his own dwelling place.
And in the morning, while Hastipāla was wandering about searching for his beloved who had gone away after her wealth was stolen, he skillfully sent his attendants to her side.
Seeing him, they then neutralized that poison— which had been consumed through the suffering of not attaining it— by means of their own spells, as if out of compassion.
"Come to our teacher's side; he is a man of knowledge and knows everything.
Having said this, they brought him into the presence of that minister.
And that elephant-keeper, having seen him adorned with the ornaments of his vow, bowed at his feet and asked about the news of his wife.
That minister, having falsely meditated upon it, described that place to him along with identifying marks—
the very place where she had been taken by other men during the night.
Then, having prostrated before him and departed together with the city guards,
that elephant-keeper reached that place and surrounded it.
He slew those wicked men who had abducted his wife,
and he recovered his own woman along with her ornaments and her wealth.
On the second day, having arrived in the morning and paid his respects,
he took his seat and extended an invitation for a meal to that impostor who claimed to be a perfected one (siddha).
For him who desired to enter a house and who spoke of eating only at night,
they prepared his meal in the elephant stable at twilight.
By the power of the mantra, the practitioner of spells took all that was hidden, placed within bamboo tubes, and having gone there, he ate it along with his followers.
Then, after the elephant-keeper had departed and the others there were asleep,
he placed him inside a bamboo tube of the elephant Bhadradanta.
Having spent that night there with a snake at Karna's ear while he was asleep, he returned to his own country of Magadha; the elephant was killed by him.
When that excellent minister had slain Dharmagopa’s elephant as if it were his own pride,
King Bhadrabāhu rejoiced.
Then he dispatched Anaṅgalīlā, that maiden, as a messenger to Vārāṇasī to ask Dharmagopa for her hand in marriage.
He too gave her to him, being weakened by the absence of that elephant;
for kings who know the right time adopt the conduct of a reed.
Thus, by means of that very wisdom, King Bhadrabāhu attained the amorous dalliance of the minister Mantragupta.
To Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was saying, "Therefore, I too shall obtain that wife through my intelligence," his minister Vicitrakatha replied:
Everything will be accomplished for you through the favor of the necklace seen in the dream;
for what could the unfailing grace of the deities not achieve?
And so, listen here to a story being told by me:
there was once a king named Bhadrākṣa in the city of Takṣaśilā.
Desiring a son, he worshipped Lakṣmī on the sword day after day with one hundred and eight white lotuses.
Once, while that king was worshipping and maintaining his vow of silence,
by chance one lotus was missing as he mentally counted them.
Having split open his own heart-lotus, he gave it to the goddess;
and she, being pleased, granted him a boon that would bestow upon him a son who would become a universal monarch.
Having restored the king’s body to its unimpaired state, he departed from sight;
then, a son was born to that king by his chief queen.
And because he was born through the grace of the lotus of his heart,
the king gave that son, who possessed auspicious marks, the name Puṣkarākṣa.
And in due course, having consecrated that virtuous son who had attained youth upon the throne, King Bhadrākṣa retired to the forest.
Puṣkarākṣa, having obtained the kingdom, worshipped Hara every day;
once, after having performed his adoration, he made a request of him through his wife.
"O son, everything you desire shall be accomplished," he then heard this voice arising from the sky.
Then, filled with joy and having gained confidence, that king, while remaining [in his palace],
once went to a forest of deer for the diversion of hunting.
There, seeing a young camel engaged in devouring a pair of serpents that were intent on copulation, he, overcome with grief, let it fall.
As soon as he was struck down, having abandoned that body of a young camel and become a Vidyādhara, he spoke joyfully to Puṣkarākṣa:
"You have done me a favor; therefore, listen to what I say to you.
O King, there is a preeminent Vidyādhara named Raṅkumālin."
Seeing that youth, Tārāvalī by name, the daughter of an eminent Vidyādhara, fell in love with him and, being herself enamored, chose him because she was captivated by his beauty.
And when they had performed their marriage according to her own wish, her father,
out of anger, cast upon them a curse that would cause separation for a certain period of time.
Then Tārāvalī and Raṅkumālin,
that couple whose love was ever-expanding, wandered together through various regions of their own domain.
Once, due to that curse, they both fell from each other's path of vision;
separated from one another, they were born somewhere in the midst of a forest.
Then Tārāvalī, searching for her husband,
eventually reached a forest frequented by perfected seers on the far shore of the western ocean.
There she saw a single great rose-apple tree in full bloom,
which seemed to offer consolation through its sweet humming, as if out of affection.
And having assumed the form of a female bee,
she sat upon a certain flower of that tree to rest, drinking the honey.
Seeing her husband returned to that very place after a long time by a stroke of fate,
she immediately sprinkled that flower with the semen flowing from her joy.
Having abandoned her body as a female bee, she went and was united with him,
her husband Raṅkumālin, who was searching for her, just as moonlight is united with the moon.
Then, when she had gone with him to her own abode, she became impregnated by his seed;
from that, a fruit arose from a *jambu* flower.
And from that fruit, through the course of time, a daughter was born;
for indeed, the potency of the divine never goes to waste.
Once, the sage named Vijitāśva came there for the sake of fruits and roots; at that moment, a ripe fruit from a jambu tree fell down.
Then, emerging from that fallen and shattered [palace], a divine maiden,
bowing low with humility, paid homage at the feet of that sage.
Having seen her with his divine vision and understood the truth of the matter, the sage, filled with wonder,
led Vinayavatī to his own hermitage and gave her that name.
There, in the hermitage of that sage, she gradually grew up;
and while traveling through the sky, I saw this Vinayavatī.
Then, deluded by pride in my physical form and by intoxication,
I approached her and proceeded to seize her by force, even though she was unwilling.
At that moment, O King, having been informed by her as she was crying out, that sage, who had conquered the Asuras, became enraged; he approached and pronounced a curse upon me.
"O you who are proud of your form, yet despised in every limb, become a young camel!
When your death is brought about by King Puṣkarākṣa, you shall be released from the curse."
"And he alone shall be the husband of Vinayavatī";
thus cursed by the sage, I was born as a young camel upon this earth for her sake.
And today, through you, that end of the curse has been born;
therefore, go from here to that forest situated on the far shore of the western ocean, known by the name Surabhimāruta.
"Obtain that divine wife, who shall take away the pride of Śrī’s beauty";
having said this to Puṣkarākṣa, the Vidyādhara went to heaven.
Puṣkarākṣa also went to his own city and, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers,
mounted a horse and set out alone during the night.
Proceeding by degrees, he reached the shore of the western ocean once more, and there he reflected: "How shall I cross the sea?"
Then he saw there a certain empty temple of Caṇḍikā;
having entered it, he bathed and bowed down before that goddess.
Having respectfully taken up a lute placed there by someone,
he began to play it for the Goddess with his own songs.
And pleased by his lute-playing, she led him, while he slept there that night,
across the ocean by means of her own host of spirits.
Then, having awakened at dawn, the king saw himself situated within a forest on the shore of the ocean, and not in that temple of Caṇḍikā.
Rising up in amazement, he wandered there and beheld the hermitage,
which seemed to bow down in welcome through trees bent low with the weight of their fruit.
Entering there, he saw the sage standing surrounded by his disciples, as if offering a welcome with the warbling of the birds.
Having approached, the king paid homage at the feet of that seer;
and the wise sage, having offered him hospitality, spoke to him.
"O lotus-eyed one, she for whose sake you have come has gone for a moment to fetch fuel and such; therefore, wait here for now."
"O King, take back that former wife this very day!"—
being thus addressed by the sage, Puṣkarākṣa reflected.
"By good fortune, this is that very sage, and this is that same forest where Vijitāsu once was; surely it is by the power of the Goddess that I have been delivered from the great ocean."
"This Citrā was previously my wife," the sage told him;
reflecting on this very thought, the king was delighted and questioned that sage.
"O Blessed One, tell me how this was my wife in a former life.
Then that sage said: "Listen, if you have curiosity."
In former times, there was a merchant named Dharmasena in Tāmraliptī,
and he had a virtuous wife whose name was Vidyullekhā.
That merchant, robbed by thieves by fate and struck by weapons,
being on the verge of death, went out with his wife to enter the fire.
And suddenly, both the husband and wife saw a pair of swans of beautiful form arriving through the sky.
Then, with their minds fixed upon that [state], those two royal swans entered the fire and died;
they were both reborn again as husband and wife.
Once, during the rainy season, while the two of them were staying in a nest in a date-palm tree at night,
a whirlwind uprooted that tree and separated them.
In the morning, while the storm had subsided, that swan,
searching for his mate among the lakes and at the ends of the quarters, did not find her anywhere.
Then, afflicted by love and having conceived a longing for another female swan on the road, he went to Lake Mānasa, which is frequented by swans at that time of year.
Having found his own female swan there and having waited until the arrival of the rainy season,
he went with her to a certain mountain peak to sport together.
There, having taken up his slain female swan and seeing that she was dead,
he observed from afar many men approaching along the road, armed with weapons.
The hunter, having taken up that slain female swan and seeing from afar several armed men approaching along the path, [acted accordingly].
Quickly cutting [the stalks] with his knife and covering her with grass on the ground,
he placed Haṃsī there, thinking, "Lest these people should see her and carry her off."
When those men had departed,
that female swan, wishing to seize him as he approached, uprooted a blade of grass while the hunter looked on.
Having regained life through the juice of the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* herb, which had been cut within that grass, he flew up into the sky and departed from there.
Meanwhile, that swan, her husband, having gone to the shore of a certain lake,
fell down bewildered among a flock of swans, his mind fixed solely on her as he gazed at her.
At that very moment, a certain fisherman, having cast his net and caught all those swans, sat down for a meal within a mere instant.
Then, having arrived at that very spot while searching for her husband, the female swan saw him ensnared in the net; distressed, she gazed toward the quarters of the sky.
Then, on the bank of that lake, he saw a jeweled necklace placed upon some clothes by a certain man who had gone there to bathe.
Having gone there, while he was looking on, she took that necklace and,
showing it to the fisherman, departed slowly through the sky.
Seeing that female swan with the necklace held in her beak, the fisherman abandoned his net, took up a club, and pursued her.
The female swan went to the mountain peak and placed the necklace far away;
out of greed for it, the fisherman also set about climbing up there.
Seeing that, the female swan went quickly to her husband’s side and struck with her beak the eye of a monkey who was fast asleep on a tree nearby.
Struck by the monkey, he fell down in terror and tore through the net;
consequently, all those swans emerged from it.
Then those two swans, husband and wife, having come together and told their respective stories to one another, rejoiced and sported as they pleased.
While searching there, that man obtained the fisherman who had arrived with the necklace around his neck, lured by the desire for its feathers; he was the very one whose necklace had been stolen.
Having taken the necklace from the hand of that fisherman, who was betrayed by his own fear,
the man severed the fisherman’s right hand with a knife.
And those two swans, having made a single lotus into a parasol,
rose from the lake at midday and wandered through the sky.
In an instant, those two birds reached the bank of a certain river,
where a sage sat, intent upon the worship of Dhūrjaṭi.
There, as the couple was passing by,
they were both struck simultaneously with a single arrow by a certain hunter and fell to the ground.
And that lotus used as a sunshade then fell upon the top of the Śiva-liṅga that the sage was worshipping.
Then that hunter, having seen them, took the male swan for himself and gave the female swan to the sage; he too worshipped Śiva with her.
O lotus-eyed King, by the power of that very lotus which fell upon the summit of that Linga, you have now been born as a swan within this lineage.
And this very Haṃsī was born in the lineage of the Vidyādharas as Vinayavatī;
for Hara was especially worshipped by her with her own flesh.
Having been told thus by the sage Vijitāsu, "She was indeed your former wife," that lotus-eyed king spoke to him again.
O Blessed One, how did that act of entering the fire, which destroys the flood of sins, result in birth in the womb of a bird; what was the fruit for us two?
To the king who had spoken thus, the sage replied:
"Whatever state a living being has cultivated within himself, that very form he attains at death."
For instance, in the city of Ujjayinī, there was formerly a young Brahmin girl named Lāvaṇyamañjarī who was a lifelong celibate.
Upon seeing the young Brahmin named Kamalodaya,
her heart suddenly went out to him, and she was consumed by the fire of love.
Without abandoning her own vow, and being absorbed in meditation on the enjoyment of that [union],
she went to the bank of the Gandhavatī and gave up her life at the sacred ford.
Why did she not become attached to sensual enjoyments through that very meditation? In the city of Ekalavyā, she became a courtesan named Rūpavatī.
And by the power of her vows at sacred fords, she herself, being one who remembered her former births,
[bestowed herself] upon the twice-born reciter, Coḍakarṇa, as an incidental consequence.
He related the secret account of his own previous births,
along with the instruction for one who is single-mindedly devoted to the practice of recitation.

And previously, even that courtesan attained a good rebirth because her resolve was pure; for in this world, a king—or indeed anyone—attains the state of being identical with whatever his mind is fixed upon.
Having spoken thus, the sage dismissed the king to bathe,
and he himself performed the midday libation.
That king Puṣkarākṣa also went to the bank of a river in the forest,
and there he saw Vinayavatī gathering flowers.
Shining with her own form like the radiance of the sun,
she had out of curiosity entered a dense forest never seen before.
While he was reflecting with eager anticipation, "Who might this be?",
she, seated there, spoke confidently to her friend.
"Friend, that Vidyādhara who formerly desired to abduct me has today come here, freed from his curse, and announced my recovery of my husband."
Having heard that, the friend replied to the hermit maiden:
"This is true; for this very morning, while I was listening, Muñjakeśa [spoke thus]."
Thus addressed by the sage Vijitāsu, his own disciple said:
"Go and bring Tārāvalī and Raṅkumālin quickly."
Indeed, today the marriage of their daughter Vinayavatī with King Puṣkarākṣa shall take place here in this city.
Having been addressed thus by his teacher, Muñjakeśa replied, "So be it," and departed.
Therefore, come now, my friend; let us go to the hermitage.
When she had spoken thus, Vinayavatī then departed from there;
and Puṣkarākṣa heard that from afar, remaining unobserved.
As if to plunge into a river to escape the torment of the blazing fire of passion,
that king went once more to the hermitage of Vijitāsu.
There Tārāvalī and Aṅkumālin met him;
they paid homage to him as he bowed, and the ascetics surrounded him.
Then, upon the altar illuminated by his own splendors, the great seer sat like a second embodied Fire who had conquered his vital breaths.
He bestowed Vinayavatī upon that king,
and Raṅkumālin gave him a divine chariot that travels through the sky.
"Rule over the earth bounded by the four oceans together with her"—
this was the boon granted to him by the great sage after he had conquered the Asuras.
Then, with her permission, the king Puṣkarākṣa, taking his new bride and mounting that celestial chariot which travels through the sky,
swiftly crossed the ocean and went from there to his own city, appearing like the rising moon to the eyes of his subjects.
And having conquered the earth there by the power of his chariot and attained universal sovereignty,
he dwelt together with Vinayavatī, enjoying pleasures for a long time.
Thus, even a task that is extremely difficult succeeds spontaneously when the deities are benevolent;
therefore, O Lord, by the grace of the beloved of the Mountain-Daughter (Śiva) seen in your dream, your own desired goal shall also be accomplished before long.
Having heard this wonderful tale from his minister, Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta, filled with longing to find Śaśāṅkavatī,
resolved together with his own ministers to depart for Ujjayinī.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave.
In this manner, Mṛgāṅkadatta [encountered] here the daughter of King Karmasena.
Desiring to obtain that Śaśāṅkavatī described by the Vetāla.
He consulted with his ministers regarding a secret departure from his own city to go to Ujjayinī in the guise of a Mahāvratika ascetic.
And that prince privately commanded his minister Bhīmaparākrama to collect the skull-topped staff, the begging bowl, and other such items.
He brought that [treasure] into his own house,
and it was soon discovered by the chief minister of King Mṛgāṅkadatta’s father.
And at that moment, as he was suddenly walking along the roof of the palace,
Mṛgāṅkadatta spat out the essence of betel-juice.
And by chance, it fell upon the head of his father’s minister,
who was walking along that path below, having remained unseen.
Having realized that the spittle had been released by Mṛgāṅkadatta, the minister,
having performed his ablutions, took that anger born of humiliation into his heart.
Then, by the power of fate, on another day, King Amaradatta, the father of Mṛgāṅkadatta, was afflicted with cholera.
Then, having found an opportunity, that minister, having been granted immunity from fear, spoke suddenly to the king in private about him who was afflicted by the disease of possession.
"O Lord, an act of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) was commenced against you in the house of Bhīmaparākrama by Mṛgāṅkadatta; for that reason, you were afflicted."
"I have learned of this from the mouth of a spy, and it is now seen before my very eyes;
therefore, expel him from the country, just as one drives a disease out of the body."
Having heard that, the king became greatly agitated and dispatched his own general to the house of Bhīmaparākrama to investigate the matter.
And having obtained that mass of hair and so forth,
the general immediately brought it and showed it directly to the king.
"Let that son of mine, greedy for the kingdom and treacherous,
be exiled from this city this very day without delay by you, together with his ministers."
Then the king, having recovered his composure, commanded his general in anger:
"For what master does not know the crooked ways of his own ministers?"
Then that general, having gone and delivered the king’s command,
expelled Mṛgāṅkadatta along with his ministers from the city.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, having attained his desired success, was filled with joy; having worshipped Vināyaka and mentally prostrated before his parents, he [proceeded].
Having departed from Ayodhyā and traveled a great distance with those companions,
he spoke to the ten ministers, headed by Pracaṇḍaśakti.
There is a great lord of the Kirātas named Śaktirakṣita;
he is my fellow student in the sciences and has been my friend since childhood.
For previously, when his father was taken captive in battle, he was offered here as a substitute for his father's religious observance so that his father might be liberated.
When his father had died, he was installed in the paternal kingdom by his father— whom I had petitioned— by means of his own power, as one born of the royal lineage.
Therefore, friends, let us first go into his presence;
thereafter, we shall proceed in due course to Ujjayinī for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī.
Having spoken thus, accompanied by those ministers who replied,
"So be it," he set out from there and reached a great forest in the evening.
In that place, devoid of trees and water, he with great difficulty reached a lake where a single withered tree grew upon its bank.
Having performed the evening rites and drunk water there, he,
being weary, slept with his ministers beneath that withered tree.
And at night, on a moon-bright night, having awakened, he saw that withered tree gradually becoming filled with leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Seeing that its ripe fruits were falling at that very moment,
he awakened [the king] and showed that marvel to his ministers.
Then, filled with wonder and being hungry, he ate those fruits of that tree, which were of excellent flavor, together with them.
And while they were all eating there and watching,
that young Brahmin in an instant became a withered tree.
Then, questioned by the astonished Mṛgāṅkadatta, he said:
"There was once a certain eminent Brahmin named Damadhīra in Ayodhyā."
I am his son, named Śrutadhi; having lost his wife during a famine, he wandered with me and reached this land.
Having received five fruits given here by someone, he,
emaciated by hunger, gave three to me and set two aside for himself.
Then, when he had gone to the lake water to bathe,
I ate all those fruits here and feigned sleep.
Then, having returned from his bath and perceiving me standing there like a log under a disguise, he cursed me: "Become a withered tree right here on the shore of this lake!"
"And at night, you shall have flowers and fruits on the Candravatī;
by satisfying guests with those fruits, you will be released from the curse."
Thus cursed by my father, I immediately became like a withered tree;
and now that you have consumed its fruit, I am at long last released from the curse.
When Śrutadhi had thus related his own story and questioned him in turn,
Mṛgāṅkadatta then informed him of his own adventures.
Then that twice-born Śrutadhi, who was without kinsmen and proficient in the science of polity,
chose from Mṛgāṅkadatta the boon of becoming his follower.
Then, having passed the night there, Mṛgāṅkadatta set out in the morning accompanied by his ministers and Śrutadhi.
And as he was going, having reached the forest named Karimaṇḍita,
he saw five men with abundant hair and hideous forms.
Approaching him with humility, they spoke to him, their wonder having been aroused:
"We were born in the city of Kāśī as brahmins who subsist on cows."
"Scorched by droughts and withered grass, we have come from that region to this forest,
which abounds in grass, along with our cows during a time of famine."
And here we have obtained a rejuvenating elixir from the water of the pond,
which is constantly infused by the three myrobalans falling from the trees growing upon its banks.
"May they always drink that [nectar] of ours; while these [beings], subsisting on milk, remain here, five hundred years have passed for us in this uninhabited forest."
Therefore, O Lord, we are such as you are, and you are now our guests;
since you have arrived here by divine providence, please enter our hermitage.
Thus entreated by them, Mṛgāṅkadatta went with his followers to that hermitage and spent that day there, subsisting on milk and other such foods.
Having set out from there at dawn, observing various other curiosities as he went, he reached the territory of the Kirātas in due course.
And there he dispatched Śrutadhi to Śaktirakṣita, the lord of the Kirātas and his friend, to inform him of his arrival.
Having learned of this, the lord of the Kirātas came forth before him and,
bowing low, led Mṛgāṅkadatta along with his ministers into his own city.
Then, having been thus attended to by him, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained there for several days, having declared the reason for his arrival.
Having stationed Śaktirakṣita there ready to assist him whenever the time for his own duty arrived, the prince took leave of him.
Then, on an auspicious day, he set out again toward Ujjayinī;
his mind was captivated by Śaśāṅkavatī, and he traveled with twelve companions.
And as he was going, having reached a desolate forest,
he saw a certain ascetic seated at the foot of a tree, wearing ashes, a deerskin, and matted hair.
"O Blessed One, why do you stay here alone in this forest where there is no hermitage? Having approached him thus, he, accompanied by his followers, questioned him.
Then that ascetic said to him: "I am a disciple of the Great Guru named Śuddhakīrti, who has attained mastery over various floods of mantras."
Once, on one occasion, I spontaneously entered a state of self-possession after encountering a certain kṣatriya youth endowed with auspicious marks.
That prince, having been possessed, was questioned by me regarding various things;
he then spoke this after enumerating the fields of the juices of perfected medicinal herbs.
In this northern region, there is a solitary *śiṃśapā* tree;
and beneath it, in the Vindhya forest, lies a great palace of a lord of the *nāgas*.
And that water, covered with moist dust,
was clearly visible at midday by pairs of swans playing there along with water-fowl and cranes.
There is a powerful and excellent nāga there named Pārāvata;
he possesses an unsurpassed sword obtained from the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Whatever man obtains that sword named Vaidūryakānti becomes a sovereign lord of the siddhas and wanders about invincible.
When it was said, "And that sword is obtained by heroes with their companions," I then performed my dismissal by him who was possessed [by the spirit].
Turning away from all else and seeking that sword, O Great Earth, I wandered about;
but failing to find my companions, I came here exhausted, desiring death.
Having heard this from that ascetic, Mṛgāṅkadatta said to him there:
"I, along with my ministers, am your ally."
Having welcomed him with joy, that ascetic went together with him and his followers to the abode of that nāga by means of a foot-ointment.
There, having established Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others at night within quarters secured by spells and reached through supernatural power, he [conducted them] with consecrated [substances].
Having made it manifest with mustard seeds and sprinkling water over it with their powder,
he proceeded to perform a fire offering (*homa*) with the *nāgadamanī* mantras.
By the power of his mantra, he conquered obstacles such as portents and clouds;
then, from that *śiṃśapā* tree, a divine woman emerged.
As if reciting a spell of delusion with the tinkling of her jewel ornaments,
she approached him in an instant and pierced his mind with a sidelong glance.
And she, whose firm breasts were pressed against him,
having robbed him of his composure, caused the vessel for the oblation to fall from the hand of him who had forgotten the mantra.
Having found an opening at that moment,
that nāga named Pārāvata rose up from his abode like a thundercloud at the end of an eon.
Seeing him, with eyes blazing like fire and a roar as terrible as thunder,
that ascetic— bereft of his celestial nymph— suffered his heart to burst.
When he had perished, the Naga, his affliction having subsided, cursed Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others who had rendered him assistance.
"Since you have done this without cause by acting against the community,
you shall therefore remain separated from one another for some time."
When the nāga had thus spoken and vanished, at that very moment all those people there found their vision obstructed by darkness and their power of hearing sounds destroyed.
Separated by the power of the curse, Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others wandered here and there, crying out and searching for one another.
And then, when the confusion of night had passed, Mṛgāṅkadatta wandered here and there in the forest, remaining there without his ministers.
When two or three months had thus passed,
