Seeing there that Gandhamālin under the power of the yakṣas,
he drove away those wretched ones, wounded by his sword, for the sake of his liberation.
Seeing that, Kālajihva, having cast off his form as a female cakravāka bird from the middle of the lake,
rose up roaring like a monsoon cloud.
And as the battle raged in the sky, Vinītamati leaped up with his horse and seized Kālajihva by the hair as he sprang forward.
Even as he wished to cut off his head with a sword, the yakṣa,
wailing piteously, sought refuge with him.
Being released, he gave him his own ring, which wards off calamity;
bowing low, he also released that Naga Gandhamālin from servitude.
Then Gandhamālin, joyful and disciplined in mind,
gave his daughter Vijayavatī to him and went home.
Then, at dawn, the skillful Vinītamati returned home, bringing with him the sword, the ring, the horse, and the jewel maiden.
There, welcomed by his father, who was pleased by the account he had heard,
and by his own king, he married that Naga maiden.
Then, on one occasion, his father Kamalamati, having augmented him with those four jewels and his own virtues, spoke to him in private.
"O King, this daughter of yours, named Putrodayavatī, who is well-trained in all branches of knowledge, belongs to this Udayatuṅga."
A wager was made by him on that occasion: "Whichever Brahmin or even Kshatriya defeats her in debate, to him I shall give her."
And all other disputants were utterly defeated in debate by her,
who was like a celestial nymph in a form that causes wonder throughout the world.
And you are a solitary hero in the doctrine of your own kshatriya lineage; why then do you remain silent? Conquer him in debate and then marry her!
Thus addressed by his father, he, with a humble mind, replied: "O father, what conversation could there be for those like me with women who are so artful?"
Nevertheless, when he replied, "I shall carry out this command of yours," his father went into the presence of the king with that mature youth.
"O King, a debate with the princess will be held tomorrow morning," Vinītamati informed the monarch there.
Having accepted the matter from the king and returned home, he related it exactly as it was to his son, Vinītamati.
Then the eloquent Vinītamati, having arrived, approached that lotus-pond of the assembly of scholars, which was inhabited by that royal swan himself.
Resplendent, he illuminated [the world] while being gazed upon by throngs of virtuous men who had taken refuge in him, with their flickering eyes like bees, as they looked toward him face-to-face.
And in another moment, that Princess Udayavatī arrived there slowly,
drawn by his virtues like the bow-staff of the God of Love.
It was adorned by its own virtuous qualities and beautiful sounds, which served as ornaments,
as if they were presenting the initial prima facie arguments from the very beginning.
If a stainless crescent moon were to appear in a faultless sky,
it would then resemble her seated upon a throne of emerald.
Then she set forth her prima facie argument, as if weaving a garland of exquisite gems of words upon the threads of the rays from her gleaming teeth.
Having rendered Sumukhī speechless at every step, Vinītamati established that faultless doctrine of ultimate truth in an instant.
Then, while he was being praised by the members of the assembly, the princess considered herself victorious even in defeat, because she had obtained a virtuous husband.
Then King Udayatunga, being delighted,
gave that daughter— won through the wager of debate— to Vinītamati.
Then Vinītamati, filled with the jewels given by him,
remained there together with those two, the daughter of the Naga and the daughter of the king.
Once, while playing at dice and being defeated by others, his mind was deeply distressed;
a brahmin approached him and, through persistent insistence, begged for food.
Then, having whispered into his servant's ear, he, overcome with rage,
covered a vessel of sand with a cloth and had it given to him.
Taking that [gold] along with the gold coins because of its weight, the upright brahmin,
thinking it was his own, went to a secluded spot and opened it out of great joy.
Having seen it filled with sand, he pushed it aside onto the surface of the earth;
thinking, "I have been deceived by him," he went to his own home dejected.
Vinītamati, however, disregarding this and casting it aside,
remained at his own home as he pleased, in the company of his beloved wife, even though he had been engaged in gambling.
And as time passed, his joints and limbs became loosened by old age;
there, King Udayatunga became incapable of bearing the burden of the kingdom.
Then, having consecrated that very Vinītamati as his son-in-law in the kingdom, he, being childless, went to the Gaṅgā for the sake of liberation from the body.
And not long after that, having attained the kingdom, Vinītamati conquered even the ten directions by the power of his horse and sword.
By the power of this plague-averting ring,
the kingdom became free from disease and famine, just like that of King Raghu.
Once, a mendicant named Ratnacandramati, a lion among the elephants of disputants, arrived there from another land before the king.

And that monk, having been treated as a guest, requested of the king—who was fond of the virtuous—for the sake of debate, and uttered such a wager: SoKss_12.5.94: "And that monk, having been hospitably received, requested of that king who was fond of the virtuous for the sake of debate, and proclaimed such a wager."
"O Indra among kings, if you are defeated, you must accept the teaching of the Sugata;
if I am defeated, I shall serve the brahmins, casting aside my monastic robes."
Having heard this and said "So be it," King Vinītamati engaged in debate with that monk for seven days.
On the eighth day, that monk defeated the lord of the earth,
by whom Udayavatī— the "hammer for the heads of disputants"— had been conquered.
Then, having conceived faith, the king accepted from that monk the teaching of the Sugata, which is rich in the merit of benefiting sentient beings.
Devoted to the worship of the Jina, he constructed monasteries, sacrificial halls, and dwellings for all, including monks, brahmins, and others.
And having been pacified by that practice, he then requested from the monk the instruction for the conduct of a Bodhisattva, which benefits sentient beings.
Then that monk said to him: "O King, the great conduct of a Bodhisattva is to be practiced here by those who are free from defilement, and not by others."
Indeed, for one such as you, there is no gross transgression to be observed; however, you should seek out subtle faults through this method and bring them to rest.
Having said this, that monk taught him the dream-māṇava;
and the king, having seen that dream because of him, spoke to him in the morning.
"O Teacher, I know that today in a dream I went to the other world;
there, men carrying staffs said to me, who was seeking food out of hunger: [5.104]"
"O King, eat these abundant heated sands that you have earned—
the very same ones which were formerly given by you to a hungry Brahmin who came as a petitioner."
"Having given ten crores of gold, you shall be liberated from this sin.
Thus addressed by those men with clubs in their hands, I awoke at the end of the night.
Having spoken thus and related that account, and having given those ten crores of gold, the king again performed the ritual for inducing dreams.
Having seen that dream again, he rose at dawn and described it:
"Even now, they have given to me, who am hungry, [this] in another world within my dream."
When they were asked by men for food of sand, they replied to me:
"Even if alms are given, why would we eat this sand? (SoKss 12.5.109)
Then they did not weep, saying, "That gift of yours was fruitless,
because among it there was one piece of gold belonging to a brahmin."
Having heard this, the king exclaimed, "I have awakened from a dream," and he bestowed ten more crores of gold upon those who sought it.
Then, during the night, he again experienced a dream of the individual soul (āṇava);
having seen that dream once more, he arose at dawn and described it.
"Even now, alas! Those men gave me that very same meal of sand in the next world; and when questioned in a dream, I was told this by them: SoKss_12,5.113.
O King, even that gift of yours has become fruitless,
because today in the forest region of your own country, a brahmin was robbed by bandits and killed.
And since your protection was not effective, that protection has thus been fruitless;
therefore, give now a gift twice as great as that which you gave today.
Having heard this, the king declared to the mendicant, "I am awakened even here," and gave his teacher twice as much as the gift he had seen in the dream.
Then he said to that monk: "O Teacher, how can such a dharma, full of many flaws, be maintained in this world by those like me?"
Having heard that, the monk said: "O King, it is not by such means alone that the wise should apply their minds to the task of protecting the Dharma with lack of enthusiasm."
The deities protect those who are steadfast, endowed with perseverance, and who do not despise their own duty;
they also fulfill their desires.
And likewise, O King, this Jātaka of the Blessed One as a boar has not been heard by you; let it now be heard by you.
Long ago, in a cave on the Vindhya mountains, there lived a certain wise boar born from a portion of a Buddha, together with a monkey who was his friend.
Always accompanied by that number of beings who act for the welfare of all,
he passed his time honoring guests according to the traditional rites appropriate for himself.
And once there occurred a storm lasting five days,
terrible because the continuous downpour cut off the movement of living beings.
On the fifth day, at night, while the boar was asleep along with the monkey,
a lion accompanied by his wife and son went to the entrance of his cave.
There, that lion said to his wife:
"On this foul day, we shall certainly die today of hunger, having failed to obtain any living creature in this vast expanse."
Having heard that, the lioness said: "We are all hungry;
we cannot survive. Therefore, eat me alone, and you two shall live."
For you are the master, and this son is our very life and all-in-all; may another woman like me become yours, or let there be only him for both of you—may it be auspicious!
Thus, at that time, the noble boar, having awakened by chance, overheard the mutual conversation between that husband and wife.
Delighted, he thought: "By good fortune, where is this night, where is this foul weather, and where is the arrival of such a guest? Oh, what an auspicious rise of merit for me today!"
"As long as no obstacle arises to that [practice], why should I not satisfy these guests with this body, which perishes in an instant? (SoK 12.5.130)
Having risen and gone out, that boar spoke to the lion with gentle words: "O noble one, do not fall into despair."
When the boar said, "I have come as food for you, along with my sons and wife;
therefore, eat me," that lion—*SoKss_12,5.132*.
Delighted, he said to his wife: "Let this child eat first;
after him I shall eat, and after that you shall eat."
When she had said "So be it," the lion then proceeded to eat the flesh of that boar, which had previously been devoured by a lion cub.
As he was eating, that Great Being, the boar, said to him:
"Drink this blood of mine quickly, before it coagulates upon the ground."
"Find satisfaction with my flesh, and let your beloved eat the remainder," he said,
speaking thus as he was gradually reduced to nothing but bones by that lion.
Even though the boar was led away, deprived of life, he did not abandon his state of being established in courage;
as if they stood there to witness the very limit of that fortitude.
Meanwhile, that lioness, exhausted by hunger, died there;
her son, the lion, went elsewhere, and the night drew to a close.
In the meantime, that monkey woke up, went outside, and seeing the boar in such a state, asked him in great agitation: SoKss_12,5.139 //
"Tell me, friend, if you are able, by whom has this state of unease been brought upon you?
Having heard that, the steadfast boar related to him exactly what had occurred.
Then, weeping and bowing at his feet, the monkey said:
"You are a portion of a divinity, by whom I have been liberated from this animal state."
"Tell me some desire of yours; I shall fulfill it for you.
Being addressed thus by that monkey, the boar said to him:
That desire of mine for my companion, which could not be accomplished even by fate,
has been fulfilled as I watched this poor lioness die of hunger.
"O friend, my heart desires that she, having regained her life, might now satisfy herself by eating once more, as she did before when she had reached my presence."
Thus, appearing before that disputant Kroḍa and touching him with his hand,
Dharma transformed the lord of sages into a body of divine form.
And he said: "This illusion in the form of a lion and so forth was created by me alone, desiring to overcome you who have girded your loins for the sole purpose of others' welfare."

By you, whose being is unbroken, who have given up your life for the sake of others, and who have conquered me, this Dharma has been attained; today you have truly reached the state of a Lord of Sages.
Having heard that and perceiving the Dharma standing before him, the sage said:
"Now, while these two monkeys have not yet abandoned their animal state, let them remain as friends."
"O Blessed One, even this attainment of the state of Lord of Sages does not please me," he said.
Having heard this, the Sage made that monkey also a follower of the Dharma.
"Association with the great leads inevitably to great fruit;
now that Dharma has vanished, Siṃhī has died and disappeared."

Thus, O King, for those who have not abandoned their enthusiasm for the Dharma through the power of their resolve, and who receive the assistance of deities, the fulfillment of their desires is not difficult to attain.
Having heard these words of the monk, King Dānaśūra, whose mind was disciplined, again performed that dream-mantra at night.
Having seen it, he related the dream to that monk in the morning:
"I know that today in a dream some divine sage spoke thus to me."
"Son, now practice the stainless conduct of a bodhisattva.
Upon hearing those words, I was awakened this very day and attained peace.
Having thus informed the monk who was his guru,
the lord of the earth undertook that great practice on an auspicious day with his permission.
And he remained there, raining down desires upon those who sought them without ceasing;
and his wealth became inexhaustible, for prosperity indeed has its root in dharma.
Then once, a needy brahmin approached him and made this request:
"O King, I am a brahmin residing in the city of Pāṭaliputra."
There, having surrounded the fire-hall, my son too was surrounded by a *brahmarākṣasa*; no means of escape is effective against him.
Therefore, I have come here to you, who are a wish-fulfilling tree for those who seek, to make this request:
grant me this ring, which destroys all evils, for my well-being.
Thus entreated by that brahmin, the king,
remaining unperturbed, gave him that very ring which he had obtained from Kālajihva.
When that brahmin had departed taking it, the fame of the king’s vow as a bodhisattva spread even to the ends of the earth.
Then, on one occasion, another guest arrived for the Lord from the northern region: a certain prince named Indukalaśa.
Having shown his courtesy to that king, whose noble lineage he knew,
and being asked by the steadfast monarch what he desired, the prince spoke to him:
You are indeed renowned on earth as a wish-fulfilling gem for the caravan of supplicants;
for even when he requests your very life, no petitioner ever turns away from you empty-handed.
"And I, having been seized by my brother named Kanakakalaśa, was exiled from the kingdom; seeking wealth for my father's sake, I have come to you."
"Therefore, O hero, give me those two jewels, the horse and the sword,
by whose power I may conquer my kinsman and obtain the kingdom."
Upon hearing that, King Vinītamati gave even those two— the horse and the sword— which were jewels for protecting the kingdom, to this prince.
And no doubt arose in that firm-minded one,
even as the ministers, with downcast faces, were letting out sighs.
Then, having obtained the horse and the sword, the prince went there;
by their power, he conquered that brother and obtained the kingdom.
His brother Kanakakalaśa, having been deposed from the kingdom,
came to that city of King Vinītamati.
And there he began with difficulty to enter the fire;
having learned of that, King Vinītamati spoke to his ministers:
"This virtuous man has reached this state because of my transgression;
therefore, by restoring his own kingdom to him, I shall now become free from my debt to him."
"What use have I for this kingdom, which serves no purpose for others?
Since I am childless, let him alone be my son and the sustainer of the kingdom."
Having spoken thus, the king summoned Kanakakalaśa and bestowed his own kingdom upon him, even though his ministers were unwilling.
Having bestowed the kingdom, he departed from that city at that very moment,
accompanied by his two wives, with a mind free from conceptual construction.
Alas, alas! Fie upon it! The full moon, the nectar-rayed one who nourishes the world, has been born and yet has been obscured by a cloud that falls out of season.
And though he was engaged in fulfilling all the hopes of every embodied being,
that king, who was like a wish-fulfilling tree for his subjects, was led away by fate to some unknown place.
Seeing this, the citizens then followed him, wailing with such cries that they were hoarse, overwhelmed with agitation, and drenching the earth with their tears.
Having with difficulty turned them back, the unshakable Vinītamati then departed for the forest with his wife, driving the chariot in reverse.
In due course, he reached a desert land created by fate to test his fortitude— a region scorched by the sun, devoid of water and trees.
Afflicted by thirst and exhausted by the fatigue of the long journey, he sat down for a moment in one part of that place and was overcome by sleep along with his wife.
As soon as he awoke and looked about,
he beheld there a magnificent and wonderful grove, brought into existence by the excellence of his own merit.
It possessed ponds filled with cool, clear water and blooming lotuses;
it was covered with dark green grass and trees bent low under the weight of their fruit.
With its smooth, broad, and lofty stone surface situated in the shade,
it was like the Nandana grove of the third heaven, drawn down by the power of his generosity.
"Is this a dream, or a delusion, or perhaps a divine favor to me?"—
as the king gazed and gazed upon that sight, he was filled with wonder.
Then he heard a voice uttered from the sky by a certain pair of perfected beings (*siddha*) in the form of a pair of swans moving through the heavens.
O King, what cause for excessive wonder is there here regarding the greatness of your own essential nature?
Therefore, dwell at your pleasure in this forest, which always bears flowers and fruit.
Having heard these words of the Siddha, Vinītamati remained there in the forest,
contented, practicing austerities together with his two wives.
And once, while sitting there upon a stone slab, he saw from afar a certain man who was intent on taking his own life by means of hanging.
Having gone quickly and having consoled him with affectionate words while warding him off from death, he questioned that man there regarding the cause.
Then that man said: "Listen from the very beginning as I speak to you:
I am Somaśūra, son of Nāgaśūra, known by the name Somaka."
Thus, because I was designated as a thief in my birth story, my father, out of fear of that, diligently instructed me in the Dharmaśāstra under the guidance of experts in those treatises.
Even after studying that, I engaged in theft due to association with the wicked;
by whom can the karma of a previous life be altered here?
Then once, having been seized from the midst of thieves by the city guards,
I was brought to the place of impalement on a stake for execution.
At that very moment, a great royal elephant, frantic with rut and having broken its tethering post,
came to that same spot while trampling living beings to death.
Out of fear of them, those executioners abandoned me and fled somewhere;
and I, having escaped from that tumultuous fray, departed from there.
I heard from the world that my father had lost his life as soon as he heard that I was being led away for execution; thereafter, I heard that my mother had followed him.
Then, afflicted by grief, wandering and exhausted, and intent on casting off my body,
I gradually reached this great, desolate forest.
As soon as I had entered here, a certain divine woman appeared suddenly; approaching me, she offered consolation and spoke.
"O son of Vinītamati, you have reached this hermitage of the royal seer;
your evil has departed, and from him you shall obtain knowledge."
Having said this, she vanished; and as I wandered about, unable to find that royal sage and desiring to abandon my life out of grief, I was beheld by you.
Having spoken thus and led Somaśūra to his own hermitage,
that royal seer introduced himself as a guest and honored him.
And having finished his meal, the royal sage, wishing to restrain him from ignorance amidst various discourses on the Dharma, spoke to that humble man.
Ignorance, my child, must be abandoned, for it belongs to those of perverted intellect; it leads to harm in both worlds. Listen now to a scriptural tradition regarding this: SoKss_12.5.204
Long ago among the Pāñcālas, there was a twice-born man named Devabhūti;
he was a follower of the Vedas and possessed a virtuous wife named Bhogavatī.
When he had gone away to bathe, she entered the vegetable garden for the sake of vegetables and saw a washerman’s donkey eating the greens.
Taking up a club, she ran after him, and that donkey,
while fleeing, fell into a pit and broke his hoof.
Having learned of this, the washerman, its owner, arrived there in a rage and beat that Brahmin woman with clubs and kicks.
Because of that, the pregnant woman suffered a miscarriage with a sudden convulsion;
then Dhāvaka, taking Khara with him, went to his own home.
Then her husband returned from bathing; having learned of this and seeing his wife, the brahmin went in agitation to the city magistrate and made his representation.

Having heard the dispute between those two, he immediately summoned a washerman named Balāsura; the fool then explained it as follows: SoKss_12,5.211: "He immediately summoned a washerman named Balāsura; having heard the dispute between those two, the fool explained this."
"Because of this donkey's broken hoof,
let this twice-born man carry the donkey's load until the donkey returns to its natural state."
"Moreover, let this washerman produce another embryo in the wife of that Brahmin by causing her to miscarry that [first] fetus."
When he had said, "This is the punishment for these two," that twice-born man,
out of anguish, consumed poison and gave up his life along with his wife.
Having learned of this, the king killed that city superintendent there— he who was difficult to overcome and a slayer of a Brahmin— and he entered the womb of an animal for a long time.
Thus, those shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, who wander on the wrong path due to their own faults and have not placed the lamp of the true scriptures before them, will certainly fall.
Having spoken thus, that royal sage, Vinītamati, addressed Somaśūra again in order to instruct him who was seeking instruction.
"My child, I shall now explain the meaning of the perfections; listen to them in due order.
Formerly, there was a king in Kurukṣetra named Malayaprabha."
Once, when the king was giving wealth to his subjects during a famine,
his son Induprabha spoke to him as he was being restrained by his ministers out of greed.
O dear one, how can you be indifferent toward your subjects because of the words of evil counselors?
For you are their wish-fulfilling tree, and they are your cows of plenty.
To his son, who was prattling thus with persistence, the king, under the influence of his ministers, spoke out of weariness: "My dear child, what inexhaustible wealth do I possess?"
If I am to become for these subjects a wish-fulfilling tree even without him,
then why do you not yourself assume the state of a kalpa-tree for them?
Having heard this from his father, that prince made a vow:
"I must either die, or the state of being a wish-fulfilling tree must be achieved by me through asceticism."
Having thus resolved, that Great Being set out for the forest of asceticism;
and as soon as he had ascended [his vehicle], that famine came to an end.
Then, having obtained his desired boon from Mahendra, who was gratified by his intense asceticism,
that wish-fulfilling tree appeared right there in his own city.
With its branches extended in all directions and with the cries of birds, it seemed as if drawing in those standing afar and calling out to those who sought it.
And day after day he granted desires even to those who sought what was difficult to obtain;
he made those subjects free from longing, as if they were dwelling in heaven.
And at that time, Mahendra approached him and spoke, tempting him:
"Your service to others is complete; come now for the sake of heaven."
Then, having become like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*), that prince said to him:
"In this place, even these other trees are delightful with their flowers and fruits."
Those who are free from desire for their own interests constantly devote themselves to the welfare of others;
how could such a person, having become a wish-fulfilling tree for them, go to heaven for his own pleasure?
"Having thus shattered the hopes of these people, I shall depart"—
hearing these noble words of his, Śakra spoke again.
"In that case, let all your subjects also go to heaven. Then the prince, who was like a wish-fulfilling tree, replied to him:
"If you are pleased, lead my subjects to heaven; I have no need for that myself.
For the sole purpose of accomplishing the welfare of others, I shall perform great asceticism."
Having praised him who had spoken thus, the lord of the gods said "So be it" to that Sugata, and taking the subjects with him, he went joyfully to the third heaven.
Having abandoned that state of being a tree and resumed his own form, the prince Induprabha, dwelling in the forest, attained the status of a Bodhisattva through his ascetic penance.
Thus have I fully described the accomplishment of those devoted to generosity;
this is your perfection of generosity—now hear the perfection of ethical discipline.
Long ago, on the Vindhya mountain, there was a king of parrots born from a portion of the Sugata;
rich in virtue practiced in previous births, he was self-controlled and named Hemaprabha.
Although he was one who remembered his former births and was a teacher of the Dharma,
he had a gatekeeper who was passionate and foolish, a parrot named Cārumati.
Once, grieving for his wife— a female parrot slain by a fowler with a snare—
he fell into a state of deep compassion, tormented by the pain of separation from her.
Then that wise king of the parrots, Hemaprabha, wishing to dispel his grief through a skillful means for his own benefit, spoke these words falsely.
"That wife of yours is not dead; she escaped from the fowler's snare. Indeed, I have just now seen her alive as she fled."
Saying, "Come, I shall show her to you," the king led Cārumati through the path of the sky to a certain body of water.
Having shown him his own reflection there within the water, he said to him: "This is that wife of yours; look, she stands here."
Having heard that and seeing his own reflection there, that fool-minded man was delighted; entering the water, he embraced and kissed her.
Not obtaining the touch of his beloved nor hearing her voice, he thought:
"Why does my beloved not give me her touch and her conversation?"
Then, fearing his anger, he went and brought an *āmalaka* fruit;
out of a desire for conciliation and thinking it was his beloved, he placed it in the reflection.
Realizing that it had fallen from his mouth after being swallowed and then spat out by his beloved,
he went with sorrow to King Hemaprabha and addressed him.
"O King, that wife does not grant me even a touch or a word;
moreover, she rejected the āmalaka fruit that was offered by me."
Having heard this, the king spoke slowly to him as if with difficulty:
"It is not proper for me to say this; nevertheless, I speak to you out of affection."
"For she is now devoted to another; how could she possibly feel affection for you?
Come, I shall show her to you directly right here within the water."
Having said this, the king led him there and showed him both his own reflection and his own reflection in the water, joined together with that [other's].
As soon as that fool saw his wife united with another man,
he turned back in disgust and informed his own king.
"O Lord, that your instruction was not heard by me, a fool—this is its ripening for me; now, command what must be done by me in this matter."
When he had thus made his request, King Hemaprabha,
having found the opportunity for instruction, spoke to the doorkeeper.
It would be better to consume the *hālāhala* poison or have a serpent bound around one's neck than to place trust in women, who are beyond the reach of jewels, mantras, and other such means.
Like whirlwinds that are exceedingly fickle and laden with much dust, women defile those who follow the true path and utterly overwhelm them.
Those of firm character and wise intellect should not be attached to those [pleasures];
rather, they should practice ethical discipline in order to attain the state of one free from passion.
Thus instructed by the king, Cārumati renounced women and gradually became one whose vital energy was drawn upward (an ascetic), equal to a Buddha.
Thus, I have described the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) as that which enables others who are rich in virtue to cross over; now hear the perfection of patience (*kṣamāpāramitā*).
On Mount Kedāra there was a great sage named Śubhanaya;
he constantly bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī, self-controlled and emaciated by his asceticism.
Once at night, thieves came there to search for gold previously buried in the ground, but they did not find it anywhere.
Then, thinking that the place was secluded, those thieves entered his hut and spoke to one another as they saw that it had been taken by that sage.
"O Dambhamuni, release the gold we have brought from the earth!
Alas, you have arrived as a thief even among thieves!"
Thus accused by those wicked men, the sage, whose purpose had not been achieved, spoke falsely:
"I have not taken anything; I have seen nothing."
Then, although he was beaten with those wicked clubs by those bandits,
that best of sages, being truthful in speech, continued to say exactly the same thing.
Then those robbers, thinking "this man is cruel," cut him apart;
they successively tore off his hands, his feet, and gouged out his eyes.
Nevertheless, perceiving him as unchanging and beyond all speech,
and considering him to be like gold from which all else has been removed, those thieves departed just as they had come.

Of that man who maintained the five sacred fires, two additional fires blazed intensely with hunger—
the digestive fires of himself and his wife, both of whom were impoverished of progeny and wealth.
Once, while he was established in austerity and seeking wealth and a son,
the blessed Fire-god instructed him in a dream.
“You have no biological son, but you shall have an adopted one;
and by his power alone, O Brahmin, your poverty shall cease.”
"Thus, that brahmin has remained waiting today for instructions from Agni;
this child must be given to him, for such is the destiny."
Having spoken thus to his beloved, he placed that child— who was seated upon a golden pitcher filled with gold and adorned with a divine garland of jewels tied around his neck— [upon her lap].
Having cast [the corpse] into the house of that twice-born man while he was asleep at night,
Aṭṭahāsa, together with his wife, departed for his own destination along with his wife.
Having awakened there, the brahmin Devadarśana, together with his wife, beheld that crescent moon of the young moon, its star-like gems shimmering.
Wondering "What is this? and looking at that golden pitcher, he remembered the Agni-svapnādeśa and rejoiced.
He took that boy, his son bestowed by fate, and that wealth;
and at dawn, he held a great festival.
And on the eleventh day, she gave her young son his appropriate name, Śrīdarśana, right there.
Then, having become very wealthy, that brahmin Devadarśana remained performing rituals such as sacrifices and enjoying various pleasures.
Śrīdarśana also grew up there in his father’s house,
and being full of vigor, he attained excellence in the sciences of the Vedas as well as in the knowledge of weapons.
In the course of time, while he was still in his youth, his father Devadarśana,
having arrived on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, passed away at Prayāga.
Having learned of this, his mother also entered the fire;
thereafter Śrīdarśana performed for them the funeral rites prescribed in the scriptures while mourning.
Gradually, his grief having subsided and still possessing no possessions, he became addicted to gambling; though wise, he was rendered friendless by fate.
And before long, as his wealth was exhausted by that evil addiction,
he experienced distress even regarding his food.
Once, while staying for three days without food in a gambling hall,
he was unable to leave because of his shame at wearing such unseemly garments.
A certain gambler friend named Mukharaka, seeing Śrīdarśana distressed because he would not eat what others had given him, addressed him: SoKss_12,6.75 //
Why do you become deluded? This very sight is the sin of the vice of gambling;
have you not realized that the dice are nothing but the falling glances of unchaste women?
Arms as a cloak, the dust as a bed, the crossroads as a home,
and a ruined wife— indeed, the Creator fashioned these for the gambler.
Why do you not eat? Though wise, why do you neglect yourself?
For what desired thing is there that a steadfast man, while living, cannot attain?
And so, listen here to this wonderful story of Bhūnandana:
there is here a region that is an ornament of the earth, known as Kaśmīra.
Having fashioned the visible enjoyment of heaven for those of meritorious deeds,
the Creator made a second [heaven] as it were, consisting of objects to be enjoyed.
That [city] was inhabited by both Sarasvatī and Śrī, who had entered as if out of mutual jealousy, each thinking, "I am the superior one here, not she."
As if to prevent the entry of the Kali age, which is hostile to the Dharma,
the Snowy Mountain protects itself by encircling its own body.
"Go far away from here, O impurity!"— thus do the waves, with hands outstretched, seem to drive away even that which is adorned within a mere span of the river, the divine Tīrtha.
In which city the lofty rows of palaces, washed with white lime,
create the illusion of the mountain ranges at the foot of the nearby Himalayas.

In that [kingdom], there was a king named Bhūnandana, who was a teacher of the social classes and stages of life, a moon bringing joy to his subjects, and one learned in the sciences and sacred scriptures.
His valor shone forth upon the pairs of breasts of amorous women, as well as upon the circles of his enemies' fingernails.
Though he was possessed of statesmanship, his subjects were constantly devoid of policy;
though his own mind was solely attached to Kṛṣṇa, their minds were far from being devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Once, on the twelfth lunar day, having duly worshipped Acyuta,
that king saw in a dream a certain daughter of the Daityas approaching him.
Having attained union with her, he woke up and did not see her;
however, astonished, he clearly saw the marks of sexual enjoyment upon his body.
"This is no dream, for it is vivid; I consider this to be a state of enjoyment.
I have surely been deceived by that woman, who is perhaps some divine being."
Having understood this, his mind became so afflicted by the pain of separation that he gradually abandoned all royal duties.
Seeing no means of attaining her, the king reflected:
"By the grace of Hari, that moment of union with her occurred for me."
In order to attain that [state], I shall go to a solitary place and propitiate Him alone;
alas, I shall cast off this noose of kingship, which has become tasteless due to separation from Him.
Having thus resolved and informed his ministers,
that delighter of the earth gave the kingdom to his younger brother named Sunanda.
Having renounced his kingdom, he went to the sacred ford named Kramasara, which arose from the footprint of Hari and was established in ancient times by Trivikrama.
It was occupied by the three gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— who, shaped like peaks, resided upon the summits of the nearby mountains.
By that same footprint of Viṣṇu, another celestial river was created in Kaśmīra, named Viṣuvatī, which is the Vitastā, as if out of envy [for the Gaṅgā].
There the king remained performing austerities, indifferent to all other pleasures;
weary and longing for a new flavor, he was like a *cātaka* bird in the heat of summer.
And when twelve years had passed while he remained there engaged in ascetic penance,
a certain ascetic, the best among the wise, arrived by that same path.
With tawny hair matted at the top, clad in bark garments, and accompanied by a host of disciples,
he descended like the Lord himself from the peak of that mountain-tirtha.
As soon as he saw the king, he was filled with joy; approaching him and bowing low, he inquired after his welfare and, after reflecting for a moment as it were, spoke.
"O King, that Daitya maiden who was your beloved dwells on Pātāla;
therefore, take heart, for I shall lead you into her presence."
"I am indeed the son of a sacrificer named Yajñasamjña from the south,
a Brahmin named Bhūtivasu, who is a teacher of yogins."
Thus, having had my knowledge transmitted by my father from the Pātālaśāstra,
I was instructed in the sequence of rituals for the mantras and tantras of Haṭakeśāna.
Having gone to Śrīparvata, I performed austerities for the propitiation of Tryambaka;
then, being pleased by that, Śiva appeared to me there in person and commanded as follows: ||| SoKss_12,6.105 |||
"Go, accompanied by the wives of the Daityas, and enjoy pleasures in the netherworld (Rasātala).
You shall come to me; hear now the means for attaining that which I shall tell you."
There are many openings to the netherworld here on this earth,
but there is one great opening made by Maya that provides light in Kaśmīra.
By whom Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa, was led into the secret garden grounds of the Dānavas and brought delight to Aniruddha, her beloved.
And then Pradyumna, in order to protect that son,
made a manifest opening on one side by means of a mountain peak.
And for the sake of guarding that gateway, he installed Durgā there,
whom he had propitiated with hundreds of hymns and who bears the name Śārikā.
That place there is even now designated by two names: Pradyumnaśikhara and Śārikākūṭa.
"Go, enter Pātāla through that opening along with your followers; by my grace, you shall achieve success therein."
Having spoken thus, when the deity had vanished, by the power of his grace,
all-encompassing higher knowledge arose within me, and I have come here to this land of Kaśmīra.
Therefore, O King, come with us to Śārikākūṭa;
there I shall lead you to the netherworld (pātāla) where you may be beside your beloved woman.
When the ascetic had spoken thus,
the king, the delighter of the earth, agreed and went together with him to that heap of śārikā wood.
When that great ascetic, endowed with the favor of the Earth, had revealed the opening by casting mustard seeds according to the prescribed rite, [the entrance appeared].
Having entered together with him and his disciples,
that king traveled along the path to the netherworld for five days, day and night.
On the sixth day, having all crossed the Ganges that flows to the netherworld,
they beheld upon the silver ground a divine forest.
It was perfumed by the fragrance of golden lotuses blooming upon the land,
and it possessed trees of rising coral, camphor, sandalwood, and agallochum.
In its center was a vast expanse, beautiful with jeweled stairways,
with golden walls and radiant with a multitude of ruby pillars.
And they joyfully beheld the lofty temple of Śiva, with its vast and pure central core constructed from moonstone.
Then that ascetic, the best among the knowers of wisdom, addressed his own disciples and King Bhūnandana, who were filled with wonder: SoKss_12,6.123 //
"This is that god Hāṭakeśvara, whose abode is in Pātāla;
he is celebrated throughout the three worlds, therefore let him be worshipped."
Then all of them, drenched in the waters of the Gaṅgā there, worshipped Śambhu with those various flowers produced in the netherworld.
Resting for a moment from that worship, they departed and reached a certain divine, great jambu tree from which ripe fruits were falling.
Seeing them, that ascetic said to them: "These fruits are not to be eaten by you, for if they are consumed, they will surely cause an obstacle."
Even upon hearing this, one of his disciples, driven by hunger, ate that fruit;
and as soon as he had eaten it, he became motionless, taking on the form of an immobile being.
Then, their desire for the fruit [of worldly life] abandoned through fear at the sight of that,
the ascetic, accompanied by those other disciples and Bhūnandana, [departed].
Having traversed a distance of one krośa, he beheld a lofty golden wall standing there,
with a gateway fashioned from excellent jewels.
On both sides of that gate,
he saw two iron-bodied rams, striking with their horns, blocking the entrance.
Having immediately struck them on the head with his staff empowered by incantations,
he drove them both away to some unknown place, as if they had been smitten by a thunderbolt.
Then, having entered through that gate, he, his disciples,
and the king beheld divine dwellings made of gold and jewels.
And at every door they saw gatekeepers, fierce with their lower lips bitten by their teeth, grasping iron clubs.
Then they all sat down there at the foot of a single excellent tree;
that ascetic, however, performed a yogic concentration (dhāraṇā) for the destruction of evil.
By the power of that dhāraṇī, all those fierce gatekeepers fled from every gate and vanished from sight.
And in an instant, from those gates there emerged courtesans adorned with divine ornaments and garments, accompanied by retinues of Daitya maidens.
Approaching each of those ascetics individually, they requested entrance from them, each according to the words of their respective mistress.
"Once you have entered within, you must not disregard the words of your beloved.
Having spoken thus to those others, that accomplished ascetic then departed.
And having entered the excellent palace together with some of them,
he obtained one preeminent Daitya maiden and all his desired enjoyments.
Others also, one by one, were led by those [maidens] into divine mansions and became vessels for the enjoyment of the daughters of the Daityas.
Then King Bhūnandana was also led by that single woman, who was bowed low with humility,
to an outer palace made of jewels.
With the reflections of his retinue and excellent women appearing on all sides upon the jeweled walls, it was as if a living painting were displayed there.
Constructed from smooth, great-blue sapphire,
it was as if it had ascended to the very surface of the sky out of a desire to surpass the celestial chariots.
With its beautiful Rāma appearing radiant with intoxication, possessing the charming grace of Pradyumna,
and enriched by the power of Acyuta, it was like the banner of the Vṛṣṇis.
Even a flower that withstands the morning sun would not serve as a comparison for the delicate nature of the bodies of women here.
Having entered there, where divine music was sounding,
the king beheld that lovely asura maiden whom he had previously seen in his dream.
When this [city] was illuminated by its own splendor, even though Pātāla was devoid of the sun and other celestial bodies,
the Creator’s fashioning of the light from jewels and such became redundant.
Beholding her of indescribable form, the king, with tears of joy,
seemed as if he had washed away the impurity of looking at others from his eyes.
And she too, seeing that lord of kings being proclaimed by the songs of the Aḷīgīs,
the young girl named Kumudinī experienced an indescribable joy.
Rising up and taking him by the hand, saying with respect, "You have been troubled by me," she seated him upon a throne.
Having rested for just a moment, bathed, and adorned with garments and ornaments,
that asura woman led him to a garden for a drinking party.
There, on the bank of a pond filled with the blood, fat,
and wine dripping from corpses hanging from trees at the water’s edge, she sat down together with him.
She gave that vessel, filled with fat and liquor, to the king for him to drink; but he did not accept it, as it was loathsome.
"If you forbid us from drinking this, there will be no safety for you," said the king to her as she spoke thus with persistence.
"I have resolved that I shall certainly not drink this, whatever it may be";
then she threw the vessel at his head and departed elsewhere.
And with his eyes and face contorted, that king was taken by her female attendants and cast into another body of water, into a large pond.
And at that very moment, as soon as he was cast down, he beheld himself arrived once again in that former grove of ascetics, at the sacred ford of Kramasaras.

And seeing that mountain there appearing as if laughing with its snow, he—dejected, astonished, and bewildered, feeling deceived—reflected: paśyaṃś ca sa himaṃ tatra hasantam iva taṃ nagam / viṣaṇṇavismitodbhrānto vañcitaḥ sa vyacintayat // SoKss_12,6.159 //
Where is that garden of the Daitya’s son, and where is this mountain Kramasaras?
Oh, what is this marvel? Is it an illusion, or is it a delusion of the mind?
Or what else is certain for him, since my word has been transgressed?
Even after hearing the words of that ascetic, this [transgression] of mine has manifested.
And yet that drink is not to be censured; it was she herself who tested me, for by that which fell upon her head, a divine fragrance reaches my nostrils.
For in every way, even great effort made for those who are incapable does not lead to fruit; for destiny turns against them in that manner.
Thinking thus, Bhūnandana approached, and there he was surrounded by bees attracted by the fragrance of his limbs, which had been moistened by drinking the wine of the asura’s daughter.
"Alas! May this hardship not bear fruit for me;
may it instead result in an undesirable outcome, like the distress of a weak person who attempts to raise a vetāla."
Thus being stung by those bees, the king, reflecting at that time,
became filled with agitation and resolved to abandon his body.
Just then, by chance, a certain son of a sage happened along that path and beheld the king in such a state.
Approaching quickly, his mind moistened with compassion, the seer warded off the bees;
and having asked about the circumstances, he spoke thus to the king:
O King, as long as this body exists, how can there be an end to suffering?
Therefore, the wise should always strive for the goal of human life through the absence of agitation regarding that [suffering].
As long as there is no realization of the oneness of Acyuta, Īśāna,
and Viriñci, the accomplishments born from the worship of their distinctions will remain indeed fragile.
Meditating upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara with the thought of their non-difference,
perform penance here for another twelve years with fortitude.
Then you will obtain that beloved woman and, in the end, eternal perfection;
meanwhile, your body has already attained success, as evidenced by this divine fragrance.
And take this black antelope skin of mine as your upper garment,
so that, when you have covered yourself with it, you will not be troubled by bees.
Having said this and given him the deerskin and the mantra, the sage departed;
and the king, having accepted them with the words "So be it," remained there at that sacred ford, his fortitude restored.
When that king had lived there for twelve years and propitiated Īśvara through ascetic penance,
the Daitya maiden Kumudī herself approached him.
Having gone to the netherworld with that beloved wife,
King Bhūnandana enjoyed pleasures for a long time and attained perfection.
Thus, those of a non-remissible nature who rely upon fortitude regain their own ground, even if they have fallen far from it.
And you, Śrīdarśana, possess auspicious marks and are destined for future prosperity;
why then do you neglect yourself out of agitation in the absence of food?
Having been addressed thus by his friend Mukharaka within the gambling hall,
Śrīdarśana, who had remained without food during the night, spoke to him.
"As you have said, though I am of noble birth, because of my shame in this city,
I am unable to go outside, being so utterly ruined by gambling."
If you do not forbid my departure for some foreign land on this very night, O Miśra, then I shall take food.
Upon hearing that, Mukharaka said, "So be it," and then, having brought food for him, he gave it; and he too then ate it.
And having eaten there, Śrīdarśana then set out toward another country together with that very friend who had followed him out of affection.
And as he was traveling along that path at night, his mother and father, who had arrived by chance through the sky, beheld him there by the power of fate.
Those two, Saudāminī and Aṭṭahāsa, by whom the newborn son of the brahmin Devadarśana was placed here in his house.

Perceiving that he had fallen into such a state— destitute by his addiction to gambling and about to depart for a foreign land— the two [gods], out of affection, spoke from the sky while remaining invisible:
"O Śrīdarśana, your mother-in-law, the wife of Devadarśana,
has placed her ornaments on the ground inside her own quarters."
Having gone there and taken them, proceed without anxiety to Mālava;
for there dwells a king named Śrīsena, possessed of exalted glory.
And because he had been so intensely addicted to gambling during his youth,
he established a large and flourishing monastery for gamblers.
Gamblers dwelling there obtain their desired food;
in that same way, go there, and it shall be well for you.
Having heard these words from heaven, Śrīdarśana went home;
from the pit in the earth, he took those ornaments together with Samiśrā.
Then, filled with joy and accompanied by his friend Mukharaka,
he set out toward Mālava, considering it to be a divine favor.
Having traveled a very long distance during that night and day,
he reached the village named Bahusasya with him at evening.
Exhausted and accompanied by his friend, he sat down upon the bank of a lake of pure water, not far from that village.
At that moment, while he stood with his feet washed in the water he had drunk,
a certain maiden of incomparable beauty came there for the sake of water.
With limbs marked by lines the color of blue lotuses, she was like Rati alone,
made dark by the smoke from Kāma when he was consumed by Hara.
Seeing Śrīdarśana, she approached him with eyes overflowing with love and spoke to him and his companion, who were delighted by the sight of her.
"Where have you two, O noble ones, come here to this calamity?
Have you fallen into the blazing fire out of ignorance, like moths?"
Having heard this, Mukharaka was bewildered; he questioned the maiden there, "Who are you? And what is this that you have said? Tell me."
Then she said: "I shall speak this in brief; listen, you two.
There is a very great and famous agrahāra named Sughoṣa."
There lived a brahmin named Padmagarbha, the most eminent among those who know the Vedas;
he had a wife of noble family named Śaśikalā.
And upon her two children were born to that man of noble birth:
a son named Mukharaka, and a daughter, who was myself, Padmiṣṭhā.
That brother of mine, Mukharaka, ruined by the vice of gambling,
left home even in his youth and went off somewhere to another land.
When my mother passed away due to that grief,
my father, afflicted by the pain of both sorrows, abandoned his life as a householder.
And taking me alone, he wandered here and there to search for that son,
and by the power of destiny, he reached this village.
And here in this great village there is a leader of a band of thieves,
known by the name Vasubhūti, though he is a brahmin in name only.
Therefore, having arrived here with his servants, that wicked man has taken away my father’s life-breaths and the gold contained within his body.
And having been led by him to his home, I was taken captive and intended to be given as a wife to his son named Subhūti.
And his son, having gone somewhere to plunder a caravan, has remained there;
he does not return even now—by my own merits, fate is now my only measure.
Therefore, once this thief sees you two, he will certainly cause you great harm;
devise some means by which you may both escape from him.
When she had spoken thus, Mukharaka, having recognized her at that very moment,
embraced the girl around the neck and said while weeping:
"Alas, Padmiṣṭhā! Here I am, your brother Mukharaka;
a traitor to my kin, O sister, ill-fated, I am destroyed—alas!"
Hearing that, Padmiṣṭhā too was distressed upon seeing her elder sister in such a state;
she was as if instantly enveloped by all sorrows out of compassion.
Then Śrīdarśana, having consoled both his parents and brothers who were grieving with intense distress, spoke what was appropriate for the occasion.
This is no time for grief; rather, one's own self must now be protected. Even by abandoning wealth, one must take action against this thief.
When Śrīdarśana had spoken thus, those three, suppressing their sorrow with fortitude, made a mutual agreement regarding what was to be done.
Then Śrīdarśana,
having become emaciated by his previous fasts, lay down upon the bank of that pond and feigned illness.
Grasping his feet, Mukharaka stood there weeping,
while Padmiṣṭhā quickly went to the side of that lord of thieves.
And at the edge of the pond, the fool said: "A certain traveler has arrived and is standing there;
he has a second companion who remains there as his attendant."
Upon hearing this, the thief dispatched his servants as spies;
they went there, saw those two in such a state, and observed Mukharaka among them.
They asked him, "O good man, for what reason do you weep so bitterly?
Having heard this, Mukharaka, filled with distress, spoke to those thieves: SoKss_12,6.221: "Having heard this, Mukharaka, filled with distress, spoke to those thieves."
"This elder brahmin, my friend, who was traveling abroad on a pilgrimage, has today arrived here with me, having slowly wandered about while overcome by disease."
And as soon as he had arrived, having become motionless, he said to me:
"Arise, my child; quickly prepare for me a bed of darbha grass."
"Bring some virtuous brahmin from this village;
I shall give him my entire fortune, for I shall not live through this night."
Thus addressed by him here in a foreign land, when the sun had set, I—
bewildered as to what should be done and afflicted by grief— resorted to weeping as my refuge.
"Therefore, bring some brahmin here while he is still alive,
so that he may give with his own hand whatever we possess to him."
For this [king] will surely not exist tomorrow night, and I am unable to endure that sorrow; tomorrow I shall enter the fire.
Therefore, O compassionate ones,
you who have gathered here as our unasked friends, please grant us this request.
Having heard that, the bandits were moved by compassion; they went and spoke those very words to Vasubhūti, and then addressed their master once more: SoKss_12,6.229 //
Therefore, come; take for yourself that wealth from him who offers it, having received it through the formal rite of acceptance (pratigraha) from the Brahmin who has cast it down.
Thus addressed by them, Vasubhūti said: "What kind of procedure is this?
To seize wealth without having first brought [the offender] to his knees is a supreme impropriety for us."
"One who has been robbed of his wealth should certainly make a plan to strike back even if he has not yet fallen [into ruin].
To him who had spoken thus, those wicked servants replied: ||| SoKss_12,6.232 ||| "In this matter..."
"What is this suspicion? Where is the abduction, and where is the acceptance of a gift from one about to die?
Or rather, we shall kill those two brahmins tomorrow morning, if indeed they still live."
"Otherwise, what fruit would there be from the sin of killing a Brahmin in vain?
Having heard this, Vasubhūti accepted it, saying, "So be it."
And he came at night to Śrīdarśana for the purpose of receiving alms;
Śrīdarśana, too, covering himself with his garment, gave him something here and there while breathing heavily.
Having thus made that ornament his own by swallowing the syllables of her speech,
the thief, his purpose accomplished, departed for home along with his followers.
Then, while the thieves were asleep during the night, Padmiṣṭhā approached the side of Śrīdarśana and Mukharaka.
Then all three of them, having consulted quickly,
departed from there toward Mālava once again by a path free of robbers.
Having traveled a great distance during that night,
they reached a vast forest that was perpetually bristling with thorns and filled with the eyes of wandering black antelopes.
Her slender body was withering away; she wailed with piercing cries from her tattered rags, as if trembling in fear of the roaring tigers, lions, and other wild beasts.
And as they were traveling upon it, the sun, seeing their suffering throughout the entire day,
withdrew its radiance as if out of compassion and went to its setting.
Then, exhausted and afflicted by hunger, they took refuge at the foot of a tree;
at twilight, they saw from afar what appeared to be the flame of a fire.
"Perhaps there might be a village here; having gone there, I shall look about.
Having said this, Śrīdarśana then proceeded, following the flames.
When he arrived there and looked about, he saw a house made of jewels;
he beheld its great magnitude and its radiance like a blazing flame.
Within that [palace], he saw a yakṣiṇī of divine form,
surrounded by many yakṣas whose feet were turned backward and whose eyes were squinting.
Seeing the various kinds of food and drink they had brought there,
the hero approached that yakṣiṇī and requested her portion as a guest.
And being pleased with the being, she caused him to be given food for himself and two others, as much as he desired, and water for his own satisfaction.
Having taken that [gift] and placed it upon the shoulder of a yakṣa commanded by him,
he arrived at the side of Padmiṣṭhā and her two companions.
Having dismissed the yakṣa, he partook there of that various divine food together with the two of them, and he drank cool, clear water.
Then, perceiving him to be a portion of the gods enriched by the power of his inner being,
Mukharaka, desiring to wish for his own good fortune, spoke with satisfaction:
"You, O Padmiṣṭhā, are surely some portion of a divinity, and this sister of mine is the sole beauty of the world; therefore, she is now fittingly given by me to you."
Hearing that, Śrīdarśana joyfully said to his friend:
"I welcome these words of yours, which I have long desired."
"I shall marry her after reaching my destination according to the prescribed rites"—
having spoken thus, he and those two spent that night in joy.
And having set out in the morning, they all then reached in due course that city of the lord of Mālava, King Śrīsena.
Then, having arrived exhausted, they immediately entered the house of a certain elderly brahmin woman for the sake of rest.
There, as if distressed, she was seen and questioned by them— those who had announced their own names and circumstances in the course of conversation— and the elderly woman spoke to them.
I am named Yaśasvatī, the wife of a brahmin called Satyavrata, who lives by serving the king; I am of pure lineage here.
When my husband died childless,
that compassionate king granted me one-fourth of his own livelihood for my maintenance.
And today, through my own misfortunes, this moon of kings, though he is the nourisher of the entire world, has been seized by a consumption that is incurable even for physicians.
Neither mantras nor medicinal herbs take effect upon him who knows that [truth];
however, one speaker of mantras made a vow in his presence.
"If there were some hero who could become my companion,
then by means of the accomplishment of a *vetāla*, I would destroy this disease."
Then, even though the drum had been beaten, when no such hero was found,
the king commanded his ministers as follows:
Regarding this great monastery here, which is famous for the sake of gamblers:
some brave gambler who has arrived here must be considered.
For gamblers are indeed indifferent, having abandoned wife, kinsmen, and wealth;
they are fearless, sleeping at the roots of trees and such, just like yogis.
Thus instructed by the ministers who had been commanded by the king, the head of that monastery spoke accordingly and constantly searched for a heroic newcomer.
"You are gamblers and you are capable in that business;

Then, released from the state of an elephant, you will become a gandharva;
and at that time, there will also be a benefit for that guest.
When Bharga had vanished after giving these instructions, Śīladhara,
seeing his body emaciated by long penance, cast it into the Gaṅgā.
In this interval, at the juncture of the narrative, there was a king previously mentioned by the name Ugrabhaṭa, residing in the city of Rāḍhā.
While he was dwelling happily with the queen named Manoramā,
a dancer named Lāsaka arrived at his side from another country.
And he demonstrated that dramatic performance to the king,
in which the nectar had been carried off by Hari from the Daityas who were in the form of women.
And there, on that ground of immortality, the king beheld the dancing daughter of that dancer, named Lāsyavatī.
Upon seeing her form, which had utterly agitated the Dānavas,
the king fell under the sway of desire as if he were truly immortal.
And at the conclusion of the dance, having bestowed abundant wealth upon her father,
he then led that maiden into his own inner apartments.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony with that dancer Lāsyavatī,
the king remained with her, his eyes fixed intently upon her face.
Once, he said to his domestic priest, named Yajuḥsvāmin:
"In truth, I have no son here; therefore, perform for me a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining sons."
Then, saying "So be it," that domestic priest duly performed that sacrifice for the king together with learned brahmins.
And having purified it with mantras, he caused that beautiful goddess Jyeṣṭhā—
who had previously been propitiated by her— to consume the foremost portion of the sacrificial porridge.
And he gave the remainder to that second daughter, Lāsyavatī;
and then those two, Śīladhara and Satyadhara, [were born] from them both.
The two previously mentioned [beings] were conceived in the wombs of both queens;
and when the time had arrived, the queen of that lord of the earth [gave birth].
Manoramā gave birth to a son endowed with auspicious marks;
this king named Bhīmabhaṭa was born, one of renowned fame.
At that moment, a very clear voice issued from the sky;
then, on the following day, Lāsyavatī also gave birth to a son.
And his father, the king, gave him the name Samarabhaṭa;
then, having received the sacraments, the two boys gradually grew up.
The elder, Bhīmabhaṭa, surpassed that younger brother in virtues;
and through their mutual rivalry, the enmity between them increased.
Once, during a playful wrestling match, Samarabhaṭa,
filled with jealousy, forcibly struck Bhīmabhaṭa on the neck with his arm.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, out of rage, encircled Samarabhaṭa with both arms, lifted him up,
and dashed him to the ground with a loud crash.
Struck severely by him, vomiting blood from all his orifices,
he was raised up and led into the presence of his mother by his own servants.
Having seen him and learned the news, she, distressed by affection,
placed her head upon his head and wept bitterly.
When the king had entered and seen this, his mind was agitated;
he asked, "What is this? and Lāsyavatī spoke thus:
"O King, this condition of my son was brought about by Bhīmabhaṭa;
he constantly overcomes him, yet I do not speak of it to you."
Having seen this, I know how there could possibly be well-being for you alone;
please consider this yourself regarding such a son.
Thus addressed by his beloved, King Ugrabhaṭa,
filled with rage, restrained Bhīmabhaṭa from his presence.
And having deprived him of his livelihood, he appointed a hundred princes with their retinues for the protection of that Samarabhaṭa.
He placed the treasury under the control of his younger brother,
but he completely excluded the elder brother, Bhīmabhaṭa, from every aspect of it.
Then his mother, Manoramā, called him and said to him:
"You have been abandoned by your father, who is infatuated with dancing girls."
Therefore, go to your maternal grandfather’s residence in Pāṭaliputra;
there, being childless, your maternal grandfather will give his own kingdom to you.
Hearing these words of his mother, "Lest this powerful enemy, Samarabhaṭa, slay you here," Bhīmabhaṭa said to her:
Being a Kṣatriya, I shall not abandon my own country like a coward out of fear.
Be steadfast, O Mother; what wretch would be able to oppress me?
When he had spoken thus, his mother said to him:
"In that case, secure for yourself many companions for protection by means of my wealth."
Then Bhīmabhaṭa said: "Mother, this does not befit you;
for if it were so, it would constitute an act of hostility toward my father."
"By your blessing alone may that welfare be mine; be at peace.
Having thus comforted her, Bhīmabhaṭa departed from there.
And when they learned of this there, all the citizens reflected:
"The King has committed a supreme impropriety toward Bhīmabhaṭa."
Samarabhaṭa does not dare to seize his kingdom;
therefore, this is the time for us to perform service to Bhīmabhaṭa.
Having thus decided, those citizens secretly nourished Bhīmabhaṭa with wealth in such a way that he remained there in comfort together with his servants.
But his youngest son was intent on nothing but his father’s execution, having inferred that intention from the preparations for the funeral attire.
At that moment, a brave and wealthy young brahmin named Śaṅkhadatta,
a friend of the two [princes], approached Samarabhaṭa and said to him:
"Hostility toward a brother is not fitting for you; this is not dharma, nor is it possible for you to oppress one who is your elder. It would only result in supreme infamy for you."
Speaking thus and reproaching him, he was reviled by him;
for wholesome advice leads only to anger in a fool, not to peace.
Then, out of anger at that, the resolute Śaṅkhadatta went forth with the desire to conquer him and formed a friendship with Bhīmabhaṭa.
Then, a certain merchant named Maṇidatta, who had arrived from another land,
brought a single, most excellent jewel among horses.
White as the moon, with a sound as pleasant to hear as that of a pure conch,
it rose up like a mass of towering waves from the ocean of milk.
It was adorned with glittering crest-jewels, armlets, and other ornaments,
appearing as if perfected by those born from the lineage of the Gandharvas.
After Śaṅkhadatta had described it, Bhīmabhaṭa went there and purchased that excellent horse from that preeminent merchant for a great amount of wealth.
At that very moment, Samarabhaṭa, having learned of this,
arrived there and sought that horse from the merchant for double its price.
When the merchant did not give him that horse which had been made dependent upon him,
he then proceeded out of envy to take the horse away by force.
Then, as the servants of both those princes rushed forward with weapons in hand, a fierce battle broke out there.
There, his followers having been struck down by the fierce staff-like arms of Bhīmabhaṭa,
Samarabhaṭa abandoned his horse and fled out of fear of him.
And as he was being broken, Śaṅkhadatta, overwhelmed by a weight of fury, ran up, seized him by the hair from behind, and struck him down.
Just then, Bhīmabhaṭa approached from behind and restrained him, saying, "Let it be;
otherwise, my father will surely suffer grief at this moment."
Then, released by Śaṅkhadatta and vomiting blood from his wounds,
the terrified Samarabhaṭa fled and went to the side of his father.
Then, a certain Brahmin approached the hero Bhīmabhaṭa, who had accepted the horse there, and leading him to a secluded place, spoke to him in an instant.
Your mother, Queen Manoramā; the domestic priest Yajusvāmin;
and your father’s minister Sumati now speak these words to you.
"You know, my child, what kind of man the king is toward you;
now that this event has occurred, he has indeed become your enemy."
If you wish to protect yourself, the Dharma, and your reputation;
if you have regard for the future; and if you consider us to be well-wishers.
Therefore, before the sun sets from here, depart unobserved;
go now to your maternal grandfather’s house for the sake of attaining success.
"Having thus sent this message, they have dispatched this casket filled with fine jewels and gold; please accept it through my hands."
Having heard this from the brahmin and having welcomed it with "So be it," the wise Bhīmabhaṭa took that vessel made of excellent gold and precious gems.
Having given him a fitting reply and dismissed that twice-born man,
he, sword in hand, mounted his horse.
Then, accompanied by Śaṅkhadatta— who had taken up gold and jewels and was mounted on a second horse— he set out from there.
Having traveled a long distance, at midnight that prince Bhīmabhaṭa reached a great forest of reeds in the middle of his path.
There, as he proceeded incessantly with his companions,
[the army] was awakened by the sound of arrows crushed by the hooves of the galloping horses.
Rising up with her two lion cubs who were roaring loudly,
she tore at the horses' bellies from below with her claws.
And at that very moment, that heroic lion, together with his companion, rendered all of them lifeless,
their limbs severed by blows from his sword.
Then Samitra also dismounted and looked; at that moment, both horses fell to the ground with their entrails spilled out.
Seeing that, he became despondent and said to Śaṅkhadatta:
"Friend, we have fled with great effort from our own kinsmen who were hostile toward us."
Tell me, even with a hundred efforts, where can we flee from Fate,
by whom we have been struck down here today, though he is incapable of enduring even the mere sound of our horses?
Even that horse for whose sake the abandonment of our country was undertaken has died;
therefore, how can we traverse this forest on foot in the night?
Thus addressed by him, his friend Śaṅkhadatta said to him:
"It is no new thing that adverse fate should triumph over human effort."
Such is his very nature; however, it is overcome by fortitude.
What could that wind do to a steadfast man who remains unshaken, any more than it could affect a mountain?
Then Bhīmabhaṭa set out from there together with Śaṅkhadatta, who said, "Come, let us go there, mounted upon horses of great courage."
Then, as he gradually traversed that wilderness with his feet lacerated by arrows, the night passed away.
Then, when the sun— the lamp of the world that dispels the darkness of night— had risen,
the lotuses of the path-lakes resounded with the sweet humming of bees.
"By good fortune, he has crossed this forest teeming with lions and other beasts,
while they look at him one after another with wide-open mouths as if they were speaking."
Proceeding by degrees, he reached the sandy bank of the daughter of Jahnu, which was strewn with the huts of ascetics, accompanied by his companions.
There, having bathed in those sweet and cool waters, which were as if infused with the nectar of the moon resting upon Śiva’s head, he found rest.
He sustained his body by means of the flesh of deer— some purchased from hunters encountered on the road, some roasted, and others brought by Śaṅkhadatta.
And seeing the full river of Jahnu’s daughter impossible to cross, which seemed to ward him off repeatedly with its uplifted hands of waves; so too— SoKss_12,7.113.
Then, having gone along its bank, he saw the son of a Brahmin,
absorbed in his private Vedic recitation, standing in the courtyard of a two-storied hut.
Having approached him, he asked, "Who are you, and what are you doing here all alone in this desolate place? Thereupon, he replied to him:
I am a resident of Vārāṇasī, the son of a twice-born man named Śrīkaṇṭha; my name is Nīlakaṇṭha, and my father performed for me the entire sequence of purificatory rites.
Having thus completed my studies at the teacher’s house, as I was returning to my own home in my youth,
all my kinsmen had perished.
Therefore, protectorless and destitute of wealth, ill-situated due to the failure of my household life, I became despondent; having come here, I have resorted to severe austerity.
Then, in a dream, the goddess Gaṅgā said to him after giving him fruits:
"Eat these and remain here until you obtain what you desire."
Having heard this, I woke up immediately; then, having gone and bathed at the end of the night, I obtained fruits that had arrived within the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having brought those things, which were as delicious as nectar, I ate them in my hut;
thus, remaining here, I continued to eat them as they arrived day after day.
When he had spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa said to Śaṅkhadatta:
"I shall give this virtuous man wealth sufficient for the life of a householder."
Having heard that and having placed his word in trust, the prince then gave that wealth, which had been bestowed upon him by his mother, to that brahmin.
For what indeed is the greatness of the great, whose treasury of being is never depleted,
if they do not instantly sever the suffering of another upon hearing of it?
Having thus fulfilled the purpose of that brahmin, he then went everywhere, searching for a means to cross the Gaṅgā; but when he did not find one, he [continued his search].
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, with his sword fastened to his head,
descended into it with Śaṅkhadatta to cross it by means of his two arms.
And in the middle of the stream, having distanced his companions by the force of the water,
he somehow reached the far shore while being carried away by the waves.
As he searched along the shore for his friend Śaṅkhadatta, who had reached the far bank but was nowhere to be seen, the sun set.
Then, despairing and crying out "Alas, my friend!
in extreme distress, he prepared to throw himself into the Ganges at the onset of night.
"O Goddess Jāhnavī, my life has been carried away by you along with me;
therefore, take now even this body of mine, which is empty of it."
Having said this, just as he desired to throw himself therein,
at that moment Gaṅgā herself appeared visibly from the midst of its waters.
At that moment, she, delighted by his intense agitation, said to him:
"O son, do not act rashly; he remains alive as your friend."
"Before long, you shall be reunited with him;
meanwhile, receive from me this vidyā known as *pratilomānulomā*."
A person reciting this [mantra] in the forward order (anuloma) becomes invisible to others;
reciting it in the reverse order (pratiloma), one may effect the manifestation of any desired form.
This is the power of this vidyā, which is adorned with seven syllables;
by its power, you shall become the king upon this earth.
Having said this and bestowed the vidyā upon him, the Jāhnavī vanished;
he too, having conceived hope for the recovery of his friend and so forth, desisted from death.
Eager to find his friend, Bhīmabhaṭa spent the night with difficulty like a lotus; then, in the morning, he set out from there, searching for him.
Then, wandering about in search of Śaṅkhadatta,
he eventually reached the region of Lāṭa all alone.
Where even the people, though of unmixed castes, abide in a state of variegated brilliance;
and which, though the abode of the arts, does not bear the name of the "mine of faults" (the moon).
There, wandering through the inner city and observing the dwellings of the temples,
he reached a hall belonging to gamblers.
Having entered there, he saw gamblers playing with dice,
who, though clad in nothing but rags around their loins, were nonetheless elegant.
With limbs that were well-proportioned and full, indicating the exercise of luxury,
he proclaimed his hidden sovereignty, which was currently supported by the pursuit of wealth.
Having conversed with them, he began a game of dice with those who had formed the intent:
"This man, along with his ornaments, is our prey."
Then, having defeated them at dice, he seized all their wealth—
that which those rogues had previously acquired by deceiving others.
When the gamblers, having lost their wealth, were preparing to go to their own homes,
Bhīmabhaṭa blocked them by placing his arms across the doorway and said to them:
"Where are you going? Take this wealth; what use have I for it? This must be given by me to those who are dear to me, and are you not dear to me? (SoKss 12.7.146)
"Where could I find dear friends such as yourselves?"—
even as he was saying this, they did not accept [his offer] out of modesty.
There, a certain gambler named Akṣakṣapaṇaka said:
"This is the convention of gambling—that what has been lost need not be paid back."
Nevertheless, if he, having become our friend,
should offer us wealth even though it has been won by his own desire, why should we not accept it?
Having heard that, others said: "If he establishes such an eternal friendship with us, then this will be appropriate."
When they had spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa, considering them to be heroes, agreed with them saying "So be it," and he formed a friendship with them and gave them that wealth.
Requested by them, he went with them and their families to a garden and spent his time enjoying the food, drink, and other provisions they had brought.
Then, questioned by Akṣakṣapaṇaka and the others, he told them his own account of his lineage and name, and likewise questioned them in turn.
Then Akṣakṣapaṇa related his own story to him:
"There was a Brahmin named Śivadatta in Hastināpura."
I am the son of that wealthy man named Vasudatta;
in my youth, I was trained in the science of weapons as well as the sciences of the Vedas.
Then my father arranged my marriage with a family of equal status;
however, my mother was extremely fierce, difficult to propitiate, and exceedingly wrathful.
Though agitated by her, my father, upon seeing that I was accompanied by a wife, abandoned his own home and went away somewhere unexpectedly.
