Seeing that, I was filled with fear and diligently enjoined my wife to win over my mother’s heart; she too, being afraid, did as I requested.
But her mother, intent on quarreling, was not satisfied with her in any way; she met her with silence, contempt, piteous talk, and deceit. (SoK 12.7.159)
Considering it to be a matter of conviction and dispute, those of evil intent [ask]:
"For who is able to cause fire to relinquish its own nature of burning? (SoKss 12.7.160)
Then, due to those hostile actions of hers, my wife soon became distressed; she departed from the house, and I know not where she has gone.
Then, though agitated and intent on abandoning my home,
I was forcibly made to undergo another marriage by my wicked kinsmen who had gathered together.
My wife as well, tormented by her in that manner out of fear,
hanged herself with a noose and brought about her own death.
Then, utterly despondent, I prepared to go to a foreign land;
to my relatives who sought to restrain me, I described the wickedness of my mother.
Regarding my father’s exile and other such matters, for those who assert various alternative causes,
that conviction which they lacked was [established] through reasoning by means of the wooden doll.
Having had her prepared for me in private, she was then married to me by a ruse;
having been brought back, she was placed within the inner house, which was secured with a bolt from another side.
A single female guard was appointed for her, appearing like a servant;
I have established this new wife in a separate house.
"You and I shall now remain right here in our own separate homes;
you must not go there, nor must she come here."
"That immature girl does not yet know how to propitiate you," I said to my mother, and she agreed with that as well.
Then, as the days passed, she was unable by any means whatsoever to reach that deceitful daughter-in-law, who remained inside the inner house behind a bolted door.
Then, having struck her own head with a stone on one occasion,
the mother, smeared with blood, cried out loudly in the courtyard of her own house.
Having heard the cry and entered, I and all my kinsmen saw her;
when asked, "Tell us, what is this?", she replied with indignation.
"Such a state has been brought upon me by my daughter-in-law through no fault of my own;
therefore, now my only atonement is death."
Upon hearing that, her kinsmen became enraged;
taking her with them, they came along with me to the place where that wooden doll was.
Having removed the bolt and opened the door, just as they were about to enter,
they saw there nothing but a woman made of wood.
Then, laughing at their own mockery and at their embarrassed mother,
those kinsmen, having gained confidence, departed as they had come.
Having abandoned that country, I wandered about and reached this region;
here, by chance, I entered a gambling hall.
There I saw these people gambling with five dice:
this one called Caṇḍabhujaṅga and this one Pāṃsupaṭa. (SoK 12.7.178)
This vetāla from the cremation ground, this kālavarāṭaka,
and this pile of bones— these heroes are equal in prowess.
And there I played at dice with them,
having mutually bound a wager that the loser should become the slave of the victor.
"Then, defeated at dice, they entered my service;
but I, conquered by their virtues, have myself come into their service."
Living together with these, I have forgotten my own suffering;
know me here as Akṣakṣapaṇa, a name appropriate to my condition.
Thus, having been born into noble families and having concealed our identities right here, we have remained together with these meritorious ones; and today you have met us here.
Therefore, you are now our master, even before this;
for we, who are devoted to virtue, have already taken that wealth as yours by our own understanding.
When Akṣakṣapaṇaka had thus related his own story in due order,
all the others, including Bhīmabhaṭa, likewise described their own adventures.
Then, concealing herself with various arts acquired for the sake of wealth, she regarded those heroic men as her friends and engaged in various other conversations.
Having spent the day in the monastery, he beheld the eastern quarter,
its face adorned with the shining ornament of the cool-rayed moon.
Then that prince Bhīmabhaṭa departed from that garden together with those six companions, Akṣakṣapaṇaka and the others, for their dwelling place.
As he remained there together with them, the rainy season arrived,
as if announcing his reunion with a friend through the thundering of the pouring clouds.
And then, there the river named Vipāśā, which flows toward the ocean,
became filled by the flood of the sea and began to flow upstream.
Having filled the sandy bank with a great flood of water,
she proceeded toward the ocean as if the torrent had been stilled.
At that time, having been brought there and cast in by the surging waters,
the great fish, due to its heavy weight, became stranded on the riverbank.
And having seen him, the people there ran forward with various weapons to kill him,
and tore open the belly of that fish.
And from that split [body], a young brahmin emerged alive;
at the sight of that marvel, the people there raised a great clamor.
Having heard that, Bhīmabhaṭa went there with those friends and saw his friend Śaṅkhadatta emerging from the fish.
And running toward him, he embraced him, drenching him with streams of tears as if washing away the stench of dwelling within the cave of a fish's belly.
Having crossed over that calamity and reached him,
Śaṅkhadatta embraced his friend and then went from one festival to another.
Then, questioned there out of curiosity by that Bhīmabhaṭa,
Śaṅkhadatta related his own adventures briefly as follows:
Then, carried away by the force of the Ganges' waves beyond the range of your sight,
I was unexpectedly swallowed by an exceedingly large fish.
Having entered that great chamber of his belly, I remained there for a long time,
eating his flesh, which was cut away by the knife, out of hunger.
"Today this very fish was somehow brought here and cast up by the Creator; it has been killed by these people, and I have been pulled out from its belly."
"I have seen you and the sun, and the directions have become bright to me.
This, my friend, is my account; I know nothing beyond this."
Having been addressed thus by Śaṅkhadatta, Bhīmabhaṭa and all those present there spoke as follows out of sheer amazement:
Where is the swallowing by a fish in the Gaṅgā, and where is its movement in the ocean?
And where, along that same path, is its settling in the Vipāśā?
Where was his slaughter, and where was his escape while still alive?
Oh, how inconceivable is the course of Fate, whose deeds are so wondrous!
Speaking thus with them, including the Akṣakṣapaṇaka and others,
Bhīmabhaṭa led Śaṅkhadatta to his own abode.
And there, with great celebration, he attended upon him with baths, garments, and other offerings—
[the king] who appeared as if born once again from the belly of a fish in that very same body.
Then, while Bhīmabhaṭa remained in that region with him,
the festival procession of Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, arrived there.
To see him, the prince, surrounded by his friends, set out for the abode of that preeminent elephant,
where a great multitude of people had gathered.
There, having bowed down before that image in the temple— which was filled with garlands resembling hosts of serpents and which resembled a pool of stagnant water— he worshipped.
Having gone to the south, he saw his great lake,
filled with red lotuses that seemed like masses of light from the jewels on [the serpent's] hoods.
It was filled with blue lotuses as if with masses of poisonous smoke,
and surrounded by trees that seemed to be offering worship with flowers falling in the wind.
To me, this small ocean appears like a mere puddle before him who possesses a splendor that cannot be taken away by another; it has been robbed of its glory by Śauri.
Thus, while he was filled with wonder and reflecting upon what he had seen,
he beheld a maiden who had come there for the purpose of bathing.
There, the auspicious Haṃsāvalī by name was born as the daughter of King Candrāditya, the Lord of Lāṭa, from his wife Kuvalayāvalī.
Although her mortal nature was concealed by other limbs that imitated those of a divine being, it was revealed by her flickering eye through its blinking.
With the tips of her body as delicate as flowers, and with shimmering virtues reaching to them,
she was like the bow-staff of the God of Love, whose middle can be grasped by a single fist.
Merely by looking with sidelong glances from her eyes like arrows,
she then bewildered Bhīmabhaṭa, piercing him to the heart.
Having entered her very eyes, that thief of the world's beauty stole away her heart’s steadfastness by his sidelong glances.
Then, through the mouth of a trusted maidservant sent secretly,
she inquired from her friends regarding his name, residence, and other details.
Then she went to her own palace, being led by her attendants;
having bathed, she turned her face away, looking back again and again with eyes fixed upon him.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa also returned to his own dwelling with his friends,
his gait faltering due to being bound by the noose of love for his beloved.
Thereupon, at that very moment, the princess Haṃsāvalī dispatched that maidservant as a messenger to him, having given her the desired message.
Approaching him in private, the maidservant said to Bhīmabhaṭa:
"O Lord, the princess Haṃsāvalī entreats you."
Seeing a person you love being carried away by the flood of passion,
it is not fitting for you to remain indifferent and stand on the sidelines, disregarding this one who is fleeing.
Having thus obtained from the messenger the nectar of his beloved’s words,
Bhīmabhaṭa, thrilled at having regained his life, then said to her:
"My beloved does not know that I am standing in the flood and not on the bank;
yet, having found a support, I shall certainly do as she says."
"Having arrived, I shall honor her tonight within the inner apartments;
and as I enter, concealed by my magic power, no one at all shall see me."
Having been addressed thus by him, the maidservant was delighted; she went and reported it to Haṃsāvalī, who then remained with her mind intent upon union with him.
At the time of dusk, he too, adorned with divine ornaments,
[performed] by reciting in the direct order the vidyā that had been crossed over the Gaṅgā.
Having become invisible and gone there, Bhīmabhaṭa entered her excellent inner apartments, which she had previously cleared for him.
There, in that place which brings delight and joy, fragrant with black aloe-wood, and beautified by heaps of flowers arranged in five colors; SoKss_12,7.232.
In that place resembling a pleasure garden of the gods, he beheld his beloved, who possessed a divine fragrance and appeared like the blossoming vine of the true knowledge of the Ganges.
Having recited that spell in reverse order,
he suddenly became attractive in the eyes of that princess.
Upon seeing him, she was instantly filled with joy, her hair standing on end, and trembling with awe; amidst the sounding music of her own ornaments, she seemed to dance at that very moment.
And with her face bowed in the modesty of maidenhood,
she asked, as it were, what was to be done, her heart intent upon news of him.
O charming one, why does your heart now conceal that very object which has already been revealed, even though you hide it out of shame? How indeed can this [object] be hidden?
With such words as, "There is a thrill in your limbs," and "Why is this bodice bursting at the seams? and with other expressions of affection, he addressed her.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having made the fair-faced Haṃsāvalī cast off her shame,
made her his wife according to the Gāndharva rite of marriage.
Having spent the night with her, delighting in the play of her lotus-like face, he took his leave,
saying, "I shall come back tonight," and went to his own abode with great difficulty.
And in the morning, his high officials, having entered the inner apartments, saw that Haṃsāvalī there, possessed of the marks of sexual enjoyment.
Her hair and locks were disheveled, and she bore fresh wounds from teeth and nails;
she appeared as if truly overwhelmed by the multitude of scars left by the arrows of the God of Love himself.
Having gone, the spies reported that very matter to his father, the king;
he too stationed secret agents there to observe during the night.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having spent the day happily with his friends,
returned again at nightfall to the inner apartments of his beloved.
Seeing that he had entered there unobserved through the power of his magic science, and considering him to be a perfected master (*siddha*), those spies departed from that place.
Having gone, they told it to the king, and he likewise commanded them:
"He who has entered here, though well-guarded, and yet remains invisible, is not a human being."
"Bring him here at once so that I may see what this is;
and you yourselves, speak to him in my name with gentle words."
Why was my daughter not openly requested from me by you?
What secret was kept? For where could there be a bridegroom with virtues such as yours?
Having been told this and dispatched by the king, those spies went and,
while still standing at the gate, reported those words to Bhīmabhaṭa exactly as they were.
Realizing, "I too am known by the king," the very resolute prince, though remaining within, addressed them forcefully.
"In my name, say to the king when you attend his court in the morning:
'I shall inform him of the truth; for at present, the night is indeed blind.'"
Having heard that, when they had departed and spoken thus, the king became silent;
then in the morning, Bhīmabhaṭa set out from there toward his friends.
And together with those seven heroes, having assumed a magnificent appearance, he went to the assembly hall of that king, Candrāditya.
When Bhīmabhaṭa, who had observed his splendor, heroism, and beauty, had honored him and was seated upon a seat appropriate for himself, the twice-born man—
His friend Śaṅkhadatta addressed that king:
"O King, this is the son of King Ugrabhaṭa, the lord of Rāḍhā."
Due to the greatness of his inconceivable knowledge, his prowess is difficult to overcome;
he is Bhīmabhaṭa by name, and he has come here for the sake of your daughter.
Having heard that account of the night's events and recognizing him as worthy, the king said, "Ah, we are indeed fortunate! and then placed his full trust in him.
Then, having arranged the elaborate ceremonies for the wedding,
he gave his daughter Haṃsāvalī to Bhīmabhaṭa with the utmost magnificence.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, having acquired many elephants, horses, and villages,
dwelt there in contentment together with Haṃsāvalī and Lakṣmī.
And after several days, his father-in-law, the aged Candrāditya, having entrusted that kingdom of Lāṭa to him, went forth as a wandering mendicant to the forest since he was childless.
Then the successful Bhīmabhaṭa, having obtained that kingdom,
ruled it together with those seven heroes, Śaṅkhadatta and the others.
Then, as the days passed, he one day heard from his spies that his father, King Ugrabhaṭa, had come to Prayāga and died.
And by him, as he was about to die, his own youngest son, Samarabhaṭa, the son of a dancer, was consecrated in the kingdom of Rāḍhā.
Then, having lamented for his father and performed the funeral rites for him,
the king dispatched a messenger to Samarabhaṭa.
"O fool, son of a dancer, what fitness do you have for my father's throne?
For that [throne] belongs to me alone, even though this kingdom of Lāṭa exists here."
Therefore, he sent a letter to that harmful kinsman, instructing him: "You must not ascend that [palace]."
And that messenger, having gone quickly, delivered the letter to him; having announced himself, he presented it to Samarabhaṭa, who was present in the assembly hall.
Having read that very inscription bearing the name Bhīmabhaṭa,
Samarabhaṭa became enraged and spoke as follows.
"This untrained man, who was formerly banished from the country by his father as being unworthy— this false pride is indeed fitting for him."
Even a jackal acts like a lion when staying within the shelter of its own cave;
yet, once it has come into the sight of a lion, it is known for what it truly is.
Having roared thus and sent that very message by means of a letter,
he too dispatched his own counter-ambassador to Bhīmabhaṭa.
The messenger, having also gone there, was announced by the chamberlain and delivered that letter to Bhīmabhaṭa, the lord of the Lāṭa country.
Then, when that letter had been read there, Bhīmabhaṭa let out a loud, mocking laugh and addressed the messenger who had come from his kinsman.
"Go, O messenger! Speak these words of mine to that son of a dancing girl:
'At the time of seizing the horse, you were protected by me from Śaṅkhadatta.'"
"You are a child and dear to your father; I shall forgive you no more and no more. I will certainly send you into the presence of your affectionate father."
"Be ready; know that I have arrived here in just a few days.
Having spoken thus and dispatched that messenger, Bhīmabhaṭa prepared for his expedition.
When that lord of kings, resplendent like the rising sun, had mounted his elephant-mountain,
the great ocean of the army surged forward with a tumultuous roar.
And it was filled with countless neighboring princes who had arrived in great numbers, setting out from all directions with their armies.
Trembling and convulsing, filled with the great speed of falling elephants and horses,
the earth cried out as if in terror from being split asunder.
Thus Bhīmabhaṭa went and reached the vicinity of Rāḍhā,
making the sky such that the splendor of the sun was stolen away by the mass of dust from his army.
And at that moment, King Samarabhaṭa, having learned of this and being unable to endure it,
armed himself and went forth at the head of his army to fight him.
And those two oceans of armies, the eastern and the western, met together;
and a great dissolution of heroes in battle commenced.
There, the fire born from the clashing of swords accompanied by sound enveloped the sky,
as if it were the fire arising from the gnawing of the teeth of the enraged God of Death.
And iron arrows flew forth, with sharp points and long feathers,
possessing the grace of the glances cast by the women of heaven as they gazed upon the heroes.
Then that stage of the battlefield, with its canopy of dust, resounding with the noise of the army and musical instruments, and featuring dancing headless trunks, shone forth brilliantly.
And here, the river of blood, carrying skeletons and garlands of severed heads,
flowed like the Night of Doom (Kālarātrī), intoxicated as it swept away the circle of living beings.
And in an instant, by Śaṅkhadatta, by that Akṣakṣapaṇaka,
and by Caṇḍabhujaṃga and the others, who were experts in hand-to-hand combat, [he was subdued].
Like a rutting elephant among powerful and heroic warriors,
that bow-wielder Bhīmabhaṭa shattered that enemy army.
When the army was broken, Samarabhaṭa, standing upon his chariot,
then rushed forward in a rage and began to act like Mount Mandara in the ocean of battle.
Then Bhīmabhaṭa, mounted upon his elephant, charged at him,
cut his bow asunder, and with arrows slew all four horses in the chariot.
Then, even though deprived of his chariot, that warrior Samarabhaṭa rushed forward and struck Bhīmabhaṭa’s excellent elephant on the forehead with a lance.
And that elephant, struck by the *tomara* spear, fell to the earth;
thereupon, both of them became foot-soldiers, deprived of their chariots.
Then those two kings, seizing shields and swords, fought as foot soldiers in a duel of fury.
Although Bhīmabhaṭa was capable of killing that enemy by making himself invisible through the power of a spell, out of regard for righteousness, he did not slay him in that manner.
But he, skilled in sword-fighting, violently attacking him, severed the head of the dancer’s son with his sword.
And when that warrior Samarabhaṭa, together with his army, had been completely slain, and cries of "Well done!
were uttered from the sky by the *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, [the king] remained there.
When the battle had come to an end, Bhīmabhaṭa— praised by bards and panegyrists—
entered the city of Rāḍhā together with his friends.
Having returned from his long exile with his enemies slain, he delighted his mother there—
she who had been longing for his sight— just as Rāma did for Kauśalyā.
Then, welcomed by the citizens, the virtuous prince sat upon his father’s lion-throne, being honored by his ministers who were fond of his virtues.
Having honored all his subjects and celebrated a festival,
he bestowed the kingdom of Lāṭa upon Śaṅkhadatta on an auspicious day.
Having dispatched him to the Lāṭa region accompanied by troops from that country,
he granted villages and wealth to those [monks], such as Akṣakṣapaṇaka and others.
Then, joined by them, he remained there governing his ancestral domain together with that queen Haṃsāvalī, the daughter of the lord of Lāṭa.
And having gradually conquered the earth and brought back the daughters of kings,
King Bhīmabhaṭa then became solely intent on enjoying their company.
Having entrusted the burden [of government] to his ministers, he sported with the women of the inner apartments;
due to his addiction to drinking and other vices, he did not emerge from the interior.
Then once, the sage Uttaṅka came by chance to see him,
as if at the very time for the ripening of the former command of Śarva.
When this Sage reached the gate and the doorkeepers announced his arrival,
the king— blinded by the intoxication of passion and the pride of sovereignty— did not, it is said, even hear him.
Then, enraged, that sage pronounced this curse upon the king:
"O you who are blinded by pride, fallen from your kingdom, you shall become a wild elephant."
Having heard that, the king, his pride shattered by fear,
went out and propitiated the sage with piteous words, bowing at his feet.
Then, his anger having subsided, that great seer spoke to him:
"O King, you shall indeed become an elephant; it cannot be otherwise."
However, the minister of Mṛgāṅkadatta named Pracaṇḍaśakti, who had been struck down by a serpent's curse, had fallen into blindness.
When you have comforted him who has become your guest and shall relate your own history to him, then you will obtain release from this curse.
And you shall attain that state of a Gandharva previously ordained by Giriśa;
and then that guest of yours shall indeed become possessed of sight.
Having spoken thus, the sage Uttaṅka departed as he had come;
and that elephant Bhīmabhaṭa was restored to life, though deprived of his kingdom.
"Know me, my friend, to be that very Bhīmabhaṭa who has become an elephant;
and you are Pracaṇḍaśakti. I know that this is the end of my curse."
Having spoken thus, Bhīmabhaṭa abandoned his elephant form and at that very moment became a Gandharva of divine splendor.
And Pracaṇḍaśakti, for whom the sight of the arisen [deity] was a festival for his eyes,
at that very moment became aware of seeing that Gandharva there.
Meanwhile, staying within the thicket of creepers, he heard their conversation;
accompanied by his other ministers, he formed a very firm resolve.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, knowing the right moment, rushed forward with impetuous speed and seized his own minister Pracaṇḍaśakti by the throat.
Seeing him, as if his limbs were sprinkled by a rain of nectar from a cloudless sky,
Pracaṇḍaśakti suddenly seized the Lord by the feet.
Then that Gandharva Bhīmabhaṭa consoled those two, who were weeping and deeply distressed after being separated for so long and now reunited.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, bowing before that Gandharva, said: "That this friend was obtained by us, and furthermore, that he has been obtained by him..."
"Having attained sight through your majesty, salutations be to you!
Having heard this, that Gandharva also spoke to the prince.
Before long, having recovered all your remaining ministers,
you shall obtain that wife Śaśāṅkavatī and sovereignty over the entire earth.
"Therefore, you should not act with such lack of composure, O auspicious one; I shall accomplish that for you, and I will remain close to you whenever you remember me."

Thus, freed from the curse and filled with the joy of attained auspiciousness, he revealed his true nature as a friend; having spoken to that prince, he—the peerless leader of the Gandharvas—suddenly flew up into the sky, making the quarters of the world resonant with the tinkling of his beautiful armlets and necklaces.
Having obtained Pracaṇḍaśakti in that forest, Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by his ministers, spent that day there with his weariness dispelled.
Thus ends the seventh wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The eighth wave: The twenty-fifth [chapter].
Victory belongs to him, the Conqueror of Obstacles, from whose dancing a shower of stars falls like rain from the sky, dislodged by the blow of Tārāvalī’s hand.
Then, having passed that night, at dawn he set out from that forest together with his ministers, headed by Pracaṇḍaśakti.
For the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, Mṛgāṅkadatta set out once more toward Ujjayinī, searching for his remaining ministers.
As he was going along, he saw on the road the minister Vikramakesarin being carried through the sky by an extremely hideous man.
And while he was being shown to the other ministers with such haste,
that minister descended from the sky into his presence.
And quickly descending from the shoulder of that man,
he approached Mṛgāṅkadatta and, with eyes full of tears, grasped his feet.
Embraced by him in his joy, and likewise by his ministers in turn, he dismissed that man with the words:
"When you are remembered, you shall come to me."
Then, having sat down out of curiosity, Vikramakeśarin was questioned by Mṛgāṅkadatta and related his own adventures in the forest.
Then, fallen from you due to the curse of the Naga and wandering about,
I thought of you for many days while searching for you.
"I shall go to Ujjayinī, for they must certainly have gone there. Having thus resolved, I set out toward that city.
Gradually reaching the village named Brahmasthala in its vicinity,
I sat down at the foot of a tree on the bank of a pond.
Having come there, an old Brahmin afflicted by a snakebite said to me:
"Rise up from here, my son; you shall attain my state."
"For here there is a great serpent, by whom, when bitten and afflicted with pain,
I am about to cast off this body into this great pond."
Having thus spoken, I compassionately dissuaded him from abandoning his body;
there, O Brahmin, I rendered him free from poison by means of the science of poisons.

Then that brahmin, having respectfully asked me for the entire account with its underlying motive, spoke thus, being pleased and having understood the matter: SoKss_12.8.15: "Then that brahmin, having respectfully asked me for the entire account with its underlying motive, spoke thus, being pleased and having understood the matter."
"O hero, you have given me back my life;
therefore, accept from me this mantra for mastering the vetāla, which I obtained from my father."
This [path], which brings about accomplishment, is suitable for those like you who are endowed with courage;
but as for these people like me, what indeed can they do, being as they are cowards?
Having been addressed thus by him, I replied to that best of the twice-born:
"Separated from Mṛgāṅkadatta, what can I do with these Vetālas?"
Having heard that, the Brahmin laughed and spoke to me again:
"Do you not know that everything desired can be obtained from a vetāla?"
Moreover, by the grace of the Vetāla, what sovereignty over the Vidyādharas was not previously attained by King Trivikramasena?
And so I shall tell you this story of his; listen. There is a region named Pratiṣṭhāna on the banks of the Godāvarī.
There, the son of Vikramasena was a king named Trivikramasena, whose prowess was like that of Śakra and whose fame was renowned. SoKss_12,8.22 (Vet_0.2) //
Every day, as that king sat in his assembly hall,
a monk named Kṣāntiśīla would approach him for the sake of service and present him with fruit.
The king, having taken that fruit,
gave it every day into the hand of the treasurer who was standing nearby.
When ten years had passed in this manner, it is said that once,
after giving the fruit to the king, the mendicant departed from the assembly hall.
That king gave that fruit to a young pet monkey, which had escaped from the hands of its keepers and entered there by chance.
The monkey ate as much of it as he could;
then, from the center of that split fruit, there emerged an unsurpassed, priceless jewel.
Seeing that, the king took it and asked the treasurer:
"Those fruits which were always brought for me by the monk—"
"Where have those things given into your hand always been kept by you?
Hearing that, the terrified treasurer replied to him:
"I did not open those [letters] which were cast by me from the window into the treasury;
if you command it, O Lord, then I shall open them and search for [the truth]."
Having spoken thus and received permission from the king, the treasurer departed; returning in a moment, he addressed his lord once more.
"I do not see those fruits here in the treasury, O Lord;
instead, I see a heap of jewels ablaze with rays of light."
Having heard that and being pleased with the treasurer for giving those jewels,
the king questioned that monk— who had arrived as before— the following day.
"O monk, why do you serve me thus every day at such expense?
I will not accept your fruit now until you speak."
To the king who had spoken thus, the monk said in private:
"I have a means for accomplishing a mantra that requires the assistance of a hero."
"In this matter, O Lord of Heroes, I request that you provide assistance.
Having heard that, the king agreed to it, saying, "So be it."
Then that ascetic, being pleased, spoke again to the king:
"In that case, on the arrival of night on the coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
"O Lord, you must come from here to my presence, as I wait beneath the banyan tree within this great cremation ground."
When the king replied, "Very well, I shall do so," that ascetic Kṣāntiśīla went to his own dwelling, filled with joy.
Then, having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that Great Being,
remembering the request made by that monk, [acted accordingly].
At twilight, dressed in blue garments and with a crest of *tāla* leaves,
he went forth from the capital at night, sword in hand and unobserved.
And he went [to a place] blackened by a mass of terrible, dense darkness,
its appearance made fearsome by the flames from the fierce eyes of the funeral pyre’s fire.
It was crowded with the skeletons, skulls, and bones of innumerable dead men,
and surrounded by nearby, leaping, and terrifying spirits and vetālas.
Like another form of Bhairava, deep and terrifying, that cremation ground resounded with the howling of great jackals; yet he remained undaunted.
Having searched for him there and found the monk beneath a banyan tree performing the ritual layout of a mandala, he approached and spoke to him.
"Here I am come, O monk; tell me, what shall I do for you?
Having heard that and seeing the king, the monk spoke to him with joy: SoKss_12,8.46 (Vet_0.26)
"O King, if you are so gracious, then go alone from here toward the south; after traveling a long distance, there stands a śiṃśapā tree."
"In that place stands a certain man, dead and hanging;
go there, O hero, bring him here, and provide me with protection."
Having heard that, the king, true to his promise, said "So be it," and then that great hero set out from there, taking the southern direction as his course.
Having traveled along a path marked by blazing funeral pyres through that darkness,
he somehow reached that śiṃśapā tree.
He saw him hanging from the shoulder of that tree— smelling of raw flesh and scorched by the smoke of the funeral pyre— like the corpse of a spirit.
Having climbed up there onto that ground, he let go of the severed rope;
and having fallen there, he suddenly cried out in agony as if in pain.
Then, having descended out of compassion and fearing for his life, he touched that limb of the king; because of that, the corpse let out a loud laugh.
Then that king, perceiving him to be possessed by a vetāla, said without trembling, "Why do you laugh? Come, let us go."
He spoke thus; he did not see the corpse with the vetāla upon the ground, but then he saw it again, hanging suspended right there in the tree.
Then, having climbed back up, he caused him to descend once more from there;
for even from a diamond, the jewel of the mind of heroes remains unbroken.
Then King Trivikramasena, having placed that corpse along with the vetāla upon his shoulder in silence, set out to go.
And as he was walking, the vetāla situated within the corpse, perched upon his shoulder, said:
"O King, listen; I shall tell you a story to divert you on your journey."
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva),
which, frequented by holy people, is like a plateau of Mount Kailāsa.
The celestial river, constantly situated near her bank and bearing abundant waters,
shines like a string of pearls upon her.
In that city, in former times, there was a king named Pratāpamukuṭa, who consumed the forest of his enemies' clans with the fire of his majesty.
He had a son named Vajramukuṭa,
who humbled the pride of both the God of Love and his enemies through his beauty and valor.
There, that prince had a high-minded minister’s son named Buddhiśarīra, who was his friend and dearer to him than his own body.
Once, while playing with that friend, the prince traveled a long distance due to his excessive addiction to hunting.
Like the chowries of the glory of valor upon the heads of lions,
he severed their maned crests with his arrows and entered a great forest.
There, while the cuckoos sang like bards, they recited at an improper place,
as if by trees that had rendered them a service with their flower-clusters serving as waving chowries.
Accompanied by that minister’s son, he beheld a lake that was like another ocean, the source of various blooming lotuses.
At that very moment, a certain maiden of divine appearance arrived at that lake for the purpose of bathing; he beheld her together with her retinue.
As if filling the lake with a torrent of loveliness,
she seemed to create a new forest of blue lotuses there with her glances.
With her face, which surpassed the moon, she seemed to reject the lotuses;
at that very moment, she captivated the mind of the prince.
The youth likewise captivated her eyes in such a way that the maiden could no longer perceive even her own modest adornment out of shame.
As he gazed upon that youth along with his followers, wondering "Who might this be?",
she employed the pretext of playful charm to communicate her name and the description of her own country.
She took a blue lotus from her flower garland and placed it behind her ear;
she fashioned her teeth for a long time, and having taken them up, she set them in place.
She placed her hand meaningfully upon his head and then upon his heart;
yet at that time, the prince did not understand her sign.
But his wise friend, the minister’s son, perceived this;
and in an instant, that maiden was led away from there by her attendants.
Having reached her own home, she lay upon a couch with her body resting there,
yet she fixed her mind upon that prince for the sake of her own mental conception.
That prince, like a Vidyādhara who has lost his magic power,
went to his own city and fell into a state of great misery without her.
Then, questioned in private by that friend, the minister’s son, he—
losing his composure as the youth described her as not difficult to attain— spoke.
"How can she be found whose name, village, and lineage are not even known? Why do you comfort me with such falsehoods?"
Thus addressed by the prince, the minister’s son replied to him:
"Did you not see that which was indicated by her through a sign?"
"Because an *utpala* lotus was placed upon your ear, she said this to you:
'I dwell in the kingdom of King Karṇotpala.'"
"Because she arranged her teeth in such a way, she said this:
'Know me there to be the daughter of a tooth-maker.'"
She who was adorned with lotuses spoke the name "Padmāvatī," and placing her hand upon his heart, she declared, "My life-breaths are in you."
In the land of Kaliṅga, there is indeed a famous king named Karṇotpala; he has a great ivory-carver who is well-known for his skill in craftsmanship.
That king named Saṅgrāmavardhana also has in the three worlds a daughter named Padmāvatī, a jewel who is dearer to him than his own life.
And this, O King, is known by me exactly as it is from the world;
therefore, I have understood that designation which indicates its location and so forth. (SoKss_12.8.86, Vet_1.28)
Thus addressed by that minister’s son, the prince was pleased with that wise youth; having found his means, he rejoiced.
Having consulted with him, he set out from his own palace accompanied by him;
seeking his beloved, he went once more in that direction under the pretext of hunting.
And halfway along the road, having outstripped his army with the speed of wind-swift horses,
he proceeded toward the territory of Kaliṅga accompanied only by the minister’s son.
Having reached that city of King Karṇotpala and having searched for it, they found the residence of that ivory-carver.
And not far from there, both the minister’s son and the prince entered the house of an elderly woman for the sake of lodging.
Having given water and fodder to the two horses and stationed them in a secure place,
the minister’s son spoke to the old woman while the prince remained there.
"Do you know, Mother, the ivory-carver Saṅgrāmavardhana?
Having heard that, the old woman spoke to him with faith.
"I am indeed her nurse; and now I have been appointed by him as the senior attendant beside his own daughter, Padmāvatī."
However, I do not go there constantly because my garments are worn out;
for a wicked son or a gambler, upon seeing my clothes, would surely steal them.
When she had spoken thus, the minister’s son, being pleased, gratified that elderly woman there by giving her his upper garment and other gifts, and spoke to her again:
"You are our mother; therefore we tell you this: do for us what must be done in secret.
Go to this Padmāvatī, the daughter of the ivory-carver, and speak to her."
"The prince whom you saw at the lake has arrived here;
out of affection, he has sent me to inform you of this."
Having heard that, the old woman, subdued by the Dānava, said "So be it," and having gone to Padmāvatī’s side, she returned a moment later.
When questioned, she said to the prince and the minister’s son:
"Having gone there, I secretly informed her of your arrival."
Having heard this, she rebuked me and struck me on both cheeks with her two hands, which were smeared with camphor.
Then, distressed by this humiliation, I came here weeping;
look, my two sons, at these finger-rings upon my face.
When she had spoken thus, that highly wise son of a minister said into the ear of the prince, who was despondent with despair: SoKss_12,8.103 (Vet_1.45) //
"Do not fall into despair; for when she rebuked me while guarding the secret, ten of her fingers, white as camphor, were pressed against her mouth."
Thus it was said: "In this bright fortnight, wait for these ten nights, which are suitable for our meeting, like the nights of the full moon."
Having thus comforted the prince, the minister’s son then secretly sold some gold he had in his hand at the marketplace.
With that old woman, he prepared a costly meal;
then the two of them ate it together with her.
Having thus spent ten days in this manner, the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī for the sake of further inquiry.
She too, being greedy for fine food, drink, and other luxuries,
went to her house out of consideration for him, and returning once more, she spoke to the two of them.
Having gone from here today, even if I remain there in silence,
she will herself again pour out that offense of speaking about you.
Struck upon this breast with three fingers stained with red lac,
I have now come here from her presence.
Having heard that, the minister’s son spoke freely to the prince:
"Do not entertain any other suspicion; for she has placed this very thing in her heart."
Having skillfully applied three finger-marks of red lac, she indicated:
"I have remained in my menses for three nights."
Having spoken thus to the prince, when three days had passed,
the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī.
She went to her house and was honored and fed by her;
there, she spent the day in joy, entertained with games of drinking and other diversions.
And as that old woman was wishing to return home in the evening,
a terrifying clamor arose outside at that moment.
"Alas, alas! This intoxicated elephant has broken loose from its tethering post and is rushing about, trampling the people!"—such was the cry of the world that was heard there.
Then Padmāvatī spoke thus to that old woman:
"It is not proper for you to travel along this path, which is clearly blocked by elephants."
Having placed you upon that platform with its securely fastened ropes,
we shall cast you down here through this large window.
Then, having climbed a tree in the house garden and leaped over this wall,
descend by another tree and go to your own home.
Having said this, she then had that old woman lowered from the window into the garden by her maidservants using a rope-swing.
Having gone there, he related everything exactly as it had happened to the prince and to the minister’s son along the path they had described.
Then that minister’s son spoke to the prince:
"Your desire is accomplished, for she has shown you the path through her skillful means."
Therefore, go this very day to that place; when the king has departed at this twilight, enter the mansion of that beloved woman by this very path.
Thus addressed by him, the prince, accompanied by that old woman, went to that garden by the path along the wall as she had described.
There he saw that rope hanging down with its seat,
watched from above by maidservants who were looking out for his path.
As soon as he saw her mounted upon it, he was quickly hoisted up by those maidservants through the window and entered the presence of his beloved.
When he had entered, the minister’s son went to his own abode;
but the prince beheld Padmāvatī there.
With a face like the full moon and a radiance spreading like the moonlight,
she was like the night of the full moon remaining hidden out of fear of the dark fortnight.
She too, seeing him, rose up and honored him with various services, such as embracing his neck, which were appropriate for her long-standing longing.
Then, having been married by her according to the Gāndharva rite,
the prince remained there in secret with his beloved, his desires fulfilled.
After staying for some days, he spoke to his beloved at night:
"My friend, who has come along as my companion, is actually the son of a minister."
"And he remains there alone in the house of your elder sister;
O slender one, having gone there and paid my respects to him, I shall return once more to your side."
Having heard that, the cunning Padmāvatī said to her beloved:
"Ah, noble son, I wish to ask you about those signs created by me."
"What did that friend, the minister’s son, say to you?
When she had spoken thus, the prince said to her:
"Nothing of that was known by me; but having learned everything, it was explained to me by that son of a minister, who is endowed with divine wisdom."
Having heard this and reflected upon it, that beautiful woman said to him:
"In that case, you have done what is improper, in that you spoke of him to me only after such a long time."
"He who is your brother and friend is mine as well; therefore, I must always first offer him the customary hospitality of betel and other refreshments."
When she had spoken thus, he was permitted by her and, following the previous path,
the prince then went at night to the presence of his friend.
And in the midst of their conversation, he related to him that account concerning his beloved,
which he had previously told her in her presence regarding the description of her name and characteristics.
But the minister’s son did not believe him, thinking it improper;
meanwhile, that night there turned into dawn for those two.
Then, while the two of them were engaged in conversation after their evening rituals had concluded,
a friend of Padmāvatī arrived, carrying cooked food and betel in her hands.
Having inquired after the welfare of the minister’s son and provided him with attendants,
she skillfully contrived there to prevent the prince from eating.

In the course of conversation, having informed his mistress— who was waiting for his arrival at the time of meals and other occasions— that he had departed, he went away from there secretly in an instant.
Then that minister’s son said to the prince:
"O King, behold a single marvel; I shall now show it to you."
Having said this, he then gave a single morsel of cooked food to the dog;
and as soon as the dog had eaten it, it perished.
Seeing that, the prince asked the minister’s son, "What is this wonder? and he replied to him.
Having recognized me as a rogue through her knowledge of signs,
she, being devoted to you, sent me poisoned food with the desire to kill me.
"If he remains here, this prince will become single-mindedly devoted to me;
and under my influence, he might abandon me and return to his own city."
Therefore, abandon your anger toward her; you should devise a plan for her abduction, which I shall tell you after due reflection, so that this high-souled man may be forced to abandon his kin.
When the minister’s son had spoken thus, the prince praised him there, saying, "Truly, you are one whose very body is wisdom."
Unexpectedly, there arose outside the clamor of people overwhelmed by grief;
"Alas! The young son of the king has perished!"—thus was it heard.
Delighted upon hearing that, the minister’s son then said to the prince:
"Ah, go this very night to the house of Padmāvatī."
There, one should make her drink it until, from the intoxication of the drink,
she becomes unconscious, devoid of movement, and as if lifeless.
Then, while she was asleep, he marked her hip with a spear heated by fire and took away her collection of ornaments.
"You should come through the window, having descended by means of a hanging rope;
thereafter, I shall know how to ensure that all goes well."
Having said this and having had one fashioned with a point resembling the bristles of a boar,
the minister’s son gave that trident to the prince.
The prince took that hook, crooked and harsh, made of solid black iron, in his hand— like the heart of two lovers toward one another.
"So be it," he replied as before; at night he went to the house of Padmāvatī, for the word of a pure minister is not to be questioned by his masters.
There, having stripped her of her ornaments and marked her on the hips with a spike while she lay motionless from intoxication, he went into the presence of his friend.
Having displayed his ornaments to him, he related everything as it had been done;
then that son of the minister also considered his desired goal accomplished.
Having gone to the cremation ground at dawn, he assumed the garb of an ascetic and freely made that prince his disciple.
And he said to him: "Go alone from here, taking this pearl necklace as if to sell it in the marketplace."
And he should declare her price to be very high, so that no one at all would take her even as she was being paraded about,
while everyone looked on.
If the city guards should seize you there, say without agitation: "My teacher gave this to me for sale. SoKss_12,8.165 (Vet_1.107) //
Thus dispatched by him, the prince then went and stood in the marketplace, wandering about while clearly wearing the string of pearls.
And being such as he was, he was seized by the city guards,
who were searching for thieves at the command of the ivory-carver’s daughter, Oṣajñapti.
And he was led by them immediately to the presence of the city magistrate;
and seeing him in the guise of an ascetic, the magistrate questioned him kindly.
"O Blessed One, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that was lost here?
For the jewelry of the ivory-carver’s daughter was stolen in the night."
Having heard that, the prince, who was in the guise of an ascetic, said to him:
"This was given to me by my teacher; let him be asked when he arrives."
Then the lord of the city approached him, bowed, and asked:
"O Blessed One, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that has come into the hands of your disciple?"
Having heard this, that rogue made the place secluded and said to him:
"I am an ascetic who wanders constantly here and there through the forests."
Thus, having arrived here by fate, I remained in this cemetery at night and beheld a circle of yoginīs assembled here and there.
And in their midst, a young prince was offered to Bhairava by a Yoginī belonging to the Single Vehicle, her heart-lotus having been opened.
And that great illusionist, intoxicated by drink, began to snatch away my rosary as I was chanting, making contortions with her face.
And in my anger, I struck her excessively on the hip with a trident whose points were set ablaze by mantras.
This pearl necklace was then taken by me from her neck;
that very same one, which is unworthy of an ascetic, is now for sale with me.
Having heard this, the city superintendent went and informed the king;
the king, too, having heard it and recognized that pearl necklace as hers, [acted accordingly].
And having heard from the mouth of a trusted elderly woman sent to observe her— that she truly possessed that very mark of the "dart of sight" upon her hips— she [acted].
Having reached the firm conclusion that "my son has been seized by that ḍākinī," he went in person to the presence of the minister's son, the ascetic.
And having asked about her punishment, he, at her word, ordered the banishment of Padmāvatī from the city while she was being grieved for by her parents.
Though she was distressed by being exiled and dwelling in the forest, she did not abandon her body,
for she had anticipated that the minister’s son would employ such a stratagem and act accordingly.
At the end of the day, as she was grieving, the minister’s son and the king’s son— both having discarded their ascetic garb— approached her mounted on horses.
Having comforted her and mounted her upon a horse, they led her back to their own kingdom;
there the prince dwelt with her in happiness.
But Dantaghāṭa, believing his daughter had been devoured by carnivorous beasts in the forest,
perished from grief, and his wife followed after him.
Having spoken thus, the vetāla addressed the king once more:
"Therefore, resolve this doubt of mine regarding the killing of this couple."
What sin did the minister’s son commit, or what indeed did the prince? Or what was Padmāvatī's fault? For you are the best among the wise.
And if, O King, knowing this, you do not speak the truth to me,
then this head of yours will certainly burst asunder into a hundred pieces.
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, King Trivikramasena, recognizing him and fearing the curse, replied to him in this manner:
"O Lord of Yoga, what is unknowable? For this is not a sin for these three; rather, that evil belongs to King Karṇotpala."
The Vetāla also said: "O King, what indeed is the fault of those three who committed that act?
What offense do the crows commit when the rice has been eaten by the swans?"
Then the king said to him: "None of those three are at fault;
for that was the business of the master, and thus it is blameless for the minister's son."
For those two, Prince Padmāvatī and the prince, were scorched by the fire of the arrows of desire; they were beyond reproach, free from fault, and intent upon their own purpose.
But King Karṇotpala, untrained in the treatises on statecraft, did not investigate the true state of affairs among his subjects, even among his own kin, by means of spies.
Not knowing the conduct of rogues and unskilled in interpreting gestures and other signs,
he incurred the sin by acting so thoughtlessly.

Having heard this, when the king had properly uttered his reply with his silence broken, the Vetāla—who was within that human corpse—immediately departed elsewhere, unobserved, by the power of illusion, in order to test the king's firmness; and the motionless monarch again made the resolve to recover him. Thus ends the ninth wave. *Sutasomakathāsaṃgraha*, 12.8.196 (Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā 1.138).
Then King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree in order to bring that vetāla there once again.
Having arrived there at night, as he looked about by the light of the funeral pyre,
he then saw that corpse fallen on the ground, groaning.
Then that lord of the earth, having placed the Vetāla residing in the corpse upon his shoulder,
proceeded silently and swiftly to bring him back.
Then, from his shoulder, the vetāla spoke again to that king:
"O King, you have fallen into this great and undeserved hardship."
Therefore, for your amusement, I shall tell you a tale; listen.
There is a land-grant village named Brahmasthala on the bank of the Kālindī.
There lived a Brahmin named Agnisvāmin, who had mastered the Vedas;
to him was born a daughter of exceeding beauty named Mandāravatī.
Having fashioned her of such fresh and priceless beauty,
the Creator surely came to loathe his own previous creation of the celestial nymphs.
And while she was in the bloom of youth, three young Brahmin sons, equal in all virtues, arrived there from Kānyakubja.
And for their own sake, each one of them requested her from his father;
he, unwilling to give her to anyone else even at the cost of his own life, refused.
Her father, however, did not give her to even one among them, fearing the death of the other two; consequently, she remained as a maiden.
And all three of them, their gazes fixed solely upon the moon of her face,
remained there day and night, adopting the vow of the cakora bird.
Then, due to the onset of a burning fever that arose suddenly,
it is said that the maiden Mandāravatī passed away.
Then those sons of the brahmin, overwhelmed with grief, took her—
who had been adorned with ornaments— and having carried her to the cremation ground, they consigned her to the fire.
And one among them, having constructed a small hut right there,
remained with a bed made of their ashes, subsisting on alms obtained without asking.
The second took her bones and went to the Bhāgīrathī;
the third became an ascetic and went to wander through other lands.
Wandering on, that ascetic reached a village named Vakrolaka;
there, as a guest, he entered the house of a certain Brahmin.
While he, thus honored, was about to begin eating there,
a certain child there began to cry.
When he did not desist even though being pacified, his wife, seized by anger, took him by the arm and threw him into the blazing fire.
As soon as it was thrown, that creature of delicate limbs was reduced to ashes;
seeing this, the ascetic guest, his hair standing on end with awe, said:
"Alas! Woe is me! I have entered the abode of a Brahmarākṣasa.
Therefore, I shall not eat this food here now, for it is indeed embodied sin."
To him who was speaking thus, that householder said: "Behold my power over this mantra, perfected through recitation, which restores the dead to life."
Having said this, he took that manuscript of mantras and, having recited them,
he scattered consecrated dust upon those ashes.
Thereupon that boy rose up alive, possessing that very same form;
then the brahmin ascetic, being satisfied, ate there.
Even though he was a householder, he placed that manuscript on a wall-bracket;
and having eaten, he went to bed there at night together with her.
While that householder was asleep, the ascetic, desiring the life of his beloved, rose up secretly and apprehensively took hold of that manuscript.
Having taken it, he departed from there and, traveling day and night,
eventually reached that cemetery where his beloved had been cremated.
And at that moment, he saw him arrive there for the second time—
the very one who had gone to cast those bones into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then he spoke to both of them— both that man and the first one— who were lying there in her ashes within their constructed hut.
"Let this hut be cleared away so that I may raise up my beloved from the ashes while she is still alive, by means of some power of mantras."
Having thus urged them with persistence and having searched through the small hut,
that brahmin ascetic opened it and read that manuscript.
Having consecrated the dust with a mantra, he scattered it upon the ashes;
thereupon, Mandāravatī rose up alive from that place.
Having emerged from the fire, that maiden then bore a body of even greater luster than before,
as if it were fashioned out of gold.
Seeing her born again in such a form,
all three of them, afflicted by love and desiring to obtain her, engaged in a mutual quarrel.
One said, "This wife was won by me through the power of mantras," and another said,
"This wife was obtained by me through the power of sacred fords."
"Since I have preserved this woman here by means of my ascetic power and her ashes,
she is my wife"— thus he spoke as the third in this matter.
O Lord of the Earth, regarding this dispute between them, please tell me your own decision: to which of these two does this girl rightfully become a wife?
"Your head shall split asunder if you know and do not speak," having heard this from the vetāla, the king replied to him thus:
He who, even after experiencing affliction, restored her to life by means of a mantra—
he was her father because he performed that act for her, but not her husband.
He who carried him away to the Ganges is considered his son;
but he who remained performing austerities while embracing that bed of ashes is [the other].
It is in the cremation ground itself that her husband is said to take delight;
for he, being deeply in love, has acted in a manner befitting that passion.
Having heard this from King Trivikramasena, who had thus broken his silence,
the Vetāla left his shoulder unexpectedly and returned to his own place.

Then the king, intent on the goal for the sake of the mendicants, set his mind once more upon attaining it; for those of steadfast character do not abandon an undertaking they have resolved upon, even at the cost of their lives.
The Tenth Wave. Now, once again, that best of kings, Trivikramasena, went to that śiṃśapā tree in order to fetch the vetāla.
Having reached him who was situated there, now again within a dead body,
he then proceeded silently to carry him away, holding him upon his shoulder.
And as he was departing, the Vetāla, seated upon his back, said to him:
"It is strange, O King, that you are not agitated by making this journey back and forth in the night."
Therefore, so that you may not grow weary, I shall describe it further; listen to this story.
There is a city known on the face of the earth called Pāṭaliputra.
There, in former times, there was a king named Vikramakesarin,
whom the Creator had made a repository for virtues as if they were jewels.
There, a parrot descended by means of a curse, possessing divine insight and knowledge of all the scriptures,
known by the name Vidagdhacūḍāmaṇi.
The prince married that princess of Magadha, named Candraprabhā, who was of similar status and had been recommended by him.
It is said that she, likewise endowed with all forms of wisdom,
was the daughter of a king named Somika, and her name was Śārikā.
And there were two, a parrot and a myna bird, staying together in a single cage;
they served their own master and mistress with their respective skills.
On one occasion, that parrot, filled with desire, said to the female shārikā:
"O fortunate one, share with me a single bed, seat, and meal."
"I do not desire association with men,
because men are wicked and ungrateful," the female myna bird replied to him.
"Men are not wicked; it is women who are wicked and cruel-hearted"—when Śuka had spoken thus once more, a dispute arose between the two of them.
Having made a mutual wager that one would become a slave and the other a wife, those two birds then approached the prince, who was presiding as the arbiter, to reach a decision.
Having heard the subject of their dispute while seated in his father’s assembly hall, he said to the śārikā bird:
"Tell me, how are men ungrateful?"
Then, saying "Listen," she told this story concerning the faults of men in order to establish her own position. SoKss_12,10.15 (Vet_3.15) //
There is on earth a great city named Kāmandikā;
in it there is a merchant of great wealth named Arthadatta.
And a son named Dhanadatta was born to him;
when his father passed away, he too became unrestrained in his youth.
And gamblers, having gathered together, cast him down during his addiction to gambling and such;
for association with the wicked is indeed the root of the tree of calamity.
Before long, his wealth exhausted by misfortune,
he then abandoned his own country out of shame for his destitution and went wandering through other lands.
And as he was traveling, having reached a place named Candanapura,
he entered the house of a certain merchant, seeking food.
Seeing that delicate youth and inquiring after his lineage and other details, the merchant,
recognizing him to be of noble birth, honored him and accepted him as his own through the turn of fate.
And he gave him his daughter, named Ratnāvalī, along with her dowry;
thereafter, Dhanadatta remained there in the house of his father-in-law.
As the days passed, having forgotten his misfortune in his happiness, he desired to go to his own country; having attained his goal, he was now facing calamity.
Then, having somehow obtained the reluctant permission of his father-in-law,
that rogue took his daughter— who was his sole progeny— and set out with her beautifully adorned.
Accompanied by his wife Ratnāvalī and one elderly woman,
he set out from there with himself as the third, according to the message.
Having gradually reached a distant forest and spoken of the fear arising from bandits,
he took the jewelry of that wife and made it his own.
Behold, alas, the heart of ungrateful men— hard as a sword— who cling to the miserable vices of gambling, harlots, and the like!
Then that wicked man, for the sake of wealth, threw his virtuous wife—
accompanied by that old woman— into a pit in order to kill her.
And as soon as he had thrown it and departed, that old woman died;
but his wife, though distressed by the thicket of creepers, did not die.
And then, because her life-force was not yet exhausted, she slowly rose from that chasm, crying out piteously as she clung to grass, shrubs, and other vegetation.
With her limbs wounded and having asked for the way at every step,
she returned with great difficulty to her father’s house by the very same path by which she had come.
There, having suddenly arrived in such a state and being questioned with agitation by her mother and father, that virtuous woman spoke thus while weeping:
"We were robbed on the road by thieves; my husband was bound and led away.
My aged mother died even after falling into a pit, yet I have not died again."
Then, a certain compassionate traveler who had arrived there pulled me out from that pit; and by fate, I have reached this place.
Having been thus addressed by her mother and consoled by her father,
the virtuous Ratnāvalī remained there, her mind fixed solely on her husband.
In the course of time, her husband Danadatta returned to his own country; having squandered that wealth in gambling, he reflected: SoKss_12,10.36 (Vet_3.36)
"I shall go back again and, having sought it out, bring wealth from my father-in-law;
and there I shall tell him, 'Your daughter is staying in my house.'"
Having thus meditated in his heart, he set out for his father-in-law’s house;
and when he arrived there, his wife saw him from afar.
She ran and fell at the feet of that wicked man;
for even when their husband is evil, the minds of virtuous women do not turn toward any other conduct.
Then, to him who was terrified, she related everything without omission—
that which she had previously described to her parents as the false accusation of theft and so forth.
Then, having entered the father-in-law’s house there with her,
he was received by his parents-in-law with joy upon seeing him and greeted with delight.
"By good fortune, he has been released from the thieves and is alive!"— with these words, his father-in-law, having gathered his kinsmen, then celebrated a great festival.
Then Dhanadatta, enjoying the splendor of his father-in-law there,
lived happily with his wife Ratnāvalī.
Once, during that night, that cruel man did something which,
though peaceful and unspeakable, is told here for the sake of the narrative.
Having killed his wife as she slept in his lap and having seized her collection of ornaments,
he then departed for his own country unobserved.
When Śārikā had declared, "Such men are wicked," the prince then said to the parrot, "Now you speak."
Then that parrot said:
"O King, women are difficult to endure in their audacity, wicked in their conduct, and sinful; likewise, let this story be heard."
There was a city named Harṣavatī,
and there lived a merchant named Dharmadatta, a leader among men and the master of many millions.
And that merchant had a daughter named Vasudattā, peerless in beauty, who was dearer to him than his own life.
And she was given by him to that man of equal status, who was endowed with beauty and youth,
and who was like a moonbeam of nectar to the eyes of excellent women.
To the virtuous son of a merchant named Samudradatta,
who resided in the city of Tāmraliptī, which is frequented by noble ones.
Once, while her husband was in his own country and she was staying at her father’s house,
that merchant’s daughter saw a certain man from afar.
That fickle woman, deluded by Māra, consorted with that handsome youth—
a secret lover brought to her in concealment through the mouth of a female friend.
From that time forward, her mind entirely fixed upon him, she always took her pleasure with him there in secret night after night.
And once, her youthful husband arrived there from his own country,
like joy itself incarnate to his parents.
On that festive day, having adorned herself for the night, she was sent by her mother; yet, even though he was upon their bed, she did not approach her husband.
Requested by him, she feigned sleep with her mind fixed elsewhere;
he too, intoxicated by drink and exhausted by the journey, was then overcome by slumber.
Then, while everyone was asleep after having eaten and drunk,
a thief slowly broke through a breach and entered that inner chamber.
At that moment, not seeing him, the merchant’s daughter also rose up and,
having made an appointment with her lover, departed from there secretly.
Seeing that, the thief, his purpose frustrated, thought:
"She is adorned with the very ornaments for whose sake I entered here!"
"She has gone out at midnight; therefore, I shall see where she is going. Having reflected thus, he went out and [confronted] that thief and the merchant's daughter.

He followed Vasudattā with his gaze fixed upon her, remaining unobserved; she too, accompanied by a single confidante carrying flowers and other offerings, proceeded according to their secret appointment.
Having gone outside, she entered a garden not very far away;
there she saw her own lover hanging from a tree.
Having found him at night at the place of appointment, the city guards, thinking him to be a thief, hung him up; he remained dead with a noose around his neck.
Then, overwhelmed and bewildered, crying out, "Alas, I am ruined!",
she fell to the ground, lamenting piteously and weeping.
Then, having brought down her lifeless lover from the tree and seated him,
she adorned him with unguents and flowers.
Embracing him while he was unconscious, her mind blinded by passion and grief,
the distressed woman raised his face and kissed it.
Then, that lifeless corpse of another man,
suddenly possessed by a vetāla, bit off her nose with its teeth.
Agitated by that, though she had retreated from there in distress, alas,
thinking "Could he perhaps still be alive?", she returned and gazed upon him once more.
And seeing him, the Vetāla gone, motionless as if truly dead,
she— terrified and humiliated— staggered away, weeping softly.
Remaining hidden for that long, the thief then observed everything and thought: "What is this that has been done by this wicked woman?"
Alas! The disposition of women is terrifying and thick with darkness;
like a bottomless blind well, it is profoundly deep and leads only to one's downfall.
Thinking, "What indeed will she do now? the thief followed her once more from a distance out of curiosity.
She too, having gone and entered that house where her husband lay asleep,
then wept aloud and spoke thus:
"Save me! By this wicked man, who is my enemy in the form of a husband, the nose of this innocent woman has been cut off."
Hearing her repeated cries, everyone there—
the husband, the attendants, and the father— woke up and rose in great agitation.
Then her father, having arrived and seen her with her nose cut off while still wet with blood,
became enraged and had her husband bound, charging him with being a traitor to his wife.
But he said nothing at all, remaining like one mute even while being bound,
while his father-in-law and all the others who were listening were utterly bewildered.
Then, having recognized that thief and once he had quickly departed,
the night gradually passed away amidst the clamor.
That merchant’s son was led by his father-in-law, the merchant,
into the presence of the king together with his wife whose nose had been cut off.
And the king, having been informed [of the truth], disregarded those words and ordered the execution of the merchant's son, thinking, "This man is a traitor to his own wife."
Then, as he was being led to the place of execution accompanied by the beating of drums, that thief approached and spoke to the king’s men: SoKss_12,10.82 (Vet_3.82)
"This man is not to be killed without cause; however, I know exactly what has occurred.
Lead me before the king, so that I may tell him everything from beginning to end."
Having spoken thus, the thief was led by them before the king while being granted protection from fear; he then reported the entire course of events during the night from its very beginning.
And he said: "O King, if you have no confidence in my words, then let that nose be examined even now upon the mouth of that corpse."
Having heard that, the king sent servants to investigate; once he had ascertained the truth of it, he released the merchant’s son from the penalty of execution.
Having cut off her ears as well, he banished that wicked woman from the country;
he punished her husband and his father-in-law, confiscating all their property.
And the king, being pleased, made that city magistrate a thief;
thus, women in this world are by nature treacherous and deceitful.
As soon as he had spoken thus, Śuka became the Gandharva named Citraratha; with his Indra-imposed curse exhausted, he departed for heaven in a divine form.
At that moment, Śārikā became Tilottamā, a celestial woman;
her curse thus exhausted, she immediately departed for heaven.
"And thus their dispute remained undecided in the assembly.
Having related this story, the vetāla spoke again to the king:
Therefore, may you tell us: are men more sinful, or rather women? If you do not speak, O Knower, your head shall shatter into pieces.
Having heard these words of the Vetāla resting upon his shoulder, the king said to him: "O Master of Yoga, women are sinful."
Indeed, some particular man might perhaps at some time or place be of such ill conduct;
however, women are almost always of that very same nature everywhere.
When the king had spoken thus, the Vetāla vanished from his shoulder as before; and the king once again undertook the effort of bringing him back.
The Eleventh Wave:
Then King Trivikramasena went once more near that śiṃśapā tree to the cremation ground there at night.
Having obtained that vetāla, who was laughing with a loud laugh and was seated within the human corpse,
he placed him upon his shoulder without trembling and departed from there in silence.
And as he was walking along, the vetāla on his shoulder spoke to him again:
"O King, for the sake of this wretched mendicant, why do you undergo such exhaustion?"
"Alas, there is no discernment in you regarding this fruitless exertion!
Therefore, listen to me as I tell you a story to amuse you on the road."
There is on earth a city named Śobhāvatī, which is also called Satyā;
and in it there was a king named Śūdraka, possessed of abundant valor.
The fire of whose majesty blazed night after night for that victorious one,
fanned by the breezes from the yak-tail whisks waved by the wives of his captive enemies.
While that king reigned, the earth was abundant with the practice of dharma unimpaired;
he even caused the kings of old, such as Rāma and others, to be forgotten.
Once,
O protector of the earth, a certain brahmin named Vīravara came from Mālava to that king, who was fond of heroes, for the purpose of service.
