When this was said by the third, the fourth spoke as follows:
"I am a brahmin named Jīvadatta, and my knowledge is of this kind."
"Even by bringing back dead creatures, I can quickly show them alive;
let her take me as her husband, one who has attained perfection through such heroic conduct."
Seeing those speakers, who were in celestial dress and form, King Vīradeva,
together with his daughter, became like one mounted upon a swing.
Having told this story, the Vetāla questioned King Trivikramasena,
who had been made fearful by the previously mentioned curse.
Therefore, O Lord of the People, please tell me first: among those four, to whom should that maiden Anaṅgarati be given?
Having heard this, the king replied to the vetāla:
"You are likely making me break my silence merely to waste time."
"Otherwise, O Lord of Yoga, tell me: how is this question so profound?
For how could a Kṣatriya woman be given to a Śūdra weaver?"
How could a Kṣatriya woman even be given to a Vaiśya, and as for that [knowledge] which has passed away—
the understanding of the speech of deer and other animals— where would such a thing be of use?
What is the use of that third brahmin here,
who has fallen from his own duty, a master of illusion who fancies himself a hero?
Therefore, she should be given to that fourth equal kṣatriya,
who wields the sword and is endowed with the power of his own vidyā.
Having heard these words of the king, that Vetāla departed swiftly from the king's shoulder back to his own place by the power of yoga, just as before.
Yet the king followed after him once more to bring him back; for in the heart of a hero, which is a solid mass of resolve, weariness finds no entrance.
The Seventeenth Wave.
Then King Trivikramasena went to that śiṃśapā tree, took up the vetāla once more upon his shoulder, and set out.
And as he was departing, the Vetāla, seated upon the back of his shoulder, said to him:
"O King, you are weary; therefore, listen to this story which will dispel your fatigue."
There was a most excellent king, renowned by the name Vīrabāhu, whose commands were placed upon the heads of all sovereign rulers.
He had a preeminent city named Anaṅgapura;
there lived a very wealthy caravan leader named Arthadatta.
That lord of merchants had a daughter named Madanasenā, a jewel among maidens, who was younger than his eldest son named Dhanadatta.
Once, a merchant's son named Dharmadatta, a friend of his brother, saw her playing in her own garden together with her circle of female companions.

Beholding her, who was like a cascading torrent overflowing with the essence of beauty, with the tips of her jar-like breasts visible and rippled by the three folds of her waist; so it is said in *Sūktimuktāvalī* 12.17.7 (*Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā* 10.7).
Like a pleasure-bathing pool for the elephant of youth,
he suddenly became one whose consciousness was stolen away by the intense heat of the multitude of Cupid’s arrows.
"Aha! This form, radiant with such an ascended intensity, has been fashioned by Māra as a crescent-headed arrow to pierce my mind."
Thus, as he meditated and gazed upon her for a long time,
the day passed away for him like that of a cakravāka bird.
Then Madanasenā entered her own house,
as did the pain of not seeing her in Dharmadatta’s heart.
As if burning with the heat of the fire of grief from not seeing him,
even the radiant sun, turning red, quickly fell into the western ocean.
Having learned that the lovely-faced woman had gone inside at night,
the moon rose slowly, as if vanquished by the lotus of her face.
Having gone home, Dharmadatta remained there reflecting upon her;
he lay down upon his bed and rolled about, struck by the rays of the moon.
Even when questioned with effort by his friends and kinsmen,
he said nothing at all, being utterly deluded by the seizure of love.
Having obtained sleep with great difficulty during the night, he saw that same beloved in his dream; full of longing, what did he not do as he sought to win her over?
Having woken up in the morning and gone there, he saw her again standing alone in that secluded garden, waiting for her friend.
Having approached her, longing for an embrace, he bowed at her feet and sought to persuade her with words tender with love.
"I am a maiden and the wife of another; I do not belong to you here at present, since I have been given by my father to the merchant Samudradatta."
"In only a few days my marriage shall take place;
therefore, go silently so that no one may see you, lest some trouble should arise from it."
Thus addressed by her, Dharmadatta spoke to her excessively:
"Let whatever may happen; for I cannot live without you."
Hearing this, the merchant’s daughter, agitated by fear of being forced against her will, said to him: "Let my marriage be performed here for now."
"May my father obtain the long-desired fruit of giving me away in marriage;
thereafter, I shall certainly come to you, won by your affection."
Having heard this, he said: "Indeed, one who has belonged to another is not desired by me as a beloved;
for when a lotus has been enjoyed by another, how can there arise any delight from it?"
Thus addressed by him, she said: "In that case, I am already married;
first I shall go to you, and after that I will approach that husband."
When the merchant’s son had spoken thus, she bound him with an oath, for he would not release her without a guarantee of truth.
Then, dismissed by him, the dejected woman entered her own palace;
and when the appointed day arrived, she completed the auspicious rites of marriage.
Having gone to her husband's house and spent that day with festivities,
she entered the bedchamber with her husband at night.
There, even though she was lying on the bed,
she did not respond to the embrace of her husband Samudradatta, as she turned away from him.
Because she shed tears even while being thus entreated by him, he thought in his heart: "Surely I am not beloved by her."
And he said: "O beautiful one, if I am not desired by you, then I have no need for you; go to him who is dear to you."
Hearing this, she, with her face cast down, slowly spoke thus to him:
"You are dearer to me than my own life; nevertheless, hear my request."
"Perform your duty with joy and grant me safety;
take an oath, O noble son, while I speak to you."
When she had spoken thus and he had done so with great difficulty,
she spoke again, feeling ashamed, despondent, and afraid.
Once, seeing me alone in the house garden,
a young man named Dharmadatta, my brother’s friend, seized me while he was afflicted by love.
In order to protect my father from the reproach that would follow from giving away his daughter,
I restrained the speech of him who had acted with such impetuosity.
"Having first performed my marriage, I shall then approach you, my beloved;
therefore, O Lord, please grant your consent so that this truthful word of mine may be fulfilled."
"Once I have gone near him, I shall return to your side in an instant;
for I am not able to transgress the truth that I have practiced since childhood."
Thus, suddenly struck by the thunderbolt of her words and bound by truth,
Samudradatta reflected for a moment.
"Alas! Woe! This woman is in love with another; she will certainly go to him. Shall I kill her for the sake of truth? Let her go; what need has she for marriage?"
Having reflected thus, he consented to her departure as she desired;
she too, rising from there, went forth from her husband's house.
At that moment, the moon ascended the summit of the palace of the lordly eastern mountain,
while the maiden of the eastern quarter laughed aloud, embraced by his rays.
Then, even as the darkness remained embracing the mountain caves as its beloveds, and as the bees frequented another bed of white water-lilies; so too did the King remain.
As Madanasenā was traveling alone at night, she was seen on the road by a certain thief who ran up and seized her by the hem of her garment.
"Tell me, who are you and where are you going? he asked her; and she, trembling with fear, replied:
"What is this to you? Let me go; I have business here."
Then the thief said, "How can you be released from me, a thief?
Hearing that, she said to him, "Take my ornaments."
Then the thief said, "O simple girl, what use have I for these stones?
[I desire her] whose face is like the moonstone and whose hair is as black as sapphires."
With a diamond-like waist, golden limbs, and enchanting feet like rubies,
I shall never forsake you, the ornament of the world.
Thus addressed by that thief, the helpless merchant’s daughter,
having related her own story, entreated him as follows:
"Forgive me for a moment while I fulfill my commitment to truth;
remaining right here, I shall come to your side with all speed."
“O good man, I shall not violate this word of truth.
Having heard this and considering her to be one who is true to her promise, that thief released her.
He remained right there, awaiting her arrival;
she, for her part, went into the presence of that merchant Dharmadatta.

And seeing her standing thus in that secluded place—though she was his beloved and had come to him—he questioned her about what had happened, reflected for a moment, and said: SoKss_12,17.53 (Vet_10.53)
"I am pleased with your truthfulness; what use have I for your wife, who belongs to another?
Go back the way you came, before anyone sees you."
Having been dismissed by him with these words, she then departed saying, "So be it," and went from there to the presence of that thief who was waiting for her on the road.
When he asked her, "Tell me, what was your experience after you had gone there?
she told him exactly how she had been released by that merchant.
Then that thief said to her: "If it is so, then you have been released by me as well, out of satisfaction with the truth; go home with your ornaments."
Thus she was abandoned by him, yet protected by her follower;
with her virtue unimpaired, she returned joyfully to her husband's house.
Having entered there in secret, she approached him with great joy;
seeing her husband, she described everything that had happened to him.
He too, perceiving that she was one whose facial radiance was undiminished, who bore no signs of sexual union,
whose conduct remained unbroken, and who was devoted to the attainment of truth— she being a virtuous woman— [concluded her innocence].
Having welcomed his wife Adṛṣṭamanas in accordance with their family tradition,
Samudradatta then remained with her in comfort as he pleased.
Having thus told this story there in the cemetery grounds at that time, the Vetāla spoke again to Trivikramasena, the lord of the earth.
Therefore tell me, O lord of men, which among these—the thieves or the merchants—is the generous one?
If you know and do not speak, your head shall shatter into a hundred pieces.
Having heard that, the lord of the earth broke his silence and said to the vetāla:
"Among these, the thief is the one who renounced, and not either of the two merchants."
For how can that man of noble birth, who abandoned her even though she was such a woman fit for marriage and not to be forsaken, continue to carry his wife once he knows she is attached to another?

Furthermore, that other husband of hers, whose sense of urgency had been worn away by time, abandoned her out of fear; once he had learned the facts, he would say to the king in the morning: "She is his."
But he was a thief who moved in secret, a perpetrator of evil deeds who acted without regard for consequences;
yet because he did not release that jewel among women along with her ornaments when he had her in his grasp, he was a man of renunciation.
Upon hearing this, the Vetāla departed from the king's shoulder and returned to his own place as before;
yet the king, his lofty fortitude unbroken, set out once more to recover him.
The Eighteenth Wave:
Then, having gone back and reached the śiṃśapā tree once more,
King Trivikramasena took that vetāla upon his shoulder and set out.
And as he was approaching, the vetāla on his shoulder said to the king:
"O King, listen; I shall relate to you a single wonderful tale."
In the past, there was a king in Ujjayinī named Dharmadhvaja;
he had three wives, princesses who were exceedingly dear to him.
Among them, one was named Indulekhā, another Tārāvalī, and yet another Mṛgāṅkavatī; they were all possessed of extraordinary beauty and virtues.
Sporting with those three queens, the king,
having conquered all his enemies and being accomplished in every way, sat there in happiness.
Once, when the festival of the spring season had arrived there,
he went to the garden with those beloved women to sport.
There he saw creepers bent with flowers, appearing like the bow-staffs of the Bodiless One, with rows of bees for their strings, as if strung by the Spring.
And he heard the song uttered by a cuckoo perched on the tip of a tree,
which was like the command of the god of love, whose sole essence is sensual enjoyment.
That king, who was like Indra himself, indulged together with his harem in the drinking of intoxicants—
the very life-force of passion and the sustenance of Love itself.
He took delight in drinking the honey-liquors that were fragrant with her breath, possessed the luster of her bimba-like lips, and remained as remnants after being sipped by his beloved.
There, as the king playfully seized Indulekhā by the hair,
a blooming blue lotus fell from the tip of her ear onto his lap.
When a wound was suddenly inflicted on the back of the lute by that blow, the noble queen, crying out "Alas!
Alas!", fell into a swoon.
Seeing this, the king and his attendants were overwhelmed with grief;
the queen was then slowly revived by cool water and fanning.
Then, having led her back to his capital, the king attended to his beloved with divine medicines prepared by physicians, after she had been bound with bandages over her wounds.
And having seen her well-settled at night, that lordly king ascended the moon-palace together with his second wife, Tārāvalī.
There, as she slept in the king's lap, the rays of that moon fell through the lattice-windows upon her body, whose garment had shifted.
Then, awakening in an instant and crying out, "Alas, I am burned!",
she rose suddenly from her bed, feeling her limbs.
"What is this? he thought, bewildered; then, having awakened, the king rose up and saw boils that had broken out upon her body.
When he questioned her, Queen Tārāvalī then said to him:
"This was done to me by the rays of the moon falling upon my naked body."
When she had spoken thus while weeping,
the king, filled with pain, called out to her attendants, who ran about in a state of frantic agitation.
Therefore, he had a bed prepared for her with lotus leaves moistened with water,
and he had her body anointed with fresh applications of sandalwood paste.
Having learned this, his third beloved, Mṛgāṅkavatī,
desiring to come to his side, departed from her own palace.
Having gone out, she heard from somewhere in a house the distinct sound of a pestle striking grain at night,
even though the night was otherwise silent and the sound came from afar.
Upon hearing this, crying out, "Alas, I am dead! and shaking her hands, that fawn-eyed woman sat down on the path, overcome by agony.
Then, having turned back and been led by her attendants to her own inner apartments, the young woman fell weeping upon her bed.
There, as he searched for her, his retinue saw his hands marked with calluses, like two lotuses with bees clinging to them, and they wept.
Having gone, he spoke to the king; the king, arriving in a state of agitation, asked, "What is this? Then Dharmadhvaja [spoke] to his beloved.
She too, showing her hands to him while afflicted by pain, spoke thus:
"When the sound of the pestle was heard, these two [hands] of mine became marked with calluses."
Then the king, overcome with wonder and grief, had sandalwood paste and other remedies applied to her hands to alleviate the burning sensation.
One woman was wounded by even a falling lotus petal;
the other, however, had her limbs scorched even by the rays of the moon.
But for this third woman, even though she has heard [the teaching],
such calluses have formed on her hands from the painful sound of the pestle.
"Alas! Now, by fate, even this quality of extreme nobility has become a defect for me simultaneously with these beloved women."
As he wandered thus through the inner apartments with these thoughts,
that night passed for the king with difficulty as if it were a hundred watches.
And in the morning, he underwent surgery together with physicians and surgeons such that,
before long, his inner apartments became restored to health and filled with joy.
Having thus told this most wonderful tale, the Vetāla,
remaining upon the shoulder of King Trivikramasena, then questioned him.
"O King, tell me which among these queens is the most noble-born!
Let that previously mentioned curse be yours if you know and yet do not speak."
Having heard that, the king said: "She was even more delicate than that;
for her calluses arose by sound alone, even before the pestle had been touched."
When the touch occurred with hands like blue lotuses and moons, on the other two [limbs] there arose wounds and pustules; therefore, those [hands] were not equal to hers.
When he had spoken thus, the vetāla departed once more from the king’s shoulder to his own place;
and the king, remaining as firm in his resolve as before, followed after him.
The Nineteenth Wave:
Then King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree, reached it, and once again placed the vetāla upon his shoulder.
And taking him, he set out in silence just as before;
then that vetāla spoke to him once more from his position upon his shoulder.
"O King, since you are thus free from anxiety, you are sufficiently dear to me.
Therefore, listen to this heart-pleasing tale that I shall relate to you for your lack of weariness."
In ancient times, there was a king named Yaśaḥketu in the land of Aṅga;
resting upon the earth for the sake of protecting Aṅga, he was like another Smara who had not been consumed by fire.
And he had a minister named Dīrghadarśin, who, like Bṛhaspati for Śakra, had conquered the entire host of his enemies through the prowess of his own arms.
Having entrusted the kingdom, from which all thorns had been removed, to that minister,
the king gradually became devoted solely to pleasure due to the intoxication of his youth and beauty.
He remained constantly within the inner apartments, a place for women that was no fit setting for his purpose; he listened to impassioned songs, but not to the words of those who desired his welfare.
And he took delight, free from anxiety, in the lattice windows;
but he never again engaged in royal affairs, which are full of many pitfalls.
But the far-sighted great minister, bearing that burden of state affairs,
remained day and night without weariness.
Having cast the king— who finds his stability in mere names— into calamity,
the far-sighted minister now enjoys the royal fortune here.
When this great rumor had arisen among the people,
Dīrghadarśin then spoke privately to his wife, named Medhāvinī.
"O dear Queen, while you were attached to pleasure, although I was bearing that burden, the kingdom has been devoured by him; thus a lack of reputation has arisen among the people."
In this world, even false public rumor causes distress to the great;
did not Rāma, too, abandon Jānakī because of the talk of the people?
When he asked, "What should I do in this matter?
his wife Medhāvinī—wise, steadfast, and true to her name—spoke to him.
"Under the pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, O high-minded one, it is fitting for you to take leave of the king with due deliberation and go abroad for some time."
Thus, this public rumor will cease for you who are free from desire;
then, while you remain steadfast, the king himself will uphold the kingdom.
Then this calamity of his will gradually come to an end,
and once he has arrived here, your counsel shall be beyond reproach.
Having been thus addressed by his wife, Dīrghadarśin replied, "So be it," and having gone there,
he made a request to King Yaśaḥketu during the course of a conversation.
"Grant me leave, O King, for I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords for some days; for that is the dharma I desire to pursue."
Having heard that, the king said: "It is not so;
is there not another dharma, such as giving and the like, which leads to heaven even in one's own home, apart from sacred fords?"
Then that minister said to him: "O King, purity of wealth and the like are sought after; however, the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as giving and so forth are eternally pure."
O King, as long as youth lasts, a wise man should pursue these [pleasures];
for since the body is not to be trusted, how could there be union with them at any other time?
While the king was speaking thus and forbidding him in this manner,
the doorkeeper entered and addressed the king.
"O King, the sun is plunging into the midst of the celestial ocean;
therefore arise, for this time for your bath is passing away."
Upon hearing this, the lord of the earth immediately rose to bathe;
intent on his expedition, he and his minister bowed to him and departed for their homes.
Having left his wife there, whom he had prevented from following him,
he set out from that place by a stratagem, unobserved even by his own servants.
Wandering alone through various regions and visiting sacred fords,
Dīrghadarśin, firm in his resolve, reached the territory of Puṇḍra.
There, having entered a port city not far from the ocean,
he sat down in the courtyard of a certain temple dedicated to Śiva.
There, a merchant named Nidhidatta, who had come to worship the deity, saw him exhausted by the heat of the sun's rays and dusted with the pollen of the long journey.
Seeing him in such a state, wearing the sacred thread and possessing auspicious marks,
and honoring him as an eminent brahmin, the hospitable host led him into his home.
There he honored him with the finest offerings, such as baths and meals;
and once he had rested, he asked him: "Who are you? From where do you come? Where are you going?"
"I am a Brahmin named Dīrghadarśin, come here from the land of Aṅga for the purpose of pilgrimage," he said to him with such depth of character.
Then the great merchant Nidhidatta also said to him:
"I am preparing to go to Suvarṇadvīpa for the purpose of trade."
Therefore, stay here in my house until I return from there;
once you have rested, weary as you are from your pilgrimage, you may then depart.
Having heard that, Dīrghadarśin said: "In that case, what is it to me here?
O caravan leader, I shall go with you yourself as you please."
When the merchant replied, "So be it," the minister then spent that night in his house, finally obtaining a bed after a long time.
Then, on another day, having gone to the ocean together with that very merchant,
he boarded a ship filled with those goods.
Traveling by that ship while beholding the ocean, wondrous and terrifying,
he eventually reached that Golden Island.
Where is his position as chief minister, and where is his crossing of the ocean?
Alas, what will virtuous men not do when they are afraid of infamy?
There, on that island, he lived for some time with that merchant Nidhidatta, who was engaged in buying and selling.
And as he was returning from there, suddenly standing upon his ship equipped with that [apparatus],
he saw a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) rising up from behind a wave in the ocean.
It was adorned with trunks as beautiful as coral branches, radiant as refined gold,
and graced with lovely fruits made of jewels and flowers.
And upon his shoulder, he beheld a maiden of most wonderful and lovely form, seated upon the lap of a couch made of the seven precious gems.
While he was reflecting for a moment, "Aha! What can this be?", that lute-playing maiden proceeded to sing as follows:
Whatever seed of karma was sown by someone in the past, that he surely experiences;
for it is not possible to alter what was previously done, even by means of fate.
Having sung this, in that very instant, the divine maiden sank right there into the ocean upon her couch and bed of a wish-fulfilling tree.
"Today I have seen here some unprecedented and wonderful marvel:
where is the ocean, and where is this tree, which vanishes as soon as it is seen, with its divine women singing?"
Or perhaps this ocean is worthy of homage, for it is the eternal source of such things as Lakṣmī, the moon, and the pārijāta tree; have they not all emerged from it?
Seeing Dīrghadarśin at that moment lost in such thought and overcome with wonder, the helmsman and the others said:
Thus this excellent maiden is always seen here;
she sinks at that very moment, and this is your first sight of her.
Having been addressed thus by them, the minister, accompanied by Nidhidatta,
traveled by ship along the ocean shore in due course, filled with wonder.
Then, together with that very merchant who had unloaded his goods and whose servants were joyful, he went to that house in a festive mood.
Having stayed there for no very long time, he said to Nidhidatta:
"O caravan leader, I have rested in your house for a long while in comfort."
"Now I wish to go to my own country; may it be well with you," having said this, he took leave of the merchant lord, even though the latter was unwilling.
That far-sighted one, with his son as his sole companion, set out from there;
having traversed the long and distant road step by step, he reached his own realm of Aṅga.
There, the scouts whom King Yaśaḥketu had previously dispatched to search for him saw him arrived outside the city.
Having gone there, the spies informed him, and the king approached him;
having himself departed from the city, he was deeply distressed by the separation from him.
Having approached and greeted him with an embrace,
the king led him— who was pale and emaciated from his long journey— into the interior of the palace.
Having abandoned us, alas, what have you taken away? Not only our minds, but even this body has been reduced to a state of cold and harshness.
Or rather, who knows the course of what is destined for the Blessed One,
since this thought of yours to go to the sacred fords and elsewhere has arisen so suddenly?
"Therefore, tell me: what countries have you wandered through, and what new thing have you seen?
Thus the king spoke there to his minister.
Then, describing the path step by step as far as Suvarṇadvīpa,
he told him about that divine maiden whom he had seen emerging from the ocean.
Dīrghadarśin related exactly as it had occurred to the king how she, who was the essence of the three worlds, stood upon the Kalpa tree singing.
As soon as the king heard this, he fell under the power of love in such a way that,
without her, he considered both his kingdom and his life to be fruitless.
And then, having led his own minister aside to a private place, he said to him:
"I must certainly see her; otherwise, there is no life for me."
I go by the path you have spoken, having bowed to destiny;
I am neither to be dissuaded by you, nor am I to be followed in any way.
"I shall indeed go alone in secret, but the kingdom must be protected by you.
Do not act otherwise than my word; you are bound under oath by my very life."
Having spoken thus and rejecting his reply,
the king dismissed the minister to his own home, longing for his kinsmen whom he had missed for a long time.
There, even amidst the great festival, Dīrghadarśin remained deeply dejected;
for when a master is beset by an incurable calamity, how can there be happiness for his wise ministers?
And on another day, King Yaśaḥketu, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his hand,
set out at night wearing the garb of an ascetic.
And as he was going along the road, he saw a sage named Kuśanābha;
there, the sage instructed him, who was dressed in the garb of an ascetic and bowing before him.
"Go forth without anxiety; having traveled upon the ocean with the merchant Lakṣmīdatta on his ship, you shall obtain that beloved maiden."
Delighted by those words, the king bowed to him;
then, traveling across countries, rivers, and mountains, he reached that ocean.
With its blossoming waves for eyebrows, white as a beautiful conch shell,
it seemed to gaze with whirlpools for eyes out of the excitement of hospitality.
On its shore, he met with that merchant Lakṣmīdatta, who was about to set out for Suvarṇadvīpa, as had been foretold by the sage.
Because he had seen the king’s footprints marked with the wheel-design along with him,
the king, bowing low, boarded the vessel and set out upon the ocean.
When the ship reached the middle of the ocean,
that maiden rose up there from the midst of the waters, standing upon the trunk of a world-tree.
As soon as the king beheld her, like a cakora bird beholding moonlight,
she began to sing thus, beautifully accompanied by the lute.
Whatever seed of karma was sown by someone in the past, that he surely experiences;
for it is not possible, even by means of fate, to alter what was previously done.
Therefore, wherever, in whatever manner, and whatever is destined to happen for someone through the conjunction of fate, there he is led helplessly to attain that; herein there is no delusion.
Reflecting upon her as she sang, thus indicating the destiny of a fortunate man,
the king stood motionless for a moment, struck by the arrows of Love.
O Ratnākara, homage to you whose heart is true and unfathomable,
by whom Hari was deceived when his splendor was concealed by you.
I have taken refuge in you, whose limits cannot be reached even by the gods, who provide shelter to the winged mountains; grant me the attainment of my desired goal.
In this manner, as the king bowed and praised that ocean,
the maiden sank there along with her tree.
Upon seeing that, the king threw himself after her along the path,
as if to extinguish the heat of the fire of passion within him, into this ocean.
Seeing that, and thinking him lost beyond hope,
the virtuous merchant Lakṣmīdatta became intent on ending his own life out of grief.
"Do not commit this rash act; there is no fear for one submerged in the ocean.
This is King Yaśaḥketu, wearing the garb of an ascetic."
"He came here for the sake of this maiden, and she was his wife in a former life;
having obtained her, he shall return once more to the kingdom of Aṅga."
Thus, comforted at that moment by the voice arising from the sky,
the caravan leader departed as he desired for the sake of accomplishing his wish.
King Yaśaḥketu, submerged within the great ocean,
suddenly beheld a divine city and was filled with wonder.
It was resplendent with palaces featuring pillars made of radiant jewels, walls shining with gold,
and windows adorned with lattices of pearls.
It was adorned with gardens that grant all desires, enriched by *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, and featuring stepped walkways and ponds lined with slabs of various precious gems.
Although that city was prosperous, when he entered house after house and found it deserted,
he did not see his beloved anywhere.
Then, searching about and seeing a single lofty palace of jewels,
that king ascended it, opened the door, and entered.

With longing, he opened her face, wondering, "Could it be she?
and as soon as he did so, he beheld that very woman whom he had desired.
With the beauty of her moon-like face laughing as the darkness of her slipping blue garment faded,

And by the sight of him, she then experienced a certain state,
like that of a traveler in the desert during the summer season upon seeing a river.
She too, opening her eyes, beheld him of auspicious form and marks who had suddenly arrived in that manner, and in her agitation she abandoned her bed.
Having been offered hospitality, she, with downcast face, as if worshipping his feet with the placement of her lotus-like blossoming eyes, slowly spoke to him:
"Who are you, and why have you entered the netherworld, which is not to be approached? Why do you, whose body is marked with royal insignia, observe the vow of an ascetic?"
"O illustrious one, grant this favor if you have grace toward me.

"O beautiful one, I am the King of Aṅga, known by the name Yaśaḥketu;

"Therefore, having assumed this disguise for your sake and abandoned my kingdom,

Having left me all alone here in my own city,

When the garlands have fallen from her hair, there is a series of nail-marks from the grasping of locks;

On her breasts, the rows of nail-marks appeared like shattered strings of rubies;

Once, while the king was thus established in the bliss of that divine enjoyment, his wife Mṛgāṅkavatī spoke these words to him.
"You should wait right here while I go somewhere for the sake of my business;

"Stay here, noble son; do not go to that crystal house, lest you fall into this pond and return to the world of mortals."
Having said this and taken leave of him, she departed from that city;

There the king beheld a rākṣasa, dark as the night and with a gaping mouth like a cavern, approaching like the underworld incarnate.
That rākṣasa, having fallen down and let out a terrible roar,

Upon seeing that, as if suddenly blazing with extreme rage,
he [struck] with his great sword, dark as a snake that has cast off its slough.
Drawing his sword from its scabbard, the lion-like king rushed forward and severed the head of that charging demon, whose lips were bitten together in a snarl.
Then, by the blood of that king, which was vomited forth by the *rakṣasa* headless trunk, the fire born of his anger was extinguished;
but not so the fire born from the separation from his beloved.
Then, while that king was blinded by the night of delusion and his course was ruined,
[the voice] suddenly emerged as if piercing the body of a Rākṣasa dark as a cloud.
Illuminating the circle of the quarters like the stainless form of the moon,
that Mṛgāṅkavatī emerged alive with her limbs unhurt.
Seeing his beloved thus delivered from that peril, the king ran toward her in great agitation and embraced her, saying, "Come! Come!"
"Beloved, what is this? Is it a dream or an illusion? Thus questioned by the king, that Vidyādharī, reflecting upon it, spoke as follows:
Listen, noble son: this is neither a dream nor an illusion;
rather, such was the curse pronounced upon me by my father, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
For although my father had many sons, while he formerly lived here,
out of excessive affection for me, he would never take food without me.
And I, always devoted to the worship of Śarva in this secluded place,
would come on the fourteenth and eighth days of both fortnights.
And once, on the fourteenth day, having come here, while I was worshipping Gaurī for a long time with flavorful offerings, the day ended by chance.
On that day, my father, though hungry, ate nothing and drank nothing while waiting for me; instead, he remained angry with me.
Then, at night, as I approached him with my face cast down in shame for my transgression, he—

Just as I am now seized by hunger due to my contempt for you,
so too [I was seized] only on the eighth and fourteenth days of every month.
While you are departing from this very city for the sake of worshipping Śiva,
a Rākṣasa named Kṛtāntasaṃtrāsa will swallow you up.
"Having pierced and pierced his heart, you shall emerge alive;
and you will remember neither the curse nor the agony of being swallowed."
"Having been told these words of a curse—that you shall remain here alone—he, my father, was gently entreated by me; after reflecting, he spoke to me regarding the end of the curse."
When the king named Yaśaḥketu becomes your husband,
he will see you swallowed by the Rākṣasa and shall slay him.
Then you shall be released from the curse, having emerged from his heart;
you will remember the curse and all your own sciences.
Having spoken thus and set a limit for the end of the curse,
my father left me here alone and went to the Niṣadha mountain on the earthly realm, accompanied by his retinue.
And while practicing in that manner, I dwelt here due to the delusion of a curse;
now that curse of mine has been exhausted, and memory has returned in every respect.
"Therefore, I shall now go to the side of my father on Mount Niṣadha;
for this is our agreement: that at the end of the curse, we shall return to our own state."
"Stay here, or go to your own kingdom; you have freedom in this matter.
When she had spoken thus, the king, filled with sorrow, made this request to her: "SoKss_12,19.145 (Vet_12.145)"
"O fair-faced one, please do not go for seven days;
let us first dispel our longing here in the garden with diversions."
"You go now to your father's place; I too shall go to my own.
To these words of his, that innocent girl agreed, saying, "So be it."
Then the king took delight there for six days with that beloved woman in the gardens and in the ponds whose eyes were like water-lilies.
"Do not depart, leaving us behind!"—
thus they seemed to cry out with the sounds of swans and cranes, as their wave-hands were tossed upward.
On the seventh day, he skillfully brought his beloved there to the house where that mechanical door-well leading to the world of mortals was located.
There, taking her by the neck,
he fell into that pond and rose up from the middle of the pond in his own city's garden together with her.
There, seeing him arrived with his beloved, the garden-keepers were delighted; they went to the minister Dīrghadarśin and told him.
The minister also approached and prostrated at his feet; seeing that the king had brought the woman he desired, he, together with the citizens, ushered the monarch into the inner apartments.
"Aha! How has this divine woman been obtained by this king—she who was seen by me like a flash of lightning in the sky, visible for but a moment?"
Whatever has been written for someone by the Creator in the lines of letters upon their forehead, that necessarily comes to pass for them, even if it is impossible to believe.
Thus, while this chief minister and other people were meditating amidst the festive celebration of the king’s arrival and the wonder of obtaining a celestial woman— SoKss_12,19.156 (Vet_12.156).
Having seen that king returned to his own country, Mṛgāṅkavatī desired to attain the state of a Vidyādharī once the full seven days had passed.
And even when remembered, her science of flight did not manifest at that time;
consequently, as if robbed, she fell into the deepest despondency.
"Why do you appear so dejected all of a sudden? Tell me, my dear," the king said to her; thus addressed by him, that daughter-in-law spoke as follows:
"Although I am released from the curse, because I have remained here for so long out of affection for you,

Hearing that, King Yaśaḥketu thought, "Ah, this Vidyādharī has been won by me," and he then celebrated a great festival to its full extent.
Having seen that, the far-sighted minister went home at night;
while lying upon his bed, he suddenly perished from a bursting of the heart.
Then, having experienced that grief, Yaśaḥketu himself, bearing the burden of the kingdom,

Having told this story on the way, that Vetāla,
remaining upon the shoulder of King Trivikramasena, spoke again to him.
Therefore tell me, O King: when such prosperity had come to you, your master, why did the heart of that great minister suddenly burst?
"Was it because my heart was bursting with grief at the thought, 'Why have I not obtained a divine woman,' or rather from the sorrow born of the king's arrival for one desiring the kingdom?"
And if you do not tell this to me, O King, even though you know it here,

Having heard this, King Trivikramasena said to the Vetāla:
"Neither of these two things is fitting for that minister of excellent conduct."
But what can be said now of that king who, having neglected his kingdom out of mere passion for women,

"Alas! Though I have acted with great hardship for his sake, on the contrary, my fault has only increased.
As that minister reflected thus, his heart burst asunder.
When the king had spoken thus, that illusory Vetāla returned once more to his own place;
then the resolute-minded king, desiring to seize him by force, again ran swiftly after him.
The Twentieth Wave:
Then King Trivikramasena, having gone back and reached the śiṃśapā tree once more, took that vetāla upon his shoulder.
And as he was approaching, the Vetāla spoke again to that king:
"O King, listen; I shall relate to you a single tale in brief."
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of Śiva; there lived a venerable brahmin named Devasvāmin, who was honored by the king.
That wealthy man had a son named Harisvāmin,
and his wife was Lāvaṇyavatī, who was exceedingly excellent.
I believe that Brahmā, having attained mastery in the creation of celestial women such as Tilottamā,
fashioned her with a beauty and loveliness beyond price.
Once, exhausted from lovemaking, Harisvāmin went to sleep with that beloved wife in a palace cooled by the rays of the moon.
At that time, a young Vidyadhara named Madanavega, traveling through the air at will, arrived by that same path.
There he saw Lāvaṇyavatī by her husband’s side,
sleeping, her fine bodily form revealed as her garments had slipped away from the exhaustion of passion.
His heart captivated by her form and blinded by passion,
he pounced upon her while she was still asleep, seized her, and in that very instant departed through the sky.
Then, awakening in an instant, the young Harisvāmin, her husband,
not seeing that mistress of his life, rose up in agitation.
"Aha! What is this? Where has she gone? Is she angry with me?
Or is she hidden away, wishing to test my mind, or perhaps mocking me?"
Thus, agitated by a flood of many such doubts,
he wandered through the night, searching for her here and there among the terraces, palaces, and upper chambers.
Searching for her everywhere throughout his palace gardens, when he could not find her anywhere,
he, tormented by the fire of grief, lamented with a voice choked with tears.
"Alas, O you with a face like the lunar orb! Alas, O you as fair as moonlight! Alas, my beloved! Why have you not been spared by this night, which seems to hate our shared virtues?"
This very moon, which once gladdened me with its sandalwood-cool rays— as if it were afraid, having been conquered by your beauty— now brings no joy since you are gone.
O beloved, now that he has found an opening, he torments me with those very same [feelings] as if with glowing coals or with arrows smeared with poison.
As Harisvāmin was thus wailing, that night passed for him with great difficulty; but the pain of separation did not pass away.
At dawn, the sun pierced the pervasive thick darkness with its rays;
yet it was not able to pierce the blinding darkness of his delusion.
Then, as if encouraged by the cakravāka birds who had passed the night there,
the sound of his piteous lamentation increased a hundredfold.
Although being consoled by his kinsmen, the young brahmin, inflamed by the fire of separation,
could find no composure without his beloved.
"Here she stood, here she bathed, here she made her adornment,
and here she wandered about"— saying this, he went from here to there, weeping.
"She is not yet dead; why then do you destroy yourself in this way?
You shall certainly obtain her again at some time or other, as long as you remain alive."
Therefore, rely upon that fortitude and search for your beloved;
for there is nothing unattainable here for one who is steadfast and resolute.
Thus, having been awakened by the words of his kinsmen and friends, Harisvāmin finally, with great difficulty,
established himself in fortitude after some days.
And he thought: "Having given away my entire possessions to the brahmins, I shall wander through sacred fords until I exhaust the accumulation of my sins."
"Only through the destruction of my evil karma might I ever find that beloved while wandering";
having reflected thus, he rose according to the circumstances and performed his ablutions and other morning rites.
And on another day, he provided various kinds of food and drink for the twice-born at the sacrificial session without restriction, and moreover, he gave away his wealth entirely.
Having departed from his own country with nothing but the status of a Brahmin as his wealth,
he then went forth to wander through sacred fords (tīrthas), desiring to find his beloved.
And as he was wandering, the lion of the summer season approached him— Bhīma—
with the fierce sun for its face and the blazing rays of that sun for its mane.
And the winds blew exceedingly hot, as if their heat had been deposited by the breaths of travelers tormented by separation from their beloveds.
With their mud dried up and cracked, and appearing as if their hearts were split asunder,
the reservoirs of water appeared with the wealth of their waters lost to the heat.
Chattering with the whirring of crickets and their lower lips withered by the heat,
the trees on the roads seemed to weep from the separation from the beauty of spring.
At that time, exhausted by the heat of the sun, by separation, by hunger and thirst,
and by the constant journey, he was withered, parched, and greyish-pale.
Seeking food, Harisvāmin, wandering about somewhere,
reached the house of a Brahmin named Padmanābha who maintained a sacrificial hall.
There, seeing many brahmins eating inside,
he stood leaning against the doorpost, silent and motionless.
Seeing him remaining in that state, his wife,
a virtuous woman, felt compassion for Padmanābha and thought:
"Alas! This thing called hunger is truly heavy; for whom would it not cause lightness?
For here stands some seeker of food at the door, with his face cast down."
Having traveled a long distance, he had bathed and was now exhausted by hunger;
perceiving that he was a worthy recipient for the gift of food, she [acted accordingly].
The virtuous woman, lifting with both hands a vessel filled with excellent rice, accompanied by ghee and sugar, brought it forward and gave it to him with humility.
And he said to him, "Go to the edge of some pond and eat this;
this place is surrounded by Brahmins who are eating while remaining in a state of ritual impurity."
Saying "So be it," he took that vessel of food and, having gone not very far,
set it down on the bank of the pond beneath a banyan tree.
Having washed his hands and feet in the pond and performed the ritual sipping of water there,
he approached that excellent food with satisfaction, ready to eat it.
Just then, a hawk, having seized a black snake with its beak and its two talons, arrived from somewhere and perched upon that tree.
As that snake was being carried away by the bird, it was attacked;
its life departed, and poisonous saliva issued forth from its mouth.
Then she fell into that food bowl situated below;
and Harisvāmin, not seeing her, went there and ate that food.
Then, for him who was afflicted by hunger, as soon as he had eaten all of that delicious food, a sharp pain from poison arose instantly.
Alas! When fate is perverse, what here does not turn upside down?
For even my food, though it contained milk, ghee, and sugar, has become poison.
Speaking thus, afflicted by poison and stumbling along, Harisvāmin went to the house of that Brahmin’s wife and said to her: SoKss_12,20.48 (Vet_13.48)
"Poison has arisen from the food given by you;
therefore, quickly bring some one to me who is skilled in the administration of antidotes, otherwise there shall be the sin of Brahmin-murder upon you."
Having spoken thus to that virtuous woman, who was distraught wondering "What is this?",

Then, although she was blameless and hospitable,
that spy, enraged by his false guest’s murder, drove his wife out of the house.

"Whose murder is this? Is it that of the snakes, the hawks, or the providers of food?"—this debate took place before Dharmarāja, but there was no final decision.

Having heard this from the Vetāla, King Trivikramasena, constrained by the curse, broke his silence and spoke these words to him:
That sin belongs to the serpent; for what fault is there on the part of this helpless one being devoured by his enemy?
Then what was wrong with that hungry hawk as well, who,

From where could there be any fault in either of those two—the husband and wife, or the giver of food—or even in one of them? For both are solely engaged in the practice of dharma.
Therefore, I consider that the sin of killing a Brahmin belongs to that dull-witted man who,

When the king had spoken thus, the vetāla once again departed from his shoulder and returned to his own abode;

The Twenty-first Wave.
Then King Trivikramasena went back to that śiṃśapā tree,
reached the vetāla once more, and took him upon his shoulder.
And as that lord of the earth was setting out, the vetāla spoke to him again:
"O King, you are weary; therefore, I shall tell you a wondrous tale—listen."
There exists a city named Ayodhyā,
which served as the capital of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of Rāma, the bringer of destruction to the race of Rākṣasas.
In that city there was a king named Vīraketu,
who, with his mighty arms, protected this earth as a rampart protects a city.
While that king reigned, there lived in this city a certain great merchant named Ratnadatta, who was the leader of a caravan of traders.
To him, by his wife named Nandayantī,
was born a daughter named Ratnavatī, acquired through the propitiation of the gods.
And that wise woman grew up in her father’s house,
together with her natural qualities of beauty, grace, and modesty.
When she reached the prime of youth, not only great merchants but even kings sought her from Ratnadatta.
But she, hating men, did not desire even Vāsava as her husband;
intent on abandoning her life, she could not endure even the mention of marriage.
Because of that, her father remained silent, distressed by paternal affection;
and that rumor spread everywhere throughout that city.
In the meantime, it is said that all the citizens, being constantly robbed by thieves,
assembled there and petitioned King Vīraketu.
"O Lord, we are constantly being robbed by thieves here night after night;
yet they are not seen by us. May Your Majesty know what is beyond this."
Thus petitioned by the citizens, the king ordered the night-watchmen to remain concealed throughout the city in order to search for the thieves.
They too did not capture the thieves, for that city was being plundered;
then one night, the king himself went out at will.
Wandering there alone with his sword grasped, he saw on one side a certain man going along the top of a wall.
He was skilled in various gaits with a silent placement of his feet,
and he looked back repeatedly with eyes trembling with apprehension.
"This is surely that thief who robs my city while wandering alone"—
thinking thus, the king approached his vicinity.
Then that thief, seeing the king, asked, "Who are you?
The king replied to that thief, "I am a thief."
Then the thief, having seen him, said: "In that case, you are my equal and a friend to me;

Having heard that, the king said, "So be it," and went with him to that house situated within an underground cavern deep inside the forest.
Richly endowed with every kind of enjoyment, illuminated by shining lamps,

When the king had entered there and taken his seat, that thief then went into the inner chamber.
At that very moment, a certain maidservant approached the king there and said:
"O noble one, how have you entered here into the jaws of death?"
"For this man is a lone thief; having escaped from here, he will surely commit a wicked act as a betrayer of trust.
Therefore, depart quickly from here!"
Thus addressed by her, the king departed quickly from there;
having gone to his own capital, he mobilized his armies during the night.
And having arrived with his army arrayed for battle,

Then, perceiving that his house was besieged and learning of the disclosure of his identity,

Having gone forth, he displayed superhuman prowess in battle;
he lopped off the trunks of elephants and cut through the legs of horses.
And alone, bearing sword and shield, he carried off the heads of the soldiers;
then the king himself rushed toward him once his army had been destroyed.
Knowing the science of swords, the king, by means of a clever maneuver,
snatched the sword from his hand and then also that dagger.
Then, having laid down his own weapon, the king— being himself unarmed—
struck down the thief with a wrestling match on the ground and captured him alive.
Having bound him along with his wealth, he led him to his own city;
and in the morning, he ordered his execution by impalement upon a stake.
And from her palace, the merchant’s daughter Ratnavatī saw that thief being led to the place of execution to the sound of drums.
Upon seeing him, though he was wounded and his limbs were smeared with dust, she, deluded by Māra,
went to her father Ratnadatta and said:
"This man who is being led away for execution—this is the husband chosen by me;
therefore, O father, protect him from the king, lest I die following him."
Having heard that, her father said to her: "What is this you say, daughter?
You who do not desire even kings as husbands, though they long for you?"
"How can you desire this wicked thief who has fallen into calamity?"—
though addressed by her father with these and other words, she did not waver from her resolve.
Then his father went quickly to the king and, even at the cost of all his possessions, begged for the thief's release from execution.
But the king did not release that thief, who had stolen everything, even for hundreds of millions of gold pieces, since he had been brought there as a stake with his own body.
Then, when her father had arrived and turned away, that merchant’s daughter,
having performed her ritual bath, prepared to die following him, even though she was being restrained by her relatives.
Having ascended his palanquin, she went to the execution ground of that bandit,
followed by her weeping father, mother, and the people.
And at that moment, the executioners impaled that thief upon a stake;
with his life-breaths failing, he beheld her thus arrived along with her kinsmen.
Having heard the account from the people, the thief shed tears for a moment and then,
laughing, he gave up his life while upon the stake.
Then, having removed that corpse of the thief from the stake,

And at that very moment, the Lord Bhairava himself, having manifested his presence in this cremation ground while remaining invisible, spoke thus to her from the sky:
"O devoted wife, I am pleased by this devotion of yours toward this very self-choice marriage ceremony; therefore, request a boon from me."
Having heard that boon from the god, she bowed and chose thus:
"O Lord, may there be a hundred sons even for my father, who is currently childless."
To this virtuous woman who had spoken thus— "By this [means], he, whose only son, will not give up his life without me"— the god spoke again.
"May you have a hundred sons for your father; choose another boon as well.
For one of such firm resolve as you deserves no less than this."
Having heard that, she then said: "If the Lord is pleased with me, then let this husband of mine live, and let him always be righteous."
"May it be so! May this husband of yours rise up unhurt and alive;
may the king be righteous, and may Vīraketu be pleased."
When Śarva, whose form was invisible, had spoken thus while stationed in the sky,
that thief rose up at that very moment, alive and with his limbs unhurt.
Then, his heart filled with wonder and joy, the merchant Ratnadatta took his daughter Ratnavatī and that thief, his son-in-law.
Having entered his own palace together with his joyful kinsmen,
he who had obtained the boon of a son celebrated a festival befitting his own joy.
And the king, delighted upon learning the news, summoned that lone hero Vīraketu at that very moment and appointed him as the commander of the army against the thief.
Then, having desisted from theft and married that merchant’s daughter,
Ekavīra lived happily, remaining on the path of righteousness and esteemed by the king.
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla, who was perched upon his shoulder, questioned King Trivikramasena with the fear of the previously uttered curse hanging over him: SoKss_12,21.57 (Vet_14.57) //
O King, tell me: having seen that merchant’s daughter standing there with her father, why did the thief weep and laugh while being impaled on the stake?
Then the king replied: "The thief wept out of sorrow;
therefore, I have not attained freedom from debt toward this friend without cause, thinking, 'I am his merchant.'"
And he laughed out of wonder, thinking: "How is it that this maiden, having rejected excellent kings, is enamored with this man? Oh, how strange is the mind of women!"
When the king had spoken these words, that supreme Vetāla, the master of illusion, departed from his shoulder by his own power to his own abode;
and the king followed after him once more, just as before.
The Twenty-second Wave:
Then, having gone back and once again reached the Vetāla at the śiṃśapā tree,
Trivikramasena took him up and set out once more.
And as that king was approaching with the Vetāla upon his shoulder, the Vetāla spoke to him once more: "O King, listen; I shall tell you this story."
In the land of Nepal there was a city named Śivapura;
in that place, long ago, there lived a king whose name was Yaśaḥketu, which was truly appropriate for him.
Having entrusted the burden of government to his minister named Prajñāsāgara,
he enjoyed worldly pleasures together with the queen named Candraprabhā.
In due time, a daughter was born to that queen from him,
named Śaśiprabhā, whose radiance was like the moon, the eye of the world.
In due course, having reached the prime of youth, she once during the month of Madhu went with her retinue to a garden to see a festival procession.
There, in one part of that place, he saw her intent on gathering flowers,
with one breast revealed by her upraised creeper-like arm.
A wealthy man’s son, a brahmin named Manaḥsvāmin who had come on a journey, saw her looking beautiful with her fingers like pincers grasping a flower-stalk from which the blossom was falling.
By that glance, the youth’s mind was instantly captivated;
though he was the master of his own mind, he became no longer its master, being utterly deluded by passion.
Is this the pleasure of the Mind-born God for the sake of his arrows,
that she herself gathers here the flowers gathered by spring?
"What does this forest deity wish to worship, Mādhava?"—
as he was reflecting thus, the princess also beheld him.
And the moment she beheld him, with his limbs like those of the god of love newly reborn,
she— filled with longing— forgot neither the flowers, nor her own limbs, nor even herself.
While the two of them remained there, their hearts overflowing with mutual love, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! suddenly arose.

he arrived there, provoked by the rage arising from the scent of another elephant that he had perceived.

Thus, due to the incident of the princess who had attained power through illusion,

Therefore, O King, tell me first: to whom does that wife belong? Cut through my doubt, for the agreement previously mentioned applies to you.

And when his son had reached youth, he— urged by virtuous men and by ministers because of that son's qualities— consecrated him as the crown prince.
And while Jīmūtavāhana was established in the position of crown prince,
his father’s ministers, desiring his welfare, approached him and spoke.
"O Lord, this Kalpavṛkṣa tree of yours, which grants all desires and is unassailable by all beings— this very tree shall always be worthy of your worship."
"For as long as he exists, even Śakra could not harm us, let alone anyone else.
Having heard this, Jīmūtavāhana thought to himself:
"Alas! Having obtained such a celestial tree as this, why have our ancestors not attained from it any such fruit as this?"
By seeking even a few objects of desire suited only for the base,
both this man and that Great Soul have been brought to insignificance in the eyes of the world.
"I shall accomplish this desire that has arisen in our minds";

There, having satisfied his father— who was seated comfortably in a secluded place— by performing every service he had been instructed to perform, he addressed him.
Therefore, you yourself know that in this ocean of existence,

Where and when have the twilight, lightning, and the goddess Lakṣmī— each dissolving as soon as its light appears for a very brief moment— ever been seen to be stable?
In this world, however, there is one thing that is imperishable: service rendered to others, which gives birth to merit and fame that remain witnesses until the end of hundreds of ages.
Therefore, dear father, for what purpose should we guard this wish-fulfilling tree in vain, while these enjoyments are so transitory?
By whomsoever this was guarded by such attachment as "this is mine," where are those former ones now? Where is he, and who is he, or what is his relation to them?
Therefore, O Father, by your command, I shall employ this wish-granting kalpa-tree for the sole purpose of accomplishing the benefit of others.
Having been granted permission by his father with the words "So be it," Jīmūtavāhana then went and spoke to that wish-fulfilling tree.
"O Lord, our ancestors' cherished desires were fulfilled by you;
therefore, fulfill this one unique desire of mine."
"Act so that I may see this earth free from poverty;

When Jīmūtavāhana had spoken thus with palms joined in reverence, a voice issued from that tree:

In an instant, that wish-fulfilling tree rose up to heaven and rained down wealth upon the earth,

Then, because of that intense compassion for all sentient beings,
Jīmūtavāhana’s fame spread throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, all those born of his lineage, unable to endure it out of envy,
[lamented] him who was now deprived of that wish-fulfilling tree that had made worldly suffering its own and destroyed all distress.
Considering him as one who had his father still alive, they united and made a firm resolve;
desiring to seize that kingdom, they armed themselves for battle.
Seeing that, Jīmūtavāhana said to his father:
"Father, when you have taken up your weapons, who else possesses such power?"
But who indeed, having slain their kinsmen out of no pity, would desire sovereignty for the sake of this evil, perishing body?
Therefore, what need have we for sovereignty? Having gone elsewhere, wherever it may be, we shall practice only the Dharma, which brings happiness in both worlds.
"Let these wretched heirs, greedy for the kingdom, rejoice!
To him who had spoken thus, his father Jīmūtaketu said:
"O son, I desire the kingdom for your sake;
if you, being filled with compassion, renounce it, what is the use of that to me, who am old?"
Having been thus granted permission by his father and mother,
Jīmūtavāhana, having renounced the kingdom, went to the Malaya mountain accompanied by them.
There, in a mountain cave with waterfalls covered by sandalwood trees,
he remained, having established a hermitage and attending upon his father.
And there he obtained a friend known as Mitrāvasu,
the son of Viśvāvasu, a king of the Siddhas who resided in that very place.
Once, while wandering there,
Jīmūtavāhana entered a temple of the goddess Gaurī situated in a grove to pay her homage.

accompanied by her circle of female friends, intent upon the worship of the Daughter of the Mountain.
The deer stood motionless as if ashamed by the beauty of her eyes, while listening to the sweet sound of the lute in its accompaniment with song.
Bearing Kṛṣṇa as its savior with its own eyes,

As if desiring to gaze upon the moon of her face through their mutual rivalry,

As he was fashioning it from the clay, his fingers were pressed together as if in a fistful;

Then Jīmūtavāhana asked her friend:

He spoke to Malayavatī with words softened by a smile:

When she said, "For this guest has arrived, who is worthy of worship by the whole world," the daughter of the Vidyādhara remained silent, her face bowed down with shame.

And Jīmūtavāhana, overflowing with love,
took that garland and placed it around Malayavatī’s neck.

fixed her gaze upon him as if it were a garland made of blue lotuses.
Thus, having approached those two who were engaged in a special self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*) where no word was spoken by either,
a certain maidservant spoke to that Siddha-maiden.
"O princess, your mother remembers you; come back without delay.

And as he stood there astonished, the courtesans approached him from that city and said:
"Arise, my lord! Come, bathe, eat, and cast off your fatigue."
Having said this, he led him inside, bathed him, and anointed him;
then, provided with excellent garments by them, he was conducted to another superior dwelling.
There within, the youth beheld a certain preeminent young woman,
beautiful in every limb, as if she had been fashioned by the Creator out of mere curiosity.
Then, rising with longing, he sat upon half of her own seat and partook there of divine food together with her.
Having enjoyed the sweetness of ripe fruit and betel-leaf, and with his natural vigor,
he partook of the pleasure of her company at night while reclining on a couch.
Having awakened in the morning, he saw only that temple of Śiva there;
neither the celestial woman, nor that city, nor his retinue was to be found.
Then, distressed, he addressed that ascetic in the morning as he emerged from his hut with a smiling face, having been asked about the comfort of his night.
"Through his grace, O Blessed One, I have dwelt happily during the night;
however, my life-breaths will depart without that divine woman."
Having heard that, the compassionate ascetic said to him with a smile:
"Stay right here; tonight will come again for you in the same way."
When that ascetic had spoken thus, by that very logic,
Candrasvāmin enjoyed those pleasures here every night through his favor.
And having gradually understood that power of knowledge,
impelled by destiny, he once propitiated that lord of ascetics and made this request.
"If it be true, O Blessed One, that you have compassion for me who has come to you for refuge,

To him who was speaking thus with persistence, the ascetic replied:
"This science is impossible for you to master; for it is mastered only beneath the water."
And there, as the practitioner recites it, this net of illusion is swiftly created for his utter delusion, by which he does not attain accomplishment.
For there he beholds himself born again as a child;
then as a youth who has taken a wife and likewise as one whose children have been born.
"He is my friend, he is my enemy"—thus he is deluded by falsehood;
he does not remember this birth, nor the practice performed for the sake of attaining knowledge.
But he who, having reached twenty-four years of age, has been awakened by the teacher’s knowledge,
remembers his birth and understands that it is a manifestation of Māyā— he is steadfast.
Under its influence, he likewise enters the fire here;
yet, having crossed over the waters, he who has mastered the vidyā perceives the ultimate reality.
This knowledge does not belong to anyone else; for it succeeds only for the disciple. If it is imparted to an unworthy person, it perishes even for the teacher.
Since the fruit is already established by my own success, what is the use of this grasping on your part?
Should my success fail, even this [grasping] of yours will surely perish.
Even though the ascetic spoke thus, Candrasvāmin, being possessed by a planetary influence, said to him:

Then that ascetic agreed to bestow that knowledge upon him;
alas, what will the virtuous not do out of consideration for those who have sought their protection?
Then, having led him to the riverbank, that practitioner of the great vow said to him:

Awakened by me through this instruction, you should enter the very fire of illusion;

the best among those who observe vows, taught that science correctly to Candrasvāmin, who was himself pure and had performed the ritual sipping of water.

As he was intent on entering the fire to attain the fruit of his divine goal,

Seeing there his aged parents and his wife intent on death,

"Let me enter that fire according to my desire," reflecting thus within himself,

Having experienced the touch of snow and being filled with wonder at the fire,

"Since this is unprecedented in the accomplishment of this science," having heard these words of the teacher, Candrasvāmin said:

Thereupon, his preceptor, desiring to test his knowledge, called that spell to mind.

Having thus told this story, the Vetāla then questioned King Trivikramasena once more, after stating the previously mentioned condition.

For even through difficult deeds performed with purity alone, a person cannot attain perfection,

But the mind of that dull young Brahmin, though awakened here, continued to conceptualize;

Thus, having uttered these words for that king, the excellent Vetāla once more vanished from his shoulder to his own place, unseen; and the king followed after him in exactly the same manner.

Then King Trivikramasena, having gone back to the śiṃśapā tree, once again took the Vetāla upon his shoulder and set out.
And as he was approaching, that vetāla spoke to him again:

There is a city named Vakrolaka, resembling the city of the gods;
in it there was a king named Sūryaprabha, who was like Indra, the slayer of Jambha.
With a form intent on ease, he gave joy to the earth;
having lifted it up like Hari, he bore it for a long time upon his arm.

Although he was enriched with every kind of prosperity, there was one thing that brought him no peace:

And at this point in the narrative, in the great city of Tāmraliptī,

And to him was born an only daughter named Dhanavatī,
a Vidyādharī fallen from her station due to a curse, who was clearly indicated by her very beauty.
And while she was still in her youth, that merchant passed away;
then, due to the lack of royal protection, his wealth was seized by his kinsmen.
Then his wife, named Hiraṇyavatī,
taking her own collection of jeweled ornaments that had remained hidden away, [departed].

Darkened both outside and within by gloom and suffering,

There, walking through the thick darkness by the turn of fate,

Still alive, he was further pained by the friction against the tip of his shoulder;
"Ah! Who has thrown this caustic upon my wound? he cried out.

"Even now, on this stake, my life-breaths do not depart.

Having heard that, just as the merchant’s wife was telling her own story,

There, while King Sūryaprabha brings the people to the happiness of good governance,

Having stayed there and cremated that body by means of a stratagem,

On another day, having secured her wealth and departed from there with her daughter,

There, having purchased a house from an excellent merchant named Vasudatta,

And at that time, there was a preceptor named Viṣṇusvāmin in that city;

Although he was endowed with learning and noble lineage, being overcome by youth,

"Mother, look at the beauty and youth of this son of a Brahmin;

Having heard this and perceiving that she was deeply in love with him,

Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a son, should not this very person be sought as a suitor by my daughter,

Having reflected thus, he dispatched a maidservant who kept secrets, instructing her with his intended purpose, in order to bring him for the sake of his daughter.
Having gone and led her to a secluded place, the maidservant told him that;

"If five hundred gold dīnāras are given for the sake of Haṃsāvalī, that is bearable; I will go for just one night."
When the merchant’s wife had been told this by the maidservant who had gone [to her], she sent that wealth to him in the servant's hand.

There he beheld his beloved, her longing intensified, adorning the surface of the earth; like a cakora bird at the sight of moonlight, he both gazed upon her and rejoiced.
Having spent that night with her in the play of sexual union,

Dhanavatī, the merchant’s daughter, also became pregnant from him;

Then, as she and her mother were completely satisfied by the birth of their son,

"Taking this boy, adorned with a thousand pieces of gold,

When the wielder of the trident had said, "Thus shall there be safety," that merchant's daughter and her mother awoke from their sleep and spoke to one another.
And having led him there, they abandoned the child— along with his golden ornaments— at the main gate of King Sūryaprabha, out of faith in the Blessed One.
And at that time, the Bull-bannered God commanded King Sūryaprabha, who was constantly distressed by anxiety for his son, even in a dream.

And having seen that boy at the main gate, together with his heap of gold, his hands and feet marked with lines, umbrellas, banners, and other signs, and possessing an auspicious form; so it is said in Sūtrakṛtāṅga 12.26.55 (Vetāla 19.55).
Saying, "This son has been granted to me by Śambhu as one appropriate for me," he took him in his own arms and entered the capital city.
He held a festival for so long, bestowing such immeasurable wealth,

Having passed twelve days with dances, music, and other festivities,

Then, in due course, that prince Candraprabha grew there both in physical form and in a flood of virtues that bestowed joy upon those who relied upon him.

Having seen him become such as that, his father Sūryaprabha,

And while that son of his, who was possessed of statesmanship, was ruling the earth,
the king abandoned his body there by practicing intense austerity.
Having learned of that misfortune of his father and having performed the funeral rites after mourning him,
the righteous King Candraprabha then spoke to his ministers:

"Having brought them, I shall cast his bones into the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite;

As the king said, "In passing, I shall also undertake a pilgrimage to the holy fords as far as the eastern ocean," his ministers addressed him thus:

"Where is the life of a wanderer, fraught with many perils, and where are kings, who are ever-protected?
Hearing these words of the minister, King Candraprabha replied:
"Enough with these doubts; it is certain that I must go for the sake of my father, and I shall visit the sacred fords as long as my youth permits."
"Who knows what will happen next in this body that perishes in an instant?

Having heard this resolve of the king, the ministers remained silent;
then that monarch prepared the requisites for the journey.
Then, on that auspicious day, having bathed, offered oblations into the fire, and honored the twice-born,
he mounted a well-yoked chariot, self-restrained and wearing peaceful attire.
He turned back the neighboring princes, the citizens, and even the people from the countryside who, though unwilling, had followed him with great difficulty as far as the borders.
King Candraprabha, having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, set out together with the Brahmins mounted on their vehicles and accompanied by his domestic chaplain.
Delighted by observing various costumes, languages, and other such sights,
and beholding many kinds of lands, he eventually reached the Ganges.
And he beheld her creating, as it were, a flight of stairs for ascending to the third heaven by means of the rows of water-waves for all living beings.
She who originates from the Himavat, who playfully seized Śambhu by the hair,
who bears the playful grace of Ambikā, and who is worshipped by the hosts of gods and sages.
Having descended from his chariot and performed his ritual ablutions there according to the prescribed rites,
he cast the bones of that king, Sūryaprabha, into it.
Having given gifts and performed the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), he then mounted his chariot and set forth;

Where the currents of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā appear like the paths of light and smoke meeting at the sacrificial fire, leading men toward the state of the Sugata.
Having fasted there and performed the auspicious rites of bathing, giving, and ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*),
King Candraprabha then departed for Vārāṇasī.

Having fasted for three days in that place and having worshipped the bull-bannered god with various offerings appropriate to himself, he set out toward Gayā.
Then, as if being praised with prostrations at every step by the trees, which were bowed down by the weight of their fruits and filled with birds warbling sweetly, he proceeded.
As if being honored by the winds with scattered wild flowers,

And having performed there a *śrāddha* ceremony according to the rules with abundant sacrificial fees,

As he was offering the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his father at Gayākūpa,

"We do not know where this body should be placed, nor what this might become.

The Twenty-Seventh Wave. Then King Trivikramasena, having gone and taken the Vetāla upon his shoulder from the śiṃśapā tree, set out once more.
As he was departing in silence, the Vetāla spoke to him from his shoulder:
"O King, what is this persistence of yours? Go and enjoy the comfort of sleep."
"It is not right for you to lead me into the domain of that wicked monk;
or rather, let there be a seizure there—listen to this one story."
There is a city named Citrakūṭa, which maintains its distinction through the arrangement of letters that do not deviate from their own lines, and which bears the name "Truth."
There, a king named Candrāvaloka, the crest-jewel of monarchs, reigned; he showered the rain of the essence of nectar upon the eyes of those who loved him.
The wise have proclaimed him to be the tethering post for the elephant of valor, the birthplace of generosity,
and the pleasure-chamber of beauty.
Although all prosperity was present, that one thing which was appropriate for him—a wife—remained unattained; this alone became the supreme anxiety in the heart of that youth.
And once, in order to dispel that distress, the king went to a great forest for the hunt, accompanied by his cavalry.
There, piercing the herds of boars with continuous arrows,

Lying upon beds of arrows, those lions fierce in battle were made formidable by their white locks of hair; yet he whose prowess surpassed even Arjuna lay there himself.
Treating the śarabhas as adversaries, he brought down those mountain-like creatures with the blows of his spears, as hard as the thunderbolt, displaying the prowess of Indra, the enemy of Jambha.
Desiring to enter the interior of the forest alone,
the king urged on his horse with a sharp kick from the heel.
Stimulated intensely by that stroke of the whip, the steed,
disregarding in an instant all uneven ground as if it were level, was spurred on by the pressure of the heel.
Then, with a speed exceeding that of the wind, he led the king to another forest,
having bypassed him by a distance of ten yojanas while his sensory faculties remained deluded.
While the army remained there, the king,
having lost his sense of direction and wandering about exhausted, saw nearby a single, very vast lake.
With lotuses repeatedly bent down and raised by the wind blowing against them, they seemed to be beckoning him with their hand-like gestures, saying, "Come this way."
Having gone there, he found the horse refreshed with a change of fodder,
