Having himself performed his ablutions, drunk water, and dispelled his fatigue,
he cast his gaze here and there upon those beautiful regions.
And in one place, beneath an aśoka tree, he saw a young female ascetic,
adorned with ornaments of freshly plucked flowers and graced by garments of bark.
The king beheld her, whose form was a marvel, accompanied by a female companion, and who was exceedingly beautiful with her mass of matted hair tied in a charming fashion.
And he thought: "Who might this woman be who has fallen within the range of the arrows of the Flower-Bowed God? Could she be Sāvitrī herself, come here to bathe in the lake?"
Has Gaurī, having fallen from the lap of Hara, undertaken asceticism once more?
Or is it the luster of the moon, which has set during the day, that has taken up a vow?
"Having approached her here, I shall slowly obtain my boon,"—
having reflected thus, the king went into the presence of that maiden.
She too, seeing him approaching, her eyes agitated by his form and her hands occupied with the flower-garland she had previously begun to weave, reflected:
Who is this man in this forest? Is he a perfected one (*siddha*) or perhaps a knowledge-holder (*vidyādhara*)?
Ah! His form brings fulfillment to the eyes of the entire world.
Having reflected thus and looking askance at him with shame,

Then that city-dweller, having approached her, spoke thus:

When the king had spoken thus, her friend, who was equally discerning,
seated her there and performed the rites of hospitality for the monarch.
Then the king, full of longing, affectionately asked her:
"O blessed lady, what meritorious lineage is adorned by this friend of yours?"
"What are these syllables of her name that drip nectar into the ears?
And why is this body of hers so delicate as a flower?"
Hearing the king’s words, “She is being made to suffer in this desolate place by a mode of life suited for ascetics,” her friend replied:
This daughter of the great seer Kaṇva was raised in the hermitage;
born of Menakā, this maiden is named Indīvaraprabhā.
Having come here to this lake to bathe with her father’s permission, she said:
"Not far from here is the hermitage of that father of mine."
Thus addressed by her, the king was delighted; mounting his horse, he went to the hermitage of the seer Kaṇva to ask for that daughter.
Having dismounted his vehicle and remained outside, he entered that place humbly,

And in their midst he saw the sage Kaṇva, surrounded by seers,
gladdening with his splendor like the moon among the planets.
Having approached him, he bowed at his feet; and that wise sage, once the guest had been settled and rested after being provided with hospitality, spoke to him quickly.
Child Candrāvaloka, listen to these words of mine for your benefit:
you know well what kind of fear of death exists for living beings in this saṃsāra.
Why then do you kill these wretched deer for no reason at all?
For the Creator fashioned the weapon of the Kṣatriya for the purpose of protecting the frightened.
Therefore, protect your subjects according to dharma and uproot the thorns [of your enemies];
achieve moving prosperity and other goals through training in elephants, horses, weapons, and the like.
Enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty, bestow wealth, and spread your fame in all directions;
abandon this predatory addiction to hunting, which is but the sport of Death.
Where the negligence of both the slayer and the victim is equal, what is the use of that which brings such great harm? Has the conduct of Pāṇḍu not been heard by you?
Having heard these words of the sage Kaṇva and having greeted them with approval,
King Candrāvaloka, who understood their meaning, replied to him.
"I have been instructed by you, O Blessed One; you have bestowed upon me the supreme favor.
I shall desist from hunting; let all living beings be free from fear."
Having heard that, the sage said: "I am pleased with this gift of safety to living beings by you; therefore, choose the boon you desire."
Thus addressed by that sage, the king, who knew the proper time, replied:
"If you are pleased, give me your daughter Indīvaraprabhā."
To the king who had thus requested her, the sage gave that suitable maiden, born of an Apsaras, who was currently engaged in her bath.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony, he took her— adorned by the wife of the sage and followed by the weeping ascetics— as far as his own hermitage.
Taking his wife Indīvaraprabhā and mounting his horse,
King Candrāvaloka then departed swiftly from that place.
And as he was going, seeing that day’s extensive activity,
the sun, as if distressed, settled upon the peak of the western mountain.
And the deer-eyed woman, her passion gradually intensified,

At that time, on the road, the king came upon an aśvattha tree standing on the bank of the water of a pond as pure as the heart of a virtuous person.
Seeing that place, its ground dark green with grass and covered by a flood of branches and leaves, he made this resolve in his heart: "I shall dwell here for the night."

Then,

and the king, with even greater resolve, ran after him again, for the steadfastness of the courageous, which surpasses the principal mountains, remains unshaken even at the end of an aeon, as they strive to attain their goal.
The Thirty-first Wave.
Then, in that terrifying cremation ground, the hero [beheld] that night-demoness, dark as the gloom, her eyes aflame with the fire of the funeral pyre.

There was once a certain regional king in the Deccan named Dharma, a leader among the virtuous and born of many lineages.
He had a wife named Candravatī, born in the land of Mālava,

And upon that wife of the king,
there was born a daughter alone named Lāvaṇyavatī, whose name was truly significant of her beauty.

As he entered it, the dew-droplets seemed to shed tears;

Then the sun, with its rays raised like hands, ascended the eastern mountain as if to ward him off,

Then, with his feet wounded by the thorns of *kuśa* grass, that king traveled on foot with his sons and wife and reached a village of the *bhillas*.
It was crowded with men who robbed others of their lives and all their possessions,
devoid of righteous people, and difficult to traverse like the city of Death.
There, upon seeing the king from afar, adorned with his garments and ornaments,
many Śabaras bearing various weapons rushed forward to plunder him.
Seeing them, King Dharma said to his son and wife:
"Before the barbarians touch you, enter the forest from here."
Thus addressed by the king, Queen Candravatī entered the middle of the forest out of fear, together with her daughter Lāvaṇyavatī.
The king too, bearing sword and shield,
slew many of those brave Śabaras who came toward him with arrows in their hands.
Then, commanded by their leader, the entire village fell upon him and killed the king alone, whose skin was wounded by their blows.
When the army of bandits had departed with the seized ornaments,
she, standing within a thicket of forest trees at a distance, beheld her husband slain.
There, Queen Candravatī, overwhelmed with distress, fled together with her daughter and entered deep into the dense forest.
There, even though the shadows had retreated into the roots of the trees along with the travelers— like those afflicted by the heat of midday— the shadows remained cool.
On one side of the lotus pond, at the foot of an *aśoka* tree,

Just then, a certain great man, a resident of the vicinity, arrived at that forest on horseback with his son for the sake of hunting.
And Caṇḍasiṃha, seeing there the tracks of their feet rising from the dust, spoke to his son Siṃhaparākrama:
"If these two women of auspicious marks and good fortune follow you and obtain you,
then choose one of them as you please."
To him who had spoken thus, his son Siṃhaparākrama said:
"She whose feet are so delicate appears to me as the one to be my wife."
"I know that she, being of very young age, is surely suitable for me;
but this one, with her large feet, is fit for you, who are advanced in years."
Having heard these words of his son, Caṇḍasiṃha said to him:
"What kind of talk is this? Your mother has indeed only recently departed to heaven."
"When such a virtuous wife has departed, where else could there be any attachment?
Having heard that, the son also spoke to Caṇḍasiṃha.
"Father, do not say so; for the house of a householder is empty and desolate without a wife.

Where does a non-fool enter that fortress known as a "house"— which is unchained— when his beloved, with her firm breasts and hips, no longer stands there watching the path?
"By my life, O father, you are adjured: if you do not accept her as a second wife for my sake, you shall be cursed."
Having heard these words of his son and having agreed with them, Caṇḍasiṃha, accompanied by his friend, followed the trail of footprints and proceeded slowly.
And having reached that lake, he beheld Queen Śyāmā, who was adorned by a multitude of pearls like stars, shining like the moon.

And full of curiosity, he approached her together with his son;

"Enough with this fear, O Mother; these two are not thieves. They have gentle appearances and are well-attired; they have surely come here for the sake of hunting."
When the queen had been addressed thus by her daughter and was wavering there,

When Manmatha was consumed by the flames of the fire from Śiva’s eye and had fallen into distress,

The thirty-third wave.
Homage to the Conqueror of Obstacles, upon whose knee-region [the moon] revolves.
Like a garland of stars fallen from a jar as he dances through the nights.
Then, at the conclusion of the conversation, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having regained Vikramakeśarī, rose up from the middle of the road, filled with joy.
Accompanied by Guṇākara as well as Vimalabuddhi,
he was endowed with various stories and possessed formidable prowess.
Endowed with fierce power and accompanied by the brahmin Śrutadhi,
he searched for his remaining friends who had been separated from him by a curse.
In order to obtain Śaśāṅkavatī, he set out once more toward Ujjayinī, having previously begun his journey, now proceeding with his own eighth self.
And in due course, he reached a forest whose waters were dried up by the summer heat,
devoid of trees, and where the sands were scorched by the fierce rays of the sun.
As he was walking through it, the prince said to his ministers:
"Behold, how difficult to traverse and terrifyingly vast is this forest!"
For this [city], strayed from its path and abandoned by people, is without refuge;
it is like the rising flames of the fire of suffering, these mirages in the desert.
With its scattered, coarse hair of grass dry and rustling,
it seemed to have its body-hairs standing on end from the terror of lions, tigers, and other beasts, as if covered in thorns.
"Appearing as if weeping due to the cries of deer exhausted by the heat and longing for water,
this vast expanse must now be crossed by us with haste."
Having spoken thus, Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with those ministers who were afflicted by hunger and thirst,
quickly traversed that forest.
And he saw before him a very great lake, filled with clear, cool water,
as if with the liquefied essences of the moon melted by the sun's heat.
It was like a jeweled mirror fashioned by the Fortune of the Three Worlds to behold her own reflection, whose expansive reach pervades the ends of the earth.
It bore the likeness of the *Mahābhārata*, with the agitation caused by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the diverse delusions of Arjuna, and the sweet flavor that provides rest.
With the supreme poison swallowed by the blue-throated one (Śiva) approaching his side,
and with Lakṣmī resting upon Acyuta (Viṣṇu), it resembled the ocean at the time of churning.
Its interior was deep and cool, untouched by the rays of the sun;
it was like the subterranean realm of Pātāla, which dwells upon the earth and is the abode of infinite lotuses.
And on the western shore of that lake,
the prince, together with his minister, beheld a great celestial tree.
With its multitude of spreading branch-arms shaken by the wind,
and with the river of clouds clinging to its crest, it was like Śaṅkara dancing.
With its exceedingly lofty head reaching up to the surface of the sky,
it seemed as if striving out of curiosity to behold the splendor of the Nandana grove.
It was radiant with fruits of divine flavor hanging from its branches,
like a wish-fulfilling tree adorned by the gods with jars of nectar.
With its swaying tips of sprouts acting as hands, it seemed to cry out again and again with the cries of birds, "Let no one touch me in such a manner!"
While the lord Mṛgāṅkadatta was thus gazing upon him,
his ministers, afflicted by hunger and thirst, rushed toward him.
Having climbed that tree to eat its fruits, as soon as they saw them,
all six of them unexpectedly attained the state of being fruits, even though they were human beings.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, seeing those friends nowhere,
became distraught and called out to each one of them by name at that tree.
When they gave no answer and were nowhere to be seen, he spoke with a voice distressed by despair: "Alas, alas! I am destroyed! (SoKss 12.33.25)
That prince fell there upon the surface of the earth, unconscious,
while the twice-born Śrutadhi remained standing at his side, having not yet climbed the tree.
And at that moment, the wise brahmin Śrutadhi, having consoled him, said:
"O Lord, though you possess perfected wisdom, why do you lose heart and despair?"
For he indeed attains prosperity who does not lose his composure in adversity;
have you not reached these very people who were freed from the serpent’s curse?
In this very way, you shall again obtain these ministers and others as well;
moreover, your union with Śaśāṅkavatī will take place before long.
Thus addressed by Śrutadhī, the prince said:
"Whence has this come? Surely this was not designed by the Creator for our destruction."
Otherwise, where would there be a vetāla at night, and where the heroic prowess of Bhīma?
And where would there be knowledge of Śaśāṅkavatī, through the occasion of her conversation with him?
And where was our departure from Ayodhyā in order to attain that [state],
and where was our mutual separation in the Vindhya forest due to the curse of the Nāga?
Then, for some among us, where was our gradual meeting?
And now, O friend, where is this separation, this abandonment of what is dear?
"For they have been seized by a spirit in this tree; without them, what is Śaśāṅkavatī to me, and what is life? Enough with these delusions!"
Having spoken thus, Mṛgāṅkadatta rose up there in the lake to cast himself in, even as Śrutadhi sought to restrain him out of grief.
At that moment, an incorporeal voice arose from the sky:
"O son, do not act rashly; for everything shall turn out well for you."
The god Gaṇapati himself dwells in this tree,
yet he has been insulted today by these ministers of yours out of ignorance.
For they were impure, having neither sipped water nor washed their hands and feet;
afflicted by hunger and desiring fruit, they had climbed up into this dwelling.
Then, once those [fruits] were touched there, they attained the state of being fruits;
for by the curse of Vighneśa, it was decreed that "whatever one's mind is set upon, to that state shall one go."
Moreover, those other four ministers of yours who came by this very same path likewise ascended it and attained the state of its fruit.
Therefore, propitiate this Leader of the Gaṇas with austerities;
through his grace, the accomplishment of all your desires shall come to pass.
Thus addressed by a voice from the sky, which seemed to pour forth a stream of nectar,
Mṛgāṅkadatta regained his resolve and desisted from abandoning his body.
Having bathed in the lake and worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas beneath that tree,
he abandoned all food and, with palms joined in reverence, praised him.

Victory to you, O Lord with the elephant’s face, who are being prostrated to by the entire world— including its mountains, forests, and the earth itself— as it bows down, weighed down by the burden of crushing the ostentation of your own cosmic dance.
Victory to you, whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by the three worlds including the gods, asuras, and humans;
O treasure-store overflowing with various supreme siddhis, whose form is like a jar!

Victory to you, whose blazing splendor is like twelve fierce suns risen simultaneously; you who bring about the untimely end of the world for the hosts of Daityas, who were invincible even to Hara, Hari, and the Lord of the Gods!
Victory to You, O Dispeller of the misfortunes of Your devotees, whose palm shines with the flame of fire held in hand like an excellent axe, as if by the torch of a playful *nīrājana* ceremony!

O Gaṇeśa, you who were worshipped by Gaurī as well for the sake of her husband’s desired success in the conquest of Tripura—to you, who have taken refuge in that [Lord Śiva], I go for shelter; let there be salutation to you!
Having thus praised the Lord of Obstacles, Mṛgāṅkadatta passed that night at the foot of that tree, fasting upon a bed of kusha grass.
In that very manner, for eleven days,
the prince spent his time devoted to the worship of Vighneśa while Śrutadhi served as his attendant.
On the night of the twelfth day, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke to him in a dream:
"Child, I am pleased with you; you shall regain your ministers, released from their curse."
And having gone with them and found Śaśāṅkavatī in due course,
you shall return to your own city and rule over the earth.
Thus instructed by Gaṇeśvara at the end of the night,
the awakened Mṛgāṅkadatta related that dream he had seen to Śrutadhi.
Having been welcomed by him, he bathed in the morning, worshipped Vināyaka,
and performed circumambulation as far as that tree where he had resided.
Then, having descended from that tree together, all ten of those ministers, who had been called "fruits," fell at his feet.
Vyāghrasena, as well as Sthūlabāhu and Meghabala,
and Dṛḍhamuṣṭi as the fourth— these six who were described here at the beginning.
Then, having suddenly met all those ministers together with a gaze agitated by emotion and a voice faltering with joy,
the son of the lord of men— accomplished in virtue— looked upon each one repeatedly with exceeding affection, embraced them, and thereafter conversed with them.
Seeing their lord emaciated like the new moon and having performed such austerities, they shed tears;
and having heard the truth as declared by Śrutadhi, they praised him and considered themselves not to have lived in vain.

Then, having regained his fortitude for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, Mṛgāṅkadatta joyfully performed his breaking of the fast with those ministers at that lake, after they had first bathed and attended to their other needs.
Thus ends the thirty-third wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The thirty-fourth wave:
Then, having broken his fast and being well-composed, he remained there on the shore of the lake.
Mṛgāṅkadatta sat down together with those ministers of his own.
Then, when those four of his own ministers arrived that day,
he respectfully questioned them regarding the events of their time apart from him.
Then he, named Vyāghrasena, spoke to him from among them:
"O Lord, please hear our story; I shall describe it."
When, due to the curse of that nāga named Pārāvata,
I became deprived of consciousness and fell far away from you, [I was lost].
Then, having wandered through the forest at night, although I regained consciousness after a long time,
I could see neither the directions nor the path, being shrouded in darkness.
And when that long night of suffering had passed with great difficulty,
the Blessed Sun arose, gradually illuminating the quarters of the sky.
I thought: "Alas, what a tragedy! Where has our lord gone?
Separated from us and all alone, how will he fare here?"
"How shall I find him? Where shall I search? What is my recourse?
It would be better for me to go to Ujjayinī; perhaps he might be found there."
"Indeed, she must go for the sake of Śaśāṅkavatī, for she remains there. With this hope, I gradually set out toward Ujjayinī.
Then, entering that difficult forest which was like a state of misfortune,
he was scorched by the sun's rays as if by heaps of burning embers.
Somehow I reached a lake whose lotuses were like blossoming eyes,
which seemed to engage in conversation through the sweet cries of swans and other birds.
With the tips of his hands extended like waves, possessing a serene and vast intention,
he is like a true being who, by the mere sight of him, removes all suffering.
Having bathed there, eaten, and drunk the water and lotus stalks,
while I was standing there, I saw these three arrive.
Then, having approached Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Sthūlabāhu, and Meghabala,
we inquired among ourselves after your welfare.
And though we were all ignorant of this, fearing some evil,
we resolved to give up our lives, unable to endure separation from you.
And at that moment, a young son of a sage named Mahātapa, the son of Dīrghatapas, came to that lake to bathe.
With his own flames made into matted locks, like Agni desiring once more to burn the Khāṇḍava forest, he took recourse in the body of Brahmā, blazing with splendor.
Clad in a black antelope skin, holding a water-pot in his left hand,
and bearing a rosary and a ring in his right hand.
Accompanied by deer who had come together and were bathing in the mud dug up by their horns,
he was joined by a few other young sons of sages who were his equals.
He approached us the very moment he saw us prepared to leap into the lake;
for the virtuous, moistened with compassion, are kinsmen to all without cause.
And he said: "You must not commit evil deeds worthy of base men;
for those who are blinded by suffering and cowardly fall indeed into the abysses of calamity."
But the wise, who have seen the true path and possess the stainless eye of discernment, do not fall into the pit; they reach what is to be reached and necessarily attain it.
And you possess auspicious forms; you will surely attain what is beneficial.
Therefore, tell me: what is the suffering that afflicts your minds? For my own heart is pained.
To that son of a sage who had spoken thus, I immediately related my entire life story from its very beginning.
Then, having been awakened by him with various words that revealed the future,
I was turned away from abandoning the body, even though he was accompanied by his followers.
Then, having bathed, that young son of a sage led us not very far from there to his father’s hermitage, desiring to offer us hospitality.

There, even the trees— with their high branches and arms raised upward, standing upon the altars as if they had begun a penance, and drinking in the rays of the sun— [seemed to be practicing austerities].
Having seated us in one place and offered us water for our feet, that son of the sage went to each of the trees of the hermitage and begged for alms.
In an instant, his alms-bowl was filled with fruits that had fallen of their own accord from those trees; then, taking it, he came into our presence.
And he gave us those fruits of divine flavor,
by eating which we then became satisfied as if by nectar.
When the day had ended and the sun had fallen into the ocean, the sky was filled with celestial lights,
as if by droplets of water splashed up by that very fall.
As if out of weariness with that [world], when the moon had taken its place upon the peak of the eastern mountain— a grove of asceticism— clad in bark garments washed white by the moonlight.
We went there to see the sages seated together in one place, who had completed all their own duties within that hermitage.
Having prostrated and sat down, we were quickly asked by those great seers—who had offered us hospitality and spoke kindly—“From where have you come? (SoKss 12.34.34)
Then that young sage related to them the entire account concerning us,
ending with our entry into his hermitage.
Then a wise sage named Kaṇva spoke to us there:
"O sirs, why have you, though being heroic men, fallen into such cowardice?"
Maintaining fortitude in adversity, remaining free from pride in prosperity, and never abandoning one's enthusiasm— this indeed is the vow of a virtuous person.
And the great ones, having crossed over great hardships through fortitude and having attained great goals, have obtained the title of "Great. (SoK 12.34.38)
This is the story of Sundarasena; hear now how he experienced suffering for the sake of Mandāravatī.
Having spoken thus, the sage Kaṇva described this story to all the great seers there while we were listening.
There is a country named Niṣadha, which adorns the face of the northern quarter;
in that place, there once existed a city called Alakā.
In that city, the people were always happy, with all their needs and purposes fulfilled;
the only thing that was never at rest were the jewel-lamps.
In that city there was a lord of the earth named Mahāsena, whose name was true to his character;
though born in the month of Śaraja, he scorched his enemies with a fierce and terrible heat.
That king had a great minister named Guṇapālita,
an abode of valor who bore the burden of the earth like another Śeṣa.
When the king had laid his burden upon him, being thus at ease and having destroyed his enemies,
a son was born to him by the queen named Śaśiprabhā.
He who was named Sundarasena, though but a child yet mature in his virtues,
was chosen as his own husband by the goddesses of Heroism and Beauty at their self-choice ceremony.
There, that prince had five heroic ministers who were his equals in age and virtue, having grown up together with him since childhood.
Caṇḍaprabha, Bhīmabhuja, as well as Vyāghraparākrama,
the hero Vikramaśakti, and Dṛḍhabuddhi was the fifth.
And all those great beings were endowed with strength and intelligence;
they were of noble birth, devoted to their master, and even understood the cries of birds.
There, in his father's house, the prince lived together with them;
though young, he remained without a wife and without a retinue, as he lacked a suitable consort.
In this world, a man is honored for valor that does not retreat, for wealth earned by one's own arms,
and for a wife who is a match for his beauty.
Otherwise, what would be the use of these three? Thus he reflected;
and then that hero Sundarasena, together with those ministers—
And once, accompanied by his armies and those five companions,
that prince went out from the city for the sake of hunting.
And as he was departing, a certain eminent female ascetic named Kātyāyanī, who had come from a distant land, saw him.
"Is this the moon accompanied by Rohiṇī, or is it the Love-god who brings no pleasure?
Thus she reflected upon that superhuman form as she gazed at it.
And having learned from his attendants that he was the prince,
she marveled, praising the Creator’s wondrous variety of creation.
Then, with a voice that was far-reaching and long-sustained, she bowed down while saying to the prince, "O Kumāra, may you be victorious!"
But Sundarasena, without even hearing that, departed at that very moment with a mind preoccupied by the conversation begun by his own ministers.
Then, making herself heard loudly, that ascetic woman spoke angrily to him:
"O Prince, why do you not listen even to my blessing?"
"Whom on earth have I not honored— whether kings or princes—
if such is this pride of yours arising from youth and the like?"
"You shall obtain as your wife that maiden Mandāravatī, the daughter of the Lord of Haṃsadvīpa, who has become the ornament of the world."
Therefore, I think that you will certainly not hear my words even from Mahendra and the other gods due to your arrogance; what then of wretched mere humans?
Having heard her speak thus, Sundarasena, full of curiosity, called her to him and, bowing low, asked that female ascetic for forgiveness.
And he dispatched his servants to the house of his minister Vikramaśakti for the sake of their rest, desiring to question him.
Then, having gone out and returned from his hunt, and having performed his daily rites,
the prince summoned her after she had finished her meal and questioned her.
"O Blessed One, please tell us: who is this maiden named Mandāravatī whom you have mentioned today? For our curiosity is indeed great."
Having heard that, the female ascetic said to him: "Listen, I shall tell you this:
for the sake of visiting sacred fords and such, I wander this earth with its various continents."
Wandering about, I arrived at Haṃsadvīpa by chance;
there I beheld the daughter of King Mandāradeva.
Worthy of being enjoyed by the sons of gods and visible only to those of meritorious karma,
she who bears the name Mandāravatī is like the goddess Śrī dwelling in the Nandana grove.
Bearing a golden form that kindles the god of love upon being seen,
she was created by the Creator as another body made of nectar, distinct from that of the moon.
On this earth, there is truly no one else equal to her in beauty;
I know that you alone, sir, emulate the perfection of her form.
"Those by whom she has not been seen, their eyes and their very birth are fruitless.
Having heard this from the mouth of the female ascetic, the prince said:
"O Mother, how can we see her form as it truly is?
Having heard these words of theirs, that female renunciant replied:
Out of passion, I carry her— painted upon a canvas at that very moment and placed inside a magic bag— if you have any curiosity, let it be seen.
When she had spoken thus to the gratified prince,
she drew [the painting] from her pouch and showed it to him.
And Sundarasena, gazing at that maiden of wondrous form— even though she was depicted in a painting— stood motionless with joy.
At that moment, he sat with his limbs covered in the bristles of horripilation,
as if nailed down by the dense arrows of the Flower-Bowed God.
Gradually, no longer hearing, speaking, or seeing anything at all,
he became absorbed in that [state] and remained for a long time as if depicted in a painting.
Seeing that, his ministers said to the ascetic woman:
"Noble lady, paint King Sundarasena here upon this canvas."
"Let us first observe your skill in painting portraits.
Upon hearing this, she painted that prince upon a canvas in an instant.
And seeing that it was so exceedingly similar, everyone there said this:
"There is not even the slightest discrepancy between the painting and the Blessed Lady."
For the thought "this is indeed the prince" arises regarding this painting;
thus, the form of Queen Mandāravatī here cannot be in error.
When the ministers had spoken thus, Sundarasena, having taken the two variegated cloths,
joyfully honored that female ascetic.
And having dismissed her, who had been living in one place, according to her merit,
he entered his inner apartments carrying the portrait of his beloved.
Is this her face? Or is it the moon, its spots washed away by her radiance? Or are these two breasts the consecration jars of the God of Love for his royal coronation?
Are these the waves of the ocean of her form, appearing as the creepers of the three folds [of her waist]?
Is this her hip, or is it the pleasure-couch of Rati?
Thus, contemplating Mandāravatī there limb by limb as she appeared in the painting, he remained prostrated upon his bed.
Remaining in that very state day after day, turning away from food and other necessities,
and overcome by the weight of the fever of passion, he became [emaciated] in just a few days.
Having learned of this, his parents, Śaśiprabhā and Mahāsena, came and privately asked his friends the cause of his ill health.
And their companions told them everything accordingly,
explaining how the daughter of the king of Haṃsadvīpa had become the cause of these events.
Then Mahāsena said to Sundarasena:
"Son, why is this attachment of yours being concealed? It is indeed appropriate."
For the jewel of a maiden, Mandāravatī, is indeed worthy of you alone;
and her father, Mandāradeva, is my supreme friend.
"What purpose is served by this harassment regarding a matter that can be accomplished by his messenger and is already appropriate?
Having spoken thus to him and consulted together, they went to ask for the girl from him.
That King Mahāsena dispatched an envoy named Suratadeva to Haṃsadvīpa for King Mandāradeva.
She gave him that portrait of Sundarasena,
painted by her on a canvas, which revealed the excellence of his beauty.
That messenger traveled swiftly and reached the city named Śaśāṅkapura on the shore of the ocean,
belonging to King Mahendrāditya.
Then, having boarded a ship, he reached Haṃsadvīpa and,
after several days, arrived at the palace of that king, Mandāradeva.
Announced by the doorkeepers, the messenger entered there, looked within,
and reported to the king exactly what had occurred, having been presented with a gift of treasure.
"O Great King, a message has been sent to you by King Mahāsena:
'Give your own daughter to my son Sundarasena.'"
For that maiden, a jewel among girls, was indeed painted on a cloth by the female ascetic named Kātyāyanī and brought here to be shown.
And because we have conceived a desire for him due to his beauty, we have painted his likeness on this cloth;
let the portrait of Sundarasena, which has been sent here, be beheld.
Moreover, this man, being unlike others in his appearance, does not desire marriage without a wife who resembles him; and your daughter alone is her counterpart.
Having thus instructed him, he said: "This cloth was presented to me by the king;
let it be seen and let the divine Mādhavī creeper be joined [to it] now."
Having heard these words of the messenger, the king joyfully had Mandāravatī and her mother, who were both asleep, brought before him.
Having opened it together with those two and seen that painted cloth, he abandoned his pride, thinking, "There is no one on earth equal to my daughter."
And he said: "If it is appropriate for this prince, then the creation of this form for my daughter will have been fruitful."
For she does not shine without him, nor does he shine without her;
for what is a lotus pond without a swan, and what is a swan without a lotus pond?
When the king had spoken thus, and while the queen was exceedingly full of faith,
that Mandāravatī immediately became infatuated with passion.
She stood upon the painted canvas with her wide-open eyes motionless,
as if presided over by him, as if asleep though awake, and as if depicted in a painting.
Then Mandāradeva, seeing his daughter in such a state,
accepted that gift and honored the messenger accordingly.
On another day, he dispatched that man as a counter-messenger,
a brahmin named Kumāradatta, to King Mahāsena.
And having gone to that Lord of Alakā, he spoke to both of them:
"In my name, speak quickly to King Mahāsena."
Out of friendship, I have already given you my daughter; therefore, let it be said:
should your son come here, or should the daughter be sent here?
Having been thus given the king’s message, those two messengers then departed quickly by sea on a ship.
Then, having reached Śaśāṅkapura by way of the land route, the two of them arrived at that prosperous city which was like the stainless Alakā.
Then, having approached and entered the royal palace as was appropriate,
they beheld King Mahāsena, who had shown them due honor.
And they delivered that message spoken by Mandāradeva to the king;
and having heard it, he was pleased and honored them both.
And having asked the maiden’s birth star from her father’s messenger,
that king questioned the astrologers regarding an auspicious moment for his son’s marriage.
And after three months, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika,
they declared an auspicious moment for that bridegroom and his bride.
At that auspicious moment, the Lord of Alakā then dispatched his son for the wedding and sent word to Mandāradeva.
Having written that upon a letter for Kumāradatta, for another messenger named Candrasvāmin, and for himself, he placed it in their hands.
And those two messengers, having gone from there and delivered the letter exactly as it was,
reported everything before the lord of Haṃsadvīpa.
The king, having said "So be it," dismissed Candrasvāmin— who had been duly honored—
along with Mahāsena’s messenger back to the presence of their own master.
When he had returned to Alakā, having determined the course of action as instructed,
all those belonging to both sides remained waiting for the auspicious moment.
And meanwhile, on Haṃsadvīpa, Mandāravatī had conceived a passion for him long before she had even seen the painted canvas.
Having learned of that auspicious moment for the wedding, she, unable to endure the passage of time,
became intensely anxious for her beloved and was deeply tormented by the fire of love.
A rain of embers upon the body, even when anointed with sandalwood paste;
a bed of lotus leaves as well, becoming a layer of scorching sand.
Alas, even the rays of the moon became like the blazing crests of a forest fire to her,
whose heart was captivated by Sundarasena.
Maintaining silence, abstaining from food, and observing a vow of separation,
she was questioned by her distressed and trusted friend and spoke thus with great difficulty.
"Friend, my wedding is far off,
and I am unable to wait for that time without the son of the Lord of Alakā as my bridegroom."
The place is distant, the time is distant, and the course of destiny is manifold;
therefore, who here in this world knows what will happen to whom?
Saying, "Therefore, I must surely die," Mandāravatī, distressed by separation, immediately fell into a critical state.
Having learned this from the mouth of her friend and having seen her in such a state,
her father, together with his wife and ministers, held a consultation.
That king Mahāsena, the lord of Alakā, is our friend;
and this Mandāravatī is unable to endure [the passage of] time here.
Therefore, let her shame be as it may; let her be sent right there, for staying by the side of her beloved, she will endure the delay with fortitude.
Having reflected thus and consoled his daughter Mandāravatī,
he placed her upon a ship together with her wealth and her attendants.
Then, on an auspicious day, she was sent from Haṃsadvīpa by way of the sea,
having had the auspicious rites performed for her by her mother according to the prescribed ritual for the sake of her marriage.
Having bestowed his own minister named Vinītamati upon him,
King Mandāradeva sent him off toward Alakā.
Then, for some days,
as the princess Mandāravatī traveled upon the great ocean by means of the ship, [the following occurred].
Suddenly, the thief-like cloud arose, thundering,
emitting a fierce wind with a whistling sound and discharging a multitude of arrow-like torrents.
And in an instant, as if drawn far away by a powerful destiny,
her ship was struck and shattered by the wind.
When that retinue had been submerged along with Vinītamati,
her entire treasury sank into the great ocean.
But the ocean, with its wave-arms, lifted up that princess while she was still alive,
carried her near, and then cast her down in the coastal forest.
Where is a fall into the ocean, and where is being carried away by a towering wave into the forest?
Alas, let it be seen: nothing is impossible for that which is destined to be.
Then, in that desolate forest, she— terrified and overwhelmed,
seeing herself all alone— plunged once more into an ocean of sorrow.
Where have I set out? Where have I arrived? And where is my retinue?
Where is Vinītamati? What is this sudden change in my condition?
"Where shall I, unfortunate as I am, go? Alas, I am ruined; what can I do?
O cursed Fate, why was I rescued from the ocean by you?"
"Alas, father! Alas, mother! Alas, noble son, lord of Alakā!
Without reaching you, I am perishing; look, why do you not save me?"
