he considered himself successful and rejoiced in his lineage.
Then the king greatly rejoiced in those three— Dṛḍhabuddhi and the others— who were bowing down along with their sons and ministers, and especially in Vindhyaketu.
Then Sundarasena also,
having bowed to his father-in-law Mandāradeva, who had been informed by his father, rejoiced exceedingly.
And seeing those two ministers, Caṇḍaprabha and Vyāghraparākrama, who had arrived earlier, clinging to his feet, he considered all his desires fulfilled.
At that very moment, King Mahendrāditya also arrived there from Śaśāṅkapura,
joyful at having heard the news with affection.
Then, together with all of them, that prince Sundarasena carried his beloved Mandāravatī, just as Naḍakūbara carried Rambhā.
Mounted upon his excellent vehicle, he went to his own dwelling in the city of Alakā—
a place that was the abode of every prosperity and teeming with many Puṇyajanas.
And there, being showered with lotus-eyes by the women of the city leaning at the windows,
he entered his father’s capital together with his beloved.
Having prostrated there at the feet of his mother, whose eyes were clouded with tears of joy,
the prince spent that day amidst a festival celebrated by all his kinsmen and servants.
Then, on the following day, at the auspicious moment indicated by the astrologers,
the son of the lord of men took the hand of Mandāravatī— whom her father had offered to him— in that marriage which she had long desired.
And his father-in-law, King Mandaradeva, who was childless, being delighted, gave him many highly precious jewels and even his own kingdom, which was destined to be his after his own death.

And her father, King Mahāsena, performed a great festival in accordance with his desire and wealth— a festival that yielded inexhaustible merit, released those held in bondage, and rained down gold and garments.
Then, seeing that Sundarasena had attained his life's purpose through his union with Mandāravatī,
and observing the entire assembly of women singing and dancing while indulging in the joy born of their wedding, [the king spoke].
Honored by King Mahāsena, King Mandaradeva returned to his own realm;
and that monarch Śaśāṅka, as well as Vindhyaketu, the lord of the great forest, likewise departed.

Then, after some days had passed there, King Mahāsena, seeing that his son Sundarasena was endowed with excellent virtues and beloved by the subjects, installed him in his own kingdom and departed for the forest.
Then King Sundarasena, having obtained the kingdom and having conquered the host of his enemies by the strength of his own arms,
ruled the entire earth together with those ministers, his joy expanding from the acquisition of Mandāravatī.
Having thus related this tale to Mṛgāṅkadatta there on the shore of the lake,
that minister named Vyāghrasena spoke to him further.
O Lord, that sage Kaṇva described this wonderful tale to us within his hermitage;
and at the conclusion of the story, the compassionate man spoke thus to comfort us.

Those sons of mine who, with steadfast hearts, endure hardships that are extremely difficult and hard to overcome—they indeed attain the supreme goals thus desired; but not others, whose strength of being has dissolved and whose efforts are ruined.
Therefore, abandon this despondency; for that Mṛgāṅkadatta, your sovereign, having recovered all his ministers, shall rule the kingdom upon the earth for a very long time in union with Śaśāṅkavatī.
Thus addressed by that great seer, we took heart and spent the night there;
then, departing from that hermitage, we have gradually reached this forest, exhausted by the journey.
"Tormented here by excessive thirst and hunger, we climbed this Gaṇanātha tree for the sake of its fruit and became fruits themselves; today, O Lord, we have been liberated by your ascetic power."
Thus, this is our story brought about by the curse of the Nāgas during our separation from you;
now that the curse has expired, depart with all of us for the accomplishment of your purpose.
Having heard this from his own minister Vyāghrasena, Mṛgāṅkadatta,
having regained his fortitude through the prospect of obtaining Śaśāṅkavatī, passed that night.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth wave in the *Śaśāṅkavatī-lambaka* of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the thirty-fifth wave:
Then, having arrived, he rose up from that shore of the excellent lake.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with all his assembled ministers...
Equipped with that wisdom acquired through learning, he bowed to the tree that conquers obstacles and set out toward Ujjayinī, desiring to win Śaśāṅkavatī.
Then he saw those various forest regions, abounding in hundreds of streams,
their expanses dark as the tamāla tree, like nights at the onset of the rainy season.
And other [forests], where kīcaka reeds were broken by roaming, fearsome, and intoxicated elephants;
where the arjuna trees appeared distorted; resembling the city of Virāṭa.
The caves of the lord of mountains, though pure and filled with blossoming flowers,
were inhabited by fierce creatures and yet resorted to by peaceful sages.
Having proceeded by stages, that hero, the prince accompanied by all his ministers,
reached the vicinity of the city of Ujjayinī.
Then, having reached the river Gandhavatī and washed away his fatigue with a bath,
he crossed it and, accompanied by his followers, arrived at the Mahākāla cremation ground.
And he saw that place, strewn with various fragments of bones and skulls,
formidable with human skeletons held aloft, and frequented by heroes.
It was crowded with many hosts of spirits, a favorite playground for ḍākinīs,
and blackened by the smoke of nearby funeral pyres.
Having passed beyond that, he beheld the city of Ujjayinī, ancient as a yuga, protected by King Karmasena.
The city gates were guarded by men bearing various weapons,
and by numerous princes born of heroic lineages who remained vigilant.
It was surrounded by ramparts shaped like the peaks of the king of mountains,
difficult for the uninitiated to enter, and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Beholding her to be thus inaccessible from every side,
Mṛgāṅkadatta became despondent and spoke to his own ministers:
Alas! For me, who have arrived here unworthy through hundreds of such afflictions, there is no entry at all; what recourse is there, then, for the attainment of my beloved?
Having heard that, they also said to him: "O Lord, what does this seem to you?
Is this great city to be conquered by force by so few as we are?"
A means must be sought here, and it will certainly be found;
for how could this, which has been repeatedly enjoined by the deities, have been forgotten?
Thus addressed by his ministers, Mṛgāṅkadatta remained for some days wandering just outside that city.
Then Vikramakesarin meditated upon the Vetāla who was already established [there],
desiring to summon his mistress from her bedchamber by means of that mantra.
He too was dark-complexioned, tall, with the neck of a camel and the face of an elephant;
he had the feet of a buffalo, the eyes of an owl, and the ears of a donkey—[he was] a Vetāla.
Having arrived there, he was unable to enter;
therefore he departed, for by the boon of Śambhu, such persons do not step upon that city.
Then the brahmin Śrutadhi, who was skilled in statesmanship, spoke to Mṛgāṅkadatta, who was surrounded by his ministers, dejected, and with his mind intent on entering [the city].
O King, why do you, though a knower of the principles of policy, become bewildered as if ignorant?
For whose prowess is esteemed here in this world without first examining the distinction between oneself and the enemy?
For in each of the four gates of this city,
there are two thousand elephants and twenty-five thousand horses.
And ten lakhs of chariots and foot-soldiers remain armored day and night for the sake of protection, invincible due to the presence of heroes.
Therefore, our sudden entry here as a mere few is nothing more than the behavior of moths; it will not lead to the accomplishment of any purpose whatsoever.
Moreover, this city cannot be attacked even by a small army;
for that conflict is one between elephants and infantry against those who possess superior force.
By that young ascetic Māyāvaṭu, the king of the Pulindas,
who had been his friend and had rescued him from the terrible danger of the crocodiles in the Narmadā river—
And by that friend of his, the exceedingly powerful Mātaṅga king,
that Piśāca of the fortress, who was devoted to him because of their kinship.
Just as by that Kirāta king,
his childhood companion Śaktirakṣita by name, who was endowed with great prowess.
Having assembled with all your forces, filling the quarters of the sky with your army,
and being fully endowed with excellent allies, accomplish this desired goal.
And how have you forgotten this: that the king of the Kirātas remained there, awaiting the news of your envoy’s arrival?
And Māyāvaṭu, having certainly arrived by the command of the King of the Mātaṅgas, remains ready with him; for he has been made acquainted with this matter.
"Let us go to that dwelling-fortress of that lord of the Mātaṅgas, named Karabhagrīva, situated on the southern flank of the Vindhya mountains."
Right there, King Śaktirakṣita was summoned by them;
then, all of them having gathered together, they made auspicious preparations for success.
Having heard these meaningful words of Śrutadhi, which were approved by the wise,
Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with his ministers, placed full trust in them, saying, "So be it."
And on another day, having paid homage to the sun— the kinsman of the virtuous,
whose rising is certain, who reveals the quarters of the world to all, and who is the eternal traveler of the sky— [he spoke].
Then he set out toward the southern slope of the Vindhya mountains,
toward the abode of that Durgapiśāca, the lord of the Mātaṅgas.
And his ministers were Vyāghrasena of terrible prowess,
Guṇākara, Meghabala, and Vimalabuddhi.
Vicitrakatha, Sthūlabāhu, Vikramakesarin,
Pracaṇḍaśakti, Śrutadhi, and Dṛḍhamuṣṭi followed him.
Together with them, he gradually traversed vast wildernesses like his own past deeds,
and dense forest regions like his own inner inclinations.
Passing by lakes and taking refuge at the roots of trees on their banks during the night,
he reached and ascended the Vindhya mountain, as lofty as his own mind.
Descending from the top of it to its southern side,
he gazed from afar at the Bhilla hamlets, which were covered with elephant tusks and deer skins.
"Where in this world could there be a dwelling for that lord of elephants?
From where shall we learn?"—thus the prince pondered within himself.
Just then, he saw a young ascetic approaching;
together with his ministers, he bowed and questioned him.
"Do you know where the house of King Mātaṅga is here, O gentle one?
For we must see Durgapiśāca."
Having heard that, the virtuous son of the ascetic spoke thus:
"Five yojanas from here lies a region called Pañcavaṭī."
And not far from there was the hermitage of the sage Agastya,
by whom King Nahuṣa had been effortlessly cast down from heaven when he became arrogant.
There, at the command of his father, Rāma dwelt for a long time with Lakṣmaṇa and followed by Sītā, staying with that sage in the forest.
There, where the moon and sun seemed to portend the destruction of the Rākṣasas,
Kabandha set out to attack Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
There, Rāma cast down the arm of Yojanabāhu,
which resembled the serpent Nahuṣa when he had been transformed into a python at the request of Agastya.
Where, even now at the onset of the rainy season, upon hearing the roar of the clouds,
they remember the sound of Rāma’s bow that filled the sky.
Beholding all directions empty, the aged deer, raised by Jānakī, gaze with tearful eyes and do not take a mouthful of young grass.
As if to protect the deer that remained after the slaughter,
the golden deer— which brought about Vaidehī’s separation— carried Rāghava away elsewhere.
Where, in many great lakes abounding with the waters of the Kāverī,
the ocean water seems to have been drunk and then vomited up by Agastya at every step.
Not very far from that hermitage, on a ridge of the Vindhya mountains,
there is a fortress named Karabhagrīva, which is crooked and difficult to access.
There dwells that lord of the Mātaṅgas, Durgapiśāca, of fierce prowess and great strength, who has conquered all rival kings.
He was the sovereign of a hundred thousand archers,
each one of whom was followed by five hundred warriors.
With those bandits, he plunders caravans, crushes his enemies,
and enjoys this great forest, disregarding various kings.
Having heard this from the daughter of the sage and having taken leave of him,
Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by his followers, departed quickly by that very same path.
And he gradually reached the vicinity of that Karabhagrīva,
the fortress of the Mātaṅga king, which was crowded with Bhilla hamlets.
And there, not far away, he saw throngs of Śabaras here and there,
carrying peacock feathers, elephant tusks, tiger skins, and the flesh of deer.
Behold those who live like animals, subsisting on forest fare;
yet it is a marvel that they call even such a lord a "demon of a fortress."
There is indeed no such thing as a state without a king; alas, someone must surely exist among the subjects!
This title "king" was created by the gods out of fear of the law of the fish (*mātsyanyāya*).
Thus, having looked upon those Bhilla friends and speaking with them, Mṛgāṅkadatta sought to discover the path to the fortress of Karabhagrīva.
Then, as he first arrived there at the foot of the Nāyabaṭa tree,
the scouts of the Śabara king beheld him whom they had seen before.
Having gone to that illusory tree-spirit, they immediately informed him of his arrival;
and he too, accompanied by his army, went out to meet him.
Having approached and seen him, that king of the Pulindas, releasing his horse, ran forward and fell at the feet of the prince.
Having embraced him around the neck and inquired after his welfare, the king led him, along with his ministers, mounted upon a vehicle, to his own camp.
And then that lord of the Śabaras dispatched a doorkeeper to announce his arrival to that king of the Mātaṅgas.
And that king of the Mātaṅgas also arrived swiftly from his own country, a demon of a fortress who bore his name according to its true meaning.
With limbs as hard as a mass of stone, with foliage as dark as the *tāla* tree,
and sinful as he was frequented by *pulinda* hunters, he was like another Vindhya mountain.
With a face terrifying due to his natural frown,
he was marked by her as if with a three-pronged trident, as though she, the dweller of the Vindhya mountains, had claimed him for herself.
Though young, he has exhausted all [other] stages of life; though difficult to behold, he is Kṛṣṇa; and though subsisting on the feet of the mountain, he is served by none other.
Like a fresh cloud bearing the variegated bow of a peacock’s tail,
he was like Hiraṇyākṣa whose body had been wounded by the fierce Boar.
Powerful like Ghaṭotkaca, assuming a haughty and terrifying form,
he was like the Kali age, in which the subjects are unrestrained and devoted to unrighteousness.
And his army, its mass filling the earth,
surged forth like the current of the Narmadā released from the embrace of Arjuna’s arms.
Is this a mass of rocks tumbling from Mount Añjana?
Or is it a premature flood of clouds at the end of an eon fallen to the earth?
Thus entertaining this suspicion, that multitude of Caṇḍāla troops advanced,
darkening the faces of the quarters with their black shadows.
And having approached him, Durgapiśāca, his lord, bowed down to Mṛgāṅkadatta, placing his head upon the ground from afar.
And today the goddess Vindhyavāsinī has been gracious to me,
since you, belonging to a most noble lineage, have come to my home.
Saying, "Therefore, I am blessed; I have achieved my purpose," that king of the Mātaṅgas gave him a gift consisting of pearls, musk, and other such items.
The prince also greeted him with affection as was appropriate;
then, right there, they all established their military camp.
That great forest was covered with elephants bound to hitching posts, horses stationed in the stables, and foot soldiers who had taken up their positions.
At that moment, as if reeling from the fortune of having attained the state of a city never before seen since birth, she could not remain established in her own self.
Then, in that grove-garden, having performed his auspicious bathing rites,
having taken his meal, and being seated comfortably in a secluded spot accompanied by his ministers—
While Māyāvaṭu was present, that Durgapiśāca, in the course of conversation,
spoke to Mṛgāṅkadatta with words tender with affection and humility.
"O Master, this young Māyā has been here for a long time;
awaiting your command, he has remained with me."
Therefore, O Prince, inform us now as to where you have been staying for so long and what has been done; let us be made aware of your own affairs.
Having heard these words from the house of this Māyāvaṭu, the prince then spoke with Vimalabuddhi.
Having met Bhīmaparākrama together with Guṇākara,
and having gone with Śrutadhi while searching for my other friends, I—
Pracaṇḍaśakti has arrived, as have Vicitrakatha and this Vikramakesarin, who has also come by way of the road.
Then, having reached the Vighneśa tree on the shore of the excellent lake, they climbed it for the sake of fruit;
by its curse, they turned into fruits.
Then, having propitiated that Gaṇeśa with some effort, I was somehow liberated;
likewise, those others who were in such a state were also released by me there in the same manner.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Vyāghrasena, Meghabala,
and Sthūlabāhu— these four are his ministers.
Dṛḍhamuṣṭi, Vyāghrasena, Meghabala,
and Sthūlabāhu— these are his four ministers.
I went to Ujjayinī together with all of them who had arrived;
and since I was without an army, I did not consider it appropriate to send an envoy.
Therefore, having deliberated, we have come into your presence;
now, my friend, you are our authority here for the sake of success.
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had thus related his own adventures,
that Ugrapiśāca then spoke to him as he approached in the form of a young brahmin:
"Be firm; how small a task is this for us!
These very lives have already been prepared for your sake."
"Let us go there, bind that king Karmasena,
and by force carry off his daughter Śaśāṅkavatī."
When the young ascetic had spoken thus with the King of the Mātaṅgas,
Mṛgāṅkadatta replied with affection and great respect.
What is not possible among you? For this very quality speaks to you:
the steadfastness of character that carries out the task undertaken for a friend.
Having taken firmness from the Vindhya mountains, valor from tigers,
and a mixed passion from forest lotuses, you were fashioned here by the Creator.
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had spoken thus, "Reflect on this and do what is appropriate," the Maker of Day (the Sun) rested upon the peak of the Setting Mountain.
Then they rested there for that night of three watches in dwellings prepared by the laborers in the military camp, each according to his rank.
And in the morning, Mṛgāṅkadatta dispatched Guṇākara to bring his friend Śaktirakṣita, the king of the Kirātas.
Having gone there and related the events, that lord of the Kirātas returned in just a few days accompanied by him and a vast army.
Ten hundred thousand foot soldiers, two hundred thousand horses,
and ten thousand rutting elephants mounted by great heroes.
Eighty-eight thousand chariots followed that lord of the earth, their banners and parasols covering the sky.
And Mṛgāṅkadatta, having joyfully gone out to meet him and honored him,
brought the king, along with his friends and ministers, into the camp.
Meanwhile, all the other friends and kinsmen of Mātaṅgarāja,
as well as those sent by Māyāvaṭu as his messengers, arrived there.
And the ocean-like camp, resounding with joyful shouts as hundreds of armies converged, increased in size, bringing delight to the heart of Mṛgāṅkadatta.
With pearls, musk, garments, loads of meat, and fruit liquors,
that Piśāca of a fortress honored those kings there.
The lord of the Śabaras, Māyāvaṭu, provided for all of them unsurpassed bathing materials, ointments, food, drink, beds, and so forth.
And Mṛgāṅkadatta ate together with all those lords of men, who were seated in their respective appropriate places.
Even that king of the Mātaṅgas he caused to eat first, from afar;
for the task, the place, and the time are more important than the person.
And when the army of Kirātas and others who had newly arrived had rested,
Mṛgāṅkadatta, on another day, sat upon an elephant throne.
Having performed the appropriate honors for the royal assembly in their proper places,
and having cleared the area of people, he spoke to his friends, including the king of the Mātaṅgas and others:
Why is time being wasted now? Why do you not proceed quickly toward Ujjayinī with this entire army?
Having heard that, the brahmin Śrutadhi said to the prince:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you here what is the opinion of those who know the science of policy."
One who desires victory must first understand the distinction between what should be done and what should not be done;
that which cannot be accomplished by any means should be abandoned as something not to be done.
That which is to be accomplished through a means is its task; in that regard, the fourfold means are traditionally known as conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force.
Among those, each preceding one is superior and each succeeding one is inferior;
therefore, the application of conciliation (sāma) is appropriate for you first here in this world.
Indeed, when King Karmasena is free from greed, neither bribery nor sowing dissension will lead to success;
for he has no angry, greedy, or insulted subjects.
And when he is stationed in a difficult location and possesses superior strength,
an expedition undertaken by kings against one previously unconquered by others brings about uncertainty of success.
Victory in battles is uncertain even for the powerful;
nor is it right for those seeking a maiden to bring about the destruction of her kinsmen.
Therefore, let an envoy first be dispatched to that king using conciliation alone;
if that fails, force will be employed when it arrives by way of compulsion.
When Śrutadhi spoke these words, they all there accepted them as such;
they placed their faith in them and praised his knowledge of the sequence of mantras.

Then, having deliberated together with those very men, they dispatched that best of brahmins, who was endowed with the qualities of an envoy and had previously been described by them, as an attendant of the Kirāta king.
Mṛgāṅkadatta dispatched a messenger named Suvigraha to the king Karmasena, carrying a letter and a verbal message.
Having gone to Ujjayinī, that messenger was announced by the doorkeeper and entered the delightful inner courtyard, which was filled with beloved horses and elephants.
Having entered the royal palace, he saw King Karmasena seated upon the lion throne, surrounded by his ministers.
Having prostrated and sat upon his seat, he was questioned in turn regarding his welfare;
then, being greeted by the king, he presented the letter to him.
Having taken that [text], which was spread out by the casting of mudrās,
the minister named Prajñākoṣa then read it aloud clearly as follows:
Hail! From the edge of the forest at the base of Karabhagrīva Fort, [this is the proclamation] of the son of the Great King of Kings, the Lord of the city of Ayodhyā.
There, the illustrious Mṛgāṅkadatta— the ornament of the earth’s surface— stood with the kings bowed down before him in submission, honoring the glorious Amaradatta.
From Ujjayinī, this is clearly sent with respect by the great king Karmasena,
the moon in the ocean of his own lineage.
"You have that daughter; she must certainly be given away—bestow her upon another!
She is suitable for me as a wife, for she has been ordained for me by the gods."
In this way, our state as kinsmen shall come to pass and our former enmity shall perish;
otherwise, I shall rely solely upon my own arms in this matter.
When this letter had been read there, King Karmasena, filled with anger, spoke to his ministers, including the counselor Prajñākośa.
They are always our adversaries because of that [self] which lacks self-knowledge;
this very point was taught by him who perceives the present disorder.
Previously, we were drawn by self-interest; later, out of contempt, we were inflated with pride, and in the end, our strength of arm was displayed. (SoKss 12.35.142)
"Therefore, a reply from me is not appropriate; what need is there even for talk of a maiden?
Go, messenger! Let your master do whatever he knows to be right."
Thus addressed by King Karmasena, that twice-born messenger,
Suvigraha, full of splendor, spoke these words in due order:
"O fool, you are only now becoming aware because you have not seen that prince;
when he arrives, prepare yourself, and you will know the difference between yourself and others."
When he had spoken thus, that royal assembly fell into agitation;
the king, enraged, said: "Go! You are not to be killed; what shall we do?"
Others there, biting their lips with their teeth and wringing their hands with their hands, said to one another: "Why do we not go and kill him this very moment?"
"Let this talkative boy go; why be angry at his words?
We shall see what he will do," said the others with fortitude.
Some stood silently with faces reddened by anger, as if signaling their readiness to string their bows with the knitting of their brows.
Thus, while the assembly was in a state of anger,
that messenger of handsome form departed and went to the side of Mṛgāṅkadatta at his own camp.
He related that which had been said by Karmasena to him and his friends;
and having heard it, the prince likewise ordered the army to set out on its expedition.
Then, tossed by the onset of the powerful wind of his master’s command, that ocean of an army—filled with men, horses, and elephants as its sea-monsters—rushed forward.
Inspiring joy in the hearts of the mountain-like kings who stood on their side, it caused a terrifying agitation among the cowards.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta set out slowly toward Ujjayinī for victory, making the earth muddy with the ichor of elephants and the foam of horses, and deafening the world with the sound of his trumpets.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth wave in the Śāśāṅkavatī-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The thirty-sixth wave begins:
Then, having crossed the Vindhya mountains, he reached [his destination] with his army arrayed for battle.
Accompanied by his friends, Mṛgāṅkadatta reached the outskirts of Ujjayinī.
Having learned of this, King Karmasena also, firm and accompanied by his army,
equipped himself for battle and then emerged from the city before him.
As those two armies drew near and came within sight of one another,
a battle that thrilled the heroes broke out between them.
That battlefield became like the abode of Hiraṇyakaśipu, crowded with cowardly demons who were broken and terrified by the roar of the Man-Lion.
Continuous, cutting down as they went, thick and traveling through the sky,
the arrows fell upon the great warriors like locusts upon grain.
The heap of pearls arising from the frontal globes of elephants struck by swords shone like a necklace of the Fortune of Battle, snapped asunder in her agitation.
With its teeth like the points of sharp spears, devouring horses, men, and elephants,
that battlefield shone like the very mouth of Death.
The severed heads of those endowed with mighty arms leaped up,
as if taking a high leap into the sky to kiss the celestial nymphs.
And here, at every step, headless trunks danced as if out of joy for the battle with their excellent master, which had been made manifest.
And so for five days that battle, which brought an end to heroes, continued— a river of blood flowing daily and abounding with heaps of skeletons.
On the fifth day, in the evening, as Mṛgāṅkadatta was gathered in private with his ministers, the brahmin Śrutadhi approached him and said:
"While you were occupied with the battle, I went from here in the guise of a mendicant, entered Ujjayinī through its unguarded gates, and [proceeded]."
O Lord, listen as I tell you exactly what was sought by me while remaining invisible even when close at hand, through the power of my knowledge.
At the very moment that King Karmasena went forth for battle,
Śaśāṅkavatī, with her mother’s permission, departed from the house.
Having departed from there, she took refuge in the temple of Gaurī located within that city,
in order to propitiate that goddess for the sake of her father’s welfare in battle.
Remaining there, she spoke in private to a trusted female companion:
"O friend, on my account this conflict has arisen with my father."
And once he has been overcome, he will hand me over to that prince;
for kings do not take account of their affection for their offspring when it comes to the sake of the kingdom.
And I do not know whether that prince is suitable for me or not;
for I would rather desire death than an ugly husband.
I think that even a poor husband who is endowed with beauty is better than one who is ugly,
even if he were the sovereign of the entire earth.
"Go from the army to see what he is like and then return;
for you, O auspicious one, are indeed Caturikā by name and by wisdom."
Thus addressed by her friend, she went to our camp with skillful means;
having seen you, O Lord, she returned and spoke to that princess.
What else, my friend? I know that even Vāsuki does not possess such a tongue as is capable of describing that beauty of the prince.
Furthermore, I declare this:
there is no other woman equal to you in beauty, nor is there any other man who is your peer.
I consider what I have said to be far too little; indeed, in these three worlds, I believe there is no one such as him—not a Siddha, nor a Gandharva, nor even a god.
Thus, by the words of her friend, Śaśāṅkavatī’s mind was placed upon you, and it was simultaneously transfixed by the arrows of Kāma.
From that moment on, desiring your welfare and that of your father,
she remained emaciated by her ascetic penance and by the separation from you.
Therefore, go secretly tonight and, having abducted her from Gaurī’s hermitage,
bring that princess here unobserved from that solitary place.
"Go from here to the house of this Māyāvaṭu; after those kings have first restrained their anger, they will come there together with me."
"Let this battle cease; let there be no further destruction of the armies.
May there be well-being for your bodies, and for the king who is your father-in-law."
For this is indeed a path of no return, wherein battle is waged by surrendering one's life;
this is proclaimed by the wise to be the lowest of all expedients.
Thus addressed by Śrutadhi, Mṛgāṅkadatta mounted his horses there at night with his ministers and proceeded in secret.
And having gone there, he entered that city of Ujjayinī, which was left with only sleeping women and children,
its gates closed and guarded by only a few slumbering sentries.
Then, clearly identified by the tokens provided by Śrutadhi,
it was known to be situated within the great garden named Puṣpakaraṇḍaka.
Illuminated by the rays of the moon, which at that time adorned the face of the eastern quarter,
the prince went to that hermitage of Gaurī.
And while her circle of friends slept, exhausted from their service and other duties,
Śaśāṅkavatī remained there sleepless and reflected:
Alas, for my sake, day after day, those various heroic kings and princes are being slain in the encounter between the two armies.
And that prince had been foretold by the goddess Ambikā in a dream:
"He was my husband in a former life; he has sought battle for my sake."
And having torn out his heart and discharged a succession of arrows,
Kāma, who has attained his mark, took it and offered it to him.
But my father will certainly not give me, one of little merit, to him;
for today I have heard from a letter that it is due to former enmity and pride.
In the left [hand] and in the moon, what certainty can there be regarding the instruction of a deity in a dream?
And upon obtaining my beloved, I do not see any direction whatsoever.
Therefore, as long as I do not hear that anything has been done to my father in battle, why should I not abandon this hopeless self?
Having risen and gone before Gaurī, the distressed woman fashioned a noose from her upper garment at the foot of an aśoka tree.
Meanwhile, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having entered that garden with his companions and tethered his horse to a tree, went to the hermitage of the temple of Gaurī.
There, having observed the princess from a distance, Mṛgāṅkadatta was addressed privately by his minister Vimalabuddhi: SoKss_12,36.44 //
"Your Majesty, behold! Here is some noble maiden who is about to kill herself with a noose; who indeed might she be?"
Upon hearing that and seeing her, the prince said:
"Aha! Who is this? Is she Rati, or perhaps Bliss personified?"
Is she the embodied radiance of the moon, or the mobile command of the God of Love?
Or perhaps a celestial nymph? But no—how could such a being be intent on casting a snare?
Therefore, let us remain here for a moment, concealed by the trees,
until we can somehow clearly discern who she is.
Having spoken thus, while he remained there concealed with his companions,
Śaśāṅkavatī, being distressed, addressed the goddess:
"O Queen, if, due to my past misdeeds, that prince Mṛgāṅkadatta has not become my husband in this life," SoKss_12,36.50.
By your grace, O Gaurī, may he be my husband even in another birth— O Blessed One, you who remove the suffering of those in distress.
Having thus addressed the queen and bowed down to her, the princess,
her eyes moist with tears, placed the noose around her neck.
And at that very moment, having awakened and being distraught by not seeing her,
her friends hurriedly searched for her and approached her side.
"Alas, alas! What is this you have begun? O friend, shame on your rashness!"—having said this, they immediately removed the noose from her neck.
Then, while that girl remained there, ashamed and dejected,
a voice arose from within the inner sanctum of Gaurī.
"Do not despair, daughter Śaśāṅkavatī;
those words that were spoken by me to you in your dream, O fortunate one, shall certainly not prove false."
Thus, this very Mṛgāṅkadatta, your former husband, has indeed arrived in your presence;
go with him and enjoy the entire earth.
Having suddenly heard these words, Śaśāṅkavatī slowly cast a timid glance around her side to see what was there.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta’s minister, Vikramakeśarin,
approached him and spoke, pointing with his outstretched hand:
"O Goddess, what Bhavānī has commanded you is indeed true;
for here before you is that prince, your husband, drawn by the noose of love."
Having heard that, she then cast her gaze sideways and beheld her beloved,
radiant, standing in the midst of his companions.
Surrounded by his attendants, he was like the moon descended from the sky;
he was a source of nectar for the eyes, beyond comparison with any other form.
Then, with her limbs bristling as if covered by the feathers of the shafts of falling arrows of the God of Love,
she remained motionless like a pillar.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta approached her and, making her abandon her shame, spoke words dripping with the honey of love, appropriate for the occasion: SoKss_12,36.64.
"O lady of curved limbs, having abandoned my own country, kingdom, and kinsmen far behind,
I have been brought here as a slave, bound by your virtues."
Therefore, [I shall endure] dwelling in the forest, sleeping upon the bare earth,
subsisting on fruit, and enduring the intense heat of the sun.
O slender-limbed one, such is the fruit obtained from the hardship of asceticism:
that this body of yours has been seen, a rain of nectar for the eyes.
O deer-eyed one, if you have such affection and regard for me,
then grant a festival for the eyes to the women of our city.
"May the battle cease; may it be well for both sides.
May my birth be rendered fruitful along with the blessing of my preceptor."
When Mṛgāṅkadatta had spoken thus, Śaśāṅkavatī then replied slowly, her eyes fixed upon the ground:
This person, purchased by your virtues, is already at your disposal;
therefore, noble son, do whatever you deem to be for our welfare.
Thus, having been satisfied and refreshed by her nectar-like speech,
Mṛgāṅkadatta, feeling fulfilled, praised and bowed down before that goddess Gaurī.
Having mounted the princess upon a horse behind him,
with her female companions likewise mounted on the backs of horses following behind, he departed.
Then, accompanied by ten heroic ministers with weapons in their hands,
the prince set forth at night, bearing his own arms.
And although those eleven saw him there, they were unable to restrain him;
for like the wrathful Rudras, he was difficult to approach, even by the guardians of the city.
Having departed from Ujjayinī, they went to the house of Māyāvaṭu together with Śaśāṅkavatī, just as Śrutadhī had instructed.
While the guards there were bewildered, wondering "Who are these people? and "Where have they gone?", that princess gradually learned in Ujjayinī that she had been abducted.
And to inform King Karmasena of this, the Great Queen swiftly dispatched the city magistrate toward the royal camp.
In the meantime, at that camp, having approached him during the night,
the chief of scouts informed King Karmasena:
"O King, at the very hour of dusk today, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having departed secretly from the army with his ministers, has gone to Ujjayinī by means of horses."
"I have correctly understood that he intends to abduct Śaśāṅkavatī while she is staying in the temple of Gaurī; beyond this, the Lord himself knows."
Having heard this, King Karmasena summoned his own general and described everything exactly as he had heard it in private.
And he said: "Accompanied by five hundred excellent horses with brave riders, go quickly and secretly to Ujjayinī."
"Slay that wicked Mṛgāṅkadatta, or having captured him, bind him!
Know that I am coming after you, with my soldiers stationed behind me."
Thus addressed by the king, that general, equipped with the forces as commanded, set out for Ujjayinī at night, saying, "So be it."
On the road, he met the city magistrate and heard from him how the princess had been carried off by certain other heroes.
Then the city superintendent returned and informed King Karmasena of all that had occurred, exactly as it was.
Having understood that and reflected upon it, the king realized it was impossible;
he desisted from the assault and passed that night in silence.
In Mṛgāṅkadatta’s army as well, the kings headed by Māyāvaṭu likewise spent that night prepared for battle, following the words of Śrutadhi.
In the morning, having inquired into the news, the wise King Karmasena dispatched a messenger to the camp of Mṛgāṅkadatta to inform the kings.
"My daughter has already been carried off by Mṛgāṅkadatta through deception;
let it be so, for who else indeed could be such a suitable husband for her?"
Therefore, let him now come with you to my house,
so that I may perform the marriage of my daughter according to the prescribed rites.
Thus the king delivered his message through the mouth of the messenger,
and those kings, together with their learned ministers, then placed their trust in it.
And they said to the messenger: "In that case, let this lord of yours go to his own city, so that we may go there and bring back the prince."
Upon hearing that and being thus described by the messenger who had gone there, Karmasena, together with his army, said "So be it" and went to Ujjayinī.
Seeing that, those kings also, led by Māyāvaṭu and accompanied by Śrutadhi, set out toward Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Meanwhile, Mṛgāṅkadatta, accompanied by Śaśāṅkavatī,
reached that city of Kāñcanapura, the home of Māyāvaṭu.
There, having had due honors paid to him by the women of the inner apartments,
he— his purpose accomplished, accompanied by his friends and his beloved— rested.
On another day, those kings, together with Śrutadhī, arrived there;
as did that heroic lord of the Kirātas, Śaktirakṣita, accompanied by his army.
That powerful Śabara chief, King Māyābaṭu,
was a hero and a formidable Piśāca, as well as the commander of the Mātaṅga army.
Seeing Mṛgāṅkadatta united with Śaśāṅkavatī, as the night-lotus is joined with the moon, they all celebrated and congratulated him.
Having shown him the honor he deserved, they reported to him Karmasena’s message and his own admission into the palace.
Then, having established his camp, which resembled a moving city,
Mṛgāṅkadatta sat down together with all of them for consultation.
"Should I go to Ujjayinī for the wedding, or not?
he asked the kings and his ministers, saying, "Let it be told."
That king is wicked; how could there be any welfare in going to his house?
There is no business at all to be done there, for his daughter has already been obtained.
When the kings and ministers had spoken thus with one accord,
Mṛgāṅkadatta then questioned that brahmin Śrutadhi.
O Brahmin, why do you remain thus in silence like one who is indifferent?
Is this indeed your own preference, or is it not? Tell me.
Then Śrutadhi said: "If you will listen, I shall tell you:
it is my opinion that we must go to the house of Karmasena."
For this was instructed by him without deceit; otherwise, how could that powerful man, upon the abduction of his daughter, abandon the battle and go home?
And what could he do even if he reached your house while accompanied by his army?
For you would have the same joy there as you would with him.
"He would indeed be our companion in the future, and moreover, out of affection for his daughter, he does not desire an improper marriage; therefore, he speaks thus according to the truth."
When Śrutadhin had then said, "The journey there is appropriate for that," they all, placing faith in his words, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! at that time.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta said to them: "Let all this be as you say;
however, without my father and mother, marriage does not please me."
"Let someone go from here to summon his mother and father;
and having learned their intention, we shall do what is appropriate."
Having spoken thus and consulted with his ministers, the hero of terrible prowess dispatched Bhīmaparākrama to the side of his parents while remaining right there himself.
Meanwhile, in that city of Ayodhyā, his father King Amaradatta learned from the people about him over the course of time.
Vinītamati falsely slandered Prince Mṛgāṅkadatta, thereby causing him to be banished from the country.
Then, having slain that evil minister along with his lineage out of anger,
he fell into a state of misery and hardship caused by the intense grief of his son’s exile.
Having departed, he stayed in a temple of Hari outside the city;
that king, together with his wives, performed austerities in the place called Nandigrāma.
While he remained there for a long time, that man of terrible prowess, having been informed of the arrival by his spies, reached Ayodhyā with the speed of the wind and a horse.
He beheld that city, distressed and bereft of the king’s son,
as if it had once again encountered the calamity caused by Rāma’s exile.
Then, surrounded by the citizens who were inquiring after the prince’s welfare,
and having heard the news from their mouths, he proceeded from there to Nandigrāma.
There he saw King Amaradatta together with his queen; the king’s body was emaciated by asceticism, and he was filled with eager longing for news of his beloved son.
Approaching the king, falling at his feet, and embracing him around the neck,
Bhīmaparākrama, having been asked about his welfare, spoke with tears.
O King, that Śaśāṅkavatī, the daughter of King Karmasena, has been won by your son Mṛgāṅkadatta through his own prowess.
And for that man devoted to his father, a marriage with anyone other than the King and the Queen does not appear auspicious in any way.
Therefore, having been dispatched by him, your son has come here with his head bowed to the ground to inform you: "Please come right here."
O King, awaiting you, he remained in Kāñcanapura,
in the house of the lord of the Śabaras, King Māyāvaṭu.

"Now listen to the account," he said, "beginning from his departure from that country and extending through the long and difficult period of dwelling in the forest and separation [from his companions]."
He of terrible prowess recounted the entire account of his own master, including the battle with Karmasena and its various wonders, ending with the conclusion of their alliance.
Having heard that, King Amaradatta, whose welfare was secured by his son, became firm in his resolve;
and at that very moment, out of joy, he ordered his own departure.
Then, mounted upon an elephant together with the queen, the kings, and his ministers,
he set out with his force of elephants and horses, eager for his son.
And in just a few days, without delay,
that king reached his son’s camp situated in the territory of the Śabara chief.
And as soon as he learned of this, Mṛgāṅkadatta, along with all the kings and his companions, went forth before him, having long been filled with longing.
Having seen them from afar, he dismounted from his horse and fell at the feet of his father and mother as they descended from their elephant.
Embraced by his father’s body, he filled the space between his father’s arms with his own,
his heart with longing, and his eyes with tears.
The mother too, having embraced her son and gazing at him repeatedly for a long time,
was unable to let him go for a long while, as if fearing separation once more.
And those kings, the friends of Mṛgāṅkadatta, having been informed of that by him, then paid homage to their lord Amaradatta along with his queen.
Both that king and his queen,
out of affection for their many sons, welcomed those companions during their time of distress.
Then, having entered the capital of Māyāvaṭu and beheld her there,
he saw Śaśāṅkavatī bowing at his feet as his daughter-in-law.
Having accepted the gift from the queen and together with his daughter-in-law,
Amaradatta went forth and took up residence in his own camp.
And having eaten there together with his son and all the kings,
he spent that day in great happiness with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
And he considered himself a man of merit by virtue of that son, Mṛgāṅkadatta, who had already attained fame and was destined to become a universal emperor.
And at that moment, King Karmasena,
being well-disposed, deliberated and dispatched a messenger here to Mṛgāṅkadatta.
Your Honor will not come here to Ujjayinī for the time being;
therefore, I shall send my son named Suṣeṇa to this very place.
"He will duly give you his own sister, Śaśāṅkavatī; therefore, O sinless one, she must not be married by you through an improper rite."
"If there is compliance with our affection," so the king commanded him; and that monarch sent this message both in a letter and through the mouth of the messenger to the prince.
When that message was heard by the prince in Rājagṛha,
his father, the king himself, gave a reply to that messenger.
Who else but King Karmasena, who possesses such noble intent, would say this? He surely has affection for us; therefore, let him send him from here.
"We shall act in such a way that the marriage of his son Suṣeṇa will bring him complete satisfaction."
Having spoken thus and dispatched that honored messenger with a reply,
the king addressed his son Śrutadhi and the other monarchs.
"Let us go now to Ayodhyā; there the wedding shall be celebrated with splendor, and there the hospitable reception for Suṣeṇa will be duly accomplished."
"Let King Māyābaṭu wait here for Suṣeṇa;
once he has arrived, you shall go to Ayodhyā together with him."
"We shall go ahead once more for the sake of the wedding preparations"—
at these words of the king, everyone there gave their assent.
Then, on another day, that lord of the earth, together with the queen, his armies,
Mṛgāṅkadatta, and those kings and ministers, set out.
Having left Māyāvaṭu there until the arrival of Suṣeṇa,
the two skillful men then set out together with Śaśāṅkavatī.
It was crowded with hundreds of waves consisting of throngs of galloping horses,
and its quarters were filled by the waters of the marching infantry, which surged forth in countless numbers.
The ocean of that army, deep and terrifying, surged forward, its hearing of other sounds drowned out by the tumultuous sound rising up.
And they made the earth, covered in dust, appear like the heavens, while the sky,
filled with thundering clouds like elephants, appeared like the earth.
Proceeding gradually along the road, the father and son reached the home of Śaktirakṣita, the king of the Kirātas.
There, he and his wife, having performed a noble service with heaps of great jewels, gold, and fine garments, together with their retinue, [honored them].
Having eaten for one day and rested with their army,
they then set out and reached their own city, Ayodhyā, in due course.
With the faces of the city women, shimmering as they leaned from the palace windows and blossoming with radiance,
it was as if the city were a lake filled with blooming, swaying lotuses.
With their eyes— restless as if they were moving blue lotuses— they were eager to behold the prince who had arrived late with his bride.
And they entered that city, which was filled with royal swans swooping down and rippling with banners fluttering in the wind, like a lake on a gale.
There the citizens rejoiced as the two were being granted blessings by the twice-born,
praised by bards, and celebrated in song by the *cāraṇas*.
If the great ocean were to behold this daughter of Karmasena, it would no longer take pride in its own daughter, Lakṣmī.
And even upon seeing the wealth of beauty possessed by Śaśāṅkavatī, people were struck with wonder; they did not say that Himavat was like Gaurī.
And then, with the echoing sounds of great auspicious trumpets, they made the quarters of the sky seem as if they were signaling to the kings that a festival had arrived.
As if overflowing with passion poured outward,
that entire city became filled with festive joy, as if dancing with vermilion.
On another day, when the astrologers had determined the auspicious hour for his son's wedding,
King Amaradatta made preparations for that marriage.
His city was filled with various kinds of jewels brought from all directions in such a manner that it surpassed even the city of Kubera.
Then, having arrived shortly thereafter, a messenger of Māyāvaṭu, announced with joy by the gatekeeper, addressed that king there.
The prince Devagata and King Suṣeṇa—
both of them stood at the boundary of this Ayodhyā as Māyābaṭu.
Upon hearing that, King Amaradatta immediately dispatched his own general, Suṣeṇa, along with his troops, to face him.
Then Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with his friends, went out from Ayodhyā to meet the prince who had arrived there with him, out of affection.
Having descended from their vehicles from afar and embraced one another around the neck,
those two princes met and inquired after each other’s welfare.
Mounted upon a single chariot out of love, they entered that city,
presenting a great festival for the eyes of the city's women.
And there Suṣeṇa, having seen the king and being highly honored by him,
thereafter went to the residence of his sister Śaśāṅkavatī.
Having risen there and embraced her as she shed tears,
he sat down and spoke to that bashful princess.
"Your father says to you: 'Daughter, nothing improper has been done by you;
for today I have learned from Ambikā in a dream what this truly is.'"
"This prince Mṛgāṅkadatta has been designated as your husband;
and for women, following the path of their husband is the supreme vow."
Having been addressed thus by him, that young woman, with her face cast downward, looked at her own heart and,
seeing that "your desired goal is accomplished," cast aside her shame.
Then Suṣeṇa took that wealth which she had personally accumulated and, having brought it, presented it before the king for Śaśāṅkavatī.
Two thousand loads of gold for the purpose of making jewel ornaments,
five well-fed young camels, and other golden vessels.
And he said this: "O father, whatever belongs to her has been sent after her;
I shall bestow it upon her in due order at the altar of the wedding."
Then all of them, having eaten and drunk there in the presence of the king,
spent that day in contentment together with Mṛgāṅkadatta and the others.
On the following day, when the appointed hour for the wedding had arrived, while the king himself was busily occupied with joy,
Mṛgāṅkadatta performed his ablutions and other rites in a manner befitting himself.
And there, the women adorned Śaśāṅkavatī— who was already full of curiosity due to her very loveliness—
merely because it was the custom.
Then, having emerged from the chamber of curiosity with the bustling Suṣeṇa,
the bride and groom took their seats upon the altar, which was like a blazing fire.
In that [ceremony], from Vyagrasuṣeṇa, he took the hand of that princess—
which was as beautiful as a held lotus— just as Acyuta took the hand of Lakṣmī.
During the circumambulation of the fire,
the face of Śaśāṅkavatī shone as if it were reddened by some heat and smoke, shedding tears even though she was not angry.
And handfuls of parched grain scattered by her in the fire shone like the smiles of the God of Love, who rejoiced at the success of his efforts.
And at that time, during the first scattering of parched grain, Suṣeṇa gave five thousand horses and likewise a hundred elephants.
Two hundred and ninety loads of gold,
along with female elephants laden with burdens of fine garments, excellent jewels, and pearl ornaments.
Her brother bestowed upon her the wealth born of his conquest of the earth, and at each subsequent scattering of parched grain, he gave her twice as much as before.
Then, amidst the resounding music of festive instruments, Mṛgāṅkadatta, having completed the auspicious marriage rites,
entered his own palace together with his newlywed bride, Śaśāṅkavatī.
And his father, the king, by bestowing upon him as was fitting elephants, horses, jewels, ornaments, food, and drink,
delighted his own subjects and citizens, from the circle of kings down to the parrots and mainas.
And at that time, the excellence of that king’s generosity was recognized here by its very sufficiency;
for the trees, laden with garments and ornaments, gave such an impression that they were mistaken for the wish-fulfilling trees of the earth.
Then that king, together with Mṛgāṅkadatta, Śaśāṅkavatī, and the other kings,
having eaten, spent that day in a drinking party along with Suṣeṇa.
Then, while the people in that house were engaged in dancing and music, having eaten and drunk well,
and had fully quenched their thirst for the essence of the earth, the sun, its course completed, entered the cave of the western mountain.
And beholding him departing somewhere, united with the twilight glowing with fresh passion,
the beauty of the day, as if angry with jealousy, rushed after him with her girdle of trembling birds.
And gradually, with a face whose pupils were trembling and whose passion had intensified,
the night-damsel appeared, beautiful in her flowing dark garment of spreading darkness, as she went forth on her secret tryst.
Then the moon, rising as radiant as fresh vermilion and resembling the curved goad on the trunk of the elephant of the Eastern Mountain,
became the brother of the sidelong glances of angry, long-eyed women.

When the darkness had departed, the eastern quarter, its favor restored, bore a smiling face like that of Indra’s consort, adorned with the moon as an ear-ornament for her play and with him as a fresh sprout upon the creeper of Rati.
Having performed the evening rites, Mṛgāṅkadatta, together with his new bride Śaśāṅkavatī,
entered their costly bedchamber for the night’s rest.

Then, by the moon of that woman’s face, which dispelled the darkness within her chamber, the interior was illuminated; thus, the excellent jewel-lamps were rendered superfluous, as if they were painted upon a wall.
And there, as she remained upon the bed, he turned toward his beloved;
by embracing her, by kissing her, and gradually by biting her lower lip, he stole away her modesty.
And he experienced that long-desired bliss, the essence of a fresh spell of enchantment, from her who uttered but a few small words of "No, no,
enough," while the broad, precious jeweled girdle fell away.
At the end of their dalliance, he delighted in her moon-like face with its disheveled locks and half-closed eyes,
and in her limbs, languid and slackened by exhaustion, with their ointments partially rubbed away.
Then, as if through the very play of their enjoyment, that night was spent and diminished;
yet their love, with its expanding flow of longing for the festival of sexual union, attained further growth.

The night has passed; now, O Lord, let this couch of dalliance, which dispels the fatigue of lovemaking, be abandoned, for these breezes from the palace chambers blow, shaking the curls of the deer-eyed women.
Like pearls fallen from the laughter of the night as she suddenly follows the moon,
the dewdrops of the dawn shimmer with clear luster, clustered upon the tips of the dūrvā grass.

Behold, O Prince, those bees who for a long time sported within the buds of the *kairava* lilies, drinking their honey and dwelling comfortably once they had gained entry during the union with the moon’s light; now that those flowers have closed and their beauty has faded, the dark bees depart elsewhere. For whom, indeed, is prosperity stable in times of adversity?

Upon merely beholding the night, whose lower lip was adorned by the rays of the sun-maker, the Mind-born [god of love] made her body marked with the spotless moon as its tilaka, and likewise smeared it with the very slight darkness of collyrium.

Thus, at dawn, with the soft and sweet words of the bards, Mṛgāṅkadatta— having cast off his sleep and the exhaustion from the end of their lovemaking— suddenly abandoned his bed, crying out for Śaśāṅkavatī.
Having risen, he performed his daily duties, for which all the necessary arrangements had been made by his father;
and once again, accompanied by his beloved, he spent many more days in that same manner with great festivity.
Then King Amaradatta, his father-in-law,
first bound the turban upon the head of Suṣeṇa, who had been consecrated.
Out of great respect, that king gave him as a fitting reward one elephant, horses, loads of gold, garments, and a hundred excellent women.
Then he [conquered] the lords of the Śabaras and Kirātas, as well as Māyāvaṭu and Śaktirakṣita,
together with their kinsmen and wives, and that king who was the commander of the Mātaṅga army.
He brought together Durgapiśāca and those ministers of Mṛgāṅkadatta, along with Śrutadhi,
by bestowing upon them territories, cattle, horses, gold, and garments.
Then, having sent those kings, headed by the lord of the Kirātas, along with Suṣeṇa to their own countries,
King Amaradatta— delighted by his son’s heroism— ruled his kingdom in happiness.
Mṛgāṅkadatta, too, having conquered his enemies and after a long time regained Śaśāṅkavatī,
remained for a long time happy together with those ministers of his, Bhīmaparākrama and the others.

Hariśikha is devoted solely to valor, while he alone is established in statesmanship.
"There is no need for those two now; however, Gomukha, being clever, is my friend in all circumstances, yet being far away, he causes me distress."
Thus speaking there, he suddenly heard a sweet and gentle voice, which dispels sleep, uttered like that of a woman: "Alas! What misery! (SoKss 14.2.60)
And having heard this, as he looked all around in that brightly lit place,
he beheld the divine face of the Noble Lady within the lattice window.
"Today the moon was seen in the sky as stained by this [cloud]," so thinking out of curiosity,
the Creator showed another stainless moon, as it were, in a place that was not the sky.

Not seeing her remaining limb and longing to behold it, his eyes drawn by her form, he thought thus at once: SoKss_14,2.63: "Not seeing her remaining limb and longing to behold it, his eyes drawn by her form, he thought thus at once."
"The Daitya Ātāpi previously obstructed the creation of Brahmā through his stratagems;
go there and see this marvel! Having said this, he was sent to the Nandana grove.
There he beheld only the foot of the woman, wondrous in its form;
yet he perished through his obsession with the desire to see her other limbs.
"In this way, even for me, this face alone must have been created by my nurse for my own misfortune"— as long as he reflects thus for a moment on this matter.
Then, from the window, a divine woman showed her sprout-like hand and signaled to him with a gesture of her finger, saying, "Come this way."
Then, having quietly emerged from the dwelling where his beloved was fast asleep, he,
filled with longing, approached that celestial woman.
While praising her husband who was infatuated with another woman, O Madanamañcukā, she cried out, "Alas, you are ruined! as he drew near.
Having heard that and remembering his beloved, Naravāhanadatta, burning with the fire of separation, questioned that beautiful woman.
"Who are you? Where was your beloved Madanamañcukā seen by you?
And for what purpose have you come to me? Let it be told."
Then, having led the mature princess far away at night, she said to the prince,
"Listen to everything," and proceeded to speak.
In the city of Puṣkarāvatī,
there was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Piṅgalagāndhāra, who was tawny from his propitiation of the fire.
Know me to be his daughter, a maiden named Prabhāvatī,
obtained through a boon from Vibhāvasu, who was propitiated and pleased.
So, in order to see my friend Vegavatī at Āṣāḍhapura,
I went there, but I did not find her anywhere, for she was established in ascetic practice.
Having learned from the mouth of her mother, Queen Pṛthivī, that Madanamañcukā was your beloved and was staying there, I went to see her.
I saw her, emaciated by lack of food, pale and greyish,
with her hair bound in a single braid, weeping and speaking only of your virtues.
She was surrounded by throngs of daughters of the Vidyādhara lords, who were shedding tears,
agitated by the rising pain and joy born from seeing her and hearing of her.
Having been told her true nature by her,
and having consoled her by bringing you there, she was overcome with compassion for her, her mind drawn by your virtues.
Having understood through the power of my knowledge that you are now situated here,
I have come into your presence for the sake of accomplishing both your purpose and my own.
"Today, seeing you here speaking of others whom you had forgotten, I cried out 'Alas, what misery! and lamented for your wife."
Thus addressed by her, the prince, filled with longing, said to her:
"Lead me there; and employ me however you wish."
Having heard that, Prabhāvatī took him up, soared into the sky,
and set out at night to go to Candravatī, a city of the Vidyādharas.
As she was going somewhere, seeing a blazing fire, she circumambulated it and took the hand of that Naravāhanadatta.
Thus, she, being mature, skillfully completed the marriage rites;
for all actions of divine beings have intention alone as their primary element.
Then, from the surface of the sky, he saw the earth like an altar,
rivers like female serpents, and mountains like anthills.
Displaying various such curiosities at every step, she gradually traveled a great distance there with her beloved.
While Naravāhanadatta was exhausted from traveling through the sky, afflicted by thirst, and seeking water,
she descended from the path of the heavens.
And he led him to the edge of the forest, near a lake whose waters were as white as moonbeams,
as if filled with liquid silver.
There in that delightful forest, his thirst for water was stilled by drinking the water;
yet, a thirst born of longing for the company of a beloved arose within him.
Then, having meditated upon Madanamañcukā, that compassionate Prabhāvatī, sighing deeply, yielded with great difficulty to the forceful pursuit during their union.
Then the [journey] of that Naravāhanadatta proceeded;
for the highest beings, intent upon the welfare of others, do not look to their own self-interest.
And he said to him: "O noble son, do not think otherwise;
I have a certain intention here, so listen to the story regarding this."
Long ago in Pāṭaliputra, there was a certain woman whose husband had died;
she was young, beautiful, poor, and had an only son who was still a child.
And she, seeking union with another man for her own gratification,
went from her house at night here and there.
"Son, I will bring you a sweetmeat in the morning," she said, comforting her young son; and so, day after day, she brought it to him.
And that boy sat silently in the house with the expectation of the sweetmeat;
once, she did not bring it for him, having forgotten that sweetmeat.
And when that fool was begging for the sweetmeat, she reportedly said to him:
"Son, I know my own lover's sweetmeat, and no other."
Hearing that, the heart of that child, who had become hopeless, broke, thinking: "My sweetmeat was not brought back by her because she was attached to another."
Therefore, my beloved, if I were to accept you even more completely as before, then,
comforted by me alone, you would be ready for the great festival of union with you.
If Madanamañcukā, having learned [of this], were to become hopeless because of me alone,
her heart, as delicate as a flower, would burst.
Therefore, having failed to comfort her with this very compassion,
I do not now desire you, my beloved who is dearer to me than life itself, in such a manner.
Having been addressed thus by Prabhāvatī,
Naravāhanadatta, filled with joy and wonder, reflected at that moment:
Oh, how the Creator is a connoisseur in fashioning ever-new wonders,
by whom Prabhāvatī was created, she whose conduct is inconceivable and sublime!
Meditating thus and praising her with love, the prince said:
"In that case, lead me to where Madanamañcukā resides."
Having heard that and taken him up, Prabhāvatī reached Mount Āṣāḍhapura through the sky in an instant.
There, she finally united with him her body, which had long been wasting away,

There Naravāhanadatta also beheld his beloved, suffering from the pain of separation, thin and pale like a digit of the moon on the day of the new moon.
Then, for the sake of attaining life, their union with one another became a source of joy to the world, like that of the night and the moon.
And that couple, tormented by the fire of separation, embraced each other and,

Then, by the power of the Prabhāvatī spell, the two of them enjoyed there at will all the pleasures prepared for them that very night.
And by the very power of that magic science, no one there saw Naravāhanadatta except for Madanamañcukā.
In the morning, as her beloved was releasing his own single-stringed lute there,
Madanamañcukā, overcome by the force of her indignation, spoke to him.
While this Mānasavega still lives, he must be slain by my noble son;

Thus was it promised by me today to you;
yet since this king still lives, I have been released, and for that reason my mind is pained.
"Though cast down upon the Fire Mountain by Vegavatī, he did not die;
and you were rendered invisible here by Prabhāvatī through her own magical power."
Otherwise, if these followers of this enemy were to wander here today in your presence, how could they endure seeing you?
Having been addressed thus by his virtuous wife, Naravāhanadatta, mindful of the constraints of time, spoke to her consolingly:
"This desire of yours shall be fulfilled; I will slay that enemy before long.
Once you have encountered him, O dear one, recognize him as the foe and wait but a moment."
Having spoken thus and comforted Madanamañcukā,
Naravāhanadatta remained there in that city of the Vidyādharas.
Then Prabhāvatī, by the power of her magic knowledge,
caused her own form to become inconceivable before him, having herself vanished from sight.
In that form, the prince remained there at his ease;
though he was manifest, he was free from fear, enjoying the pleasures attained through his magical powers.
This companion of Vegavatī attends upon this Madanamañcukā out of affection for her and under the influence of her own friendship.
Thinking that he was thus exerting his power while his true form remained concealed,

Then one day, in the course of conversation, Madanamañcukā related her own story to Naravāhanadatta.
Then Mānasavega, having brought me here by his own magic power,

Then the Blessed One, manifesting in a terrifying form with drawn sword and lolling tongue, uttered the syllable "Hūṃ" and spoke.
"This is the wife of the future universal monarch among the lords of the Vidyādharas; how can she be insulted by you while we are present?"
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, that wicked Mānasavega fell upon the surface of the earth, vomiting blood from his mouth.
Then, when the god had vanished, he was comforted in an instant;
having returned to his own palace, he once again turned toward me with cruelty.
Then, as I was terrified, afflicted by separation, and intent on giving up my life here,
the maidservants of the inner apartments approached me, comforted me, and spoke these words:
In former times, having seen a certain beautiful daughter of a sage, this Mānasavega forcibly abducted her; consequently, he was cursed by her kinsmen.
"O wicked one, when you go to another man's wife against her will,
then this head of yours shall split into a hundred pieces."
Therefore, he shall not approach another's wife by force; do not fear.
By the command of the gods, your union with your husband shall surely take place once again.
When I had spoken thus, the maidservants immediately brought Vegavatī, his sister,
in order to awaken Mānasavega to reason.
Pervaded by compassion upon seeing me, she comforted me by bringing you;
how she arrived is already known to you.
Then, with garments white as moonlight, she was like the stainless body of the Moon;
with her very gentle appearance, she seemed to drench me with nectar.
The virtuous Queen Pṛthivī, mother of this evil-minded Mānasavega, spoke these words to him with affection: 138.
Having renounced food that results in auspicious consequences, why do you neglect yourself?
And do not harbor in your heart the thought, "How shall I eat the food of the enemy?"
"In this kingdom, my daughter Vegavatī has a portion assigned to her by her father;
she is your friend, having been married by your husband."
That wealth belongs to your husband and is indeed your own as well; enjoy it, for you have acquired it through knowledge. Knowing this, I tell you the truth.
Having spoken thus with an oath, she, bound by her affection for her daughter, then fed me food appropriate to my condition.
Then, having come here with you, he was defeated by Vegavatī;
O brother, you were protected here, and I do not know what remains of him.
And I too, remembering the words of that deity regarding the attainment of Vegavatī, did not give up my life, which was sustained by the hope of attaining you.
Therefore, by the power of the highly majestic Prabhāvatī,
you have now been found by me even in this peril from enemies.
But if my anxiety were to be dispelled here by Prabhāvatī, your form would perish;
what then would become of us?
Reassuring Madanamañcukā as she spoke these and other words,
the hero Naravāhanadatta remained there together with her.
And once, when Prabhāvatī had gone to her father’s palace,
at the time of dawn that [palace] lost its splendor due to her absence.
Seeing Naravāhanadatta there in human form, he became agitated, thinking, "An adulterer has entered here."
Out of fear, the entire retinue went to the royal palace and spoke [to the king],
having set aside the terrified Madanamañcukā even as she was trying to restrain them.
Then King Mānasavega, accompanied by his own forces,
rushed there and surrounded Naravāhanadatta.
Then his mother, the goddess Earth, having approached him in haste, said to the king: "O son, this man must not be killed by you, nor by me."
For this son of the King of Vatsa, Naravāhanadatta, is not an adulterer; he has come here to his own wife.
"By the power of my knowledge I know: blinded by anger, do you not see that this son-in-law of ours is worthy of honor and born of the lunar lineage?"
When he had been addressed thus by his mother, Mānasavega, feeling provoked and thinking, "In that case, this man is my enemy," spoke to her.
Then his mother spoke to him again out of affection for her son-in-law:
"My son, no unrighteous act can be committed in this world of the Vidyādharas."
"For here there exists an assembly hall of the Vidyādharas for the sake of dharma and worldly affairs;
there, in the presence of its presiding authority, cast the blame upon his head."
Therefore, whatever is done for him that is fitting will shine; otherwise, the Vidyādharas would manifest their powers and the deities would not tolerate it.
Accepting these words of his mother out of respect for her, Mānasavega proceeded to bind him, intending to lead him to the assembly hall.
Unable to endure his captivity, Naravāhanadatta uprooted a pillar from the archway and slew many of his captor's servants there.
From among them, having seized the sword of one who had been slain,
that hero of divine prowess instantly struck down the others as well.
Then Mānasavega, by means of his own divine magic power,
bound him along with his wife and led them into that assembly hall.
There, summoned by the great sound of the drum, the Vidyādharas gathered from here and there, just as the gods assemble in the Sudharmā hall.
Then King Vāyupatha, surrounded by his courtiers and the Vidyādharas, arrived and sat down there upon a jeweled lion-throne.
While he was being fanned with chowries that seemed to shake off unrighteousness,
the wicked Mānasavega stood before him and spoke these words.
"Though he is a mortal, he is a destroyer of the inner apartments and a ravager of his own sister;
this enemy of mine must be put to death today, for he truly has no desire for our lordship."
Having heard that, the hero Naravāhanadatta was questioned by that courtier regarding the reply, and he spoke with confidence: SoKss_14,2.167 //
That is an assembly where there is an assembly member; he is an assembly member who speaks according to the Dharma;
that is the Dharma where there is truth; and that is truth where there is no deception.
"I am bound by illusion and remain right here on the ground, while you, however, are seated upon a seat and are liberated; what dispute can there be between us two who are equal in this regard?"
Having heard this, Vāyupatha seated him upon the ground and,
according to the rule, caused Mānasavega to be released.
Then, while everyone there was listening, Naravāhanadatta spoke this reply in the presence of Vāyupatha:
"If I have obtained my own wife Madanamañcukā, who was carried off and brought here by him,
whose inner apartments have I then desecrated?"
If, having approached her because of her beauty, I have deceived her and become the husband of this sister, what fault of mine is there in that?
"If I am one who desires sovereignty, whose desire does not arise for what, and where?
Having heard this and reflected upon it, King Vāyupatha then spoke.
"This great-souled one has spoken what is righteous; he will attain a very great exaltation.
O Mānasavega, my good friend, do not commit unrighteousness toward him."
When he had spoken thus, Mānasavega did not turn away from unrighteousness because he was blinded by delusion; rather, Vāyupatha directed his anger toward him there.
Then, together with Mānasavega and his arrayed army,
there arose a great agitation for him who was devoted to the Dharma.
For the wise, who perceive only what is right, seated upon the throne of Dharma, recognize even the weak as their own, regardless of whether they are strong or another.
Abandoning deceit, fight clearly with me;
behold my prowess as I slay you with but a single blow.
Thus, gazing at the divine maidens who were filled with curiosity, Naravāhanadatta spoke then to Mānasavega.

And while those Vidyādharas were engaged in mutual quarrels there, suddenly from the very center of an excellent pillar situated within the assembly hall, a deity in a terrifying form indeed emerged with a loud crash.
Pervading the sky, dark as collyrium, and obscuring the sun, with the rays of his eyes flashing like flickering streaks of lightning,
and with rows of teeth shining like a flight of cranes, he was as fierce as a roaring cloud at the time of the great dissolution.
"There is no defeat for this rogue, the future Wheel-Turning King of the Vidyādharas," saying this,
the Lord [Śiva] cast down Mānasavega with his face turned downward, gladdening Vāyupatha.

Taking Naravāhanadatta by his two arms for the sake of protection, the Blessed One quickly brought him to the auspicious and excellent mountain Ṛṣyamūka; having established him there, he then indeed vanished from sight.
Then that agitation among the Vidyādharas in that assembly subsided;
and Vāyupatha, together with them and his own other followers, departed from there just as he had come.
And that Mānasavega, placing Madanamañcukā before him—
