Thus ends the second wave in the fifth book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave:
I believe that Fate intends only what is auspicious for a man, even when it appears contrary to his expectations.
He repeatedly and deeply examines his steadfastness in the face of pleasure and pain.
In various foreign lands, at every step, he united Naravāhanadatta with this or that wife and then separated him from them.
Then, having approached Naravāhanadatta as he was staying on that Ṛṣyamūka mountain, his beloved Prabhāvatī spoke to him.
"Indeed, because of the fault of being possessed by intoxication, you were then led away from that assembly hall by Mānasavega, who desired to do you harm."
Having understood that, I arrived at that very moment and, by means of the power of my magic knowledge (*vidyā*), created a grand display of divine manifestation and brought you here.
For on this mountain, even the extensive magical powers of the mighty Vidyādharas do not prevail, since this is a field of perfected ones (siddhakṣetra).
"Even my own power of knowledge does not succeed here for this very reason;
therefore, it is a source of sorrow to me: how indeed will you subsist on forest food?"
When she had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta remained there with her, awaiting the appointed time while meditating upon Madanamañcukā.
He bathed in the purifying Pampā lake near that mountain and partook of roots and fruits of divine flavor.
He drank the meritorious water of the pond, seasoned with venison,
along with the succulent and fragrant fruits fallen from the trees on the bank.
He dwelt at the roots of trees and within the interior of mountain caves,
following the conduct of Rāma as he lived in the forests of that region.
And having seen the hermitages of Rāma there,
Prabhāvatī described to him those various episodes from the Rāmāyaṇa for the sake of diversion.
Here, Rāma, accompanied by Saumitri and followed by Sītā,
dwelt in the forest at the foot of a tree where he had constructed a hut, together with the ascetics.
With Anasūyā as her unguent and Sītā perfuming the forest,
she dwells here among the wives of the sages, clad in garments of bark.
In this regard, the Daitya Dundubhi was slain by Vālin in a cave;
he was the cause of the enmity that existed in the past between Vālin and Sugrīva.
For Sugrīva, believing through delusion that Vālin had been killed by the Daitya,
fled in fear after blocking the entrance of the cave with mountain crags.
And Vālin, having broken through that gate and emerged,
drove Sugrīva away, thinking, "He has bound me here out of a desire for the kingdom."
Having fled, that Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys,
established his residence here on this ridge of Ṛṣyamūka together with those headed by Hanumān.
Then, having approached and deceived the mind of Rāmadeva with the guise of a golden deer, Rāvaṇa carried off the daughter of Janaka.
Then, seeking news of Sītā, that scion of the Raghus formed an alliance here with Sugrīva, who was himself seeking the death of Vālin.
And there, to demonstrate his strength, he pierced seven palm trees with a single feathered shaft;
even Vālī, though possessed of great power, could only split one of them with difficulty.
Having gone from here to Kiṣkindhā, that hero, having slain Vālin with a single arrow released with ease, bestowed his sovereignty upon Sugrīva.
Then, while Sugrīva’s followers, headed by Hanumān, set out in the four directions to obtain news of Sītā, [the following occurred].
Here, during the rainy season, Rāma dwelt together with the resounding clouds, which, with their falling torrents of rain, seemed as if they shared his sorrow.
And when it was learned through great effort that Hanumān had crossed the ocean at the word of Saṃpāti, [Rāma] went forth accompanied by the monkey forces.
Having bound the ocean with that bridge and slain his enemy, the Lord of Laṅkā,
he brought back the divine Jānakī by way of this celestial chariot.
In this way, noble son, you too shall attain prosperity;
for fortunes come of their own accord to steadfast men in times of adversity.
While Prabhāvatī was speaking in this manner and so forth,
Naravāhanadatta remained there, sporting with her here and there.
Once, while he was at Pampā, two Vidyādharīs,
Dhanavatī and Ajināvatī, descended from heaven and approached him.
By means of those two, he was led from the city of the Gandharvas to Śrāvastī,
where Bhagīrathayaśas was married by him.
When Prabhāvatī had joined her as a friend at Ajināvatī,
Dhanavatī spoke thus to Naravāhanadatta:
"This daughter of mine, Ajināvatī, was previously given by me in word; therefore, marry her, for your time of prosperity is near at hand."
Out of affection for her friend, Prabhāvatī and Naravāhanadatta both welcomed these words of Dhanavatī, saying, "So be it."
Then Dhanavatī gave that daughter Ajināvatī to the son of the Lord of Vatsa according to the appropriate rite.
And she brought to completion that auspicious marriage ceremony for her daughter, made beautiful by the magnificent divine preparations fashioned through her own supernatural power.
Then, on another day, she said to Naravāhanadatta:
"My son, it is not proper for you to remain here for long in such a place."
The people of the Vidyādharas are illusory, and you have no business here;
therefore, go now to your own Kauśāmbī together with your wife.
And I myself shall come there with my son Caṇḍasiṃha and with the lords of the Vidyādharas for your prosperity.
Having spoken thus, Dhanavatī ascended, making even the day appear as if filled with moonlight by the radiance of her white body and garments.
And Prabhāvatī and Jināvatī brought that Naravāhanadatta through the air to the city of Kauśāmbī.
Having arrived there at that garden and descended from the sky,
Naravāhanadatta was seen by his own attendants.
"This prince has arrived; by good fortune we are prospering!"—thus a roar arose from the people there on every side.
Then, having learned of this, King Udayana, together with Vāsavadattā, was filled with joy as if suddenly drenched by a shower of nectar.
Padmāvatī and her brides, Ratnaprabhā and the others, as well as Yaugandharāyaṇa and the other ministers of the Lord of Vatsa, [departed] swiftly.
Kaliṅgasenā and her own ministers, Gomukha and the others,
approached him as was fitting, like travelers approaching a lake in the heat of summer.
And they saw him in their midst, seated between his two wives like Kṛṣṇa between Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā— [he who belonged to] the noble lineage of the Daśārhas.
As if out of fear that their own limbs might shatter,
they closed their eyes with tears of joy upon seeing him.
And Vatsarāja and the two queens, having at last embraced their son,
were unable to let him go from their limbs, as if he were pinned there by thorns.
Then, while that great festival was proceeding with the sounding of musical instruments,
there was the daughter of Vegavatī, the wife of Naravāhanadatta.
Having descended through the path of the sky, Vegavatī, the sister of Mānasavega,
arrived there after learning [the way] through the power of her perfected vidyā.
Having prostrated at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, she,

"Because of you, I became weak; having mastered the sciences in the forest of asceticism, I have now returned to your presence, O auspicious one."
When she had spoken thus, and was welcomed by her husband and the others,

While she was being embraced by those two and seated there in their midst,
Mātājināvatī and Dhanavatī also arrived.
And those various lords of the Vidyādharas arrived together with her,

Her son was the hero Caṇḍasiṃha of mighty arms,

And that Piṅgalagāndhāra, the powerful father of Prabhāvatī,
was also Vāyupatha, the presiding lord of the assembly who had previously entered [the path].
And that heroic King Hemaprabha, endowed with great strength, was addressed by Ratnaprabhā together with his son Vajraprabha.
The Gandharva king Sāgaradatta also arrived, accompanied by his daughter Gandharvadattā and Citrāṅgada.
Having arrived, they were duly honored by the King of Vatsa together with his son, and they sat down upon the seats as was appropriate.
Then King Piṅgalagāndhāra addressed his son-in-law, Naravāhanadatta, who was standing in the assembly, for a moment.
"You are a universal monarch, created by the gods for all of us;
out of the power of great affection, we have all come to you."
This Queen Dhanavatī is your mother-in-law, firm in her vows;
she possesses divine knowledge and wears a rosary, a black antelope skin, and garments of bark.
Exerting herself to protect you, she is like the Blessed Mother in person,
or like Sāvitrī, a perfected lore praised by the highest of the Vidyādharas.
"Therefore, the accomplishment of your purpose is possible; however, listen to what I say:
here on Mount Himavat, there are two divisions of the Vidyādharas."
The northern and the southern [peaks] are situated on different levels of the mountain ridges;
indeed, the northern one is beyond Kailāsa, while the southern one is on this side.
Therein, for the sake of supreme sovereignty, this Amitagati now performed difficult austerities and completely satisfied Śaṅkara.
"Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch, will fulfill your desire; having been commanded by him, he has come to you."
There, a chief king named Mandaradeva resides, who is evil-minded;
though he is powerful, he cannot withstand you once you have attained the vidyā.
But he who is in the middle of the south, known as Gairimuṇḍa,
is a king of evil nature, exceedingly difficult to conquer by virtue of his power of knowledge.
And he is the supreme friend of his enemy Mānasavega;
as long as he has not been won over here, the task will not be accomplished.
"Accomplish the supreme reality quickly, for the power of your knowledge is great.
When Piṅgalagāndhāra had spoken thus, Dhanavatī sang in reply:
"Thus it is, my son; as this king tells you, so it shall be.
Having gone from here to the field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), [worship] the Lord for the sake of attaining the vidyā."
"Exert yourself in propitiation, for without his favor, how can there be success?
Moreover, these kings gathered here will protect you."
Then Citrāṅgada spoke thus again:
"Let this Vijaya be made the foremost of us all."
Then, having resolved upon this very course and performed the auspicious rites for his departure,
he bowed at the feet of his parents and his elders, who were both shedding tears.

"The bath of one who is not a universal monarch does not succeed here;
yet today that sovereignty of yours has been achieved," so spoke a divine voice.
Having heard that, the universal monarch entered into the midst of those waters and sported together with his harem, like the Lord of Waters in the ocean.
There he took delight in gazing upon his beloveds, whose eyes were as red as lotuses from being washed, whose hair-braids were loosened, and whose wet garments clung to their limbs.
The rows of birds flying up from this lake with a rustling sound shone like the girdles of its glories coming forth to meet them.
And the lotuses there, surpassed by the loveliness of the faces of those brides, sank into the waves of water as if out of shame.
And having bathed that day on the very bank of that lake,
Naravāhanadatta dwelt there together with his retinue.
There, having stayed with his wife and minister in pleasant conversation and discourse, that successful man, mounted upon his celestial chariot at dawn, set forth from there with his army.
Then, while traveling along the path of the wind, having reached a city by the force of his course,
he stayed there for that very day in accordance with its requirements.
There he beheld a maiden he had seen before, the sister of Vāyupatha,
named Vāyuvegayaśas, who was standing in a garden and longing for him.
She wandered in the groves on the banks of rivers with golden sands;
her face was like the full moon, and she was delightful with her gentle speech.
With a white smile, burdened by the weight of her heavy hips, and graced with excellent limbs, she—
her heart already enamored of him upon seeing him arrive— then vanished from that spot.
Then Naravāhanadatta, feeling embarrassed as he realized she was averse to any other motive, returned to his own quarters.
There, Marubhūti, by virtue of Gomukha’s cleverness,
having learned that account of the king's conduct from his companion, [related it].
The queens performed various jests against that sovereign,
while Gomukha stood there abashed due to Marubhūti’s lack of cleverness.
Then Gomukha, seeing the king abashed and having comforted him,
went to that city desiring to know the mind of Vāyuvegayaśas.
Then Vāyupatha, seeing him as if he had suddenly arrived to behold the city,
offered him hospitable welcome with joy and, leading him to a private place, spoke to him:
I have a sister, a maiden named Vāyuvegayaśas;
she has indeed been declared by the Siddhas to be the future wife of a universal monarch.
"Therefore, I wish to give that here as a gift to Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch; please accomplish this desire of mine."
"I have set out to come into your presence for this very purpose," said Vāyupatha; to him, the minister Gomukha replied:
"Even though this lord of ours has set out for the purpose of conquering his enemies, nevertheless, you must make this request; I shall accomplish it for you."
Having spoken thus and taken his leave, Gomukha went and reported that the task was accomplished to Naravāhanadatta, without even having to ask for it.
And on another day, the wise Gomukha came there to Vāyupatha in person and addressed the king regarding this matter: SoKss_14,4.166: "The wise Gomukha spoke to that king."
"O Lord, you must not cause Vāyupatha’s request to fail;
for one who is devoted believes that whatever he says to his master must be carried out."
Then King Vāyupatha also accepted that proposal;
he brought his own younger sister and gave her to him, even though she was unwilling.
While being led away for marriage, she said, "I am unwilling; I was given [in marriage] by my brother by force. Therefore, O World-Protectors, there is no unrighteousness in me."
While she was speaking thus, all the women of Vāyupatha raised such a clamor that no others could hear her words.
Then, in order to discover the king's intention regarding the words he had spoken,
Gomukha wandered here and there to search for a suitable means.
Having wandered about, he saw in a secluded spot four Vidyādhara maidens who were preparing to enter the fire simultaneously.
When questioned by him regarding the cause, those slender-waisted women told him that it was Vāyuvegayaśas who had violated their agreement.
Then Gomukha went and reported the matter exactly as it was to Naravāhanadatta in the presence of the king and all his attendants.
When the king was struck with wonder upon learning this, Vāyuvegayaśas then said:
"Arise! Let us go quickly to protect him."
"Noble son, I shall then explain the reason for those maidens.
Having been addressed thus by her, the king went there together with everyone.
And he saw those maidens before him with blazing fires; and having restrained them, Vāyuvegayaśas spoke to the king: SoKss_14,4.177 //
This one is named Kālikā, the daughter of the Lord of Kālakūṭa;
this second one is Vidyutpuñjā, born from Vidyutpuñja himself.
O King, this third one is Mataṅginī, the daughter of Mandara;
O Lord, this fourth one is Padmaprabhā, the daughter of Mahādaṃṣṭra.
And on the fifth day, having seen you performing austerities at the field of the Siddhas, we, deluded by Māra, made a mutual pact.
"This beloved husband is to be carried away by all five of us equally; he must not be surrendered to him by any one of us who has become estranged."
If one [of the sisters] should separately perform a marriage with him,
then fire must be entered by the others, having aimed it at that betrayer of her friend.
Fearing this very situation, I did not desire a separate marriage;
nor, O Noble Son, is my person surrendered to you even now.
My noble son and the world-protectors themselves are witnesses here,
if this agreement has even now been transgressed by me according to my own will.
Therefore, noble son, accept these friends of mine;
O friends, this must be cultivated by you and not otherwise.
When she had spoken thus, the maidens rejoiced and embraced one another, having escaped death; and the king also rejoiced within himself.
Having learned of this, their fathers arrived there at that very moment and presented those daughters to Naravāhanadatta.
At that time, even those lords of the Vidyādharas, who were the foremost followers of Kālakūṭapati, accepted the teaching of his son-in-law.
Thus, having obtained these five together, Naravāhanadatta, the son of a great Vidyādhara, attained supreme greatness therein.
And he remained there for several days with them;
then the commander-in-chief, Hariśikha, spoke to him as follows:
"O King, though you are a knower of the treatises, why do you act by transgressing political ethics?
At this time for war, what is this indulgence of yours in the pleasures of desire?"
Where is this undertaking of a military expedition to conquer that Mandaradeva,
and where are these many days spent here in recreation with the ladies of the inner apartments?
When Hariśikha had spoken thus, the great king said:
"What you have said is fitting; however, I have no effort here for the sake of enjoyment."
"For this union with my wife, which grants me the acquisition of kinsmen,
has now been welcomed by me as the primary factor in crushing the enemy."
"Let these armies of mine now advance for the sake of conquering the enemy"—
to the king who had spoken thus, his father-in-law Mandara replied:

O King, that Mandaradeva is difficult to conquer; he possesses all the jewels that are the limbs of a universal monarch who has not yet attained his sovereignty, and he dwells in a terrain far removed and inaccessible.
Indeed, this place is guarded by the cave named Triśīrṣa, which stands at the entrance protected by the great hero Devamāya and occupies the foremost position.
And that cave was entered by the wheel-turning monarch Siddharatna;
and that sandalwood tree, O King, is the wheel-treasure of that wheel-turner.
First, accomplish that which exists on this earth for the sake of attaining your desired goal;
for no one who is not a universal monarch comes near that tree.
Having heard this, Naravāhanadatta, fasting at night and firm in his vow, went toward that sandalwood tree on Mount Mandara.
Though being terrified by most dreadful obstacles as he went,
the hero was not afraid there, and he reached the root of that great tree.
And having seen that great jewel with its lofty railings fixed upon it, he approached,
ascended by the stairs, and paid homage to the sandalwood tree.
"O Cakravartin, I am this *candana* tree, perfected for you; I shall appear before you whenever you remember me. Therefore, depart from here now."
From there, you will obtain Govindakūṭa and other jewels;
thereafter, you will conquer Mandaradeva with ease.
Having been addressed thus by that incorporeal voice there at night,
he said "So be it," and having prostrated before that perfected divine tree, he departed.
Then Naravāhanadatta, the great lord of the Vidyādharas, returned to his own camp, traveling through the path of the sky in high spirits.
Then, having passed that night, he related in the morning,
in the presence of the entire assembly, the whole account of how the sandalwood tree had been produced during the night.

Having learned of this, his beloved wives, his young ministers, and those trusted Vidyādharas such as Vāyupatha and others, along with Citrāṅgada and the rest of the Gandharvas who had accompanied him, were overwhelmed with joy; they praised the greatness of his fortitude, which was characterized by the power of courage, energy, and steadfastness, now that he had forcibly achieved such great success.
Having consulted with them, the king—traveling in a divine celestial chariot—then set out to conquer Mandaradeva’s pride;
meanwhile, for the sake of obtaining other jewels from the remaining sandalwood trees, he went to Mount Govindakūṭa.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the fifth book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
And here concludes this fourteenth book, the Pañcalambaka.
// Śrī //
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The fifteenth book, named "The Great Consecration.
Long ago, it is said, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the Lord of Mountains.
Those who, having attained supernatural power free from obstacles, forcibly savor [the nectar] and bear the burden of the gods upon this earth, do so by the grace of Bhava.
May the Conqueror of Obstacles destroy your darkness, as if nourishing the stars with the spray from the hissing of his trunk raised high in a dance during the nights. (First Wave)
Then, Naravāhanadatta, that universal monarch, while seated in his assembly hall upon Govindakūṭa, was approached.
That Vidyādhara named Amṛtaprabha traveled through the celestial path by which he had previously protected him when he was cast by his enemies onto the Fire Mountain.
Having arrived and announced himself, he bowed down before the wheel-turning monarch;
after being offered hospitable greetings that brought him joy, that Vidyadhara spoke to him.
There is a great mountain named Malaya situated in the southern direction;
in a hermitage there dwells the great ṛṣi Vāmadeva.
"O Lord, he is summoning you alone for the sake of some business;
it is for this purpose that I have been sent to you today."
"You are my master from whom I acquired [this wealth] in the past; for that reason, I have come here.
Therefore, come, let us go quickly to the presence of that sage for the sake of attaining success."
When he had spoken thus, he left his wives and armies right there with that vidyādhara, saying, "So be it."
Flying swiftly through the sky and reaching Mount Malaya,
Naravāhanadatta approached the sage Vāmadeva.
And he saw him, tall of stature and white with age,
with the sockets of his eyes devoid of flesh and the true jewels of the pupils shimmering within them.

The Himalaya mountain, its thickets of matted hair swaying, was the abode of the jewels of the lords of the Vidyādharas; it appeared as if it had come along with him for the sake of assisting in his spiritual attainments.
Then he paid homage at the feet of that sage,
and the sage, having offered him hospitality, addressed the king in this way:
Although you were previously consumed by fire, you have been made a universal monarch of all the lords of the Vidyādharas by Śambhu, who was pleased with Rati.
"In this hermitage of mine, within a deep inner cave, there are jewels; perform those tasks as directed by me."
For Mandaradeva shall indeed become your Siddharatna;
it is for this purpose that you have been summoned here by me at the command of Giriśa.
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, delighted and instructed in the ritual by that very sage, entered the cave.
Having conquered those various floods of obstacles therein, the hero beheld a rutting lord of elephants charging toward him with a roar from its throat.
Having dealt a blow with his fist to the mouth and placed his feet between the tusks,
that king, through his agility, mounted the intoxicated elephant.
"Excellent! O Cakravartin, the great elephant-jewel has been accomplished for you"—thus did an incorporeal voice arise from within the cave at that time.
Then he beheld a sword resembling a great lord of mountains; and having descended, he grasped it as if it were the tresses of hair belonging to the Fortune of Universal Sovereignty.
"Excellent, O subduer of enemies! Your precious sword has been perfected as a conqueror.
Thus, once again, an incorporeal voice arose within the cave.
Then he accomplished the jewel of moonlight, the jewel of beautiful women,
and the jewel of knowledge known by the name Vidhvaṃsinī.
Thus, together with the first two, along with *sarasā* and sandalwood (*candana*),
there are seven [substances] suitable for use at the time of the rite, which bestow greatness.
Having accomplished the acquisition of the jewels, he then emerged from the cave and reported everything that had been achieved to the seer Vāmadeva.
Then that sage spoke with affection to the universal monarch:
"Son, you who have accomplished the great jewel of a universal monarch, go now."
Victory to that Mandaradeva who dwells on the northern side of Kailāsa;
enjoy the powerful imperial glory of both those flanks.
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the universal monarch Sāmṛtaprabha, his purpose accomplished, bowed to him and then departed through the sky.
In an instant, he reached his own camp situated at Govindakūṭa,
where he was welcomed by his mother-in-law Dhanavatī, who possessed great power.
There, he was greeted with great joy by his own Vidyādhara lords who had come out onto the road, as well as by their wives and ministers.
Then, having sat down, he related to those who questioned him his vision of the sage Vāmadeva,
his entry into the cave, and his attainment of the jewels.
Then, there, with the divine musical instruments silenced and joy destroyed, the great festival became one where the Vidyādharīs were dancing and the people were intoxicated by drink.
And on another day, he was [confronted] by a malefic planet situated in the house of the enemy,
while a benefic planet, possessing self-sufficient power, occupied the house of the thorn (kaṇṭaka).
Having performed auspicious rites at a moment endowed with every excellence,
he ascended that celestial chariot fashioned by Brahmā, which had been granted by Śarva.
Then Naravāhanadatta, accompanied by his army and the ladies of the harem, set out through the air from that place in order to conquer Mandaradeva.
And those followers— those heroic lords of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas— remained surrounding him, both devoted and fearful.
Following the command of the general Hariśikha,
Caṇḍasiṃha, together with his mother Dhanavatī and Sumedhā, [departed].
The hero Piṅgalagāndhāra, as well as the powerful Vāyupatha, Vidyutpuñja, Amitagati, and he who is the lord of Kālakūṭa.
Mandara, Mahādaṃṣṭra, his friend Amṛtaprabha,
and the hero Citrāṅgada, together with Sāgaradatta— these were also there.
These and others who were there, taking refuge with Gaurimuṇḍa,
all together, endowed with their forces, pursued him as he sought victory.
Then, the sky being covered by that army, the sun sank away somewhere as if out of shame, its radiance eclipsed by their brilliance.
Then, having crossed Lake Mānasa, which is frequented by hosts of celestial sages,
and having passed beyond Gaṇḍaśaila, the pleasure garden of the heavenly nymphs;
That universal monarch reached Mount Kailāsa, which possessed a luster as white as crystal, as if it were the very root of his own mass of glory.
There, on the bank of the Mandākinī, the wise Vidyādhara lord Mandara addressed him with these charming words as he sat there: SoKss_15,1.43
"O Lord, please stay right here today on the bank of the celestial river;
it is not fitting to proceed further ahead, bypassing this Kailāsa."
For the knowledge of this abode of Hara perishes through transgression;
one must go to its northern side by way of the Cave of the Three Heads.
And that [king] is addressed by the king as "Devamāya";
since he is exceedingly arrogant, how can we depart without first conquering him?
When Mandara had spoken thus and Dhanavatī had approved,
Naravāhanadatta remained right there for that day.
Remaining there, he dispatched a messenger to Devamāya with conciliatory words;
yet, despite this peaceful overture, the latter did not accept his command.
Then, on the following day, that lordly universal monarch set out toward Devamāya together with those various kings, all clad in armor.
Devamāya also, having learned of this, came with his army to do battle,
preceded by Varāha, Vajramuṣṭi, and many other kings.
Then a battle broke out there between those two armies on Mount Kailāsa, while the sky was covered by the celestial chariots of the hosts of gods.
With the terrifying downpour of hailstones that were the rows of severed heads,
and with the thundering roars of the heroes, that terrible onset of the battle-cloud took place.
When Caṇḍasiṃha slew Varāha, the commander-in-chief and foremost warrior of Devamāya, there was nothing at all surprising about it.
But it was truly marvelous that even Devamāya, though himself a master of illusion,
was bound by Naravāhanadatta— who was no magician— and rendered unconscious in battle by his blows.
And once he was bound, that army,
together with Vajramuṣṭi, Mahābāhu, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, and the others, was broken by the great chariot-warriors.
Then, when the gods stationed in their celestial chariots cried out, "Excellent!
Excellent!", everyone rejoiced in that victorious universal monarch.
Then the Great Lord, having consoled him who had been brought there bound,
favored Devamāya with his grace and released him.
He, along with Vajramuṣṭi and the others, bowed down and accepted the command of that wheel-turning monarch, Bāhujita.
Then, when that battle had ceased and the day had passed,
he arrived at the morning assembly hall and stood by the side of the universal monarch.
Being thus questioned by him who desired to enter, Devamāya explained that tradition of the Three-Headed Cave exactly as it truly is.
Long ago, O Lord, on Kailāsa, which was inhabited by the foremost of the Vidyādharas,
there were two sides, southern and northern, whose empires were divided.
Then, by the god Śambhu, who was pleased by his asceticism,
he named Ṛṣabha was designated as the sole universal monarch over both riverbanks.
Once, while crossing over Mount Kailāsa on his way to the northern side,
he fell from heaven, his magical powers lost through the wrath of Śiva who stood below.
Then, having propitiated Hara once more through severe asceticism,
Ṛṣabha requested of him that he be granted sovereignty as before.
"O Lord, I am not yet able to leap over Kailāsa; by what path shall I go?
For on both sides, O God, I am the sovereign emperor."
Having heard that, the wielder of the Pināka bow split Mount Kailāsa on its northern side and created a great cave-opening for him to pass through.
Then, pierced and distressed, Kailāsa addressed Śiva:
"O Blessed One, this northern side of mine is inaccessible to humans."
"Now this cave has been made accessible even to them;
therefore, act in such a way that this boundary of mine is not violated."
Thus addressed by Kailāsa, Hara stationed guardians of the cave:
the elephants of the quarters, venomous-eyed serpents, and lords of the Guhyakas.
To his right, at the gate, is Mahāmāya, the lord of the Vidyādharas;
and to the north are Kālarātri and Aparājitā Caṇḍikā.
Having thus appointed the guardians of the cave and produced great jewels, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara established the regulations there.
This land of two continents shall belong to the Cakravartin Siddharatna,
together with his wives and messengers, as well as to the sky-dwellers.
And those kings who hereafter shall be authorized by him—
for them alone is this cave accessible, and not for anyone else here.
When the Three-Eyed One had thus commanded,
Ṛṣabha then waged war out of pride against the gods for imperial sovereignty, and was slain by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt.
Such, O Lord, is the traditional account of this cave known as Triśīrṣa;
and indeed, this cave is inaccessible to others except for those such as you.
And from time to time, in the lineage of this guardian of the cave-door,
Mahāmāya, I was born as this Devamāya, the Lord.
Born among the Vidyādharas, he is invincible by enemies in battle;
and whoever shall conquer him here will become a universal monarch (cakravartin).
"Therefore, he must be your master, and you must follow that lord"—
thus did a divine voice speak to me at my birth.
Thus I have been conquered by you; you are one who has attained the jewels and possesses great power.
You are our lord here, the sole universal monarch over both sides of Kailāsa.
"Having crossed this cave of Triśīrṣa, conquer the remaining enemies," said Devamāya; thus addressed, the Cakravartin replied.
"Let us go today; let us dwell for now at the entrance of the cave.
Having made our preparations, we shall enter that cave tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta went there and, together with all those kings, took up residence at the entrance of the cave.
And he beheld that cave, its interior deep and without light,
like the birthplace of the darkness at the end of an eon, where neither sun nor moon exists.
And on the second day, having honored her, he entered that celestial chariot,
accompanied by his retinue and aided by excellent jewels that appeared as soon as they were thought of.
He [dispelled] the darkness with the jewels of moonlight, the venomous serpents with sandalwood,
the elephants of the quarters with the jewel of a state elephant, and the *guhyakas* with the jewel of a sword.
Having warded off other obstacles with various jewels, he emerged from that cave through its northern gate together with his army.
And having emerged from the interior of the cave, he beheld the northern side of Kailāsa, which resembled another world of living beings where there is no rebirth.
"Excellent! O Cakravartin, by the majesty attained through the power of the jewels, this cave has been crossed by you"—thus a voice arose from the sky at that time.
Then Dhanavatī and Devamāya said to that lord:
"O Lord, Kālarātri is always present at the door."
And she was previously produced by Viṣṇu during the churning for the nectar of immortality,
as a means to shatter the lords of the Dānavas who desired to seize that nectar.
This very cave has been designated by Śarva here to guard it,
so that no one else may cross over it except for those like you who have been described.
"You are a universal monarch who has crossed over and attained the jewels;
therefore, this cave must be honored by you, for it is worthy of worship for the sake of victorious accomplishment."
In this manner, as Dhanavatī and Devamāyā were speaking,
that day passed away for Naravāhanadatta right there.
And the northern slopes of Kailāsa became crimson with the twilight,
as if foreboding the sprinkling of blood from the imminent battle.
The darkness, having acquired strength, enveloped the king's camp as if remembering the bitterness of its defeat by the cave-dwelling.
Like sprouts of disrespect, dejection, the night of death, and wrath,
throngs of bhūtas, vetālas, ḍākinīs, and jackals wandered about.
In an instant, the entire army of Naravāhanadatta became unconscious, as if asleep; he alone remained unconfused.
Then the Cakravartin, perceiving that display to be the manifestation of the Night of Doom enraged by his lack of worship, honored her with flowers of speech.
Skilled in the movement of the wheel from the navel to the head, you are the syllable Om;
I bow to you, the life-force of living beings, who sustains their existence.

O you who have the form of Durgā, salutations to you, by whom the three worlds were comforted with the streams of blood from the throats of the Mahiṣas as you drank them in, and by whom the splendor of the trident was displayed!
With hands whirling filled with the blood of Ruru and holding a skull-cup, you dance as if holding a vessel for the protection of the three worlds; victory is yours!
With eyes turned upward, a radiant lamp-vessel, and a skull, you are Kālarātri;
O beloved of Bhava, with a skull in your hand, you shine like the sun and moon together.
Thus praised, Kālarātri was pleased there;
yet he desired to worship her with the offering of his own head, for that [which she had granted] was not enough for him.
"Do not act rashly, my son; I am already accomplished for you, O hero.
Let this army of yours return to its natural state; may you attain victory."
Thus spoke that goddess to him as he held his sword; at that very moment, his entire army became like one who has just awakened from sleep.
Then his wife, his friends, and all those Vidyādharas praised the power of that universal monarch.
Then the Hero, having performed the necessary duties such as taking food and drink as prescribed, passed that night of three watches as if it were a hundred watches long.
And having worshipped that Kālarātrī in the morning,
he then set out toward Dhūmaśikha, whose path was blocked by the foremost of the Vidyādharas.
A battle took place between that universal monarch and King Mandaradeva, who was accompanied by his chief ministers; it was such as that.

There, having forcibly captured Dhūmaśikha in battle and brought him back,
that universal monarch honored him and made him accept his command.
And on that day, he stationed the army right there in that city,
like a fire whose mass of smoke-crests has been stilled after its fuel has been consumed.
On the second day, having learned from his scouts that Mandaradeva was approaching to fight, and having already understood the situation beforehand, he [prepared].
Then Naravāhanadatta, having fixed his resolve upon conquering him, set out toward him together with those lords of the Vidyādharas.
Having gone a short distance, he saw before him the army of Mandaradeva, accompanied by a great multitude of kings, having arrived and formed into a battle array.
Then, having arranged a counter-array and surrounded by kings,
Naravāhanadatta charged against the enemy's force.
Then the battle commenced between those two armies,
which resembled the surging, agitated floods of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
Then those great chariot-warriors, Caṇḍasiṃha and the others, fought on one side,
while the heroes led by the king named Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra fought on the other.
Making the three worlds tremble and shaking the great boundary mountains,
that battle unfolded like the onset of the winds at the end of an eon.
Then Kailāsa followed the Lord of Gaurī, its one side crimsoned with the saffron-like blood of heroes, while its other side was white with ashes.
With the fierce radiance of many solar discs rising from the blades of swords,
that great battle was truly the time of universal dissolution for the heroes.
Such was that battle that even Nārada and others, who had witnessed the combat between the gods and the asuras, were filled with wonder upon seeing it.
Thus, in that terrible battle, Caṇḍasiṃha rushed forward and struck him on the head with a fearsome mace, using his golden fangs [as a grip].
Seeing her son fallen from the blow of the mace,
Dhanavatī cursed both armies with the power of her magic knowledge and rendered them unconscious.
And Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch,
as well as Mandaradeva— these two alone remained conscious after that destruction by force.
Then, seeing Dhanavatī enraged and capable of destroying the world,
even the gods traveling through the sky fled in all directions.
Then, seeing that sole universal monarch Naravāhanadatta, Mandaradeva rushed toward him with his weapon raised.
Naravāhanadatta also, descending from his celestial chariot and drawing forth his precious sword, quickly seized him.
Then Mandaradeva, desiring victory through illusion,
assumed by means of his own vidyā the form of a rutting and fierce elephant.
Seeing that, Naravāhanadatta, endowed with the excellence of his magical sciences, assumed by means of his own *māyā* a very great lion-form.
Then, his body shattered and his lion-like form clearly abandoned,
that universal monarch engaged in battle with the god Mandaradeva.
Performing various and diverse movements with their limbs and gestures,
those two holders of the foremost mandalas shone like two engaged in a dramatic dance.
Then Naravāhanadatta, by means of a clever stratagem, took from Mandaradeva’s hand his sword, as if seizing victory itself in person.
And there, while his sword had been taken away and his dagger drawn,
the universal monarch likewise suddenly seized that [dagger] from him as well.
Then, having seized Mandaradeva by the ankles as he fought with his bare arms, being unarmed, the king threw him down upon the ground.
And with his feet placed upon the chest of his enemy, the Emperor drew him by the hair and began to sever his head with a sword.
Then a maiden named Mandaradevī,
the sister of Mandaradeva, approached him and, seeking to dissuade him, spoke thus:
"Having seen you staying in the forest of asceticism, I previously designated you as my husband;
therefore, O King, do not slay this brother of mine, who is like a son-in-law to you."
Thus addressed by Sudṛśā,
the steadfast Great King, casting aside his conquered modesty, spoke to that Mandaradeva.
"I have released you; let there be no shame for you, O Lord of the Vidyādharas.
For victory and defeat in battle are indeed fickle for the brave."
Thus addressed by the king, Mandaradeva said to him:
"What is life to me now, having been protected in battle by a woman?"
Therefore, I am going into the presence of my father who dwells in the forest for the sake of asceticism;
you alone have been appointed here as the sovereign emperor over both halves of the Veda.
"And this matter was previously indicated to me by my father.
Having said this, the proud man went to his father's side in the ascetic grove.
"Excellent! Having conquered your enemies, you have rightly attained universal sovereignty," so the gods dwelling in the sky then exclaimed.
Then, when King Mandaradeva had departed, Dhanavatī restored her son and both armies to consciousness by means of her own power.
Thus, like those who have awakened from sleep, all the ministers and others, perceiving that their enemy was defeated,
congratulated the victorious Naravāhanadatta.
Moreover, those kings belonging to Mandaradeva— such as Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra, Aśokaka, Raktākṣa, Kālajihva, and others— accepted his command.
Recalling the blow from that mace received in battle upon seeing Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra,
Caṇḍasiṃha grew furious, brandishing his excellent sword which was gripped firmly in his clenched fist.

"Enough with this battle here, my child; who could possibly defeat you at the front of the fray? However, by a stratagem, I have for a moment employed an illusion for the sake of protecting both armies from destruction."
And so speaking, Dhanavatī then pacified her son from his great anger and,
through her own supernatural power, brought joy to the entire army along with King Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch.

When he had attained the sovereignty over the northern slopes of Mount Śarva— a realm free from the turmoil of battle because the enemy heroes had been conquered, humbled, or fled— King Naravāhanadatta, whose circle of friends remained unharmed, experienced supreme joy.

Then, accompanied by his beloved wife and his ministers, and joined by a multitude of eminent kings, that virtuous king spent the day drinking wine— which was like the very majesty of his enemies— amidst the loud-sounding musical instruments struck for the festival of victory over his foes, and graced by the beautiful dancing and singing of the celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the first wave in the Mahābhiṣeka-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The Second Wave:
Then, on the following day, having risen from that peak of Kailāsa, he departed.
This Naravāhanadatta is a powerful universal monarch.
At the command of King Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra,

And he reached that city, beautiful with its lofty golden walls,

There, the elders of the royal harem approached the sovereign, who was seated in an improper place and surrounded by kings and sky-dwellers, and addressed him.
Now that King Mandaradeva has been defeated by you and has departed, his queens, having heard this, are seeking to enter the fire; the Lord knows this now.
Thus addressed by them, the universal monarch, having dissuaded them from death,

Thus, that emperor brought the entire host of Vidyādhara lords under the fetters of his affection.
And there, out of gratitude, he consecrated that previously designated King Amitagati in the kingdom of Mandaradeva.
And he entrusted those kings,
Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra and the others, to that king, who was devoted and steadfast.
And there he sported for seven days in the magnificent gardens,

Then, although he had attained the status of a universal monarch over the Vidyādharas and the rulers of the earth— each occupying half of the two worlds— he became one whose desire was for even more.
Though restrained by his ministers, he set out to conquer the regions inhabited by the gods, where Mount Meru stands as an insurmountable boundary, situated in that direction.
Exceedingly accumulated [merits], though they may remain without the attainment of distinction,
do not persist for those possessed of splendor, like blazing forest fires.
Then the sage Nārada, having approached him, spoke thus:
"O King, though you are a knower of policy, what is this exertion of yours toward an improper object?"
One who proceeds with pride and arrogance is defeated in what is impossible,
just as Rāvaṇa was when, out of insolence, he attempted to uproot Kailāsa.
For even Meru is difficult to scale here for the sun and the moon;
yet sovereignty over the Vidyādharas was ordained for you by Śarva, not sovereignty over the gods.
"For Himavat, the realm of the Vidyādharas, has been conquered by you;
what business have you on Meru, the land of the gods? Abandon this stubborn obsession."
"The father of Mandaradeva, who is named Akampana—
he should be visited by you, desiring welfare, once you have gone to where he dwells in the forest."
Having spoken thus, the sage Nārada, after taking leave of that universal monarch who had agreed, saying "So be it," departed as he had come.
Even the Cakravartin, though he knew what was to be done, was dissuaded by Nārada as he recalled hearing from Devamāyā about the destruction of Ṛṣabha.
Having reflected thus by his own intellect, he turned back from there and went to see that royal seer Akampana, who was staying in a grove of asceticism.
And his penance grove was filled with great seers established in yoga,
seated in the lotus posture, as if it were the world of Brahmā.
There he saw that aged man, wearing matted hair and bark garments,
Akampana, who was surrounded by forest-dwelling sages like a great tree frequented by birds.
Approaching there, he prostrated at the feet of the ascetics;
and that royal sage, having offered him hospitality, spoke to him.
"O King, you have done well by coming to this hermitage;
for had you passed it by, these great seers would have cast a curse upon you."
While that royal seer was speaking thus to the universal monarch,
he remained there in the penance grove, having taken up the vows of a sage.
Then Mandaradeva also came into the presence of his father,
accompanied by his sister, the maiden Mandaradevī.
And Naravāhanadatta, seeing him, embraced him around the neck;
for among the wise, affection alone is appropriate toward enemies who have been conquered and pacified.
Then, seeing Mandāradevī arrived together with her brother,
the royal seer Akampana spoke to that sovereign:
"O King, this daughter of mine is Mandaradevī by name;
she has been declared by a divine voice to be the queen of a universal monarch."
When the royal sage had said, "Therefore, accept this [girl] bestowed by me upon you, O Cakravartin," his daughter then spoke.
"In this place, I have four companions who are excellent maidens;
one is a girl named Kanakavatī, born of Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra."
The second was a daughter named Kālavatī, born to Kālajihva;
the third was the offspring of Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, known by the name Śrutā.
The fourth was the daughter of King Protra, named Ambaraprabhā;
and I am the fifth among those daughters of the Vidyādhara lords.
Wandering about, we five, having previously seen this noble son in the forest of asceticism, were filled with longing and made a mutual agreement.
"This husband must be obtained by us all equally;
she who would treat him as distinct from the others—alas, her very self must be destroyed by the others immediately."
"Without those friends of mine, my marriage cannot take place; for how could women like me commit such a rash act of transgressing their nature?"
When that mature woman had spoken thus, her father Akampana summoned those four fathers of the Vidyādhara lords.
He related the matter to them exactly as it was; and they, considering themselves to have achieved their purpose at that very moment, brought forth those maidens and sons.
Then, beginning with Mandaradevī,
Naravāhanadatta married these other five women here in succession.
And there he dwelt with them for many days,
bowing to the sages at the three junctions of the day, having prepared festive ornaments.
"O King, go now to Mount Ṛṣabha for the sake of the great consecration.
When this was said by Akampana, Devamāya then spoke to him.
"O King, you must act exactly in this way, for it was on that mountain that Ṛṣabha and the other former universal monarchs were consecrated."
Having heard that, as he was praising the auspicious Mandara mountain nearby, these words arose from the sky concerning the consecration of Hariśikha: SoKss_15,2.45.
"O King, all [the Buddhas] indeed received the great consecration on Mount Ṛṣabha in the past; you too should go today to that place of accomplishment."
Having been thus addressed by the divine voice and having bowed to the Sākampana sages,
Naravāhanadatta set out from there on an auspicious day.
And he reached the northern gate of the cave named Triśīrṣa,
accompanied by all the lords of the vidyādharas, headed by Amitagati.
There, having entered that cave through that gate where Kālarātri was worshipped, the emperor emerged by the southern exit.
Having set out together with his army for the palace of Devamāya, he rested there with his retinue on that day at the king's request.
While staying there on Kailāsa, he, accompanied by Gomukha, reflected upon Hara who was present there and went of his own accord to see him.
Having reached his hermitage and likewise beholding Surabhi and the bull, he bowed down and approached the gatekeeper, Nandin.
Having been granted permission by him through a gesture of circumambulation, he opened the door and,
having entered, beheld the Bull-bannered Lord together with the Goddess.
Even from afar, she brought delight with the rays of the moon upon her crest,
which seemed to have gone here and there as if to rival the radiance of Gaurī’s face.
He was playing with his beloved at dice, as if by mere whim,
with those pieces that were fickle yet under his control, having been granted autonomy for their own purpose.
And having seen him, he fell at the feet of that bestower of boons and of the goddess,
the daughter of the mountain, and performed two circumambulations.
It is fitting that you have come here; otherwise, there would indeed be fault for you.
Now, however, your spells shall become forever unbreakable.
Therefore, my child, go to that field of accomplishment, Ṛṣabha Mountain;
there, quickly obtain the great consecration when its time has arrived.
Having been thus commanded by the King, the Cakravartin replied, "So be it," and after bowing to him along with his wife, he went to the palace of that Devamāya.
"Where had you been, noble son, that you appear so joyful?
Have perhaps five other maidens met you here as well?"
Having spoken these and other such playful words, he sat there happily, gladdening Queen Madanamañcukā, who had been told the truth of the matter.
On another day, accompanied by the entire host of Gandharvas and Vidyādharas,
he made the sky appear as if it held two suns by means of his own radiant splendor.
Then Naravāhanadatta, mounted upon his excellent celestial chariot, accompanied by his harem and his ministers, set out for Mount Ṛṣabha.
And he reached that divine mountain, where the trees— with their tangled creepers shaken by the wind and their scattered blossoms— seemed like ascetics offering a guest-offering (*argha*).
There, those various lords of the Vidyādharas brought for him the requisites for the great consecration, befitting the power of the Lord.

And at his consecration, all the Vidyādharas from every direction arrived with gifts in their hands— those who were devoted, those who were terrified, those who were conquered, and those who were respectful.
Then those Vidyādharas asked him: "O Lord, who here is to be consecrated upon half the throne in the position of Mahādevī?"
"Queen Madanamañcukā is to be consecrated by me as my equal,"—
when the king had spoken thus, those sky-dwellers immediately entered into meditation.
Then an incorporeal voice arose from the sky:
"O Vidyādharas, this Madanamañcukā is no mortal woman!"
For this Rati has descended here as the wife of this Lord Kāma;
she was not born from Madanavega and Kaliṅgasenā.

For this [child] was not born from a womb; indeed, the gods, having transformed him through their illusory power (māyā), deposited him there at that very moment when she had given birth to her own embryo.
The one born from her who was named Bharga was handed over by the Creator to Madanavega and remained by his side; he is known as Akasa.
Therefore, this Madanamañcukā is worthy of half the throne of her husband;
for in the past, Hara, pleased by her ascetic penance, granted this boon to her.
Having spoken thus, that voice ceased, and those Vidyādharas rejoiced and praised Queen Madanamañcukā.
Then, on an auspicious day, while the domestic priest Śāntisoma was busily engaged,
there arose the sounds of auspicious musical instruments and the beautiful songs of celestial nymphs.
While the brahminical chants of the Brahmins pervaded the ten directions,
Madanamañcukā stood at his left side as he sat upon the lion throne.
The great seers consecrated Naravāhanadatta with waters drawn from various sacred fords and brought in golden jars.
It was a marvel that by the waters falling upon his head, purified by mantras,
the deep-seated stain of enmity toward his foes was washed away from his mind.
The goddess Lakṣmī, as if out of a sense of kinship toward the ocean water used for his consecration,
followed him and visibly enveloped his body along with it.
A continuous garland of flowers, released from the hands of celestial nymphs,
shone upon his body as it fell of its own accord like the Ganges with its many streams.
Then the sun, adorned with the ruddy glow of dawn as if by its own majesty,
shone forth as it stood upon the horizon, having bathed in the waters of the ocean.
Wearing a garland of bound mandāra flowers, radiant with fine garments and ornaments,
and having donned a divine crown, he bore the splendor of Śakra.
And Queen Madanamañcukā, having received her consecration,
shone at his side with divine ornaments like Śacī beside Indra.
With the sounding of drums like thunderclouds and a rain of flowers falling from the sky,
that day became a wondrous storm, surrounded by celestial women like flashes of lightning.
Then, in the city of the Lord of Nagas, even the creepers shaken by the wind did not fail to dance, let alone the excellent women of the Vidyādharas.
During that great festival, when the drummers struck the kettledrums there,
even the mountain seemed to play music itself, as its caves resounded with echoes.
Surrounded by Vidyādharas reeling from intoxication with the finest divine liquors,
even that mountain appeared as if it were itself spinning from the drinking.
Having witnessed the splendor of this consecration as it was thus described,
even Indra, while traveling in his celestial chariot during his own consecration, became dejected in spirit.
Thus, having obtained the consecration as a universal monarch according to his desire,
Naravāhanadatta then remembered his father with longing.
Having consulted together immediately with his ministers, Gomukha and the others,
the sovereign emperor summoned the king and commanded him to go to Vāyupatha.
"Naravāhanadatta remembers you with great longing.
Having said this and related the news, he added, "Go, and bring my father here."
"You should likewise bring his queens and ministers by means of that same speech.
Upon hearing this, Vāyupatha said, "So be it," and departed through the sky.
In an instant, he reached Kauśāmbī, surrounded by seven crores of Vidyādharas, beheld by the citizens with a mixture of fear and wonder.
And there he beheld Udayana, the King of Vatsa, together with his ministers and the queens,
all showing him due respect as was fitting.
Then, having sat down and inquired after his welfare,
that lord of the Vidyādharas, being gazed upon by everyone with curiosity, spoke to the king.
Your son Naravāhanadatta, having propitiated Śaṅkara and having beheld him in person,
shall obtain all the sciences that are difficult for enemies to conquer.
Having slain Mānasavega and Gaurimuṇḍa in the south,
and having conquered Mandaradeva in the north, he became the lord of half the altar.
Having attained the great rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the kings of the Vidyādharas who hold half of both Vedis and who uphold the teachings.
O King, having now attained the great consecration on Mount Ṛṣabha,
he remembers you with longing, together with your queen, ministers, and others.
And I have been sent by him with the command: "Come quickly from here!
For those possessed of merit behold their own lineage as exalted. (SoK 15.2.100)
Having heard this from Vāyupatha, the King of Vatsa, filled with intense longing,
assumed the grace of a peacock delighted by the roar of rain clouds.
And having followed those words, at that very moment,
he ascended a palanquin through the sky by the power of those vidyās.
Followed by Kaliṅgasenā and accompanied by his wife and ministers,
he went and reached that great divine mountain named Ṛṣabha.
There he saw his son seated upon a divine lion-throne,
standing in the midst of the lords of the Vidyādharas and accompanied by many wives.
Seated upon the summit of the eastern mountain, adorned by the host of planets,
he resembled the moon surrounded by a multitude of stars.
Sprinkled by the nectar-essence of that vision, his heart uplifted,
the king assumed a certain resemblance to the ocean at the rising of the moon.
Naravāhanadatta, too, seeing his father after a long time,
rose up in agitation and, filled with longing, approached him along with his retinue.
Then, embraced by his father and placed upon his lap,
he was drenched once more, as it were, by a flood of tears of joy.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, having embraced her son for a long time,
bathed him with the milk flowing from her breasts at the sight of him, thereby reviving her memories of childhood.
And Padmāvatī, as well as the ministers headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa,
and her paternal uncle Gopālaka, beheld him after a long time.
They drank in his nectar-like form with thirsty eyes,
like cakora birds gazing at a sovereign who has been honored according to his merit.
Upon seeing him as her son-in-law and her own daughter, Kaliṅgasenā could not contain herself even within the three worlds, let alone within her own limbs.
And Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others, seeing their sons headed by Marubhūti, who had attained divinity through the grace of their lord, offered them their congratulations.
The goddess Madanamañcukā was adorned with divine ornaments,
as were Ratnaprabhā, Alaṃkāravatī, and Lalitalocanā.
Karpūrikā, Śaktiyaśas, and Bhāgīrathayaśas,
as well as the sister of Ruciradeva who possessed a divine form.
Vegavatī, Ajināvatī, as well as Gandharvadattā, Prabhāvatī, Ātmanikā, and likewise Vāyuvegayaśas; SoKss_15,2.116.
Then her four friends, Kālikā and the others, as well as Sulocanā,
and furthermore Mandaradevī and five other excellent women [spoke].
There, the queens of the universal emperor Naravāhanadatta bowed at the feet of their father-in-law, the Lord of Vatsa.
In the same manner, they likewise increased the joy of Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī with appropriate blessings.
When the King of Vatsa, accompanied by his harem, had seated himself upon the appropriate throne,
Naravāhanadatta ascended his own great seat.
And Queen Vāsavadattā, beholding those various new daughters-in-law, rejoiced as she inquired after their families and names.
Beholding that divine splendor of Naravāhanadatta, the Lord of Vatsa and the others considered their lives to have achieved their purpose.
Then, while that great festival of the reunion with kinsmen was underway,
the brave warder Rucideva entered and spoke.
"Let this banquet hall be prepared; therefore, please come here.
Having heard that, they all went to that auspicious banquet hall.
It was like a garden lotus-pond, with various jeweled goblets as its blossoming multicolored lotuses and strewn with many scattered flowers.
The city was filled with matronly women carrying jars brimming with intoxicating wine,
who created the illusion that the nectar produced by the arms of the Moon’s snatcher had been brought forth.
There, that wine— which shatters the shackles of shame for women in the inner apartments,
which is the very life-essence of Love, and the minister of amorous play— they drank.
Their faces, flushed and blooming with honey,
shone like the red lotuses of lakes at the touch of the fresh morning sunlight.
As if terrified by the very sight of union with them, the cups of wine, surpassed by the lips of the host of goddesses,
concealed their own liquor through the radiance of their own [red] luster.
Even at a time when anger was imminent, the queens of Naravāhanadatta, though touched by intoxication, had their eyes reddened and their brows knitted.
Then they gradually arrived there at the dining hall,
which was captivating with various kinds of food produced by the power of their magical knowledge.
With its spread cloths, its abundance of vessels, and its curtain-screens,
it was like a stage for the arts of fortune, featuring various kinds of savory flavors.
There, having taken their prescribed meals at sunset along with the twilight,
they then rested in their sleeping quarters once the sun had settled upon the mountain of setting.
And Naravāhanadatta, having divided his body in many ways by means of his magic science,
remained present in the dwellings of all the goddesses.
In truth, he took his delight with his beloved Madanamañcukā— whose face was like the moon, who was composed yet possessed flickering pupils— just as one might take delight in seizing the night.
The Lord of Vatsa also spent that night with his followers, enjoying celestial pleasures,
as if he had attained another birth through that very same body.
Having awakened in the morning, they all likewise enjoyed those various pleasures in the gardens,
palaces, and other dwellings of the accomplished masters of knowledge.

Thus, as many days passed while they were engaged in various diversions there, the joyful King of Vatsa, desiring to go to his own city, approached his son—the king of all sky-goers—and spoke thus to him as he stood bowed before him: SoKss_15,2.138 //
"O son, what conscious person would take delight in these divine pleasures? Or rather, what draws humans away from their love for dwelling in their own birthplace?
Therefore, let us go to our own city; as for this Vidyādhara prosperity, you may enjoy it, for these lands are suitable for one who possesses both divine and human nature."

"Furthermore, my son, we should be summoned again on a future occasion; for this is the fruit of our birth here, that we behold this moon-like face of yours, lovely and composed of the nectar-essence to be drunk by the eyes, and that we rejoice upon seeing your divine splendor."
Having heard these very words of his father, the Lord of Vatsa,
King Naravāhanadatta quickly summoned the Vidyādhara lord Devamāya and commanded him with a voice faltering from the weight of his tears.
"Father is indeed departing for his own capital city, accompanied by his mother and joined by his ministers and others;
therefore, dispatch ahead of him a full thousand loads of gold and jewels, to be carried by thousands of celestial beings acting as his porters."
Thus commanded with affection by his master, Devamāya bowed low and said:
"O honorable one, I shall go myself, accompanied by my followers, as far as Kauśāmbī to accomplish this task."
Then the universal monarch gave Vāyupatha and Devamāya, along with their followers, as attendants for his father, who had been honored with garments and ornaments.
Having mounted a divine vehicle, the Lord of Vatsa, together with his retinue,
turned back his son who had followed from afar and departed for his own city.
Queen Vāsavadattā, her longing intensified a hundredfold at that moment, turned back her prostrating son while weeping; gazing after him, she somehow managed to go on.
And that Naravāhanadatta, followed by his ministers and having taken leave of his elders,
returned with his face clouded by tears to that very mountain, Ṛṣabaka.
There, that universal monarch dwelt together with his childhood ministers headed by Gomukha, and with hosts of Vidyādhara lords;
accompanied by his harem and joined by Madanamañcukā, he remained insatiable in the constant pleasures of divine enjoyments.
Thus ends the second wave in the Mahābhiṣeka-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa; and here concludes the fifteenth Lambaka, named Mahābhiṣeka. Śrī!
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.

The sixteenth book, named Suratamañjarī. This nectar of stories, it is said, was long ago churned forth from the ocean of Hara’s mouth by the churning of the Mountain-King’s Daughter as the mountain-staff.
Those who, having attained supernatural powers free from obstacles, taste [the nectar] by force and bear the burden of the gods upon this earth, do so through the grace of Bhava.
First Wave:

May the Conqueror of Obstacles protect you— he whose decoration of vermilion on his cheeks flies upward like a *tāṇḍava* dance, as if he were vomiting forth and then drinking back the power of all impediments.
Thus it was for Naravāhanadatta, as he remained on that Ṛṣabha mountain together with his wives and his ministers.
Once, while he was enjoying supreme prosperity as the sovereign emperor of the Vidyādharas,
experiencing manifold pleasures, spring arrived.
After a long time, the beautiful moonlight of the one marked by the deer became serene;
the earth, embraced by fresh green grass, became as if covered in perspiration.
And the rows of trees on the mountain slopes, repeatedly embraced by the nearby Malaya breezes,

The cuckoo, acting as the doorkeeper for the flower-bowed god, gazing at the mango branch,
seemed to restrain the pride of the proud woman with its warbling.
From the flowering creepers there flew forth swarms of bees with a humming sound,
