Having thus observed that manifestation of honey,
the ministers Gomukha and the others then made their report to Naravāhanadatta.
"O King, behold! Now this very mountain Ṛṣabha has become something else entirely, made of flowers, its forest thickets filled with blossoming madhūka trees."
With flowers struck against one another, they were like cymbals of bell-metal;
shaken by the wind, they seemed to sing along with the humming of the bees.
O King, behold the creepers, which are like women proceeding to the garden prepared for spring— the abode of the God of Love— adorned with veils of pollen.
"Behold this mango blossom-cluster, its string of bees serving as a slackened bowstring;
it is like the vine of the bow belonging to Kāma, who has rested after conquering the world."
Therefore, O King, come now to this beautiful garden on the bank of the Mandākinī and let us go to enjoy this spring festival.
Thus addressed by his ministers,
Naravāhanadatta, together with the women of the harem, then went to the bank of the Mandākinī.
There he sported in the garden, which resounded with the songs of various birds and was adorned with cardamom, cloves, bakula, aśoka, and mandāra trees.
And having seated himself upon a vast slab of moonstone,
he placed the Great Queen Madanamañcukā at his left side.
Accompanied by other members of his harem and surrounded by various lords of the Vidyādharas, headed by Caṇḍasiṃha and Amitagati; so it was.
While enjoying the drinking hall there and engaging in various conversations,
the Emperor, having reflected upon that season, spoke to his ministers.
The southern breeze was pleasant to the touch and gentle; the quarters were stainless, and at every step there were fragrant groves in full bloom.
Sweet are the songs of the cuckoo and the pleasures of drinking games;
what happiness is there not in spring? Yet, in this season, separation from one's beloved is unbearable.
Let alone others; even among animals, the pain of separation here is bitter. Behold this cuckoo, exhausted by the pangs of longing.
For she, having searched for her lost beloved for a long time while warbling,
and not finding him, now stands by the mango tree, silent as if dead.
To the sovereign who had spoken thus, the minister Gomukha replied:
"It is true that at this time, separation is unbearable for all living beings."
For instance, O King, listen as I relate what occurred in Śrāvastī:
there was a certain prince who lived in a village and served the king.
To him, who was named Śūrasena, there was a suitable wife born in the land of Mālava named Suṣeṇā, who was dearer to him than his own life.
Once, when he had been summoned by the king and was preparing to go to the royal camp,
Śūrasena was addressed by his devoted wife:
"Noble son, you ought not to depart leaving me all alone;
for I shall not be able to remain here for even a moment without you."
Thus addressed by his beloved, Śūrasena said to her:
"O slender one, summoned by the king, I do not go; do you not understand why?"
"For I am a prince who lives as a servant, dependent on others.
Hearing that, his wife, her eyes filled with tears, spoke to him:
If you must go by necessity, I shall somehow endure it,
provided that you do not pass even a single day and arrive in the springtime.
Having heard this, he also said to her at last with certainty: "My dear, even if I must abandon my duty, I shall come on the first day of Caitra."
Having spoken thus and being somehow permitted by his beloved,
Śūrasena went to the royal camp in the presence of the king.
His wife also remained there with hope,
counting the days and watching for the day that marked the beginning of spring as the limit for his return.
Then, as the days passed, the festival day of spring arrived,
with the warbling of cuckoos shimmering like the incantations that summon the god of love.
The sound of bees, intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers,
was heard like the twang of the bow being strung by Kāma.
"Since this honey festival has arrived, my beloved will certainly come today"—
thinking thus on that day, his bride [spoke] to Śūrasena.
Having reflected thus, she performed her bath; with Smara worshipped by Suṣeṇā and having prepared her ornaments, she stood waiting, gazing along the path for him.
When her husband did not return even at the end of the day,
she, distressed by despair during that night, reflected thus:
"The time of death has arrived for me, but that husband of mine has not come;
for what affection indeed can there be toward one's own kin among those who are solely devoted to the service of others?"
As she was thinking thus, her mind fixed entirely upon him,
her life-breaths departed as if being consumed by the forest fire of love.
Meanwhile, having somehow freed himself from the king,
Śūrasena, longing for his beloved, did not let the day pass by.
Having mounted an excellent young camel and traversed the long road,
he arrived at his own home in the final watch of the night.
There he saw his beloved, adorned with ornaments but deprived of life,
like a creeper with blossoming flowers uprooted by the wind.
As soon as he saw her, he was overwhelmed; while holding her in his arms, the life-breaths of that man, who was separated from her, departed in an instant along with his lamentations.
Seeing that couple thus fallen into calamity, the family deity,
the boon-granting goddess Caṇḍī, restored them to life out of compassion.
Then, having regained their breath, from that time forward they both remained inseparable,
having seen their mutual affection.
O Lord, in this way, during the spring season, fanned by the Malaya breeze,
for which embodied beings is the fire of separation not unbearable?
When Gomukha had spoken thus, Naravāhanadatta, while reflecting upon those very words, suddenly became as if despondent.
For great-souled ones, whether in distress or at ease, their inner self indicates future good or evil even without a cause. (SoK 16.1.49)
Then, when that day had ended, the Emperor, having performed his twilight devotions,
entered his bedchamber and rested upon his couch.
At the end of the night, in a dream, he beheld his own father being dragged away by a dark woman and led toward the southern direction.
Upon seeing that very [dream], having become awakened and fearing for his own misfortune,
he meditated upon and questioned the vidyā named Prajñapti who had appeared before him.
"Tell me, what is the news of my father, the King of Vatsa?
For it is because of him that I am anxious due to this vision of an evil dream."
Having been addressed thus by him, that Vidyā appeared in bodily form and spoke to him:
"Listen, O Lord, to the account of what befell your father, the King of Vatsa."
While staying in Kauśāmbī, he suddenly heard from a messenger arrived from Ujjayinī that King Caṇḍamahāsena had perished.
From him he heard that Queen Aṅgāravatī had likewise followed him in death, and out of delusion he fell to the ground.
Having regained consciousness after a long time,
he, together with Queen Vāsavadattā and his retinue, grieved for his parents-in-law who had gone to heaven.
In this fragile existence, who possesses stability? And that king is not to be mourned, whose son-in-law you are and whose son is Gopālaka.
Then, having been awakened by his ministers who informed him that Naravāhanadatta was his grandson, he offered the water libation to his parents-in-law.
Then the Lord of Vatsa, his throat choked with tears, spoke to Gopālaka, his brother-in-law, who stood by his side at that time, afflicted with grief out of affection: *Ślokavārttika* 16.1.60.
"Arise, go to Ujjayinī, and protect your ancestral kingdom;
for the subjects are indeed waiting for you"—this was heard from the mouth of a messenger.
Having heard that, Gopālaka wept and said to the King of Vatsa:
"O Lord, I am unable to go, having abandoned you as well as my sister."
And I do not venture even to look upon my own city, now bereft of its father;
therefore, let my younger brother, who is its protector, be king here with my permission.
When Gopālaka spoke thus and did not desire the kingdom,
he then dispatched Rumaṇvat as commander-in-chief to the city of Ujjayinī.
The Lord of Vatsa,
having received permission from his elder brother, consecrated that younger brother-in-law named Pālaka upon the throne there.
Having perceived that everything is unstable, he became dispassionate toward sense-objects and said this to his ministers, Yaugandharāyaṇa and the others:
In this essence-less existence, all things are ultimately devoid of flavor;
we have already ruled the kingdom, enjoyed pleasures, and conquered our enemies.
Thus we have seen our son attain the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas;
now, however, our own age has passed along with that of our kinsmen.
We have been seized by old age by the hair to be delivered unto death,
and our bodies have been overtaken by wrinkles as if by a kingdom of eunuchs.
Therefore, having gone to Mount Kālañjara, I shall cast off this impermanent body and attain here the eternal state as it has been described.
Having been addressed thus by the king, all his ministers deliberated upon that matter,
and Queen Vāsavadattā, being of the same mind, spoke to him.
"O Lord, by your grace, we too shall attain our respective desired goals,
and in the next world as well, we shall reach the supreme state."
Thus addressed by those who were like himself, the king, having made his resolve, spoke to Gopālaka, his maternal cousin and chief minister, who was standing there: *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra* 16.1.73.
"Naravāhanadatta and you are both my equal sons;
therefore, protect this Kauśāmbī, for the kingdom has been bestowed upon you by me."
Thus addressed by the Lord of Vatsa, Gopālaka said to him:
"Whatever be your destiny, that shall be mine; I do not wish to abandon you."
While he was thus speaking at length out of affection for his sister,
the King of Vatsa addressed him, assuming a feigned anger.
This very day you have become independent and have followed me in vain;
for who indeed would heed the command of one who is falling from his own position?
Thus addressed harshly by the king, Gopālaka, weeping with his face cast down, turned back for the time being,
though he had already resolved to go to the forest.
Then the king, mounted upon an elephant together with Queen Vāsavadattā and Padmāvatī, set out accompanied by his ministers.
As he departed from Kauśāmbī, the citizens followed after him, including women, children, and the elderly, crying out with loud lamentation and their faces clouded with tears.
Having somehow consoled them with the words, "May Gopālaka protect you," and having turned them back,
that Lord of Vatsa departed for Mount Kālañjara.
Having reached him and ascended [the chariot], and having bowed to the bull-bannered Lord,
he took the lute Ghoṣavatī, which is dear to him at all times, in his hand.
Accompanied by his two queens at his sides and together with those ministers headed by Yaugandharāyaṇa, he fell from the precipice.
Even as he was falling, that king, shining brightly, went to heaven together with his followers, having arrived in a radiant celestial chariot.
Having heard this from the mouth of Vidyādharī Mukha, Naravāhanadatta cried out, "Alas, father! and fell there upon the ground, unconscious.
Having regained consciousness, he lamented for his father, his mother, and his father’s ministers,
together with his own ministers whose fathers had also passed away.
O Goddess, even though you know the true nature of this cyclic existence— which is momentary and like a magical illusion— how is it that you are so bewildered?
And why do you grieve for your fathers, who are not to be mourned and have accomplished all that was to be done, since you,
the sole universal monarch of the Vidyādharas, are their son?
Thus enlightened by the lords of the Vidyādharas and by Dhanavatī,
he offered water to his ancestors and questioned her once more regarding that science.
"Where is my maternal uncle, that cowherd? Where does he stay and what has he done?
Then that science spoke again to the emperor.
Having grieved for that King Vatsa at the great mountain on the road,
and having considered his sister to be impermanent, he remained outside the city.
Having summoned his brother Pālaka from Ujjayinī,
Gopālaka bestowed upon him even this kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
And while his younger brother remained in the two kingdoms, he,
out of world-weariness, departed for the forest of asceticism and went to Kaśyapa’s hermitage on Mount Asita.
There, having taken up bark garments and practicing austerities in the midst of sages,
your maternal uncle Gopālaka now dwells, O Lord.
Having heard this, Naravāhanadatta, eager to see his maternal uncle, went with his retinue to the Black Mountain by means of a celestial chariot.
Having descended there from the sky, surrounded by the lords of the Vidyādharas,
he beheld that hermitage of the sage Kaśyapa.
It seemed to offer a glance through the delusions of many black antelope deer,
and it seemed to perform a welcoming rite through the warbling of birds.
With the rising columns of smoke from the offerings of the *agnihotra* sacrifices,
it was as if [the city] were showing the path of ascent to heaven for the ascetics.
Resorted to by many mountain-kings and hosts of monkeys,
it was like an unprecedented netherworld situated above the earth, free from darkness.
There in the midst, he beheld his maternal uncle, with matted hair and clad in the bark of trees, surrounded by sages like tranquility incarnate.
The cowherd, seeing his nephew approach,
rose up, embraced him closely, and wept with tearful eyes.
Then, their grief renewed, the two of them lamented for their kinsmen;
for whom does the fire of suffering not burn when fanned by the wind of seeing one's own people?
Then, having approached even those animals who were afflicted by the sight of that suffering,
the sages, Kaśyapa and the others, comforted them there.
Then, when that day had passed, at dawn, the sovereign entreated Gopālaka,
saying, "Come, you shall dwell in my sovereignty."
Gopālaka also said to him: "My son, is this not enough for you, merely by seeing me?
If you have affection for me, then dwell right here in this hermitage during this arrived rainy season."
Having been addressed thus by his maternal uncle at that time, Naravāhanadatta,
accompanied by Sāricchada, remained on that Black Mountain in the hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the first wave in the Suratamañjarī book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.

Then, on that Asita mountain, he made this request to the king as he sat in his assembly hall:
Once, his own army commander [spoke] to that Naravāhanadatta.
"Today, O King, while standing upon my palace roof guarding the troops at night, I saw a woman being carried away through the sky by a divine being."
Having found her crying out, "O son of a nobleman!"— she who had stolen away the very essence of his beauty—
he realized she had been brought there by the moon, powerful at that moment.
"O wretch! Having abducted another's wife, where will you go in the kingdom of King Naravāhanadatta, the protector?"
In the sixty thousand yojanas of the Vidyadhara realm, even animals do not commit unrighteousness; what then to say of others?
Having said this, I myself, together with my attendants, quickly ran forward,
bound that man, and brought him down from the sky along with the woman.
And having brought him down, we saw that he was your brother-in-law, O Lord—

When we asked him, "Who is this woman born of Queen Kaliṅgasenā from Madanavega? Why do you carry her away? he replied: SoKss_16,2.8 //
This is the daughter of Matangadeva, the lord of the Vidyādharas,
born of Aśokamañjarī, and named Suratamañjarī.
This very woman, who had indeed already been promised to me by my mother in words,
has now been bestowed here upon another man by her own father.
"Therefore, if I have now recovered and taken my own wife, what fault is there on my part? Having said this, Ityaka ceased speaking.
"By whom were you married, noble lady, and how did you come to be with this man?
Thus was Surata-mañjarī questioned by me, and she then spoke.
In Ujjayinī there is a glorious king named Pālaka;
he has a son, a prince named Avantivardhana of noble name.
Therefore, having been married by him, I was sleeping on the roof of the palace today when I was carried off by this wicked man while my noble husband was asleep.
When she had spoken thus, both she and that Saṃyatatthika Ityaka were established by me here; now the Lord is the authority.
Having heard this from the general Hariśikha with doubt,
the Cakravartin went to Gopālaka and told him this.
Gopālaka also said: "My dear boy, this was not known to me;
I only now know that she has been married by the son of Pālaka."
"Let the prince be brought from Ujjayinī together with his minister Bharataroha; then we shall know the true state of affairs."
Having heard those words of his maternal uncle, the cakravartin dismissed the vidyādhara Dhūmaśikha, the younger brother of his maternal uncle.
He had both of them brought into the presence of King Pālaka:
that prince from Ujjayinī and his minister.
When they had arrived and offered their salutations, he, accompanied by the cowherds,
honored them with affection and respect, and questioned him regarding the matter at hand.
While Avantivardhana, who shone like the moon at the end of night, was established there,
and while his father Setyaka was likewise [established] along with Suratamañjarī.
While Kaśyapa remained silent among the Vāyupatha and others, the minister Bharatarohaka spoke thus to the others: SoKss_16,2.23
"Listen from the very beginning, O King: once, it is said, all the people of Ujjayinī assembled together and addressed King Pālaka in this manner."
"Today, O Lord, there is a festival in this city called the 'Gift of Water';
if the reason for it has not been properly heard by you, then let it be heard."
Formerly, your father Caṇḍamahāsena, in order to obtain an excellent sword and a wife, propitiated the goddess Caṇḍī through ascetic penance.
She gave him her own sword and spoke thus for the sake of marriage:
"After you have slain the asura named Aṅgāraka, [marry] his daughter, who will soon be born."
"You shall obtain a worthy wife named Putrāṅgāravatī.
Having been thus instructed by that goddess, the king remained there with his mind fixed upon her.
In the meantime, whosoever became the ruler of the city in Ujjayinī was devoured night after night by some being.
Then Caṇḍamahāsena, wandering at will through the city at night to search for him, encountered a man committing adultery.
With his sword, he cut off that head adorned with ornaments;
and as soon as the neck was severed, a certain *rākṣasa* approached and seized it.
"Surely this is the command of the city's ruler; he must be here!"—having thus exclaimed, the king seized the rākṣasa by the hair and began to kill him.
Then that rākṣasa said: "O King, do not kill me falsely;
he who devours the lords of cities here is someone else entirely."
"Who is he? the king asked him; and the Rākṣasa replied once more:
"There is here an Asura named Aṅgāraka, whose abode is in Pātāla."
O scorcher of enemies, O Lord, at nightfall he issues commands to the city governors and forcibly carries off princesses from every side.
And he is preparing an escort for his daughter Aṅgāravatī;
when you see him wandering in the forest, kill him and be successful.
Having spoken thus, the king released that rākṣasa and went to his own palace;
and on one occasion, he then departed for a hunt.
There he saw a massive boar with eyes blazing with anger,
appearing like a peak of a mountain of collyrium rising up from a cave.
"Could such a creature not be a boar? Might it be the illusory Aṅgāraka?"—thinking thus, the king struck that boar with his arrows.
Disregarding those arrows and shaking off his chariot,
he went forth and entered a vast cavern in the earth like a boar.
The heroic king also entered right after him into that very place;
there he beheld a celestial city, but he did not see the boar.
And sitting there on the bank of the pond,
he saw a maiden surrounded by a hundred girls, like Rati herself in embodied form.
That maiden, having approached and asked the reason for his coming there,
looked at him with tearful eyes and, love having arisen within her, spoke to him:
"Alas! Where have you entered, that a boar was seen by you?
That demon is named Aṅgāraka; he possesses a body of diamond and great strength."
Having now abandoned his boar-form, he sleeps within;
however, upon waking at the time for food, he will do you great harm.
And I, O fortunate one, am this Aṅgāravatī, his daughter;
and fearing some misfortune for you, my life-breaths have reached my throat.
Thus addressed by her, the king, remembering the boon granted by the goddess and feeling confident that his purpose would be accomplished, replied to her.
If you have affection for me, then do this at my word:
go and weep by the side of your father when he has awakened.
"O lovely-eyed one, if someone should kill you while you are heedless, what would become of me?"— thus should he who asks for the reason be addressed by you.
"If this is done, there will certainly be welfare for me as well as for you.
Having been addressed thus by the king, she departed, infatuated with passion.
Having sat down by the side of his father who had awakened, she wept;
and when questioned, she explained to him the cause of her fear, which arose from the slaying of her [mother].
Then that Daitya said to her: "Who indeed can slay me, Vajrāṅga?
For this bow, which is in my left hand, protects my vital organ."
The king, remaining hidden, overheard those words;
then that Daitya proceeded to bathe and worship Hara.
Manifesting at that very moment,
the king, with his bow strung, challenged that Daitya— who had maintained a vow of silence— for battle.
That Daitya also, raising his left hand while his other was occupied,
gave a signal to the king, saying, "Wait a moment."
At that very moment, the Daitya was struck by the king with an arrow that had found its mark at the vital point; he fell to the earth.
"If he who has struck me down while I was tormented by thirst does not satisfy me with water year after year,

Having spoken thus, when that Daitya had perished, the king took his daughter,
Aṅgāravatī, and came to this city of Ujjayinī.
And having married that queen, O gods, your father, the god,
caused the giving of water for Aṅgāraka to be performed every year.
Everyone here celebrates the great festival known as the offering of water;
since that [festival] has arrived today, perform for your father whatever he used to do.
Having heard these words of his subjects, King Pālaka then inaugurated in that city a festival for the distribution of water.
While that [festival] was underway and the people were intent upon it in a tumultuous uproar,
suddenly an intoxicated elephant, having snapped its tethering post, rushed toward them.
That elephant, having overcome the goad and shaken off its driver,
wandered about within the city and in an instant killed very many people.
Although the mahouts ran forward accompanied by their attendants,
and the citizens as well, no one was able to restrain that elephant.
As the elephant wandered through it in due course and reached the Caṇḍāla quarter,
a certain Caṇḍāla maiden emerged from there.
As if delighted that the moon had been conquered by her face— her own enemy—
she illuminated the earth with the splendor of a lotus clinging to her feet.
For one whose mind has withdrawn from other objects and remains motionless,
it bestows rest upon the eyes of the entire world, like sleep itself.
That maiden, having struck that lordly elephant with her trunk as it approached directly before her,
lashed it with those crooked side-glances.
Stupefied by the touch of her hand, his face bent down, and pierced by her gaze as he looked at her, that elephant did not move even a single step from that spot.
Then that excellent maiden, having fashioned a swing between his two tusks with her own upper garment, leaped up, climbed upon it, and began to play.
Seeing her afflicted by the heat, the elephant went for the shade of a tree;
having witnessed this great marvel, the citizens there spoke thus:
"Aha! This maiden must be some divine being, for by her form and power, which surpass all others, she has even captivated the animals."
In the meantime, having learned of this, Prince Avantivardhana went out to see the spectacle and beheld that maiden.
As he watched, the deer of the prince’s mind, having rushed toward her— the snare of the hunter Madana— was captured.
She too, beholding him with her heart captivated by his beauty,
took from the swing made of the tusks of a lordly elephant the upper garment he had placed thereon.
Then, as the elephant was mounted by the driver, she went to her own home, looking at the prince with both shame and affection.
When the commotion caused by the elephant had subsided, Avantivardhana too,
his mind carried away by her, returned to his own palace feeling empty.
There, tormented by separation from that excellent maiden and having forgotten the festival of giving water he had begun, he questioned his friends.
"Do you know whose daughter she is, and what the name of that maiden is?
Having heard this, his companions spoke to the prince.
In this city, within a quarter for the Caṇḍālas, there was a certain Mātaṅga named Utpalahasta;
his daughter was Suratamañjarī by name.
Her beautiful form, whose sole fruit is the sight of her by the virtuous, is like that of a figure in a painting; it is not fit for physical enjoyment.
Having heard that from his companions, the prince said to them:
"I believe she is certainly not the daughter of a Mātaṅga; she is surely some divine being."
For such a form as that could not belong to the daughter of a Caṇḍāla;

Speaking thus with his ministers, whom he could not restrain,
the prince became exceedingly tormented by the fire of separation from her.
Then Queen Avantivatī and King Pālaka,
his parents, having learned of this, became deeply distressed for a long time.
"How could a son born of a royal lineage desire a woman of the lowest caste?
When the queen had spoken thus, King Pālaka replied:
Since my son’s mind runs thus toward her,

Whether attached or detached, the mind of the virtuous speaks of what ought and ought not to be done;

Formerly, in the city named Supratiṣṭhita, during the time of King Prasenajit,

a certain young Caṇḍāla, sword in hand, rushed forward there.
Having slain that great elephant with a sword-stroke as it was cutting him,
that heroic man liberated the princess.

"He is my protector from the elephant, or my husband, or even death itself"—
thinking thus, she remained there, distressed by separation from him.
And that Caṇḍāla youth, having slowly returned to his own home,
his heart captivated by her form, brooded upon her and was consumed with anguish.
Where am I, born in my final birth, and where is that princess?

This is a mockery that I can neither speak of nor ignore;
therefore, in this perilous situation, death alone is my refuge.
Having reflected thus, he went to the cemetery at night;
having bathed and prepared a funeral pyre, he kindled the fire and made this petition:

To him who had spoken thus and was preparing to cast himself into the fire,

In this city there dwells a preeminent brahmin named Kapilaśarman;
in his shed, I reside visibly as the letter *sa*.
There, once, out of lust for her beauty, I made his daughter—
who had reached marriageable age and whose blemishes had been removed by a boon— my wife.
At that very moment, my dear son, you were born from my seed;
yet, out of shame, she cast you onto the street at that instant.

Therefore, there shall be no impurity in you, who were born from my own splendor;
and you will surely obtain that wife, the princess Kuraṅgī.
Having spoken thus, the Fire vanished; and he too, filled with joy, the artificial son of the Mātaṅga, having gained confidence, went to his own home.
Then King Prasenajit, urged by fire in a dream,
sought out the truth and gave that daughter to the son of the Fire-god.
"Thus, O Goddess, divine beings always remain hidden on earth;
therefore, this Suratamañjarī is surely some divine being herself, not one of low birth."
For that jewel of my son is surely something quite other;
she is his beloved from a previous birth, as described by the passion of his gaze.
While King Pālaka was speaking thus and we were standing by,
I related there this story concerning the fisherwoman.
Long ago, there was a king named Malayasiṃha in the city of Rājagṛha;
he had a daughter named Māyāvatī, who was peerless in beauty.
Once, while she was playing in the Madhū garden, she was seen by a certain young fisherman who was endowed with beauty and youth.
And Suprahāra, having seen her, fell under the power of love;
for destiny does not regard whether something is possible or impossible.
Having gone to his own home and abandoned the catching of pāṭhīna fish and other such activities,
he remained on his bed with his mind fixed solely upon that, having renounced all food.
When questioned further, he explained his intention to his mother named Rakṣitakā; she, in turn, spoke to her son.
"Abandon your despondency, my son; take food with certainty.
I myself shall accomplish this desired goal of yours through my own skillful means."
Having spoken thus, when he had been comforted, had regained his confidence, and finished his meal,
she took some delicious fish and went to the house of the King’s daughter.
There, having been pointed out by the maidservants from the vicinity of the service-quarters,
that fisherwoman Rakṣitikā entered and gave her that gift of fish.
And by giving this very thing day after day in that same sequence,
she propitiated the princess, who was longing for a word [of reassurance].
"Tell me what you desire from me; I shall do it, even if it be difficult," the princess said to the fisherwoman, being pleased with her.
Then that fisherwoman, having been granted safety, spoke to her in secret:
"O Queen, my son is languishing without you, whom he saw in the garden."
Having shown him hope, I have saved him from the loss of life;
if you have compassion for me, then restore my son to life by your touch.
Thus addressed by that fisherwoman, the princess,
feeling both shame and a sense of obligation, reflected and spoke to her in this way:
"Bring that son of mine secretly to my palace tonight.
Upon hearing this, the maidservant was delighted and went at once to her son.
And at night, having adorned herself according to her means,
she brought her son to that prince’s inner apartments.
There, the princess, having felt affection for him, took Suprahāra— who had long been yearning for her—
and placed him upon the bed.
And she comforted him, whose limbs were exhausted by the fire of separation,
with the touch of her hand, cool as sandalwood, as she massaged them.
Like a fisherman’s son suddenly sprinkled with nectar, he too felt his purpose fulfilled; having rested for a long time, he was instantly overcome by sleep.
And while he was asleep, the princess went elsewhere and slept;
she, the daughter of a fisherman won over by stratagem, had thus prevented the disaster.
Then, as he was awakened by the cessation of that touch of her hand,
he beheld his beloved slipping away, having fallen from the very palm of his hand.
Like a treasure-jar to one who is utterly destitute and despondent,
the life-breaths immediately departed from the fisherman’s son, who was now hopeless.
Having learned of this and come there, the princess reproached herself and resolved to mount the funeral pyre with him at dawn.
Then her father, King Malayasiṃha, having learned of this, came there; seeing that she was beyond restraint, he sipped water for purification and spoke these words:
"If it is true that I am a devotee of the three-eyed God of gods, then tell me,
O Guardians of the World, what must be done by me as is appropriate."
When the king had spoken thus, a divine voice spoke these words:
"This daughter of yours was formerly the wife of this young fisherman."
Long ago, in a village named Nāgasthala, there lived a most virtuous Brahmin named Baladhara, the son of Mahīdhara.
When his father had gone to heaven, he was robbed of his wealth by his kinsmen; filled with world-weariness, he went with his wife to the bank of the celestial river.
Standing there without food, intending to cast off his body, he beheld fishermen eating fish and, out of hunger, believed it with his mind.
Then, when he had passed away there, defiled by his own mental constructions,
his wife— whose intentions were pure— followed him even while remaining established in asceticism.
Born due to the fault of his own volition, this twice-born man was born into a family of fishermen;
and she, Sutaṃtapā, became his wife—she has been born as your daughter, O King.
Therefore, O King, let this blameless daughter of yours restore her former husband— who has lost half his life— to life with half of her own lifespan.
Indeed, by the power of this asceticism and likewise by the greatness of that sacred ford,
this son-in-law of yours, having become purified, shall become king.
Having been thus addressed by the divine voice,
the king gave that daughter, along with half of his own life-span, to Suprahāra, whose life had been restored.
Having become a successful king through the jewels of land, elephants, and horses given by him,
Suprahāra remained there, having obtained the daughter of that [king] as his wife.
Thus, a connection from a previous birth generally leads to affection for embodied beings;
moreover, hear this story concerning one who was related to him as his own son.
In Ayodhyā there was a king known as Vīrabāhu,
who always protected his subjects without distinction, as if they were his own offspring.
Once, the citizens approached that king and informed him:
"O Lord, thieves are plundering this city every night."
"Even while we are awake, they cannot be detected by us.
Having heard this, the king stationed spies there during the night.
They too did not capture the thieves, nor was the disturbance quelled;
therefore, the king himself set out at night to search for them.
Wandering everywhere alone with sword in hand,
he saw a man moving upon the top of the rampart.
Out of fear, he took light steps with eyes as flickering as a crow's,
looking like a lion as he repeatedly turned his neck.
It was marked by the rays of swords drawn from their scabbards,
as if with ropes stretched out for the purpose of seizing the bright jewels.
Having seen him, the king thought: "I know for certain that this is a thief;
surely my city is being plundered by this man who wanders alone."
Having reflected thus, the king approached that clever thief;
the thief also, filled with apprehension, asked him: "Who are you?"
Then the king, burdened by many misfortunes, said to him:
"I am a reckless thief; tell me, who are you?"
The thief also said: "I am a lone wandering robber with great wealth;
come, therefore, to my house so that I may fulfill your desire for riches."
Having heard that, the king agreed, saying "So be it," and went with that bandit to his dwelling at the edge of the forest, which was constructed by being excavated into the surface of the earth.
It was presided over by excellent women, illuminated by many jewels,
always providing fresh enjoyment, and resembling a city of serpents.
Then, once that thief had entered the inner chamber,
a certain compassionate maidservant spoke to the king, who remained in the outer area.
"Where have you entered? Come out quickly, you betrayer of trust!
For this [man], fearing that his secret might be revealed, will surely kill you as you wander alone."
Having heard that, the king went out and quickly returned to his own palace;
then, having summoned the commander-in-chief, he came back again accompanied by his army.
Having arrived and blocked that house, he caused brave men to enter within,
and having seized the thief who had plundered the store of wealth, he brought him out.
When the night had passed, that thief— whose arrest had been ordered by the king—
was led through the middle of the marketplace to the place of execution.
"O father, if this man who is being led to the execution ground with the drum beaten for him should not become my husband, then know me to be dead."
Then, seeing that she was impossible to restrain, her father went to the king and begged for the release of that thief even at the cost of ten million pieces of gold.
The king also became enraged at that merchant, but not at the thief;
he released him without delay and impaled him upon a stake.
Then that merchant’s daughter, named Vāmadattā,
taking the corpse of that thief, entered the fire out of her deep affection for him.
Thus, since those beings are dependent upon their connections from previous births,
what future entity could one transcend, or who could prevent what for whom?
Therefore, O King, this Suratamañjarī belongs to your son Avantivardhana, created by some prior connection.
Otherwise, how could this prince of noble birth have such an attachment here for that woman of the Mātaṅga caste?
"Therefore, O Lord, let that Mātaṅga, her father, whose hand holds a blue lotus, be asked for his daughter; let us see what he says."
Thus addressed by me, King Pālaka then dispatched messengers with blue lotuses in their hands to request that maiden from him.
And being thus entreated by those messengers, Mātaṅga said to them:
"This is my wish; however, [I shall give it] to whoever feeds me in my own house."
"To that man, I must give my daughter Suratamañjarī, along with eighteen thousand Brahmins who reside in the city."
Having heard those words of his, which were accompanied by such a vow,
those messengers returned and reported it exactly so to King Pālaka.
Considering this to be the cause, the king, having related the entire account to the brahmins assembled in the city of Ujjayinī, spoke:
"Eat here in the house of this Mātaṅga, who holds a blue lotus in his hand;
you eighteen thousand shall not wish for anything else."
Thus addressed by the king, those twice-born ones, terrified of the Caṇḍālas and bewildered as to what should be done, took refuge in Mahākāla and performed austerities.
"Eat food from his house without hesitation; he has blue lotuses in his hand.
For this man, along with his family, is a Vidyādhara, not a Caṇḍāla."
Having been thus instructed in a dream by that Śambhu, those brahmins rose,
went to the king, reported it to him, and spoke again:
"O King, let this man cook pure food elsewhere than in the Caṇḍāla quarters; then, with Utpala in hand, we shall eat it here. (SoKss_16.2.183)
Having heard that, King Utpalaha built another house for him;
pleased, he had pure artisans cook food for him there.
When he had bathed and stood before me with lotuses in his hands and wearing clean garments,
eighteen thousand Brahmins were fed there.
When they had finished eating, he approached King Pālaka in the presence of the court; bowing with a blue lotus in his hand, he addressed him.
There was a lord of the Vidyādharas named Gaurimuṇḍa;
I became his dependent, known by the name Mataṅgadeva.
O King, when this daughter of mine, Suratamañjarī, had been born, Gaurimuṇḍa spoke these words to me in secret: SoKss_16,2.188.
"This son of the Lord of Vatsa named Naravāhanadatta,
who is to become the future universal emperor here, is spoken of by us gods."
Therefore, as long as that Kaṇṭaka has not attained the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), go by means of your own magic power and strike him down; do not delay!
Thus impelled then by the wicked Gaurimuṇḍa,
as I was traveling through the sky for that purpose, I saw Maheśvara before me.
Enraged, that Lord uttered the sound "hum" and immediately cursed me:
"O wicked one, how can you desire to commit sin against a person of great soul?"
"Therefore, with this very body, accompanied by your wife and daughter,
go to Ujjayinī and fall among the Caṇḍālas, O evil-minded one!"
When he feeds eighteen thousand Brahmins residing in the city as a fee for the gift of his daughter, [he will attain success].
"At that time, the end of the curse will come to someone in your house;
you must give your daughter in marriage to him who provides her dowry."
Having spoken thus, when Śambhu had vanished, I then fell [into another womb];
in others, I was named Utpalahasta, yet there was no confusion between me and them.
"Today that curse of mine has been pacified through the grace of your son;
therefore, I give this daughter, Suratamañjarī, to him."
And now I depart for my own Vidyādhara abode,
for the sake of serving Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch.
Having spoken thus and entrusted his son, that Mataṅgadeva, accompanied by his wife, rose into the sky and came, O King, into the presence of your feet.
King Pālaka, having realized the truth, was delighted and then performed the marriage of his daughter with that Suratamañjarī.
And his son, Avantivardhana, having obtained that Vidyādharī as his wife,
became one who had achieved his life's purpose through the attainment of more than he could have ever imagined.
And once, while that prince was sleeping with her in his palace,
he woke at the end of the night and suddenly did not see his beloved.
Having searched for her and not found her,
he lamented and suffered so intensely that even his father, the king, became utterly distraught upon learning of it.
"This city is well-guarded; no stranger may enter it at night.
Surely she has been carried off by some wicked sky-walker."
While we were thus speaking and had gathered there at that moment,
your Vidyādhara Dhūmaśikha descended from the sky.
Therefore, this Prince Avantivardhana has been brought here;
and I, having related the circumstances, sought him from King Pālaka.
And here she stands, Suratamañjarī, together with her father;
such is her story, and Your Majesty knows what follows from this.
When the minister Pālaka had thus spoken and ceased, O Bharatarohaka,
the members of the assembly questioned Mataṅgadeva in the presence of Naravāhanadatta.
"To whom have you given this Suratamañjarī? Tell me!
He replied, "I have indeed given her to Avantivardhana."
Then Cetyaka, questioned by them, "Tell us, why do you take her away?
replied, "In the first place, she was given to me by my mother's word."
"If you have a father, who is your mother? And as for the giving of her, who here is your witness?
"Therefore, she is another's wife; you are a sinner! thus the members of the assembly said to him.
When he had been thus rendered speechless by them and forcibly brought under control,
King Naravāhanadatta, enraged by his ill-behavior, issued an order for his punishment.
"Forgive this one single offense of his here; for he is indeed your brother-in-law, the son of Madanavega.
Thus entreated by the eminent sages, Kaśyapa and others, the king, having rebuked him somewhat, released him with great difficulty.
Furthermore, he dispatched his own nephew Avantivardhana,
together with his ministers, to his own city, accompanied by his wife and placed in the hands of Vāyupatha.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Suratamañjarī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave.
In this manner, on that Asita mountain, [he found] the virtuous Suratamañjarī.
Thus, she was carried off from that brother-in-law who had threatened her.
Having recovered him and presented Naravāhanadatta— who was standing in the midst of the sages— to his husband, the seer Kaśyapa spoke to him.
O King, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a universal monarch like you,
whose mind— while seated upon the throne of Dharma— is not under the sway of passion and the other afflictions.
Blessed indeed are those who always behold you as one of meritorious deeds;
for even in such sovereignty, not the slightest fault exists in you.
For in former times, other universal monarchs such as Ṛṣabha and others were seized by various kinds of defects; they perished and fell from their royal splendor.
Ṛṣabha, Sarvadamana, and the third, Bandhujīvaka—
all of them met their downfall at the hands of Śakra due to excessive pride.
Jīmūtavāhana, the lord of the Vidyādharas, having arrived, was questioned by the sage Nārada regarding the cause of his attainment of the station of a universal emperor.
He recounted the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree as well as that of his own body;
by that proclamation of his meritorious deeds, he was cast down from his station.
And he who was the universal monarch named Viśvantara here, when his son Indīvarākṣa had been slain by the king of Cedi; ||| SoKss_16,3.9 |||
Deprived of his fortitude by grief and delusion over his wicked son, he perished through that [woman] named Vasantatilakā, who brought about the destruction of his family.
O Indra among kings, having become a human being with a singular vision,
he attained the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among the *vidyādharas* through his well-performed deeds.
Having enjoyed the wealth of universal sovereignty for a long time without encountering any misfortune,
he eventually abandoned it of his own accord out of dispassion and went to the forest.
Thus, the Vidyādharas are generally deluded by the attainment of their own status;
blinded by passion and other afflictions, they do not remain on the proper path and fall.
You must constantly guard yourself from straying from the path of truth;
likewise, these subjects of the Vidyādharas must be protected from transgressing the Dharma.
Thus addressed by Kaśyapa, King Naravāhanadatta, having placed full faith in his words, respectfully questioned him as follows.
O Blessed One, please describe to us how Tārāvaloka, while still a human being, formerly attained sovereignty over the Vidyādharas.
Having heard that, Kaśyapa said: "Listen, I shall tell you:
there was a king among the Śibis named Candrāvaloka."
That Lord had a beloved named Candralekhā as his chief queen;
she was of a lineage as pure as the Ocean of Milk, stainless, and equal in her steadfastness to the Gaṅgā.
And he had an elephant, the crusher of enemy armies,
known on the earth as the great Kuvalayāpīḍa.
By the power of that [merit], even though he was powerful, that king was never overcome by any enemy or anyone else in his kingdom, which had the citizens as its masters.
And when his youth had passed away, a son endowed with auspicious marks was born to that lord of the earth by Queen Candralekhā.
And he, named Tārāvaloka, gradually grew up together with innate virtues such as generosity, righteousness, and discernment.

The one of great intelligence studied the entirety of the meaning of all branches of knowledge; there was not a single word or meaning he did not learn, yet he never failed to grant the desires of those who sought his help.
Though young in years, he was old in his conduct;
though resembling the sun in brilliance, he was exceedingly gentle in appearance.
He was as beautiful as the full moon, possessing the splendor of the entire collection of its digits;
he was like Kandarpa, the god of love, bestowing longing upon the whole world.
He was born as one who had surpassed Jīmūtavāhana through his service to his father,
and was marked by the manifest signs of a great universal monarch (cakravartin).
Then, for the sake of that son, the king Candrāvaloka brought from the lord of Madra a maiden named Mādrī.
And when he had completed his marriage, the great king, his father, gratified by the excellence of his virtues, consecrated him as the crown prince at that very time.
And there, having been consecrated as crown prince by his father according to his command,
Tārāvaloka established alms-houses for the distribution of food and other necessities.
And rising from his bed, he would always mount the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa to personally inspect those alms-bowls.
Whatever anyone requested, he gave that to them, even his own life;
by this, the fame of the crown prince spread in all directions.
Then two twin sons were born to him by Mādrī;
and his father gave them the names Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
And those two children grew up as the very embodiments of their parents' affection and joy,
even more beloved than life itself by their own grandparents.
These two, Tārāvaloka and Mādrī, could not have had enough of gazing upon those two who were bent like bows with their virtues fixed upon them.
Then, seeing Kuvalayāpīḍa the elephant and the two sons of Dātṛyaśas, the enemies of Tārāvaloka spoke to their own brahmins: SoKss_16,3.35 //
"Go to the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa and beg him from Tārāvaloka;
if he is available, he will surely give him to you."
Then we shall seize the kingdom from him once he is deprived of it;
he will not give it, and thus his reputation for generosity will perish.
Having been addressed thus by them, those brahmins said, "So be it," and having departed from there,
they then requested that [gift] from King Tārāvaloka, beginning with the hero among givers.
"What indeed was the purpose of that elephant king when he was requested by the twice-born?
I know for certain that these [birds] were employed against me by someone."
Therefore, let it be so: this best of elephants must first be given by me;
for how can a petitioner go away with his desire unfulfilled while I am still alive?
Having reflected thus, Tārāvaloka gave that best of elephants to those brahmins with a perfectly steady mind.
Then, seeing that excellent elephant being led away by those twice-born men,
the citizens of Candrāvaloka went in anger into the presence of the king.
And they said: "This kingdom has now been abandoned by your son, who, having renounced everything, has taken up the dharma of a sage."
Behold this great elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, the very root of royal fortune, who, like an elephant with temples broken by rut-fluid, has been given to supplicants.
Therefore, either send this son away to the forest for asceticism,
or bring back the elephant, or else we shall make another king.
Thus addressed by those citizens, Candrāvaloka caused his son to hear that very same thing through the mouth of the doorkeeper.
Having heard that, his son Tārāvaloka said:
"I have already given away an elephant; indeed, there is nothing that I cannot give to those who seek my favor."
But what use have I for such a kingdom as this, which depends upon the citizens? And what use have I for wealth that flickers like lightning and is of no benefit to others?
Therefore, dwelling in the forest among trees that possess the splendor of fruits edible by all is better for me than living here amidst such royal beasts.
Having spoken thus, accompanied by his wife whose resolve was equal to his own,
he meditated upon the feet of his parents and gave away his store of wealth to those who sought it.
Having donned bark garments, Tārāvaloka departed from his own city together with his two sons, consoling the weeping brahmins.
Seeing him set out in such a manner, even the beasts and birds,
wailing piteously, drenched the earth with streams of tears.
Then, as Tārāvaloka was traveling along the road with nothing remaining for his vehicle but a single chariot for his two sons, he was requested by other brahmins for their chariots and horses.
Then he gave those [gifts] to them and himself drew the chariot,
together with his wife, in order to lead those two delicate youths to the forest of asceticism.
Then, approaching him as he was exhausted and situated in the midst of the Avīci hell,
another brahmin there begged even for his horseless chariot.
Having given that [gift] to him without hesitation, the steadfast man, together with his wife and his son, somehow reached the forest of asceticism on foot.
There, having performed noble service for him by his own wife Mādrī,
he remained with his retinue of deer, making his dwelling at the foot of a tree.
With beautiful fly-whisks of flower-clusters trembling in the wind,
with umbrellas of broad-shaded trees, and with stone seats and beds of leaves;
The forest regions attended upon that hero, who was established in the sovereignty of dispassion, with the songs of female bees and the juices of various fruits.
And once, when his wife Mādrī had gone outside the hermitage herself to gather fruits, flowers, and other provisions for him, [the deer approached].
A certain aged brahmin, having approached Tārāvaloka as he sat in his leaf-hut, requested his two sons, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
"It would be better for these two children to be taken away— even though they are infants—
than that this petitioner, whose desire has been frustrated, should ever again be sent away empty-handed."
Thinking, "This rogue Vidhi indeed desires to witness the destruction of my fortitude," he gave those two sons to that brahmin.
As the two were being led away by that brahmin, they did not proceed;
thereupon, the brahmin struck them on their bound hands with creepers.
And that cruel man led them away while they were crying out repeatedly for their mother,
turning back again and again to look at their father with tearful eyes.
"My child, though Tārāvaloka beheld this, he was not disturbed;
rather, by his fortitude, the entire host of beings, both moving and unmoving, was shaken."
Then, having gradually gathered flowers, fruits, roots, and other provisions,
that virtuous Mādrī, though exhausted, returned from the edge of the forest to her husband’s hermitage.
She saw her husband with his face cast downward, but she did not see those two sons,
whose clay horses, chariots, and elephants used for play lay scattered about.
With a heart fearing the undesired, she asked her husband in great agitation: "Alas, I am ruined! Where are those two sons of mine?"
He too spoke softly: "O blameless one, these two sons were given by me to that poor brahmin who entreated me."
Having heard that, the virtuous woman, her delusion abandoned, said to her husband:
"In that case, you have acted rightly; how could one who seeks [a favor] be turned away?"
When she had spoken thus, because of that shared resolve of the husband and wife,
the world trembled and Indra’s throne shook.
Then Indra, through his supernormal power of mental concentration, beheld the world shaken by the power of the generosity and virtue of Mādrī’s two sons, Rāhula and Avalokita.
Then, having become a brahmin and desiring to test him, he went to the hermitage and asked Mādrī, the devoted wife of Tārāvaloka, for her hand.
Tārāvaloka, free from hesitation, proceeded to give that forest-dwelling companion to him with water poured from his own hand.
"O royal sage, what do you seek to accomplish by giving away even such a wife?"—
when he was thus addressed by Śakra in the form of a brahmin, he replied:
"I have nothing whatsoever to be accomplished; this is my only desire, O twice-born one: that I may always give even my own life to the Brāhmaṇas."
Having heard that, Śakra assumed his own form and said to him: "I am pleased with you, having fulfilled my desire to test you; therefore, I shall speak to you."
"Your wife shall not be given back, and you shall soon become a universal monarch among the Vidyādharas"; having said this, he vanished.
In the meantime, that old brahmin, having received the two sons of Tārāvaloka as his sacrificial fee, became lost on the way.
Wandering on, they reached by chance the city of that lord Candrāvaloka,
and proceeded to offer the two princes for sale in the marketplace.
Having recognized those two there, the citizens went and informed the king, and brought the two, along with the brahmin, into the presence of Candrāvaloka.
Seeing his two grandsons and questioning that brahmin with tears in his eyes, he remained for a long time immersed in a state of both joy and sorrow, filled with the account related by him.
Then, having perceived the excellence of his son’s character, he abandoned all desire for the kingdom; though entreated by the citizens, he [dismissed] those two brahmins.
Having purchased his two grandsons from him with wealth,
he took them along with their belongings and went to the hermitage of his son, Tārāvaloka.
There he saw him with matted hair and wearing bark garments,
like a great tree whose splendor had been enjoyed by birds arriving from every quarter.
When he had run from afar and fallen at his son's feet,
he took him onto his lap and bathed him with the water of his tears.
That very [power] then became the commencement of his ascent to the lion-throne, preceded by the consecration for the sake of the sovereignty over the Vidyādharas.
Then the king gave those two sons, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
to Tārāvaloka, saying, "These two were purchased by me for you."
While they were there engaged in conversation concerning one another's adventures,
a four-tusked elephant and Lakṣmī descended from heaven.
And when other lords of the *vidyādharas* had also descended,
Lakṣmī, holding a lotus in her hand, spoke to that Tārāvaloka:
"Mount this elephant and come to the abode of the Vidyādharas;
enjoy the glory of that empire, won through the power of your generosity."
When Lakṣmī had spoken thus, accompanied by his wife and son,
he bowed at the feet of his father while observing those dwelling in his hermitage.
Having mounted that divine elephant and surrounded by the lords of the Vidyādharas,
Tārāvaloka traveled through the sky to the realm of the Vidyādharas.
Having enjoyed sovereignty there for a long time and being supported by the sciences,
he eventually developed dispassion and retired to a grove of asceticism.
Thus, in former times, though he was a mere human, Tārāvaloka attained the sovereignty of all the Vidyādharas through his stainless meritorious deeds.
But others, even having attained that [state], fall away from it due to lapses;
therefore, you must guard against such a transgression, whether by yourself or through others.
Having thus related this story, the sage Kaśyapa instructed Naravāhanadatta; and the emperor, saying "So be it," accepted his advice.

"Listen, O Vidyādharas! From this day forward, whoever among my subjects commits a transgression against the Dharma shall certainly be put to death by me. Having said this, he then caused a proclamation to be circulated all around Mount Harā.
Then, his command upheld by the sky-dwellers with bowed heads,

The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Haṭṭa.

Thus, there on Mount Asita, in the hermitage of the sage Kaśyapa and near his uncle Gopālaka, who was engaged in ascetic penance.

There exists here on earth a city renowned by the name of Vārāṇasī;
adorned by the celestial river, it is like the very embodiment of Śiva, bestowing liberation.
With the banners of the celestial palace being lowered and raised by the wind, it seemed as if it were constantly saying to the people: "Come here; go to liberation."
With its white palace pinnacles, it is the dwelling place of the Moon-crested Lord;
crowded with hosts of Śiva’s attendants, it shines like the plateau of Mount Kailāsa.
In that city, in former times, there was a king named Brahmadatta;
he was solely devoted to Śiva, venerable to Brahmins, heroic, generous, and intent on forbearance.
His command did not stumble even in difficult terrains, nor did it sink even in oceans;
as it wandered over the earth, there were no islands that it did not cross.
Queen Somaprabhā was his beloved, bestowing joy upon him like a cakora bird; she too became for him a draught for the eyes.
And his minister was a brahmin named Śivabhūti,

Once, while that king was lying on his bed in the moon-palace at night,

Made of glowing Jāmbūnada gold and surrounded by rows of royal swans,

When that most wonderful being had passed beyond the range of his sight, the king,

When the king had spoken thus, the minister Śivabhūti said to him:

Through the application of diverse karma,

Therein, amidst that which consists of suffering, sentient beings— due to delusion and conceiving the notion of pleasure— become attached through their relish for dwelling, food, drink, and so forth.

And there he saw those two golden swans from afar and paid them homage;

Their bodies were made of pure gold, their eyes consisted of pearls and gems,

Observing those two swans who had approached him with confidence,

There he saw Jayasena’s daughter, the princess named Candralekhā, who was holding a fly-whisk for the queen and gazing at him with longing.

In this regard, O King, hear this wonderful account concerning those two, Piṅgeśvara and Guheśvara.
On this earth there is a royal grant known as Yajñasthala;

To him were born two sons in their middle age:
Harisoma was the elder of them, and Devasomaka the younger.
When those two had emerged from childhood and been initiated,
the wealth of that brahmin, along with his wife, was first exhausted by their lifespan.
Then those two sons of his, wretched, deprived of their father, and lacking a livelihood,
having had their estate seized by kinsmen, consulted with one another.
"Since we were born with the single practice of begging for alms, yet we do not obtain alms,

"Even though we have both fallen from our status, who here would believe that we have come of our own accord?

Thus addressed by their two maternal uncles, Hari and Somadeva, with throats choked with tears, accepted those words, saying, "So be it."
Then, having led the cattle into the forest, the two of them guarded them constantly;
and being exhausted, they returned home in the evening, taking the animals with them.
Likewise, as the two of them were tending their cattle, being cursed by fate,

Then, while those two maternal uncles were thus distressed, once upon a time,
their two sacrificial animals— a cow and a goat— disappeared somewhere.

the two of them fled and, searching for a place, entered the forest far away.

There, as soon as they saw him, the gatekeepers, suspecting them of being thieves,
seized those two thieves and cut off their ears and noses.
Once they were bound in such a manner, those thieves then led them to the presence of the chief criminals, while being beaten with blows from clubs.
There, questioned by those leading thieves, the two of them, overwhelmed by fear and afflicted by the suffering of hunger, related the account of their own conduct.
Then, out of compassion, those chief thieves released the two from their bonds and said, "Stay here and eat; let there be no fear for you."
"Today, on the eighth day, at this occasion for the worship of the army leaders, you two have arrived as our guests; you are worthy of a share here."
Having spoken thus, those thieves, who had worshipped the goddess and fed the two [boys] from their own plates,

Then, as they gradually committed acts of theft together with those bandits,

And once, having heard from a wandering thief that there was a great city— a sacred site of Śiva—
those two generals set out at night with their armies to plunder it.
Even when the signless was seen, as long as that [state] did not cease, they two, having attained it,

Then the god Hara, being incensed, was invoked by the inhabitants of that place who sought refuge; he rendered those thieves crippled and blind.
Seeing that suddenly and realizing it was Śarva’s grace,
the citizens gathered together and struck down those bandits with clubs and stones.
Remaining invisible, the hosts threw the thieves into chasms;
some they crushed, having struck down those bandits upon the ground.
And as soon as people saw those two generals and sought to kill them,
they both turned into tailless dogs.
Remembering their former birth in such a state,
they danced before Śaṃkara without hesitation and took refuge in him alone.
Seeing that, all the people—the brahmins, the merchants, and the rest—were struck with wonder;

With their delusion stilled and awakened, those two dogs, for the sake of ending the curse,
renounced food and then resorted to austerity dedicated to Śiva.
In the morning, the citizens there, having celebrated a festival and worshipped the Lord,
beheld two dogs absorbed in meditation, turning their faces away even when food was offered.

"Tell me first how Padmāvatī, having emerged from the state of mortality caused by the curse, reached [her destination];

Having heard that, those two birds described the story as follows:
"There was a lord of the Daityas named Vidyutprabha, who was invincible even to the gods."

Ten lakhs of elephants, fourteen [lakhs] of chariots,
thirty lakhs of horses, and ten koṭis of foot soldiers.
In each watch, they take turns guarding this city;
and that rotation of watches for them returns every seven years.
Having heard that, Vidyuddhvaja said: "Fie on such a kingdom, which is indeed protected by the arms of others and not by one's own arm!"
Having performed that, I shall practice such intense austerity that this mockery shall not befall me, whose enemies have been conquered by my arms.

Having spoken thus with certainty and having bid farewell to his parents,
the asura Vidyuddhvaja performed ascetic penance for the propitiation of Viriñca.

Then Brahmā, observing that his asceticism was capable of agitating the world,
approached him and gave those weapons, beginning with the Brahma-weapon, to him who requested them.

except for the fierce Pāśupata weapon, which is beyond our reach.
"Desiring victory, you must not employ this at the wrong time.

Agitated by the wind of indignation and overflowing with hundreds of armies,
the ocean of battle swelled, with its leaping horses and elephants as its crocodiles.
Then, as the dual combats between the gods and the asuras proceeded,
Vidyutprabha— the father of Vidyuddhvaja— also approached Śakra in a rage.
Then, as Śakra was being gradually overwhelmed by that enemy of the gods in a battle of missiles against counter-missiles, he hurled his thunderbolt at him.
Struck by the vajra, that Daitya fell there, deprived of life;
then Vidyuddhvaja, out of rage, rushed toward Śatakratu.
When there was no longer any doubt of his survival, Brahmā first hurled the Brahmā-weapon at him,
and other great asuras struck him with various other weapons.
Then, having meditated for a moment upon the Pāśupata weapon commanded by Īśvara,
Śakra worshipped it as it appeared before him and hurled it at his enemies.
That asura army was consumed by that weapon of the fire of time;
however, Vidyuddhvaja, because of his youth, was not killed but fell down unconscious.
For that weapon does not strike a child, an elder, or one who has turned his back;
then the gods, having achieved victory, all went to their own abodes.
Vidyuddhvaja, having been struck down, regained consciousness after a long time;
lamenting and fleeing, he spoke to the remaining soldiers who had gathered together.
"Though we were victorious, we have today been defeated, for the Brahma-weapon has been countered.
Therefore, having gone to the battlefield and approached Śakra, I shall sacrifice my life."
"If my father hates me, I shall not be able to go back to my own city again"—
to him who had spoken thus, his aged paternal minister said:
The Brahma-weapon, discharged at an improper time, was rendered sluggish by other weapons already loosed;
indeed, it was thwarted by that great weapon of Ishana, which cannot be endured by other weapons.
"You ought not to provoke an enemy who has recently achieved victory at an improper time;
for in doing so, you would only cause his own growth and your own destruction."
For the steadfast man, by protecting himself and waiting for the time when the enemy's strength is reached,
achieves world-renowned glory after having administered a retaliatory blow to his anger.
When he was thus addressed by the elder, Vidyuddhvaja said:
"In that case, you all go for the sake of protecting our kingdom; as for me, however—"
"I shall go and propitiate that very Śiva, the Lord of All," he said;
and having spoken thus, he dismissed his followers even though they were unwilling to leave.
Having gone there with five companions who were sons of Daityas,
he took up his residence at the foot of Kailāsa on the bank of the Gaṅgā to practice asceticism.
In the midst of the five fires, in the cold, and in water,
he remained for a thousand years, meditating on Śiva and subsisting on fruits.
The second was eating roots, the third eating water,
the fourth subsisting on air, and the fifth was fasting entirely.
He did not regard the Lotus-born one highly, even though he had come for the sake of granting a boon;
and having seen him, he said, "The power of your boon has been witnessed; you may depart."
After he had remained for that same length of time without food,
with great smoke rising from his head, Śambhu himself appeared before him.
When he was told, "Choose a boon," that Daitya replied to him:
"O Lord, by your grace, may I slay Śakra in battle."
"Arise! There is no difference between one who is conquered and one who is slain.
Therefore, you shall conquer Indra in battle and dwell in his place."
Having spoken thus, the god vanished; and Vidyuddhvaja, considering his desire accomplished, broke his fast and returned to his own city.
There, welcomed by the citizens and having met with that minister of his father’s who had performed arduous penance for his sake, he celebrated a festival.
Having summoned the hosts of asuras and arranged the preparations for battle,
he dispatched a messenger to Indra, saying, "Be ready for war!"
And the sky, rent by the thunderous roar of the armies,
trembled as they covered it with their banners, creating a calamity for the dwellers of heaven as it were.
Indra too, perceiving that he had arrived having obtained the boon, was distressed;
after consulting with the preceptor of the gods, he summoned the celestial armies.
Then, when Vidyuddhvaja had arrived, a great battle broke out between those two armies,
in which the distinction between one's own side and the enemy was no longer known.
The Daityas led by Subāhu fought with the Vāyus;
those led by Piṅgākṣa fought with the Kuberas, and those led by Mahāmāya fought with the Agnis.
The Iron-bodied ones and others were subdued by the Sūryas; the Ākampanas and others by the Siddhas;
the Daityas by other Vidyādharas; and the Gandharvas and others by still others.
Thus there was a great battle between them for twenty days;
on the twenty-first day, the gods were broken by the Daityas in combat.
And those [demons], broken, fled and entered within Triviṣṭapa;
then Vāsava himself, mounted upon Airāvaṇa, went forth.
And surrounding him, the divine armies emerged once more,
together with the lords of the sky-dwellers, headed by Candraketu.
Then, as the battle commenced and the Asuras and gods were being slaughtered,
Vidyuddhvaja rushed toward Indra, incensed by the killing of his father.
As the lord of the Daityas countered his weapons with counter-weapons,
the king of the gods repeatedly severed his bow with arrows.
Then, empowered by the boon of Maheśvara, Vidyuddhvaja took up a mallet and rushed with speed toward Vāsava.
Leaping up and placing his foot upon the tusks of Airāvaṇa,
he ascended the top of its frontal globe and struck down the driver.
And he dealt a blow with a mallet to the King of the Gods,
and the King of the Gods quickly struck him back with a club.
Vidyuddhvaja struck him again with a mallet;
Indra fell there, unconscious, upon the chariot of Vāyu.
Vāyu, with the speed of thought, carried Indra away on his chariot elsewhere;
Vidyu-dhvaja, who had leaped after him, fell to the ground behind.
"This is not the time; withdraw Indra from the battle quickly!"—thus at that moment a voice issued forth from the sky.
Then, after Śakra had been driven away by Vāyu,
Vidyuddhvaja, mounted upon his chariot, pursued him with the speed of that vehicle.
Then Airāvaṇa, enraged and unrestrained, rushed forward,
crushing and routing the armies, and went toward where Śakra was.
Then, having abandoned the battle even as Indra pursued him,
the preceptor of the gods led the terrified Śacī to the abode of Brahmā.
Then Vidyuddhvaja, having achieved victory and found the city empty,
entered Amarāvatī accompanied by his shouting armies.
Indra, having regained consciousness and seeing that it was no longer the right time,
went together with all the immortals back to that very abode of Brahmā.
"Now, this is the power of Hara’s boon; do not grieve.
You shall once again attain your own station," the Grandfather consoled her thus.
He gave him his own place called Samādhisthala, a site that brings all happiness and is situated in a certain region of the Brahma-world, for his residence.
There the lord of the gods dwelt together with Śacī and Āvaṇa;
and at his word, the lords of the Vidyādharas went to the world of Vāyu.
The lords of the Gandharvas went to the invincible world of Soma;
others, abandoning their respective abodes, went to other worlds.
And Vidyuddhvaja, having caused the drums to resound upon the earth of the gods,
seized the kingdom in Triviṣṭapa and ruled it without restraint.
In the meantime, at this juncture in the story, the lord of the Vidyādharas, Candraketu, who had long resided in the world of the Wind-god, thought to himself as follows:
How much longer must I remain here, fallen from my own station?
Even now, the power of our enemy Vidyuddhvaja’s asceticism has not yet waned.
I have heard that my friend Padmaśekhara,
the lord of the Gandharvas, has departed from the world of Soma to the city of Śiva for the sake of ascetic penance.
"I do not yet know whether or not the King has shown him favor;
having learned that, I shall understand what must be done by me."
While he was thus meditating,
his friend, the king of the Gandharvas, who had obtained a boon, approached that lord of the Vidyādharas.
Embraced by Candraketu and offered a welcome,
the lord of the Gandharvas was questioned regarding his own adventures and replied.
Having gone to Śivapura, I gratified Śambhu with ascetic penance; and he commanded me: "Go, for a most excellent son shall be born to you."
Furthermore, you shall regain your kingdom and even the most excellent maiden;
the hero who shall be her husband will be the slayer of Vidyuddhvaja.
"Having been thus instructed by Hara, I have come to tell this to you," [said the messenger].
Upon hearing these words from the lord of the Gandharvas, Candraketu said:
For my part, in order to pacify this suffering, Maheśvara must be propitiated;
for without propitiating him, the desired accomplishments do not come to pass.
Having thus resolved, Candraketu went with his wife Muktāvalī to a divine field of the Trident-bearer for the sake of ascetic practice.
Having related his own excellent account to Indra regarding the destruction of his enemies,
Padmaśekhara, filled with resolve, departed for the world of Soma.
Then the Lord of the Gods, remaining there at that site of meditative concentration,
conceived hope for the destruction of his enemy and called to mind the Teacher of the Immortals.
When he had been remembered and appeared there, Padmaśekhara bowed humbly and, having honored him, spoke; Śiva, pleased by his asceticism, commanded him thus.
"He is indeed the slayer of Vidyuddhvaja and my future son-in-law;
let there first be an end to this evil deed of his, but for me, it will be long."
O Blessed One, I dwell here in despondency, distressed by my fall from my own station;
therefore, I contemplate here the imminent danger that will swiftly come to pass.
Having heard these words from Śakra, the preceptor of the gods said to him:
"Granted that the depletion of that enemy's ascetic power has been brought about by his own evil deeds."
Therefore, this is our opportunity to employ our own efforts;
come, let us speak to Brahmā, and he will tell us the means.
Having been addressed thus by the Guru, Śakra, filled with that thought, went into the presence of Brahmā;
and having prostrated before him, he related what was in his own mind.
Then the Self-Existent One said: "Is this concern not mine as well?
However, that which was done by Śarva can only be averted by Śarva himself."
And that god is attained only after a long time; therefore, let us go to him who is non-different from Hari himself—he will tell us the means.
Having thus deliberated, Brahmā, Śakra,
and that preceptor of the gods mounted their swan-vehicle and arrived at Śvetadvīpa.
In this [state], every person bears the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the mace;
with four arms, both in form and in mind, they consist of the Blessed One.
There, within a palace of great jewels, they beheld the god Hari,
reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa, his feet served by Kamalā.
Having offered salutations to him, they were honored by him according to their merit;
and being revered there by the celestial sages, they sat down as was appropriate.
When asked about their welfare by the Blessed One, those gods informed him:
"O Lord, what welfare can there be for us while Vidyuddhvaja exists?"
For the Lord surely knows all that we have done for him;
this visit of ours was for his sake, and therefore the Lord knows what lies beyond this.
When the gods had spoken thus, Janārdana said to them:
"Do you not know that my established order has been shattered by that asura?"
However, that which was done by the Lord himself, the destroyer of Tripura, can only be undone by him;
it cannot be altered by me.
From that very [knowledge] shall come the destruction of that evil-minded Daitya;
if you will hasten, listen as I tell you the means.
There is a divine field of Maheśvara named Siddhīśvara;
there the Lord Hara is ever-present.
And this very Lord, manifesting in the form of a blazing linga,
previously spoke to me and to Prajapati concerning that which is difficult to grasp.
Therefore, let us go there and entreat him through asceticism;
he alone will pacify this affliction of the worlds.
Having been thus instructed by that god Viṣṇu,
they all went to Siddhiśvara together with him, traveling on the vehicles of Tārkṣya and the swan.
Untouched by old age, death, or disease, that sole abode of happiness is a place where even the deer, birds, and trees are made of gold and jewels.
There, having worshipped the Linga of the Wielder of the Trident— which manifests different internal forms moment by moment and assumes various jewel-like appearances— he should pay homage.
Devoted to that [task], those four— Hari, Brahmā, Devendra, and the preceptor of the gods— performed difficult penance directed toward Hara.
In the meantime, Śiva, gratified by his intense asceticism,
granted a boon to that lord of the Vidyādharas, Candraketu.
"Arise, O King! That great hero shall be born as your son, who will slay your enemy Vidyuddhvaja in battle."
He who had descended into human existence due to a curse and was deprived of his immortality regained it through the power of the asceticism of Padmāvatī, the daughter of the Gandharva king.
Having regained his own station together with that very wife,
he shall exercise the sovereignty of all the Vidyādharas for ten kalpas.
When the god had thus granted the boon and vanished, Candraketu, together with his wife, returned at that very moment to the realm of Vāyu.
Then, pleased by their intense asceticism, Hara, having been seen within the linga even there at Siddhīśvara, spoke joyfully to Nārāyaṇa and the others:
"Arise! Enough with this distress; I have been gratified by the Vidyādhara lord Candraketu and his ascetic penance, which was performed on your behalf."
From my portion, a heroic son named Śambhava will be born,
who shall soon slay that Daitya Vidyuddhvaja in battle.
Then, having fallen from his divine state into the human realm due to a curse for the sake of another deity's purpose,
