the daughter of the Gandharva Padmaśekhara will deliver him.
Together with his wife named Padmāvatī, who was born from a portion of Gaurī,
he will rule the empire of the sky-dwellers and then come to me alone.
"Therefore, fulfill this desire of yours even slightly.
Having spoken thus to Acyuta and the others, Śiva vanished from their sight.
Then the joyful Brahmā, Hari, Śakra, and those two preceptors of the gods returned once more to those very places from which they had come.
Then the beloved Muktāvalī of that lord of the Vidyādharas,
Candraketu, became pregnant and in due time gave birth to a son.
He was illuminating the quarters with his invincible splendor,
like the newly risen sun rising to remove the affliction of darkness.
And as soon as he was born, a voice from heaven was heard there, saying:
"O Candraketu, this son of yours shall be the slayer of the asura Vidyuddhvaja."
"Know him by name as Muktāphalaketu, the subduer of enemies.
Having said this to Candraketu, her speech ceased amidst a festive atmosphere.
A rain of flowers fell; having understood the matter, Padmaśekhara, Śakra, and those gods who were standing there in concealment went to that place.
Relating to one another the account of Hariprasāda,
they experienced great joy and returned to their own respective abodes.
And that Muktāphalaketu, refined by all the formative processes (*saṃskāra*),
gradually attained growth together with Ānanda among the gods.
Then, after some days had passed following the birth of his son,
a daughter was also born to Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas.
"O son of the Gandharva king, this daughter of the enemy of Vidyuddhvaja shall become your wife;
she will be named Padmāvatī, the lady of the Vidyādharas."
When she was thus born, a voice rose up from the sky;
thereafter, Padmāvatī gradually grew up there as a maiden.
She was radiant with a flood of loveliness that surged like waves, as if it were nectar transferred from its birthplace in the world of the moon.
That high-minded Muktāphalaketu also became a youth;
filled with devotion to Śiva, he constantly performed austerities such as vows and fasts.
Once, while he was absorbed in meditation and had fasted for twelve days,
the Blessed Lord, the husband of Girijā, appeared before him in person and spoke.
"I am pleased with this devotion of yours; by my grace, those weapons, as well as the sciences and all the arts, shall manifest for you."
And take from me this sword named Aparājita,
by means of which you shall exercise sovereignty, unconquered by adversaries.
Having spoken thus, the Lord gave him a sword and vanished;
and that prince immediately became possessed of the power and prowess of great weapons.
In the meantime, once upon a time, that great asura Vidyuddhvaja,
while staying in the third heaven, engaged in water-sports in the waters of the celestial river.
He beheld her vast water, brownish with the pollen of flowers,
permeated with the scent of rut, and agitated by ripples.
Then, puffed up with pride in his own arms, he said to his followers:
"Who is playing with water even over my head? Go and see!"
Having heard that, they went upward and saw in the water the bull of Śarva sporting with the elephant of Indra.
Having arrived, they said to that lord of the Daityas: "O Lord, the bull of Śambhu, accompanied by Airāvaṇa, has gone up above and is sporting in the water."
Hearing that this water was mixed with the ichor from Airāvaṇa’s temples and his flower garlands,
that asura, disregarding Śarva out of intoxication, became enraged.
Deluded by the ripening of his own evil deeds, he said to his servants:
"Go, bind those two—Āvaṇa and Āvaṇa—and bring them here with oxen."
Then, as soon as those asuras went there desiring to seize them, the two—
Vṛṣa and Dvipa— rushed forward in anger and slew them.
Those who remained after the slaughter went and reported this to Vidyuddhvaja;
enraged, he dispatched against those two a very great army of asuras.
Having crushed that army, which was brought to destruction by the ripening of its own sins,
Vṛṣa went into the presence of Hara, while Airāvaṇa approached Indra.

Then Indra, having observed those actions of the son of Diti, perceived that his enemy— the one who had even insulted the Blessed Lord, the husband of Gaurī— had reached the moment of his destruction, along with the hosts of guards following Airāvaṇa.
Having informed the Lotus-born One (Brahmā) and then having assembled with the hosts of gods accompanied by the Vidyādharas and others,
Śakra— having mounted his preeminent celestial elephant and having had auspicious rites performed for him by Śacī— set out to slay that enemy.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Third Wave.
Then, having reached Triviṣṭapa, that Indra surrounded it.
With forces whose strength was gained through the opportune moment and through the enthusiasm born of Hara’s grace.
Seeing that, Vidyuddhvaja set out with his army fully equipped;
as he was departing, then various ill omens occurred for him.
Lightning struck the banners, vultures circled above,
great parasols were shattered, and jackals howled inauspiciously.
Disregarding those ill omens, that asura went forth;
and then a great battle broke out between the gods and the asuras.
Then, when the wielder of the thunderbolt asked, "Why does that Muktāphalaketu not yet arrive?",
the lord of the sky-goers, Candraketu, informed him.
"Having forgotten it, I did not tell him as I was coming in haste;
but once he has realized this, he will surely follow after me with great speed."
Having heard this, the Lord of the Gods dispatched a swift chariot with Vāyu as its charioteer to bring that illustrious Muktāphalaketu.
And his father, Candraketu, dispatched a doorkeeper followed by a chariot to summon him along with his army.
And Muktāphalaketu, having learned that his father had gone to the battle with the Daityas, prepared with his followers to go to that very place.
Then, mounted upon his victorious elephant and having had auspicious rites performed for him by his mother,
he set out from the world of Vāyu, bearing the divine sword.
As he set forth, a rain of flowers fell from the sky;
the gods beat their drums, and auspicious winds blew.
Then those hosts of gods gathered together and surrounded him;
meanwhile, those who had fled and remained hidden out of fear of Vidyuddhvaja [now emerged].
Traveling with that great army,
he saw on the way a vast mountain hermitage named Meghavana.
Not transgressing that [command], he descended from the elephant with devotion,
gathered divine flowers, and proceeded to worship the Goddess.
In the meantime, Padmāvatī, the daughter of Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas, having reached the bloom of youth, arrived surrounded by her female companions.

Having taken leave of his own mother, who was established in asceticism for the sake of the welfare of her husband who had gone forth to battle, he departed from the world of the moon by means of a celestial chariot.
Seeking Śiva as her father’s kinsman and her desired husband,
she went to that very same divine abode of Gaurī for the sake of ascetic penance.
"Even now, no suitor has been determined who stands ready for battle;
moreover, for the sake of your father’s welfare, your mother has taken up ascetic practice."
"But you, my friend, for whose sake do you wish to perform penance as a maiden?
Thus addressed on the road by her friend, Padmāvatī spoke this.
"O friend, for maidens, the father alone is the deity who grants all success;
and as for the groom, one with qualities not shared by others has indeed been chosen by me."
"He who was born from the lord of the Vidyādharas to slay Vidyuddhvaja— he,
Muktāphalaketu, has been designated by Śambhu as my husband."
I heard this from the very mouth of my father when he was questioned by my mother:
"He will either go, or having gone, he will certainly be my boon in battle."
Therefore, desiring victory for both that husband and my father, I propitiate the Blessed Gaurī through the power of asceticism.
To the princess who was speaking thus, her friend said:
"In that case, even regarding a future matter, this resolve of yours is appropriate."
"May that which you desire be accomplished," said her friend to her;
thus addressed, she reached a large, auspicious lake near the temple of Gaurī.
It was covered with radiant, full-blown golden lotuses,
as if they were suffused by the splendor rising from her own lotus-face.
Having descended there, that daughter of the Gandharvas gathered lotuses for the worship of Ambikā,
and while she was about to perform her bath—
While that battle between the gods and asuras was thus proceeding, and while the rakshasas were greedily seeking flesh as they rushed forward, two female rakshasis arrived by that path.
With tawny, upward-pointing hair from which flames are vomited from mouths made terrible by fangs;
with a massive body dark as smoke and pendulous breasts and belly.
As soon as those two night-stalkers saw the daughter of the Gandharva king, they pounced upon her, seized her, and carried her off toward the sky.
And as long as the presiding deity of that celestial mansion [remains], and as long as those two Rākṣasīs [are present], he shall hold her back;
meanwhile, her attendants cry out in distress.
Then Muktāphalaketu, having performed his worship, emerged from the goddess’s temple;
hearing the cry of distress, he came to that very place.
He saw her, possessed of radiant splendor, held by the pair of rākṣasīs like a flash of lightning caught amidst a mass of dark clouds.
Having rushed toward Padmāvatī, the Great Hero liberated her;
he struck those two Rākṣasīs with his palms, casting them senseless upon the ground.
And he beheld her, who flowed like a cascade of the essence of beauty,
graced by a waist made lovely by the waves of the three folds.
She seemed as if she had been fashioned by the Creator himself, who displayed his supreme mastery in creating celestial brides, having concentrated therein the very essence of all beauty.
And having seen her, his senses dulled by the delusion of Kandarpa, he—
though steadfast— stood there for a moment motionless, as if fixed in a painting.
When the agitation caused by the rākṣasīs had subsided, having recovered as if in a mere moment,
Padmāvatī also beheld Muktāphalaketu.
A form that was a festival for the eyes of the world and a source of intoxication for women,
as if fashioned by Fate by uniting the Moon and Kandarpa into one.
Then, with her face cast down in shame, she spoke softly to her friend:
"May it be well with her; I shall depart from here, from the side of this strange man."
While she was speaking thus, Muktāphalaketu asked her friend, "What does this young woman say?"
She too said: "This Sukanyā has been given to you as a blessing for saving her life;
she says to me, 'Come, let us depart from the presence of this other man.'"
Hearing that, Muktāphalaketu spoke to her in agitation:
"Who is she? Whose daughter is she? And to what man of auspicious deeds has she been given?"
Thus questioned by him, her companion said to him:
"O fortunate one, this maiden named Padmāvatī is our friend."
She was born from the self of Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Gandharvas;
and Śambhu has ordained that Muktāphalaketu shall be her husband.
The son of Candraketu, the lord of the Vidyādharas, beloved by the world,
the ally of the king of the gods, and the destroyer of Vidyuddhvaja.
Desiring victory for her father, her lord in battle,
she has now come to this sanctuary of Gaurī for the sake of ascetic penance.
Having heard this, the followers of Candraketu’s son gladdened that princess, saying, “By good fortune, O Queen, he is indeed your husband!”
Then, their own selves filled with joy from recognizing one another,
it was fitting, O Mother, that those two— the maiden and the suitor— did not [remain] as they were.
While the two remained there, gazing at one another with mutual affection through side-long glances, the sound of musical instruments was heard.
Then the army was seen, and the chariot joined by Vāyu,
as well as Candraketu’s doorkeeper, both arriving with haste.
And those two, Vāyu and Pratīhāra, having abandoned their mounts out of humility,
approached Muktāphalaketu and spoke to him.
"The Lord of Gods and your father call you from the field of battle;
therefore, mount this chariot and come quickly."
Then, although bound by his love for Padmāvatī, that son of the lord of the sky-goers, out of regard for his teacher's duty,
ascended the chariot together with those two.
And having quickly fastened the divine armor sent by Śakra, he set forth,
turning his neck to look repeatedly at Padmāvatī.
And Padmāvatī, beholding him as he passed beyond the range of her sight,
struck down the two night-stalkers with a single blow of her palm.
Thinking only of him, she bathed and worshipped Ambikā and Hara,
and from that time forward, she performed austerities right there for his ultimate welfare.
Reflecting upon that vision, Muktāphalaketu reached the auspicious battle between the gods and the asuras, which portended victory.
And seeing that hero arrive, well-armored and accompanied by his army,
all those great asuras rushed toward him.
With his shower of arrows,
that hero, at the commencement of the festival of battle, made an offering to the deities of the quarters with their heads shattered into fragments.
Seeing his army being slaughtered by that Muktāphalaketu,
Vidyuddhvaja himself rushed toward him in a fit of rage.
As that Daitya was falling, he was struck with arrows by the diligent [hero];
consequently, the entire Asura army rushed toward him from all sides.
Seeing that, Vāsava, accompanied by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and gods,
immediately rushed toward that army of Daityas.
Then there arose a tumultuous battle, with falling arrows, darts, spears, javelins, and axes, in which countless soldiers were slain.
Rivers of blood flowed, with elephants and horses for their bodies, crocodiles for their forms, ivory and pearls for their sands, and the heads of great heroes for their stones.
For the beings intoxicated by the wine of blood and seeking flesh,
that festival of battle became a source of joy as they danced together with headless trunks.
In that ocean of battle between the Daityas and the gods, the fortune of victory,
as fickle as a great wave, moved for a moment this way and for a moment that way.
Thus the battle lasted for twenty-four days,
watched by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā as they stood in their celestial chariots.
On the twenty-fifth day, when both armies were nearly exhausted and the principal duels had commenced in that battle, so it was said.
Then a duel commenced between Śrīmuktāphalaketu and that Vidyuddhvaja, one mounted on a chariot and the other upon an elephant.
One should counter the darkness-weapon with the sun-weapon, the winter-weapon with the summer-weapon, the mountain-weapon with the thunderbolt-weapon, and the serpent-weapon with the garuḍa-weapon.
Having warded off the driver and the elephant of that asura,
Muktāphalaketu struck them down with a single arrow each.
When he had mounted his chariot, Vidyuddhvaja resorted to a magical illusion because [the prince] had slain his charioteer, his horses, and his chariot.
Becoming invisible to the entire army, he ascended into the sky and rained down rocks and various weapons upon the celestial host from all sides.
And that impenetrable net of arrows which had been released by Muktāphalaketu was then obstructed by that Daitya,
who consumed it with showers of fire.
Then, having consecrated with mantras the Brahmā weapon capable of destroying the universe, Muktāphalaketu released it toward that enemy and his followers.
By that weapon, the great asura Vidyuddhvaja, though accompanied by his army, was slain and, deprived of life, fell from the midst of the sky.
The remaining ones, including the sons of Vidyuddhvaja and others together with Vajradaṃṣṭra, fled out of fear and went to the depths of the netherworld.
And the gods, following his voice, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
and they honored the illustrious Muktāphalaketu with showers of flowers.
Then, once the enemy was slain, Śakra regained his kingdom and entered Triviṣṭapa;
and throughout the three worlds, there was a great festival.
The Lord of Creatures himself came there, preceded by Śacī,
and he fastened the finest crest-jewel upon Muktāphalaketu.
Indra, too, placed upon the neck of that prince— who was radiant with victory and destined to bestow the kingdom— a necklace from his own throat.
And he seated him upon a seat equal to his own,
while various blessings were bestowed by the gods who were filled with joy.
And having dispatched his doorkeeper to the city of the asura Vidyuddhvaja,
he accepted the additional wealth of his own city, intending to bestow it upon him when the occasion arose.
Then the Gandharva Padmaśekhara,
wishing to give Padmāvatī to the prince, looked meaningfully at the face of the Dhātṛ.
And the Creator, having understood his intention, said to that lord of the Gandharvas:
"There is a certain remaining task; therefore, endure for a little while longer."
Then, resounded by the songs of Hāhā and Hūhū accompanied by their own musical instruments,
and by the dances of Rambhā and others, there arose a festival of victory for Indra.
When the festival and the joy had passed and the Creator had departed, the slayer of Vṛtra,
having honored the world-protectors and others, dismissed them each to their own respective abodes.
And he dismissed that king of the gandharvas, Padmaśekhara,
after honoring him and his retinue, sending him back to his own city of the gandharvas.
And Hari sent the honored Śrīmuktāphalaketu and Candraketu to his own city of the Vidyādharas for the festival.
Having removed all thorns from the world and followed by many kings of the Vidyādharas,
Muktāphalaketu then returned to his capital, accompanied by his father.
And at that time, adorned with excellent jewels and garlanded with banners and silken streamers,
the city shone when the victorious prince returned after a long absence together with his father.
And immediately his father, Candraketu, having gratified the circle of his kinsmen and servants in the city,
spread a magnificent festival for his son’s victory, raining down wealth like a cloud pouring forth water.
And although that Muktāphalaketu had attained the fame of subduing Vidyuddhvaja,
he found no pleasure in his own enjoyments without Padmāvatī.
Furthermore, his mind being comforted by his friend named Saṃyata, who reported the commands of Śarva and other matters, he passed those days with great difficulty.
Thus ends the third wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Fourth Wave.
In the meantime, that king of the Gandharvas [returned] to his own city.
Padmaśekhara entered, amidst a widespread and resplendent festival.
Having learned from the mouth of his wife that [the sage] was performing austerities in the hermitage of Girijā out of hope for victory over him, he summoned his daughter Padmāvatī.
And as his daughter, emaciated by asceticism and by separation, approached and fell at his feet, he spoke to her, bestowing his blessing.
"O child, you have undergone great hardship through penance for my sake;
therefore, [slay] that son of the king of the Vidyādharas, the destroyer of Vidyuddhvaja."
"Quickly obtain as your husband that illustrious Muktāphalaketu, the refuge of the world, the victorious one, whom Śambhu himself has ordained."
While Vinatā remained there with her face cast down after her father had spoken thus,
her mother Kuvalayāvalī addressed the king.
How was that such asura slain in battle by that noble son, the prince who grants fearlessness to the three worlds?
Having heard that, the king described to her the prowess of that prince,
including his battle with the gods and the asuras.
Then, by Padmāvatī’s friend named Manohārikā,
the ease with which she had slain the pair of rākṣasīs was also related.
Then, having learned of the conduct of his son and his daughter, their mutual seeing of one another, and their affection for each other, both the king and the queen attained great satisfaction.
And they both said: "Who are those two Rākṣasīs? By whom the hosts of the Asura armies were swallowed up, just as the ocean was by Agastya."
And by that gale of descriptions regarding the excellence of his manly prowess,
the fire of Padmāvatī’s passion blazed up all the more intensely.
Then, having departed from her parents' presence, that princess ascended in an instant, full of longing, to the jewel-adorned palace within the inner apartments.
There, in a place where pearl lattices were fastened to pillars inlaid with jewels, and where there was a noble couch and a comfortable seat set upon a jeweled floor;
Though she dwelt in a place delightful with various divine enjoyments that appeared at her mere thought,
she suffered intensely from the fire of separation from her beloved.
And then he beheld from behind him a divine, prosperous garden, covered with golden trees and creepers, and filled with hundreds of jeweled ponds.
And having seen it, he thought: "How wonderful is this supreme city of ours, more beautiful even than the world of the Moon, the birthplace of my lineage!"
Yet I have not seen this crest-jewel of the Himalayas,
where there is such a city grove that surpasses even the Nandana garden.
Therefore, having gone there to that excellent, secluded place, cool and providing good shade,
I shall somewhat allay this torment of the fire of separation.
Having reflected thus, that young woman then slowly and alone,
having skillfully descended from there, set out to go to the city garden.
Unable to go on foot, she was carried to that garden by birds that appeared through her own supernatural power and served as her vehicle.
There, within a house consisting of a grove of plantain trees, he sat upon a bed of flowers while the sound of divine songs and other music was being heard.
She found no delight therein, nor did her passion subside;
for without her beloved, the fire of desire increased all the more.
Then, eager to behold even that beloved one depicted in a painting,
she took from her store of accomplishments a painted tablet and colored pigments.
Since even the Creator cannot again produce a second being equal to him, how can I, with my hand faltering and filled with longing, paint his likeness?
"Nevertheless, for the sake of my own diversion, I shall paint him however I can.
Having thus reflected, she began to paint him upon a wooden board.
Just then, her friend named Manohārikā, searching for her and distraught at not seeing her, arrived at that very spot.
Standing behind her, she saw the princess there alone in the bower of creepers, longing [for him] and holding a painted panel.
"Let me see what she is doing here all alone. Having reflected thus, her friend remained there concealed.

Meanwhile, Padmāvatī, her lotus-like eyes filled with tears, spoke thus regarding her beloved, who was depicted in a painting: “Padmāvatī, her lotus-like eyes filled with tears, spoke thus regarding her beloved, who was depicted in a painting.”
Having slain the Asuras who were defeated by falsehood, you protected Indra by a mere word; why then do you not protect me from the Māras?
Even the wish-fulfilling tree fails to give, and even the Sugata lacks compassion for one of meager merit; even gold turns into stone for such a person.
And being unacquainted with the fever of love, you surely do not know my suffering;
what can that wretched flower-arrowed god do for you, since he has been conquered by the Daityas?
What more shall I say? Fate is adverse to me, since it seeks to veil my eyes with tears, desiring that I should not behold you even in a painting.
Having spoken thus, the princess began to weep,
with drops of tears like large pearls falling from her broken necklace.
At that very moment, her friend Manohārikā approached her;
the princess, having covered that painting, said to her:
"You have not been seen for so long, my friend; oh, where have you been?
Hearing that, Manohārikā said to her while smiling:
"O friend, searching for you alone, I have wandered for a long time; therefore, why do you hide this from me? Is it a wonder that has been seen by me, or is it a wonder that has been heard?"
Thus addressed by her friend, Padmāvatī,
with her face bowed in shame, spoke to her while holding her hand, her voice faltering with tears.
"Friend, everything was already known to you; why is it being concealed?
At that time, by that prince, in that hermitage of Gaurī—"
Though she was rescued from the midst of a most terrible fire of rākṣasīs,
she has been cast into the submarine fire of passion, where the flames of unbearable separation blaze.

Therefore, I do not know where I should go, to whom I should speak, or what I should do; nor do I know what recourse or means to rely upon, for my mind is attached to that which is difficult to attain.
To the princess who was speaking thus, her friend said:
"O friend, this attachment of your mind is appropriate; it is well-placed."
Indeed, the union of you two is for each other's mutual adornment,
like the crescent moon and the matted-hair crown of Śarva.
"And let there be no lack of resolve in this matter;
he will certainly not remain without you. Have you not observed him to be such as that?"
Even women, greedy for beauty, desire the state of manhood upon seeing her; who then would not be desirous of you, since you possess such equal beauty? Furthermore, how much more so!
Is even Śarva a speaker of falsehood, by whom you two were told that you are a married couple?
For when a desired object is not yet attained, who can maintain their composure?
"Therefore, take heart; that very man shall soon become your husband.
No one is difficult for you to attain, but you are difficult for everyone else to attain."
Having been addressed thus by her friend, the princess said to her:
"Friend, although I know this, nevertheless, what shall I do?"
But this mind of mine, so attached to him, cannot endure for even a moment without that lord of my life; nor can it endure the god of love.
For as I remember him alone, my mind finds no peace for even a moment;
my limbs burn with anguish, and my life-breaths seem to be departing.
Speaking thus, deluded by infatuation, that princess, as delicate as a flower, fell into the lap of her companion.
Then, with the sprinkling of water, the leaves of plantain trees, and the fanning of breezes,
that female companion gradually comforted her while shedding tears.
The lotus-fiber necklace, the bracelets, the moist unguent of sandalwood,
and the bed of lotus leaves— these were the things she prepared for her friend.
In contact with her, those [lotuses] too, being joined with her intense heat,
became heated and, as if sharing her sorrow, withered away.
Then the distraught Padmāvatī said to her friend:
"Why do you distress yourself in vain? My anguish will not be stilled in this way."
"If you do that by which [the king] will be pacified, it will lead to his welfare.
To her, who had spoken thus and was standing there, her friend replied:
"What might I do that I would not do for your sake? Tell me that, my friend.
Having heard this, the princess spoke somewhat bashfully.
"Go quickly, dear friend, and bring that beloved one here for me;
otherwise, there can be no peace for me, nor will my father cease his anger."
"On the contrary, he will give her to me as soon as she has come here.
When she had spoken thus, her friend also spoke to her with enthusiasm.
"If this is so, then take heart; how small a task is this!
O friend, here I go myself to bring your beloved."
The excellent city of your father, the lord of the sky-dwellers, Candraketu, is known by the name Candrapura; be at peace—why grieve?
Having been thus consoled by her friend, the princess said:
"Therefore, arise; may your path be auspicious; go with all speed."
O friend, you must speak with affection to that hero, my lord of life, who is the protector of the three worlds, conveying these words of mine.
Why did you not protect me from the fear of the rākṣasīs in that temple of Gaurī,
while I was being struck down by the woman-killer Makaraketu?
O Lord, what kind of dharma is this for those like you who are capable of uplifting the world,
that you remain indifferent in the face of calamity, even though the people previously relied upon you?
"Speak thus to her, O auspicious one, or as you yourself know best. Having spoken these words, Padmāvatī dismissed that friend.
And she, mounted upon her own self-manifested vehicle drawn by birds,
set out toward the city of the Vidyādharas, captivating his mind.
And Padmāvatī, having regained some measure of fortitude through that hope,
entered her father’s palace taking with her the painting board.
There, having entered her own dwelling surrounded by female servants,
she bathed, worshipped the Lord of Gaurī with devotion, and made this request:
O Blessed One, in these three worlds, nothing desired by anyone— whether much or little— is accomplished here without the favor of your will.
"If you do not give me that desired husband, the son of the noble Vidyadhara universal monarch, I shall cast off my body before you."
Having heard this declaration made by the one who bears the moon upon his crest,
the retinue, both distressed and filled with wonder, spoke.
"O Goddess, why do you speak thus, showing such disregard for your own body?
Is there anything in these three worlds that is truly unattainable even for you?"
For even the Sugata, when entreated by you, would surely relinquish his self-restraint;
thus, he alone here is truly virtuous whom even you entreat in this manner.
Having heard this, the princess, drawn by his virtues, said:
"He who alone is the refuge of the gods, including Śakra himself."
By whom alone was the demonic host destroyed, as darkness is by the sun;
and who is the giver of life to us—how could he not be sought after?
Speaking thus with longing, she remained there with that very story,
together with the attendant women who had arrived.
In the meantime, her friend Manohārikā also quickly reached that city of the lord of the Vidyādharas, Candrapura.
Having built the city of the gods, Viśvakarman, as if still dissatisfied, fashioned this wondrous place of extraordinary splendor.
There, not having found Muktāphalaketu, she searched for him; while remaining in the air, that Manohārikā arrived at his city garden.
It possessed the inconceivable power of supernatural accomplishment, with trees made of radiant jewels,
upon which clusters of blossoms of many different species grew from a single tree.
Beholding that place, beautiful with the songs of birds mingled with the sound of divine music and featuring stone slabs of various jewels, she took her delight there.
And having been seen by the garden-keepers, who were of various bird-like forms,
they approached and entreated them with very clear words and pleasant speech.
Having seated her at the foot of the Pārijāta tree upon a throne of Tārkṣya-jewel stone,
worship was performed for her with appropriate offerings.
Having accepted that worship, we then reflected there:
"Oh, how wonderful are the diverse manifestations of the supernatural powers of the lords of the Vidyādharas!"
For those whose garden is such that its enjoyments arrive inconceivably,
where celestial women perform music and winged beings serve as attendants.
Having reflected thus and questioned those very garden-keepers,
she reached a grove of trees other than the *pārijāta*.
There she beheld Muktāphalaketu lying upon a bed of flowers sprinkled with sandalwood paste, looking like the Kalpa tree itself.
Recognizing him as one she had previously seen at Gaurī’s hermitage, she thought to herself while remaining hidden: "I shall observe what is the cause of his distress."
While his friend Saṃyataka was thus comforting him with snow, sandalwood, and breezes, Muktāphalaketu said to him:
"Embers placed upon snow, the fire of chaff upon sandalwood,
and a forest fire against the wind— these, I am certain, have been employed by Smara against me."
"O friend, why do you thus exhaust yourself fruitlessly, while this [wind] spreads its heat on all sides, born of the torment of separation?"
Even with the diversions of beautiful women, dance, song, and the like,
my mind is distressed in this grove which surpasses even Nandana.
"Without that Padmāvatī, born of Padmaśekhara and lotus-faced,
this fever from the arrows of Love does not subside for me."
I do not dare to speak this to anyone, nor do I find any composure;
yet there is only one means for its attainment that I possess.
"I am going to the sanctuary of Gaurī, where my heart was uprooted by the arrows of her sidelong glances and carried away by that beloved who has been seen by me."
There, having united with the daughter of the first king,
Śambhu— propitiated by me through asceticism during that union— will provide the means for me.
Having said this, just as the prince desired to rise,
Manohārikā, her heart filled with joy, revealed herself.
"Friend, congratulations! By good fortune your desire has been fulfilled;
I have come as a friend to see you in the presence of that beloved woman."
"For I saw her at Ambikā’s hermitage standing by his side," Saṃyataka said to the prince out of joy.
Then, upon seeing his beloved’s friend, the prince fell into a certain state agitated by throbbing joy, wonder, and longing.
Having seated her nearby, he then questioned that woman— who was like a rain of nectar for his eyes— concerning the welfare of his beloved’s body.
Then she spoke thus: "O Lord, my friend’s welfare is certain as long as you are her protector; however, at present, she is indeed suffering."
From the moment her heart was stolen by you upon being seen, she has been distracted ever since;
she neither hears nor sees.
Having cast off her young maidens' ornaments, she wears a necklace of lotus fibers;
abandoned by her couch, she rolls upon a bed of lotus leaves.
She who formerly could not endure even a mention of her husband out of modesty—
she has today reached this state in his absence.
Thus, O best of the accomplished ones, her own limbs— now white with sandalwood paste drying from the heat of her fever— seem to laugh at her.
Having spoken thus to you,
she recited for you those songs of Padmāvatī’s message composed by Manohārikā.
Having heard all that, Muktāphalaketu was freed from his distress;
he greeted Manohārikā with joy and spoke to her.
Sprinkled as it were with nectar by your words, this consciousness of mine has been revived; breath has returned, fortitude has arisen, and exhaustion has departed.
And today my former good deeds have borne fruit,
since even that daughter of the Gandharva king is thus partial toward me!
But while I might somehow be able to endure the pain of separation,
how indeed could she, whose limbs are as delicate as the śirīṣa flower, ever bear it?
Therefore, I shall go to that very hermitage of the Daughter of the Mountain;
there you must bring your friend, so that our union may take place this day.
"Go, O auspicious one, and quickly console that friend of yours;
and take this [garland] bestowed upon me by the Self-Existent One himself out of his great satisfaction."
"Give her this crest-jewel that destroys all suffering;
and this necklace, obtained by me from Śakra, is your reward."
Having spoken thus, the prince took the crest-jewel from his head and offered it to her;
he then placed the necklace from his own neck around her neck.
Then, having bowed to him with joy, Manohārikā set out from there,
mounted upon her bird, toward her friend Padmāvatī.
And Muktāphalaketu, his fatigue dispelled by great joy,
quickly entered his own city together with Saṃyataka.
Having reached Padmāvatī’s side, Manohārikā told her of that beloved’s fever of longing, exactly as she had desired.
He recalled those words, affectionate, tender, and sweet, exactly as he had heard them,
along with that appointment for their meeting which had been spoken at the hermitage of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then he gave her that crest-jewel sent by him,
and he showed her the necklace given as a reward by him.
Then Padmāvatī, having embraced that successful friend,
honored her and forgot the pain of the fire of love.
Having tied that crest-jewel in her topknot as if it were bliss itself,
she prepared for her journey to the forest of Gaurī.
In the meantime, by chance, the sage Tapodhana arrived at that grove of Gaurī together with his disciple named Dṛḍhavrata.
And there the sage spoke thus to his disciple of firm vows:
"In this divine grove, I have maintained meditative absorption for a moment."
"Standing at the door, you must not allow anyone to enter here;
having entered into meditative absorption, I shall worship Pārvatī."
Having spoken thus, the sage stationed his disciple at the gate of the garden and,
beneath the pārijāta tree, entered into meditative absorption.
Having arisen from his meditative absorption, he entered within to worship Ambikā;
yet he did not speak of that matter to his disciple who was waiting at the door.
Just then, Muktāphalaketu arrived there,
having adorned himself and mounted a divine camel along with Saṃyataka.
And as he was entering that garden, he was stopped by that disciple of the sage, who said, "Do not, do not! My teacher is situated here in meditative absorption."
"Perhaps my beloved has come here while the interior is spacious,
and the Sage is staying in one corner"— thinking thus, he became full of longing.
Having passed out of the sight of this son of a sage, the prince,
accompanied by his friend, entered that garden by way of the sky.
And as long as he gazed at that, so long did he enter there,
the disciple of the sage, in order to observe the completion of his teacher’s meditative absorption.
He did not see his teacher there, nor did he see him with his companions;
rather, he saw Śrī Muktāphalaketu having entered by an unauthorized path.
Then that disciple of the sage, filled with wrath, cursed the prince:
"Because of this lack of discipline, go to the human state along with your companions."
"Since you have broken my concentration here and disregarded me, O Guru," having thus pronounced this curse, he followed after that very guru himself.
And Muktāphalaketu, when his desire was nearly accomplished,
fell into profound despondency due to the falling thunderbolt of the curse.
Meanwhile, Padmāvatī, eager for union with her beloved,
arrived there mounted upon a bird, accompanied by Manohārikā and the others.
Seeing her who had come to choose him for herself, yet was separated from him by a curse,
the prince fell into a painful state composed of both joy and sorrow.
And at that moment, as Padmāvatī displayed her lack of courtesy,
her right eye throbbed and her mind trembled.
Then, seeing her beloved there looking distressed, the princess thought:
"Could he be troubled because I arrived before him?"
And when she had approached him with humility, the prince said to her:
"My dear, our desire has been frustrated; though it was accomplished, fate has thwarted us."
Hearing that, the prince, with agitation, described his own curse to her as she asked, "Alas! How was it broken?"
Then, distressed and afflicted by the curse, they all went to their preceptor, the sage,
who was staying in the temple of the goddess, to entreat him for an end to the curse.
Seeing them approach and bow down, the wise great sage spoke with affection to Muktāphalaketu.
"You have been cursed by this fool, who acts without foresight;
you did nothing at all for me, for I arose from that state of my own accord."
In this matter, you must act solely for the sake of the cause; for you have a divine task that must necessarily be performed while in human form.
"By the power of fate, upon seeing this very Padmāvatī, you will become afflicted with love;
then, casting off your mortal body, you shall quickly be released from the curse."
With this very body, you shall again protect this mistress of life; for you are the protector of the universe, and you truly ought not to endure the curse for long.
Since even the children, the elderly, and others were slain by the Brahmāstra weapon employed by you,
that slightest trace of unrighteousness is the cause of your [suffering] in this matter.
Having heard that, Padmāvatī, with tears in her eyes, entreated the seer:
"O Blessed One, may whatever be the destiny of my noble husband now be mine as well."
"I shall not be able to remain even for a moment separated from this," said Padmāvatī as she made her request; to her, the sage replied:
"This is not so; you must remain right here for now and perform austerities, by which he shall soon be released from his curse and marry you."
Then, accompanied by this Muktāphalaketu,
you shall rule the empire of the sky-dwellers and the asuras for ten kalpas.
"This crest-jewel given by me shall protect you while you remain in asceticism;
it has arisen from the water-pot of the Creator and possesses great power."
To the sage of divine vision who had thus spoken to Padmāvatī,
Muktāphalaketu, bowing low, made this request:
"O Blessed One, may I have unbreakable devotion toward you in my human existence.
Padmāvatī then cursed that offending disciple.
When the sage had said, "So be it," Padmāvatī, being exceedingly distressed, cursed that offending disciple of his.
"Because you have cursed the noble son out of folly, you shall become his very mount in this human world— capable of assuming any form at will and moving according to your desire."
Thus, when he had been cursed by her and was despondent,
that sage, whose wealth was his asceticism, vanished along with his own disciple.
Then Muktāphalaketu said to Padmāvatī:
"I am going to my own city; let me see what will happen there for me."
Hearing that, Padmāvatī, terrified of separation, fell instantly to the ground with her flower ornaments, like a creeper broken by the wind.
Having somehow consoled her as she was weeping, he, accompanied by his friend,
departed from there with his eyes repeatedly turned toward Muktāphalaketu.
And when he had gone, Padmāvatī, lamenting and deeply distressed,
spoke to her friend Manohārikā who was trying to comfort her.
"Friend, I know that today in a dream I beheld the goddess Pārvatī;
she even attempted to cast a garland of blue lotuses around my neck."
"Let it be; I shall give you more," she said, and then she ceased.
Thus, she has indicated this obstacle to my attainment of my beloved.
As she was thus grieving for her, that friend then said to her:
"This dream was shown to you at that time in order to console the Queen."
The Sage has spoken likewise, and the command of the gods is the same:
therefore, take heart; before long, you shall have a reunion with your beloved.
By these words of her friends and by the power of the crest-jewel,
Padmāvatī then established her resolve and remained in the hermitage of Gaurī.
And she performed austerities at the three junctions of the day, worshipping here the Lord united with the Daughter of the Mountain;
and likewise, she treated the portrait of her beloved—which had been brought from her own city—with the same devotion as she did the deity.
"Do not, for the sake of an object that is certain to come to pass as you desire, undergo the fruitless toil of asceticism"—
thus her parents, having approached her with tears and knowing her purpose, sought to dissuade her, to which she replied as follows:
Now that my new husband has suddenly been struck by the misery of a curse by the gods, how could I dwell here in comfort? For the husband is the supreme soul of virtuous women.

"When this evil has been exhausted through asceticism and Śambhu has attained satisfaction, my reunion with my beloved will occur before long; for indeed, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by ascetic practices."
When Padmāvatī had thus spoken with firm resolve,
her mother Kuvalayāvalī addressed her father, the king.
"O King, do not perform this painful austerity; why weary yourself further in vain?
This must come to pass for her. There is a cause for it here; I shall tell you, so listen."
A maiden of the lord of the Siddhas named Devaprabhā, performing very great asceticism in order to obtain her desired husband, resided for a long time in Śivapura.
Approaching her, he said, "She has gone there with me to see King Padmāvatī;
how is it that you are not ashamed for the sake of your husband because of your asceticism? and he laughed at her.
"O fool, you laugh out of childishness; you too shall perform asceticism that brings only suffering for the sake of a husband.
Thus she then cursed her with anger in the presence of the Siddha maidens.
Therefore, that hardship caused by the curse of the Siddha’s daughter must necessarily be endured;
who else is able to alter it? Thus, let her do whatever she does.
Thus addressed by the queen,
the Lord of the Gandharvas, accompanied by her, took leave of her with some difficulty and departed for his own city, as his daughter bowed at his feet.
She too, traveling through the sky every day, worshipped that Siddhīśvara who is served by Brahmā and the other gods;
and having been told in a dream by Hara, "In this hermitage of the Daughter of the Mountain," Padmāvatī remained devoted to her vows and silent recitations.
Thus ends the fourth wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The fifth wave begins:
While Padmāvatī was thus engaged in asceticism in order to attain him...
Meanwhile, that Muktāphalaketu reached his own city.
Fearing his imminent descent into human birth due to the power of a Brahmin’s curse,
the son of the Vidyādhara lord sought refuge in Śiva.
While worshipping him, he heard a voice from that inner sanctum:
"Do not fear; for you shall suffer no pain from dwelling in a womb."
In human existence, you shall experience neither suffering nor a long stay;
you will be born as a prince of great strength and prowess.
From the sage whose wealth is asceticism, you shall obtain the entire collection of weapons;
and my attendant, known as Kiṅkara, shall become your younger brother.
Having conquered your enemies with their assistance and accomplished the task of the gods,
you shall once again exercise sovereignty over the sky-dwellers, united with Padmāvatī.
Having heard these words, the prince then stood firm in his resolve, as if awaiting the arrival of the fruit of that curse.
In this interval of the narrative, in the eastern direction,
there was a city named Devasabha, which surpassed the assembly of the gods in its splendor.
There, a universal monarch named Merudhvaja reigned as king;
he was the ally of the King of the Gods when the war between the gods and asuras broke out.
That high-souled one had no greed for fame, nor did he covet the property of others;
his sharpness was found in his sword, not in his punishment, and his fear arose from sin, not from enemies.
Curvature appeared in his eyebrows during anger, but not in his heart; roughness was found on his arm, marked by the scars of the bowstring, but never again in his speech.

He who, in battle, directed his efforts toward piercing the enemy rather than guarding his treasury; who placed his delight in the practice of dharma rather than in women; and who had faith in the protection of the poor rather than in gold coins.
Two thoughts were constantly present in the heart of that king:
first, that not even a single son had yet been born to him.
And the second [reason] was that previously, after the great battle between the gods and asuras,
those asuras who remained after being slain had fled to the netherworld (pātāla).
Having departed from there, they repeatedly went to the netherworld (pātāla) after destroying his holy fords, shrines, and hermitages from afar by means of deception.
The king did not find those who move through the underworld and the sky;
consequently, that radiant one felt distressed, even though he was without rival upon the earth.
Agitated by these reflections, he once went to the abode of the gods in a noble chariot sent by Śakra, there at the arrival of a bright day in the month of Caitra.
For at the beginning of every year, there was a grand assembly for Śakra;
King Merudhvaja always went there by means of that chariot.
But then, even though that place was filled with the dancing and singing of celestial women,
and even though he was honored by Śakra, the king sat there sighing.
Having seen that, the King of the Gods, who knew his heart, said to him:
"O King, I know what sorrow you have; let it not be yours."
A son named Muktāphaladhvaja, an incarnation of Śiva, shall be born to you;
he is one manifestation of a Gaṇa, and the second is Malayadhvaja.
Muktāphaladhvaja, along with his younger brother, shall obtain from the sage whose wealth is asceticism the sciences, a vehicle that assumes any form at will, and various divine weapons.
And having again obtained the great Pāśupata weapon, that invincible one,
having slain the asuras, will bring both the earth and the netherworld (pātāla) under his control.
And you, take from me these two sky-travelers equipped with great weapons,
as well as the elephant Kāñcanagiri and likewise Kāñcanaśekhara.
Having spoken thus and given him his celestial elephant, he was then dispatched by the wielder of the thunderbolt;
delighted, Merudhvaja returned to his own city upon the earth.
But those asuras, having incurred blame through their deceit, did not attain the state of moving through the air even after he had reached the underworld for refuge.
Then, having heard this from Śakra, the king, desiring a son, went on his divine mount to the hermitage of that seer whose wealth was asceticism.
Having approached that seer there and informed him of Śakra’s command, he said to him:
"O Blessed One, instruct me quickly on the means to achieve this. SoKss_17,5.28 //
And that sage, for the sake of his swift attainment of the desired goal,
prescribed for the king and his wife the vow of propitiating Śambhu.
By means of that vow, the lord of the earth propitiated Śiva;
and the all-pervading Lord, being pleased, spoke thus to the king in a dream:
"Arise, O King! You have reached [the time] for the destruction of the remaining Asuras; without delay, you shall obtain two invincible sons in due course."
Having heard this and awakened, he spoke to the sage at dawn;
then, having broken his fast together with his wife, O King, he returned to his own city.
There, after a few days, that queen Merudhvajā, who possessed auspicious marks, reached her season.
Having abandoned his Vidyādhara body by the power of that curse, Muktāphalaketu unexpectedly came to be conceived within her womb.
And that body of his remained there in his own city of Candrapura,
preserved by his kinsmen and kept from decaying through the power of his magic spells.
There, in the city of Devasabhā, Queen Merudhvajā, having become pregnant, brought joy to her husband, King Merudhvaja.
And just as that queen became increasingly languid from the weight of her pregnancy,
so too did her husband, the king, become filled with enthusiasm.
And when the time had arrived, she gave birth to a son who resembled the sun—
a child of fierce splendor, like Pārvatī giving birth to Kumāra.
A festival arose not only throughout the entire surface of the earth,
but even in the vault of heaven, as the drums were struck by the gods.
Then the sage, rich in asceticism and possessed of divine vision,
came there in person to congratulate King Merudhvaja on his good fortune.
Together with that sage named Śakra,
the king, having held a great festival, made Muktāphaladhvaja his son.
Then, after that sage had departed, at the end of a year,
a second son was born to the king by that queen.
And the king gave him the name Malayadhvaja,
together with that very same sage who had arrived out of joy.
Then that Saṃyataka, the son of the minister, was born from the curse;
and his father gave him the name Mahābuddhi.
Then those two princes grew like lion cubs,
together with that minister’s son, in due course and along with their splendor.
Then, when about eight years had passed,
that sage rich in asceticism came and performed the initiation ceremony for those two sons of the king.
And for another eight years, those two were trained by him in the sciences, the arts, and in all the great weapons.
Then, seeing those two youths, who were skilled in all weapons and capable in combat,
King Merudhvaja considered himself a man of great achievement.
Then, as the sage desired to go to his own hermitage, he said to him:
"O Blessed One, please accept this desired sacrificial fee now."
O Lord of the Earth, this alone is the desired sacrificial fee from you:
that you, together with your son, shall slay the Asuras who destroy the sacrifice.
To the great seer who had spoken thus, the king replied:
"Therefore, O Blessed One, you must now accept a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."
Therefore, commence that sacrifice; the asuras will come to obstruct it, and at that time I too shall go there along with my sons.
O sage, in former times, those Daityas, having committed an offense against you through deceit,
flew up into the sky and, plunging into the ocean, went to the netherworld (pātāla).
"But now I possess two sky-faring elephants given by Indra;
with them, I shall reach those who travel through the air along with my sons."
Having heard that, the sage was pleased and said to that lord of men:
"In that case, prepare for me the necessary materials for the sacrifice as is appropriate."
"Having gone as far as my fame has spread throughout the world, I shall commence a sacrifice there;
and I send you this disciple of firm vows as my messenger."
Having assumed the form of a great, powerful bird, wild with passion,
this very one shall become the vehicle for him whose banner bears a pearl.
Having spoken thus, the sage departed for his own hermitage, and the king immediately dispatched all the necessary provisions after him.
And when that sacrifice had begun, with the assembly of gods and sages gathered together,
the Dānavas dwelling in the netherworld became agitated upon learning of it.
Knowing this, the sage dispatched that disciple of firm vows to the city of Devasabha, where he had assumed the form of the Lord of Birds as fashioned by Śāpaka.
Having seen that he had arrived there and having recalled the words of the Sage,
King Merudhvaja readied those two divine elephants.
He himself ascended the principal of those two golden mountains,
and he gave the one with the golden peak to his younger son.
And Muktāphaladhvaja, having taken up his divine weapons and being saluted by a multitude of bards, mounted that king of birds, Dṛḍhavrata.
Then those three heroes set forth on their aerial vehicles,
having been granted blessings by the best of the twice-born and preceded by soldiers dispatched ahead.
When they had reached his hermitage, that sage, with a joyful mind, granted them this boon:
"May you be impenetrable by all weapons."
And at that moment, the host of Dānavas arrived to destroy the sacrifice;
seeing this, Merudhvaja’s army charged forward, roaring.
Then a battle commenced between the Daityas and the humans;
the Daityas, remaining in their own positions, oppressed the humans who stood upon the earth.
Then that Muktāphaladhvaja, whose vehicle was a bird, having rushed forward, cut down and struck the Daityas with a rain of arrows.
And seeing him seated upon the bird, blazing as if with splendor,
the remaining Daityas fled, filled with apprehension toward Nārāyaṇa.
Having gone to Pātāla out of fear, they reported everything exactly as it was to Trailokyamālin, the king of the Daityas, at that very moment.
Having learned of this, he quickly searched for him through his spies;
and having discovered that Muktāphaladhvaja was a mere mortal, he could not endure being overcome by a human being.
Having assembled all the Dānavas of the netherworld,
the lord of the Asuras came to that hermitage to fight, even though he was being dissuaded by the birds.
Muktāphaladhvaja and the others remained there, fully attentive; as soon as they saw the lord of the Dānavas with his army, they rushed toward him.
Then, as that great battle between mortals and asuras commenced once more,
the gods, headed by Rudra and Indra, arrived in their celestial chariots to witness it.
And there Muktāphaladhvaja beheld before him the great Pāśupata weapon, which had appeared at that very moment with an irresistible splendor.
Of immense proportions, with upward-flaming tongues of fire, three eyes, and four faces;
having one leg and eight arms, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon.
"Know me to have come at the command of Śaṅkara for your victory.
Having spoken thus, the prince honored him and accepted his offer.
And meanwhile, from the sky, the army of Merudhvaja, standing below and suffering, was afflicted by various showers of missiles discharged by those asuras.
Then, in order to protect it, Muktāphaladhvaja, a versatile warrior,
spread a net of arrows in the midst and fought with the asuras.
Seeing him together with his father and brother upon that sky-faring vehicle,
Trailokyamālin, the lord of the Daityas, released the serpent-weapon (pannagāstra).
As he emerged from there, Malayadhvaja struck down countless, terrifying venomous serpents with Garuḍas produced by the *Gāruḍa* mantras.
Then, whatever weapon that lord of the Daityas, together with his son, discharged,
Muktāphaladhvaja effortlessly repelled each one of them.
Then, enraged, that enemy of the gods, his son, and the other Dānavas simultaneously hurled at him weapons such as the Āgneya and others.
Seeing those blazing weapons standing before him like the Pāśupata weapon,
all the other missiles became terrified and turned away in an instant.
Then, while those terrified Daityas were fleeing as far as they wished,
the hero Muktāphaladhvaja, perceiving their intention, [acted].
At that very moment, he bound an impenetrable net of arrows above them and in the four directions, resembling a cage of thunderbolts.
There, as those Dānavas were wandering about like birds, he,
together with his father and brother, struck them down with sharp arrows.
And the hands, feet, bodies, and heads of those Daityas fell; their severed limbs flowed away as rivers of blood.
Then, when the gods had offered shouts of "Well done! accompanied by a rain of flowers, Muktāphaladhvaja discharged the *mohana* (stupefying) weapon at those enemies.
He rendered those Asuras, along with the king, who were thus bewildered and fallen to the ground,
bound by fetters with the Vāruṇa weapon.
Then that sage, whose wealth was asceticism, spoke to King Merudhvaja:
"This army of asuras, which remains after being slain, must certainly not be killed."
For by accepting this very [weapon], you shall enter the subterranean realm (rasātala);
meanwhile, this lord of the Daityas, together with his sons and his ministers, shall be bound and led away.
Accompanied by great asuras, wicked nāgas, and chief rākṣasas,
he should be established within a cave of the White Mountain near the assembly hall of the gods.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, Merudhvaja said to the Daitya warriors:
"Do not fear; you are not to be slain by us, along with our brother."
"Follow now the teaching of this Muktāphaladhvaja!"—
having been addressed thus by the king, the Dānavas joyfully accepted it.
Then that king brought the Daitya king Trailokyamālin,
together with his sons and the others, to Mount Śveta.
And he placed him,
bound and guarded by the principal ministers endowed with the strength of Bhūriśravas, inside that cave.
Then, when the battle had ceased, the gods in their celestial chariots— having released a rain of Mandāra flowers—
departed, and a festival for the world commenced.
There, King Merudhvaja, the victorious, said to his two sons:
"I am staying right here for the time being in order to protect the sacrifice."
"Go both of you to Pātāla with these soldiers of yours,
accompanied by the multitude of Daitya chariots and the remaining forces of the Asuras."
Having comforted and brought under your control those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla),
and having appointed leaders over them, you shall return here after taking possession of them.
Having heard this, saying "So be it," the hero Muktāphaladhvaja, whose vehicle was the divine wish-fulfilling cow, and Malayadhvaja also quickly departed.
Both brothers, together with their armies, entered Rasātala,
accompanied by the Dānava host who marched before them in submission.
Having slain the guards and the adversaries stationed at their posts,
those two there beat the drum of fearlessness for the rest of the people.
And toward people who trusted and bowed down to them, these two accepted [offerings] from the seven underworlds,
consisting of hundreds of cities filled with various kinds of jewels.
And they enjoyed those delightful [gardens], which fulfilled all desires,
with ponds featuring staircases made of a single jewel and filled with divine liquors.
There, the wives of the dānavas and their daughters beheld those two of wondrous form within the trees, their bodies concealed by illusion.
And then, there, for the sake of her husband’s welfare while he was bound,
his wife named Svayaṃprabhā undertook ascetic penance.
And her two daughters, Trailokyaprabhā and Tribhuvanaprabhā,
likewise began to practice austerities for the welfare of their father.
And those two princes, having honored all the people there in Pātāla—
who were now at ease, having attained tranquility— with various pleasing gifts, [remained there].
And having appointed Saṅgrāmasiṃha and the other officials,
they went to the vicinity of their father’s hermitage in the forest of asceticism.
At that point, the sacrifice of the sage reached its conclusion;
then the gods began to depart for their own abodes, and likewise the ṛṣis.
Then Merudhvaja addressed Śakra, who was well-pleased:
"O Lord, if you are pleased with me, please come to my city."
Having heard that, Vāsava took leave of the sage and went to the city of the assembly of the gods together with his beloved and the king along with his son.
And there, that king, the lord of two worlds,
attended upon Śakra in such a way that he forgot his celestial happiness.
Then Śakra, being pleased, led that lord of the earth together with his son, mounted upon a divine celestial vehicle, to his own heaven, Triviṣṭapa.
There, in that place made beautiful by the pleasure of the music of Nārada, Rambhā, and others,
he caused Merudhvaja— who was accompanied by Malayadhvaja— to rest.
And Indra, having given Muktāphaladhvaja garlands made of *pārijāta* flowers along with divine crowns, honored him and sent him home.
Having come here to the world of men and moving back and forth to the netherworld (pātāla),
those god-like kings exercised sovereignty over both worlds.
Then Merudhvaja said to Muktāphaladhvaja:
"O son, you two brothers have conquered your enemies; you are both young men."
The princesses are under my control and have been sought out by me;
since the time has arrived, let the taking of a wife be performed.
When his father had spoken thus, Muktāphaladhvaja then replied:
"Father, my mind does not yet incline toward marriage."
"I shall now practice austerities in order to propitiate Hara;
let this son of mine, Malayadhvaja, however, perform his marriage."
Having heard this, his younger brother Malayadhvaja said to him:
"O Noble One, since you have no wife, how could marriage be appropriate for me?"
"Or, if you remain without the kingdom while I am in power, I shall indeed follow your path.
When this was said by Malayadhvaja, the king replied:
Merudhvaja said to his eldest son, Muktāphaladhvaja:
"What has been proposed by this younger brother of yours is indeed appropriate."
But you speak what is improper; for while you are still in this very youth, what indeed is the time for asceticism? This is truly your time for enjoyment.
"O son, this evil obsession is not appropriate for the present time; let it be relinquished.
Even though he was addressed thus by the king, the eldest son remained there.
When he did not accept the marriage now with certainty,
the king remained silent, waiting for the right time.
In the meantime, in the netherworld (pātāla), those two daughters of Trailokyamālin,
who were engaged in ascetic penance, spoke to their mother Svayaṃprabhā.
"O Mother, while we two were only seven or eight years old, our father became self-restrained;
yet why has this loss of kingdom occurred for us, who have performed no meritorious deeds?"
"This is now the eighth year that we two have been performing austerities, yet Hara is not pleased with us,
nor is our father released from his bonds even to this day."
Therefore, as long as there shall be no defeat by our enemy,
let them sacrifice this body, devoid of its marks, into the fire.
Having been addressed thus by her two daughters, Svayamprabhā spoke in this way:
"Daughters, wait for now; for there will be a reunion for us again."
For while I was established in asceticism, I remember that in a dream the god Śiva said to me:
"Daughter, maintain your fortitude; your husband shall regain his kingdom."
This Muktāphaladhvaja and likewise Malayadhvaja shall both become the husbands of your two daughters, O Prince.
"Do not think that these two are merely humans;
for one is a preeminent Vidyādhara, and the second is my own Gaṇa."
"Thus commanded by Īśvara at the end of the night, I was awakened;
with this intention, I endured this great suffering."
Therefore, I inform you of this matter regarding your lordly father;
and by his will, I shall strive for the accomplishment of your marriage.
Having thus comforted her two daughters, Queen Svayaṃprabhā spoke to an elderly woman of the inner apartments named Indumatī.
Go to the presence of the noble son at the cave of the White Mountain;
falling at his feet, represent my words to him.
"O Great King, I was created by the Creator from a different kind of wood;
for even now I am not consumed by the blazing fire of separation from you."
"But my own self has not been abandoned by me, for I still hope to see you again.
Having said this, you should report to me the instruction from Śiva that appeared in my dream.
"Therefore, you must ask him regarding the marriage of my daughter; whatever he says, you must come and tell it to me, and I shall act accordingly."
Having spoken thus to Indumatī, she sent her forth;
and she, having departed from Pātāla, reached the well-guarded entrance of that mountain cave.
Having entreated the guards, she entered within and,
beholding Trailokyamālin bound there, she took hold of his feet with tears in her eyes.
Being skilled in reading his mind, she slowly related all of her wife's message to him; then the king spoke.
"Let that attainment of sovereignty which was prophesied for us by Śarva come to pass exactly so;
but what need is there to mention the giving of daughters in marriage to the two sons of Merudhvaja?"
"I would rather perish right here than give this gift to my two human enemies while I am held in captivity."
Having spoken thus, Indumatī was then sent by the king;
she returned and reported those words to her husband’s wife, Svayaṃprabhā.
Then, having heard this, those two daughters of the lord of the Daityas, Trailokyaprabhā and Tribhuvanaprabhā, spoke to their mother, Svayaṃprabhā.
"Since fire alone is now our refuge out of fear for our youth,
O Mother, let us enter it on this fourteenth day."
When those two had thus made their resolve,
her mother as well, along with her retinue, then likewise made a resolve for death.
And when the fourteenth day arrived, they all performed the funeral rites at the sacred ford named Pāparipu, after having worshipped Hāṭakeśvara.
At that very time, on that lunar day, King Merudhvaja arrived together with his son and his wife to worship Dhāṭakeśvara.
As he was traveling with his followers toward that sacred ford of Pāparipu to bathe there,
he saw from afar smoke rising up from within the forest on its bank.
To that king, who was asking, "From where does this smoke arise?",
Saṅgrāmasiṃha and his other personal officials in charge of Pātāla replied:
O Great King, Trailokyamālin’s wife, Svayaṃprabhā,
was established here in ascetic practice together with her two daughters, who were still maidens.
"Surely they are performing some fire-ritual or the like here today;
or perhaps, exhausted by extreme asceticism, they are entering the fire."
Having heard that, the king went there with his two sons, his wife, and those officials to see him, having forbidden all other attendants.
And standing there in concealment, he beheld those two Daitya maidens together with their mother, worshipping a well-kindled funeral pyre.
With the outpourings of the mass of beauty from their faces, they seemed to create hundreds of moon-disks throughout all directions and even down into the netherworld.
With their two golden jars of breasts, they performed, as it were, the consecration of Kāma for the conquest of the three worlds, using the streams of water from their dangling necklaces.
Bearing her broad hips, which were encircled by a girdle,
she was like the forehead of the elephant of Smara, marked with a garland of stars.
And their two masses of hair flowed like two serpents fashioned by the Creator to guard the treasury containing the very essence of their beauty.
Having seen them, the king reflected with wonder arising within him:
"Aha! The creation of the Creator of the Universe is a shimmering, ever-new marvel."
Between these two daughters of the lord of the asuras, even Rambhā, Urvaśī, or Tilottamā do not attain equality in beauty.
While the king was thinking thus, that eldest daughter of the Daityas, Trailokyaprabhā, having worshipped the fire, made this request:
Ever since my mother told me the dream-omen regarding the bridegroom,
from that time forth I have indeed fixed my mind upon him as my husband.
"O Blessed One, may that very prince Muktāśphaladhvaja, who is a treasury of virtues,
become my husband once again in another birth."
In this life, although my father, while remaining in self-restraint,
desired to give me away, and my mother also intended to give me to him, I was not accepted by him.
Having heard that, Tribhuvanaprabhā likewise chose Malayadhvaja, the son of Hutāśa, as her husband in another birth.
Then King Merudhvaja, thrilled upon hearing that,
and his queen, the Mahādevī, spoke to one another:
"If these two sons of ours were to obtain these two wives,
then the fruit of conquering both worlds would be attained by them."
Therefore, as long as they do not throw themselves into this fire,
why do we not approach and stop them, together with their mother?
Having thus consulted with the queen, the king approached them and said:
"Do not commit this rash act; for I shall indeed pacify your suffering."
Having heard these words of the king, which were like a rain of nectar for the ears,
and having seen him, all those celestial women bowed down before him.
"Though we were looking on before, we were not noticed because we were concealed by illusion;
today, however, we have been seen here by you, the Lord of the two worlds."
And for those seen by you, the end of our suffering surely comes before long;
how much more so when a boon is granted by the Lord himself in his own voice at our request?
Therefore, having accepted seats, please accept the water for the hands and feet and other offerings;
for you are worthy of worship by the whole world, and this is our hermitage.
When Svayaṃprabhā had spoken thus, the king said with a smile:
"Let water for the feet and the guest-offering be given by you to these two sons-in-law."
Then, by his own power, the bull-bannered god said to them:
"Let the guest-offering and other honors be presented by you today; let it be accepted."
Then Merudhvaja said: "I have now taken all this;
you, however, must desist from your preparations for death and turn back from here at once."
"Enter and remain together in one of your own cities, which fulfills all desires;
then I myself shall ensure that everything becomes well for you."
To the king who had spoken thus, Svayaṃprabhā replied:
"At the command of the gods, we have desisted from our resolve to abandon the body."
"But while our lord is confined in prison, how can it be fitting for us to remain in our own homes?
Therefore, O King, let us stay right here for the time being."
"Until our Lord himself shall uphold the boon granted to us,
he will liberate our master along with his sons and ministers."
Once liberated, he will become your successor and shall rule the kingdom;
and by your own will, he will hand over the kingdom to you alone.
And he will establish such a binding covenant;
we, meanwhile, shall remain here together with the inhabitants of the netherworld.
"And take for yourself the jewels belonging to us from the netherworlds.
To her who had spoken thus, King Merudhvaja replied:
"I myself shall understand this; you must simply remember your own words," having said this, the king bathed and worshipped Hāṭakeśa.
And those two daughters of the Daitya king, having thus seen for themselves,
became single-mindedly focused on their two sons.
Then King Merudhvaja, the virtuous one, having been prostrated to and entreated for liberation by all the inhabitants of the netherworld (rasātala) belonging to Trailokyamālin, [consented].
Shrouding the quarters with parasols as white as his own fame, accompanied by his wife, sons, and servants,
he departed from that world of the asuras and returned to his own city.
There, his son Malayadhvaja, brooding over that younger daughter of the Dānava king,
passed the night afflicted by the fever of love, with eyes closed even though he was not asleep.

Even though he had heard of her from his father, the young Muktāphaladhvaja remained unmoved in heart; for although she was the daughter of the lord of asuras, her love for him was firmly fixed, and she was superior even to those whose minds are the domain of the great sages, capable of inciting the transformation of passion. Yet, despite having previously requested a boon from the sage, he did not waver in spirit.
But Merudhvaja, having learned that his son had been forbidden from marriage, that Malayadhvaja was under the sway of passion,
and that the great Asura was averse to giving his daughter in marriage, became anxious in his mind as he sought to devise a stratagem.
Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the sixth wave:
Then King Merudhvaja [spoke] to Malayadhvaja in that manner.
Seeing [him] thus overcome by the fever of love, he spoke to his own goddess in this way.
"O Pātāladṛṣṭa,
if your daughter were not to become the wife of my two sons, what would have been gained by me?"
Except for the youngest of those two, my son Malayadhvaja—
his fire of desire concealed by shame— is being cooked by the process of *puṭapāka*.
And for that purpose, although I have already promised liberation to the wife of Trailokyamālin, it has not yet been swiftly carried out even by me up to this day.
"Released from bondage, he would never give his two daughters to my two human sons out of pride in their divine nature. (SoKss 17.6.5)
"Let us now speak of this matter to him with gentleness for his benefit";
having reflected thus together with the queen, he gave orders to the doorkeeper.
"Go to the cave of Śvetaśaila and, with affection and according to my words, speak to that lord of the Daityas, Trailokyamālin, who remains there bound."
O Lord of the Daityas, you have long been afflicted here by the turn of fate;
therefore, now follow my words and bring an end to this suffering.
"Give your two daughters, who are enamored with my two sons, to them;
being thus released from here and having established confidence, rule your own kingdom."
Having spoken thus, the steward was sent by the king; having gone there into the interior of the cave, he delivered that message of the king to the lord of the Daityas.
"I will not give my two daughters to mere mortals," he replied;
and having been answered thus, the steward returned and reported it to the king.
Then, while King Merudhvaja was searching for a means,
as the days passed, his wife learned of the news concerning him.
Sent once again from Pātāla by that Svayaṃprabhā,
Indumatī arrived there as a messenger bearing a message.
Having arrived and announced her presence through the mouth of the female doorkeeper,
she entered the presence of the Great Queen, having been received with due honor by her.
Having prostrated, she said to her: "O Goddess, O Goddess Svayaṃprabhā, what is it that you have forgotten—your own previous promise?"
The oceans and the auspicious *elā* plants may become otherwise at the time of universal dissolution;
but even then, the word of those such as you would never become otherwise.
"Even though our master has not agreed to the offering of his daughter,
how could he, being thus bound, give his two daughters as a gift?"
If he is released by you for the sake of providing assistance in accordance with propriety,
then he will certainly repay your favor by giving you his daughter in marriage.
Otherwise, that Svayamprabhā might even give up her life along with her daughter;
therefore, you would neither obtain the daughter nor fulfill your promise of truth.
Therefore, O Goddess, act in such a way through the means of the pledge (samaya), signs of conviction (pratyaya), and so forth,
that the king may release him, our lord, for the sake of all our success.
And accept this ornament, created by me spontaneously,
which is inlaid with various divine jewels that bestow powers such as the ability to travel through the air.
When Indumatī had spoken thus, the queen said to her:
"How can this be accepted by me from one who is so sorrowful?"
If you do not take this upon yourself, we shall remain unsettled;
but once it is taken, we consider our own suffering to be stilled.
Thus, having been diligently exhorted by Indumatī,
that queen accepted those jeweled ornaments for the sake of consoling her.
"Stay right here, noble lady, until the king arrives," she said,
and she had the queen remain in that very place.
Just then the king arrived there, and Indumatī rose;
announced by the queen, she bowed to the monarch with due respect.
And she presented to that king the crest-jewel, which had appeared spontaneously and bestowed itself,
removing poison, demons, old age, and disease.
To that king who was saying, "I shall uphold my own truth and accept this," the mature Indumatī addressed him thus:
If what has been undertaken by Your Majesty is true, then it is already preserved;
if this is accepted, our confidence will become even greater.
When she had spoken thus, the queen said, "Well said," and taking that crest-jewel from the head of the king, she bound it upon her own head.
Then Indumatī again related to that king exactly what Svayamprabhā had said to the queen.
Then, having been addressed in the same manner by the queen, the king said to Indumatī:
"Wait right here today; I shall speak with you tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus and passed that night, King Merudhvaja summoned his ministers at dawn and addressed Indumatī in this manner:
Having informed King Trailokyamālin along with these ministers,
go and bring the asura women from Pātāla.
