[He gave] all the principal inhabitants of Pātāla, beginning with Svayaṃprabhā,
as well as the sealed treasure-water connected to Hāṭakeśvara.
The one who wears the garland of the three worlds must always remain under my control;
the nāgas, along with their servants and kinsmen, must become destroyers of the crops.
In this matter, having touched the feet of my lord in the presence of my minister,
may Svayaṃprabhā and the others become our witnesses through their oaths.
Likewise, let all the inhabitants of the netherworld act as sureties;
and let all [the gods], together with their kings, establish their offspring [as witnesses].
And let all the kings together have this written down,
and let them drink the entire reservoir of water from Hāṭakeśvara.
"Then I shall release Trailokyamālin from prison," having said this to Indumatī, the king dismissed her along with her ministers.
Having gone there and spoken with Trailokyamālin in the presence of his ministers,
Indumatī— having gained his trust— entered the netherworld in that very same manner.
Then she brought Svayaṃprabhā and the others, as well as the treasury water;
at the king's command, she caused all of them to perform everything before the ministers.
And King Merudhvaja released Trailokyamālin from prison along with his retinue, once the required conditions had been fulfilled.
Having brought him home and duly honored him along with his retinue, he—
having accepted a flood of divine jewels— dismissed him back to his own kingdom.
Trailokyamālin, having returned once more to his own Rasātala and attained sovereignty,
rejoiced together with his servants and kinsmen.
And Merudhvaja filled the earth with accumulations of wealth originating from the netherworld,
just as a rain cloud fills it with waters.
Then Trailokyamālin, having consulted with his own wife and desiring to give the two jewels of daughters to her two sons in his own home, [acted accordingly].
Remembering the favor he had received, the lord of the Daityas went in person from Pātāla to invite King Merudhvaja, along with his kinsmen, to come [to him].
Having arrived and received the rites of hospitality, he said to that king:
"At that time, you did not see the subterranean realm (rasātala) with complete composure."
"Since we are now intent on serving you, please come and show yourself;
and for the sake of our two sons, let my jewel of a daughter be accepted."
When this had been said by that king of the asuras, Merudhvaja then had his wife and both his sons summoned to that very place.
To them he related that speech of the lord of the Asuras, ending with the gift of his daughter;
then his eldest son, Muktāphaladhvaja, spoke to him.
"I shall not perform a marriage without having propitiated Śaṅkara;
what I said previously must be forgiven for this transgression of mine."
When I have departed for my home, let Malayadhvaja make his dwelling there;
for indeed, without that daughter of Pātāla, he can find no peace at all.
Having heard that, the younger brother said to him: "While you are present, noble sir, I would not perform such a dishonorable and unrighteous act."
Then, although King Merudhvaja endeavored to persuade him,
Muktāphaladhvaja did not desire his own marriage ceremony.
Then Trailokyamālin, having addressed that distressed king,
departed for his own Pātāla with his followers, just as he had come.
Having related the events there to his wife and son, he said to them:
"Behold what kind of fate this is for us, which is intent solely upon our humiliation!"
"Even though I previously requested these two human maidens, they were not accepted by them for me to give; yet today, they have not been taken by those two. (SoKss 17.6.59)
Having heard that, the two of them said: "Who knows how this was situated in the mind of the Creator? For how could the word of Śambhu be otherwise?"
Having understood what they were saying, they made a vow there regarding the two maidens, Trailokyaprabhā and Tribhuvanaprabhā.
If, while we two remain without food for twelve days,
the god does not grant the favor of the successful completion of our marriage, [then...]
Therefore, we two must enter the fire together with you;
this body must not be preserved for the sake of humiliation or for the sake of livelihood.
Having thus made their vow, the two daughters of the lord of the Daityas stood before the God, abstaining from food and devoted to recitation and meditation.
Having learned of this, their mother and father, the lord of the Daityas,
being deeply affectionate toward their daughter, likewise remained there without food.
Then Svayaṃprabhā quickly dispatched Indumatī back again to her mother, the great queen of Merudhvaja, to tell her that.
Having gone there, she reported the distress in her master’s house;
then King Merudhvaja learned of it from that queen.
Then, out of consideration for them, that couple abandoned their food there, as did their two sons who were devoted to filial piety.
Thus, while the two royal cities were in such distress,
Muktāphaladhvaja, fasting, meditated upon Śiva as his refuge.
When six nights had passed, the prince woke up in the morning and spoke first to his friend Saṃyataka, who possessed great intelligence.
"Friend, I know that today in a dream I mounted my own vehicle, which was granted by the ascetic sage, capable of assuming any form at will and moving as fast as thought."
Having fallen into a state of humiliation, out of world-weariness he went to the divine abode of Gaurīśa on the side of Mount Meru, which is very far from here.
There I saw a certain celestial maiden emaciated by her ascetic penances;
and a man wearing matted locks, smiling, spoke to me regarding her:
Having fled from one maiden, you have come here in this manner;
look, this second one has also arrived and stands here before you.
Having heard those words of his, while still unsatiated in beholding the beauty of that maiden, I suddenly awoke at the end of the night.
Therefore, I shall go to that very place to obtain that divine maiden;
if I do not find her there, I will enter the fire.
Having abandoned that Daitya maiden who was thus offered to me, my mind is now enamored with this woman seen in a dream; what can be done against fate?
"Once I have gone there, there will certainly be good fortune for me," he said, and then he called to mind the vehicle given to him by the sage.
Having ascended that, he attained the state of a celestial chariot (vimāna) together with his friend—
a vehicle that assumes any form at will and reaches whatever place is conceived by the mind.
Muktāphaladhvaja set out for that divine abode of Gaurī’s Lord;
having reached it and beholding it exactly as he had seen it in his dream, he rejoiced.
Then, at that sacred bathing place named Siddhodaka, he proceeded to perform his ablutions and other rites, attended solely by his friend.
Meanwhile, having learned that he had gone somewhere unknown, his father,
King Merudhvaja, accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, [set out at once].
Emaciated by fasting, he experienced the agitation of suffering while staying in his own city;
at that very moment, all of this was likewise perceived even in the netherworld (pātāla).
Then Trailokyamālin, having taken his two daughters,
went right there into the presence of the king, fasting and accompanied by his wife and others.
"He has surely gone somewhere today on the fourteenth day to worship Hara;
therefore, let us wait for him right here for this day."
"If he has not returned by morning, we shall go to that very place where he is";
thus they all made this firm resolve regarding what was to happen.
In the meantime, while staying in that hermitage of Gaurī in Meghavana,
Padmāvatī also spoke to her own companions on that day:
"Friends, I know that today in a dream, as I had gone to Siddhīśvara,
a certain man with matted hair emerged from a temple and spoke to me."
"Suffering has come to an end; O daughter, your reunion with your husband is near.
Having spoken thus, he departed, and for me too, sleep and night both passed away.
Having said, "Therefore, let us go there," she departed for that abode of Gaurīśa,
Padmāvatī, situated on the side of Mount Meru.
There, seeing Muktāphaladhvaja from afar bathing in the Siddhodaka water,
she was filled with wonder and spoke thus to her own companions:
"Look at what kind of man this is; he resembles my beloved.
It is a marvel—could it be he himself? No, for he is indeed a human being."
Having heard that and having seen him, her friends said this to her:
"O Queen, this man is not only very similar to your beloved."
Look, even this companion here attains a resemblance to your beloved’s friend, Saṃyataka.
O Goddess, from the dream-vision that you have described today,
we clearly understand that you two have manifestly entered the state of humanity due to a curse.
These very two have been brought here by the Lord through his own power;
otherwise, how could there be a human arrival in this divine realm?
Thus addressed by her friends, Padmāvatī, who had worshipped the Lord,
remained concealed near the god, eager to test him.
Having bathed, Muktāphaladhvaja arrived there to worship the deity;
looking all around, he spoke to Mahābuddhi.
That very same variegated abode which was seen by me in the dream— the form of Gaurīśa, visible within the *liṅga* and composed of jewels— is this very place.
I see those very same regions now here, as seen in my dream,
with trees shimmering with the light of jewels and divine birds.
I do not see that divine maiden here whom I beheld at that time;
if she is not attained, I shall certainly cast off my body here.
When he had spoken thus, her friends said to Padmāvatī in private:
"Listen; surely he has come here after seeing you in a dream."
"O Goddess, without even seeing you he intends to give up his life;
therefore, remaining hidden, let us observe his resolve."
When they had thus remained there in concealment, Muktāphaladhvaja entered within, worshipped the deity, and came back out.
As soon as he had gone out and performed three circumambulations with devotion,
both he and his friend remembered their own former births.
And while they were joyfully recounting their past adventures to one another,
Padmāvatī came within the range of their vision.
And Muktāphaladhvaja, remembering his deeds in a previous birth,
as soon as he saw her, spoke to his friend, overflowing with joy:
"I have seen this Queen Padmāvatī here in a dream;
by good fortune she has been found, so I shall now quickly pay my respects to her."
Having said this, he approached her and, with tears, spoke to her: "O Queen, do not go anywhere now; I am that Muktāphalaketu, your beloved."
"By the curse of Dṛḍhavrata, having become human, my former birth has been remembered today," she said; and he, eager, desired to embrace her.
But she, bewildered, vanished from sight and remained there with tearful eyes;
and that prince, no longer seeing her, fell to the ground out of delusion.
Then, with great sorrow, her companion said in the sky:
"O Goddess Padmāvatī, that was the purpose for which you underwent the hardship of asceticism."
"How was he found? Why do you not speak thus to him?
I am Saṃyataka; he too was a friend of your beloved."
"Since you have been cursed for my sake, why do you not speak kindly to me?
Having said this and comforted him, he spoke to the prince.
Since the daughter of the Daitya king was abandoned by you despite her having approached you with such passion,
this fruit of that sin has now come upon you.
Having heard that, Padmāvatī, remaining concealed, then said to her friends:
"Listen; it is said that he does not set his heart upon the daughters of the asuras."
Then her friends also said to her, "Everything appears to be consistent;
do you not remember what was said by your beloved at the time of the curse?"
"May my mind not go elsewhere in this human state except for Padmāvatī"—
this boon he previously obtained from that sage whose wealth was his asceticism.
"Surely it is because of his power that he does not take pleasure in other women.
Upon hearing this, the princess became overwhelmed with doubt.
Then Muktāphaladhvaja, having seen his beloved vanish, cried out:
"Alas, my dear Padmāvatī! Why do you not look upon me?"
"The curse that I incurred in Meghavana while in the state of a Vidyādhara—
I shall undoubtedly meet my death here today for your sake."
Having heard his lamentation beginning with these words, Padmāvatī said to all her companions: "Even though all these tokens of recognition correspond [to him],"
Nevertheless, my mind does not arrive at the certainty that these [teachings] might have been heard by these two two through some traditional succession. (SoKss 17.6.123)
"I cannot bear to hear his distressed words; I am going now to that temple of Gaurī, for it is my time for worship there."
Having spoken thus, she went with her companions to the hermitage of Padmāvatyambikā;
and having worshipped the goddess, she made this request: SoKss_17,6.125 //
"If he whom I saw at Siddhiśvara is truly my former beloved,
then act in such a way that there may be a swift reunion with him."
While Padmāvatī remained there with longing,
Muktāphaladhvaja likewise stayed at Siddhiśvara.
Previously, he spoke to his friend Saṃyataka, who possessed great intelligence:
"I know, my friend, that she has gone to her own abode, that temple of Gaurī."
Saying, "Therefore come, let us go right there," he mounted that mind-moving celestial chariot,
and he too arrived at that very hermitage of Ambikā.
Seeing him descending from the sky in his celestial chariot from afar,
his friends said to Padmāvatī, "O Queen, behold this wonder!"
"He has indeed come here even now by means of a divine celestial chariot;
how can such a divine power belong even to a human being?"
Then Padmāvatī said: "Friends, do you not remember that firm-vowed giver of the curse whom I cursed?"
"When you have descended into human existence, you shall become his vehicle, assuming any form at will and following his every desire."
By means of that vehicle belonging to the disciple of the Sage,
he certainly wanders everywhere at will, assuming the form of a celestial chariot.
When she had spoken thus, her friends said to her: "If you understand it to be so, then why, O Queen, do you not believe this? What do you look for?"
Having heard these words of her friend, Padmāvatī spoke again: "It is possible, my friends; yet even now I have no certainty."
Even if it were true that he is indeed this very person, nevertheless,
how could he be accessible to me while residing in another body, not supported by my own?
"We shall watch his movements here while he remains thus concealed," she said to the princess, and then she remained hidden, surrounded by her companions.
Then, having descended from his celestial chariot right there at Ambikā’s hermitage,
Muktāphaladhvaja, filled with longing, spoke to his companion:
Previously, I perceived her there, terrified by a rākṣasī; now she has been seen again here in the midst of the garden, having come of her own accord to choose a husband.
And here, at that time, my beloved Padmāvatī, who was intent on following me even though I had received a curse, was turned back with great difficulty by the lord of sages.
"Look, my friend, she herself is fleeing from the path of my sight this very day.
Having heard these words of his, Padmāvatī spoke to her friends:
"Truly, my friends, this is indeed that very same person, though not dependent upon his former body.
But how shall I reach him? In this matter, the Lord of Siddhas is my refuge."
"Since that very dream was granted by him,
he alone will provide the means," she decided, and returned once more to Siddhiśvara.
"Either bring about a reunion with my beloved as he existed in his former body, or grant me death; there is no third course for me."
Having thus addressed Dhūrjaṭi after honoring him,
she remained right there in the temple courtyard together with her companions.
Then, having searched for her at Gaurī’s hermitage there and not finding her, Muktāphaladhvaja became distressed and spoke to his companion.
"O Yavus, she has not returned from that abode of Śambhu;
if I do not find her even there, then I shall enter the fire itself."
Having heard that, his friend said: "Surely there will be only good fortune for you;
the word of the sage cannot be false, nor can the prophetic dream of Śambhu."
Having been thus consoled by that friend, Muktāphaladhvaja ascended the celestial chariot and set out for Siddhiśvara together with him.
Seeing that he had arrived there, Padmāvatī remained unobserved;
she said to her friends, "Look, he has arrived right here!"
Having entered the foremost of the gods' abodes and seen the deity freshly worshipped,
Muktāphaladhvaja addressed that companion of his:
"Friend, look! This Lord has just now been worshipped by someone.
Surely that very beloved of mine is standing here somewhere, having performed this worship."
Having said this, when he searched there and did not find her, the lover then cried out repeatedly in separation: "Alas, my beloved Padmāvatī!"

He mistook the peacock feather for her conversation due to the thought of her speech, for her braid due to the thought of her hair, and likewise for the lotus due to the delusion that it was her face.
As he ran about, helpless under the influence of the fever of love,
his friend consoled him with great difficulty and spoke to the prince after having entreated him.
"Why have you undertaken this while exhausted by many fasts?
Why do you neglect yourself, which has conquered both the world of men and the netherworld?"
While you have not yet returned, your father Merudhvaja,
King Trailokyamālin, and your father-in-law, the lord of the Dānavas, [are all waiting for you].
And that daughter of yours, Trailokyaprabhā, also desires you;
so too does your mother Vinayavatī and your younger brother Malayadhvaja.
"Everyone who fears what is undesirable abandons their life-breaths while fasting;
therefore, come, let us go and protect them, for the day is drawing to a close."
To that speaking friend, Muktāphaladhvaja said:
"Go yourself in my celestial vehicle and comfort them."
Then his friend said to him: "How can that disciple of the sage, who has become your mount by means of a curse, be brought near to me?"
To his friend who had spoken thus, the prince said:
"Then stay here for a while, my friend; let us see what will happen in this matter."
Having heard that conversation, Padmāvatī said to her friends:
"I know by the correspondence of these tokens of recognition that he is my former beloved."
Granted that one dwelling in a human body is thus tormented by a curse,
yet this fault of the curse is mine as well, arising from my derision of the Siddha’s daughter.
Even as she was speaking thus, the moon, with its copper-red hue—
the forest fire for those separated from their lovers— arose.
And gradually he filled the world with moonlight on all sides,
as well as that Kandarpadahanajvālā [fire] upon Muktāphaladhvaja.
Then, crying out like the one called Kālacakra, the prince was addressed by the distressed Padmāvatī while she remained concealed.
O prince, even if you are that very same person who was my beloved in the past,
nevertheless, residing in another body, you are to me a stranger.
"I am here, as are your wife's paramours; why do you cry out again and again?
If the word of that sage is true, a remedy will surely come to pass."
Having heard these words of hers and not seeing her,
Muktāphaladhvaja fell into a state of mind made uneven by joy and despair.
And he said: "O Goddess, having remembered my previous birth, I recognized you upon seeing you, as you were assuming your very own body."
But you, having seen me while I was residing in a Vidyādhara body,
how is it that you now recognize me when I am situated in a mortal body?
"Therefore, I must certainly abandon this wretched body," he said, and then became silent; his beloved wife also remained hidden there.
Then, when the night had mostly passed and his friend, that great sage Pūrṇa Saṃyatika, had fallen asleep from exhaustion;
Knowing that Padmāvatī was unattainable with that body,
Muktāphaladhvaja gathered pieces of wood and kindled a fire.
O Blessed One, by your grace, having resumed that former body of mine,
I shall before long attain my beloved Padmāvatī.
Speaking thus and bowing down to Śaṃkara in his form as the Liṅga,
the prince offered his body into that blazing fire.
Then that one of great intelligence awoke; not seeing Muktāphaladhvaja even after searching for him, he beheld a blazing fire.
Reflecting upon that friend who had sacrificed himself and was distressed by separation,
he too, out of grief for him, threw himself into that very fire.
Seeing that, Padmāvatī, afflicted with grief, said to her friends:
"Alas, shame! The hearts of women are harder even than a thunderbolt."
Since I have not departed with my life-breaths while witnessing this slaughter,
how much longer must I, an unfortunate soul, continue to sustain myself?
"Even for a sage, there is no end to my suffering today due to my lack of merit;
his word has proven otherwise. Therefore, death is better for me."
It is not proper for me to enter here into the midst of other men; therefore, this noose is indeed my path, for it is free from exertion.
Having spoken thus, the princess approached an *aśoka* tree in front of Śambhu and proceeded to fashion a noose from its creeper.
While her circle of friends was trying to dissuade her with words that offered hope, that sage, whose wealth was his asceticism, arrived there.
"Do not act rashly, my daughter; let those words of mine not prove false.
Be steadfast now, for you shall see your beloved here this very moment."
By your very ascetic power, the exhaustion of his curse has occurred without delay;
how then can you have no regard for your own asceticism?
"And since your marriage is imminent, why this despondency?
Having understood all of this through my meditative concentration, I have come here."
Seeing the sage approaching and speaking thus,
Padmāvatī bowed to him and for a moment became as if mounted upon a swing.
Then, having abandoned his mortal body through cremation and assumed a Vidyādhara form,
Muktāphalaketu arrived there with his companion, beloved by her.

Beholding that son of the Vidyādhara lord descending from the sky, Padmāvatī experienced an indescribable joy in her heart— like a female cātaka bird at the sight of a fresh cloud, or like a night-lotus at the rising of the full moon.
And that Muktāphalaketu rejoiced upon beholding her with his very eyes, drinking her in like a traveler,
exhausted by long wandering in a desert land, who encounters a river.
And at the end of that night of the curse, both of them, having attained union like a pair of cakravāka birds,
reached a state of satisfaction by prostrating at the feet of that sage who possessed the splendor of the sun.
"If you two have returned here once more, joyful at having crossed over the curse, that alone is today the complete satisfaction of my heart"— thus did the great sage then welcome them.

When the night had passed, King Merudhvaja also arrived there, mounted upon Indra’s elephant, accompanied by his youngest son Dāraka; likewise did Trailokyamālin, the lord of the Daityas, arrive together with his daughter Trailokyaprabhā, traveling in a celestial chariot, along with his inner court and his followers.
Then the sage, having shown Muktāphalaketu those two, described their history:
how he had attained human birth through a curse for the sake of a specific purpose, and how he subsequently achieved liberation from it.

Having understood that instruction given by the sage, Merudhvaja and the others, who were on the verge of throwing themselves into the fire, performed the ritual bath in the water of success, the worship of Hara, and other rites; they immediately became free from sorrow.
Then, by means of that Trailokyaprabhā, having quickly recollected her birth, she thought: "Alas, I am Devaprabhā, the daughter of the Lord of Siddhas."
"May the lord of the Vidyādharas be my husband"— thus, while performing austerities,
Padmāvatī was mocked and entered the fire to achieve her own desire.
Thus I was born into this family of the sons of Diti, and here I have found one to whom I am devoted;
and now this prince has also regained his own body as a Vidyādhara.
And it is not fitting for him, being of another form, to approach with this body;
therefore, I offer this asura-body into the fire once more in order to attain that state.

Having reflected thus in his heart and informed his parents, the Fire-god himself appeared, bringing with him her former body which had been offered out of compassion, as she had entered the fire of Muktāphaladhvaja; and he spoke.
"O Muktāphalaketu, she has cast off her body for your sake;
therefore, accept this Devaprabhā, daughter of Siddheśa, as your wife."

As soon as he had said this, the fire vanished; then Brahmā arrived there along with the immortals headed by Indra, as did the king of the Gandharvas together with Candraketu and Padmaśekhara, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
Then the prosperous king of the Gandharvas, having bowed down before him who was greeted with joy by all, and being assisted by them with attentive care,
bestowed his daughter Padmāvatī upon Muktāphalaketu according to the prescribed rites.

And there, having finally attained that beloved for whom he had long yearned, the prince of the Vidyādharas felt as though he had reaped the fruit of the tree of his birth; then he took to himself that maiden of the Siddhas.

And there, Malayadhvaja, the prince, was united with that beloved daughter of the lord of the Daityas, who had been bestowed upon him by her father according to the prescribed rites, and who possessed the splendor of the three worlds.
Then, having consecrated his son Malayadhvaja in the sole sovereignty over the circle of the earth with its islands because of his maturity,
Merudhvaja went to the forest with his wife to practice asceticism.
Then Trailokyamālin, the sovereign of the Daityas, departed for his own abode along with his retinue;
thereafter, Śakra bestowed upon Muktāphalaketu the royal fortune of Vidyuddhvaja.
"Let this Muktāphalaketu enjoy the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas and Asuras,
and let the gods return to their own abodes"— thus a voice resounded from the sky.
Having heard that, Brahmā, Śakra, and the others departed from there, filled with joy; and the sage Tapodhana, having been released from the curse, went along with his disciple.
Then Candraketu, accompanied by his son Muktāphalaketu, who shone with two wives, returned to his own Vidyādhara realm.
And having enjoyed there for a long time the fortune of a sovereign of the sky-dwellers together with that son, the king,
becoming dispassionate, entrusted the burden of his own kingdom to him and, along with the queen, took refuge in the ascetic grove of the sages.
And that Muktāphalaketu, having previously attained the sovereignty of the asuras from Indra,
and having subsequently regained from his father that status as the universal emperor of the Vidyādharas—
Together with Padmāvatī, for ten kalpas,
that man of merit enjoyed the glorious happiness of a prosperous universal sovereignty over both realms, as if accompanied by personified bliss.
Having observed that all phenomena are ultimately devoid of essence, and having finally taken refuge in the forest of the Lord of Sages,
he attained the supreme light through the excellence of his asceticism and reached union with the Lord Dhūrjaṭi.
Having thus heard this story of the lakes from the pair of swans and having obtained knowledge from their mouths, King Brahmadatta attained a divine state;
and his wife, his minister, and those two birds all went to Siddhīśvara, cast off their bodies born of a curse, and regained their own original status as attendants of Śiva.
Thus, O sages, having heard this story from Gomukha regarding my separation from Madanamañcukā,
I diverted my mind with fortitude for a mere moment.
When Naravāhanadatta, the universal monarch, had thus finished his tale,
the sages at Kaśyapa’s hermitage, together with Gopālaka, were thoroughly delighted.
Thus ends the sixth wave in the *Padmāvatī* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
This seventeenth book, the *Padmāvatī* book, is now complete.
// Śrī //
The Ocean of the Streams of Story, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa. The eighteenth book, named Viṣamaśīla.
Long ago, it is said, this nectar of stories emerged from the ocean of Hara’s mouth, churned by the Mandara mountain of his love for the daughter of the king of mountains.
Those who, having attained supernatural power through the removal of obstacles, forcibly savor [the nectar] and bear the divine burden upon this earth, do so by the grace of Bhava.
The First Wave:
Homage to him whose body is half-moon-faced, whose splendor is white as moonbeams,
whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and who bears the crescent moon upon his head.
May that elephant-faced one protect you, who shines as if bestowing supernatural powers with his trunk, its tip curled and playfully raised.
Then, on that Mount Aśita, in the hermitage of the sage Kaśyapa,
Naravāhanadatta addressed those sages in this way:
Moreover, while I was separated from the Queen, Vegavatī, out of her affection for me,
took me and placed me in the care of Abhirakṣita to be looked after by him.
Then, seeking to cast off my body, separated from my beloved and wandering in a foreign land,
I beheld the great sage Kaṇva at the edge of a forest.
Seeing me prostrate at his feet and perceiving my vow,
the compassionate sage led me, who was filled with sorrow, to his own hermitage and spoke to me.
Having become a hero born of the lunar dynasty, why indeed do you lose your composure?
What lack of faith can there be in the command of the gods, which is certain; what [value] have you for union with a wife?
Even meetings with those who seem impossible for men to encounter do occur in this world;
for instance, I shall relate to you the story of Vikramāditya—listen.
In the land of Avanti, there exists a famous city named Ujjayinī, built by Viśvakarman at the beginning of the eon, which serves as the dwelling place of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva).
Like a virtuous wife, she was unassailable; like a lotus pond, she was graced by beauty; like the wisdom of the virtuous, she was rich in righteousness; and like the earth, she was full of wonders.
In that city there was a world-conquering king named Mahendrāditya,
who, like Maghavan in Amarāvatī, was the destroyer of the forces of his adversaries.
In valor he was like the wielder of various weapons and missiles; in beauty, he was like the god whose weapon is the flower.
He who was "open-handed" in generosity became one with a "fisted hand" in his refusal to give up [the throne].
That lord of the earth had a wife named Saumyadarśanā,
who was like Śacī to Indra, like Gaurī to Śambhu, and like Śrī to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The lord had a chief minister named Sumati,
and a doorkeeper named Vajrāyudha who had served in his family for generations.
Ruling the kingdom together with them and propitiating Hara,
that king constantly observed various vows out of a desire for a son.
In the meantime, in that mountain cave inhabited by hosts of gods,
which was as beautiful as the laughter of Kubera rejoicing in his conquest of another quarter, [the following occurred].
The gods, including Indra, distressed by the oppression of the Mlecchas, approached Purāri, who was staying on Kailāsa, the lord of mountains, accompanied by Pārvatī.

Having prostrated and sat down immediately thereafter, those immortals, having offered praise and been asked the purpose of their arrival, addressed the god in this way: *praṇāmānantarāsīnāste kṛtastutayo 'marāḥ / pṛṣṭāgamanakāryāste devamevaṃ vyajijñapan //* SoKss_18,1.18 *//
Those asuras who were slain by you, O Lord, and those who were slain by Viṣṇu,
have today been born once again on the surface of the earth in the form of Mlecchas.
They cause obstacles to arise, they destroy rites such as sacrifices, and they carry off the daughters of sages; what evil do these wicked ones not commit?
O Lord, the world of the gods is perpetually nourished by the earth-world,
for the oblation offered into the fire by the brahmins serves for the satisfaction of the inhabitants of heaven.
And when the world of mortals is overrun by barbarians and devoid of the auspicious sound of *vaṣaṭ*,
the world of the gods languishes due to the cessation of sacrificial portions and other offerings.
Therefore, devise a means for this purpose and bring down some great hero to the earth who shall exterminate those mlecchas.
Thus addressed by the gods, the Enemy of Tripura said to them:
"Go; you need have no anxiety here; be at ease."
"I shall undoubtedly devise a means for this here before long," having said this, the Lord of Ambikā dismissed the gods to their own celestial abodes.

When they had departed, the Blessed One summoned the group known as Mālyavat and, together with Parvatī, gave this command: SoKss_18,1.26: "When they had departed, having summoned the group known as Mālyavat, the Blessed One, together with Parvatī, gave this instruction."
"O you who have descended as a son, be born in the human world in the great city of Ujjayinī as the heroic son of King Mahendrāditya."
That king is indeed a portion of myself, and his wife is born from a portion of Ambikā;
being born in their house, accomplish the task of the gods.
"Slay all the Mlecchas without exception, who are destroyers of the dharma of the three Vedas;
and by my grace, you shall become a king, the lord of the seven continents."
Even yakṣas, rākṣasas, and vetālas will remain under your control;
and after enjoying human pleasures, you shall come back to us again.
Thus commanded by the Conqueror of Cities, the Gaṇa Mālyavat replied:
"Your command is not to be transgressed by me; however, what pleasures are there in the human realm?"
Where there is the unbearable separation from kinsmen, friends, and servants,
and where there is the agony arising from the loss of wealth, old age, disease, and the like.
Thus addressed by that host, Dhūrjaṭi replied to him:
"Go, O sinless one; these sorrows shall no longer be yours."
"By my grace, you shall be happy at all times.
Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, Mālyavat then became invisible.
Having gone to Ujjayinī, that best of Gaṇas was conceived in the womb of the queen of King Mahendrāditya at the time of her season.
And at that time, the Lord, whose crest was adorned with a digit of the moon,
commanded King Mahendrāditya in a dream:
"I am pleased with you, O King; therefore, a son shall be born to you, who by his prowess will traverse the earth with its seven continents."
The Hero will bring under his control even the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others who dwell in the netherworld and the sky; he will slay the hosts of mlecchas.
For this very reason, he shall be known by the name Vikramāditya;
likewise, he shall be called Viṣamaśīla because of his hostility toward his enemies.
When the god had vanished after saying this, the lord of the earth woke up and,
delighted, reported that dream to his ministers in the morning.
Then those ministers, filled with joy, reported to the king in due order that dream-instruction of Hara which had resulted in the attainment of a son.
Then the maidservants of the inner apartments came and showed the fruit directly to the king, saying, "In a dream, Śambhu gave this to the Queen."
Then that king rejoiced, being congratulated by his ministers, saying again and again:
"Truly, a son has been granted to me by Śarva."
Then that queen, possessing intense splendor, became pregnant,
like the eastern quarter at dawn bearing the orb of the rising thousand-rayed sun.
And she shone upon her breasts with the dark luster of her nipples,
like the seal of protection for the milk of a sovereign still dwelling in the womb.
Then, in her dream, she crossed all seven oceans while being prostrated to by all the yakṣas, vetālas, and rākṣasas.
And when the time had arrived, she gave birth to a glorious son,
by whom the dwelling was illuminated with his youthful splendor as if by the sun in the sky.
And when he was born, the sky shone, laughing with a shower of falling flowers and resounding with the noise of the celestial drums of the gods.
At that time, the city became as agitated by the joy of the festival as if it were intoxicated, possessed by a spirit, or overwhelmed by a disturbance of wind.
And at that time, while wealth was raining down incessantly upon the king,
there was no one who was not a follower of the Sugata, nor anyone who was not a sovereign.
His father named him Vikramāditya according to the word of Hara,
while King Mahendrāditya named him Viṣamaśīla.
As other days passed there,
a son was born to that king’s minister, Sumati, named Mahāmati.
To Kṣattṛ Vajrāyudha was born a son, Bhadrāyudha;
and to Mahīdhara, the family priest, a son named Śrīdhara was born.
Together with those three ministers,
the prince Vikramāditya grew here like [one increases] through splendor, heroism, and strength.
For him who had been initiated into the sciences, his teachers became merely instrumental causes;
those sciences, however, manifested spontaneously for him without effort.
Whatever science or art he employed,
that very one was perceived by those who knew it to be unsurpassed by him.
And seeing that prince fighting with divine weapons,
the people became indifferent even toward stories of Rāma and other archers.
The kings who had submitted after being attacked gave him beautiful maidens;
his father brought them to him like so many other goddesses of fortune.
And then, seeing him established in youth and possessed of abundant prowess,
he duly consecrated his son, who was beloved by the people, in the kingdom.
King Mahendrāditya, along with his wife and ministers,
being advanced in years, went to Vārāṇasī and took refuge in Śiva.
Having obtained his father’s kingdom,
Vikramāditya also gradually began to blaze forth as a king, like the sun in the sky.
As soon as he saw the string fixed upon his bending bow,
even the kings, though their heads were already held high, bowed down in every direction as if by that very training.
Possessing divine power, he even subdued vetālas, rākṣasas, and others,
and correctly instructed those who were following the wrong path.
Adorning the quarters of the sky upon the surface of the earth, the armies of that Vikramāditya set forth like the rays of the sun.
Though he was a great hero, he was timid regarding the next world;
though brave, he was not fierce; and though a lord of the earth, he was beloved by women.
He was the father of those who were fatherless, the kinsman of those without kin, and the protector of the helpless; among his subjects, who was there that he did not become?
In the creation of Śvetadvīpa, the Ocean of Milk, Kailāsa, and the Himālaya mountains,
his fame was surely the model for the Creator.
And once, when King Vikramāditya had entered the assembly hall, the doorkeeper Bhadrāyudha approached and addressed him.
When he was dispatched with an army for the conquest of the southern region,
it was Vikramaśakti whom the King sent as his companion.
"O Lord, this messenger Anaṅgadeva has arrived and stands at the gate;
he is accompanied by a companion, his face is joyful, and he speaks auspiciously."
When the king said, "Let him enter," the doorkeeper respectfully ushered Anaṅgadeva into his presence along with his companion.
Having entered and uttered the words of victory with a respectful salutation, the messenger sat down before him; then he was questioned by the king.
Is that king Vikramaśakti, the commander-in-chief, well?
And are the other kings, such as Vyāghrabala and the rest, also doing well?
Regarding the other princes and the leaders in that army,
I hope all is well with the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Thus questioned by the king, Anaṅgadeva spoke for the welfare of Vikramaśakti,
his entire army, and all people.
The western region was conquered by Your Majesty, as were the southern lands,
the Middle Country together with Saurāṣṭra, and the eastern direction including Vaṅga and Aṅga.
The region of Kaśmīra and the northern quarter were made to pay tribute;
those various strongholds and islands were also conquered.
The hosts of Mlecchas were slain and the survivors were brought under subjection;
those various kings entered the camp of Vikramaśakti.
And that Vikramaśakti, having joined with those kings,
O Lord, is indeed staying only two or three marches away from here on his expedition.
When he had spoken thus, King Vikramāditya, being pleased, rewarded the messenger with garments, ornaments, and villages.
Then the king questioned that excellent messenger again:
"Anaṅgadeva, which countries were seen by you upon your journey here?"
"O good man, tell us where and what curious thing was seen by you. Thus addressed by the king, Anaṅgadeva proceeded to speak.
"By Your Majesty's command, O Lord, I have come here from there,
arriving in due course at the side of Vikramaśakti with that assembly of Your Majesty's army."
It was adorned by the glorious lion-like lords of infinite nāgas gathered together,
vast like the ocean, and inhabited by winged mountains.
And having arrived there, I was received with great honor by that Vikramaśakti, who bowed down to me and said, "I have been sent by my lord."
While I remained there, gazing upon the form of Vijaya,
a messenger connected to the Lord of Siṃhala arrived.
"Anaṅgadeva, who has become like the very heart of the king, stands near him"—
this was told to me by messengers who have returned from your presence.
Therefore, send this Anaṅgadeva to my presence with haste;
I shall tell him something auspicious regarding a certain matter of state business.
Thus that messenger, having come from Siṃhala, spoke these words of his sovereign in my presence to that Vikramaśakti.
Then Vikramaśakti said to me, "Go quickly;
go to the presence of the Lord of Siṃhala and see what he says in your face."
Then, together with that envoy of the Lord of Siṃhala,
I went to the island of Siṃhala by ship along the path of the ocean.
And there I saw the royal capital, fashioned of gold,
with its palaces of variegated jewels, like the city of the gods.
And there I beheld that Vīrasena, the lord of Siṃhala,
surrounded by his disciplined ministers like Śatakratu by the gods.
Having received me with respect and inquired after the welfare of my lord,
the king comforted me there with great hospitality.
On another day, that king, having entered the assembly hall, summoned me and,
displaying his devotion toward you, spoke in the presence of his ministers:
"I have a daughter, a maiden who is the singular beauty of the mortal world;
her name is Madanalekhā, and I give her to you, O Kings."
She is his suitable wife, and he is her worthy husband;
for this reason you have been summoned by one desiring to recover what belongs to your master.
And go with my messenger before your master to say:
"I shall send my daughter here immediately after you."
Having spoken thus, the king had his daughter brought there,
adorned with an abundance of ornaments and endowed with beauty, grace, and youth.
Having seated her on his lap and shown her to me, he said, "This maiden has been given by me to your master; let her be accepted."
And having seen that princess, I was struck with wonder at her beauty;
delighted, I said, "I desire her for the sake of the king."
And I thought: "Aha! Fate is never satiated in its wondrous ways, since even after creating Tilottamā, it has fashioned this most excellent woman."
Then, having been honored by that king, I set out from that island together with this messenger, Dhavalasena.
Having boarded the vessel, as we were traveling upon the ocean,
we suddenly beheld a great sandbank in its midst.
In their midst, we beheld two maidens of wondrous form:
one with limbs as dark as the priyaṅgu plant, and the other with a radiance as pure as the moon.
Adorned with garments and ornaments appropriate to their respective castes, they offered salutations with joined palms,
the sound of which was accompanied by the tinkling of jeweled bracelets.
In front of them, they were making a young play-deer dance—
a creature made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with jewels, yet truly alive.
Seeing that, we both, filled with wonder, said to one another:
"Aha! What is this marvel? Is it a dream, an illusion, or perhaps a delusion?"
Where in the ocean is there a sandbank so suddenly? And where, upon it, are two such maidens?
And where is a living golden deer, its limbs variegated with such jewels, for these two?
O King, even as we were speaking these words in wonder,
a wind suddenly began to blow, tossing up the ocean.
Thinking that our ship was reeling, it was destroyed;
and the people on board, being devoured by sea-monsters, sank down.
And those two maidens approached us, took hold of our arms,
lifted us up, and carried us to the sandy bank before we had even reached the mouths of the sea-monsters.
And as that bank was being filled by the waves, we were overwhelmed;
then, having comforted us, we were made to enter [the cave] by them, as if into the interior of a mountain cavern.
Then we looked about at that divine forest with its various trees;
there was neither ocean nor shore, nor was there the young deer, nor the two maidens.
"Is this a painting? Surely it is some kind of illusion," we said as we wandered there for a moment; then we saw a great lake.
Like the disposition of the great, it was naturally pure, profound, and vast;
like Nirvana personified, it quelled the torment of craving.
And there we beheld a certain excellent woman, surrounded by her attendants, who had come to bathe and appeared like the very goddess of the forest in person.
Having descended from her palanquin and gathered appropriate lotuses,
she bathed in the lake and meditated there upon the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva).
Just then, rising from the lake with wonder,
Śiva in the form of a linga approached her in person, right before us both.
Having worshipped that lute made of divine jewels with various enjoyments suited to her own wealth, the beautiful woman took it up.
Taking the right path, she played that [instrument] while singing it correctly with proper pitch, rhythm, and lyrics, through her focused attention.
Just as their hearts were drawn by hearing that [sound], the Siddhas and others who had come through the sky remained there motionless, as if they were painted.
Then, having withdrawn the Gandharva music, she performed the dismissal of Śambhu;
and there, at that very spot, the god submerged himself in the lake.
Then, having risen and boarded the vehicle along with her attendants,
that deer-eyed woman set out to proceed slowly.
Although we both asked repeatedly with great effort, "Where is she?",
none of her attendants gave any answer as we followed after her.
Then, wishing to demonstrate your power to this envoy of the Lord of Siṃhaladvīpa, I spoke these words to her aloud:
"O auspicious one, you are bound by an oath upon the touch of King Vikramāditya’s feet:
if you depart without revealing your true nature to me, you shall be a mere illusion."
Having heard that, she dismissed her retinue, descended from the vehicle, approached me, and spoke with sweet words: SoKss_18,1.128.
"I hope the lord Śrī Vikramādityadeva is well;
or rather, Anaṅgadeva, what need is there for me to ask, since everything is already known to me?"
Indeed, it was by me alone that you were brought here after displaying this illusion;
for the sake of that king, he is one who is to be honored by me, as he is my savior from great danger.
"Come then to my house; there I shall tell you everything—who I am, how the king is to be honored by me, and what his purpose is."

Having spoken thus, she who had gracefully released her vehicle proceeded on foot along the path; bowing low, that fair-faced woman led them to her own city, which was like unto heaven, adorned everywhere with various jewels and wrought gold, and at its gates occupied by heroic men bearing diverse weapons and assuming various forms.

There, in a screened enclosure, she honored us with baths, ointments, fine garments, and ornaments by means of brides who were like personified successions of all divine enjoyments and accomplishments, and she now allowed us to rest.
Thus ends the first wave in the *Viṣamaśīla* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The Second Wave.
Having spoken thus to King Vikramāditya as he sat in his assembly hall, [he continued:]

Then, after the meal was over, she, standing in the midst of her friends, said to me:
"Anaṅgadeva, listen now; I shall tell you everything."
"I am Madanamañjarī, the daughter of Dundubhi, the king of the yakṣas, and the wife of Maṇibhadra, the brother of Dhanada."
Thus, on the banks of rivers, upon mountains, and in delightful groves, I always lived happily with my husband.
And once, it is said, I went to Ujjayinī together with my beloved to enjoy myself in a garden named Makaranda.
There, by chance at dawn, a certain wretched Kāpālika mendicant saw me, who had awakened after sleeping in the monastery’s rest-house.
That wicked man, enslaved by desire, went to the cremation ground and began to employ me through the performance of a fire sacrifice and the chanting of mantras in order to win me as his wife.
Having understood this through my own supernatural power, I informed my husband;
he, in turn, reported it to his elder brother, Dhanada.
Having gone, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) made his request to the Lotus-born (Brahmā);
and that Blessed One, having meditated thus upon Brahmā, spoke to him.
It is true that Kapālin was intent on abducting your brother’s wife;
for such is the power of those mantras used for the propitiation of yakṣas.
But she, being drawn by that mantra, must cry out to King Vikramāditya; he will then protect her from that [danger].
Having approached my husband, Dhanada spoke these words of Brahmā;
and my husband told them to me, whose soul was terrified by the evil spell.
And at that moment, while performing a fire-oblation in the cremation ground, that Khaṇḍakāpālika himself drew me forth by means of a mantra perfected through successive stages.
And I, drawn by the mantra, fled in terror from there and reached a fearsome cemetery,
abounding in bones and skulls, frequented by spirits.
There I then saw that wicked Kāpālika,
who had offered oblations into the fire and was presiding over a mandala established upon a consecrated, upturned corpse.
And that Kāpālika, seeing me arrive, was deluded by pride;
by some chance, he went to a nearby river to perform his ritual rinsing.
At that moment, having forgotten the words of Brahmā, I thought:
"Why do I not cry out to the king? He might perhaps wander here during the night."
Having reflected thus, I cried out loudly there:
"Save me, O Lord, King Vikramāditya!"
O jewel that guards the waking world, behold this virtuous woman by force—
this wife of Maṇibhadra, the younger brother of the Lord of Wealth!
"This Kāpālika is intent on destroying me within your kingdom; he is a Yakṣī named Madanamañjarī, the daughter of Dundubhi."
Even as she was thus crying out, I beheld that king approaching with sword in hand, as if blazing with splendor.
And he said to me, "O blessed lady, do not fear;
be at ease. O auspicious one, I shall protect you from this Kāpālika."
"Who indeed is capable of committing such unrighteousness in my kingdom?
Having said this, he summoned a vetāla named Agniśikha.
And he, being summoned, arrived while still blazing, with his hair standing erect like dust;
having approached, he said to the king, "What shall I do? Command me."
Then the king said: "This wicked Kāpālika, who has committed the theft of another's wife, must be killed by you and eaten."
Then Agniśikha, having entered that corpse which was positioned within the circle of worship,
sprang up and rushed forward with his arms and mouth wide open.
That Vetāla seized the Kāpālika by the calves from behind as he was returning from having sipped water for purification and was intent on flight.
Having whirled him about in the air and swiftly dashed him against the ground,
he crushed both his body and his aspirations together into dust.
Seeing the Kāpālin slain while the creatures were greedily craving the flesh,
a fierce Vetāla named Yamaśikha arrived there.
Having approached, he took that corpse of a Kāpālika;
then the Vetāla Agniśikha, who had been there before, spoke to him.
"By the command of His Majesty Śrī Vikramādityadeva, this wicked Kāpālika has been slain by me; who are you to him?"
Having heard this, Yamaśikha said, "In that case, tell me: what is the power of that king? Then Agniśikha replied:
If you do not know its power, then listen as I tell it to you:
In this city there was a very resolute gambler named Ḍākineya.
Once, having had all his possessions stolen by the deceptive magic of gamblers,
he was bound by them for the sake of recovering an excessive amount of wealth they had extorted from others.
Because he possessed no sense of ownership, he did not give; and being beaten by them with those very clubs and other weapons, he remained standing like a stone, as if dead.
Then, having led him away by all those wicked courtiers,
he was cast into a great blind well, anticipating that there would be no remedy for him while he remained alive.
And there, in that exceedingly deep well, the gambler Kitava,
having fallen in, saw two great persons in the fire.
Seeing him fallen there and terrified, the two of them questioned him with gentle words:
"Who are you, and from where have you fallen into this well? Let it be told."
Then, having related his own story to the gambler, he asked them as well:
"Tell me, who are you two and from where have you come here?"
Having heard that, the two men situated in the pit said:
"O gentle one, we are two brahmarākṣasas in her city, in the cremation ground."
And we two took those two maidens right here in this city—
one the daughter of the chief minister, the other the daughter of the chief merchant.
And no one on earth, not even a master of mantras possessing blazing spells, was able to liberate the two maidens from our presence.
Then King Vikramāditya, who was devoted to his father, having learned of this,
went to that place where those two maidens were staying together with their father’s friend.
Upon seeing that king, although we both wished to flee after leaving those two maidens, we were simply unable to go from there.
We saw all the directions blazing with his splendor;
then, seeing us, that king bound us by means of his own power.
Seeing them thus distressed by the fear of birth and death, he commanded:
"O you two sinners, dwell within this blind well for the duration of one year!"
"Therefore, you two who have been released must not act in such a way again;
if you do so, I shall then restrain you."
Having commanded thus, we two were cast into this blind well by that King Viṣamaśīla; yet, out of compassion, we were not put to death.
With these eight days, the limit for our dwelling in this well will be fulfilled; after one year from now, we two shall be released from there.
"If you give us these few days' worth of food,
friend, we shall pull you out from that well and cast you outside."
"If you do not grant us what we have extracted as our food,
then we shall certainly devour you once we have departed from here."
Having spoken thus, those two brahmarākṣasas then agreed to his request,
saying "So be it," and cast the gambler out from the well.
Having emerged from the well and seeing that his goal could not be attained otherwise,
he entered the cremation ground at night to trade for human flesh.
While standing there at that time, I saw that gambler saying, "Let someone take it; I am selling human flesh."
When I replied, "I shall take it; what price do you seek?", he said, "Give me your own beauty and power."
When I asked him again, "O hero, what are you doing with those two?
that gambler told his entire life story and spoke thus:
Therefore, by means of your form and power,
I shall draw those enemies together with their courtiers and give them as food to the *brahmarākṣasas*, you gamblers.
Having heard that, being pleased by his fortitude, I granted to that gambler the powers of form and influence, speaking thus for seven days.
Having dragged those wrongdoers out by means of those two and cast them into the well one after another,
he led them to become food for the brahmarākṣasa within seven days.
"Today, no food was given by me for those two on that eighth day;
therefore, having emerged from my body, those two brahmarākṣasas will devour me."
"Therefore, tell me what must be done by me in this matter, for you are my friend.
To him who had spoken thus, I replied out of affection born from our long acquaintance:
"If this is so, then those gamblers were indeed eaten by those two rākṣasas for your sake; therefore, I shall eat those two rākṣasas again on your behalf."
"Show me that friend," he said; and at those words, the gambler led me to his presence, saying, "So be it."
And while I was looking down into that well without hesitation,
he gave me a half-moon blow and threw me into its depths.
Then, having fallen into the interior of a well and been seized by two rākṣasas who regarded me as food,
a hand-to-hand struggle ensued between them and me.
When they were unable to overcome my strength of arm, they abandoned the fight and asked me, "Who are you? SoKss_18,2.67.
Then, after I had related my own history starting from the account of the Ḍākineya, those two showed me friendship and said to me:
"Alas! What a state has been brought upon you two, upon us, and upon those gamblers by that wicked gambler!"
What trust can there be in those gamblers who possess the sole science of deception, whose minds are untouched by friendliness, compassion, or kindness?
Recklessness and disregard for consequences are innate to gamblers;
likewise, let the story of Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla be heard by you.
In this very city of Ujjayinī, he had previously been a gambler named Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, a formidable man whose name was truly significant.
As he was constantly losing at dice, those other players who were victorious gave him a hundred cowries every single day.
Having purchased wheat flour from that shop at the close of day,
he kneaded it with water in a potsherd somewhere and made cakes.
Having gone to the cremation ground and cooked them over the fire of the funeral pyre, she returned before Mahākāla and ate them, anointed with the ghee from that lamp.
And right there, in the courtyard of the temple of the god Mahākāla, he always slept upon the ground at night with his arm used as a pillow.
Once, at night there in the abode of Mahākāla,
as he was looking on, the images of the circle of Mothers, the Yakṣas, and other deities [appeared].
As these [omens] quivered due to the presence of the mantra, this thought arose in his mind:
"Why do I not employ a skillful means here through reasoning for the sake of my purpose?"
"If he succeeds, it is well; or if he does not succeed, what loss is there for me?
Having reflected thus, he spoke while casting those deities into the game of dice.
"Come now, sirs! I shall play with you here; I myself shall be the member of the assembly, the caster of the dice, and the one who immediately pays what is won. (SoKss_18.2.80)
When they remained silent after being addressed thus by him,
Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla cast down those variegated cowries, having made a wager.
"If the gambler does not object, his acceptance constitutes a forfeiture"—
for such is always the established rule for gamblers everywhere in the game of dice.
Then, having won much gold, he said to those deities:
"Give me the wealth that was promised when you were defeated."
When those deities did not say anything at all, even though they were addressed repeatedly by that gambler, he then spoke out in anger.
If you remain silent while standing there, then that which is done for the gambler—
who stands like a stone, having lost his wealth through what was not given— will be done for you as well.
I shall perform for you the tearing apart of your limbs with a saw as sharp as the tips of Yama’s fangs; indeed, I have no concern whatsoever.
Having said this, just as he was taking up a saw and rushing toward him,
those deities gave him gold according to what he had won.
And having caused that to be lost, he returned at night and in the same manner that very morning,
he again extracted wealth from the group of Mothers by means of a fraudulent game of dice.
"O goddesses who have mountains as their deities, this is the custom regarding gambling: he who says, 'I have come out from here after being challenged at dice,' is not to be summoned back."
"Therefore, when he calls out, dismiss him by saying that very same thing.
Thus addressed by Cāmuṇḍā, those goddesses took it to heart.
When that gambler arrived at night and was summoned to the game of dice,
all the deities said, "We have departed from this gambling match."
Thus rebuffed by them, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla challenged that very lord Mahākāla to play dice.
Thinking that he had found an opening for a forced game of dice, the King indeed said: "I am departing from this gambling match."
Alas! Even the gods, as if powerless, fear a wicked person who has not exhausted his faults and who is devoid of the fear of the uneven paths of desired and undesired results.

Thus, having been defeated by the fraudulent stratagems of Durodara’s conduct, that distressed Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla thought as follows: SoKss_18,2.96: "Thus, having been defeated by the fraudulent stratagems of Durodara’s conduct, that distressed Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla thought as follows:"
"Alas! Having learned the ways of gambling from the gods, I have been cast out.
Therefore, I now take refuge in this very Lord of the Gods."

Having reflected thus in his heart and having clasped the feet [of Mahākāla], Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, praising him, made this request to Mahākāla: *ityākalayya hṛdaye parigṛhyaiva pādayoḥ / stuvaṃṣṭhiṇṭhākarālastaṃ mahākālaṃ vyajijñapat //* SoKss_18,2.98 //
I bow to you as you sit naked, with your cheek resting upon your knee, while the goddess’s moon, bull, and elephant skins have been won at dice.
While those gods grant various such powers merely by their will,
he is free from desire, possessing only matted hair, ashes, and a skull as his belongings.
Today you have become full of greed; O one of meager merit, how is it that you seek to deceive me, for such a trivial reason? Alas! SoKss_18.2.101
"Even the wish-fulfilling tree certainly does not fulfill the hopes of the unfortunate;
for though you support the entire universe, O Bhairava, Lord, you do not support me."
O Blessed One, O Sthāṇu, you ought to forgive even my transgression, for I have taken refuge in you with a mind overwhelmed by grievous calamity.
You have three eyes, and I am just like you; there is ash on your body, and that is on mine as well.
Just as you eat from a skull-cup, so do I; therefore, have compassion for me.
Having conversed with you, how indeed could I converse again with gamblers? Therefore, rescue me who am thus fallen.
With these and other words, the gambler thus praised Bhairava;
meanwhile, the god, being thoroughly pleased, spoke to him directly:
"O Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, I am pleased with you; do not be distressed.
I shall grant you enjoyments; stay right here in my presence."
Thus, by the command of the god, that gambler remained there at that time,
enjoying an abundance of pleasures brought about through his grace.
And once, having seen the Apsarases who had come there at night to bathe at the Mahākāla-tīrtha, that god commanded him.
"Of all these celestial women who have set out to bathe,
quickly seize the garments laid upon the bank and bring them here."
"As long as they do not give this Apsaras maiden Kalāvatī to you, do not release their garments."
Thus addressed by Bhairava,
Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla went and stole the garments of those women with the eyes of celestial deer as they were bathing.
"Release, release our garments; do not leave us naked!"—to those who were speaking thus, he replied with the power of Hari: "So be it."
"If you give me this maiden Kalāvatī, then I shall release these garments for you; not otherwise."
Having heard that, having seen him who was difficult to overcome, and having remembered Śakra’s curse upon Kalāvatī as it had been, they accepted this.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, they gave that daughter of Alambuṣā, Kalāvatī, to him who had cast off his garments, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla.
Then, after the apsarases had departed, that Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla remained together with Kalāvatī in a dwelling created by the will of the gods.
And Kalāvatī would go to the celestial realm by day to attend upon the Lord of the Gods,
and she would always return to her husband at night.
"And sometimes, out of affection, she would say to me, 'O beloved, by the very cause of my attaining you, I have been made to receive a boon through Śakra’s curse.'"
Having been asked by her husband Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla about the cause of that curse, the virtuous Kalāvatī, a celestial nymph, spoke as follows: SoKss_18,2.120
Having once seen the gods in the grove, I praised the enjoyments of mortals; yet now, censuring those divine enjoyments, I see that they grant nothing but the pleasure of mere sight.
Having learned of that, the king of the gods cursed me: "Go;
you shall eat, for you have been wedded by a mortal; you shall experience those human pleasures."
Therefore, this union between us has come about, mutually agreed upon;
tomorrow I shall come from the sky without delay, and let there be no anxiety in you.
"O beloved, Rambhā will indeed perform a new dance before Hari;
we must remain there until its conclusion."
Then Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, doting with love for her, said:
"I shall see that dance; lead me there in secret."
Having heard this, Kalāvatī said to her husband: "How can this be appropriate for me? For if the King of the Gods learns of it, he will surely be angry."
When he persisted in his insistence even after being told this,
Kalāvatī then consented to take him [home] out of affection.
In the morning, having concealed his supernatural power within the lotus on her ear,
she led Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla to the palace of Mahendra.
Seeing that [palace], whose gates were adorned with divine elephants and which was as beautiful as the Nandana grove, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, considering it to be a celestial realm, was filled with joy.
And there, in the assembly hall of the enemy of Vṛtra inhabited by the thirty gods, he beheld the wonderful festival of Rambhā’s dance, accompanied by the singing of throngs of celestial nymphs.
He heard all kinds of musical instruments played by Nārada and others;
for when the Supreme Lord is pleased, what is there in this world that cannot be attained?
Then, at the conclusion of the performance, a divine jester in the form of a goat rose up there and began to dance with celestial gestures.
Seeing him and recognizing him, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla thought:
"Aha! Here I behold that very goat from Ujjayinī! (SoKss 18.2.133)
"Even here before Indra's city, such a dancer of mockery appears;
alas, this divine illusion is some truly wondrous and inconceivable thing!"
While Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla was thus reflecting in his heart,
at the conclusion of Chāgabhaṇḍa’s dance, Śakra returned to his abode.
Then Kalāvatī, delighted, brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla back to his own place, just as he had been resting upon the lotus on her ear.
And on another day, seeing him arrived in Ujjayinī in the form of a goat, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla spoke out of pride to Devabhaṇḍa: SoKss_18,2.137 //
"Dance before me as you dance before Indra; otherwise, I will not forgive you. Show that dance, you buffoon! (SoKss_18.2.138)
Having heard that, the goat was struck with wonder and remained silent, reflecting: "How is it that even this human knows me so well?"
When he was addressed with persistence, the goat did not dance at all;
therefore, Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla struck him on the head with clubs.
Then, having gone to Śakra, the goat reported everything exactly as it had happened, with his head dripping with blood.
Indra also, through his supernormal resolve, perceived it as clearly as if he were in heaven;
he brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, who had been led away by Kalāvatī during her dance of the plantain tree.
