Out of passion, you have secretly brought here that man for whom you have brought this goat to such a state for the sake of his dance.
Therefore, go to the city of Nāgapura; in a temple built by King Narasiṃha, become a statue upon a pillar.
Having been addressed thus by Kalāvatī’s mother, Alambuṣā,
Śakra was entreated with difficulty and ordained an end to the curse as follows:
When that celestial palace, which has endured for many years,
perishes and becomes level with this earth, then the end of its curse will occur.
Thus Kalāvatī, with tears, related to Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla the beginning and end of Indra’s curse, and she reproached him.
Having given him his own ornaments,
she vanished and entered a small statue atop a pillar in a temple in the city of the Nāgas.
Then Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, struck by the poison of separation from her, could neither see nor hear; he fell to the ground in a swoon.
"Alas! Though I knew it was a secret, it has been revealed by me, a fool;
for how can there be restraint in those like me who are naturally fickle?"
"Now this terrible separation has come upon me," he cried;
having regained his senses, the gambler lamented in this way.
In an instant he thought: "This is not the time for despondency on my part;
having summoned my fortitude, why do I not strive for the sake of ending her curse?"
Having reflected and deliberated thus,
that rogue assumed the garb of a wandering mendicant— complete with a rosary, a deerskin, and matted hair— and went to Nāgapura.
There, in the forest outside the city, he buried four jars filled with beautiful ornaments in the ground, placing them in the four directions.
And at night, within the city, he buried a fifth [treasure] filled with great jewels on the ground of a marketplace belonging to the chief gods, in a secluded spot.
Having done this, he remained there on the bank of the river, having constructed a hut,
relying upon deceitful asceticism and practicing artificial meditation and recitation of prayers.
Performing three ablutions daily while eating alms-food washed with water upon a stone slab, he attained the renown of a great ascetic.
Although he had gradually come within the range of hearing and was entreated by the king,
because he did not come into his presence, the king went to his side.
After they had stayed for a long time conversing, as the king desired to depart there at evening,
a jackal suddenly raised a cry from a distance.
Hearing that, the gambler disguised as an ascetic laughed;
and when asked, "What is this?", he replied, "What does it matter? (SoKss_18.2.161)
And when the king questioned him persistently, that deceiver spoke thus:
"In the forest to the east of this city, beneath a cane thicket..."
"O King, there is a jar full of jewel ornaments; take it," thus was I told by this auspicious woman, who understands the cries of animals.
Having spoken thus, he led the king, who was filled with curiosity, to that spot;
then, having dug up the ground and extracted it, he gave that jar to him.
Then, having received the ornaments, the king, his confidence restored,
regarded that ascetic— who was free from desire— as a man of wisdom and truthful speech.
Having brought him to his own hermitage and having bowed repeatedly at his feet,
he went to his palace at night with his ministers, praising his virtues.
As the king approached him in this manner, the rogue, under the pretext of the bird's cry,
caused him to procure three other jeweled jars from other directions.
Then that king, the citizens, the ministers, and the women of the inner apartments became devoted solely to that ascetic; they were entirely absorbed in him.
Once, while being led by the king to inspect the temple,
that wretched ascetic heard the cawing of a crow in the marketplace.
Then he said to that king: "O King, you have heard the crow's words:
'Right here in this marketplace, before the god, it remains buried in the ground.'"
"Why is that jar, filled with the seven precious gems, not taken?"—this was said by the crow; therefore, come and take possession of it.
Having said this, that false ascetic led him there, lifted him up from the ground,
and presented him along with the jar of excellent jewels to the king.
Then, out of excessive satisfaction,
the king himself took hold of that pseudo-knower by the hand and entered the temple.
There, having shaken off his weariness upon the pillar, the wandering mendicant beheld that statue of a *sāla* tree, which had been entered by his beloved Kalāvatī.
And Kalāvatī, assuming the form of that statue,
seeing her husband in such distress, began to weep there.
Seeing that, the king, accompanied by his followers, filled with wonder and despondency, asked Jñānābhāsa: "O Blessed One, what is this?"
Then that rogue, appearing dejected and bewildered, said: "Come to my own home; there I shall tell you this, even though it is something that should not be spoken."
Having said this, he led the king to the capital and spoke to him:
"This temple has been built by you in an improper place and at an inauspicious moment."
"Whatever has been done will become harmful to you on the third day;
therefore, from the sight of you, this pillar-statue wept."
O King, if you have need of that body,
then crush it today itself and quickly make this temple level with the ground.

Since you are building a temple for the gods here at an auspicious place and a favorable moment, may this [hostility] come to rest without cause; may there be well-being for you and your entire kingdom.
Having been addressed thus by him, that king, out of fear,
gave orders to his subjects and leveled that temple with the ground in a single day.
And in another place, he began to build a temple once again.
Alas! Even lords are deceived by rogues through their guiles after having been inspired with trust.
Having accomplished his purpose, the gambler Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla then cast off the garb of a wandering mendicant, fled,
and departed from there for Ujjayinī.
And Kalāvatī, having learned of this and being released from her curse,
approached him joyfully on the road, comforted him, and went to heaven to see Indra.
Indra too, having learned from the mouth of the keeper of that [garden] of that illusion of the gambler, was amazed, and he both laughed and rejoiced.
Then Bṛhaspati, standing by his side, said to Śakra:
"Gamblers are always like this, possessing such diverse illusions."
In a former age, there was once in a certain city a gambler named Kuṭṭinīkapaṭa, who was an expert in fraudulent gambling.
And when he had gone to the other world, the King of Dharma reportedly said to him:
"O gambler, by virtue of your own sins, you must dwell in hell for an eon."
Yet for one day, by virtue of your gift to a knower of Brahman, you possess the status of Indra; for indeed, at some time, you gave even a single piece of gold to one who knows the Veda.
"Therefore, tell me first: which shall you enjoy, hell or the state of Indra?
Having heard that, the gambler said, "I shall enjoy the state of Indra first."
Then, dispatched by Dharmarāja,
that gambler raised Indra from heaven for a single day and was consecrated in the kingdom by the gods.
Having attained the sovereignty of the gods, he summoned his friends, the gamblers, along with the courtesans,
and by virtue of his lordship, commanded the deities in heaven.
"Having led us to all the sacred fords— both celestial and terrestrial, even those situated throughout the seven continents— bathe us all in an instant."
"Having entered into all the kings on earth this very day,
bestow great gifts incessantly for our sake."
Thus instructed by him, the gods performed all of that at that very moment;
purified of sin by those merits, that rogue attained a stable state of lordship.
And his companions and courtesans whom he had brought to heaven also attained immortality through his grace, their sins having been destroyed.
On the second day, Citragupta reported to Dharmarāja that the gambler had attained a stable sovereignty over the gods through his own intelligence.
Then, having understood his virtuous conduct, the King of Dharma was struck with wonder, exclaiming, "Alas! We have been deceived by this gambler!"
"O wielder of the thunderbolt, such are these gamblers! Having said this, when the Guru had ceased speaking, Indra sent Kalāvatī as a messenger and brought Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla to heaven.
There, the King of the Gods, pleased with his discernment and fortitude, honored him,
gave him Kalāvatī, and made him stand by his own side.
Then that wise Ṭhiṇṭhākarāla, together with Kalāvatī, lived happily like a god in heaven by virtue of Śaṅkara’s grace.
Such is the course of deceit and recklessness among gamblers;
therefore, O Vetāla, what is so strange in that which is done by a gambler, even if it be like a flame of fire?
"You have been cast into this well by the Ḍākinī through her illusory power;
therefore, come out, for we two, your friends, shall emerge from this pit."
Having been addressed thus by the two Brahma-rākṣasas, I emerged from that pit and,
afflicted by hunger, encountered a Brahmin traveler in this city during that night.
And as I ran toward that Brahmin with the desire to seize him,
he cried out to King Śrī Vikramāditya.
And as soon as he heard this, the king, blazing like fire, came forth and cried out from nearby, "Ah, you sinner! Do not kill the brahmin! and thus struck me down.
As he proceeded to cut off the head of the man in the painting,
my throat was severed by him and became drenched with flowing blood.
Then, clinging to his foot, I was protected by him alone, having been released from the birds;
such is the power of that divine King Vikramāditya.
"By his command, this Khandakāpālika was slain by me;
therefore, O Vetāla, release this Yamaśikha, who is my food."
Although addressed thus by Agniśikha, Yamaśikha, out of pride, struck the body of the Kāpālika Khaṇḍa with his hand.
Then the illustrious Vikramāditya, having manifested himself there,
drew a man upon the ground with his own blood and severed its hand with his sword.
When his hand was cut off by him, it fell upon Yamaśikha;
thereupon, abandoning that corpse, he fled away out of fear.
And Agniśikha devoured that corpse of the skull-bearer;
and I too, fearless, witnessed all of that by the power of the king.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, that Yakṣa-wife Madanamañjarī spoke to me again regarding your power.
Then that King Aṅgadeva spoke sweetly to me:
"O Yakṣī, leave the Kāpālikas and go to your husband's home."
Then, having bowed to him, I have come here to my own home,
reflecting on how to repay that king for his kindness.
"In this way, my life, my family, and my husband were given to you by my lord;
and when she tells your name, she will recognize my story."
And today it has been learned that the daughter of the King of Siṃhala, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, has been sent by him as a bride to choose her own husband for that king.
And all those kings,
acting together with envy, resolved to seize her after killing Vikramaśakti, the vassal of that [king].
Therefore, go to Vikramaśakti and inform him of this,
so that he may remain attentive in providing a remedy for them.
And I shall make such an effort that,
having slain those enemies, King Vikramāditya will attain victory.
For this purpose you were brought here by me through my own power of illusion,
so that you shall tell all of this to the king along with his vassals.
And I shall send such a gift to that lord of yours,
so that I might offer some small measure of recompense for his kindness.
Even as he was speaking,
those two maidens whom we had seen in the ocean, accompanied by the deer, arrived there.
One had limbs as white as the moon, while the other was dark as the priyaṅgu plant;
they were like the Gaṅgā and Yamunā attending upon the Lord of Rivers.
When they two were seated, I, O Goddess, asked that yakṣī:
"O Queen, who are these two maidens, and what is this golden deer?"
Having heard that, O Great King, the yakṣiṇī spoke to me:
"Anaṅgadeva, if you have curiosity, listen as I tell you."
Formerly, at the time of the creation of beings by Prajāpati,
two terrible Dānavas named Ghaṇṭa and Nighaṇṭa, who were invincible even to the gods, came forth as obstacles.
And Vidhātṛ, desiring their destruction, created these two maidens,
whose beauty of form was unrestrained and intoxicating to the world.
Upon seeing these two exceedingly wondrous great asuras carrying them away and fighting one another, both of them went to their destruction.
Then Brahmā entrusted these two daughters to the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhyakṣa), saying:
"These two should be given by you to some suitable husband."
Dhanada gave these to my husband, his own younger brother;
and my husband likewise gave them to me for the sake of the boon.
I have envisioned Śrī Vikramāditya as the husband for these two;
indeed, an incarnation of a god is the fitting consort for them both.
O maidens of such form, listen to this narrative concerning a deer:
there is a beloved son named Jayanta, the offspring of the Lord of Śacī.
While being carried through the sky by celestial nymphs,
that child once saw, down upon the earth, princes playing with young deer.
Then, out of childishness, deprived of his pet fawn,
he went to heaven in a state of agitation and wept before his father.
For his sake, Śakra had Viśvakarman fashion a deer made of gold and jewels, its very life infused by the sprinkling of nectar.
Then Jayanta played with him and was well-pleased;
that young deer also remained there, sporting in the celestial realm.
At that time, Indrajit— the son of Rāvaṇa whose name was truly meaningful—
having seized the deer, carried it from the sky to his own city, Laṅkā.
And when time had passed, due to the wrath arising from the abduction of Sītā, Rāvaṇa and Indrajit were slain by the two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
That wondrous deer, made of jewels and gold, remained in the palace of Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who had been consecrated in the kingdom of Laṅkā.
And on one occasion during a festival, Vibhīṣaṇa, out of affection for his brother-in-law, brought me to his home and presented me with a deer as a mark of honor.
"This divine young deer now dwells in my house;
I must present it as a gift to your lord."
While that yakṣiṇī was thus recounting the sequence of my story,
the sun, the beloved of the lotus, went to its setting.
Then, after she had instructed me regarding the evening rites in her residence,
both this messenger of the Lord of Siṃhala and I lay down to sleep.
Having awakened in the morning, they honored him and inquired after his welfare;
then, he wished to ask them about the message from the Lord of Siṃhala.
Then, reflecting upon that manifestation of the Yakṣiṇī’s power,
we two went immediately to the side of Vikramaśakti, filled with wonder.
As soon as he saw him, having honored him and inquired after his welfare,
he wished to ask about the message from the Lord of Siṃhala and concerning the ship.
Meanwhile, those two divine maidens, whose true nature had been described by the yakṣiṇī,
and that young deer arrived there surrounded by a host of yakṣas.
Seeing them, King Vikramaśakti, suspecting them to be the illusion of evil spirits and the like, asked me out of doubt: "O Lord, what is this? (SoKss 18.2.251)
Then, in due course, I described to him the mission of the Lord of Siṃhala,
as well as the pair of Yakṣiṇī maidens and the deer’s tooth.
Having heard from the mouth of the yakṣī that this was the unanimous view of all,
I then reported to the king that effort which was hostile to kings.
Then, having honored us and both those celestial maidens, he,
the vassal lord, being overjoyed, made his army ready for battle.
In an instant, the great roar of the army's trumpets was heard here, O King;
and in an instant, the vast force of the opposing kings along with the Mlecchas was seen.
As the two armies, our own and the enemy's, charged at one another out of anger upon seeing each other, a battle broke out between them.
Then, by those yakṣas dispatched by the yakṣiṇī, some struck the army of our enemies,
while others, possessed by our own warriors, struck them down with their own hands.
Filled with masses of dust from the armies, dense with the edges of swords,
and resounding with the roars of heroes, a terrible storm of battle arose.
With the heads of our enemies falling as they were severed,
the Goddess of Victory shone upon us as if she were playing with balls.
And in an instant, those kings who remained after the slaughter, their armies broken,
bowed down and sought refuge in the camp of your subordinate.
Then, O Lord of all the earth, when you have destroyed the barbarians and the six continents of the four quarters have been brought under cultivation, [the time will come].
Appearing together with her own husband, that Yakṣiṇī spoke thus to King Vikramaśakti and to me: SoKss_18,2.262
"That which I have performed here as mere service for you, my lord, must be reported to him;
furthermore, he should be petitioned by me with these words."
"You must marry these two maidens created by the gods;
you must look upon them with favor, and this deer as well must be cherished."
Having said, "This is indeed my gift," the yakṣī presented a heap of jewels and, together with her husband and her followers, vanished from sight.
On another day, that daughter of the King of Siṃhala, Madanalekhā, arrived with a vast retinue and great splendor.
Then, having gone out to meet him, Vikramaśakti,
bowing down with great joy, led him into his own camp.
On the second day, having taken her and both those celestial maidens,
as well as that golden-jeweled deer which was a marvel to the eyes of the three worlds, he departed.
Having accomplished his task, he came here out of a desire to behold the feet of Your Majesty;
thereupon, Vikramaśakti set forth together with the kings.
"O King, that neighboring vassal has arrived nearby;
we have been sent before you by him to inform Your Majesty."
Therefore, O King, out of regard for the Lord of Siṃhala and the Yakṣiṇī,
let Your Majesty go forth to meet those kings as well as their daughters and the deer.
Thus addressed by Anaṅgadeva, King Vikramāditya remembered how he had accomplished that difficult task of protecting the yakṣiṇī.
Having heard of that requital, he did not value it even as much as a blade of grass;
for those of great magnanimity consider even a great service to be but a small one.
And being delighted, he further filled Anaṅgadeva— who was accompanied by the envoys of the Lord of Siṃhala— with elephants, horses, villages, and jewels.
Having thus spent that day with the princess of Siṃhala and those two daughters of the Lotus-born One,
the lord of the earth then set out from Ujjayinī together with his armies, accompanied by elephants and horse-drawn vehicles, to go forth to meet them.

Satkuñjara was the elephant of Añjanagiri; Mattadvipa was that of Raṇabhaṭa; Kālamegha belonged to Siṃhaparākrama; and Ripurākṣasa was the elephant of the heroic Vikramanidhi, who achieved victory in battle.
Pavanajava was the horse of Jayaketu; Vallabhaśakti had Samudrakallola; Bāhu and Subāhu had Aśvavega and Garuḍavega respectively.
Śyāmā Kuvalayamālā was the mare of Kīrtivarman from Kokkaṇa;
Karkā Gaṅgālaharī was the excellent Sindhu-bred mare of Samarasimha.
Thus, as those kings also set out, the voices of the officials in charge of the army were heard on all sides as they distributed the elephants and horses, and now that the king himself had departed.

As that king, the sovereign of all continents, proceeded upon his path, the earth became composed of his army; the quarters of space were filled solely with the great roar arising from it; even the sky was filled with the dust shimmering from the trampling of the advancing host; and all voices became utterances of praise for the greatness of that wonderful power.
Thus ends the second wave in the *Viṣamaśīla* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
The third wave begins:
Then that Vikramāditya reached that army of victory.
It was presided over by his own general, Vikramaśakti.
Accompanied by the king and his entire retinue, he entered his own army with that very same longing, his body bowed in devotion.
This Gauḍa is Śaktikumāra, this Karṇāṭa is Jayadhvaja,
this Lāṭa is Vijayavarman, and this Kāśmīra is Sunandana.
"O Lord, here is Gopāla, this Sindhurāja, this Bhilla Vindhyabala,
and this Parasīka Nirmūka— all these kings bow down before you."
Thus, in that assembly hall, the emperor honored the kings announced by the doorkeepers,
as well as the vassal lords and the soldiers.
He honored those divine maidens, including the daughter of the King of Siṃhala, and those golden deer along with Vikramaśakti, according to their respective merit.
On another day, the skillful King Vikramāditya set out from there with his army together with them, and he reached the city of Ujjayinī.

Then, when the kings had been honored and dismissed to their own countries, and the festival of the spring season—the delight of the world—had arrived; so it is said in the Sūtrakṛtāṅga Sūtra, chapter 18, section 3, verse 8.
While the female bees seemed to adorn the creepers with ornaments of flowers and to perform a concert with their humming.
While the forest groves, embraced by the winds, seemed as if they were dancing,
and the cuckoos with their melodious calls seemed as if they were reciting auspicious hymns.
Thereupon, on an auspicious day, Vikramāditya married that daughter of the King of Siṃhala and those two celestial maidens.
The elder brother of the King of Siṃhala’s daughter,
Siṃhavarman, arrived together with her and offered a vast collection of jewels upon the altar.
And at that moment, Madanamañjarī, having approached those two yakṣiṇīs who were celestial maidens, gave them countless heaps of jewels.
"O Lord, am I capable of repaying the debt of your good deed?
Yet, I have done nothing at all to demonstrate my devotion."
"Grace should be shown toward these two maidens and the deer," she said,
and having been honored by the king, that yakṣī vanished from sight.
Then, having regained those wives and the earth with its islands,
the accomplished King Vikramāditya ruled his kingdom free from all thorns.
And he dwelt happily at that time in garden grounds,
in the waters of lakes during the summer, and in houses with fountains.
During the rains, amidst the inner apartments resounding with the enchanting sounds of rising drums;
and during the autumn, upon the delightful palace terraces where the rising moon was the centerpiece of the drinking feast.
In the winter, the king, surrounded by the women of his harem, dwelt in palatial residences where comfortable beds were spread and which were fragrant with black aloe-wood incense.
To such a king there belonged a painter named Nagarasvāmin,
who enjoyed the revenues of a hundred villages and had surpassed Viśvakṛt [the Creator] in his craft.
Every two days, that painter would present to the king a portrait of a young woman,
each painted with a different style of form.
Once, due to the occasion of a festival, that puppet had been forgotten and was not painted by the artist for the sake of the king; it was only by chance that it remained.
And when the day for the presentation arrived, the painter sat there agitated, thinking, "Alas! What shall I offer to my lord? (SoKss 18.3.23)
Just then, a certain traveler who had come from afar suddenly addressed him;
placing a small book in his hand, he quickly departed for some unknown place.
And as soon as the painter, out of curiosity, opened it,
he saw there inside a figurine depicted on a cloth.
Upon seeing her of such wondrous form, he took her and presented her to the king,
exultant and thinking, "On the contrary, such a gift has been accomplished by me today."
But upon seeing her, the king was filled with wonder and said to him:
"My good man, this line of yours is not [ordinary]; this line belongs to Viśvakarman."
"For how could a mere human know how to paint such a form?
Having heard this, the painter related to the king exactly what had occurred.
Then that king, whose gaze was fixed on no other, constantly beholding that statuette,
saw in a dream in another continent a maiden of exactly that same form.
As long as he maintained that union with her, who was full of longing,
so long was he awakened by the watchman at the end of the night.
Having awakened and having his pleasure from that dream-encounter shattered,
the king, out of anger, banished that watchman from the city.
Where is the traveler? Where is his book? Where is the painted figure within it?
And where is the sight, even in a dream, of that very figure coming to life?
Thus, this stroke of fate tells me that the maiden exists;
yet I do not know that island—how indeed might I reach her?
Reflecting thus and finding no delight anywhere, the king,
his retinue thrown into turmoil, burned with the fever of love.
And being questioned slowly by Vijaya Kṣatra Bhadrāyudha regarding the cause of his distress, that lord of the earth spoke thus:
Listen, friend, I shall tell you this which you have already understood:
that picture of a maiden which was given to me by that painter.
Thinking of her, I fell asleep and in a dream I perceived that I had crossed the ocean, reached a city, and entered one that was exceedingly beautiful.
There I saw many maidens before me, armed with weapons;
seeing me, they raised a great clamor, crying out, "Kill him! Kill him!"
Then, I believe some female ascetic approached me in great haste,
led me into her own home, and spoke these words briefly:
"O son, this princess named Malayavatī, who is averse to men,
has arrived here while wandering at her own will."
"As soon as he sees a man, he has him killed by these maidens;
for that reason, you have been brought here by me for protection."
Having said this, the female ascetic immediately assumed a woman’s dress for me;
considering those maidens to be inviolable, I too endured that.
Just as I saw that princess with her daughter enter right here, I beheld her standing in a painting; it was she herself whom I had seen before.
And I thought: "I am fortunate that, having seen her depicted in a painting, I now behold her again in person—she who is as dear to me as my own life."
And that princess, along with her daughter, spoke to that female ascetic:
"We have seen a certain man who entered here."
"Whence comes this man? This guest is the daughter of my sister," she, the female ascetic, replied to her, pointing me out.
Then, even upon seeing me in the form of a woman, that princess immediately forgot her hatred for men and fell under the power of love.
Her hair stood on end as she remained motionless, as if lost in thought;
she seemed pinned down by Kāma, who had found his opening and struck her with all his arrows at once.
And in an instant, that washerwoman’s daughter addressed the female ascetic:
"Then, Noble Lady, why is it that your sister’s daughter is not also my guest?"
"Come to my house; I shall send this woman away after she has been honored.
Having said this, she took me by the hand and led me to her own residence.
And having gained her confidence, I knew that it was so, and I went there;
that clever old female ascetic also gave me her consent.
Then I remained there with that princess,
as she played with other maidens in diversions such as mock marriage ceremonies.
And she, whose eyes were fixed on me, did not leave my side for even a moment;
there was no activity that she found pleasing which did not involve both her and me.
Then those maidens, having made that princess their bride and me her groom, performed our marriage in jest, as I well know.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony, we entered our chamber at night;
there, that princess fearlessly took me by the neck.
At that moment, having revealed myself, I embraced her;
seeing me, she was thrilled at the fulfillment of her desire, yet for a moment she stood with her face bowed in modesty.
While I was thus engaging in amorous play with her,
having stripped away her modesty, I was awakened here by that wicked-minded watchman.
Therefore, Bhadrāyudha, having seen her in both a painting and a dream,
I have no desire to live without that Malayavatī now.
Having understood that the king had spoken thus while dreaming,
the warder Bhadrāyudha consoled him and spoke as follows.
If the entire city is remembered correctly, then let it be painted upon the cloth;
the deity shall investigate the means for this.
Thus addressed by Bhadrāyudha,
the king immediately drew that entire excellent city and its whole history upon a cloth.
Taking that painted cloth, the doorkeeper immediately had a new monastery built and hung it there upon the wall.
And there, in the monastery, he established a charitable feast for bards who had come from distant lands,
providing them with food of six flavors, along with pairs of garments and gold.
"If anyone comes who knows this city as it is depicted in the painting,
let him inform me"— thus he gave his command to those residing in the monastery.
In the meantime, he saw the summer forest, where the breeze was fragrant with jasmine,
where travelers sat in the shade, and where the *pāṭala* trees were in full bloom.
Dark as a rain cloud, with a deep and heavy roar,
and with the full-blown *ketakī* flower for its trunk, the intoxicated elephant of the rainy season arrived.
At that moment, King Vikramāditya’s forest fire of separation flared up, as if fanned by an easterly wind.
"Hāralatā, give me snow! Citrāṅgī, sprinkle me with sandalwood paste!
Pattralekhā, prepare a cool bed of lotus leaves! (SoKss 18.3.68)
"O Kandarpasenā, provide a breeze with plantain leaves!"—
such were the words heard then from the women of his harem.
Gradually, the king’s onset of the rainy season, fierce as lightning, subsided; yet his fever of passion, burning with the flames of separation, did not.
May travelers proceed on their paths; may news of those far away reach their loved ones;
may dear things be united with the dear; and may their reunions come to pass.
Then, as if giving such instructions with the cries of swans, Autumn arrived,
her face a blossoming lotus and her smile the *sakaśa* flower.
Once, having heard of his fame, a bard who had come from afar entered that very monastery built for the steward, seeking food alone.
Known by the name Śambarasiddhi, having taken his meal in this monastery and received a pair of garments, he beheld that painted cloth on the wall.
Having perceived that city there as if it were depicted in a painting, he was struck with wonder and said: "Aho! By whom has this city been painted?"
I know that what was seen by me alone has been written down by him [the scribe] and by that second person; I know it was not by anyone else.
Having heard this which had been said by the people of the monastery concerning Bhadrāyudha,
that bard himself went and led him into the presence of the king.
"Was that city truly seen by you? Thus questioned by the king regarding his accomplishment of the Śambara-vidyā, he spoke as follows:
Having crossed the ocean and wandered over the earth, I beheld that great city named Malayapura, situated in the midst of an island.
In that city there was a lord of the earth named Malayasiṃha;
he had a daughter of incomparable beauty named Malayavatī.
And she, who had been hostile toward men, once saw a certain great man in a dream as she was departing from the monastery.
Merely by her looking at him, that evil obsession of hatred for men departed from her mind at that very moment, as if terrified.
Then, having led him to her own palace and having made it as if in a dream,
she entered the residence of Indra together with him after their marriage.
There, while he was enjoying the festival of love with her for as long as he wished,
she was awakened at the end of the night by a maidservant staying in the dwelling.
Then, having had that maidservant banished out of anger, she burned with the fire of separation as she remembered her beloved whom she had seen in a dream.
Seeing no way out and rendered helpless by love,
she rose again and again from her bed, only to collapse once more with her limbs trembling.
Like one mute, like one possessed by a spirit, or as if stupefied by darkness,
she gave no answer at all to her attendants who questioned her.
Having been discovered by her father and mother and questioned with great difficulty,
she then related the account of her dream through the mouth of a trusted female friend.
Then, comforted by her father, she made this vow:
"If I do not reach that fire within six months, I shall enter it."
"Five months have passed since today; who knows what will happen to her?"—such was the report concerning her that I heard throughout the city.
When Śambarasiddhi had thus spoken in conversation with him,
and the king was delighted by his certainty regarding the matter, Bhadrāyudha addressed him:
O Lord, that country, together with its king, will indeed have its purpose accomplished and come under your control;
therefore, let us go there before the sixth month passes away.
When the Kṣatriya had spoken thus, Śambara, having explained the full details of what had been told,
placed that Siddha— who was honored with abundant wealth— at his front.
The king seemed to cast his own pallor upon the rays of the sun, his whiteness upon the clouds, and his emaciation upon the waters of the rivers.
Having thus become free from fear, Vikramāditya set out at once toward his beloved, accompanied by a small army.
Having traveled by stages and crossed the ocean, as soon as he reached that city,
he saw before him a crowd of people agitated by a great clamor.
Today, when her six-month period has come to an end, this Princess Malayavatī, having failed to obtain her beloved, intends to enter the fire.
Thereupon, having heard this from people whom he questioned,
the king went to that place where his funeral pyre had been prepared.
When the people had withdrawn upon seeing him, that princess beheld him there,
a sudden rain of nectar for her eyes.
"Therefore, this lord of my life, who was my husband in a dream, has arrived;
tell my father quickly," she said to her friends.
Having gone there and spoken thus to his father,
that king, his suffering now gone and filled with joy, approached the monarch with humble reverence.

At that moment, the bard Śambarasiddhi, who was skilled in discerning the proper occasion, raised his arm and recited this aloud: SoKss_18,3.102: "At that moment, the bard Śambarasiddhi, who was skilled in discerning the proper occasion, raised his arm and recited this aloud."
Victory to you, who have subdued the hosts of spirits by your own splendor; victory, O God, forest fire to the jungle of barbarians, Lord of the proud Earth bounded by the seven oceans!
Victory to you, whose exceedingly weighty command is borne upon the bowed heads of all conquered kings!
Victory to you, Viṣamaśīla, ocean of valor, Vikramāditya!
When the bard had spoken thus, King Malayasiṃha, realizing that Vikramāditya had arrived, fell at his feet.
And having been offered hospitality by him, he entered his own palace together with that daughter,
Malayavatī, who had been delivered from death.
And that king gave his daughter to King Vikramāditya,
considering himself to have accomplished his purpose through that son-in-law.
Just as in a painting, so in a dream; and just as in a dream, so too did he behold his beloved Malayavatī in person, resting upon his lap.
And Vikramāditya also considered that wonder to be the fruit of the celestial tree of grace belonging to the Beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then, taking that bride Malayavatī— who was like personified bliss—
he crossed the ocean, which was surging with waves as if it were his own long separation.
Being saluted at every step by kings with various gifts in their hands,
Vikramāditya returned to his own city, Ujjayinī.
And beholding there that power of his, which made various wonders come true according to his will, who was not amazed?
Who did not rejoice? Or who did not hold a great festival?
Thus ends the third wave in the Viṣamaśīla-lambaka of the Kathāsaritsāgara composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
Now begins the fourth wave.
Then, once during a conversation here, regarding this Vikramāditya—
The queen named Kaliṅgasenā spoke thus to her co-wives.
"What the king has done for the sake of Malayavatī is not surprising;
for this lord is renowned throughout the world as one whose character is always unpredictable."
"I am not married; why has he, having seen my daughter who resembles me and being overcome by the power of the god of love, forcibly leaped upon me?"
This story which was told to me by the traveler Devasena for this very reason—I shall relate it to you; let it be heard.
To me, who was grieving, thinking, "How have I been married by the king without the proper rites?", that kārpaṭika spoke thus, comforting me: SoKss_18,4.5 //
"Do not harbor resentment, O Queen, for you are possessed of supreme faith;
having set aside your excessive agitation, hear the story from its very beginning."
"Once, while serving as a kārpaṭika in attendance upon your lordship,
I saw from afar in the forest a very large boar."
His mouth was formidable with fangs, his complexion dark like the *tāla* tree;
he appeared like the dark fortnight itself in embodied form, devouring the crescent moons.
Having arrived, O Queen, I informed the king of that very matter;
and the king too, drawn by the desire for its flavor, went out for the sake of hunting.
Having reached the deer forest and causing the destruction of tigers and deer,
he saw that boar from afar, as I had informed him.
Having seen that marvel and considering it to be some kind of causal omen,
he mounted the horse named Ratnākara, the offspring of Uccaiḥśravas.
For at midday, the sun always remains in the sky for a single muhūrta;
during that time, the horses are released by Aruṇa for bathing and drinking.
Once, when Ucchaiḥśravas was released from the sun’s chariot in the forest,
he approached the king’s mare he had seen and begot that horse.
Having mounted it, the king pursued from behind that fleeing boar with the speed of the wind-horse, as it ran toward a land far more distant.
There, that boar, which was even swifter than the horse Uccaiḥśravas, vanished from his sight somewhere or other.
Then the king, not finding him and having cast aside his retinue from afar, saw me alone following him and questioned me thus: SoKss_18.4.16 //
"Do you know how far we have traveled?
Having heard that, O Queen, I then replied to the king.
“We have come from three hundred yojanas, O Lord.
Then the king said, “In that case, how have you come on foot?”
Thus questioned by the king with astonishment, I said to him:
"O King, I possess an ointment for the feet; hear now the account of it."
Formerly, having departed on a pilgrimage due to separation from my wife,
I reached a temple with its gardens on the road in the evening.
Having entered there to pass the night, I saw a certain woman within; I stayed there, treated with hospitality by her.
And at night, having placed one lip in the sky and the other on the ground, she opened her mouth wide and said to me: "Have you ever seen such a face anywhere?"
Then, drawing my dagger with a frown, I said to her without fear: "Have you ever seen such a man anywhere? (SoKss 18.4.23)
Then, assuming a gentle form and free from her transformation, she said to me:
"I am a Yakṣī named Caṇḍī; I am pleased with your fortitude."
"Therefore, tell me now: what pleasing service may I do for you? To her who had spoken thus, I, the yakṣiṇī, replied:
If you are truly well-pleased, then do this for me:
that I may wander to all the sacred fords without any hardship.
Thus addressed by me, that yakṣī gave me an ointment for the feet;
by means of it, I wandered through sacred fords and have now pursued you here today.
"Coming here every day to this forest region,
I eat fruits and then return to Ujjayinī to serve you."
"Thus, O Queen, the king was informed by me;
with a gracious look, he spoke of me as a suitable follower."
Again I petitioned the king in this way: "I shall bring the deities here, if their very sweet fruits may be enjoyed by you, O Lord."
"I shall not eat; nothing has been served to me.
You, however, are weary, so please eat something," the king thus commanded me.
Then, having obtained a karkaṭikā fruit there, I ate it;
and as soon as it was consumed, I became a python.
And seeing me suddenly turned into a python, O Queen,
the King became despondent and filled with wonder at my transformation into such a cruel nature.
And there, being alone, he called to mind the Vetāla Bhūtaketu,
who had previously been subdued by him after being liberated from an eye disease by his very glance.
That Vetāla, summoned by his recollection, appeared and bowed before the king, saying:
"Why have I been remembered, O Great King? Let your command be given."
Then the king said to him, "My good man,
restore this petitioner, who has suddenly turned into a python, to his own natural state."
The Vetāla also said: "O King, I do not possess such power;
powers are restricted in their scope—does water ever extinguish the fire of lightning?"
Then the king said, "In that case, friend, let us go to this village;
perhaps some means might then become known to us from among the Bhillas."
Having reflected thus, the king went to that village accompanied by the Vetāla;
there, seeing him adorned with ornaments, the thieves surrounded him.
While they were raining down showers of arrows, those five hundred were devoured by that Vetāla Bhūtaketu at the king’s command.
The survivors fled and went to their own general, saying;
then one named Ekākikesarin arrived with his forces in a rage.
Having learned this from the mouth of a certain servant who recognized him,
that general approached the king and grasped his feet.
Then the king, having greeted the general who had announced himself and bowed low, and having inquired after his welfare, spoke to him: *SoKss_18.4.43*
"My servant, having eaten a *karkaṭikā* fruit in the forest, has become a python; devise a means for his release."
Having heard these words of the king, the general said:
"Let this Devānuga show him to my son."
Then he, having come with that Vetāla and his son,
restored me to my human form as before by means of the juice of medicinal herbs.
Then we, filled with joy, approached the presence of the king;
and the king informed me, as I prostrated at his feet, of that news.
Then that solitary lion, the leader of the Bhillas,
having invited the king to his own home, led him away accompanied by us.
And we beheld his dwelling, surrounded by Śabara women, with high walls inlaid with ivory tusks and possessing the hue of tiger skins.
Where garments are made of peacock feathers, necklaces are strings of *guñjā* berries,
and the flow of elephant ichor serves as the women’s ornament.
There, the general’s wife herself performed service for him;
her garments were scented with the fragrance of musk, and she was adorned with pearls and other ornaments.
Then, having bathed and eaten, the king saw his aged sons there and that youthful commander-in-chief, and he questioned them.
"Commander, let this wonder of mine be explained by you:
you are young, yet how is it that these sons of yours are so old?"
Thus addressed by the king, the lord of the Śabaras spoke this:
"O King, this is a great story; listen if you have a curiosity."
"I am a Brahmin named Candrasvāmin who formerly lived in Māyāpurī;
once, at my father's command, I went to the forest for the sake of wood."
There, a monkey stood blocking my path, yet without causing any obstruction;
looking with distressed eyes, he pointed out another way. (SoK 18.4.56)
"He will not eat me for now; therefore, it is better that I go by another path.
By showing him this, I shall observe the disposition of this monkey."
Having reflected thus, I set out upon that path;
and that monkey went before me, looking back at me as he moved forward.
Having gone a long distance, that monkey climbed a jambu tree;
and upon its back, thick with a network of creepers, I fixed my gaze.
There I saw a female monkey whose limbs were bound by a circle of creepers,
and I understood that it was for this purpose that I had been brought here by him.
Then, having climbed the tree and cut that snare of entwined creepers with my axe, I liberated that female monkey.
Then, having descended from the tree, both that monkey and the female monkey grasped the feet of me as I had descended.
Having set down that female monkey clinging to my feet for a moment,
that king of monkeys went away, returned, and gave me a divine fruit.
Taking that and gathering firewood, I returned home;
there, together with my wife, I ate that most excellent fruit.
When he had eaten it, old age and disease departed from me along with my wife;
thereafter, a calamity of famine arose there in our country.
The local people, overwhelmed by him, fled in every direction;
by chance, I too reached this region with my wife in due course.
At that time, there was a chief of the Śabaras here named Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra;
taking up his weapon, I entered into service under him.
And having seen me as the leader in various battles,
that Kāñcanadaṃṣṭra then consecrated me to the command of the army.
And by means of a single meal, I then propitiated that Lord;
though he was childless, he bestowed the kingdom upon me alone at the time of his end.
While remaining here, twenty-seven hundred years have passed for me;
yet there is no old age for me, because of my consumption of that fruit.
Having thus related his own story, that king of the Bhillas, Ekākikesarī, addressed the astonished monarch once more: SoKss_18,4.71.
"By me, through the fruit of the monkey and so forth, long life was achieved;
today, that [longevity] has reached its fullness, and the fruit of it is this sight of your feet."
Therefore, O Lord, I entreat you: let this favor which has been shown to me today by your coming to my home be carried to its full satisfaction.
"In my Kṣatriya wife, O God, a daughter was born who is peerless in beauty, named Madanasundarī."
And that jewel of a maiden does not shine anywhere except for him;
therefore, I give her to you—marry her according to the prescribed rite.
"I am your slave, O Lord, and I follow you with two hundred thousand bows.
When he had thus entreated him, the king agreed, saying, "So be it."
And under an auspicious lunar mansion, he married his daughter to him—
the giver of hundreds of camels laden with burdens of pearls and musk.
Having stayed there for seven nights, the king then set out together with Madanasundarī and that army of Bhilla warriors.
In the meantime, while the king had been carried away by his horse in that hunting forest, Bhadrayudha, the Kṣattṛ, spoke to our army which stood there in distress: SoKss_18,4.79.
Enough with despair; your lord will arrive before long.
Nothing whatsoever can cause harm to one who possesses such divine power.
Do you not remember how he went down to Pātāla,
married the Nāga maiden named Surūpā, and returned here alone?
And having gone to the world of the Gandharvas, the hero returned from there,
taking with him Tārāvalī, the daughter of the lord of the Gandharvas.
Having spoken thus, they were all comforted by that Bhadrāyudha;
they remained at the entrance of the forest, watching for the path of the king.
The king also, together with the Śabara soldiers, proceeded along the clear path while Madanasundarī moved about as she pleased.
Mounted upon a horse, accompanied by Vetāla and myself,
he entered that forest out of a desire to see the boar he had previously beheld.
And as he had entered there, a boar appeared before him;
upon seeing it, the king struck it with five arrows.
O Queen, from the belly of that slain man, which had been ripped open by the Vetāla as he ran, a handsome man suddenly emerged.
Just as the king, filled with wonder, asked him, "Who are you?",
a wild elephant, resembling a moving mountain, arrived there.
As soon as the king saw that elephant charging toward the forest,
he struck it in a vital spot with a single arrow and brought it down.
When he too was split open by him,
a divine man and a woman beautiful in every limb emerged from within the belly of that vetāla.
And as the king was desirous of asking questions, that man emerged from the belly of the boar and said:
"O King, listen; I shall tell you my own story."
"We two are celestial youths; this one is named Bhadra and I am Śubha. While wandering about, we saw the sage Kaṇva absorbed in meditation."
"Out of playfulness, we assumed the forms of an elephant and a boar; having done so, we terrified the great seer out of delusion, and he cursed us. (SoKss 18.4.93)
"In the forest, you two shall become exactly such an elephant and a boar;
slain by King Vikramāditya, you will attain liberation."
"Thus, by the sage's curse, we two became an elephant and a boar;
today we have been liberated by you. But this woman must herself tell her own story."
Touch this boar by the neck and this elephant by the back;
for these two shall indeed become a divine sword and shield for you.
Having spoken thus, he vanished along with his companion;
and the boar and the elephant of the king, when touched by his hand, were transformed into a sword and a shield.
Then, being questioned regarding her own story, that woman spoke thus:
"I am the wife of a merchant lord named Dhanadatta in Ujjayinī."
"While I was sleeping on the roof of the palace, this elephant came, swallowed me whole, and brought me here;
yet there was no man inside it."
"A man has emerged from my split belly along with me.
To her, who had spoken thus and was distressed, the king said to that woman:
"Be steadfast; I shall lead you to your husband's home.
Go together with my own retinue, free from fear."
Having said this, he had her brought and handed her over to Queen Madanasundarī, who was departing by a different path, by means of the vetāla.
Then, when the vetāla had returned, we suddenly beheld two princesses there in the forest, accompanied by a vast and magnificent retinue.

And the king sent his high officials to fetch me; when asked, "From where? Who are they? And who are these two maidens? they replied: SoKss_18.4.104: "From the city of Śrāvastī, O King, we have come with these two maidens, the daughters of Anāthapiṇḍada. SoKss_18.4.105: "We have brought them here to offer them to you, O King, for you are the lord of the earth, the protector of the world, and the master of all people. SoKss_18.4.106: "Therefore, O King, please accept these maidens as wives for your son; let him enjoy them as he pleases. SoKss_18.4.107: "Having heard this, the king was delighted and spoke thus to those ministers: 'I shall give my consent; let the marriage ceremony be performed. SoKss_18.4.108: "Then, having summoned the astrologers, he had them determine an auspicious day for the wedding. SoKss_18.4.109: "The astrologers, having observed the stars, declared that the day was auspicious and free from obstacles. SoKss_18.4.110: "Thereupon, the king gave orders to prepare the wedding feast and to decorate the city. SoKss_18.4.111: "He ordered the streets to be swept, sprinkled with water, and strewn with flowers, and had banners and canopies hung everywhere. SoKss_18.4.112: "He commanded the musicians to play and the singers to sing, and had the city filled with the sound of festive drums. SoKss_18.4.113: "He ordered the courtesans to adorn themselves and the dancers to perform, and had the city made radiant with various spectacles. SoKss_18.4.114: "He instructed the cooks to prepare many kinds of food and drink, and had the city provided with every variety of delicacy. SoKss_18.4.115: "He ordered the palaces to be decorated and the couches prepared, and had the city filled with the fragrance of incense. SoKss_18.4.116: "He commanded the servants to bring the bridegroom's party and the brides' party together at the appointed time. SoKss_18.4.117: "Then, on that auspicious day, the king led his son forth with great splendor to the house of Anāthapiṇḍada. SoKss_18.4.118: "There, he saw the two maidens, who were like goddesses descended from heaven, endowed with beauty and grace beyond compare. SoKss_18.4.119: "The prince, beholding them, was struck with wonder and felt a surge of affection, as if he had found a treasure long lost. SoKss_18.4.120: "The king then performed the marriage rites according to the sacred tradition, and the two maidens became the lawful wives of the prince. SoKss_18.4.121: "Having enjoyed their company for some time, the prince, being devoted to the Dharma, resolved to renounce the world. SoKss_18.4.122: "He informed his father of his intention, and the king, though grieving, permitted his departure out of respect for his son's resolve. SoKss_18.4.123: "The prince then took leave of his parents and his relatives, and set out for the forest, accompanied by a small retinue. SoKss_18.4.124: "In the forest, he encountered the Buddha, the Blessed One, and upon seeing him, his heart was filled with joy and faith. SoKss_18.4.125: "Approaching the Buddha, he prostrated himself at his feet and requested ordination; the Buddha, knowing his mind, granted him the going-forth. SoKss_18.4.126: "Having become a monk, he applied himself with diligence to meditation and study, and soon attained the state of an Arhat. There is an island named Kaṭāha, an abode of all prosperity;
there dwells a king named Guṇasāgara, whose name is true to his character.
To him, by his chief queen, was born a daughter named Guṇavatī, who,
by her beauty, bestowed wonder even upon the Creator himself.
And he was designated as her husband—the lord of the seven continents—by the perfected ones (siddhas).
Thereupon, his father, the king, consulted with his ministers.
"King Vikramāditya is a worthy suitor for this daughter of mine;
therefore, I shall send her to him alone for the purpose of taking his hand in marriage."
Having deliberated thus, the king placed his daughter, together with her attendants and her wealth, upon a ship in the ocean and dispatched her.
Having reached the vicinity of Suvarṇadvīpa, by fate that ship—
along with the princess, the people, and the cargo— was swallowed by a large fish.
And that great fish, having been carried by the tide of the ocean as if by the course of destiny, was cast upon the shore and lay exhausted, clinging to that island.
Upon seeing this, the people ran there with various weapons,
slaughtered that wondrous fish, and cut open its belly.
Then that great vessel departed full of people;
having learned of this, the king of that island came there out of wonder.
And King Candraśekhara learned from the people exactly what had happened concerning his brother-in-law, who was traveling on a ship, from Guṇasāgara, the lord of the earth.
Then, having learned that his sister’s daughter was virtuous,
the king brought her into his own capital and, out of joy, held a festival.
And on another day, that king intended to give his daughter, named Candravatī, whom he had previously prepared for the purpose, to King Vikramāditya.
At an auspicious moment, he placed her, along with her virtuous attendants, upon a ship laden with abundant wealth for her sake, and dispatched her.
These two princesses here, having crossed the ocean, are proceeding step by step; we have arrived here as their retinue.
And when those two very large crocodiles and elephants charged at us who had reached this place,
O Lord, we cried out in this manner.
"Since these two maidens have come of their own accord to the self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) of King Vikramāditya,
you Lokapālas must protect them according to dharma."
Having heard that, those two boars spoke to us in clear voices:
"Be steadfast; there is no fear for you by the mere mention of the king's name."
"You shall see that king arrive right here this very moment.
Having said this, those two divine beings, the elephant and the boar, departed from there.
When those elders had said, "This is our story," I said to them,
"O Queen, this is that very king."
Then those two princesses, Guṇavatī and Candravatī, joyfully prostrated themselves at his feet and presented them to that king.
The king, having thus commanded the vetāla, had those two Sundarīs brought;
all three of them went together with Madanasundarī.
And having been joined by that Vetāla who had arrived there in an instant,
O Queen, he flew up into the air together with me.
And as we were traveling through the forest, the sun went down;
at that time and place, the sound of a drum was heard by us.
When the king asked, "From where does this sound of a drum come?
the Vetāla replied, "O King, there is a temple here."
And that divine spectacle was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
there, O Lord, this sound of the drum arose during the evening performance.
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, the king and I, out of curiosity,
went there, restrained the horse, and entered.
There we beheld a great, worshiped linga made of the jewel of Tārkṣya, and before it, a strikingly beautiful lamp that was brilliantly radiant.
There, beautiful women of divine form danced for a very long time to the four kinds of musical instruments, accompanied by song and the art of music.
At the conclusion of the performance, we witnessed there a marvel: having entered within, the dancing girls merged into the statues upon the pillars.
"Even among singers, musicians, and others depicted in paintings, [these qualities exist];
having seen this, while the king was struck with wonder, the vetāla spoke as follows:"
"O divine one, this is such an inexhaustible illusion created by Viśvakarman;
for it always occurs during both twilights."
When he had spoken thus, as we were wandering about there,
we beheld on one side a pillar-statue of extraordinary beauty.
But the king, upon merely beholding her, was utterly captivated by her beauty;
for a moment he became vacant and motionless, as if carved in relief upon a pillar.
And he said: "If I do not see a woman with such a form as this while I am still alive, then what is the use of my kingdom and what is the use of my life?"
Having heard this, the Vetāla said: "This is not difficult to attain;
there is a daughter of the King of Kaliṅga named Kaliṅgasenā."
Seeing her, a sculptor from the city of Vardhamāna, desiring to capture her beauty, fashioned this statue of a Salabhañjikā.
Therefore, O Lord, go from here to Ujjayinī and request that maiden from King Kāliṅga; or else, seize her by means of valor.
Thus the king took the Vetāla’s words to heart;
then, having spent that night there, we set out in the morning.
And as we went, we saw two noble men at the foot of an Aśoka tree;
they both rose up and bowed down to the king.
When the king asked them, "Who are you two, and why are you staying in the forest? one of them replied: "O King, listen; I shall tell you."
I am named Dhanadatta, the son of a merchant in Ujjayinī. Once, while I was asleep on the roof-terrace of my palace together with my wife, [a snake bit me].
Having awakened in the morning, when I looked, my wife was not there for me— neither in the palace nor in the other mansions, gardens, and so forth.
Her mind was not otherwise disposed, and her conviction in this matter was firm:
"If I am indeed virtuous, then this [garland] will certainly not wither. (SoKss 18.4.147)
That garland was given to me by her, and it remains unfaded;
I do not know where it has gone—has it perhaps been carried off by a spirit or some such being?
Reflecting thus, searching, crying out, lamenting, and weeping,
I remained without food, consumed by the fire of separation from him.
Then, comforted by his kinsmen and having taken some food,
he remained in the temple, dwelling there in sorrow while feeding the brahmins.
There, once, when he was exhausted, this brahmin addressed me;
then I rested him with bathing, food, and other such comforts.
When asked, "Where are you from?", after he had finished eating, he replied to me, "I am from a village situated near Vārāṇasī."
Having been told by my servant about my suffering, he spoke again:
"O friend, why have you desponded over yourself like one who lacks effort?"
"For one who is resolute, my friend, attains even that which is difficult to reach. Arise; let us search for your wife, for I am your friend. (SoKss_18.4.154)
"How can she be sought when not even her general direction is known?
To me, who had spoken thus, he then replied again with affection:
"Do not say so! Did Keśaṭa not previously obtain a wife named Rūpavatī, whose union was considered impossible? Listen to this story."
In the city of Pāṭaliputra, there lived the son of a wealthy Brāhmaṇa named Keśaṭa,
a young man of the twice-born caste who was like a second Kāma in beauty.
Seeking a suitable wife, he departed from his home without his parents' knowledge and wandered through various lands under the pretext of visiting sacred fords.
And in due course, having reached the bank of the Narmadā, he once beheld a great multitude of people on a wedding procession coming along that very road.

And having seen him from afar, an elderly leader of the twice-born came out from among them, addressed Keśaṭa, and spoke to him affectionately in private: dṛṣṭvā ca dūrāt tanmadhyād etyaikas taṃ dvijāgraṇīḥ / saṃbhāṣya keśaṭaṃ vṛddhaḥ prāha sapraṇayaṃ rahaḥ // SoKss_18,4.160 //
I request something from you that is easily accomplished by your play;
if you grant me my full desire, I shall speak it.
Having heard that, Keśaṭa said: "Noble sir, if you speak what is possible, then let that be certainly performed by me; let it be a service to you."
Then the elder brahmin said: "Listen, my son;
you have a son who is the foremost among the deformed, yet like you, he is handsome."
He had protruding teeth and a flat nose; he was dark-skinned with timid eyes, a large belly, crooked feet, and ears shaped like winnowing baskets.
Out of affection for such a person, I described his form and requested a maiden from the Brahmin named Ratnadatta.
And she, named Rūpavatī, had been promised in marriage by her father;
therefore, as her name was significant of her beauty, today the taking of their hands [the wedding] shall take place for him.
"We have come for that purpose, and now that we have seen my son, a kinsman would not give his daughter; thus this undertaking would become fruitless."
While contemplating a means in this matter, I have found you here;
therefore, fulfill this desire of mine immediately by means of your word.
"Come together with us, marry that maiden, and today bestow her upon my son; for you are indeed a suitable match for the bride."
Having heard that, and taking Keśaṭa who had said "So be it," the old brahmin crossed the Narmadā by boat and went to the opposite bank.
Having reached a certain city, he and his followers then rested outside;
meanwhile, the traveler of the sky, the sun, also settled upon the western mountain.
Then, as darkness spread along the water's edge, Keśaṭa,
having gone there to perform his ablutions, beheld a terrible rākṣasa who had arisen.
"I am devouring you; where will you go from me, Keśaṭa? To the Rākṣasa who had spoken thus, Keśaṭa replied:
"Do not devour me yet; I shall come to you again once I have certainly fulfilled the task promised to the brahmin."
Having heard that and having made him swear an oath, the Rākṣasa then released Keśaṭa; he, for his part, went to the army of his bridegroom.
Then that elderly brahmin, taking Keśaṭa— who was adorned with excellent ornaments— together with his groomsmen, entered that city.
There, amidst the sounding of various musical instruments, he caused Keśaṭa to enter the house of Ratnadatta, where the sacrificial altar had been prepared.
And Keśaṭa duly married that fair-faced maiden Rūpavatī there, for whom her father had bestowed great wealth.
The women there rejoiced upon seeing the bride and groom as a match,
and Rūpavatī too was delighted to see that such a husband had been obtained.
Her friends also, upon seeing him, became filled with love;
but Keśaṭa at that time was overcome by despondency and wonder.
And at night, upon the bed, seeing her beloved with his face turned away, absorbed in thought, Rūpavatī feigned sleep.
Then, at midnight, thinking her to be asleep, Keśaṭa went out and approached that rākṣasa in order to keep his word.
That beautiful woman, having risen of her own accord and being noticed by others,
followed after her husband with curiosity, remaining faithful to him.
And when Keśaṭa had arrived there, the Rākṣasa said to him:
"Well done, O Keśaṭa! You have preserved the truth; you are a being of great courage."
That city of Pāṭaliputra and its father, Deśaka, have been purified by you; therefore come, so that I may devour you!
Hearing that, Rūpavatī approached suddenly and said this:
"Eat me; for if this husband of mine is devoured, what refuge would there be for me?"
When the *rākṣasa* said, "Alms are your refuge," she replied to him:
"O Great Being, who here will give alms to a woman like me?"
"Whoever does not give you alms when asked shall have their head split into a hundred pieces," said the rākṣasa; and she replied:
"In that case, give me this very alms-offering of a husband," he said;
and as soon as he spoke, that Rākṣasa’s head shattered and he died instantly.
Then, taking Keśaṭa— who was utterly amazed by her conduct—
Rūpavatī went to her home, and by that time the night had come to an end.
And when the next day had dawned, that army of his, having taken their meal,
set out from there and reached the bank of the Narmadā together with the bride and the groom.
Then, having placed the beautiful bride and her attendants on a boat,
that chief elder brahmin himself boarded another boat.
But that rogue, having made a secret agreement with the boatmen, took Kesaṭa onto the boat separately, having first stripped him of his ornaments and other belongings.
Then that brahmin, together with his wife's kinsmen, crossed over and proceeded;
however, Kesaṭa was led far away through the middle of the river by fishermen.
Having cast that boat and Keśaṭa into the great current, they took the wealth from the old brahmin and departed, having crossed the river by swimming with their arms.
But Keśaṭa, though possessing a ship, was swept away by the surging river;
cast into the ocean by the force of the wind, he was eventually deposited on the shore by a wave.
There, because his life-force still remained, he took heart and reflected:
"Aha! This service has been rendered to me by that brahmin."
Or rather, why did he not declare that very same thing—that son’s lack of dharma and foolishness—since he united his son with another man’s wife by having him married? (SoKss 18.4.198)
While he sat there, overwhelmed by such reflections, the night arrived,
during which the circles of sky-faring women roamed about.
Waking up during that fourth watch, he heard a clamor in the sky and saw before him a handsome man who had fallen from the heavens.
After a long time, having perceived that he was unaltered, Kesaṭa, though terrified, asked him, "Who are you? Thereupon, that man replied.
"Tell me first who you are here, and then I shall tell you mine.
Having heard that, Keśaṭa described his own life story to him.
Then that man said: "In that case, you are in the same state as I.
Therefore, friend, listen now as I tell you my own story."
On the bank of the river Veṇā, there is a city named Ratnapura;
there I lived as a householder, a wealthy son of a twice-born man, known by the name Kandarpa.
Thus, at nightfall, seeking water, I descended into the river Veṇā;
having slipped there, I fell and was carried away by the force of the current.
Having been carried a great distance by that night, at the arrival of day,
I was deposited by him in a grove of trees situated on the marshland by the force of fate.
Having climbed up by hanging from a branch and rested near the bank,
I saw there a large, empty temple of the Mothers.
Having entered there and seen the Mothers within, as if throbbing with splendor, I bowed to them with my fear stilled, praised them, and made this request:
O Blessed Ones, grant protection to me, a wretched man;
for I have today come before you as one who has sought refuge.
Having thus made my request, as I rested there— exhausted by the torrent of the river—
the day, my friend, gradually came to its rest as well.
Then there came Raudrī, the ascetic woman of the night, richly adorned with a garland of stars for bones, white as the moonlight, and possessing a skull as bright as the moon.
At that moment, I perceived that from within the circle of Mothers,
a host of yoginīs emerged and spoke to one another.
"Today we must go to Cakrapura for the wheel-assembly;
and here, in this place teeming with beasts of prey, what protection can there be for this brahmin?"
Therefore, let him be taken and established wherever it may be well for him;
we shall bring him back again, for he has come to us for refuge.
Having spoken thus, they took me through the air, adorned me, and placed me in the house of a certain wealthy brahmin in a certain city; then they departed.
There I saw that everything was prepared for the maiden’s wedding— the altar was ready and the auspicious moment had arrived— but the groom’s party had not yet arrived.
Then, seeing me standing there in divine and excellent attire,
all the people said, "At last, this boon has been obtained."
Then, having led me to the altar and brought forth his daughter who was beautifully adorned,
that brahmin householder gave her to me there according to the prescribed rite.
"By good fortune, through the attainment of a husband of equal status,
the beauty of this Sumanas has now borne fruit," the women said to one another.
Then, having performed the marriage ceremony there with that Sumanas,
I slept in the palace, comforted by great luxuries.
Then, during this final watch of the night, the yoginīs came from the assembly circle (*cakramelaka*) and,
having seized me by their own power, flew up into the sky.
As they were traveling through the sky,
I fell here from their hands while they were engaged in a struggle with others who wished to seize me.
I do not know that city where I married Sumanā,
nor do I know what will happen now.
Thus, this succession of miseries that was bestowed upon me by fate has today reached its end in happiness through my meeting with you.
To Kandarpa, who had spoken thus, Keśaṭa said:
"Do not fear, friend; now the yoginīs have no power over you."
I possess a certain power that is entirely unimpeded, by which we shall wander together; destiny will ordain what is for our highest good.
As they were thus conversing with one another, the night passed away;
at dawn they set out from there, and both had crossed the ocean.
In due course, Keśaṭa and Kandarpa reached the city named Bhīmapura, situated near the Ratnanadī river.
Then, having heard that clamor on the riverbank, the two of them went there and saw a fish that had filled both banks.
Cast out by the ocean tide, his body bound by its great size,
he was being torn apart by people seeking flesh with various weapons in their hands.
As he was being cut open, a woman emerged from his belly;
watched with astonishment by the people, she, terrified, fled to the shore.
Then, seeing her, Kandarpa was delighted and said to Keśaṭa: "Friend, this is that very Sumanas whom I married."
I do not know, moreover, how her dwelling came to be within the belly of a fish;
therefore, let us both remain here in silence until the truth becomes manifest.
When Keśaṭa replied, “So be it,” as the two of them remained there, Sumanas was questioned by the people: “Who are you? What is this? *Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra* 18.4.234.
Then, with great difficulty, she said: "In the city of Ratnākara, I am the daughter of the eminent Brahmin named Jayadatta."
"By name I am Sumanā; I was married by a certain noble and suitable son of a Brahmin during the night."
On that very night, while I was asleep, my husband departed for some unknown place;
though my father searched for him with great effort, he was not found anywhere.
Then, in order to extinguish the fire of separation from him, I threw myself into a river;
I was swallowed by this fish and have arrived here by the power of destiny.
While she was speaking thus, a certain Brahmin named Yajñasvāmin emerged from the midst of the crowd, embraced her, and said this:
"Come, come, daughter; you shall be my sister's daughter.
For Yajñasvāmin is indeed your brother, born of the same womb as your mother."
Hearing that, Sumanas uncovered her face and, looking at him, recognized her uncle; with tears in her eyes, she grasped his feet.
Having shed a moment’s tears, she said to him: "Give me wood;
for me, separated from my noble husband, there is no other resort than fire."
Since she did not waver from her resolve even though being exhorted by us,
Kandarpa, having examined her mind, approached her.
Seeing him approach and recognizing him, the wise and gracious Sumanā fell at his feet and wept.
When questioned by the people and by her maternal uncle,
that high-minded woman declared, "This is my husband."
Then, while everyone was rejoicing, Yajñasvāmin led her home,
as well as her husband Kaṃdarpa, accompanied by Keśaṭa.
There, accompanied by his family, he attended to those who had related their respective stories with great hospitality and affection.
As the days passed, Keśaṭa said to Kandarpa there:
"By obtaining your beloved wife, you have already attained the fulfillment of your purpose."
Therefore, go now to your own city of Ratnapura with your wife;
I, however, shall not return to my own country until I have accomplished my purpose.
"O friend, I shall wear away this body by wandering from sacred ford to sacred ford.
Having heard that, Yajñasvāmin, who was staying there, said to Keśaṭa:
Why do you speak thus out of agitation? Everything is attained by those who live; therefore, listen as I tell you the story of the one whose weapon is flowers.
In the city named Caṇḍapura, there was a twice-born man named Devasvāmin;
he had a daughter of exceeding beauty named Kamalalocanā.
And the disciple was the son of a brahmin named Kusumāyudha;
that disciple and her daughter were mutually in love with one another.
Once, having been decided by her father to be given to another suitor,
that maiden quickly spoke through the mouth of her friend to that god whose weapon is the flower.
"My father has resolved to give me to another, yet you were my previously chosen husband; therefore, take me from here by some stratagem."
Then, having made an agreement with her, that Kusumāyudha stationed a swift-footed servant outside at night, before he departed.
Having gone out at her own will, she mounted that vehicle with the servant;
he did not lead her into his presence, but led her elsewhere to take her for himself.
And having led that lotus-eyed woman far away at night, he reached a certain city; in the morning, that virtuous woman said to him:
"Where is that master of yours? Why do you not lead me to my husband?
Hearing this, that rogue said to her, who was alone and traveling to a foreign land: "SoKss_18,4.259"
"I shall marry you; what of him, and where is he now?
Hearing this, she replied: "You are wise, for you are exceedingly dear to me."
"Why do you not marry me here this very day? Alas!
Then, having stationed her in the city garden, that evil-minded man went to the marketplace to fetch the wedding requisites.
Having fled for that long, the girl, accompanied by the mule,
entered the house of a certain elderly florist.
Having related her own story there, she remained with him, treated with hospitality;
he too, failing to obtain her, departed from the garden dejected, accompanied by his wicked servant.
Having gone there, she spoke to that lord, the flower-weaponed god who was questioning her:

She did not escape at all until she was seen by the people there;
while I was being held back by those others, that mule was carried off.
"By some stroke of fate, I have now escaped and come here.
Hearing this, Kusumāyudha reflected and remained silent.
Once, urged by his father, he set out for Vraja for the sake of marriage and reached that city where the lotus-eyed woman resided.
There, in a nearby park where a multitude of people had settled,
that lotus-eyed woman saw him wandering alone.
She told that gardener everything that had occurred while she was staying in his house;
he too went and, having related the account, brought her husband there.
Then, with the necessary preparations gathered and having long been desired,
the marriage of that bridegroom and that bride was immediately performed.
Then the Flower-Armed One, having restrained that wicked servant and having married her,
