Accompanied by those two brides, he returned joyfully to his own country, having come for the sake of marrying that second maiden as well.
In this way, even an inconceivable reunion occurs for those who are fortunate;
therefore, Keśaṭa, you too shall regain your beloved before long.
When Yajñasvāmin had spoken thus,
Kandarpa, Sumana, and Kesaṭa remained in his house for several days.
And having set out for their own country, they reached a great forest and became separated from one another due to the panic caused by the attack of wild elephants.
As he traveled alone and sorrowful among them, Keśaṭa eventually reached the city of Kāśī and there found his friend Kandarpa.
He went with him to his own city of Pāṭaliputra;
there, welcomed by his father, he dwelt for some time.
There, he described to his parents his own history, beginning from his marriage to Rūpavatī and ending with the account of Kandarpa.
In the meantime, Sumanā, fleeing out of fear of the elephant, entered the forest;
she arrived there, and the sun went to its setting.
"Alas, my husband! Alas, my father! Alas, my mother!"—thus lamenting at the onset of night, she desired to cast her body into a forest fire.
Meanwhile, that circle of Yoginīs, supremely compassionate toward Kāmadeva,
conquered other Yoginīs and reached their own abode.
There, having recollected Kandarpa and realized through their own higher knowledge that his wife had been lost in the forest, they took counsel together.
The wise man Kandarpa shall obtain his desire by himself;
but his wife, lost in the forest, that young woman will surely give up her life.
"Let us take her to that city of jewels and cast her there,
so that she may dwell together with her co-wife in the house of Kandarpa’s father."
Having deliberated thus, those yoginīs went to that forest, comforted Sumanas there, and having carried her away, they left her in Ratnapura.
When the night had passed, that Sumanas, wandering there in the city,
heard this being said by the people as they ran about:
This is Anaṅgavatī, the wife of the twice-born Kaṃdarpa;
since her husband has gone elsewhere, she has spent some time longing for his return.
That virtuous woman, not having found him and now devoid of hope, has departed;
pursued by her two suffering parents-in-law, she has now gone forth to enter the fire.
Upon hearing this, Sumanā immediately went to that cremation ground and,
approaching Anaṅgavatī, restrained her in this manner.
"Noble lady, do not act rashly; for your husband is indeed alive.
Having said this, she related the entire account of his adventures from the very beginning.
And he showed the jeweled ring belonging to Kandarpadatta;
then everyone congratulated her, having realized that her words were true.
Then, having honored the satisfied Anaṅgavatī and her daughter-in-law Sumanas, Kandarpa’s father, being pleased, settled them in his home.
Meanwhile, Kaṃdarpa departed from Pāṭaliputra to search for Sumanas;
he went forth without telling Keśaṭa, even though the latter was unwilling.
When he had gone, Keśaṭa too, suffering in the absence of Rūpavatī,
departed from his parents' house without their knowledge and wandered here and there.
It is said that even Kandarpa, while wandering about, by chance reached that city where Keśaṭa had married that beautiful Rūpavatī.

Then that old Brahmin, having thus deceived Keśaṭa,

"I do not see my noble son; why is he not here while everyone else is departing? Hearing this, that aged brahmin showed him his son and said: [verse 18.4.302]

Speaking thus, having abandoned food and drink out of fear of the king,

Then Rūpavatī said:

Having said, "Indeed, this was heard by me from the mouth of the Rākṣasa," she related to him in its entirety the story of both her husband and the Rākṣasa.
Then his father went there and, seeing the Rākṣasa lying dead,
gained conviction regarding the true nature of that couple and was deeply gratified.
Having comforted his daughter with the hope of her eventual recovery,
he dispatched her toward Pāṭaliputra to seek out the side of Keśaṭa’s father.
Having gone there and returned before long, they spoke thus here:
"We have seen that teacher of our master residing in Pāṭaliputra."
When asked there, "Where is that son of yours, Keśaṭa?", he replied with tears: "How could our son Keśaṭa be here?"
For even though my friend named Kandarpa arrived together with him,

"Having heard these words of his, we have come here in due course.

When she could not be restrained despite speaking thus,

After he had stayed there for some days, being treated with honor,

Where Keśaṭa married your friend named Rūpavatī,

O beloved, having reached their respective countries, Kesaṭa and Kandarpa, now possessing beautiful forms and joyful minds, remained there enjoying worldly pleasures.
Thus, those of firm character, though separated from their beloveds by adverse fate,

Therefore, rise quickly, my friend; let us go. While searching, you too may eventually find your wife.

I am Candrasvāmin, the son of a twice-born man, residing in the preeminent agrahāra of Brahmasthala; I have a beautiful wife who lives with me in my home.
Once, when I had gone to the village on business by my father's command,

As soon as she saw him, she was seized with a fever and died that evening;
then my kinsmen took her away and placed her upon the funeral pyre at night.

When I had gone to the vicinity of the funeral pyre, that Kāpālika arrived,
with a dancing khaṭvāṅga staff resting on his shoulder and the loud, resounding blast of his ḍamaru drum.
O Lord, when the funeral fire was extinguished by the scattering of ashes,

Taking up that skull-bowl which had been drawn after him by the *siddhi*, he fled swiftly; and I, equipped with bow and arrow, pursued him.

"If you have need of me as your lord,

"So be it," replied the Lord of Kaliṅga;

And on another day, O Queen, your father, the lord of Kaliṅga,

"O Queen, you were wedded by the king with such deep affection and at the risk of his own life according to the prescribed rites, not out of a desire for victory over his enemies."
Thus, O friends, having heard from the mouth of the pilgrim Devasena this [account] born of humiliation, I abandoned my resentment.
"In this manner I was married by the King upon seeing a statue on a pillar,

Thus Kaliṅgasenā, the beloved of Vikramāditya,

And thus Vikramāditya, accompanied by all of them as well as by Malayavatī, remained established in his imperial sovereignty.
Then once, a certain prince named Kṛṣṇaśakti, who had been humiliated by his own kinsmen, arrived there from the Deccan.
Having arrived at the main gate, he adopted the vow of a mendicant attendant (*kārpaṭika*) to the king,

While the king was engaged in his heroic conduct at night, listening in secret,

O Lord, in separation from you, these sighs of mine—hot, long, and trembling—issue forth incessantly;
yet it is my breaths that depart, not my life.

Having heard this repeatedly from that royal attendant as he spoke thus, the king returned to his own capital and reflected: *iti vācayatastasmātsamrāṭ kārpaṭikānmuhuḥ / śrutvā sa rājadhānīṃ svāṃ gatvā rājā vyacintayat //* (SoKss_18,5.59)
"Alas, this distressed traveler, burdened by a wife and failing in his purpose,

Thinking, "I must not allow him any delay," the king immediately sent a maidservant and had the kārpaṭika summoned.

"There, by this instruction, enjoy the village granted by me;

"What desire for victory can I have for a single village that brings only shame? Nevertheless, the command of my lord must be carried out," he thought, and traveling on, he remained dissatisfied.

"Do you know, sirs, where Khaṇḍavaṭaka might be here?

"Tell me, my lady, where is Khaṇḍavaṭaka here?

Having entered the royal palace there, which was surrounded by seven courtyards, he ascended to the upper story of the mansion, which was constructed of jewels and gold.

"O man, why have you sat here upon the royal throne?

Having heard that command and having seen him, the Rākṣasa bowed to him and said:

"The command of King Vikramāditya is indeed unbroken everywhere.
Having said this, that Rākṣasa summoned all the subjects.
The ministers and the royal retinue arrived there,
and that city was filled with the fourfold army.
Then, being saluted by everyone, that joyful pauper performed all his rites, beginning with bathing, according to royal protocol.
Then, having become a king there, he reflected with astonishment: "Aha!
What an extraordinary power this King Vikramāditya possesses!"
The wondrous and unprecedented majesty of that Lord’s profundity bestows even such a kingdom as this, he says, by merely uttering the word "village."
Thus, filled with wonder, he dwelt there ruling his kingdom;

And after some days, that eager kārpaṭika approached King Vikramāditya to pay his respects, while the king’s army caused the earth to tremble.
When he had arrived and prostrated at his feet, Vikramāditya said to him:
"Go and restrain the sighs of my wife, for whom this letter was sent."
Having spoken thus, he was sent away by the lord of the earth; accompanied by his friends, that Kṛṣṇaśakti returned to his own country, filled with wonder.
Having sent away his kinsmen and gladdened his wife, who had long been yearning for him,

Thus, King Vikramāditya, whose conduct was so marvelous,

And he asked him, "O Brahmin, why are you such as this?

O King, there was a brahmin named Agnisvāmin in Pāṭaliputra;

In due time, having mounted my horse with a single servant, I went to my father-in-law’s house to bring her back while she was still in the prime of youth.
Honored by my father-in-law, I then departed from there with my wife, who had mounted her horse and brought along a single female servant who had come as an attendant.
And on the way, when my horse was weary, my bride indeed dismounted and went to the riverbank under the pretext of drinking water. (SoKss_18.5.95)
As long as she did not return for a long time,
I dispatched a servant who was stationed right there with me to keep watch over her.
"Since he has not yet arrived, I myself have come here;
having stationed that maidservant there to guard the mare."
When I went there and looked, I saw that my servant had been reduced to nothing but bones by that wife of mine, whose face was smeared with blood as she devoured him.
Terrified, as I was heading toward my mare,
she too was devoured by that same maidservant in the very same manner.
Then, having fled from there, I went away; yet even now, because of that terror, the state of my body hair and head hairs standing on end does not cease, though it remains within me.
When that twice-born man spoke thus, "In this matter, O Lord,
my refuge is you," Vikramāditya, by his command, rendered him free from fear.
"Alas! Shame! There is no trust to be placed in women, who are the very ground of recklessness.
While the king was saying this, one minister spoke as follows:
O King, such are indeed the ill-born women;
and have you not heard here what happened to the brahmin Agniśarman?
Right here there is a twice-born man named Agniśarman, the son of Somaśarman;

A daughter of a twice-born man from Vardhamānapura was married by him; and because she was still a child, she was not abandoned by her wealthy father at home.
And when she had reached the prime of youth, her parents said to Agniśarman: "Son, why do you not bring that wife of yours even now?"
Having heard this and without even taking leave of his parents,
that dull-witted Agniśarman then set out alone toward his wife.
As he had departed from his home, a partridge appeared on his right,

That fool also welcomed it, crying out, "Live!
Live!", while the deity of the omen, remaining invisible, laughed upon hearing him.
Having reached his father-in-law’s abode and as he was about to enter it,

and that deity presiding over the bird also reflected upon it.
"Aha! This fool rejoices in what is inauspicious as if it were auspicious;

While that deity was thus reflecting, Agniśarman, filled with joy, entered the residence of his father-in-law.

Embracing his body, her nose bitten off by his teeth,

"Alas, alas! I am dead, truly dead, because of this causeless act committed by my husband against me—this mutilation of my nose which he has performed after rising up."

"First, he has already obtained the fruit of the signless through this:
that he said, 'Live, live!'—therefore, on his account, I shall protect him from death."
Having reflected thus, that hidden deity spoke from the sky:
"O executioner, this son of a brahmin is blameless; he must not be killed."
"Go between the teeth of the thief impaled on the stake and look at his nose," she said,
and then she related that account of her daughter-in-law's night.
Then, based on that report, the executioners informed the king through the mouth of the chamberlain after they had seen that nose situated between the teeth of the thief.
Having released Agniśarman from execution, he sent him home;
but he punished that wicked woman and also fined her daughters-in-law.
"O King, such are women," when this was said by that minister,
King Vikramāditya agreed, saying, "So it is."
Then the rogue Mūladeva, standing in the presence of the king, said:
"Your Majesty, virtuous women do not exist at all; what then [is there] among some who are unvirtuous?"
Are there not mango creepers even amidst poisonous vines?
Listen, therefore, to this which was experienced by me alone: SoKss_18,5.130
I previously went to Pāṭaliputra together with Śaśin,
considering it a field of urbanity out of a desire to behold its cleverness.
There, seeing a woman washing clothes at a lake on the outskirts, I asked her, "Where can travelers stay here? (SoKss 18.5.132)
On these shores, the cakravāka birds dwell among the fish, the bees in the water, and the lotuses; no lodging for travelers has been seen by me here.
Having been thus answered with an indirect remark by the old woman, I,
feeling embarrassed, entered the interior of the city together with Śaśin.

There, as the finest rice-porridge stood hot in a bowl before him at the door of the house, the Moon saw a child weeping and spoke: SoKss_18,5.135: "There, as the finest rice-porridge stood hot in a bowl before him at the door of the house, the Moon saw a child weeping and spoke."
"Alas! This child is devoid of intelligence, for he does not eat the first-offered supreme rice-milk;
he needlessly torments himself with further weeping."
Hearing that, the boy wiped his eyes and said with a smile:
"You are fools; you do not know the benefits of my weeping."
As the finest rice cools, it gradually becomes more palatable;
furthermore, it acts differently [from when it was hot], and the phlegm goes to its depletion.
"These are my virtues; I do not weep out of folly. You, however, are vulgar and foolish, for you do not understand my intention."
When this was said by that boy, both Śaśin and I, abashed by our own lack of cleverness and filled with wonder, withdrew to another place.
There too, we saw an excellent maiden gathering mangoes from the trunk of a mango tree, while her attendants remained at its base.
"O auspicious one, give us also some mango fruits," we said;
and thus addressed by us, that maiden spoke as follows.
"Should I eat mango fruits that are warm, or perhaps those that are cool?
Having heard that, desiring to know this marvel, I spoke to that maiden:
"Let us eat these warm ones first, and then others as well, O beautiful one.
Having heard this, she threw the mango fruits onto the ground among the dust.
Having rendered them free of life-force by means of the breath from our mouths, we consumed them;
then that maiden, together with her retinue, laughed and said:
"These mango fruits were previously given to you while still warm;
yet, having blown upon them after they were given, you ate them."
"Take these cool fruits, which have not been blown upon, onto your garments. Having spoken thus, she cast the fruits onto the hems of our clothes.
Taking those [gems] from that place, we departed feeling embarrassed;
then I spoke to my other companions and to Śaśin.
"I must certainly marry this clever maiden;
otherwise, how could I remedy the mockery? What other artifice could there be?"
Thus, having searched for her father’s residence according to my instructions,
we went there on the following day, disguised by our altered appearance.
While we were studying the Veda there, that twice-born man, the father of the girl, approached us as we were reciting and asked, "From where have you come, O Yajñasvāmin? (SoK 18.5.151).
"We have come here from the city of Māyā for the sake of learning";
having been addressed thus by us, that wealthy and best of brahmins then spoke.
"In that case, dwell right here in my house for these four months; show me your favor, for you have come from a distant land."
"O Brahmin, having heard this, we said:
'We shall do as you say, provided that at the end of four months you will grant us what we request.'"
Thus addressed by us, that brahmin Yajñasvāmin replied:
"Whatever it is for the sake of which you are searching, I shall certainly give it to you."
When he had thus promised, we remained in his house;
then, when the four months were complete, that brahmin was addressed by us:
"We shall go; give us that which we have requested as previously stated.
To him who asked, "What is that?", the Moon replied, pointing toward me.
"Let this maiden be given by you to him who is our chief";
then that brahmin Yajñasvāmin, bound by his word, reflected.
"I have been deceived by these men; let this be, for he is virtuous.
Having reflected thus, that brahmin gave his daughter to me in accordance with the prescribed rites.
And one night, laughing in the bedchamber, I said to that bride:
"Do you perhaps remember those mangoes, both warm and cold?"
Having heard that and recognized me, she said to me with a smile:
"In this very way are country folk mocked by city-dwellers."
Then I also said to her: "Stay here happily, O lady of the city;
I, a man of the village, shall go far away, having made a vow to leave you."
Having heard this, she too made a firm vow:
"I shall certainly capture you and bring you back by means of a son born of you."
When they had thus made their mutual agreement, she lay down with her face turned away;
and while she was asleep, I placed my own ring upon one of her fingers.
Having departed from there and reunited with those companions of mine,
I went to my own city of Ujjayinī, desiring to witness her cleverness.
That daughter of a brahmin, having woken up in the morning and not seeing me, yet seeing the ring marked with my name, thought to herself: ||| SoKss_18,5.166 |||
"He has already departed, leaving me behind; thus he has fulfilled his vow.
I too must fulfill my own vow, casting away all regret."
The name "Mūladeva" is seen upon this ring;
therefore, he is certainly that very one known as the rogue Mūladeva.
"He is said by people to be residing constantly in Ujjayinī;
therefore, having gone there by means of a stratagem, I must accomplish my desired objective."
Having thus made this resolve, she spoke this falsehood to her father:
"Father, my husband has suddenly departed, leaving me behind."
"How can I remain here at ease, separated from him?
Therefore, I shall go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords; I weary this wretched body."
Having spoken thus, and having with great effort obtained his permission even though he was unwilling,
she then set out from there with her wealth and her retinue.
Having traveled by stages and having assumed the highly precious attire appropriate for a courtesan, she,
the world’s peerless beauty, entered the city of Ujjayinī.
And having made an agreement regarding what was to be done with her retinue,
Sumaṅgalā gave the name Viprasutā to her own self.
"She is a courtesan named Sumaṅgalā, who can assume any form at will and enjoys great liberality;
let her be summoned here by the servants," so it was proclaimed.
Then the preeminent courtesan there, named Devadattā,
approached her and offered her own separate residence, which was worthy of a king.
While she was staying there, my friend Śaśin, captivated by her fame, first spoke to her through the mouth of a servant, saying, "Let my fee be accepted."
"Whoever would follow our word, let him enter here as a lover;
we have no need for hirelings, nor for other men who are like beasts."
Having been addressed thus by Sumaṅgalā through her very mouth,
Śaśin said, "So be it," and went to her palace at the onset of night.
Having reached the first gate there and announced himself, he was addressed by the gatekeeper: "Do as our mistress commands."
"Even though you have already bathed here, bathe once more; otherwise, there is no entry for you.
Having heard that, Śaśin agreed to the bath, saying, "So be it."
Then, while he was being confidently bathed by the female slaves following the application of oil and fragrant unguents, the first watch of the night passed away.
Having bathed, he then reached the second gate, where he was addressed by the gatekeeper: "You have bathed; therefore, first perform the rite of adornment."
When he had said, "So be it," his female attendants performed their adornment until the second watch of the night had also passed away.
Then, having reached the third courtyard gate, he was addressed by the guards:
"Eat first, and then enter the interior."
When he had said, "So be it," those female servants delayed him with various kinds of food until the third watch had passed.
Then, having somehow reached the fourth door of the bedchamber,
he was thus reviled there by the doorkeeper:
"Village lover, depart; do not suffer humiliation!
Is this the time for a courtesan’s new union in the final watch of the night?"
Thus insulted by him, like the moon whose luster has faded before Time personified, he departed from there just as he had come.
In this way, other lovers were also deceived by that daughter of a Brahmin who, in the guise of a courtesan, bore the name Sumaṅgalā.
Having heard that, out of mere curiosity, I made the messenger go and return;
then, well-adorned, I went to her house at night.
There, I gratified the doorkeepers at every gate by bestowing wealth;
then, without delay, I reached the door of her inner apartments.
When the time was right, having been released by the gatekeepers and entering that place,
I beheld my beloved, who was unrecognized as being in the house of a courtesan.
Having recognized me, she then rose to greet me and so forth; like a cunning courtesan, she attended upon me as I sat cross-legged on the couch.
Then, having spent the night with her, the peerless beauty of the world,
my passion was so firmly bound that I was unable to leave her house.
She too, her passion firmly fixed, did not depart from my side at that time,
until after some days she became pregnant, her nipples turning dark blue.
Then that clever woman, having composed a forged letter, handed it over to me, saying, "The king, my lord, has sent this letter; let it be read."
Then, having released it, I read the letter as follows:
"From illustrious Kāmarūpa, the glorious King Mānasiṃha."
She addresses Sumaṅgalā: "Why do you remain here so long?
Come quickly, abandoning your curiosity for other lands."
When I had thus read the letter, she spoke to me as if in sorrow:
"I am going; do not harbor resentment toward me, for I am dependent on another."
Having thus made this pretext, she departed for Pāṭaliputra;
but I, though full of love, did not follow her, thinking, "She is dependent on others."
And she, residing in Pāṭaliputra, in due time gave birth to a son;
and as he grew, even as a child, he mastered all the arts.
And when that boy was twelve years of age, out of childish fickleness,
he once struck a fellow slave of his own age with his foot.
And being struck, that slave-boy, weeping in anger, said to him:
"You strike me, you whose father is not even known!"
"Since you were born here and there while your mother was wandering in foreign lands,"—
having been told this by him, he went and questioned his mother out of embarrassment.
"Mother, who is my father, and where does he dwell? Tell me!
Then that mother, the daughter of a twice-born, looked at him for a moment and spoke to him.
"Your father, named Mūladeva, abandoned me and went to Ujjayinī";
having said this, she related her entire life story to him from the very beginning.
Then that boy said to her, "Mother,
I will go and bring back that father of mine, bind him, and fulfill your promise."
Having spoken thus to his mother, the boy set out from there;
lacking the token she had mentioned, he reached this city of Ujjayinī.
Seeing me there playing with dice and certain of my identity by my distinctive marks,
he went to the gambling hall and defeated everyone at the game.
Even in his childhood, he was a great deceiver who caused wonder in everyone;
he gave to those who asked the wealth he had won from gambling.
Having come by her own device at night and lightly placed me upon a heap of cotton, she carried off my bedstead as I slept.
Then, having woken up, I saw myself upon the back of a cotton mattress;
suddenly, I was filled with shame, laughter, and wonder at being without a bedstead.
Then, O Lord, having slowly entered the marketplace and wandering about,
I beheld that very boy selling that same bedstead.
Approaching him, I asked, "How much will you give for this bed as its price? Thereupon, that boy said to me:
O crest-jewel of rogues, this bed cannot be obtained for a price;
it is obtained only through the narration of unprecedented and wondrous tales.
Having heard that, I then said to him: "I shall tell you something wonderful, which is true in its essential reality; understand this and, if you so desire, grant me your consent."
But if you should say that it was untrue because of my lack of trust,
then you would be born of an adulterer, and I would fall upon my bed.
Listen, my dear, as I tell you of a wonderful event from this period:
formerly, there was a famine in the kingdom of a certain king.
With the great torrents of water from his elephants' trunks,
the king himself performed the plowing upon the back of the beloved of the boar.
Then that lord of the earth, enriched by the grains that had arisen and honored by the people, brought an end to the famine for his subjects.
When I had spoken thus, that boy then laughed and said:
"Clouds are the vehicles of the Nāgas; the earth is the beloved wife of the Boar."
For she is said to be the most beloved of Viṣṇu in his form as the Boar;
what wonder is there if grain is produced by her through the waters of the clouds?
Having said this, that rogue of a boy spoke again to me as I stood there amazed:
"Now I shall tell you something unprecedented."
If, having understood it, you accept this as the truth according to reality, then I shall give you this bedstead; otherwise, you shall become my slave.
When I replied, "So be it," that rogue of a boy then said this:
"O Lord of Rogues, long ago there was a certain boy here."
He who, as soon as he was born, shook the earth with the weight of his footsteps,
immediately became a grown man and set foot in the other world.
When that boy had spoken thus, not understanding his meaning, I said to him:
"This is false; there is no truth whatsoever in this, alas! (SoKss 18.5.228)
Then that boy said to me: "When Hari was born in the form of a dwarf, did the earth not tremble when his feet stepped upon it?"
Having grown powerful at that very moment, what position did he not establish?
He has conquered you in the heavenly world; indeed, you have been made my slave by me.
"All these people here in the marketplace are witnesses to our wager;
therefore, wherever I go, come along with me."
Having said this, the wise boy grasped my arm with his hand;
and all the people standing there likewise gave him their testimony.
Then, having bound me under oath, he, along with his followers,
led me to my mother’s presence in the city of Pāṭaliputra.
Then his mother, seeing him, said to me:
"Noble son, I too have today fulfilled my own vow."
"He has been brought here, held fast by a son born of you yourself!
Having said this, the virtuous woman related the entire account in the presence of everyone.
Then all her kinsmen, having held a great celebration, congratulated her— she whose desires had been accomplished by her own wisdom and who was cleansed of the family's reproach by her son.
Having achieved my purpose, I dwelt here for a long time with that wife and that son, and then I came to this city of Ujjayinī.
Thus, there certainly exist here on earth noble women devoted to their husbands;
yet, it is not the case that all women are in every way of wicked conduct.
Having heard this story from the mouth of Mūladeva,
King Vikramāditya, together with his ministers, was greatly pleased.
Thus, hearing, seeing, and performing these wonders,
King Vikramāditya conquered and enjoyed the earth with all its continents.
Having thus related this tale of Viṣamaśīla, which is filled with unions and separations,

Take heart, O son of the King of Vatsa;

Thus, having gained fortitude through the words of the sage Kaṇva, and having spent the period of separation,
I then gradually obtained my wife, the sciences, and the sovereignty over the sky-dwellers.
And that [teaching], O great sages, I have already described to you in its entirety, exactly as it was obtained by me through the grace of Śambhu, the giver of boons.
Having thus related his own story to all the sages and his maternal uncle Gopālaka, Naravāhanadatta delighted them in that hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Having spent those days there during the arrival of the rainy season, and having taken leave of his maternal uncle and the sages dwelling in the forest of asceticism,
he then departed with his wife and ministers, ascending a celestial chariot that filled the sky with its army of sky-goers.
Having reached in an instant his own mountain abode, Ṛṣabhaka, he dwelt there for an eon among the lords of the sky-dwellers, enjoying the pleasures of sovereignty,
together with Queen Madanamañcukā and Ratnaprabhā and the others.
Thus, this *Bṛhatkathā* was formerly narrated on the slopes of Kailāsa by the Moon-crested Lord, who was inspired by the entreaty of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain;
thereafter, it attained incomparable renown through Puṣpadanta and others, who, having been born on the surface of the earth due to a curse, assumed the forms of Kātyāyana and his ilk.
"Whoever recites this excellent tale that has issued from my mouth, or whoever listens to it with devotion, or whoever preserves it, shall before long have his sins destroyed and,
having become a perfected being, will surely attain the status of a true Vidyādhara and reach my own realm"— thus did the beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter then grant this boon for the story.
Thus ends the fifth wave in the *Viṣamaśīla* book of the *Kathāsaritsāgara*, composed by the great poet Śrī Somadeva Bhaṭṭa.
This eighteenth book, the *Viṣamaśīla*, is completed;
and this *Kathāsaritsāgara* is finished.
The author’s eulogy:
There was a lord of the earth named Saṅgrāmarāja, who was the *pārijāta* tree of the ocean that is the illustrious Sātavāhana dynasty;
having descended [to earth] and being attended by various learned men, he transformed the region of Kaśmīra into a second Nandana grove.

To him was born a son named Śrī Ananta, a universal emperor who was a wish-fulfilling tree for his lineage; his footstool was polished by the mass of rubies from the crowns of all prostrate kings, and he was a singular mass of valor.
And at the threshold of his gate, the head of the king— its neck severed and its belly cast out—
rolled along, as if Rāhu had attained satisfaction upon hearing the beautiful fame of [the king] who had conquered the great discus of Hari while arriving for service.
Then that moon among kings took as his queen Sūryavatī, the daughter of the lord of Trigarta,
who dispelled the darkness of her people like the sun, and who was like the radiant dawn, worthy of universal homage.
Like sacred traditions (āmnāyas) served by hundreds of Brahmins born in various lands,
and like oceans filled with jewels that provide refuge even to kings who harbor fear.
By that queen, Kaśmīra was adorned with preeminent monasteries, which were as noble as wish-fulfilling trees that daily dispel the suffering of those who approach them with hope.
The celestial mansions, constructed on banks two *vitastis* wide with flowing pure waters and white as the plaster of palaces,
bear a striking resemblance to the peaks of the Himalayas encircled by the celestial river.
Though she was given countless mountains of jewels, gold, great land-grants, black antelope skins, wealth, and thousands of cows,
the Goddess— who indeed always supports the entire universe— was neither satisfied nor even supported [by them].

The illustrious King Kalaśadeva—though a unique ornament of the earth's circle, he was free from falsehood; though a kinsman of the virtuous, he was composed of thick nectar; though inauspicious to the assembly of his enemies, he was an incarnation of Śiva. He was the son [of that king].

That city belongs to him, the excellent king named Śrī Harṣadeva, who was created by the gods as a new-born Agastya from a jar— capable of bending all the lofty mountains and able to drink even the seven oceans— and who is steadfast.
For that goddess, whose constant exertion was bound to the rites of worshiping Giriśa, performing fire-offerings, and various acts of charity,
and whose fatigue was always spent in listening to the scriptures as prescribed, there was this [moment] for some slight diversion of her mind.

This compendium of the essence of the *Bṛhatkathā*— which consists of the nectar of various tales and is like a full moon for the ocean of the minds of virtuous people— has indeed been composed by Soma, the son of Rāmā, who is beloved for his many virtues and is a preeminent Brahmin.
This Kathāsaritsāgara, composed by Soma of pure intellect with its exceedingly expansive waves of narrative, may it be for the joy of the hearts of the virtuous.
